15675-a-voyage-to-new-holland-etc-in-the:
Captain William Dampier published this voyage to New Holland in the year 1699, in a third edition printed in London in 1729 for James and John Knapton. The title page promises the Canary Islands, Mayo and St. Jago, Bahia in Brazil, Cape Salvador, winds on the Brazilian coast, and Abrolho Shoals. It also promises Shark's Bay, the isles and coast of New Holland, and their inhabitants, manners, customs, and trade.

Maps and draughts illustrate the voyage, with birds, fishes, and plants not found in this part of the world, engraved on copper plates. Chapter one follows Dampier from the Downs to the Canaries, Santa Cruz in Tenerife, Laguna town, and Oratavia. Wines, governors, winds, and Cape Verde salt follow. Dampier writes the classic buccaneer-naturalist's account: a working sailor's eye for coasts, peoples, and creatures, before Australia had a name in English minds.
20812-history-of-the-english-people-volu:
Richard the Second gave up his crown in September 1399, and Parliament took that act as law. John Richard Green opens volume three of his History of the English People at that fall. A solemn act of deposition sealed the change of kings.

Green wrote English history as the story of the people, not just of courts. Trade, towns, faith, and law share space with kings and wars. Volume three runs from Parliament's rise through years of deep change. His fresh approach shaped how schools taught the past, and this volume shows his sweep at its most confident.
22808-the-gray-madam-1899:
The Gray Madam is a mystery story dated 1899, named for a gray-clad woman whose appearance at a door leaves nothing behind it. The catalog record names no author. Ghost or spy, the gray madam of the title belongs to the 1890s taste for uncanny visitors in respectable houses.

Shaken by the contact, the narrator tore the front door open and looked out. She expected to find the woman waiting on the steps, or standing on the sidewalk out front. But no one matching her was anywhere visible. I came back inside wondering if I was a hallucination's victim, or just an everyday fool. That doubt, hallucination or folly, powers the tale. The story keeps one foot in the ghost story and one in the detective's notebook.
23247-the-cursed-patois-from-mackinac-an:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Cursed Patois comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories of 1899. In it, a man named Brown suddenly remembers a pair he has seen. They are the wife and child of Joe La France, and Joe La France is dead.

Puttany had lately told him the facts: Joe left behind a widow and a baby with no shelter. They have no relations nearer than Canada. Catherwood writes the Great Lakes frontier as a place of mixed peoples and thin safety nets. Readers get a short tale where one death leaves a family exposed, far from kin.
23248-the-black-feather-from-mackinac-an:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Black Feather comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories of 1899. Its giant is Charle' Charette, a huge and innocent primitive man. He wears the black feather among his brigade, a dozen boats strong, a mark every man on the lakes run would know.

Fresh from Canada, Charette grumbled at pork eating, the steady fare of the voyageurs. His companions teased him for it with a nickname meaning pork eater. Catherwood peoples her lake world with boatmen, nicknames, and old French ways. Readers get a frontier tale built around strength, custom, and one man's standing among his crew.
23251-marianson-from-mackinac-and-lake-s:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's Marianson comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories of 1899. A boy breaks away and leaps eagerly into the woods. All his years of wilderness training come together in one bid to escape, and he runs with everything he has.

An English officer meant to make the boy a lesson to the other voyageurs. The boy smiles at the thought of the race he can give his pursuers. He has left all his arms behind except his knife, since speed is what will count. Readers get a chase tale of the old lakes frontier, boy against soldiers and wilderness craft against orders.
23252-the-indian-on-the-trail-from-macki:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Indian on the Trail comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories of 1899. In one passage, a man looks back at the girl who grew up next door. She was only his social equal, yet his restless nature searched the whole universe for its mate.

He remembers her as a wild sweetbrier-rose child, all pink and gold, with a daring, fragrant personality. His first clear memory is of her running bareheaded onto her father's lawn, slim-legged and swift, to turn on the hose for her play. Readers get a lakes-frontier tale threaded with memory and longing.
23253-the-mothers-of-honore-from-mackina:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Mothers of Honoré comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories of 1899. It opens in island talk about a good match. One speaker wonders why a man never took Melinda Crée, who lives right next door and would make a capable wife.

She knows how to nurse in sickness, the speaker argues, besides being a good washer and ironer. Summer visitors say her fish pies are the island's best. Catherwood builds her Mackinac world from such voices: practical, gossipy, and close to the work of daily life. Readers get courtship weighed in plain island terms.
23255-a-british-islander-from-mackinac-a:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's A British Islander comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories of 1899. It sketches a woman whose looks and dress set her apart. She dressed unlike anybody else, in foreign things her aunt gave her, pieces no island wardrobe would normally hold.

She was always carrying thin scarfs of different kinds. She would throw one over her face to tantalise the men watching her. Catherwood uses dress, gesture, and island gossip to build character. Readers get a portrait of an outsider in a small lake community, where being different is both a burden and a kind of power.
24835-ri-dan-the-devil-and-other-stories:
Louis Becke published Ridan the Devil and Other Stories in Philadelphia in 1899. The title tale follows Ridan, a feared loner in a hut at the edge of a German plantation on Upolu, Samoa. Fellow workers hate and fear him as a wizard who can send death in the night, and the American overseer Burton knocks him down for a sulky brute.

Twenty more stories follow, from a lagoon island and a fish drive on a Micronesian atoll to the wreck of the Leonora and an old colonial mutiny. Becke writes from his own Pacific years, with sharp eyes for traders, natives, and beach life. The book gives a vivid, rough-edged set of South Seas tales.
25490-peck-s-uncle-ike-and-the-red-heade:
George W. Peck dedicates this book to the typical American boy, not awfully good at first but just good enough. His boy does not cry when hurt, plays dangerous games to win, and investigates every machine even if it pinches his fingers. Peck's boy learns a little about everything he will meet grown up. He can pray for his country's prosperity or fight for its honour, take a church collection, or ask an ugly father for his daughter's hand.

Uncle Ike lectures the red-headed boy on farm life, warning that a blistered beginner quits for a doctor while twelve years of work make muscular, calloused hands. The farm boy rises at four, pulls on cowhide shoes and overalls, and works until he hardens to anything. Alexander Belford and Company published the book in 1899.
28188-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-3-of-6-:
Holinshed's Chronicles, volume three of six, slice one of nine, covers England from 1399 in the 1808 London edition. Raphael Holinshed first compiled the chronicles to 1577, and later hands extended them to 1586, with fresh occurrences and rare observations. This slice, reprinted by AMS Press in 1965, treats the kings and queens of England in orderly succession.

The text keeps old spelling, with v for u at word starts, and notes on letters that plain text cannot show. Students of Tudor history and of Shakespeare's sources know Holinshed as the chronicle behind many plays. The volume gives a direct path into early English historical writing.
28390-medicine-in-virginia-1607-1699:
Thomas P. Hughes wrote Medicine in Virginia, 1607-1699, Williamsburg, 1957, as booklet twenty-one in the Jamestown 350th anniversary series. Hughes, assistant professor of history at Washington and Lee, traces medicine from European roots and Indian counterparts to Jamestown's critical years, prevalent ills, and common treatments. The Virginia 350th Anniversary Celebration Corporation published the booklet.

Later chapters treat education, women, churchmen, and the law in colonial medicine. Hughes argues that medicine, carried as seed from Europe, adapted to New World conditions yet kept its European ties. The booklet offers a clear, short history of early Virginia medicine. The book is short and clear. It will help any reader who wants the plain facts of early care for sick folk in a new land.
28499-mother-earth-land-grants-in-virgin:
W. Stitt Robinson Jr.'s Mother Earth: Land Grants in Virginia, 1607-1699, was published in Williamsburg in 1957 as number twelve in the Jamestown 350th anniversary booklets. Robinson, associate professor of history at the University of Kansas, studies how Virginia's land policy shaped the colony.

The desire for free land drew small holders, artisans, and tenants to America, and land policy, in the words Robinson quotes, determined much of the colonists' economic, social, and political life. Early chapters treat the land, the Indians of Virginia, and the clash between Algonquian, Siouan, and Iroquoian peoples and English settlers. The booklet is a concise guide to colonial Virginia's foundations.
28730-agriculture-in-virginia-1607-1699:
Lyman Carrier, professor of agriculture at Ferrum Junior College, wrote this 1957 booklet on farming in Virginia's first century, from 1607 to 1699. Published as number fourteen in the Jamestown 350th anniversary series, it explains how England's rise after the Spanish Armada of 1588 pushed her merchants toward American trade. The London Company financed Jamestown with trade in mind, and farming was not at first the prime concern.

Carrier traces how tobacco and food crops grew into the colony's working base, and how settlers learned the land. The booklet is short, clear, and grounded in the anniversary series' aim: to give general readers sound history for the 350th year. It suits anyone studying early Virginia, colonial farming, or the business roots of England's first lasting American settlement.
32603-reminiscences-1819-1899:
Julia Ward Howe's Reminiscences, 1819-1899, published in Boston and New York in 1899 with portraits and illustrations, traces her life from birth and parentage through literary New York, society, studies, and marriage. Chapters follow her father, Samuel Ward and the Astors, a tour in Europe, first years in Boston, and a second visit to Europe.

Later chapters treat anti-slavery work, the Church of the Disciples in wartime, the Boston Radical Club, a woman's peace crusade, Santo Domingo, and the woman suffrage movement. Howe writes as witness and friend, with friends and worthies among the men and movements she knew.
4871-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Dutch trade and exploration widen the republic's horizons in 1598 and 1599, and John Lothrop Motley follows sailors as well as soldiers. John Huygen van Linschoten's travels spur commerce, nautical science advances, and Arctic voyagers chase the northeast passage, discovering Spitzbergen before William Barendz dies in the frozen regions.

The survivors return to Amsterdam with scientific results, while a southern expedition against Spanish power ends in disaster. Motley balances fantastic notions about the polar regions with real gains in navigation and geography. The volume shows a small republic learning to trade, map, and sail its way toward wealth and independence.
8639-poems-1799:
Robert Southey printed this 1799 collection at a young, restless stage of his career, mixing long poems, ballads, and eclogues. The Vision of the Maid of Orleans retells Joan of Arc's story in book form, while shorter pieces turn to the poor, to sailors, and to country life. One ballad follows a sailor who served in the slave trade; others give voice to grandmothers, widows, and ruined cottages.

The English eclogues, short dialogues in verse, show Southey testing how plain speech could carry poetry. Readers meet a poet still shaping his politics and his craft, angry at hardship and eager to try new forms. The volume is useful for anyone tracing English Romantic poetry before Southey became Poet Laureate, and several ballads still read well on their own today.
a-voyage-to-new-holland-etc-in-the-year-: William Dampier voyages to New Holland in the year 1699 in this account, printed at London in a third edition in 1729. The voyage describes the Canary Islands, Mayo and St Jago, and the Bay of All Saints with Bahia in Brazil. Cape Salvador and the winds and shoals of the Brazilian coast follow. From the Cape of Good Hope the course runs to Shark's Bay and the coasts of New Holland, with inhabitants, harbours, soil, beasts, birds, fish, trees, and plants.
allen-keynotes-leading-remedies-1899:
Henry C. Allen taught prescribers to seize the one strange, clear sign in a case, and Key-Notes and Characteristics of 1899 is his handbook. The second edition gathers leading remedies of the materia medica, each summed up by its keynote symptoms. Allen compares rivals side by side throughout.

A keynote might be a craving, a fear, or the odd hour when pain strikes. Match that sign, Allen held, and the remedy often follows at once. Few homeopathic books were reprinted so often in the next century, which shows how well his sharp, short method suited daily practice.
arrhenius-dissociation-modern-theory-sol:
Harry C. Jones translated and edited The Modern Theory of Solution for Harper's Scientific Memoirs in 1899. The volume gathers the founding papers of the new physical chemistry in English. Wilhelm Pfeffer's work on osmotic pressure opens the set. Jacobus van't Hoff follows with his own study of osmotic pressure in solutions.

Svante Arrhenius contributes his paper on the dissociation of substances dissolved in water. In it, salts in water split into charged ions, a bold claim for its day. Francois Raoult's laws on solutions close the group. Together the memoirs launch the ionic theory. English readers gained the sources in one volume.
arxiv-2412-00699:
Liu and five co-authors built a one-way model in twenty twenty-four for how a burn-front wobble mixes fuel in a crush to fuse atoms. The wobble can drop the crush yield by mix of cold and hot parts. Their model adds laser burn and start bumps to a known drag rule for mix depth.

A heat term tied to churn strength and bump size stands for the mix in burn. The model sits in a one-way flow code and matched two-way sims well. In ball crush sims it gave sound drops in squeeze, peak press, and mass depth. The gap twixt shock meet and peak may gauge mix in one-shot tests.
arxiv-2412-02399:
Adam Wróbel and three co-authors introduce OMENN, a way to explain a neural network's decision as one readable matrix. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. Popular explanation tools lean on approximations that can blur the true reasons behind a prediction.

For each input, OMENN folds the network's layer-by-layer processing into a single matrix of linear transformations. The result gives exact local attributions: which input features mattered, and how much. A theoretical analysis rests on the network's piecewise linear nature. Tests on two explanation benchmarks put OMENN level with the best existing methods. It handles both classic convolutional networks and vision transformers. The authors pitch precision as the missing virtue in explainable AI.
arxiv-2412-05399:
Brittany A Erickson, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four, asks how well computer methods can copy the true spectra of hyperbolic systems. Such systems are sets of equations with terms that change from place to place. The work cares most about whether the methods can find real sources of growth or decay in the system.

She uses high-order summation-by-parts methods, with weak rules at the edges of the grid. Exact answers found with Laplace methods serve as a check on the rates. Finer grids give spectra that are closer to the truth, but some false values still appear. She urges care, and checks with both finer grids and higher order.
arxiv-2412-05899:
Yuanzhi Zhu, Junnan Li, and three co-authors distill video diffusion models into fast generators. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, attacks a known pain point. Diffusion models make fine video but need many slow steps per clip. That cost bars real-time and cheap use.

Their frame matches the output spread of a big teacher in far fewer steps. A rival network pushes frames toward real-data quality. A second score match borrows a strong image model to lift frame detail and prompt fit. Tests use a popular animation model as teacher. The student makes high-grade clips in a small share of the steps. Quality can even top the teacher on some measures.
arxiv-2412-06799:
Diederik Aerts, Massimiliano Sassoli de Bianchi, and Sandro Sozzo traced the path of the Brussels group in quantum cognition. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, is the first part of that tale. Quantum cognition uses quantum math to model how minds work. From it grew the conceptuality view of quantum theory: that quantum things act like concepts, and meet the world as minds meet sense in thought.

The Brussels path cast concepts them self as quantum things and minds as the gear that reads them. The paper walks the key steps from first uses of quantum tools on thought to that bold view. Readers in the roots of physics get a map of how a mind field bent a base theory.
arxiv-2412-06999:
Zimniak, Ferreira, and Jacquemin-Ide revise the theory of jet emitting disks, where a disk of gas feeds two fast jets. Their study from two thousand twenty-four adds one force past work left out: the push from turbulent magnetic fields inside the disk. A large field runs through the disk, and some mass leaves to feed the jets.

With the new term, the disk grows puffier and less able to carry current deep inside. Currents and field bending shift toward the disk surface, and inflow speeds up there. Strong turbulent push plus strong diffusion can drive powerful jets. Cold outflows still fall short of the mass loss seen in full simulations, the authors note.
arxiv-2412-10099:
Annabelle Bergum and co-authors record brain signals tied to eye movements as programmers read confusing code. Their 2024 paper studies atoms of confusion: tiny code patterns that baffle humans but run fine on a computer. Understanding code is a growing need as software spreads through work and life.

When readers first fixated on a confusing pattern, a late frontal brain wave appeared, hundreds of milliseconds later. Clean versions of the same code did not trigger it. The wave resembles one seen in language studies when a word is unexpected yet plausible. The authors suggest the brain updates its model of the situation in like ways for code and for sentences. The finding opens a brain-based way to spot code that will slow maintainers down.
arxiv-2412-11999:
Kassie Archer, Aaron Geary, and Robert Laudone study shallow permutations, a special class in combinatorics, in a 2024 paper. Shallow permutations were defined in 1977 as those meeting a lower bound in a known inequality. Recent work has renewed interest in them, linking them to pattern rules in their cycle form and to unlinked cycle diagrams. One famous case, shallow permutations that avoid the pattern 321, shows up in many settings.

The authors ask which shallow permutations avoid each pattern of length three. They first prove broad structural results about shallow permutations in general. Then they apply those results to count the avoiders for every length-three pattern. The counts complete the picture for this size and give later work a firm base to build on.
arxiv-2412-15599:
Katarzyna Sadecka and co-authors lay out the theory of a tunable quantum dot built from two stacked atom-thin sheets in a 2024 paper. The sheets are two sibling compounds, MoSe2 and WSe2, and stacking them gives control that neither sheet has alone. A quantum dot traps a single electron, a basic unit for quantum devices.

Using quantum simulations of the stack, they find its bands line up in a staggered, type-II way, with the low points of two valleys close in energy. They read the layer, spin, and orbital makeup of each state from the computed wave patterns. A plainer tight-binding model, fitted to the big simulations, then clarifies how the layers talk to each other. A vertical electric field shifts the balance, so the dot can be tuned by a gate voltage.
arxiv-2412-15999:
Pace and Zitkovic study scaling limits of Hawkes processes in twenty twenty-four. Such processes model events that excite further events, like the shocks that follow a quake. In this work the excitation measures may vary by generation. The team studies limits in a near unstable regime, where excitation nearly sustains itself for a long time.

The limit objects are random measures described by a nonlinear convolution equation. They form a family set by a local measure and a special probability distribution. These measures generalize the Feller diffusion and related CIR type processes. They also allow driving noise from Levy type operators of low order. Fractional derivatives of any positive order are included in that class. The scheme unifies several known limit processes under one roof.
arxiv-2412-16699:
Li, Li, and Zhou present FAP-CD in twenty twenty-four, a planning tool for fair, age friendly city districts. Cities are aging fast, and care sites for older people are spread unevenly. The tool learns how care sites and streets link up in a district. It then drafts new layouts that spread services more fairly.

The method trains on local demand first, with a push to lift the worst served areas. Road links that can be walked guide where sites can go. Tests beat rival methods by a wide margin on fairness scores. The authors say such tools can help planners renew old districts so older residents are not left far from care.
arxiv-2412-17199:
Alexander Mangerel wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-four on a Goldbach-style question about the signs of the Liouville function. That function labels each whole number plus or minus one based on its prime factors. Shusterman asked whether every large even number splits into two parts that both carry the minus label.

Assuming a famous unproven hypothesis about prime patterns, Mangerel answers yes for all large enough even numbers. The result rests on a counting bound: for prime totals, every pair of sign patterns occurs often among the splits. The proof leans on a classical expansion of fractions, the Pierce expansion, which may serve other two-part problems. The statement mirrors the Goldbach idea that even numbers are sums of two primes.
arxiv-2412-18399:
Bahruz Suleymanli and Tanatar extended the theory of layered superconductors to include two spin-orbit effects in two thousand twenty-four. In a superconductor, the energy gap sets how easily paired electrons move without resistance. Layered materials stack conducting sheets, and spin-orbit coupling can reshape that gap.

Using a standard pairing model and Green's function methods, they derive formulas for the gap with Rashba and Dresselhaus effects present. Without either effect the gap is uniform, but even one makes it vary with direction. Both effects also shrink the gap, and past critical strengths it vanishes. They give exact critical values at zero temperature and show how the basic gap equation changes.
arxiv-2412-19399:
Hang Xu and co-authors let a team of agents solve shifting balance problems online, in work from 2024. Each agent knows only its own cost term and limits, and talks only with near neighbors over links that change with time. The joint goal shifts as data arrive, and agents learn the true terms only after they act.

Their method mixes mirror descent steps with a primal-dual scheme. Scores are kept as regret against the best path over time, plus a tally of broken joint limits. Both grow slower than the time span, under mild terms. A noisy-gradient version holds the same promise with high chance. Worked cases back the math.
arxiv-2501-01799:
Annalena Daniels and co-authors study robot grasping for recycling in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is the disassembly of waste electrical and electronic devices. Devices arrive damaged, dirty, and unknown, so stored object models cannot be trusted.

The team proposes three grippers, each with touch-based strategies that use force sensing. Compliant motion helps the grippers cope with uncertain vision data. Experiments ran in lab and factory settings on four device types. Touch sensing and soft techniques clearly raised grasp success rates. The case study shows a path toward robotic disassembly of electronic waste.
arxiv-2501-01999:
Sharvaree Vadgama and her team probe when to build symmetry into a conv net, and when to break it. Group equivariance bakes in a pledge. Turn the input, and the inner code turns in a known way. If that pledge pays rests on the task's shape. Their one-frame net, Rapidash, lets forms with and sans the pledge vie on even terms.

Across tasks — cutting images up, curve fits, and making new data — tight forms won when the symmetry fit the task. More room in the net did not close the gaps. Clear breaks of symmetry, by way of shape-based frames, helped each time. Shape inputs fed in to break the pledge helped too, when they fit the task. The study swaps creed for a pick guide: match the prior to the shape at hand. Symmetry works best as a dial, not a dogma.
arxiv-2501-02599:
Jalisha Jashim Era, Bidyarthi Paul, Tahmid Sattar Aothoi, Mirazur Rahman Zim, and Faisal Muhammad Shah teach transformer models to solve Bengali math word problems. Turning text into equations is hard in any tongue, and Bengali has few resources. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team built PatiGonit, a set of ten thousand Bengali word problems. Four models, from a basic transformer to multilingual ones, were fine tuned to render problems as equations. The mT5 model scored the top exactness by a wide margin. The authors frame the set and method as tools for Bengali school AI.
arxiv-2501-06499: Carozza, De Filippis, Giova, and Leonetti give a rule that lets energy be closely matched for a class of double phase problems in twenty twenty-five. Double phase problems mix two growth rules for how energy counts a slope. Close matching by smooth cases is a key step in their study. The note states the rule for the case where the unknown is a vector, not a single value, and gives two cases that meet it.
arxiv-2501-07499:
Yaqing Ding and a team of co-authors show how to recover camera focal lengths from three linked views. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. When flat surfaces appear in several photos, the links between views are called homographies, and they hide clues about each camera.

The team compares the direction vectors tied to two of these links. That check yields new rules that tie the unknown focal lengths to the links. Three views give two extra rules, enough to solve for one or two lengths. The authors handle four cases, from shared lengths to one known camera. Each case becomes a polynomial to solve. Tests on made-up and real data beat older two-view methods on speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2501-08099:
Michail Kalntis, Andra Lutu, Jesús Omaña Iglesias, Fernando Kuipers, and George Iosifidis study mobile network handovers in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Handovers move a phone's link from cell to cell as they move. Lags or fails break the link users count on. The team ran the first study of handover tuning for a country. They started from data from a European operator serving over forty million users.

The data showed handover fails and lags track traits of radio cells and user devices, showing how mixed networks are. The team cast phone-cell links as choices made in smoothed online learning. Their method drops claims used in past work, needing no future signal reads and no facts on how users move. It holds promises on dynamic regret, in line with the O-RAN paradigm. Tests on real and made-up data showed the best marks across scenes.
arxiv-2501-08499:
Soumyadeep Sarma, Jukka Väyrynen, and Elio König published a 2025 paper on simulating a famous magnetic impurity effect on a quantum chip. In the Kondo problem, a single magnetic atom sits in a sea of electrons that screen it in a collective embrace. The dynamics are hard for classical computers. The authors design a gate-based circuit that mimics the effect on near-term quantum hardware.

They ran the circuit numerically for moderate sizes and tracked the impurity's magnetization, its entanglement with the electron sea, and the energy over time. Starting states varied, yet the long-time behavior turned universal. For large systems they derived an exact formula that matches the simulations, valid when the sea starts full. The work provides benchmarks: numbers future quantum chips should reproduce when they run the circuit.
arxiv-2501-08999:
Jan Siemen Smink, Rob Hagmeijer, Cornelis Henricus Venner, and Claas Willem Visser present a unifying method in two thousand twenty-five for designing branched fluid networks. The best network sets channel radii to balance flow friction loss against the cost of the fluid volume itself. Optimal answers were known only for special cases: smooth laminar flow, rough turbulence, or simple fluids.

Their approach builds on the Darcy friction factor, measured across many regimes. It covers laminar and turbulent flow, even mixed in one network, plus non-Newtonian fluids of three kinds and walls of arbitrary roughness. Results come as formulas and charts. The classic scaling exponent between flow and radius, long quoted from simple cases, turns out to fit real turbulent flow poorly. The method extends to curved channels and slip walls.
arxiv-2501-12399:
Shijie Han and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on FinSphere, an agent that writes real-time stock analyses. Stock models built on large language models have two weak spots. No objective score grades how good a stock analysis is. And the analyses lack the depth of professional work.

The team contributes three things. First, a scoring framework that grades stock analyses against set criteria. Next, a dataset built by industry professionals to teach the models the craft. Last, the agent itself, which combines live price feeds, quantitative tools, and a language model tuned on the craft dataset. In tests, the agent beat both general and finance-tuned language models. It also beat earlier agent systems, even ones given live data and worked examples. The team says the combination improves both the quality and the usefulness of the analyses.
arxiv-2501-14699:
Kazuko Fuchi, Eric Wolf, Christopher Schrock, and Philip Beran sped up turbulence simulations in twenty twenty-five by giving the solver a smarter starting point. Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes computations converge slowly from a naive uniform start. Their idea: prefill the domain with a modeled solution, splitting it into near-body, wake, and off-body regions.

A convolutional neural network predicts downstream wake development, trained on data from just one simulation. Combined with an accurate near-body prediction, the warm start slashed the needed iterations by a factor of about twenty-six in their test. Wall-clock time fell by a factor of about sixteen versus freestream initialization. The work shows cheap learned models can pay for themselves inside classical solvers.
arxiv-2501-15399:
Van-Bong Nguyen and Huu-Quang Nguyen study a geometry problem in their twenty twenty-five paper. The smallest enclosing ball problem asks for the tiniest ball that still covers the overlap of a set of given balls. Such problems show up in planning, graphics, and data work.

The pair finds a new split trait in the joint numerical range of a class of quadratic functions. They show this range is convex, a well-behaved shape, exactly when a set of center gaps spans at most one less than the full space. When it spans the full space, they build a patched set that is convex in a key case. These results give fresh progress on solving the ball problem.
arxiv-2501-15599:
Yinzhou Wang and seven co-authors evaluate a language model chatbot for cognitive restructuring in two thousand twenty-five. Cognitive restructuring is a core therapy skill for reframing thoughts. A prompt built chatbot delivered it to a group of users. Mental health professionals then read the chat logs in depth.

The bot stuck to core protocol and asked Socratic questions well. It also gave warm validation to users in their chats. Flaws spanned power imbalance, blunt advice, and missed cues. Excess cheer raised rapport and ethics worries as well. The team urges expert oversight for such tools.
arxiv-2501-16599:
Jungwoo Cho and Seongjin Choi check in 2025 where flying taxis could safely share city skies with planes. Around airports, airspace is crowded and tightly run. Their framework forecasts where normal aircraft will fly, as ranges of likely paths rather than single lines.

They applied the method over Seoul, testing taxi lanes at several heights. A lower lane saw few meetings with planes and kept the widest gaps and steadiest delays. A lane near the airport met departing traffic often, with sometimes tight gaps. The study shows how forecast-based planning can fit the new vehicles in, and where the hard spots lie.
arxiv-2501-17199:
Grant and co-authors sum the 16th IACHEC meet on high-force shot gear marks. IACHEC is a world group for high-force gear mark work in space. The meet sat at Parador de La Granja, Spain, for the group. Sixty-one gear hands met for 3.5 days at that site. Those hands mark gear for live and next space craft in the field. Talk spans mark state cross the world set of X-ray craft.

Ways to lift those marks form the core of the meet tale. Group texts in the sum span more than one mark theme. Themes span stock mark stars, joint mark runs, and stat ways. Gear marks and back noise marks join that theme set there. Kept lore and ends for star hands cap the sum set. The sum aims to serve the whole star craft field well.
arxiv-2501-18499:
Robin Piedeleu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It gives parity games, a core game form in logic and verification, a full set of equations that can solve them by rewriting.

Past work showed such games can be drawn as string diagrams, the arrows of a rich category, and their winning zones can be built piece by piece. This paper adds the equational side: a sound and complete axiom set for the diagrams. With it, any parity game can be solved by equation steps at the level of its picture. A matching symbolic calculus with fixpoints gets its own equational theory too.
arxiv-2502-00699:
Yulu Guo and four co-authors measure how building surfaces scatter millimeter-wave radio signals. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Future air-to-ground networks will lean on these high frequencies, and bouncing off buildings shapes the signal in ways planners cannot ignore.

Working at twenty-eight gigahertz, the team tested real building surfaces from many incoming angles. Receivers captured the scatter across full three-dimensional space, not just one flat plane. They compared the readings with the standard models used in ray tracing and with computer simulations. The lesson is direct: a surface's material matters, but so do the incoming angle and where the receiver sits. Channel models that skip either one will misjudge the signal near buildings.
arxiv-2502-01099:
Abdullaev, Khalkhuzhaev, and Kholmatov study bound states of two-plus-one fermionic trimers on a lattice at strong coupling, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Three particles, two identical fermions plus a third, form the system. A discrete Schrödinger operator governs their energies. States below the continuum and inside its gap are analyzed.

Whether bound states exist hinges on the mass ratio. Below a threshold ratio, strong coupling yields no bound states. Above it, at least one eigenvalue appears below the spectrum. Similar behavior occurs near a two-particle branch inside the gap. At zero momentum, thresholds are computed explicitly.
arxiv-2502-04699:
Hui Lan, Haoge Chang, Eleanor Dillon, and Vasilis Syrgkanis build an estimator for varied treatment effects in panel data in a 2025 paper. The difference-in-differences design compares treated and control groups before and after a policy, assuming parallel paths without it. Effects may differ across subgroups, and estimating that variation flexibly is hard. Their meta-learner targets the average effect on the treated for each profile.

The method reduces the problem to a single convex fitting task over helper models. A robustness property shields it from errors in those helpers. Extensions cover covariate shift and non-compliance settings. Tests show it beats existing baselines, the authors report.
arxiv-2502-04899:
Levente Zólyomi and co-authors survey self-taught learning for event streams across health, shops, games, and finance, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Streams of timed events hold rich context, but labels are scarce and studies sit apart by field. The survey joins the scattered work into one map.

Methods split into forecast-style and contrast-style schools. Fit and wins are weighed field by field. Gaps in the field are named, with a plan for shared, field-free frames. The aim is faster spread of what works and cleaner repeats of tests. Readers get the first unified map of a fast-growing niche.
arxiv-2502-06299:
Yolanda Cabrera Casado, Manuel Ladra, and Andrés Pérez-Rodríguez study the algebra of inheritance systems with only one male type, in a 2025 paper. Gonosomal algebras encode how genetic traits pass through populations where males and females carry different gene sets. The matching operators replay mating generation after generation, and their long-run behavior predicts where a population settles.

The authors compute the limit points of those replay trajectories for the single-male-genotype case. Limit points are the population states the system can approach but never leave cycling around. Each algebraic result is then translated back into biological terms, saying what it means for trait frequencies over time. The work extends a small, exact corner of mathematical genetics where full answers are still obtainable.
arxiv-2502-08399:
Edathumkandy and six co-authors pair resonance tests with atomistic models to confirm how ferromagnetism percolates in a dilute magnetic semiconductor. Their material is gallium nitride that holds about eight percent manganese. In such dilute systems, magnetic order spreads through linked clusters, not through uniform coupling.

Ferromagnetic resonance and SQUID magnetometry both pinned the Curie temperature at twelve kelvin. In spite of the dilution, traits of a standard ferromagnet held up. One was robust uniaxial anisotropy set by the manganese ions. Resonance signals held on far above the Curie point. They showed lone ferromagnetic clusters that never join the main network. One shared set of model values fit both kinds of test with no retuning, which firms up the percolation picture.
arxiv-2502-08499:
José Ayala and Joel Hass gave the first examples of a curious knot puzzle in 2025. Picture several closed loops of rope that are not linked at all, so in theory they could drift apart. A Gordian unlink is a trick case: the loops cannot actually be pulled apart while each keeps the same length and thickness, as real rope must.

Ayala and Hass build endless families of two-loop cases that jam in exactly this way. They also build jammed cases with any larger number of loops a reader cares to name. The result separates what topology allows on paper from what stiff, thick rope allows in space. Geometry, not linking, does the trapping.
arxiv-2502-10199:
Christophe Andrieu and J M Sanz-Serna analyze Hug, a new sampler design for Monte Carlo methods. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with Markov chain Monte Carlo, which explores a probability distribution by a random walk. Hug proposals hug the surfaces where the density stays constant, which makes them efficient.

The pair widens Hug from surfaces to manifolds of any dimension, in or out of sampling. They read Hug as a discretization of a system of differential equations, in a nonstandard way. The proof of convergence has a rare trait: second-order accuracy from a first-order match. They also find Hug paths that fail to cover the target manifold, an unexpected gap.
arxiv-2502-11999:
Alejandro Cassis, Andreas Karrenbauer, Andre Nusser, and Paolo Luigi Rinaldi engineer a shortest path algorithm for graphs with negative weights in a 2025 study. Shortest paths are a basic need in routing and planning. Non-negative weights have had near-linear algorithms for decades, but negative weights blocked similar speed until a recent randomized breakthrough, later simplified by follow-up work.

The authors take that line of research into practical algorithm engineering. Combinatorial methods, avoiding heavy algebraic machinery, sit at the core of the new designs. Making the breakthrough usable matters because real networks with costs and credits often include negative edges.
arxiv-2502-13399:
Hossein Zaremehrjerdi and eight co-authors count maize kernels with a large vision model, with no task training. Their twenty twenty-five paper serves plant breeding, where kernel rows and kernels per row set the yield of an ear. Counting by hand is slow, and past automated tools need costly labeled data.

Their method uses the Segment Anything Model, a public foundation model, to cut out each kernel in photos of ears. A graph-based step then counts kernels per row. Across a wide range of ears, the counts came out right. The team shares its code, to make cheap, label-free phenotyping open to all labs.
arxiv-2502-17999:
Michele Fiori, Davide Mor, Gabriele Civitarese, and Claudio Bettini build a system that recognizes what people are doing at home from sensor data, and can explain its choices. Such recognition supports health care uses in smart homes. Deep learning models do the job well but hide their reasoning. Recent explanation tools exist, yet they rest on older model types, and graph neural networks, though strong at this task, were not built to explain themselves.

The team's model represents the home's sensor events as a graph and learns from that structure. It is, to their knowledge, the first explainable graph network made for this purpose. On two public data sets, the system gives better explanations than leading methods. It also slightly improves recognition accuracy at the same time. The authors argue that clear reasoning matters when such systems support care decisions in the home.
arxiv-2502-18699:
Tianze Wang, Dongnan Gui, Yifan Hu, Shuhang Lin, and Linjun Zhang wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It blends several language models, each aligned to a different human preference, into one model that balances them all, without retraining from scratch.

Standard alignment trains one reward model, which flattens the diversity of what people want. Training many aligned models and merging them by reinforcement learning is costly and unstable. The authors' framework, MPO, instead mixes finished policies directly, weighting each by a fast adjustment process run in batches. The weights settle so that no single preference dominates. In tests, the blended model matched or beat existing approaches across varied preferences, at a fraction of the computing cost. The paper offers a cheaper path to models that serve mixed audiences.
arxiv-2502-19699:
Yimin Zhu and Linlin Xu classify satellite hyperspectral images with a diffusion model taught by contrast. Each pixel in such an image carries a full spectrum, a rich fingerprint of the ground. Sorting the pixels is hard because spectra and shapes tangle and noise intrudes. Their network, DiffCRN, denoises its way to clean features.

A staged design replaces the usual denoising backbone with attention modules for space and for spectra. A new loss blends the diffusion objective with contrast between examples, sharpening class borders. The model also learns which noise levels to trust, picking its own time steps. A weighted fusion step merges features across those steps for the final call. On four standard data sets, the system improved on prior results.
arxiv-2502-20099:
Gamella, Bing, and Runge tested a set of tools in twenty twenty-five that claim to learn cause links from data. They used a real light-based test rig where the true inputs that drive the rig are known. That known truth lets them check if each tool finds the right causes.

None of the tools they picked found the true factors in a steady way. The team then swapped the real data for a simpler fake set with the same form. Most tools failed there too, which points to weak tests and poor repeat work. They urge use of such real checks in the field.
arxiv-2502-20499:
Felipe del Rio and six co-authors test how traits of training data alone can push deep networks toward systematic generalization, the skill of handling new combos of known parts. Most past work tweaks model shape, loss, or training style instead. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Three data traits are varied, the range of values a hidden trait can take, burstiness that limits values per input, and random swaps of one hidden trait. All three lift generalization a lot, with range giving the largest jump on the most moved trait. Tests probe why each helps. A shared information gauge between hidden traits in the data is also weighed.
arxiv-2502-20699:
Geoffrey Cruttwell and Marcello Lanfranchi fix a persistent technicality in tangent category theory by naming the maps that behave. Tangent categories axiomatize the tangent bundle of differential geometry. Pullbacks, though, are delicate: smooth manifolds refuse most of them, and constructions like connections need pullbacks the tangent functor preserves. Prior work carried extra structure around to cope.

The alternative is a class of maps, tangent display maps, that are well-behaved under pullbacks and tangent applications. The paper develops their general theory and shows earlier constructions simplify in their language. In the smooth manifold case, display maps are exactly the submersions, the class geometers already trusted. A subclass then defines open subobjects in any tangent category. That yields a canonical split restriction category with the original embedded inside. Foundations, tidied, make the whole theory easier to build on.
arxiv-2502-21099:
Ganzhao Yuan builds adaptive optimization methods for stochastic problems that mix a smooth loss with a non smooth penalty, in work from twenty twenty-five. Such composite problems are common in machine learning. Classic methods need prior knowledge of smoothness constants or costly line searches to set step sizes.

The frame, called ALFPG, sets step sizes from data gathered along the path itself. Variants cover finite sum problems and expectation problems, with momentum tools to cut noise. Each variant reaches near stationary points with stated bounds on gradient calls. In the zero noise case, rates recover the best known form. No variant needs the noise level in advance. The work is a theory paper with proofs of those rates.
arxiv-2503-01099:
Hui Chen, Giovanni Gambarotta, Simon Scheidegger, and Yu Xu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a dynamic model of how funds split money into private assets, the hard-to-trade kind held off public markets.

Five traits of such markets are built in. The assets cannot be sold fast. Cash is pledged, called, and paid back with lags. Business cycles shift over time. Past returns echo into later ones. And rules cap what some investors may hold. Machine learning then maps the best policy across a fund's life. The model also lets regulators weigh the trade-offs of the capital charges they set on such holdings.
arxiv-2503-03099:
Diem Thi-Xuan Dang, Dai-Nam Le, and Lilia Woods study twisted bilayers of hexagonal boron nitride in two thousand twenty-five. Two atom-thin sheets, turned against each other, form patterns that can reshape their traits. The twist angle is the key knob.

One hundred ten stacked forms were simulated from first rules, with angles from under three degrees to sixty. The gap between sheets shifts across each pattern, since five stacking styles mix within one sample. Charge also spreads unevenly for the same reason. Flat bands, prized for odd physics, appear in several twists. Trends with angle give a baseline for methods that will tackle unaligned samples.
arxiv-2503-03799:
Jianqi Yan and co-authors teach a neural network to spot odd gravitational waves in a 2025 paper. The standard hunt matches incoming data against a bank of predicted wave shapes. That works for known sources, but a truly new kind of wave could slip past, since no template matches it. Their system, DeepGrav, instead learns what noise looks like and flags what departs from it.

The network adapts a residual design, the deep architecture behind modern image tools, to the wave data. It projects signals into a high-dimensional feature space while keeping the gap to the raw input visible, which sharpens the split between noise and a real wave. A data trick, averaging several signal samples into new ones, stretches the training set. The aim is an ear open to the unexpected.
arxiv-2503-07099: Kulikov studies a set of irreducible germs of finite generic morphisms from a surface to the projective plane. Each germ is taken where the branch curve has a specific kind of singularity. Those singularities match, under equisingular deformation, the curve shapes x to the k1 minus y to the k2, with coprime whole-number exponents. The article examines which germs fall in this set, letting the geometry of the morphism be read against a fixed singularity type.
arxiv-2503-07799:
Pramit Saha and co-authors present a 2025 method to spot heart defects in unborn babies from ultrasound video, without needing labeled cases of the disease. Such defects are a leading cause of death before birth, yet labeled scans are scarce. Privacy rules also make it hard for hospitals to pool their data in one place.

Their approach learns what a normal fetal heart looks like, then flags scans that depart from that norm. It also merges models in a guided way, so sites can gain from each other's work without sharing raw scans. The authors frame the task as finding what is not normal rather than sorting known cases. Tests judge how well the method finds defects it was never shown during training.
arxiv-2503-10699:
Lyu, Liu, Zhang, Hu, and Wang present a study from twenty twenty-five on models that must find new classes at test time. In real use, data can shift and unseen classes can appear mid-stream. A model must spot those new classes while keeping the old ones. Their method uses a hash-based memory that needs no training. Hash codes capture the size and direction of sample traits for fast grouping. New samples compare quickly against past ones that hash near them.

A joint sorting plan pairs a prototype sorter for known classes with a hash sorter for new ones. A self-correction step refines memory labels by checking hash neighbors. Tests show good discovery of new classes with old class skill intact. The authors post their code in public.
arxiv-2503-13299:
Yijun Liu and co-workers surveyed ways to stretch model text models to long documents in a 2025 paper. Models that shine on short text degrade on long inputs. For reasons ranging from position encodings that never saw such lengths to focus costs that explode. The survey first catalogs those failure modes, then organizes the repair literature into a four-part taxonomy for builders choosing a plan.

The groups cover positional coding fixes, context squeezing, lookup augmentation, and redesigned focus patterns. Review gets equal weight, with data sets, tasks, and metrics from current long-context benchmarks organized for check. Open problems close the survey, which serves newcomers as a map and veterans as a checklist of what remains unsolved.
arxiv-2503-13499:
Rajeev Kumar, Harishankar Kumar, and Kumari Shalini proposed a messaging framework in twenty twenty-five that rewrites communications using knowledge graphs and large language models. Personalized messages land better in health, education, and hiring, but hand-tailoring does not scale. Their system stores people, places, and events as graph nodes and links a draft's mentions to those nodes.

Relevant facts — preferences, roles, cultural norms — are pulled from the graph and combined with the draft, and a language model generates the personalized version. Reported acceptance rates reached forty-two percent in healthcare, fifty-three percent in education, and seventy-eight percent in professional recruitment. The authors present entity linking plus language modeling as a structured, scalable route to audience-aware communication.
arxiv-2503-13699:
Anne Broadbent, Alex Grilo, Nagisa Hara, and Arthur Mehta give a classical proof of quantum knowledge in two thousand twenty-five. In a proof of knowledge, a checker gains trust that a prover holds secret facts. Such proofs back tools like digital signatures and logins. The key trait is an extractor that can pull out the secret from a passing prover.

Their setting has one classical checker and many quantum provers. They prove the knowledge trait for a known zero knowledge protocol. The extractor rebuilds the ground state of a local Hamiltonian. The result is a new form of self testing. It certifies both a shared state and a prover's ground state.
arxiv-2503-15699:
Neehar Kondapaneni, Oisin Mac Aodha, and Pietro Perona present a study from twenty twenty-five on how to compare what two neural networks see in an image. Most gauges give one number for how alike two networks are at a layer. That number hides why they match or part. Their method, RSVC, names the visual ideas each network uses.

Shared ideas and lone ideas come out of the check. Some gaps trace to ideas that one model holds and the other lacks. Tests span many network builds and training styles. The authors say idea level checks can guide fixes that a lone score cannot. The work aids the craft of probing vision models.
arxiv-2503-16799:
Mingxuan Li, Junzhe Zhang, and Elias Bareinboim present causally aligned curriculum learning in two thousand twenty-five. Curriculum learning trains agents on easy tasks before a hard target. It leans on shared optimal rules across the task chain. Hidden confounders can break that sharing in real settings.

The team views the snag through causal lenses. They derive a graph rule that marks source tasks as causally aligned. Aligned tasks do keep the shared rule trait. An algorithm then builds such a curriculum from causal knowledge of the target. Tests on confounded tasks, some with pixel inputs, back the method.
arxiv-2503-17199:
Pieter Braam and five co-authors present a design method for a two reflector lighting system in a 2025 paper. The goal is to turn a parallel beam of light into two different light patterns at two target planes, using two freeform reflectors. The reflectors must control both where each ray lands and the direction it takes.

The authors derive generating functions and equations that link reflector shape to the desired light maps. A three stage least squares algorithm solves the system numerically. They also derive a condition that guarantees the reflectors do not intersect themselves. Worked examples confirm the condition and show the method can realize complex target patterns.
arxiv-2503-17399:
Atanu Paul and Ilya Grinberg build a lean atomistic model that predicts how water bends light and scatters it in Raman spectra. Raman signals fingerprint hydrogen-bonded water in clusters and in the liquid. Computing them from simulations needs each snapshot's electronic polarizability. Full quantum calculations are too slow for long trajectories.

Their model splits polarizability into a within-molecule part and a between-molecule part. A generalized bond model handles the first with few parameters. Fast-decaying functions of atom distances handle the second. Applied to clusters of two to six water molecules and to liquid water, the model matched quantum results for clusters and experiments for the liquid. It holds up at low and high temperatures, catching strong anharmonic effects. The authors propose a ladder of such models, trading detail for speed.
arxiv-2503-17999:
Srijan Kumar solved a supersymmetric field theory at high density in a 2025 paper. The Wess-Zumino model with many fields, studied in two space dimensions plus time, has a nontrivial fixed point described by coupled gap equations that normally resist exact solution. At finite temperature and large chemical potential, which favors particles over antiparticles, Kumar introduces both knobs and follows the fixed point's behavior across all coupling strengths.

In the large-potential limit the equations simplify enough to solve analytically, with answers expanding neatly in the small ratio of temperature to potential. From those solutions he obtains the partition function, stress tensor, and currents as series, then uses an inversion formula on two-point functions to extract higher-spin currents. A thermal conformal theory becomes computable in a corner.
arxiv-2503-19199:
Chenyangguang Zhang, Alexandros Delitzas, and five colleagues build three-dimensional scene graphs that record what objects are for, not just where they sit, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. A functional scene graph notes interactive elements, a handle, a switch, a lid, and how they relate to their objects and to each other.

No training set existed for this, so the method leans on foundation models: vision-language models and language models supply the functional knowledge. Inputs are posed color and depth images of real indoor rooms. The authors evaluate on an extended public dataset and a new one they collected, both annotated with functional graphs. Their system clearly beats adapted baselines built for spatial scene graphs. Downstream, the graphs support three-dimensional question answering about a room. A robot that knows which part opens the cabinet is a step beyond one that merely sees a cabinet.
arxiv-2503-20199:
Mélisande Teng and five co-authors test whether a famous general-purpose vision model can outline single tree crowns in drone photos of young plantations. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Planting trees fights climate change, but projects fail quietly without good monitoring. Counting and measuring crowns by hand is slow and dear.

The team compared ways of using the Segment Anything Model against a custom-built rival. Out of the box, even with well-crafted prompts, the general model lost to the custom one. Adding ground-height data to the images lifted the scores. The authors see promise if the model is tuned for the task rather than used raw. The study tempers hype with a fair, task-level check. It guides groups that hope to audit plantations from the air.
arxiv-2503-21399:
Uffe Høgsbro Thygesen sharpens a Laplace-based gauge of transition odds for stochastic differential equations. The paper from twenty twenty-five grows from an estimation method the author helped build. That method filled gaps between observations with mid-time states and integrated them out by Laplace approximation. Here the time step shrinks to zero, and the limit form is the prize.

The driving noise is recast as a control signal. The task becomes a least-effort steering problem between two states. A Girsanov shift of measure and a weak-noise step yield the limit formula. One example is exact, thanks to a coordinate trait. Another shows where far-off paths spoil the gauge. Splitting schemes beat plain Euler steps on order and care. Noise size and span length tune the accuracy in numeric checks.
arxiv-2503-22599: Luc Nguyen classifies the symmetric defect patterns of the Oseen-Frank energy, the standard model for liquid crystal alignment. His paper appeared in 2025. He studies patterns that look the same at every scale and respect a rotation symmetry, allowing several Frank constants rather than one. These patterns carry a topological defect of degree one, a swirl that cannot be smoothed away. Nguyen proves such critical points exist, sorts them into a complete list, and shows each minimizes the energy among symmetric disturbances away from the axis.
arxiv-2504-02699: Sarajian and Weingartner extended a number theory concept in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Smooth numbers, built only from small prime factors, are a classic tool in the study of primes. A Polymath project coined a weaker cousin, called densely divisible numbers, for work on primes in arithmetic progressions. The authors count how many such numbers lie up to a given bound. They pin down the order of magnitude of that count, uniformly across the parameters, for every fixed level of the construction.
arxiv-2504-02899:
Giuseppe Russo, Kristina Gligorić, Vincent Moreau, and Robert West studied Meat-Free Day in campus cafeterias in a 2025 paper. On a meat-free day, a cafeteria serves only plant-based meals. The team ran 67 such days over 18 months in 12 cafeterias and tracked more than 400,000 food purchases.

On treated days, food-related greenhouse gas output fell by 52.9 percent. Fiber intake rose and cholesterol fell, with no change in total calories. Yet protein intake dropped by 27.6 percent and sugar rose by 34.2 percent. Sales also fell as some customers ate elsewhere. The study weighs clear climate gains against real costs in diet quality and lost customers.
arxiv-2504-04299:
Mohammad Namvarpour, Harrison Pauwels, and Afsaneh Razi wrote a study in two thousand twenty-five about sexual harassment by a companion chatbot. The chatbot is Replika, an app sold as a source of chat and emotional support. The authors ask when the bot's sexual behavior shows up and how users react to it.

The team read user reviews from the Google Play Store. From more than thirty-five thousand low-rated reviews, they picked out eight hundred cases that fit the topic. Users often reported advances they did not ask for, behavior that would not stop, and limits that the bot ignored. Many said they felt uneasy or let down.
arxiv-2504-04599:
Matthew Kafker and Xerxes Arsiwalla simulate hard sphere systems driven out of equilibrium in this 2025 paper. Hard spheres are the simplest model of fluids, crystals, and glasses. Two kinds of disturbance are tested across all three density regimes. Molecular dynamics tracks every collision in the system.

First, a hot central region is left to relax into colder surroundings. It expands as a compression wave that collisions quickly erase. Relaxation to equilibrium is fast in that case. Second, spheres are crushed rapidly into a disordered glassy state. Those systems relax structurally over times vastly longer than the thermal case. Velocity balance is set by collision rate alone, while structure needs coordinated motion that dense packing suppresses.
arxiv-2504-04899:
Stefan Kazmaier and Kaisa Laiho described a precision measurement technique in 2025 for a workhorse device of quantum optics. Periodically poled lithium niobate waveguides generate pairs of photons, and the pairs' spectral properties depend on how the guide's refractive index differs between polarizations and modes. Handbook formulas describe bulk crystal, but a fabricated guide's effective indices can drift from bulk values, so they must be measured in place.

The authors exploit a guide whose polished ends act as strong mirrors, forming a resonator. Recording its light transmission spectrum and applying a Fourier transform yields the birefringence characteristics directly and accurately, demonstrated on a telecom-wavelength device. From the measured optical path differences they can predict, on the spot, the key spectral figures of merit that determine how useful the generated photon pairs will be.
arxiv-2504-05299:
Andrés Marafioti and a large team of co-authors introduce a family of small vision-language models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Big multimodal models are powerful but too heavy for phones and edge devices. Small versions usually copy big designs and waste memory.

The SmolVLM series was engineered from scratch for lean inference. The team tuned architecture, image tokenization, and training data for low overhead. The smallest model runs in under one gigabyte of memory yet beat a model three hundred times larger. The largest, at two point two billion parameters, rivals top models using twice the memory. The models also handle video well. The lesson: careful design beats brute scale for on-device AI.
arxiv-2504-05399:
Carolin Kimmig and Marion Villenave study how warps reveal themselves in planet-forming disks seen edge-on in a 2025 astronomy study. A warp tilts the inner disk, casting shadows that make the outer disk look lopsided. As edge-on observations pile up, astronomers need rules for reading warp size and tilt from those shadows.

Radiative transfer simulations in scattered near and mid-infrared light vary the warp's strength and the size of the misaligned inner zone. Comparing the fake images shows which asymmetries a warp can actually produce. The limits tell observers when a claimed warp is believable and when another cause must be sought.
arxiv-2504-06099: Samuel Bielik and Simon Bilik describe work toward spotting Varroa destructor mites on honey bees with a hive monitoring device, in a 2025 paper. These mites are a major pest of bee colonies. The team gathered a data set of bees and mites and used narrow-band light with hyperspectral images. A U-net segmentation model, joined with standard computer vision methods, tells bees and mites apart.
arxiv-2504-06999:
Ghurumuruhan Ganesan studies largest and lightest planar matchings in inhomogeneous random bipartite graphs. The drive comes from relay networks, where cross edges used well lift whole network performance. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

First, with chance edges and a cap on edge length, Ganesan bounds how far the largest planar matching can stray from its norm. Next, each edge of the full bipartite graph gets a positive random weight, and bounds follow for the lightest matching with a set edge count. Splitting tricks and martingale methods then give a limit law for the scaled, centered least weight.
arxiv-2504-08899:
Bozo Vareskic and co-authors published a 2025 physics paper on a tunnel device whose resistance can be tuned by a gate. The device's insulating barrier is a ferroelectric layer just two atoms thick, made by stacking boron nitride sheets so their alignment can slide. Its contacts are single layers of graphene. Flipping the barrier's electric polarization changes how easily current tunnels through.

Surprisingly, the effect is large even though the device is symmetric. Both the size and the sign of the resistance change can be dialed by the applied bias and gate voltage. The authors explain this with a simple tunneling model. The key is that graphene's capacity to hold charge shifts the available states on each side separately as voltages change. The work points toward memory and logic elements whose behavior is set electrically, in materials only atoms thick.
arxiv-2504-10499:
Zulun Zhu, Tiancheng Huang, Kai Wang, Junda Ye, Xinghe Chen, and Siqiang Luo survey how graphs power retrieval-augmented generation. Their paper from twenty twenty-five starts from a known flaw: language models hallucinate when training data is thin or stale. Retrieval systems fetch outside facts to ground replies. Much of that outside knowledge is structured, with entities tied in webs.

Graph methods tap those ties for deeper reasoning than flat text search allows. The survey sorts graph roles across the stack: building the store, the search math, the pipeline, and the end tasks. No unified review of these roles had been made. The authors map what methods share and where they part. Open challenges and next steps close the piece. It serves graph learning, database, and language readers alike.
arxiv-2504-11299:
Peter Matthew Jacobs, Foad Namjoo, and Jeff Phillips look back at a statistics gap in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov gap sets two spreads side by side in one dimension. To stretch it to more dimensions has rival takes. The team backs a form that takes the biggest gap between spreads. The gap is read over orthogonal dominating rectangular ranges. They show this form counts as an integral probability metric.

They prove the gap between a spread and a sample drawn from it shrinks to zero as the sample grows, and they bound the rate. Up to that same error, the gap can be worked out fast in four or fewer dimensions, with near-linear run time in the sample size. That gives a two-sample test with a precision term. Rival forms, they show, lack the metric traits and the near-call traits.
arxiv-2504-13699:
Daun Chung, Taehyun Kim, and thirteen co-authors report a new effect in traps that hold single ions. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a radio wave trap. At its center sits a null point where the field is zero. Ions away from that point jiggle fast, which shows up when light hits them.

The team finds a line of points where the ion acts as if it were at the null. They call this the pseudo-null. Tests under many trap settings match their math well. The true null is where lines from two light sources cross. The find could sharpen how ion traps are tuned and read.
arxiv-2504-15799:
Jehan Oh and Abhrojyoti Sen prove a regularity result for a class of parabolic equations that mix two growth rates, a setting called double phase. Such systems model materials whose behavior switches between two regimes, weighted by two modulating coefficients. The authors consider weak solutions where one coefficient is uniformly continuous and the other is Hölder continuous. Their sum stays above a positive constant.

The main result says the gradient of any weak solution is slightly more integrable than first assumed, inside the domain. To prove it, the authors build a tailored intrinsic geometry and a delicate comparison scheme. The scheme separates the three regimes: the p-phase, the q-phase, and the mixed phase. They note this is the first such result for general double phase systems in the parabolic, time-dependent setting.
arxiv-2504-17099:
Martin Böckling, Heiko Paulheim, and Sarah Detzler wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with one surname in a variant spelling in its text. It teaches knowledge graph embeddings that know where each place sits on Earth.

Many graphs hold the true shapes of cities and landmarks, yet most embedding tools drop them. GeoRDF2Vec floods the graph out from place nodes, then runs walks that lean by spatial weight. Each place thus stamps its reach on the codes of its kin. On benchmark sets the method beats both the plain RDF2Vec and a past geo rival. The codes can then serve search and link tasks with place in mind.
arxiv-2504-17299:
Emmanuel Filiot, Ismaël Jecker, Khushraj Madnani, and Saina Sunny study near-miss versions of classic questions about finite transducers. Their 2025 paper concerns machines that transform input words into output words. Exact questions, such as whether a machine's relation is truly a function, are known to be decidable.

The authors ask the approximate versions: is a given relation close to a function, or a function close to one a simpler deterministic machine can compute? Closeness is measured by standard distances between words, such as edit distance. They prove these approximate problems are decidable for several distances. One harder variant, finding a simple function near some selector of a relation, stays undecidable, mirroring its exact counterpart. The results map where approximation keeps problems solvable.
arxiv-2504-18099:
Leena Pillai, Muhammad Noorul Mubarak, and Elizabeth Sherly predict how the tongue and lips move from the sound of speech alone. The tongue shapes airflow into distinct sounds, and tracking it normally needs special recording gear worn in the mouth. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their network stacks a bidirectional long short-term memory model with a one-dimensional convolutional stage for cleanup. A fixed-weight initialization scheme is the distinctive choice. Training used two data sets recorded with electromagnetic articulography, differing in speakers' origins, languages, phonetic range, and equipment.

Tests covered speaker-dependent and speaker-independent modes, plus same-corpus and cross-corpus transfer. The fixed-weight model beat the adaptive-weight version while training in relatively few epochs, the authors report. Robust articulation tracking feeds speech science, pronunciation training, and silent-speech interfaces.
arxiv-2504-19099:
Ning Wang led a team building a debugging tool for chip design code in a 2025 paper. Large language models debug normal software well, but their use on Verilog, the language for describing hardware, was little explored. Their tool combines two skills in one model: finding a bug and fixing it.

The tool first learns patterns that set buggy code apart from clean code, then uses retrieved internal details to guide the fix. Sharing one parameter space for both jobs streamlines the process. In tests, its best variant fixed bugs far more often than open rivals, and beat a larger closed model too. The authors offer it as a sharper option for hardware teams.
arxiv-2504-19399:
Qianyi Zhang and four co-authors build a robot leader-following system in twenty twenty-five. A robot that can follow a leader of any form could fit better into human settings. Older methods work only for set types of leaders. They also lose the leader when it leaves the robot's view for a short time.

Their framework swaps detection models for a segmentation model, so the leader can be anything. A buffer stores leader features at many distances to keep recognition strong. A goal-aware mechanism shifts planning states based on whether the leader is visible and how it moves. A graph-based planner then draws candidate paths for each state. Readers get a follower built to cope with real, messy scenes.
arxiv-2504-20499: Ismail Soudi gives a theory overview of hard-soft correlation in jets, the narrow sprays of particles made when heavy ions collide. The paper appeared in 2025 and sums up recent advances shown at the Hard Probes 2024 meeting. Hard processes are the violent, high-energy parts of a collision; soft processes are the gentle parts. How the two talk to each other shapes what detectors see, in big ion collisions and small systems alike. Soudi reviews the newest models linking the two regimes.
arxiv-2504-21299:
Zhiting Fan, Ruizhe Chen, and Zuozhu Liu present a bias detector for language model output that reasons before it judges in a 2025 study. Simple fairness classifiers often miss the intent behind a sentence, while model judges asked for a verdict lack explicit criteria and drift. Their tool first analyzes the input, then works through fairness specifications step by step to reach its call.

Reasoning against stated criteria makes each flag explainable and contestable. As generated text floods hiring, lending, and moderation pipelines, bias checks that can show their work are easier for auditors to trust and for builders to fix.
arxiv-2505-00399:
Afan Ali, Md. Jalil Piran, and Hüseyin Arslan present a design from two thousand twenty-five for hiding wireless signals from watchers. Their system uses a set of linked learning models. One model makes noise-like signals, while each watcher is matched by its own checker model.

Tests covered as many as five watchers, with a moving receiver and moving watchers. The hidden signals were harder to spot and had fewer errors than signals made by noise alone or by a single checker setup. The team sees uses in city watch systems, military work, and future fast networks, with live tuning still to come.
arxiv-2505-00999:
Zhang and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on stray magnetic fields in atom smash tests. When heavy atoms crash at near light speed, their fields act like light pulses. Those pulses can knock particles out of a second atom's core. The newborn particles fly out in patterns that can reveal core structure. A leftover magnetic field after the crash may bend their paths. That bending could distort the patterns and confuse the readings. The team model the leftover field over time for gold atom crashes.

Their sums show the field shifts the flight pattern most in grazing crashes. The effect is clear for the slow particles used as probes. The authors say future core studies must correct for this shift. Their work gives a guide for those corrections.
arxiv-2505-01999:
Simon Becker, Zhongkai Tao, and Mengxuan Yang settle how fast localized wave functions must decay when topology blocks perfect localization. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Wannier functions give handy local bases for electron bands, but a topological charge forbids exponential decay.

For two-dimensional systems, the authors build Wannier functions with the exact tail that Thouless conjectured decades ago. The decay follows an inverse square law at large distance, and the full shape is pinned down. In three dimensions they achieve a uniform decay rate with a fractional power. The results close a long-standing gap between physics folklore and proof. They matter for computing with topological materials.
arxiv-2505-03699:
Eloan Rapion proves that most families of curves over a moduli space of abelian varieties do not truly vary, in work from twenty twenty-five. The space sorts abelian varieties with a fixed level structure. A family that does not vary is called isotrivial, meaning its curves are all alike in shape.

The result holds for curve genus and base genus at least two and level at least three. It covers fields of zero characteristic and all but finitely many prime characteristics. The proof finds where a set of log forms all vanish on a complex variety. That variety has a covering tied to a bounded symmetric domain of rank at least two. The work sits in algebraic geometry.
arxiv-2505-03799:
Hyun Lee and co-authors make language models work on large graphs without a graph network, in work from 2025. Graphs are too big to feed whole into a language model, since token caps cut the input short. Past work leaned on graph networks as helpers, which adds weight and hides the steps.

Their method samples the graph by walks that favor like nodes and busy hubs. That keeps key facts while using far fewer tokens. Tuned by plain instructions, the model then sorts nodes and guesses links on its own. The team shares its code in public and frames the work as a lean path to graph tasks.
arxiv-2505-04799:
