Jian Cui, Zichuan Li, Chi Wang, Luyi Xing, and Xiaojing Liao present Maris, a privacy enforcement paradigm for multi-agent collaboration systems, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Such systems let language-model agents solve problems together, but their constant message exchange risks leaking sensitive data.

Maris embeds reference monitors into key conversation components to enforce rigorous message flow control. The authors built it into the AutoGen and LangChain frameworks and tested it under emulated threats such as eavesdropping and prompt injection. Across three task suites Maris blocked sensitive data leakage while keeping a high task success rate, moving protection into the development process itself.
arxiv-2505-05599:
Seraj Al Mahmud Mostafa and four colleagues improve object localization in satellite imagery with a modified detection network. Their targets are upper-atmospheric gravity waves, mesospheric bores, and ocean eddies, each with variable scale and appearance amid noise, clouds, and city lights. Their model, YOLO-DCAP, extends a standard YOLO architecture in two ways.

A multi-scale dilated residual convolution block captures features at several dilation rates. An attention-aided spatial pooling module then focuses selection on globally relevant regions. Across all three datasets, the model beat its base network by about twenty-one percent in mean average precision and thirty-two percent in overlap accuracy. It also surpassed state-of-the-art alternatives consistently.
arxiv-2505-05899:
Boccardo, Palladino, and Picerni present a math paper from twenty twenty-five on stability of solutions to variational inequalities. The problems involve an obstacle that solutions must stay above. Constraint sets may shift, and the question is whether solutions shift gently too. A convergence notion for sets, named after Mosco, frames the study. The operator is of Leray-Lions type with a fast-growing lower-order term. The team prove solutions stay stable as constraint sets converge in that sense.

Classical stability results thus extend to natural-growth problems. Such growth terms long resisted the standard theory. The result supports obstacle models with realistic nonlinear terms. It also gives a base for approximation schemes in this class.
arxiv-2505-06099:
Zahra Hamed-Labbafian, Mostafa Tavakoli, Mojgan Afkhami, and Sandi Klavžar compute a rare color count for a class of graphs built from the ring of counts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A packing coloring splits a graph's points into classes by color. Points of a high class must sit far apart, with the needed gap set by the class. The least count of colors that works is the packing chromatic number. The team finds that count for the unitary Cayley graph of the ring. They also give two search methods, of the kind that use smart rules of thumb, to compute the count in hard cases.
arxiv-2505-06499:
Liao, Ma, Wang, and Zhao built a code tool in twenty twenty-five to trace how a set of particle acts shift with scale. The acts sit in a broad field frame past the standard model of parts. Their tool solves the flow rules at one loop for a class of size-seven acts.

It can run flows for size-five and size-seven acts between scales past the weak scale. As a test they use a rare decay where two like parts split with no neutrino seen. With flow in, that decay bounds far more parts of the frame than a plain tree check. Shared code notes come with the tool.
arxiv-2505-08499:
Sersante, Penoyre, and Rossi followed pairs of stars past a giant black hole in this paper from twenty twenty-five. When a binary wanders too close, tides can rip it apart, fling one star out, or capture the other. Some pairs survive and swing back for another pass. The team tracked fates through up to three encounters.

They started with round binaries on plunging orbits around the Milky Way's central black hole. A lean three-body model let them scan many orbit settings at once. Disruption was the most common fate, above all for deep, head-on, or stretched encounters. Repeat passes raised disruption odds by a fifth or more. In one worked example with real star sizes, mergers happened about a third of the time.
arxiv-2505-08799:
Loay Abdelrazek and colleagues argued in 2025 that mobile network security cannot be improved until it can be measured. Fifth-generation networks and their successors count as critical infrastructure, carrying traffic that individuals and industries depend on. Security work usually lists threats and defenses, but an objective reading of a network's current security state has been missing. Without measurement, operators cannot tell whether changes help.

The authors introduce a state machine model that follows the security life cycle of network functions. It tracks the states a function can occupy and the transitions between them. The model can be computed locally at each node or rolled up hierarchically for a network-wide view. Such a formalism turns security posture from an opinion into a quantity with defined states. That is the kind of foundation standards bodies need for future network generations.
arxiv-2505-08899:
Mullhaupt and Peng bound the best test zone with gap grades in this twenty twenty-five paper. A test's false call rates trace a zone whose floor is the best curve. That floor has long been set by one stock law in the field.

Inside, any gap grade yields a floor bound for the zone in their proof. Stick-type grades give the best such bound, tight to the true floor. One prime gap grade then beats a famed bound from the lore. A closed form caps the zone from top with a mix grade as well. The pair also shows how to build law pairs that hit set floors.
arxiv-2505-11999:
Liu and a team including Yan, Sui, and Wen guess food fleet routes from a web of task links in this twenty twenty-five paper. Food fleets must call each rider's next stops to pair tasks well and keep waits low. Hand rules use few task traits and miss how riders pick for themselves.

Inside, tasks are cast as nodes in a web tied by space, time, and pick-drop links. A graph-aware net reads that web to learn how tasks sway each rider's picks. A route builder then weighs rider traits and live gap cues as it lays the route. Tests on past fleet data from towns of all sizes top the chart. On a live fleet hub, the tool beat the hand rule by a clear grade.
arxiv-2505-14499:
Jun Cao, Jiyi Li, Ziwei Yang, and Renjie Zhou wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on reading feelings about specific things in posts that mix text and images. A review may praise a phone's camera but pan its battery, and the image matters too.

Small trained models do this job but often miss fine links between words, pictures, and feelings. Large language models read such detail well yet still trail tuned small models on this task. The team's framework, LRSA, feeds explanations written by a large model into a small one as extra hints. A dual cross-attention step then blends the text and image features more deeply. Across three standard benchmarks, the blend beat both baselines. The authors say the pattern should lift most small models used for this task.
arxiv-2505-14999:
Eric Hanchen Jiang and a team of co-authors rank chains of thought with a tiny energy-based verifier. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles shaky math reasoning in large language models. Checking many candidate proofs is costly with big reward models. Their EORM scorer has a small fraction of the usual size. It learns from plain right-wrong labels, with no costly step notes.

EORM scores each chain by an energy value and picks the best of a pool. A mid-size open model jumped to high marks on grade-school and contest math sets with its help. The gains match heavy best-of-many sampling at a sliver of the cost. The scorer also travels to new problem types and new models unseen in training. The team reads this as a sign it learned true marks of valid reasoning.
arxiv-2505-15699:
Jessica Enright, Samuel Hand, Laura Larios-Jones, and Kitty Meeks advanced the theory of temporal graphs in twenty twenty-five. In temporal graphs, edges exist only at set times, which models real networks but makes many problems harder than in static graphs. Width parameters tame that hardness by bounding how many vertices must be tracked at once.

The authors introduce tree-interval-membership width, a new parameter that generalizes several earlier ones. They then give meta-algorithms that work for whole families of problems at once under both the new and the older parameter. This yields a clean characterization of which problems become tractable. Applications include time-respecting Hamiltonian paths, dominating sets, matchings, and edge deletion to limit reach. The work replaces many case-by-case proofs with one reusable engine.
arxiv-2505-16199:
Rikuhei Umemoto and Keisuke Fujii wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It fills in player speeds for soccer matches where only event records exist, snapshots of who touched the ball and where, without the steady tracking that speeds normally need.

Event data are cheap and common, but they lack the flow of motion that richer analysis wants. The authors set the task of estimating every player's velocity at each event, all at once. They test rule-based guesses against neural networks that use time patterns and the web of player and ball relations. The networks won clearly on accuracy. Space ratings computed from the filled-in speeds also landed closer to ratings from true tracking data. The method could open deep movement analysis to the many matches that have only event logs.
arxiv-2505-17299:
Tuckman and Neuscamman speed up calculations of charge transfer excitations in twenty twenty-five. Charge transfer, where an electron moves between parts of a molecule, is hard to model well. A coupled cluster method with orbital relaxation is accurate but scales poorly. Large molecules in real environments strain it further.

They derive a cheaper second order perturbation variant of the method. A small coupled cluster treatment is nested inside it to restore accuracy. Formal cost drops sharply compared with the parent method. An early implementation handles about one hundred atoms on a single node. Errors in excitation energies were typically below a tenth of an electron volt. That beats a standard method of higher cost by a clear margin.
arxiv-2505-17499:
Tianxiang Dai and six co-authors present Neuroshaper, a way to design tiny light devices by letting a neural network hold the shape. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Freeform nanophotonic parts can beat standard designs, but shaping them while honoring factory limits is hard. Each tweak must keep the part buildable.

In Neuroshaper, the layout is written as an analytic neural network rather than pixels. That over-rich form smooths the search space for the optimizer. Local rules can reshape the whole device in a controlled way, including its topology. The team shows the method on a spread of devices, in simulation and in built hardware. Shapes stayed within design and manufacturing constraints throughout. The work suggests neural shape holders can widen what optical designers dare to try.
arxiv-2505-18799:
Hao Chen and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a cheap way to align large language models to new tasks. Full fine-tuning costs a lot. Past cheap routes lean on small data sets or on data driven picks of key parts, which ties them to that data. Their method, ALPS, finds the most task keen attention heads with no such tie.

Training then updates only those heads. Just a small share of attention weights is live in each run. Scores beat baselines on three tasks by a clear gap. The heads found for one task carry to new data sets. Old knowledge fades less in this mode too.
arxiv-2505-18999:
Xurong Liang, Tong Chen, Wei Yuan, and Hongzhi Yin shrink graph based recommenders so they fit on small edge devices, in work from twenty twenty-five. Graph recommenders learn user and item codes and pass signals along a user item graph. The codes cost storage, and the passing costs time and power.

Their method keeps a codebook design from prior work but squeezes the codes with quantization. More base codes then fit in the same storage. The full graph is pre trained on big servers, then weak nodes are cut to build a sparse rewired graph. The lean codes and graph move to edge devices. The result cuts memory and compute while holding recommendation quality under tight limits.
arxiv-2505-19399:
Juan Sosa, Eleni Dilma, and Brenda Betancourt build Bayesian models to find groups in networks in two thousand twenty-five. Their aim is to spot hidden blocs in complex ties. They start from the stochastic block model, a standard tool for such tasks. Two new forms add space or cross terms to how group ties are set.

The team applies the models to a network from the armed conflict in Colombia. Towns link when armed groups, violence, and illegal trade co-occur. The groups found match known zones of control and trade routes. They also test the models on fake data and on two known data sets. Full inference runs through sampling methods.
arxiv-2505-19999:
Frederik Vonhoff, Maximilian Schilcher, David Reichman, and David Egger analyze how charge carriers actually move through halide perovskites in a two thousand twenty-five materials paper. These solar-cell materials have unusual vibrations and electron-phonon coupling that make transport hard to predict.

Working with the two prototypes MAPbBr3 and MAPbI3, the authors use a dynamic disorder model and track temporal orbital occupations. Both material-specific on-site energy levels and spin-orbit coupling strength shape how transport channels fill over time. Energy gaps between on-site levels and the halide's spin-orbit strength govern the filling. The analysis identifies the pp-pi channel as a critical bottleneck and explains differences between electron and hole transport.
arxiv-2505-20099:
Ma, Chen, Wu, Khan, and Wang wrote in twenty twenty-five a survey of combining large language models with knowledge graphs for question answering. Language models answer fluently but can reason poorly, use stale facts, and invent details. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked nodes, which can ground those answers. Recent systems mix the two in many different ways. The survey proposes a taxonomy sorted by question type and by the graph's role. It compares leading methods on strengths, limits, and graph needs.

The authors match each approach to the challenges of complex questions. They summarize progress, scoring metrics, and benchmark data sets across the field. Open problems and chances for new work close the survey. The map should help builders pick the right blend for their task. It also shows where hybrid systems still fall short.
arxiv-2505-20399:
Benedikt Diemer wrote a solo paper in two thousand twenty-five presenting a tiny fluid dynamics code for teaching. Fluid flow is hard to teach because most real problems need numerical solving. Production codes are so large that their complexity hides the physics from first-time users.

His code, ULULA, solves fluid flow and gravity in two dimensions in under eight hundred lines of Python. Parts such as the solvers and boundary rules can be swapped to show their effect. Classic test problems are included and run in minutes on a laptop. The code is open-source, heavily commented, and documented for classroom use.
arxiv-2505-23499:
Masaki Murooka, Mitsuharu Morisawa, and Fumio Kanehiro control the balance point motion of humanoid robots that touch the world at several points, in two thousand twenty-five. Multi-contact moves, such as bracing a hand on a wall, help humanoids work in varied settings. Standard predictive control for such moves is costly to compute.

Their method uses preview control, which looks ahead cheaply, in place of the heavier standard approach. Feedback on the balance state adds robustness against pushes. A force-sharing step keeps every contact within its limits. In simulations, the robot performed a range of multi-contact motions stably. The drastic cut in computing cost is the central claim.
arxiv-2505-24699:
Alexandr Grebennikov and Matthew Kwan bound the chance that a random signed sum of vectors lands inside a given set, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Each vector is added or subtracted at random, and the question is how concentrated the total can be. Questions of this shape are called Littlewood-Offord problems.

Their idea is to turn probability into counting: the chance is controlled by how many lattice points the target set contains. With that bridge, they import tools from Diophantine geometry to handle concrete shapes. They prove bounds when the set is points in convex position, an algebraic variety, or a semialgebraic set. Along the way they settle conjectures posed by other researchers. Corollaries cover polynomial versions of the problem for polynomials built from few linear forms. The framework gives a geometric handle on a classic anti-concentration question.
arxiv-2506-00499:
Diogo Landau and co-authors build a shared learning frame to predict how much life is left in aircraft engines, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Airlines hold too few full run-to-failure records to train good models alone. Privacy worries keep them from pooling records in one place.

Their frame trains one shared model while data stays with each airline. A new check method validates the model without any data sharing. Four new merging rules harden the model against noisy sensor data. In a six-airline test, shared learning beat solo models for five of the six.
arxiv-2506-02699:
Aleksandar Miladinovic proves a broad trait for math forms built from discs set with group link. The work came out in 2025. These disc forms are high-tier math tools. They code acts spread over small discs. To frame them with a group G ties the shape work to that set of turns.

Fix a tight Lie group G and a finite part group H. The claim says one class of forms match an next class with no loss. The first holds G-disc forms framed by the split G/H. They take worth in a G-linked class set. The next holds H-disc forms framed by a form of H. They take worth in the base H part. The man plans to use the match to sharpen a move on real Hochschild counts. He would lift a two-part link to the full O(2) group.
arxiv-2506-05299: Sourdis wrote this short mathematics paper in twenty twenty-five on Bose-Einstein condensates, clouds of ultracold atoms that act as one quantum fluid. It studies a linear equation that arises when two such components separate from each other. The setup linearizes the system around a one-dimensional solution inside an infinite strip, with zero and repeating boundary conditions. Sourdis obtains sharp invertibility estimates for the Fourier modes of the system. Notably, the estimates do not require the usual extra orthogonality conditions.
arxiv-2506-06499:
Alex Havrilla, Edward Hughes, Mikayel Samvelyan, and Jacob Abernethy present SPARQ, a way to grow training data for AI reasoning, in a 2025 paper. Teaching models math needs many good practice problems. Most methods copy a bigger model's work or start from human-written problems, which limits scale.

SPARQ lets one model invent its own problems and rate each by how often it can solve them. That solve rate stands in for difficulty. Starting from a small seed set, the method produced more than twenty million problem and solution pairs. After filtering for the right difficulty, training the same model on its own output raised scores by up to twenty-four percent. Tests also show quality and variety matter more than sheer volume.
arxiv-2506-06799:
Robbert Beerten, Vida Ranjbar, Hazem Sallouha, and Sofie Pollin cut power use in cell-free networks in a 2025 paper. In such networks many access points serve users jointly, but past work chased throughput at peak load and counted only transmitted power, not what amplifiers actually consume. Their penalty method minimizes true consumed power under a realistic nonlinear amplifier model, and it scales far better with network size.

The method also favors sparse power allocations, switching effort to fewer access points. Counting the nonlinear consumption honestly saved up to about a quarter of the power, they report.
arxiv-2506-07899:
Ke Wang, Yiming Qin, Nikolaos Dimitriadis, Alessandro Favero, and Pascal Frossard present MEMOIR, a way to edit language models over a long life of use. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles a hard task: adding new facts to a model without full retraining. Past edit methods often broke old edits or failed to scale.

MEMOIR keeps edits in a spare memory block apart from the model's core. Each edit touches only a small slice of that block, picked by a mask tied to the input. Slices for distinct facts barely overlap, so edits clash less. At query time the system wakes only the slices that match the prompt. Tests on fact questions and false-claim fixes show top scores. The method held up through thousands of edits in a row with slight loss.
arxiv-2506-09099:
Joshua Barron and Devin White train small transformer models from scratch to probe how size trades memory against generalization, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Two toy tasks split the skills: arithmetic stretch for generalization and fact recall for memory. Models of many sizes faced each task alone and then both together.

Small models stretched arithmetic to unseen cases but failed to memorize facts. Large models memorized yet failed to stretch. A mid-size model drifted toward memory as well. Trained on both tasks, no model of any size could stretch. The authors say pretraining itself may force a choice between the two modes.
arxiv-2506-09399:
Kaiyu Guo and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about spotting data that differ from what an AI model was trained on. Such out-of-distribution detection guards the trust we place in AI systems. One family of methods reads the shape of the training data and measures distance in that shaped space.

The authors argue that badly spread training samples can warp that shape, and a fixed shape cannot correct itself. Their method updates the shape as new inputs arrive, shrinking it along the direction of each new input while guarding the main space. Tests on image benchmarks with several pretrained models, including a self-taught vision model, showed clear gains in detection. Code is released with the paper.
arxiv-2506-10399:
Zhaoxuan Kan and seven co-authors set out FicGCN in twenty twenty-five. It is a way to run graph convolutional networks on encrypted data. Cloud GCN services raise privacy fears for graphs in health and finance that hold secrets. Homomorphic encryption lets a cloud compute on ciphertext. But its spins and multiplies make graph work painfully slow. The sparsity of a GCN promises speed. Yet its rough shape adds cost back.

FicGCN balances two steps, aggregation and combination, at a global scale. A latency-aware packing scheme trims cost. A sparse within-ciphertext aggregation method trims rotations. Adjacency-driven reordering of the data trims more. On several standard data sets it beat all rivals it was tested on. It beat the newest design by up to about four times. The work pushes private graph learning toward real use.
arxiv-2506-10499:
Alexander Freiszlinger, Dirk Pauly, and Dirk Praetorius prove that an adaptive simulation method, in a 2025 preprint, really does drive its error to zero. The method is the boundary element method, which solves problems by working on a surface mesh alone. Adaptive versions refine the mesh where error estimates say it is needed. A recent scheme uses functional error estimates that judge the solution inside the domain, not just on the boundary.

Those estimates rest on extra problems solved on thin strips along the boundary. The strips change shape as the mesh adapts, which makes a proof hard. It also sets the scheme apart from the more common residual-based estimators. The authors show that for the Galerkin form of the method, the adaptive loop shrinks the potential error to zero. The proof needs new ideas, they say, because of that structural difference.
arxiv-2506-12399:
Dominik Trnka builds a two-way bridge for operads that take their worth from sets of classes. The work came out in 2025. Operads are math tools that code acts with more than one input. Class-based operads add a rich space of ways to run each act.

The bridge is a Grothendieck build fit for operads with no swap rule for inputs. It makes a two-tier class set that lies in fibers over a base class set. That base holds finite lined sets and maps that miss no point. Trnka then gives the flip build as well. Side by side, they give an exact match. Class-free operads of this kind match the fibered two-tier sets over that base. The shape echoes the known match for class-based sheaves and fibered sets. Sets with less rich form sit inside these class sets, so the find spans them too.
arxiv-2506-14999:
Ruize Ma, Michele Pizzochero, and Gaurav Chaudhary present a physics study from twenty twenty-five on thin strips of graphene as a base for rare quantum states. Strips with a zigzag edge can act as magnets and block current. A strong field across the strip, or a layer of a boron and nitrogen sheet, can turn them half metallic.

The team builds a simple model of such a strip joined to a rare type of superconductor. They show that pairing from the superconductor can open a new kind of gap in the half metal phase. That phase is not plain; its edge can host Majorana zero modes. Gates can tune shifts in the phase, which makes the strip a hopeful base for quantum work.
arxiv-2506-16399:
Shushanta Pudasaini and colleagues built the first generative language model for Nepali in a 2025 paper. After ChatGPT, thousands of language models appeared, yet none could generate Nepali text, which blocked fine-tuning and other downstream work for the language. The team set out to close that gap with a model, a corpus, and a benchmark built together.

They gathered text from many sources into a Devanagari corpus for training. They also created the first Nepali question-answer benchmark, with thousands of pairs for scoring. Reported generation scores include low perplexity and strong causal coherence and consistency ratings. Nepali speakers gain a base model that later tools, from tutoring to translation help, can build upon.
arxiv-2506-18399:
Mostafa Saeed and Nizar Habash tackle Arabic lemmatization in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Lemmatization cuts words back to their dictionary base forms. It counts much for Arabic, with rich word forms and spelling that can be read more than one way. Tools now in use face mixed standards and cover few kinds of text. The team puts forth two ways, both treating it as sorting into a tag set: lemma, part of speech, and an English gloss.

One way draws on machine translation; the other groups by meaning. The team built a new test set. It spans many kinds of text; older sets were brought to one standard next to it. Character-level sequence-to-sequence models did well. But they could give lemmas only, not the tag set, and at times made up odd forms. The sorting and grouping ways gave stronger, clearer output and set marks.
arxiv-2506-18999:
Yuan Yao and five co-authors distill a diffusion transformer into a Mamba model in two thousand twenty-five. Self attention costs grow with the square of image size. That cost bites hard at high resolution generation. Mamba state space models scale in a line instead.

Training Mamba from scratch for images proved hard in practice. Their pipeline, T2MD, transfers a trained transformer into that form. A hybrid model and layer level teacher forcing ease the swap. Feature based distillation carries the teacher's skill across. Light tuning then pushes output to very high resolution. Quality stays high at low overhead.
arxiv-2506-20499:
Shaw wrote in twenty twenty-five about designing geographic marketing experiments that scale to large markets. Geo experiments split markets into groups to measure added return on ad spending. Few units and large differences between places make design hard. The ideal grouping problem is formally NP-hard, meaning exact solutions explode in cost. Shaw's two-stage framework first compresses place data into readable embeddings. A solver then picks a grouping that balances outcomes and background factors.

Theory argues the result lands near the global optimum under stated assumptions. Tests on synthetic data matched plain randomization in estimation error. Balance between groups was tighter than randomization gives. Spectral embeddings performed much worse in the same tests. The method solved a two hundred ten market case in under a second. Older exact methods were projected to take weeks for the same task.
arxiv-2506-21499:
Asgariandehkordi and three co-authors clean sound pics with a net taught on the pic itself in this twenty twenty-five paper. Plane-wave shots take many aim turns to build one clear pic. Few turns cut frame pace, yet leave noise and smear in the pic.

Inside, the aim turns split in two sets, each set builds its own pic. Both pics share true flesh forms but bear unlike noise and smear. Those twin pics drill a two-coat net built just for the one pic at hand. The net learns flesh form as what stays put tween the two pics. No drill bank or clean ref pic is asked for at all.
arxiv-2506-21699:
Thuy Le, Phuong Nguyen, and Loc Nguyen attack a hard imaging problem in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The problem is to see inside a medium when detectors record wave intensity, not phase. The task is to rebuild a dielectric constant that shifts across space, from phaseless backscattering under single-point illumination, modeled by the Helmholtz equation. With phase gone, the problem is ill-posed and nonlinear.

Their frame stacks a set of steadying ideas. First, a phase retrieval step rests on a Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin near call, getting the lost phase back by solving an optimization problem. A Fourier-based cut in dimensions then turns the problem into a steadier system of elliptic equations with Cauchy boundary data. Last, Carleman convexification builds a strictly convex cost functional. Its global minimizer near-matches the true solution. Runs with noisy synthetic data got back scatterers' spots and contrasts, showing robustness.
arxiv-2506-21899:
Zuffer, Burke, and Harandi survey continual reinforcement learning in this 2025 review. Reinforcement learning agents usually master one task at a time. Real settings demand learning task after task while keeping old skills.

The review explains the core concepts of this continual setting and the challenges it raises, such as forgetting. It surveys the main methods researchers have built to acquire and reuse knowledge across tasks. Recent progress in robotics gets special attention, since robots face changing tasks in the physical world. The authors also summarize the test environments used across the field, which helps newcomers start. They close with limits of current work and promising directions.
arxiv-2506-22199:
Jakub Peleška and Gustav Šír present ReDeLEx in two thousand twenty five. Relational databases store most structured data in practice today. Deep learning on them treats tables as graph structures for learning. That young field lacked broad cross database analysis until now.

ReDeLEx benchmarks models of varied complexity across many relational databases in depth. Over seventy databases form the most diverse set yet available anywhere. Classic methods run alongside the graph neural models for contrast. Relational deep learning wins overall in their comparisons. Model complexity, database size, and structure shape the scores.
arxiv-2506-23499:
The unbounded knapsack problem asks how to fill a bag of fixed size with the most value when each item type can be used any number of times. Boris Rubinstein, a solo author, treats it as a case of a wider counting problem: finding whole-number solutions to two matching equations at once. Back in the nineteenth century, Sylvester and Cayley proposed cutting such a double count down to a sum of single counts by removing one unknown at a time.

Rubinstein gives that old method a geometric reading, picturing the counts as shapes rather than algebra alone. He then applies the picture back to the knapsack problem. The note links a practical packing question to a classic corner of counting theory.
arxiv-2506-23599:
Toshihisa Kubo and Victor Perez-Valdes generalize a tool for building operators that break symmetries step by step in a 2025 mathematics study. Symmetry breaking operators map representations of a group to those of a subgroup, and a method called the F-method constructs them from a symbol, a simpler polynomial shadow. That symbol existed only when a certain radical was abelian, which excluded many cases.

Their truncated symbol works for non-abelian radicals too, and inverting it revives the F-method in full generality. As a test they classify intertwining operators on the full flag variety of the three-by-three special linear group.
arxiv-2507-00399:
Randles and Yan study the long-run spread of random walks on grid-like groups with no extra assumptions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Most past work forced walks to be able to reach all points with no fixed rhythm. Those rules hide a natural back-and-forth rhythm the authors call the dance. A simple walk on whole numbers dances between even and odd steps.

Their main result splits long-run odds into two parts. One part is the smooth bell-shaped spread seen in most walks. The other part is the dance, which cycles with a fixed pattern. The dance part comes from an average over a subgroup of a dual group. The result recovers many classic theorems as special cases.
arxiv-2507-00499:
Dan Bower and co-authors model the early air of small rocky planets in a 2025 paper, using a free software package they built called Atmodeller. Young planets pass through a magma ocean stage, when melted rock and air trade gases freely. As the air cools, gases react and some condense into solids or liquids, changing what an observer would see.

For a planet like TRAPPIST-1e, the runs mostly start with carbon monoxide air that cools into carbon dioxide air a few hundred bar thick. About 40 percent of the runs end with liquid water plus graphite, sulfur, and a salt on the surface. For puffier sub-Neptunes, very high pressure bends the gas rules and favors methane-rich air. The tool helps astronomers read what telescopes see on such worlds.
arxiv-2507-00699:
Guoliang Duan and five co-authors present a benchmark in two thousand twenty-five for code instruction following by language models. Models write code well, but obeying layered, detailed constraints is less tested. Real development work mixes functional demands with style and format rules.

Their benchmark, MultiCodeIF, spans nine categories and twenty-seven constraint types, arranged in levels. An automated pipeline built over two thousand tasks in fourteen programming languages, with multi-turn variants driven by feedback. Six leading models were tested, and the best met only about sixty-three percent of constraints on average. Models handled explicit rules well but stumbled on implicit ones. Stacked constraints cut success sharply, while structured feedback raised scores over four rounds.
arxiv-2507-02099:
Amgad Abdrabou and co-authors join two math tools in a 2025 paper for computing electromagnetic fields in mixed materials. Fields inside gadgets and tissues that mix many materials are hard to compute. A pure volume method wastes effort on empty space, while a pure surface method cannot handle messy interiors. Their hybrid splits the world in two.

The inside, where materials vary, is handled by discrete exterior calculus, a grid-free frame that keeps the field's topology intact on rough meshes. The outside, uniform and endless, is handled by surface integral equations, which naturally send waves off to infinity. The whole setup is written in potentials under a standard gauge, which dodges a known low-frequency failure and pairs well with other physics. The design aims at accuracy without excess cost.
arxiv-2507-02999:
Krisanu Sarkar, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, builds new bounds on how well neural networks can do on fresh data when the data lie on curved spaces. Past theory used flat-space tools.

Flat tools miss the true shape of data that sit on a curved, low-dim sheet inside a high-dim space. Sarkar brings the sheet's own traits into the count of cases a net must cover: its bend, how its bulk grows, and how far one can go before paths cross. The new bounds match the flat results when the bend is zero. They grow in sharp ways where the bend is strong, in both the up and down sense.
arxiv-2507-04899:
Narutaka Ozawa proves a result on total sequences and the lower frame inequality in two thousand twenty-five. The setting is a Hilbert space, the home of frame theory. A total sequence reaches every part of that space. Frames add norm bounds that make expansions stable and useful.

Ozawa shows each total sequence meets the lower frame bound after scaling. A plain rescale of the terms is all it takes. The claim began as an exercise posed on a public math forum. Its proof closes a neat gap in frame theory. The note is short and self contained in scope.
arxiv-2507-06199:
Dane Grundvig and Matthias Heinkenschloss develop an optimization method in a twenty twenty-five paper. The method solves smooth problems where some rules must hold exactly. Each check of the goal and the rules can be costly, as when it needs a full physics simulation.

Their version of sequential quadratic programming swaps the true functions for cheap models with tunable accuracy. The method sets how exact each model must be, based on progress so far, and uses error bounds to stay in zones where the models can be trusted. It keeps the same convergence promises as the classic method. A test case steers flow in a heated fluid model.
arxiv-2507-10599:
Maya Okawa, Bo Zhao, and five co-authors study how large language models sort human feelings, in work from two thousand twenty-five. As such models power chat agents, how they read a user's mood has clear stakes for safe use. The team draws on emotion wheels, a frame from mind science that sorts feelings in a tree-like order.

They find that models form such trees on their own, close to human ones, and larger models grow richer trees. They also find bias: models read the feelings of some social groups worse than others, with the worst gaps for groups at crossed lines of low status. Human tests show like patterns, which hints that models pick up human social views.
arxiv-2507-13199:
Kenji Terao sorts the grades of points with rational j-invariant on two sets of modular curves. The j-invariant is a curve's mark, like a print of a thumb. Rational marks flag curves with rare traits in number work. Points on these curves stand for curves with extra level form. Their grades gauge how far the number field must stretch. Terao finds which grades can show up.

Grades that show up without end are worked out with no strings. Grades that show up just a few times are set, if one takes a claim of Zywina as true. The tool is new: closures of subgroups of the adelic general linear group. They sit under two fixed sets of subgroups. Work on those closures, for images of Galois maps, does the hard lift. A use lists the lone rational j-invariants.
arxiv-2507-14199:
Ebrahim Abu-Helalah, Jordi Serra, and Jordi Perez-Romero split image segmentation between a weak sender device and a receiver to save bandwidth. Their paper appeared in 2025. Semantic communication sends meaning instead of raw pixels, but running a full segmentation model on a small device is heavy, and sending everything is wasteful. Their design does part of the work on the device and the rest at the receiver, tuning the split to conditions.

Simulations measured computing load, bit rate, and accuracy against doing everything at the sender. The split cut the bit rate by up to about seventy-two percent while holding segmentation quality. Device computing demands fell too. The authors say the balance suits drones, cameras, and other small senders on variable wireless links.
arxiv-2507-14399:
Jiangyong Jia explains the puzzling rise-and-fall shape of radial flow fluctuations in quark-gluon plasma, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The measure, a new probe of the matter made in heavy-ion collisions, wiggles with particle momentum much like directional flow does. Its pattern had no accepted explanation.

Jia's rescaling framework splits the signal into a shape factor and a dynamical factor. The shape factor, set by the particle spectrum's bend from exponential to power law, generates the rise-and-fall on its own. The dynamical factor flags genuine suppression or enhancement. Collider data show it straying from one by twenty to forty percent in central collisions. Predictions for a lower-energy collider show strong energy dependence from shape alone. The split tightens constraints on the plasma's properties.
arxiv-2507-14599:
Shiyang Hu, Yuxiang Zuo, Dan Li, and Chen Deng study magnetic fields on a Novikov-Thorne accretion disk in two thousand twenty-five. The disk rings a Kerr black hole that spins in curved spacetime. Disk spectra need orbital traits of its particles, which are hard in such space. Their work finds those traits by numeric means.

Iteration, finite differences, and interpolation yield the needed values. From them they build flux, heat, and blackbody spectra of the disk. Spin, view angle, and field strength all vary in the runs. When field and spin align, disk glow grows with field strength. A least field size that telescopes could spot is derived.
arxiv-2507-15499:
Jongseok Lee, Timo Birr, Rudolph Triebel, and Tamim Asfour present a robot learning system that asks humans for help as data streams in. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The task is semantic perception: a robot must name what it sees. When the model fails on a new scene, a person can step in with a fix.

Their system, CLEVER, takes that fix and updates the network on the spot. A Bayesian frame holds prior knowledge about the task, which guides when to ask and how to learn. Tests with users, and with humanoid and soft objects, show the design works. They claim the first such stream-based active learning on a real robot.
arxiv-2507-15799:
Pei Jiang Low, Nicholas Zutt, Gaurav Tathed, and Crystal Senko run quantum algorithms on a single atom with many levels in a 2025 experimental study. Most quantum hardware uses two-level qubits, but an atom offers many internal states at once. Using more of them in one particle, called a qudit, could pack more computing power into less hardware.

Working with a barium ion, the team prepares and reads out up to twenty-five internal levels with high fidelity. They probe superpositions spanning nearly all those states and track how errors grow with dimension. Naming the main error sources shows what must improve for qudit processors to scale.
arxiv-2507-18099:
Naman Srivastava and co-authors compare methods that map land use and land cover from satellite images, in work from twenty twenty-five. Such maps guide city planning and resource care. The study uses images from an Indian Cartosat sensor over Hyderabad, a fast growing city.

A lookup table step first cleans the images for air effects. Then a deep segmentation model and a semi supervised model sort the land into classes. A dynamic weighting tweak lifts the trust of guessed labels in the semi supervised run. Time based images show urban sprawl, shrinking green space, and growing industrial zones. The authors judge which method serves planners best for tracking such change.
arxiv-2507-19799:
Mouyang Cheng and co-workers built lab common sense into a crystal generator in a 2025 paper. Spread models can invent new stuff, but many invented forms break a basic rule: oxidation states must balance, or the crystal cannot exist. Checking balance afterward wastes most samples. Their CrysVCD setup puts the rule inside making itself, in two stages.

A model text model over elements first puts forth compositions that already balance valence. A spread model then builds the crystal form for each mix, checking valence far faster than post-screening allows. Tuned for stability, the generator produced mostly thermodynamically stable options, and it can aim at targets like heat-conducting semiconductors and high-grade dielectrics. The module plugs into other pipelines.
arxiv-2507-20699:
Joan Martínez Canals and four co-authors proposed curved apertures in twenty twenty-five for shaping radio beams along custom paths. Beam shaping bends a signal's path to dodge obstacles and reach users around corners. Today's methods use flat apertures, whose geometry limits how freely a path can bend.

The authors give a general formulation for wave path design that works with apertures of any shape. Math and simulations show curved apertures steer propagation better than flat ones. They also tolerate the limits of real phase controls more gracefully. Power stays denser along more of the wanted path. The idea could widen options for future wireless networks in cluttered indoor and urban spaces, where straight-line links often fail.
arxiv-2507-21299:
Alex Guo and Michael Graham blend data with physics to model chaotic systems cheaply. Their twenty twenty-five paper builds hybrid reduced-order models. Full simulations of chaotic flows are costly to run repeatedly. Pure data models can drift away from real behaviour over time.

An autoencoder first finds a low-dimensional surface for the dynamics. The known physics model is projected onto that surface. Data then either corrects the physics flow or updates it as prior knowledge. Tests used two classic chaotic equations with rich patterns. Hybrid models beat data-only models in every data setting tried. They even helped when the physics model had wrong settings. Forecasters gain accuracy without paying for full simulations.
arxiv-2507-22199:
Jacob Knight, Farid Kaveh, and Gunnar Pruessner work out how much entropy a self-propelled particle produces when its engine stays hidden, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Entropy production tells equilibrium from non-equilibrium, but hidden parts of a system block exact calculation. Active particles, which move under their own power, are a prime case.

Their step-by-step framework computes a partial entropy rate from the visible motion alone. Two symmetry traits of the hidden drive decide the answer: whether it looks the same mirrored, and whether it runs the same backward in time. Real production only appears at sixth order in the swimming speed. They test the scheme on a switching drive and on diffusion with random resets.
arxiv-2507-22299:
Afonso Martini Spezia and co-authors compare ways of splitting data into folds when testing machine learning models. Their paper appeared in 2025. Standard cross-validation can create folds that miss the variety of the full data set, which biases the score. Cluster-based splitting first groups similar cases, then deals them across folds so each fold mirrors the whole. The team tested several clustering methods.

They also propose a new split that joins fast mini-batch clustering with class balancing. Tests ran on twenty data sets with four learning algorithms, scoring bias, variance, and cost. The new split won on bias and variance for balanced data, though it saved no computing time. On lopsided data, plain stratified splitting stayed best on all three counts.
arxiv-2507-22699:
Thuy Tran, Ruochen Chen, and Shaifali Parashar present a fast method for rebuilding deforming shapes from images in this 2025 paper. Shape from Template starts with a known 3D template and bends it to match video frames. Older methods need point matches between image and template, which fail when parts are hidden. Newer methods need huge training data.

Their method uses only image cues such as color, edges, and silhouettes. A mesh constraint keeps the surface from stretching, as real cloth and skin resist stretch. The result runs about 400 times faster than the best prior unsupervised method. It also captures finer detail and handles heavy occlusion better. Code was released with the paper.
arxiv-2507-23299:
Soo-hyon Phark and colleagues tuned the spin of single titanium atoms sitting on an oxide film in a 2025 paper. Lone atoms on ultrathin insulators are candidate qubits: identical by nature, yet addressable one by one with a microscope tip. The team placed titanium atoms on magnesium oxide over silver and read their spin with combined scanning tunneling microscopy and electron spin resonance, an unusually direct probe of single spins.

Two spin states appeared, a half and a full unit, depending on the landing site and the film thickness underneath. Calculations trace the switch to charge shifting between orbitals that favor or oppose polarization. Site choice thus becomes a dial for engineering surface spin qubits.
arxiv-2508-00199:
Chris Hull and Neil Lambert analyzed a conformal field theory in 2025 arising from Sen's formulation of chiral gauge fields. Sen's action describes chiral bosons, fields that move in only one direction, using two scalars that couple to two different metrics. In two dimensions, when the two metrics coincide, the theory becomes a system that forms a conformal field theory with an unusual, non-unitary character.

The authors argue that the link between Sen's version and the ordinary theory of two same-direction chiral scalars can be viewed as a bosonisation, a standard kind of duality in two-dimensional physics. They show that the familiar vertex operators of the scalar theory appear as vertex and line operators in Sen's formulation, and they derive how correlation functions translate between the two pictures. The discussion extends to higher dimensions for self-dual gauge fields.
arxiv-2508-01099:
Ramírez-Garrido and three co-authors compute a set of screen masses for forty spin-free states made of quarks, in a simple contact model of strong forces. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The states span light, heavy, and mixed quark pairs, in both meson and paired-quark forms. The model keeps the core symmetries and, at zero heat, remakes known traits of such states well. The team pushes the work to high heat. They find the dressed masses of the lightest states near their bare values as heat grows. Twin states of unlike parity meet in mass past a set heat, a sign of a deep shift.
arxiv-2508-01299:
Gioni Mexi and colleagues built a fast heuristic for hard quadratic optimization problems in a 2025 paper. Quadratic mixed-integer problems, with both discrete choices and curved objectives or constraints, model everything from portfolio design to process engineering, and exact solving is slow. Their heuristic extends the Boscia framework, a solver using Frank–Wolfe iterations inside branch-and-bound for convex problems, into the nonconvex quadratic world, reformulating nonlinear constraints and adding preprocessing.

A suite of tricks exploits the integer-feasible points the Frank–Wolfe iterations generate along the way: rounding strategies, gradient-guided variable selection, and large neighborhood search. On benchmark QPLIB instances the method improved results within minutes, and it took first place in the Land–Doig MIP Computational Competition 2025, per the authors. Good feasible answers, fast, are often worth more than proofs of optimality.
arxiv-2508-01799:
Jing Lan and nine colleagues teach a model to predict how drug molecules bind to proteins while respecting the liquid they sit in, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. A drug's shape bends differently in different solvents, and that bending can change how well it fits its target.

Older prediction methods often miss these solvent-driven shape changes and train on one task at a time. The team's pre-training feeds the model ensembles of ligand shapes generated under varied solvent conditions. Three training goals work together: rebuild the molecule's structure, predict distances between its atoms, and contrast shapes across solvents. The contrast goal pushes the model toward features that stay stable when the solvent changes. The authors report clear gains from this solvent-aware recipe, including a few points of improvement on their measures. The approach targets more realistic computer-aided drug discovery.
arxiv-2508-04499:
Miri Son classified smooth actions of a major symmetry group on closed spaces in a 2025 geometry paper. The group SL(n,R), matrices with determinant one, can act on a manifold by reshaping it while respecting the group law. Knowing all such actions in a dimension range reveals how rigid these symmetries are. Fisher and Melnick had settled the case where space and group dimensions match.

Son extends the classification to spaces up to nearly twice the group dimension, for actions described by real-analytic formulas. Separately, she classifies smooth actions with no fixed points in that range. A consequence sorts out when such fixed-point-free actions are structurally stable, dense among all actions or not. The range covered roughly doubles the earlier frontier.
arxiv-2508-05799:
Yoseph Berhanu Alebachew presents a hybrid tool to help programmers understand very large code bases, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Developers spend much of their time just grasping how a system fits together. Older visual tools show structure but do not adapt or answer questions in context.

The system pairs classic reverse engineering with a large language model that reads the user's intent. It offers diagram views, a dynamic interface, past project context, and shared features for teams. A prototype for Java shows the approach can work. Planned next steps include user testing, support for many languages, and richer screen-driven interaction with the model. The goal is a workspace that matches how developers think.
arxiv-2508-07299:
Jia and co-authors ask when a practice task helps a model learn its real task. In semi-supervised and self-supervised learning, models first train on unlabeled data. The wrong practice task can waste time or even hurt results. In the past, teams could judge fit only after full training. The authors derive what makes a practice task useful.

They find three factors: how well the model can learn the task premise, how true that premise is for the data, and how fully it covers the target. From these they build a cheap test that predicts final scores. A test set of over one hundred tasks backs the claim. Predicted scores matched real scores from large training runs.
arxiv-2508-09299:
Umar and a large team propose in twenty twenty-five a shared, open way to forecast weather without one central hub. Central forecast systems face security risks, growth limits, and single points of failure. Their design trains models jointly across many sites, so raw local data never needs to move. A public ledger then checks each model update in the open.

A voting system based on track record weighs how much to trust each submitted model. Files are stored off the ledger in a shared network to save space and cost. Tests showed better forecast accuracy than the baselines used, plus stronger resilience as the network grows. The team sees the design as fit for real, high-stakes use.
arxiv-2508-09499:
Liyan Jia, Chuan-Xian Ren, and Hong Yan present, in twenty twenty-five, a fast docking method that uses geometry to predict how a drug molecule fits a protein. Docking is a key step in rational drug design. Deep learning dockers are fast and accurate, but many rely on graphs and language-style encoders. They often miss shape details, which leads to wrong pocket location and unrealistic poses. Their method, CWFBind, adds local curvature features, which describe how the surface bends, during feature extraction.

A degree-aware weighting step sharpens the model's sense of spatial structure and interaction strength. A dynamic radius strategy and an improved loss tackle imbalance in pocket prediction. Tests across docking benchmarks show competitive accuracy at good speed, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-10799:
Fernand Pelletier and Patrick Cabau take Dirac structures into spaces with no finite size limit. Their paper came out in 2025, as the second part of a pair. Dirac structures give the math frame for motion that must obey set rules. The pair work in a broad space type, the convenient kind, which spans the Hilbert, Banach, and Fréchet cases. That kind, unlike the plain locally convex kind, still lets variational methods work.

They first adapt past work on those methods for a Lagrangian held to a subbundle of a Banach manifold. Then they treat the same task when the bound comes from a singular distribution. Last, they apply the results to normal geodesics for a conical Finsler metric on a Banach manifold. The aim is to learn which finite case results still hold in such vast spaces.
arxiv-2508-12699:
Do Quang Tam and three colleagues wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It measures how the strength of a key nuclear force fades with distance, for neutrons bouncing off four kinds of atomic nuclei at low energy.

Nuclear reaction math uses an optical potential, a stand-in for the messy forces inside a nucleus. Part of that potential is nonlocal, meaning its effect at one spot depends on nearby spots. The team computed it from a detailed nuclear model with no free knobs to turn. They found the nonlocal reach varies with position in the nucleus, the neutron's energy, and the target's mass. Values ran well above the textbook constant used for decades. The authors argue that precise reaction work needs this reach spelled out case by case, not one fixed number.
arxiv-2508-13599:
Park, Son, and Kim merged tokens to speed vision state space models in this paper from twenty twenty-five. State space models process images as token sequences, and trimming tokens cuts cost. But careless cuts can wreck the sequence order these models depend on. Their method, MaMe, scores each token's worth using the model's own timing parameter.

Tokens are then merged under arrangements that keep information flowing in order. Tests showed better speed-versus-accuracy trade-offs than rival reducers, for tuned and off-the-shelf models alike. The method stayed robust even under aggressive cutting. It also generalized beyond still images to video and audio tasks. The authors offer it as a general efficiency tool for the model family.
arxiv-2508-13899:
Xu and a team of colleagues proposed CARE in twenty twenty-five, a network for segmenting ultrasound images. Segmentation means outlining a lesion or organ in the scan. Ultrasound is hard because lesions blend with nearby tissue and artifacts of similar look, a problem the authors call target-context entanglement.

Instead of only strengthening feature extraction, CARE reorganizes how evidence is stored. It sorts encoded responses by how relevant they seem to the lesion, splitting target cues from interference. The two streams then interact, letting buried lesion cues resurface while false context signals get corrected. This sharpens the target-context split without hurting localization. On three public benchmarks, BUSI, BUSIS, and TN3K, CARE beat prior methods consistently, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-14799:
Eduardo Esteves and Felipe de Leon Saenz Angel answer a question, in a 2025 preprint, about a family of geometric spaces built from nets of linear maps. Linked projective spaces arise when tracking how families of divisors degenerate. They sit inside products of projective spaces of one fixed dimension. A natural guess says each such space is a degeneration of the diagonal, a very symmetric special case. That guess is still open. The authors settle a weaker but telling point: the spaces share the diagonal's Chow class.

The Chow class is a coarse algebraic fingerprint of a space's shape and size. Matching it means the linked spaces are, in that accounting, indistinguishable from the diagonal. The proof leans on tilings built from polymatroids, combinatorial structures that tile the relevant parameter space. The result supports the degeneration guess without proving it. Specialists gain a new invariant check for these limit spaces.
arxiv-2508-15099:
Siddharth Chaudhary and co-authors published a 2025 paper presenting Hydra, a language model design built for long documents on modest hardware. The standard transformer design grows costly very fast as text lengthens, which blocks use in tight settings. Hydra swaps the core for a state-space backbone, a design whose cost grows gently with length. Extra parts are added modularly.

The model routes work between sparse attention for long-range links, a mixture of expert sub-networks, and two kinds of memory: a scratch workspace for reasoning and a key-based store for lookup. The team evaluated a 29-million-parameter version. It processed text about three times faster than equal-sized transformers at eight thousand tokens. On multi-step logic chains, its accuracy rose tenfold. Removing each part in turn confirmed each one earns its place.
arxiv-2508-15399:
Skuratovskii studies generating sets for an extended form of the special linear group, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The pack names the creator only as a single letter, while the text head gives the full name used here. Such groups are sets of matrices with a unit product of their rows and columns, in a broad sense.

He looks at sets made of three involutions, items that undo themselves, where two of them can swap order freely. That build is barred for some three-by-three groups, which makes the case of interest. He gives a closed form for roots in one such group, and a step-by-step form for roots in the two-by-two case.
arxiv-2508-17199:
Hyeyeon Kim, Sungwoo Han, Jingun Kwon, Hidetaka Kamigaito, and Manabu Okumura introduce a task: generating a cover image, plus a short summary, for a document that has only text. Their paper came out in 2025. No dataset existed for this job, so they built one cheaply by pseudo-labeling.

They started from documents that already carried several captioned images and a summary. Images and captions were ranked separately against the summary. An image earned the label only when both it and its caption ranked first together, a double agreement that filters noise. Documents that referred to their images in the text were removed. The resulting dataset beat text-only and image-only labeling methods, and models trained on it produced better covers. Code is released publicly.
arxiv-2508-18499:
Arlen Fan, Fan Lei, Steven Corman, and Ross Maciejewski present Skeptik, a tool to flag false or weak claims in online news. Much false news does not rest on made-up facts. It rests on flawed thought and on fallacies, which are errors in how a claim is argued. Normal fact checks catch those weak spots poorly.

Skeptik works as a browser add-on. It pairs large language models with rule-based checks. It marks lines that may hold a fallacy, says what the flaw is, and gives steps to help readers judge the story. The team backs the design with case studies, counts, ease-of-use tests, and expert reviews. They also give a fallacy list that can grow over time.
arxiv-2508-19099:
Thomas Compton, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, argues for transparent, hybrid methods in quantitative discourse analysis. Heavy reliance on black box software such as MAXQDA and NVivo can hide how results were produced.

A case study in historical political discourse demonstrates a custom Python pipeline built on NLTK, spaCy, and Sentence Transformers. The workflow pairs precise lexical searches with semantic topic modeling through BERTopic, using UMAP reduction, HDBSCAN clustering, and class-based TF-IDF keywords. Multiple tuned runs improved topic coherence and coverage. Compton concludes that combining lexical and semantic layers, with code open to inspection, strengthens triangulation, reproducibility, and researcher control.
arxiv-2508-19399:
Tobias Vente, Michael Heep, Abdullah Abbas, and three colleagues build a tool for choosing recommender system datasets in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Dataset choice shapes offline experiments, yet most papers never justify it. The authors note that eighty-six percent of recent RecSys papers give no justification, and nearly all lean on the same four datasets. Algorithm Performance Spaces were proposed to guide selection by mapping how algorithms perform across datasets, but nobody had built an approachable explorer for them.

The APS Explorer is a web-based visualization tool with three interactive features. A principal component plot shows dataset similarity through performance patterns. A dynamic meta-feature table supports direct comparisons between datasets. A third view specializes in pairwise algorithm performance. The authors aim to make dataset selection a deliberate, data-driven step in recommender research rather than a habit.
arxiv-2508-19699:
Yupeng Zhang and co-authors taught a fast 3D scene renderer to also say what everything in the scene is. Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting builds scenes from millions of soft 3D blobs and renders them quickly and beautifully, but it cannot segment objects. Their method, LabelGS, attaches an object label to each blob, guided by labeled images from several viewpoints.

Three added components keep labels consistent: one handles places where objects hide each other, one lifts the main labels from images into 3D, and one filters out blobs with conflicting labels. A random region sampling scheme speeds the whole process. LabelGS beat the leading earlier method on segmentation quality while training about twenty-two times faster at high resolution.
arxiv-2508-19999:
Zhang and co-authors pick show cases for in-tale learn in straight time. In-tale learn primes a tool with picked cases for a new ask. From n cases, the ask is which k best prime the tool. Past picks leant on how like case words sit to the ask. Weights stay froze in such learn, which bound past ways. Their way uses slopes of outs in the in-feed space.

A first-rank take on outs from those slopes does the guess work. That take runs on more than one chance-picked sub-set in the way. Sub-set ends then merge in a sway score per show case. Top k scores form the prime set for the ask in the runs. One pass of outs and slopes feeds the whole pick path. Pace thus runs straight in tool and set size in the work.
arxiv-2508-20699:
Junhyeok Hur and nine co-authors published a 2025 experiment on many-body localization, a state where a disordered quantum system refuses to settle into thermal balance. Whether this state can truly survive in two dimensions has been debated for years. The team used ultracold atoms arranged in grids of up to 24 by 24 sites, larger than computers can simulate.

They tracked a measure of imbalance over long times under two kinds of disorder. With random disorder, the boundary for localization moved to stronger disorder as the grid grew, matching a theory in which rare ordered patches spread. With patterned disorder, no such shift appeared. That contrast suggests localization may be genuinely stable in two dimensions under the right conditions.
arxiv-2508-20799:
Marco Saponara, Elias Fernández Domingos, Jorge Pacheco, and Tom Lenaerts ask why bias evolves in two thousand twenty five. Humans often expect better futures than reason warrants. Evolutionary game theory tests whether such bias can be adaptive. Agents use level k reasoning in the Incremental Centipede Game.

Positive bias tilts inference toward higher but uncertain rewards. Selection favors that bias again and again in their model. Pure rational play can even go extinct in the runs. Biased agents coexist with non reasoning agents at a new balance. Longer games strengthen the pull toward positive bias.
arxiv-2508-21399:
Sabrina Kletz, Klaus Schoeffmann, Jenny Benois-Pineau, and Heinrich Husslein find surgical tools in laparoscopy video in two thousand twenty-five. Surgery videos record each step of a procedure in detail. Auto indexing of that footage is still hard due to its odd content. Their case is gynecology done through small cuts.

A region based network segments each tool apart from its background. A second task asks which type of tool each region is. With a modest count of training cases, regions were found with high accuracy. Naming the exact tool stayed hard, since tools look much alike. The study maps both the reach and the wall of the method.
arxiv-2509-00199:
Chen Zheng and Zhenyu Zhao name and study algorithm adaptation bias in online recommender experiments in 2025. A/B tests are the gold standard for launch choices, yet many biases can skew their results. Adaptation bias stems from the flywheel among live models, user data, and training pipelines.

A new model is judged on user data shaped by the incumbent system, or only in a small test group. Its measured effect can thus diverge far from its true effect at full launch. In practice, tests favor the high-traffic live variant and underrate the small-traffic test variant. That skew can cause teams to miss real gains and launch the wrong variant.
arxiv-2509-00499:
Dongwon Son, with two co-authors, Hojin Jung and Beomjoon Kim, presents NeuralSVCD for robot safety. Swept volume collision detection checks a moving robot part against obstacles along its whole path, not just at sampled points, which can miss a hit between points.

Son and his co-authors build a neural encoder-decoder, a network that compresses shape into a code and then expands it for a decision. Their design uses shape locality and time locality, the idea that nearby shapes and times behave alike, to speed work without losing accuracy. Broad tests show NeuralSVCD beats prior leading methods on both accuracy and speed across varied robot manipulation tasks, with code and videos shared.
arxiv-2509-00899:
O. B. Zaslavskii is the sole author of this 2025 research paper on black hole physics. The paper sets out a general method for round, static models that follow a vacuum-like rule. Under that rule, radial pressure and energy density are equal in size but opposite in sign.

For any chosen rule linking sideways pressure to density, the author works out the full metric in closed form. The resulting family covers both tight objects much like the classic Schwarzschild case and far more spread-out systems. Some members have a smooth centre, while others have a singular one, and one special case recovers the known Kiselev black hole.
arxiv-2509-00999:
Zbigniew Palmowski and Pawel Stepniak price an American put option capped by a drawdown event. The model is the Black-Scholes model. The option is perpetual, so it has no fixed expiry date. It ends at the first drawdown epoch beyond a predefined level. A drawdown is a fall from a peak in the asset price.

They derive an explicit price for this option. The optimal exercise strategy has a simple form. The holder should execute when the asset price first falls below a threshold. The proof relies on martingale arguments. It also uses the fluctuation theory of Levy processes. Numerical analysis complements the theoretical findings. The result links option pricing with drawdown risk in a tractable way.
arxiv-2509-01499:
Electricity prices that vary by time of day match real supply costs better than flat rates, especially as weather, renewables, and electrification widen peak gaps. Nathan Engelman Lado, Richard Chen, and Saurabh Amin study who loses when markets move from flat to time-varying pricing. The fairness effects, above all for low-income households, have been little studied.

Their theoretical framework allows consumers to differ in demand, and it counts the loss from power needs that go unmet. They derive sufficient conditions that identify when a consumer loses utility from the reform, and they compare effects across consumer types. Vulnerability, they find, depends on the interplay of when a household uses power, how flexibly it can shift that use, and how sensitive it is to price. The work guides pricing design that seeks efficiency without quiet harm.
arxiv-2509-01799:
Mario U Gaimann and Miriam Klopotek explore how swarms of active matter can serve as computers. Reservoir computing uses a complex system as a fixed processor and trains only a simple readout. Their reservoir is a simulated active matter system, meaning units that move on their own, driven by a chaotic input signal. The open question is whether how the signal enters changes what the system can compute.

Switching the drive from pushing away to pulling in reshapes how the system computes. Yet the maps of predictive success stay nearly the same in shape. A nonlinear drive helps by freeing single units from the driver motion. Liquid droplet phases of the swarm work best of all. The broad success maps suggest the approach is robust and adaptable.
arxiv-2509-01899:
Zhimeng Luo leads five co-authors on pulling medical entities from chief complaints without hand labels. A chief complaint is the visit reason in the patient own words, vital for quick triage and text mining. Wording varies wildly across sites, blocking standard records and mining. Their weakly supervised method first builds rough labels by splitting and matching text against a medical ontology, a structured term list.

Rough labels cover more than a million real de-identified records cleared by an ethics board. A BERT based model trains on those labels to find mentions and link them to the ontology. Wide tests beat prior methods that also used no hand labels. The approach scales to new sites without costly annotation rounds.
arxiv-2509-01999:
Junyang Liu leads five co-authors in a rigorous error analysis of a real valued direction finding algorithm. Direction of arrival estimation locates signal sources from sensor array data, serving radar and wireless systems. The root-MUSIC family reads directions from polynomial roots, but mirror roots create ambiguity. Standard beamforming usually suppresses those false roots, leaving theory incomplete.

Their analysis works in the non-asymptotic regime, where sample counts stay finite rather than huge. A conjugate extension builds an equivalent subspace that treats true and mirror roots alike. Perturbation formulas cover the noise subspace and both root types in turn. Monte Carlo tests confirm the formulas. The results ground parameter tuning for real sensing systems.
arxiv-2509-02099:
Alejandro Alonso leads five co-authors in a push to lift trait reads on street shots by fixing training data, not the model. The task reads traits like garb and gear from shots of folks on foot. Rare traits lag most, since data sets hold few of them and models learn them poorly. Their data first route starts by finding which traits read weakly in each set.

A prompt led pipeline that makes images from noise then makes fake shots of folks on foot. The fake shots keep the look and rules of the real data sets. A merge plan folds fake shots into training with prompt based tags and a tweaked loss. Rare trait reads rise, and whole model scores rise past the aimed traits. New scene skill grows with no change to the model build.
arxiv-2509-02399:
Haji Gul, Abdul Ghani Naim, and Ajaz Ahmad Bhat wrote a 2025 paper on a proposed score for dataset difficulty. The task is link prediction in knowledge graphs, where models guess missing links between facts. The score is called Cumulative Spectral Gradient. Its makers claimed it scales with class count and tracks model quality.

The authors vary two settings that drive the score. One is the count of sampled points per class. The other is the count of nearest neighbors used. Tests run on standard graph benchmarks, such as FB15k-237 and WN18RR. The score swung a lot with the neighbor setting. So it does not scale as claimed. Its values also showed weak or no link to mean reciprocal rank, a standard quality score. The paper calls for sturdier difficulty scores.
arxiv-2509-02499:
Junxi Wu and six co-authors present a 2025 text analysis paper on spotting AI-generated writing as language models improve. Many detectors ignore writing style and use one fixed threshold, which caps their accuracy.

Their MoSEs framework mixes several stylistics experts, models tuned to style cues, and estimates its threshold for each input. A reference repository supplies matching style examples. A router picks the right references, and a threshold estimator combines word statistics with semantic features to set the cut-off and report confidence. Average detection scores rose clearly over baselines. Gains were much larger when training data was scarce, a common real-world case. The authors release their code for reuse.
arxiv-2509-02599:
Piotr Giedziun and nine co-authors present a 2025 computational pathology paper reporting their MIDOG 2025 challenge entry for spotting mitotic figures, dividing cells, in tissue slides. Scanners, stains, and tissue types vary widely, so models must generalise across domains.

Time limits forced the team to drop a planned two-stage design and refine a single-stage detector instead. They used RF-DETR, a transformer-based detector, with hard negative mining, which feeds the model its most confusing non-cell examples during training. Training drew on the MIDOG++ collection. When the preliminary test set was scored, the method posted a solid F1 score with recall ahead of precision. The authors stress that training data balance and hard negatives matter most for crossing domain shifts.
arxiv-2509-03099:
David Senjaya and Supakchai Ponglertsakul studied a tabletop analog of a rotating black hole in a 2025 physics paper. In a photon-fluid model, light flowing through a medium behaves like sound in a fluid, and a swirling flow can mimic a black hole's horizon. The team worked in two space dimensions plus time.

They examine quasibound states, waves trapped near the analog hole, and scalar clouds, clouds of a simple field held in balance around it. Exact solutions to a wave equation let them compute the analog version of Hawking radiation, the faint glow real black holes are predicted to emit. Other techniques give formulas for superradiance, where scattered waves leave stronger than they arrived. They find such amplification for co-rotating waves in a stated energy window.
arxiv-2509-03199:
Sina Hinzmann and 6 co-authors tested sound cues for outdoor navigation in augmented reality in a 2025 user study. As AR headsets move into daily life, audio may need to guide walkers when eyes are busy. The team asked which kinds of sounds feel effective and pleasant to follow.

Twenty participants walked five outdoor routes wearing a commercial headset, guided by sound alone. Cue families included artificial sounds, nature sounds, musical instruments, everyday auditory icons, and spearcons, which are spoken words sped up and compressed. Ratings differed mainly on novelty and stimulation, where artificial sounds and instruments beat spearcons. Overall favorites split evenly between nature and artificial sounds. The authors suggest designers build in novelty and engagement, not just clarity.
arxiv-2509-03299:
Mwdansar Banuary, Ashish Kumar Gupta, and Nimrod Moiseyev gave 2025 conditions for slowing a chemical reaction inside a dark infrared cavity.
