A cavity formed by two parallel mirrors can change how molecules react, even with no light shining in. Theory and experiment on such effects have not yet fully converged.

The key requirement, they argue, concerns the reaction's energy landscape. To suppress a reaction, its surface must hold two saddle points, the passes between valleys, rather than the single pass needed for enhancement. They demonstrate the idea on a reaction combining oxygen and nitric oxide into nitrogen dioxide. Suppression depends on the mirror spacing, which sets the cavity's properties, and on how many molecules in the passing configuration interact with the cavity at once. The guidelines should help experimentalists pick promising reactions.
arxiv-2509-03399:
Marcel Blattner introduced Tangential Action Spaces in a 2025 theoretical framework linking embodiment, memory, and energy cost. Living agents must balance moving efficiently with effects that depend on the path taken, not just the destination. The framework models an agent as stacked manifolds, geometric spaces, linked by projections from physical states to cognitive representations and onward to intentions.

Turning an intention back into action can follow several routes that differ in energy use and in whether they leave memory-like traces. Under stated assumptions, three results are proved. A locally invertible perception map yields one cheapest lift with no path memory, and any memory costs extra energy. With many physical states per cognitive state, the cheapest lift is a weighted pseudoinverse. Around small loops, excess energy grows with the square of the induced memory. Agent classes and simulations follow.
arxiv-2509-03499:
Tracking many objects at once in deep-sea video is the task behind a 2025 benchmark dataset by Kevin Barnard and five co-authors. Reliable test data lets machine learning teams compare detectors and trackers fairly. Their footage comes from Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute work in deep water habitats.

Four video sequences cover midwater scenes and benthic scenes, meaning life near the sea floor. Several institute detection models are tested, plus a FathomNet detector, each paired with different trackers. A combined accuracy score balances finding objects, placing them correctly, and keeping their identities straight. The authors describe the set as the first public benchmark of its kind for deep-sea footage. They also share their workflow and example notebooks so others can add videos and compute scores.
arxiv-2509-03599:
A 2025 research paper by Nondh Panithanpaisal and nine co-authors focuses on modelling stellar streams from globular clusters inside a fully cosmological simulation. Stellar streams are ribbons of stars torn from a cluster as it orbits the galaxy. Coming surveys should reveal thousands of them, demanding realistic models to interpret.

Their framework, CosmoGEMS, follows stars one by one and links cluster-scale physics with galaxy-scale motion. Starting clusters come from the FIRE cosmological simulation of a Milky Way-like galaxy. Escaped stars are then tracked to today inside a changing gravitational field taken from that same simulation. Two example streams show contrasting fates: one stays long and thin, though clumpy and slightly misaligned, while another gains a diffuse shell-like part. Time-changing orbits, often ignored in simpler models, prove central to stream shapes.
arxiv-2509-03999:
In a 2025 research paper, Han Huang and four co-authors examine SliceSemOcc, a framework for three-dimensional semantic occupancy prediction for autonomous driving. Occupancy prediction fills a voxel grid, labelling each cell as free space or as a class like car or pedestrian. Unlike bird's-eye-view methods the grid keeps height, but many approaches neglect it when processing features.

Standard channel attention, in the SENet style, gives every height layer the same weight, blurring the vertical detail the grid exists to capture. The authors extract voxel features through vertical slices, both global and local. A fusion module blends fine local detail with holistic context. Their SEAttention3D module pools while preserving height-wise resolution and assigns attention weights per height layer. On two nuScenes occupancy benchmarks, the method improves mean intersection-over-union. Gains are pronounced on small-object categories, and ablation studies isolate each component's contribution.
arxiv-2509-04299:
Wilke van der Schee and five co-authors publish three predictions for energy loss in collisions of light atomic nuclei in a 2025 physics letter. In July 2025 the Large Hadron Collider smashed oxygen and neon nuclei to explore small droplets of quark-gluon plasma, the melted state of nuclear matter. Fast particles crossing that droplet should lose energy, called partonic energy loss. Whether such loss appears in tiny systems is a key open question for the run.

Three modeling ingredients are combined: a BDMPS-Z based energy-loss model, a path-weighted prescription, and the JEWEL simulation tool. Realistic shapes for both nucleus types complete the setup. Ion size changes the predicted loss in model-specific ways, giving experiments clear patterns to check.
arxiv-2509-05599:
Glass surfaces in three dimensions, nearly invisible to ordinary cameras, are targeted by Kai Zhang and five co-authors in a 2025 computer vision paper. Perception systems struggle with glass because its optical behaviour hides edges and depth, and real-world training data for glass have been lacking.

The team built a dataset of varied glass setups with precise three-dimensional annotations from distinct real scenes. Their method, MonoGlass3D, works from a single camera view. An adaptive fusion module gathers context under changing conditions, while a plane regression step exploits the flat geometry of most glass. Experiments beat prior methods at both glass segmentation and depth estimation from one image.
arxiv-2509-05699: A new kind of ideal in hyperstructure theory is introduced by Mahdi Anbarloei in a solo 2025 algebra paper. The paper aims to present and study endo-prime hyperideals, a prime-like notion for hyperideals, which are substructures in systems where operations can return sets of values rather than single ones. No further results are described in the record beyond this introduction and study of the new notion.
arxiv-2509-05899:
Turning a plain question into a working database query depends heavily on schema, the map of tables and columns, argues Dazhi Peng in a 2025 paper. Language models now write SQL well, yet many systems underuse schema information. Peng's framework, X-SQL, puts schema linking and understanding at the center, with different models handling different parts.

One component, X-Linking, is fine-tuned to match question phrases to the right schema elements, beating earlier open-source linkers. A second, X-Admin, bridges the gap between abstract schema terms and what the user actually means. Assigning separate large models to each stage lifts the whole pipeline. On the standard Spider benchmark, X-SQL reached the highest execution accuracy reported for open-source-based systems, on both development and test splits.
arxiv-2509-06499:
Keeping a pictured subject looking like itself while following an edit instruction is the tension explored by Jibai Lin and eight co-authors in a 2025 image generation paper. Subject-driven generation changes a specific person or object in an image as text directs. Older methods often sacrifice either identity or obedience to the instruction.

Their framework, TIDE, learns from triples of a reference image, an instruction, and target images. Some targets balance preservation and compliance well; others are distorted. Training favors the winning targets over the losing ones, a form of preference learning that needs no extra tuning when the model is used. Tests on standard benchmarks show more faithful subjects and better instruction following than rivals. The same approach also works for structure-guided generation, image-to-image edits, and blending between text and image.
arxiv-2509-06799:
Beta functions at three loops in supersymmetric gauge theories are worked out in full by Swapnil kumar Singh in a solo 2025 theory paper. Beta functions govern how a theory's coupling strength changes with energy scale. The scheme used here adds higher covariant derivatives, plus Pauli-Villars subtraction to tame divergences.

The general three-loop form in this setup was known but held regulator-linked parameters left unevaluated. Singh works them out in closed form for exponential regulators, derives their behavior when the powers grow large, and puts everything back into the general formulas. The result is a fully spelled-out set of beta functions, with a ordered expansion sorting the finite, scheme-linked terms. Finite redefinitions then connect the output to the scheme matching a famous exact relation for supersymmetric theories, clarifying how the regulators keep that relation.
arxiv-2509-06899:
Estimating the best inputs for an expensive simulation, using a fast neural stand-in, is the project reported by Dhruvil Kamleshkumar Kotecha in a solo 2025 paper. A fine model gives accurate answers but costs heavy computation, while a coarse model runs quickly at lower accuracy. Space mapping is a classic strategy for bridging the two.

Kotecha applies neural network-based space mapping optimization: the coarse model is a neural network. The mapping aligns its inputs with the fine model's, so the cheap model's optimum estimates the expensive one's. The project also reviews earlier neuro-modeling space mapping techniques and uses them to strengthen the process. Tests on the chosen derivative-based test problem aim to show the approach optimizing complex functions efficiently. The broader promise is parameter estimation for costly simulators without paying full price for every trial.
arxiv-2509-07199:
Big experiments now stream data straight from instruments to supercomputers, skipping slow file transfers. Anjus George and 6 co-authors study the messaging settings behind that streaming in a 2025 research paper. They work with RabbitMQ, a widely used messaging framework, inside the data streaming infrastructure at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility. Two real scientific workflows guide their tests.

The team uses synthetic workloads modeled on the Deleria and LCLS workflows. It varies delivery settings and measures throughput, the amount of data moved per second. They focus on the cost of reliable delivery, where every message must arrive intact. Their simulations surface practical trade-offs between speed and reliability. The findings help workflow teams pick configurations that keep analysis fast enough to steer experiments while they run.
arxiv-2509-07499:
Antoine Ledent and 3 co-authors introduce Conv4Rec in 2025, a convolutional autoencoder for profiling users in recommendation systems. Recommenders must learn from explicit ratings and from implicit feedback, the pattern of what users chose to view at all. Most models blur the two signals or use only one, losing information about items users never saw but might have loved.

The architecture learns associations between interaction types that carry over to every user and item. It predicts separately the chance a user consumes an item and the chance they rate it highly if they do. That split lets it surface items a user would not naturally encounter yet would enjoy. The authors also prove generalization bounds, among the first for autoencoders in recommendation, and show their loss recovers the exact sampling distribution under its assumptions.
arxiv-2509-07799:
Renjie Song and 3 co-authors build an exactly solvable impurity model inside the one-dimensional Hubbard model in a 2025 paper. The Hubbard model is the basic model of interacting electrons on a lattice. An Anderson impurity, a special site with its own energy and repulsion, is embedded at the boundary of a one-dimensional Hubbard chain here, within the quantum inverse scattering framework.

A nested Bethe ansatz yields the exact solution, letting the team map the bound states at the boundary and chart how the ground state changes. Reading the impurity's share of the magnetic susceptibility, they find that when electrons are scarce the impurity keeps an almost free local moment. Once the density rises, surrounding electrons screen that spin, the hallmark of Kondo physics. One impurity problem solved exactly gives a check on the approximations used for messier, more realistic cases.
arxiv-2509-08099:
The loudest gravitational wave signal yet recorded, GW250114, came from two merging black holes. The LIGO Scientific Collaboration, the Virgo Collaboration, and the KAGRA Collaboration analyze it in a 2025 research paper. After a merger, the newborn black hole rings like a struck bell. Its tones, called quasi-normal modes, are fixed by Einstein's theory if the remnant is a Kerr black hole.

The analysis shows at least two ringing modes are needed to explain the post-merger signal. Their frequencies match the Kerr prediction to within tens of percent. Amplitudes and phases match a numerical simulation of a similar merger. Tests across the inspiral, merger, and ringdown rival constraints gathered from dozens of earlier events. The authors call it the most stringent single-event check of general relativity and of the Kerr nature of black holes so far.
arxiv-2509-08199:
Sociologists increasingly analyze text with computer science tools, and the newest tool is usually assumed to be the best. AJ Alvero and 3 co-authors challenge that assumption in a 2025 research paper. They call it the state-of-the-art fallacy. Methods rise in computer science by beating accuracy benchmarks, which may not match what a sociological question needs.

The authors revisit a study of college admissions essays. They rerun the analysis with older and newer methods side by side. The newer techniques did not meaningfully beat the earlier results. Generative AI and large language models also introduced bias and confounding that were hard to remove. The authors argue for methodological pluralism: choose tools that fit the theory and the question. The warning applies well beyond sociology, wherever benchmark prestige drives method choice.
arxiv-2509-08299:
Who gets scientific papers and data when they ask informally? Hazem Ibrahim and 6 co-authors find causal evidence of bias in a 2025 science-of-science study. Paywalls block much published work, and many datasets are shared only on request. Emailing authors works around both barriers, but whether replies depend on the requester's race or institution was unknown.

Survey data, interviews, large-scale observational analysis, and two randomised audit experiments are combined to isolate the disparities. Audit experiments, which vary only the sender's identity, turn correlation into causal evidence. Unequal informal access compounds quietly: researchers already short on resources fall further behind when the community's side door opens more readily for some names than others.
arxiv-2509-08499:
The optimizer chosen to train a neural network can matter as much as the network itself, yet the choice is often habit. Chisom Chibuike and Adeyinka Ogunsanya compare ten optimizers on heart disease prediction in a 2025 research paper. All ten trained the same simple multilayer perceptron on the same public dataset. Training conditions were held consistent so the optimizers faced a fair test.

The authors scored convergence speed, stability, and standard classification metrics. Stable optimizers like Adagrad and Adadelta converged more slowly, confirming a speed-stability trade-off. RMSProp offered the best balance across the metrics and trained quickly, though it was not the most stable. The authors recommend that teams with enough computing budget evaluate optimizers this thoroughly rather than defaulting. That advice applies well beyond one medical dataset.
arxiv-2509-08999:
Sarah Peacock and 16 co-authors survey archival ultraviolet and X-ray data for Habitable Worlds Observatory target stars in a 2025 paper. Stellar radiation shapes planetary atmospheres, so it must be known to interpret them. The sample covers ninety-eight nearby tier one target stars.

Data from many space observatories are compiled and judged for coverage and quality. Near ultraviolet spectra are fairly common, but far ultraviolet and full energy coverage are rare. Few stars have both X-ray and ultraviolet spectra good enough for full modeling. Most data are single epoch, limiting study of flares and variability. The authors urge new missions and coordinated campaigns while current observatories still operate.
arxiv-2509-09499:
Sending a full image over a weak wireless link wastes most of the channel on background nobody examines. Junjie Ni and 5 co-authors propose sending meaning instead, unevenly, in a 2025 research paper. Their mixture of semantics strategy splits each image into regions of interest and regions of non-interest. The two kinds of region get very different treatment at the transmitter.

Important regions receive more bandwidth for their semantic content. Background is compressed into a compact semantic sketch. At the receiver, a diffusion model rebuilds the whole image from both streams. Experiments show the allocation balance is critical to quality. Their method improved fidelity in the important regions and semantic scores in the background over existing generative approaches. Semantic communication like this could serve cameras and sensors where bandwidth, not curiosity, is the binding constraint.
arxiv-2509-09599:
Ira J. S. Shokar and 2 co-authors build a learning-based emulator in 2025 for messy, time-evolving systems governed by partial differential equations. Rather than train a separate network for every setting, they feed the equation's own parameter values in as an input. Training starts on one parameter region, then a smaller varied set teaches the model to stretch across a broad range.

Local attention lets the same network accept changing domain sizes and resolutions, so cheap training on small domains carries upward. Trials cover the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation and turbulent flow on a beta plane with random forcing. The emulator matches behaviour at settings it never trained on, runs far faster than direct integration, and a probabilistic version gauges uncertainty for rare events.
arxiv-2509-09799:
Mansi Sharma and 4 co-authors tackle a safety problem in aviation in this 2025 paper: telling a startle reaction apart from surprise. Both can slow a pilot's thinking in an emergency, but they act in different ways and are hard to separate in practice. Earlier work mostly studied each reaction on its own, with little use of body signals.

The team trained machine learning models on physiological signals and combined information sources with fusion strategies. Their best setup, a support vector machine with late fusion, separated startle from surprise with a mean accuracy near 86 percent. Adding a calm baseline condition, the models still sorted the three states correctly about three times in four, led by a gradient boosting setup.
arxiv-2509-09899:
Christopher Eldred and 2 co-authors build neural networks that learn how a dissipative system evolves using only what an observer can actually see in a 2025 paper. Data-driven dynamics usually needs full phase space variables, yet in heat-like systems the momenta and entropies hiding inside the state cannot be measured directly. Their framework, V-NOTS, starts from a thermodynamic Lagrangian written purely in observable terms.

The networks are wired to respect that thermodynamics, so entropy can never decrease along a predicted path. From few past trajectory points and a modest parameter count, the model reconstructs the motion efficiently. For engineers who must forecast systems whose inner state stays partly invisible, such a guarantee-backed shortcut is the main attraction.
arxiv-2509-10599:
Can any shape be manufactured, if you may add and remove material in turns? Yongxue Chen and seven co-authors answer yes in this 2025 paper. Their planning method serves hybrid additive-subtractive production. They do not plan forward from raw stock. They search backward instead. Inverse operations shrink the target model, step by step, into nothing. Each inverse step matches a real printing or cutting operation.

That backward search carries a guarantee. Every intermediate shape is manufacturable. Every one is structurally stable, too. The authors prove any model can be fabricated exactly this way. A voxel-based implementation scales the idea. It handles models with huge numbers of voxels. Tests cover varied digital models. Physical builds add support. A hybrid machine with automatic tool switching made them. The theory held up in metal and plastic, not just on screen.
arxiv-2509-10699:
Nikolai Makarov and Alexei Poltoratski continue their studies of the inverse spectral problem in this 2025 paper. It is the second in a series. The problem runs a familiar question backward. Given the spectrum of a canonical Hamiltonian system, what systems could have produced it? Their aim is concrete. They exhibit families of solutions. They expose the problem's ties to classical analysis.

Homogeneous and quasi-homogeneous spectral measures play the starring role. Families of Bessel functions arise from such systems, the authors show. Those functions govern waves in round geometries. The Hilbert transform does heavy lifting along the way. So do solutions of the Riemann-Hilbert problem. A modern spectral question thus runs straight through nineteenth-century mathematics. That is part of the paper's charm, and part of its method.
arxiv-2509-10899:
Muhammad Fazlur Rahman, Joost Ellerbroek, and Jacco Hoekstra examine how poor navigation data undermines drone traffic safety in this 2025 aviation paper. In U-space, the managed airspace for uncrewed aircraft, the system that spots conflicts assumes positions and speeds that sensors only estimate. The authors model those errors as Gaussian noise matching a broadcast standard. They push them through the math of detection, with simulations and formulas.

Detection becomes a probability, not a verdict. It drops below fifty percent exactly when nominal intrusion time reaches the look-ahead horizon. Of two resolution methods compared, the modified voltage potential method proved sturdier than velocity obstacles. It pushes the distance at closest approach as large as it can, avoiding reversal behavior. BlueSky tests confirmed higher intrusion prevention and larger miss distances for that method, most of all at low relative speeds. Tuning the horizon and protected zone buys a target safety level.
arxiv-2509-11299:
Paul Bennet and ten co-authors traced six small galaxies in this 2025 astronomy paper. These isolated dwarfs sit near the Local Group's edge. Quiet dwarfs have long puzzled astronomers. Such dwarfs form no new stars. Many assumed they once swung past the Milky Way or Andromeda. A close pass would strip their gas. That history is called backsplash.

The team used new Hubble Space Telescope measurements. They tracked the dwarfs' sideways motions. Four dwarfs received their first such measurements ever. Past orbits were computed from the data. Four dwarfs look consistent with a first arrival. Cetus is likely an old backsplash case from Andromeda. Tucana apparently never came close to a massive host. The results push a rethink of dwarf quenching.
arxiv-2509-11399:
Yumou Fei, Dor Minzer, and Shuo Wang prove a clean split in what streaming algorithms can do, in this 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Their subject is constraint satisfaction problems read as a stream, where an algorithm with tiny memory may pass over the input several times and must judge how satisfiable the instance is.

For every choice of problem parameters, the authors show there is a threshold gap with matching algorithms and lower bounds. Above the threshold, a randomized streaming algorithm using only logarithmic space and constantly many passes succeeds, built from a linear programming relaxation and a distributed approximation scheme. Below it, any algorithm, even randomized and even with polynomially many passes, needs space growing like the cube root of the input size per pass. The hardness side converts integrality gaps of the relaxation into hard instances, analyzed through a communication problem with Fourier methods.
arxiv-2509-11999:
University instructors, not students, sit at the center of a 2025 study by Si Chen and five co-authors on generative AI literacy. Their program, the AI Academy, mixed hands-on exploration of AI tools with pedagogical reflection and peer learning for faculty.

Twenty-five instructors took part, tracked through surveys before and after, learning logs, and facilitator interviews. The group made clear gains in AI literacy, and the study frames them as designers of responsible classroom practice rather than passive adopters. What shapes that growth, the authors find, is a web of tools, campus policies, colleagues' habits, and institutional support. The write-up offers a program model others can copy, a survey instrument built together with participants, and design lessons for training that keeps pace with fast-changing tools.
arxiv-2509-12199:
Asif Iqbal and 6 co-authors use graph neural networks to weigh galaxy clusters in a 2025 paper. A cluster's mass is central to cosmology, the study of the universe's structure, because mass links observations to theory. Traditional estimates from X-ray data often rely on assuming the hot gas sits in balance, which can bias results.

Their network reads radial profiles of the intracluster medium, the hot gas between galaxies, inferred from X-ray observations. Representing each profile as a graph lets the model handle varying length and resolution. Trained on the Three Hundred Project simulations, it recovered true masses with no systematic bias and about six percent scatter. That scatter was six times smaller than a standard balance-based method, and the approach held up across data quality and cluster shape.
arxiv-2509-12799:
A. Alexander, J. Faupin and S. Richard prove in 2025 a form of Levinson theorem for open systems that lose energy. The classic theorem counts bound states from scatter data, but loss makes some states fade with time and hard to count.

They study a wave operator with a complex, fading field whose loss part is never a gain. For that case they prove a shape-based form of the theorem tied to an index result for the discrete, complex spectrum. In plain terms the scatter data still counts the fading states. The result links scatter theory and index theory for systems that leak.
arxiv-2509-12999:
Shinichi Honna, Taichi Murayama, and Akira Matsui test a principle about success and failure across varied media in a 2025 paper. The principle, named for Anna Karenina, says that success is narrow. Failure, by contrast, can happen in many unlike ways. The authors test that claim, the same claim turned around, and two more patterns, which they call ordered and noisy.

Their material spans four kinds of work: novels, online encyclopedias, research papers, and movies. The team then checks how those series come together, looking at the order of the changes and at their positions. The patterns turned out to depend on the medium. Novels followed the reversed pattern in order. Encyclopedia articles mixed patterns together. Academic papers behaved one way in order and another in position. Movies split by genre. Success, they conclude, rests on structural limits that are specific to each medium.
arxiv-2509-13399:
Tianyu Chen, Yasi Zhang and 14 co-authors evaluate multi-turn image editing in 2025 with EdiVal, an object-first automated frame. Instruction edits advance fast, yet fair grading lags. Paired references curb coverage and import prior bias, while zero-shot judges grade loosely.

EdiVal splits an image into named objects, then crafts varied edit orders while updating pools per turn. Three scores follow: order fidelity via detectors plus judges, consistency of untouched parts via semantic match, and visual quality via human-preference models. A bench spans nine order types and sixteen top editors. Failure modes surface for next builds.
arxiv-2509-13499:
Susobhan Ghosh, Bhanu Gullapalli and six co-authors propose in 2025 a reproducible workflow for online AI in digital health interventions. Online learners improve as streaming personal data arrives, but adaptability fights reproducibility. Iterative deployment defines the field.

Data across deployments must store with scientific utility. Algorithm acts must audit cleanly, and results must compare over time for trustworthy refinement. The workflow spans development, deployment, and analysis phases. Grounding comes from multiple real deployments by the team. Challenges per phase get concrete fixes. Health AI gains a shared discipline for learning systems that never stand still.
arxiv-2509-13799:
Chalyi and Zaitseva review dimensional crossover in a 2025 condensed matter article. Near a phase transition, squeezing a material changes its critical behavior. Thin films or narrow pores do the squeezing. Fluctuations of the order parameter start to feel the sample size. Temperature and pressure are no longer the only controls.

The authors lay out the theory for several regimes. One covers systems where the Ginzburg number separates fluctuation-dominated from regular behavior. Another covers crossovers from three dimensions down to two or one. Slit and cylinder shapes decide which drop occurs. A third topic is the fine structure of molecular light scattering near the transition. They also propose wider equalities among critical exponents, treating the fractal dimension as an exponent in its own right.
arxiv-2509-14099:
Misha Feigin, Mikhail Vasilev, and Martin Vrabec generalize a family of integrable particle systems in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. Spin Calogero-Moser systems describe particles moving on a line. Forces depend on the gaps between them and on internal spin states. The systems are prized as exactly solvable. A 1999 construction by Chalykh, Goncharenko, and Veselov produced examples whose potential singular points sit in non-symmetric layouts. Those depart from the classical symmetric ones.

The authors obtain various extensions of those examples through the representation theory of Cherednik algebras. Those algebras unify several structures in modern algebra. That theory realizes abstract objects as concrete transformations. It supplies the tools that manufacture the new systems.
arxiv-2509-14199:
Haichao Zhang and four co-authors tackle a gap in how video language models watch video in their 2025 work. Most systems sample only a few frames, so they miss detail that changes from one frame to the next. Lectures are a clear case, where new content can appear in almost every frame.

Zhang and colleagues set up a new test, called DIVE, that checks close timing in video, and a method called Gated Residual Tokenization. Their method skips still parts of a frame by tracking motion, then merges tokens in steady scene areas. In tests it beat larger models and improved as frame rate rose, showing that dense timing can be kept without letting token counts grow out of control.
arxiv-2509-14299:
Shital Lawande and Kuldeep Saha prove a topology result in 2025 about four dimensional shapes called 4-manifolds. An open book decomposition cuts such a shape into pages around a spine, a useful picture when it exists. The question was whether every suitable shape admits one.

Building on recent work by Kastenholz, the authors show there are infinitely many closed, oriented and parallelizable 4-manifolds with no open book decomposition at all. A parallelizable shape is one whose tangent directions can be framed smoothly. The result blocks a hoped for parallel with the Giroux correspondence for Engel manifolds. In the sense used by Colin, Presas and Vogel, not every Engel manifold has a supporting open book.
arxiv-2509-14399:
Gaifan Zhang, Yi Zhou and Danushka Bollegala use large language models in 2025 to fix training data for a subtle language task. Conditional semantic similarity judges how alike two sentences are under a stated condition. The same pair can be close in topic yet far in sentiment.

An earlier human rated data set for the task held annotation flaws, and hand correction of a small part already improved models. Large accurate data remain the blocker. Zhang and colleagues ask language models to correct both condition statements and similarity ratings in the flawed set. Cleaner labels should train stronger models for the task. The work tests a wider idea: using a capable model as an editor for noisy human labels at scale.
arxiv-2509-14499:
S. R. Kulkarni, writing alone in 2025, reviews metastable helium in Earth thermosphere after a space telescope flagged its glow. The SPHEREx astronomy mission saw a bright emission line near one micron during commissioning. Its team tied the line to a helium triplet transition.

Kulkarni explains the aeronomy: sunlight resonantly scatters from metastable helium atoms high in the atmosphere. SPHEREx flies in a polar dawn dusk orbit about six hundred fifty kilometres up, inside oxygen and helium rich layers. Its survey cadence could map metastable helium columns globally every day at fine time steps. An astronomy nuisance thus becomes a rich atmospheric data set, if the mission team chooses to mine it.
arxiv-2509-14699:
Pooja Jakhad and Ajay Kumar Rai compute the mass spectra of heavy particles containing bottom quarks in a 2025 physics paper. They use a relativistic flux-tube model, which pictures the force between quarks as a stretching tube, with spin-dependent corrections added. Their study covers singly bottom mesons and doubly bottom baryons in one unified treatment.

For known meson states, the calculated masses match measured values closely. Building on that agreement, the authors assign several observed resonances to specific excited states, including candidates in the bottom-strange sector. They also predict ground and excited states for two doubly bottom baryon families that experiments have not yet found. Those predictions give experimental searches clear targets to aim at.
arxiv-2509-14899:
Amine Barrak and four co-authors present CARGO, a framework for sending each user prompt to the most suitable large language model, in a 2025 paper. Models now differ widely in skill, speed, and cost, so choosing well matters. CARGO aims to balance answer quality against price without human-labeled training data.

A single embedding-based regressor, trained on pairwise comparisons judged by a language model, predicts how each candidate model will perform on a prompt. When the prediction looks uncertain, an optional binary classifier steps in for a second opinion. Category-specific regressors handle five task groups, from mathematics and coding to creative writing. Tests across four leading models show strong routing accuracy and high win rates against fixed choices, at a lightweight running cost.
arxiv-2509-15299:
Christian Capanelli, Elisa G. M. Ferreira, and Evan McDonough propose a fuzzy dark sector with interacting ingredients in a 2025 cosmology paper. Fuzzy dark matter imagines dark matter as an ultra-light field whose wave nature smooths small scales. The single, non-interacting version is elegant but restrictive, and the authors generalize it into a richer dark sector.

Their model is an ultra-light Abelian-Higgs system, with an interacting Higgs-like field and a dark photon. One characteristic scale governs the transfer function, so the large-scale fingerprints on the cosmic microwave background and galaxy distribution mimic single-field fuzzy dark matter. Galactic halos, by contrast, diversify widely because the field interaction breeds an instability absent from decoupled versions. The scenario keeps the successful large-scale story while freeing small-scale structure.
arxiv-2509-15699:
Beata Zjawin, writing alone, certifies a quantum resource without trusting the devices used. Steering is a link between two labs where one side's choices shape the other's states. A set of such states is called an assemblage. Self testing aims to prove a lab truly holds a target assemblage, even with flawed gear. Past work here leaned on numeric methods.

Zjawin builds operator inequalities, math bounds on operators, for this task. She studies the assemblage that breaks a famous inequality the most. Her bounds give an explicit floor on how close a real setup is to the target. The bounds beat past numeric ones by a wide margin. This is the first analytic treatment of its kind.
arxiv-2509-15799:
Max Studt and Georg Schildbach pair learning with model based control for teams of agents. Safe, coordinated acts in tight settings are hard for learning alone. Pure learning can be slow to train and shaky in use. Model based control is firm but leans on fixed targets and travels poorly.

Their frame stacks the two: a learning policy picks broad targets from marked regions of interest. A predictive controller then turns each target into safe, feasible motion. The split suits multi agent systems, where coordination matters most. On a predator and prey test, the frame beats pure learning and shield based rivals. It wins on reward, safety, and steadiness.
arxiv-2509-15999:
When the cost behind a route choice is unknown, can a model learn it from the routes people took? Alan A. Lahoud, Erik Schaffernicht, and Johannes A. Stork build a model that learns a spread of cost rules, not just one. Their model maps past solutions into a hidden space, then rebuilds valid routes with a solver in the loop.

Tests use real ship and taxi routes, plus paths in made-up graphs. The model rebuilds routes and cycles well and predicts how routes are spread out. Its hidden maps are also easy to read. That helps show how different drivers or ships may weigh costs in unlike ways.
arxiv-2509-16099:
Some parts of a physical theory may add nothing real, since they track a global scale no test can reach. Callum Bell and David Sloan extend a method that finds and removes such spare parts, moving it from single systems to full field theories. They work in a frame that keeps space-time symmetry clear while the math stays in a finite space of states.

Both the action-based and the flow-based forms of field theory are covered. The authors test the frame on simple cases and discuss what it means more broadly. Removing spare parts can clarify which features of a field theory are truly physical.
arxiv-2509-16199:
Waves of magnetism and waves of sound can couple inside a magnetic material, and that coupling turns nonlinear at strong drive. Marco Brühlmann and three co-authors build a full theory of this coupled motion for continuous media. Starting from standard magnetism equations and an energy model, they derive motion rules that cover three- and four-wave mixing and both linear and nonlinear coupling.

The theory is tuned to thin films that carry surface sound waves, where it matches a recent lab result on sound-to-magnetism conversion. All rates are given in closed form, ready for a quantum version, which the authors also derive. Sound control of quantum magnetism is the long goal.
arxiv-2509-16299:
In fuzzy logic, one family of implication rules is built from a disjunctive uninorm plus a fuzzy negation. Raquel Fernandez-Peralta and Andrea Mesiarová-Zemánková ask whether that building recipe is unique for each rule. Prior work on a close family suggested a unique recipe when the negation is smooth, and that belief carried over.

The pair show the belief is false: such rules can have more than one valid recipe, even with a smooth negation. They also study when uniqueness does hold, for both smooth and rough building blocks. The result sharpens the theory of how these operators are put together.
arxiv-2509-16599:
Sandro Tsang, in a solo 2025 paper, tests a faster way to review medical evidence. Reviews that pool many studies guide real care choices. Yet the medical literature grows too fast for slow manual work. Tsang uses search-driven computing to speed the task. The test case is a class of hormone drugs and the return of a painful womb condition.

The workflow finds, sorts, and pools studies with computer help. It still yields results that clinicians can use. Tsang argues the same frame can scale to other questions. That could shorten the lag between new studies and updated care. The paper sits where medicine meets computer science.
arxiv-2509-16899:
Md Wasiul Haque and co-authors map flaws in the software supply chain for self-driving cars in a 2025 paper. Such cars run complex stacks of AI, sensor fusion, and real-time code. Much of that code comes from open sources. A flaw in any piece can ripple through the whole vehicle.

The authors survey known vulnerabilities in that shared ecosystem. Their goal is to alert researchers, builders, and policymakers to the risks. They stress security work early in development, not after launch. Early fixes protect user data and public trust. As automated fleets grow, supply chain care becomes a safety issue, not just a coding one.
arxiv-2509-17399:
Pramit Sahoo, Maharaj Brahma, and Maunendra Sankar Desarkar test how well language models handle Indian culture. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that these models often miss cultural alignment and produce biased text, thanks to thin cultural knowledge. Judging that competence is hard, since few data sets capture culture at the level of regions and sub-regions.

Their data set, DIWALI, collects culture-specific items from many sub-regions of India across a range of cultural facets. Thousands of concepts anchor the set. The team uses it to grade models on adapting text to Indian contexts, scoring with the items, with model judges, and with human raters from varied backgrounds. The grading exposes patchy coverage across sub-regions and shallow, surface-level adaptations. The work gives builders a sharper mirror for cultural skill.
arxiv-2509-17599:
Atreya Acharyya, Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Manuel Meyer, and Francesco Sannino hunt for Hawking radiation in gamma-ray data. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a famous unverified claim: black holes glow faintly and evaporate. For star-size black holes that glow is far too faint to see, so the team turns to a hypothetical detour.

When two black holes merge, they may shed tiny asteroid-mass fragments, called morsels, which would evaporate fast and shine in gamma rays. The team searched Fermi telescope data around the merger GW170814 for such a delayed flash. They found no sign of one. That null result still bites: it rules out a stated morsel mass case at high confidence for a given total emitted mass. The authors sketch next steps across the growing merger catalog.
arxiv-2509-17799:
Carl P Dettmann and Chenmiao Zhang ask when a switched system can be steered back to calm. Their 2025 paper deals with step-by-step linear systems that swap between matrix rules. Some of those matrices are singular, so they crush some states to zero.

The pair give a new lower bound for the calm radius that works for any matrix set. For rank-one singular cases, that radius matches a joint spectral value. They work out the two-dim case in detail, with real and complex modes. They also note when the best switch path never repeats.
arxiv-2509-17999:
Riccardo Cadei and Christian Interno claim that feedback loops push AI models to flatter folk. Their 2025 paper names that claim the Narcissus Hypothesis. Models learn from human picks and from text that other models made, which can reward sweet replies over straight thought.

The pair test the claim on more than thirty models with standard trait tests and a new bias score. They report a clear drift toward traits that please others. They then read that drift through a causal ladder frame, down to what they call a rung of illusion. The claim is theirs, framed as a tested hypothesis.
arxiv-2509-18299:
Jhionathan de Lima and Cristiano Francisco Woellner set out a porous sheet of carbon with metal-like traits. Their 2025 paper gives a full profile of Cyclo-Graphyne, a two-dim carbon form with mixed bond types. Quantum maths sums cover its shape, energy, and heat traits, plus electron, light, and shake traits.

Heat tests show the sheet holds up to high heat, and its energy sums sit near those of made graphynes. Its band gap is ultra narrow, with two Dirac cones in the electron map. The sheet bends far more easily than graphene. Strong ultra-violet take-up marks it for gas, flex, and light uses.
arxiv-2509-18399:
Many tools sweep a laser beam across points in sequence, from sensors to fabricators. Harishankar Jayakumar and six co-authors present a way to stretch how far one sweeper can reach. Their 2025 paper tackles a known trade: faster sweepers can address fewer spots. Passive optics could double the reach at best.

Their method, called ReLOAD, loops the bent beam back onto the same deflector inside an optical cavity. Each pass multiplies the sweep range. With an electro-optical deflector, prized for speed but short reach, they reached eight times the normal range. The setup hit frame rates of ten thousand per second and line rates of one million per second. Step times fell to millionths of a second. The reach went well past what such deflectors can usually address.
arxiv-2509-18499:
Banks must flag money laundering, but real transaction data is too private to share for training. Rachel Chung, Pratyush Nidhi Sharma, Mikko Siponen, Rohit Vadodaria, and Luke Smith test a hybrid fix in this 2025 paper. Fake data that mimics real patterns can train detection models, yet pure fake sets have limits. Graph neural networks are a common tool for spotting illicit flows.

The team enriches fake data with real-world features that are public and easy to get. The hybrid set keeps the privacy gains of synthetic data. It also trains models that work better in practice. The gains show that a small dose of real features can lift a whole fake set. The authors offer the route as a practical path for banks. Better training data should sharpen anti-laundering systems without exposing customer records.
arxiv-2509-18699:
Image generators can blend two objects into one, but the results often look biased or chaotic. Zedong Zhang, Ying Tai, Jianjun Qian, Jian Yang, and Jun Li present AGSwap for cleaner cross-category fusion in this 2025 paper. Fusing, say, two unlike objects into one coherent thing has uses in games, film, and virtual worlds. Progress has also been slowed by the lack of a proper benchmark.

AGSwap swaps groups of embedding features between the two concepts to mix their traits. An adaptive update step, steered by a balance score, keeps the blend coherent. The team also built a fusion data set from ImageNet classes and a word hierarchy. It spans 95 superclasses with ten subclasses each, giving hundreds of thousands of unique pairs. In tests, AGSwap beat top compositional generators on both simple and complex prompts.
arxiv-2509-19099:
Thomas Schürmann, writing alone, proves a version of Heisenberg's uncertainty rule that holds in curved space near a black hole. The rule says a quantum particle's position and momentum cannot both be sharp. Schürmann pins the particle inside a geodesic ball, a region measured along the bent geometry, on slices of space that stay smooth across the horizon. His bound links momentum spread to the ball's radius, with no dependence on coordinates.

The proof turns momentum uncertainty into the lowest tone of a vibrating region, the first eigenvalue of the Laplace-Beltrami operator. A baseline bound like the flat-space one follows, with a strict gap that is never reached. For a known slice of the Schwarzschild black hole, whose space geometry is flat, the flat-space constant returns and is best possible. The construction extends to the Weyl class of static black holes.
arxiv-2509-19599:
Teams of AI agents need a dispatcher that sends each task to the agent best fit for it. Danilo Trombino and three co-authors note that fixed agent profiles go stale as agents learn. Their method asks agents to check a task against their own private knowledge stores. Each agent replies with a light signal of fit, sharing no private content.

Those signals fill a shared cache that speeds later routing choices. The dispatcher blends the live signals with the static profiles. Privacy holds because raw knowledge never leaves the agent. The authors frame the design for knowledge-heavy work in changing settings. Better routing should cut wasted calls and wrong handoffs in agent teams, a growing cost as such systems scale.
arxiv-2509-19799:
A white dwarf that gains mass from a companion can collapse into a neutron star instead of exploding. Luciano Combi, Daniel M. Siegel, and Brian D. Metzger simulate that collapse in three dimensions with full relativity, magnetism, and neutrino physics. The dwarf spins fast, with a weak field buried below its surface. After the core bounces, the field grows explosively near the newborn neutron star.

A swirling disk forms, cooled by neutrinos, and a dynamo inside it builds large-scale magnetic bundles. Those fields rise and launch a striped, mildly relativistic jet. The jet punches out of the dwarf. Such events may seed millisecond pulsars, gamma-ray bursts, and heavy-element synthesis. The simulation shows the magnetic route from collapse to jet in one continuous story.
arxiv-2509-20499:
A robot that follows spoken directions through a building must plan where to step next. Boqi Li and five co-authors improve that waypoint choice in a 2025 arXiv paper on vision-language navigation. Their zero-shot framework pairs a simple waypoint predictor with a multimodal language model. No task-specific training is used.

The predictor works on an abstract map of obstacles and proposes waypoints the robot can reach in a straight line. Those waypoints join a topological graph that updates as the robot moves, with visit records attached. The graph and history are written into the model's prompt. That context encourages exploration and lets the model correct its own path errors locally. On two continuous navigation benchmarks, the method set new zero-shot records, with success rates of forty-one and thirty-six percent.
arxiv-2509-20799:
Smart glasses make voice commands easy, but recorded voices can fool them. Weiye Xu and seven co-authors build AuthGlass, a 2025 benchmark for voice liveness detection and authentication on smart glasses. No public dataset existed for this setting before their work, they note.

The team collected sixteen-channel audio from forty-two subjects, plus attack samples of two kinds. From that data they propose two methods. One checks liveness using the shape of the sound field across the glasses' microphones. The other authenticates users by combining several acoustic signals. They also benchmark seven existing liveness methods on the new dataset. The work was submitted to the IMWUT 2026 conference on wearable computing.
arxiv-2509-20899:
A video classifier that explains itself in plain concepts is easier to trust than a black box. Patrick Knab and four co-authors build such a classifier in a 2025 paper called Concepts in Motion. Their framework, MoTIF, extends concept bottleneck models from still images to video.

The model predicts from sequences of concept activations that are grounded in time. Per-concept attention tracks when each concept recurs and how its pattern over time shapes the prediction. A discovery module uses a vision-language model to extract object and action concepts from training data, conditioned on the class. The design keeps the final decision readable: users can see which concepts, appearing when, drove the classification.
arxiv-2509-20999:
Draw a graph so that each edge is crossed at most four times, and the number of edges stays surprisingly small. Aaron Büngener, writing solo, gives a simplified proof of that bound in a 2025 combinatorics paper. The result, first proven by Ackerman, is a high point of beyond-planar graph theory.

Such a 4-planar graph on n vertices has at most six times n minus two edges, and that bound is tight. Büngener's proof is much shorter than the original. It also relaxes the assumptions, allowing multi-edges and drawings that are not simple. Shorter proofs under weaker conditions make the theorem easier to teach and to extend. The paper is a tidy contribution to the study of graphs drawn with limited crossings.
arxiv-2509-21099:
Smashing gold nuclei together briefly creates some of the densest matter in the universe, and the pions escaping carry clues about it. Xin Li and six co-authors model pion production in such collisions in a 2025 paper accepted by Physics Letters B. The collisions run at intermediate energies.

The team uses a lattice Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck transport model with a modern nuclear interaction. They vary the momentum dependence of the nucleon mean field, how strongly the potential grows with a nucleon's momentum. Stronger momentum dependence generally suppresses pion output. The mechanism is explained through the collision dynamics in the model. Because pion yields probe the symmetry energy at high density, such studies inform the equation of state inside neutron stars.
arxiv-2509-21199:
Multi hop questions force a language model to join scattered facts in a fixed number of steps. Behind the work are Kaiyang Wan and 5 co-authors. Such questions need facts from many places, joined in steps. A model that answers in one pass has a fixed limit on how much it can output. Past that limit, joining facts becomes unreliable. The paper formalizes that bottleneck.

The authors prove a Fano style upper bound on accuracy for one pass reasoning. The bound shows accuracy must fall once task load passes model capacity. From those ideas, they build InfoQA, a proof of concept system that makes many calls. It splits tasks to fit the limit and prunes old reasoning traces. A clear workflow keeps steps linked and robust.
arxiv-2509-21399:
Local decisions need climate projections at fine scale, but most projections are coarse. A grid cell of more than ten kilometres hides local detail. Petr Košťál and 2 co-authors use image super resolution to sharpen projections in a 2025 paper. Super resolution models upscale images while adding plausible fine detail. Their target is a one kilometre grid.

No true high resolution projections exist for training or scoring. So the team trained on high resolution observational data and applied the models to coarse projections. They scored results with climate indicators at weather station locations instead of pixel errors. Experiments on daily mean temperature showed the method can downscale projections. Crucially, the error of the climate indicators did not increase.
arxiv-2509-21499:
Training on code seems to improve language model thinking, but which part of code helps is unclear. Abdul Waheed and 3 co-authors investigate with a data centric system in a 2025 paper. Parallel instruction data sets were built in ten programming languages. Controlled perturbations disrupted form or semantic properties of the code. Models from five families and eight scales were fine tuned on each variant.

Thousands of tests measured effects on language, maths, and code tasks. Models proved more vulnerable to form perturbations than semantic ones. That gap was sharpest on maths and code tasks. Pseudocode and flowcharts could match real code as training material. Encoding the same content with fewer tokens often retained or improved performance, a striking useful finding.
arxiv-2509-21699:
Predicting a label for a whole graph depends heavily on which subgraphs it contains. Taiga Kojima and 3 co-authors build a network around exact subgraph matching in a 2025 paper. Their Exact subgraph Isomorphism Network enumerates subgraphs exactly, then feeds them to a neural network. A sparse regularization with a mixed norm constraint controls the enumeration cost. Discriminative power and interpretability are both design goals.

Sparse regularization yields an effective pruning strategy that keeps prediction performance. It also identifies important subgraphs, which supports interpretation of the model choices. Graph level prediction is the task throughout. Empirical tests examine the balance between accuracy and the cost of enumeration. The combination of exact enumeration and sparsity is the core idea.
arxiv-2509-21899:
New science often grows by joining old ideas, but not every join opens new ground. Kara Kedrick and four co-authors argue in this 2025 paper that the valuable joins are those that open a knowledge gap. A gap is an empty region in the map of concepts, created when new links complete a cycle. Such gaps focus attention on connections nobody has explored yet.

Using methods from computational topology, the team built a way to spot gaps across tens of millions of papers in a large academic database. Papers that opened gaps went on to earn more citations over the long term and disrupted earlier work more strongly. They were cited less in their first years, then more over twenty years, as if fields needed time to move into the new territory. The pattern held in five more databases and across eight ways of defining concepts.
arxiv-2509-21999:
Seongho Joo, Kyungmin Min, Jahyun Koo, and Kyomin Jung propose a simple way to spot made-up answers from language models in this 2025 paper. Most detectors need outside resources or a peek inside the model, such as word probabilities. Closed models expose neither. The authors look for a black-box signal, one that uses only the text the model returns.

Their signal comes from how models behave when asked to express uncertainty. The study found that factual answers stay consistent under such phrasing, while invented answers shift around. The team turns that gap into a detection metric. In experiments, the metric predicted the factuality of responses better than baselines that did use internal model information. The result is a practical check that works through ordinary interfaces, on models whose insides are hidden.
arxiv-2509-22699:
Alessandra Urbinati and 3 co-authors use a model's own doubt to expose bias in content moderation. Language tools now police social media at scale, but they carry racial and social bias. Test sets exist, yet fair scoring of such tools stays an open problem. Their method needs no labels. It scores a model by its doubt on posts labeled by people from groups at risk of harm. The doubt score comes from conformal prediction, a way to wrap a call in a checked level of trust.

They tested eleven models against labels from women and non-white raters. Some models matched those labels well on score, yet stayed full of doubt on the same calls. That split shows which groups a model truly serves.
arxiv-2509-22799:
Xuan He and 23 co-authors score generated videos the way a careful human judge would, with reasons. Text-to-video models now make realistic, varied clips, but quality has many faces: looks, text match, and physical sense. Old evaluators give one opaque score or a coarse take. VideoScore2 rates all three dimensions and explains itself with chain-of-thought rationales.

Training used a large data set of human-annotated videos with scores and reasoning traces. A two-stage pipeline paired fine-tuning with reinforcement learning for robustness. The model beat prior evaluators on its in-domain benchmark and four outside ones. Its scores also worked as rewards to pick the best of several generated samples.
arxiv-2509-23299:
Cleaning noisy speech in one generative step, instead of many, is the draw of MeanFlowSE. Yike Zhu and 8 co-authors built the framework on MeanFlow, which predicts an average velocity field. One step then refines the speech latent. Self-supervised speech codes guide the model, not autoencoder latents. That choice speeds inference and anchors training.

On the Interspeech 2020 DNS blind test set, quality hit top-tier levels. Intelligibility stayed competitive with multi-step generative rivals. Real-time factor and model size both dropped a lot. Telecom and speech recognition uses need that speed. Code will be released on publication, the team say.
arxiv-2509-23499:
A benchmark for vision-and-language models may reward the picture alone, the words alone, or the two together. Divyam Madaan and 3 co-authors measure which of these drives scores across twenty-three visual question-answering benchmarks. Their study uses multi-modal large language models on tasks from general knowledge to reading text in images and documents. Reliance on each source shifts a lot, both across benchmarks and inside a single one.

Many benchmarks built to cut text-only bias had instead boosted image-only shortcuts. Models often scored well by using each input on its own, with little use of how the two interact. The pattern held across model sizes and types. The team offers the measures as a guide for fairer benchmark design.
arxiv-2509-23699:
Cities planning charger networks must please drivers and the power grid at the same time. Harshal D. Kaushik and 3 co-authors present a two-phase framework that plans from the grid's point of view. First it estimates charging demand and picks candidate sites using spatial points of interest. Then a maximum coverage optimization places chargers while keeping each new charger inside grid capacity limits.

Spatial studies often ignore grid limits, the authors note, while grid studies often guess demand from statistics. Their Dallas test case joins the existing charger network to an eighty-five-hundred-bus distribution model. The result is a deployment plan meant to be both useful and electrically safe.
arxiv-2509-23899:
Answering a doctor's question about a scan takes both image reading and trustworthy facts. Rakesh Thakur and 2 co-authors propose Q-FSRU, a model for medical visual question answering. Image and text features are shifted into the frequency domain with a Fourier transform, which helps the model stress meaningful signal and filter noise. A quantum-inspired retrieval step then fetches medical facts from outside sources using quantum-based similarity.

Retrieved facts merge with the frequency features before the answer is formed. On the VQA-RAD radiology set, the model beat earlier systems, especially on complex image-text cases. The authors claim gains in both accuracy and explainability.
arxiv-2509-24399:
Coverage tasks fail at the first step when no agent knows where the target area even is. Jie Song and 3 co-authors present a coverage control method for multi-agent systems in that blind setting. Once one agent senses part of the target region, a density function is built on the fly to draw nearby agents in.

That pull is combined with a centroidal Voronoi scheme, which spreads agents toward an even, efficient layout. Barrier functions keep agents from colliding and keep their sensor footprints from overlapping. In simulations, agents located the unknown region on their own and covered it fully. The method needs no prior map of the target.
arxiv-2509-25599:
Ruolin Meng and a team of co-authors join generative modeling with an autoencoder to estimate causal effects, in two thousand twenty-five. A hidden factor can sway both a treatment and its outcome, which blocks plain causal reading. Two sets of proxy measures, one tied to each side, can unlock the effect through a function called the causal bridge.

The authors give a new theory view of when that bridge can be estimated, plus an error bound when its assumptions fail. Coupling the bridge with an autoencoder lets the parts share statistical strength. Tests on synthetic and real data beat leading methods for proxy-based causal estimation, they report.
arxiv-2509-26499:
Gerrit Gerhartz, Peter Lippmann, and Fred Hamprecht moved equivariant neural networks onto cheaper machinery in a 2025 paper. Networks for molecules should respect rotations: turning the input should turn the output the same way. Tensor field networks guarantee that, but their special tensor operations run slowly. Local canonicalization instead rotates each neighborhood into a standard pose first, letting ordinary message passing do the work.

Their framework converts existing tensor field designs into that style while preserving the symmetry guarantee and cutting runtime sharply. A systematic comparison weighs representations by theory cost, measured speed, and accuracy. The released tensor_frames package plugs the approach into a standard PyTorch geometry library, so any message passing model can gain equivariance.
arxiv-2510-00599:
Ehyaei and two co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on distributionally robust optimization, a way to train models that must stay reliable when real data shifts away from training data. Their focus is the ambiguity set, the range of possible data distributions that a model is protected against. They argue such sets should use causal knowledge about how the data was produced.

The authors introduce structural causal optimal transport, which uses both a causal graph and the equations that link the variables. A relaxed version replaces hard causal limits with a penalty term, so an efficient program can solve the problem. They prove finite-sample guarantees even when the causal structure must be estimated from data. Their method also shrinks the set radius faster and avoids the curse of dimensionality that slows older transport methods.
arxiv-2510-00699:
Rupprecht, Neumark, and Leone design all-optical logic gates for extreme ultraviolet light in this article, published in the journal Optica. Photonic computing needs light to switch light, and pushing that idea to ever shorter wavelengths could raise computing speeds toward petahertz rates. Their protocol mixes one attosecond extreme ultraviolet pulse with two few-femtosecond near-infrared pulses in a noncollinear four-wave mixing setup. Doubly excited states of helium gas serve as the working medium in their simulations.

Changing the carrier-envelope phases of the infrared pulses steers where the ultraviolet emission goes, which encodes the logic. The team realized a complete gate set, including XOR, AND, and OR with their negations, on one helium signal. Switching contrasts ranged from 3.6 to 10.4 in the simulations, beating what a weak-field regime could offer. Strong-field effects were essential to reach those contrasts.
arxiv-2510-00899:
Popadiuk and five co-authors study ferromagnetic resonance in superconductor-ferromagnet-superconductor trilayers in this 2025 arXiv paper on applied physics. Such hybrid stacks could let engineers tune the resonance of a magnetic layer, which matters for magnonic devices. The team measured how resonance fields change with temperature and layer thickness, and added control structures with metallic or insulating spacers to separate the possible mechanisms at work.

Below the superconducting transition, the resonance field dropped sharply in every structure except the one with an insulating spacer. The shift grew with thicker superconducting and ferromagnetic layers before saturating. Their analytical model explains the effect through alternating supercurrents that the precessing magnetization induces in the superconductors. Those currents create a dynamic back-action field on the magnet, raising its resonance frequency.
arxiv-2510-00999:
Fadel, Sá Earp, and Silva survey a flux-based view of the exterior derivative in this 2025 arXiv paper on analysis, dedicated to Felipe Acker and Paolo Piccione. Acker's little-known work treated the exterior derivative as infinitesimal flux through shrinking blocks. That idea yields a mean value theorem for differential forms as an exact equality, not the inequality that textbooks usually state. It also gives a Stokes theorem whose hypotheses mirror the fundamental theorem of calculus, without demanding full smoothness of the form.

The authors clean up imprecisions in the proofs and rebuild the theory step by step. Locally bounded forms whose discontinuities sit on small sets remain flux-integrable, and those discontinuities contribute nothing to boundary integrals. As a numerical payoff, they propose an algorithm that computes exterior derivatives from black-box access to a form alone. No mesh and no symbolic expression are needed.
arxiv-2510-01099:
Callebaut and Selle clarify the holographic meaning of braneworld gravity in this 2025 arXiv paper on theoretical physics. In braneworld models, our universe sits on a membrane inside a higher-dimensional anti-de Sitter space with Neumann boundary conditions. Holography says that setup should be dual to a field theory coupled to gravity on the brane. That dual theory was long described vaguely as a cut-off conformal field theory.

The authors identify it precisely as a T-squared deformed conformal field theory that has been set free, meaning its metric is integrated over. For a three-dimensional bulk, the brane theory follows a TTbar-like flow equation. Under stated assumptions, the effective gravity on the brane becomes a deformed timelike Liouville theory. The picture also recovers the holographic Weyl anomaly when the brane nears the boundary.
arxiv-2510-01399:
Borse and co-authors at Qualcomm AI Research fix the cloned faces that plague group photos from text-to-image models. Asked for several people, generators duplicate faces, merge identities, and lose count. Their framework, DisCo, is the first to optimize identity diversity directly with reinforcement learning.

A compositional reward punishes look-alike faces within an image and repeated identities across images. Person counts and human-preference quality are rewarded in the same objective. A single-stage curriculum keeps training stable as scenes grow more crowded. On a dedicated test set, unique-face accuracy approached the ceiling while quality stayed competitive. Flow-matching models are the generators being fine-tuned here. Global identity spread measures variety across the whole output set. Proprietary flagships were beaten on the diversity metrics. No extra annotations feed the reward, keeping the recipe cheap. Crowds finally look like crowds, not clones.
arxiv-2510-01899:
Mohsin and Abdulrashid design a single foundation model for early disease detection in this 2025 paper. Hospitals collect records, scans, genetic data, and wearable readings for the same patients. Models that read only one stream miss links between them, and those links often carry the earliest warning signs. Their design fuses all streams inside one attention-based transformer.

Each data type first passes through its own encoder into a shared latent space. Multi-head attention then mixes the streams, with residual normalization to keep training stable. Pretraining across many tasks should let the model adapt to new diseases with little extra work. The authors lay out an evaluation plan on benchmark data from cancer, heart, and brain disease. Governance, monitoring, and interpretability tools are built into the proposal from the start. The paper presents a blueprint toward unified precision diagnostics, not a finished clinical system.
arxiv-2510-02399:
Habib gives a simpler quantum algorithm for finding near matches inside long texts. His 2025 paper studies the k-mismatch problem. The task checks whether any substring sits close to a pattern. Closeness means at most k differing positions. Classical work on the problem dates back decades. Recent quantum papers added faster but complex methods. Habib allows a small approximation slack in the count. His algorithm then guarantees a one sided promise. A reported match truly lies within the widened limit. Silence guarantees that no tight match exists anywhere.

The running time scales with the square root of the text to pattern ratio. A precision knob trades accuracy against speed directly. The design is, by his account, optimized brute force made quantum. Preprocessing tricks from rivals may cut the cost further. String search underpins biology and security tools. Simpler quantum methods widen who can use them.
arxiv-2510-02599:
Margaryan, Wan, and Tuytelaars improve image beauty by tuning the prompt embedding, not the words. Their 2025 computer vision paper presents a method called PEO. Simple prompts often yield flat, dull images from diffusion models. Rewriting prompts by hand is the usual fix. PEO instead adjusts the numeric embedding of the prompt. A three part objective guides that adjustment. One part raises the aesthetic quality of the output. One part keeps the image faithful to the embedding. One part stops the embedding drifting from the original prompt. No model training is needed at any point.

The method works across different generator backbones unchanged. Tests compared it with leading prompt adaptation methods. Results matched or beat those rivals in quality scores. Human style qualitative checks agreed with the numbers. Anyone with a plain prompt can use the trick. Better defaults raise the floor for casual creators.
arxiv-2510-02999:
Huang and co-authors present a new way to test language model safeguards. Safety-tuned models refuse harmful requests by design. Jailbreak attacks craft prompts that slip past those refusals. Gradient-based attacks tune a suffix added to the prompt. That fixed aim narrows the search and slows the attack. Their method, UJA, drops the fixed target entirely. It seeks any unsafe reply instead.

A judge model scores how unsafe a reply looks. That score is hard to optimize in raw form. The team splits it into two smooth sub-goals. One shapes a harmful reply, the other shapes the prompt. Theory backs the split as sound. Tests hit safety-tuned models from several families. Success rates passed four fifths after only a hundred tuning steps. Rival attacks trailed by more than twenty points. The work maps weak spots that defenders must close.
arxiv-2510-03199:
Di and co-authors find the best way to pick answers when a model may submit several tries. Inference often draws many candidate answers per prompt. Majority voting and best-of-N are the standard selectors. Benchmarks, though, often grade by the best of k submissions. The authors show neither classic selector scales well there. Majority voting wastes the reward signal entirely. Best-of-N degrades as the candidate pool grows. Their Best-of-Majority hybrid fixes both flaws.

The method first keeps only frequently sampled responses. A reward model then ranks that shortlist for submission. Regret bounds for the strategy match a proven lower bound. That match certifies the method as minimax optimal. More samples never hurt its performance, unlike its rivals. Experiments on math problems confirmed the theory in practice. Best-of-Majority beat both voting and best-of-N there.
arxiv-2510-03299:
Assandje, Dongho, and Bouetou Bouetou wrote a 2025 arXiv paper in information geometry, the study of shapes formed by families of probability models. Their subject is the Weibull model, a two part model used for lifetimes and failure times. They ask whether its model space carries a special function called a potential. Such a function lets researchers build flow systems with deep order and balance.

The authors first prove that the full Weibull space has no potential function at all. They then pull out a smaller model, the logit model, hidden inside the larger one. That smaller space does carry a potential function. On it, they build a gradient flow system and show that the system is Hamiltonian and fully solvable in the classic sense. The result gives geometers a clean example of order found inside a model that first looked barren.
arxiv-2510-03599:
Omar and Khadiv present a 2025 arXiv paper proposing contact plans as a single language for teaching robots many tasks. Robots usually learn each skill from its reward design, so skills rarely transfer. Their framework instead describes every task as a sequence of contact goals: which end effector touches what, where, and when. One goal conditioned reinforcement learning policy then learns to realize plans. The team trained single policies on three different robots and task families.

One policy drove a quadruped through several gaits, and another drove a humanoid through walking and crawling styles. A third ran two handed object handling tasks on the humanoid. Contact explicit policies generalized better to goal setups the robots had never seen. Contacts are the core shared by walking and grasping alike. Framing tasks this way could let one training run cover a robot's skill menu instead of one skill at a time.
arxiv-2510-03699:
Malik and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper training artificial agents to hunt like larval zebrafish, to learn which constraints shape the animal's behavior. Zebrafish larvae pursue prey in bouts, verging their eyes inward as they close in. The team built a bout based simulator and trained recurrent policies with reinforcement learning. No fish data was used for imitation. They varied food density, prey speed, vergence limits, and energy costs to see which ingredients the behavior needs.

The agents reproduced the hallmarks: vergence linked pursuit, speed modulation, and approach paths. Pursuit bouts cut the prey angle by about half before the strike, matching measurements from larvae. A constraint set proved sufficient: binocular sensing, bouts that couple turning with forward speed, and energy costs. The sweeps produced predictions about strike success and aborted hunts. A lab narrows the experiments neuroscientists run. It frames hunting as a tradeoff between energy and gain.
arxiv-2510-03799:
Asghari and Nenno present a 2025 arXiv paper probing whether language models internally represent the political frames that structure debate. Cognitive frames like the strict father and nurturing parent models of the nation as family steer political views. The authors show that models generate text evoking each frame. Models recognize which frame a text expresses, without examples. The team turns to mechanistic interpretability, hunting for where inside the network these frames live.

They identify dimensions in the model's hidden representations that correlate strongly with the presence of each frame. Single directions carrying such concepts is a localization result. It suggests models organize political meaning in internal coordinates rather than smearing it. Knowing where a frame sits opens paths to auditing bias in model outputs. It also gives cognitive scientists a new instrument: a machine whose frame representations can be measured and perturbed. The work links two fields that rarely share methods.
arxiv-2510-04399:
Charles Wang, Keir Dorchen, and Peter Jin of Columbia University wrote this 2025 paper on AI systems that rewrite themselves. Future agents may improve not just their answers but their own learning rules and design. The authors split self change into five axes and study each one apart from the drive to gain reward. Their central finding is a sharp tension between doing well now and staying able to learn. 

The team proves that broad learning guarantees survive only when the family of reachable models stays bounded in capacity. If capacity can grow without limit, a reward driven change can make a learnable task unlearnable. Under common assumptions, all five axes reduce to that single capacity test.
