A two gate policy, which checks both gains and capacity, kept learning intact. The paper gives builders of self improving systems a clear line that safe change must not cross.
arxiv-2510-04499:
Gerui Chen and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on the thermodynamics of black holes. Black holes carry entropy tied to the area of their horizon, a fact first drawn from Euclidean gravity methods. The usual derivation uses a conical singularity at the horizon, which turns ill defined in broader gravity theories. Chen and coauthors take a different route. They work with a Euclidean black hole that has a corner instead of a cone.

With the corner in place, the Wald formula for entropy follows. The derivation works for a family of gravity theories built from the full curvature tensor. The action with a corner term and the action without one agree to first order, so either may be used. That match shows the corner itself, not its term, carries the entropy data. The team then uses a special symmetry move to derive the energy conjugate to the horizon Killing field.
arxiv-2510-04599:
Marta Volonteri wrote this 2025 review chapter on how theorists model the first black holes. Telescopes, above all the James Webb Space Telescope, now find heavy black holes startlingly early in cosmic history. Their seeds, growth paths, and observable signs all strain the older picture. The chapter began as lectures at the Saas Fee advanced course on galaxies and black holes. Volonteri distills two decades of work into physical intuition rather than detail.

Early sections set out basic black hole properties and the current high redshift view. Middle sections treat formation channels and growth mechanisms at early times, where feeding and mergers race the clock. Later sections review modeling tools, with weight on cosmological simulations, and how model outputs turn into observable predictions. The closing section tests the new telescope population against that whole body of theory. Volonteri flags where models speak with confidence and where the ground is still soft.
arxiv-2510-04899:
Ong and ten coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a benchmark for machine understanding of human behavior. Systems that read feelings, thoughts, and social moves are trained task by task. Separate data and models block transfer between skills that overlap. The authors curated the Human Behavior Atlas, a set of over one hundred thousand samples. The samples span text, audio, and video, and cover feelings, thinking states, disorders, and social processes.

On this base they trained three versions of a model family called OmniSapiens. Variants used plain supervised tuning, a behavior aware method, and reinforcement learning. Training beat multimodal language models across the tasks. Pretraining on the atlas transferred to behavior data sets the models had never seen. Adding behavior descriptions brought gains in their tests. One training ground for behavior skills cuts cost and redundancy. It lets strengths in one skill, like reading tone, support another, like spotting distress.
arxiv-2510-04999:
Nilay Kumar, Priyansh Bhandari, and G. Maragatham survey text-to-video generation in this 2025 arXiv paper. These systems turn a written prompt into a short video clip. The field promises tools for education, marketing, entertainment, and accessibility. It has moved fast, from early adversarial models to today's diffusion designs.

The survey traces each generation of models and explains why the field shifted designs. It catalogs the datasets used for training and testing. Unusually, it also lists training setups in detail, down to GPU counts and batch sizes. The authors review the standard scoring metrics and their blind spots. Open problems include prompt alignment, long-range coherence, and the heavy cost of training.
arxiv-2510-05199:
Wout M. Goesaert and six co-authors watch a nearby galaxy feed its central black hole in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Circinus galaxy hosts the closest bright active nucleus, only about 4 megaparsecs away. A dusty torus should funnel gas inward, but the feeding mechanism was unclear. The team imaged the nucleus with ALMA at resolutions down to a quarter parsec.

They found spiral arms of dust and molecular gas crossing the surrounding disk. Two arms connect directly to the torus and carry material inward. The arms' uneven gravity appears to drive the feeding, at up to several solar masses per year. Over 88 percent of that inflow is expelled again in a multi-phase outflow. A warped accretion disk likely launches or collimates the ionized part of that outflow.
arxiv-2510-05399:
Kangwoo Yi and six co-authors compare deep learning recipes for forecasting solar proton storms in this 2025 arXiv paper. Solar proton events endanger satellites, astronauts, and polar communications. Operators need the full 24-hour flux profile after an event begins. The authors test LSTM sequence-to-sequence models on GOES satellite data.

Their dataset holds 40 well-connected events from 1997 to 2017, each tied to a strong western flare. One-shot forecasting consistently beat autoregressive prediction by avoiding error accumulation. Proton-only inputs beat proton-plus-X-ray inputs on raw data. Trend smoothing flipped that ranking by calming the noisy X-ray channel. Yet the single best model overall trained on original data, showing architecture can outweigh preprocessing.
arxiv-2510-05499:
Tikhomirov extends a central idea of dynamical systems into infinite dimensions. Hyperbolicity describes maps that stretch one set of directions and squeeze another. It explains why some systems stay predictable under small changes. Classic theory covers maps on compact, finite-dimensional spaces, but many real systems live in Banach spaces instead.

Tikhomirov defines a generalized structure that merges two earlier frameworks for this setting. The new notion allows the stretch-squeeze split to jump from point to point. It also replaces exact invariance rules with weaker inclusion rules. Morse-Smale systems fall inside the new framework as well. For maps on reflexive Banach spaces, the structure yields shadowing of true orbits and resists small disturbances. With one added smoothness condition, he also obtains a weak form of structural stability. He suggests the notion can play the role that Axiom A plays for compact spaces.
arxiv-2510-05699:
Tong and colleagues expose a privacy leak hiding in a small part of language models. Membership inference attacks test whether a text was inside a model's training data. Testing them on full models is costly and plagued by mislabeled samples. Their 2025 study attacks the tokenizer instead, the piece that splits text into tokens.

Tokenizers train cheaply from scratch, and their data mirrors the model's pretraining data. The team devised five attacks that read overfitting signals from tokenizer training. Experiments on millions of internet samples show real leakage in current tokenizers. Shadow-based attacks performed especially strongly in their evaluations. The authors also propose an adaptive defense against the attacks. That defense works, but it costs tokenizer utility. The work marks the first study of membership leakage through tokenizers. It urges privacy mechanisms designed for tokenizers themselves, not just models.
arxiv-2510-05999:
Do Ó and co-authors study a nonlinear elliptic equation set in a half-space in a 2025 analysis paper. The equation contains a weight that depends on distance from the boundary, so diffusion runs unevenly through the region. A matching nonlinear condition governs what happens on the boundary itself. Equations of this kind also model diffusion with uneven coefficients in applied work.

The authors prove regularity results for weak solutions and build a new identity of Pohozaev type to test when solutions can exist. Their main finding reverses textbook expectations from the classical Laplacian case. In some parameter ranges the weighted problem has positive solutions where the unweighted one has none. In other ranges the weight destroys solutions that the classical problem allows. The result warns that adding a simple weight can flip solvability in boundary value problems.
arxiv-2510-06099:
Propp and seven co-authors tackle slow links throttling early quantum networks in a 2025 paper. Quantum communication rates are low, so qubits sit longer in noisy memories and some network applications become impractical. Multiplexing, which bundles signals into one channel, is the standard remedy.

The authors first pin down classical limits on how much multiplexing helps a quantum protocol. They then introduce two strategies that pass those limits. Quantum multiplexing allows uneven resource use and links among more than two parties. Multi-server multiplexing lets many servers, or one server with several communication qubits, serve a single client. In toy models, both improve the rate–fidelity trade-off as the multiplexing resource grows. The gains matter most for qubit-hungry protocols such as blind quantum computation. The paper advises network builders to combine every multiplexing style available.
arxiv-2510-06799:
Somasekhara Sontti and Arnab Atta simulate droplet formation inside a microfluidic T-junction. Their 2025 paper, published in a chemical engineering journal, uses a three-dimensional volume-of-fluid model. Droplets of a plain liquid form inside a surrounding non-Newtonian liquid. Such controlled droplets serve chemistry, biology, and drug screening in tiny channels.

Formation falls into three regimes called squeezing, dripping, and jetting. Flow rates, surface tension, and the surrounding liquid's flow properties decide which regime appears. A deformation index records how far each droplet strays from a sphere. Droplets stay nearly spherical in the dripping and jetting regimes. In the squeezing regime they take a plug shape instead. Raising the effective viscosity made droplets form more often but with smaller volume. The flow properties strongly shifted droplet length and the active regime. The study supplies design rules for making uniform droplets in thick, complex liquids.
arxiv-2510-06999:
Markus Reuter leads a team fixing a quiet failure mode in AI systems that answer legal questions. Their 2025 paper studies retrieval-augmented generation over large legal databases. Such databases hold many structurally similar documents, which confuses retrievers. The team names the failure Document-Level Retrieval Mismatch, where the system pulls text from entirely the wrong document.

Their fix is Summary-Augmented Chunking. Each text chunk gets a synthetic summary of its whole document attached. That restores the global context that plain chunking throws away. Across several legal retrieval tasks, the trick cut mismatch errors greatly. Precision and recall at the text level improved as well. A generic summarizer beat one guided by legal expert knowledge, a surprise result. Adding keyword search on top helped little and cost compute, so they dropped it. Legal question answering depends on citing the right document. This cheap change makes that far more likely.
arxiv-2510-07199:
Shoushtari, Chandler, and Kamilov rethink how networks clean up grainy, low-light images. Their 2025 paper concerns Poisson noise, the grain that appears when few photons reach a sensor. Standard training teaches a network to predict the single most likely clean image. That average hides how uncertain the answer is. The authors instead train a network in the log domain.

Their log-network learns the average of the log of the clean image. The team proves that this target unlocks the higher moments of the full answer distribution. From those moments, users can rebuild an estimate of the whole range of plausible clean images. On simulated data, the method cleaned images as well as standard models. It also delivered the uncertainty information those models cannot give. That knowledge matters when a cleaned image guides a diagnosis or a scientific claim.
arxiv-2510-07299:
Plantinga and co-authors compare human clinicians and a speech model at detecting Parkinson's disease from voice alone. Their 2025 paper uses five speaking tasks, from sustained sounds to describing a picture. Speech carries clues about the disease, which can speed diagnosis. The team ran listening tests with experts and, in parallel, experiments with a detection system built on the Whisper speech model. Both judged the same recordings.

The machine matched or beat the experts across the tasks. Its edge was largest exactly where humans struggle most: younger patients, mild cases, and women. The authors credit the model with picking up faint acoustic cues that ears overlook. Human experts still bring context and multiple senses that audio alone lacks. The study suggests pairing the two: let the model flag hard cases for closer human review. Earlier flags could shorten the long road to a firm diagnosis.
arxiv-2510-07399:
Martinez-Mirave and Tamborra compute the combined neutrino glow of every star in the Milky Way. Their 2025 paper models this galactic stellar neutrino flux from first principles. Stars emit neutrinos through both heat-driven and fusion-driven processes across their lives. The team evolved a suite of stellar models spanning tiny dwarfs to hundred-sun giants using a standard evolution code. Star counts across the galaxy's bulge and disks were sampled from Gaia survey data, together with a modeled history of star formation.

The combined flux spans energies from about a thousand to ten million electronvolts. Thermal processes shape the low-energy end, while fusion dominates the high end. Stars heavier than the Sun in the thin disk contribute most of the signal. Much of it originates five to ten thousand parsecs away, not from our neighborhood. Detectors already watch for solar neutrinos at these energies.
arxiv-2510-07799:
Jiang and ten coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on how teams of AI agents should talk to each other. In multi-agent systems, the communication topology decides who messages whom. Static patterns waste tokens on easy tasks and bottleneck hard ones. Hand-crafted chains and stars cannot adapt to a task's real needs. The authors propose generating the topology for each task instead of fixing it in advance.

Their framework, Guided Topology Diffusion, builds the network step by step with a graph diffusion model. A light proxy model scores each partial design on accuracy, utility, and cost. That guidance steers construction toward task-fitting networks without gradient updates. Across benchmarks, the generated topologies were sparser and cheaper than rivals while performing better. They also held up when individual agents failed. The work treats agent wiring as a design problem that a model can solve per task.
arxiv-2510-07999:
Strunk wrote this 2025 paper on how smooth gradients of solutions to certain diffusion equations must be. The equations are parabolic, so solutions evolve in time. Their diffusion degenerates widely, switching off entirely whenever the gradient stays inside a fixed bounded convex set. Outside that set the diffusion behaves regularly.

Strunk proves that a transformed version of the gradient is always continuous. He assumes only mild integrability on the equation's data term. Any continuous function of the gradient vanishing on that set produces a continuous quantity across the space-time domain. The result extends an earlier theorem from the stationary elliptic case into the parabolic setting. The proof is delicate, since the regularized equation needs carefully chosen test functions. Gradient continuity is often the first step toward predicting how solutions behave.
arxiv-2510-08099:
Liu and five coauthors wrote this 2025 quantum optics paper proposing a way to watch a magnetic sphere deform in three dimensions with picometer precision. The spheres, made of yttrium iron garnet, anchor magnomechanical systems where magnetism couples to vibration. Their scheme reads the deformation optically. A deformed sphere scatters light into higher-order spatial modes, which postselection and balanced homodyne detection extract sensitively.

With realistic parameters, precision reaches the picometer level along all three axes. A higher-order probe beam improves things further, as Fisher information analyses confirm. The method newly exploits a second-order mode tied to beam waist changes. Real-time measurement would let researchers identify specific mechanical modes and characterize backaction directly. It also enables feedback control for cooling the vibration. Precise mechanical readout is a quiet enabler for hybrid quantum devices mixing light, sound, and spin.
arxiv-2510-08199:
Di Bella, Seibold, Brown, and Tavoni wrote this 2025 energy policy study asking whether Europe can decarbonize its heavy industry without pricing it out of world markets. They modeled the most energy-intensive sectors with an open-source European energy system model. Two futures frame the analysis: continued industrial decline, or a competitiveness-driven resurgence. Deep decarbonization proved technically feasible, led by electrification and green hydrogen. Competitiveness hinged on policy choices.

Moving production inside Europe saved only modest energy costs and faces practical constraints. Strategically importing green intermediates, like green methanol and hot briquetted iron, lowered system costs and carbon prices substantially while keeping domestic production and jobs. Subsidies proved essential to stop industry leaving Europe entirely. Yet under strong reindustrialization, subsidy bills become unsustainable. The authors advise prioritizing sectors like ammonia and steel finishing. The corridor between green and competitive is narrow but real.
arxiv-2510-08799:
Choudhury and colleagues speed up video enhancement by skipping the easy parts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion-based super-resolution rebuilds sharp frames from blurry ones, but it spends the same effort on every pixel. Much of a typical frame is flat or low in detail and gains little from that work. The team's insight is that those dull regions can be spotted directly in the low-quality input.

Their framework, SkipSR, marks the low-detail regions and leaves them out of the costly rebuilding step. Only areas that need refinement go through the diffusion model. The trick works with both standard and one-step versions of that model. On standard benchmarks with high-definition video, the method cut total processing time by up to sixty percent. Viewers could not perceive any loss in quality, according to the team's checks.
arxiv-2510-08899:
Luo and co-authors improve how a language model learns from its own reasoning attempts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is reinforcement learning with checkable rewards, where the model earns credit only for final answers that verify. That all-or-nothing signal blurs which middle steps helped, and training can also collapse early onto a few habits. The team's framework attacks both problems in phases.

First, a curriculum matched to problem difficulty steadies exploration. Reasoning traces are split into meaningful segments, and an attribution method judges how much each segment contributed. That judgment regulates the model's randomness, holding off early collapse. A split reward system then assigns credit step by step, in proportion to each step's measured contribution. On hard contest-style benchmarks in mathematics, the method significantly beat the strongest existing approaches.
arxiv-2510-08999:
Wang, Jiang, Lin, and Song shrink neural networks two ways at once, in this 2025 arXiv paper on model compression. Pruning deletes unneeded connections, and quantization stores the survivors in fewer bits. Applied separately, each method usually gives up compression to protect accuracy. The team's framework, SQS, performs both together inside a Bayesian learning scheme that treats the weights as probabilities rather than fixed numbers.

A spike-and-slab prior, which mixes a sharp spike at zero with a broad slab, naturally switches many weights off. The remaining weights are modeled as mixtures of bell curves, which suits storing them at low precision. The authors prove their approximation stays consistent as data grows. Experiments compressed vision and language models, including a large chat model family, and beat a line of existing methods on compression rate. The performance lost stayed comparable to what rivals sacrifice for less shrinkage.
arxiv-2510-09199:
Buciulea and co-authors work out how to recover a network's wiring when every node reports a whole matrix of data instead of one number, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Graph learning infers structure from observations, but standard methods assume one scalar signal per node. Real signals often vary along a second dimension too, such as time or sensor settings. The team models these as matrix signals produced by filtering along both dimensions at once.

Their framework describes the hidden network as a product graph, built by combining two smaller graphs in standard ways. A stationarity assumption, meaning the signal statistics stay aligned with the network, ties the data to the structure. The resulting optimization problem can be solved efficiently, and the authors prove it recovers the true product graph. On synthetic data, the method estimated the network more accurately than existing approaches while costing less computation.
arxiv-2510-09499:
Parhom Esmaeili and five co-authors, among them Sebastien Ourselin and Jorge Cardoso, propose a fairer way to test interactive medical image segmentation in a 2025 arXiv paper. Interactive segmentation lets a clinician guide an algorithm with clicks or strokes to outline structures in scans. It promises robust, general tools, but inconsistent and unrealistic evaluation habits make rival methods hard to compare.

The authors define evaluation tasks and metrics grounded in clinical practice and built a software framework that produces standardised test pipelines. Running leading algorithms on varied, complex tasks, they draw five lessons. Keeping user input lossless matters most for robustness, and adaptive zooming speeds convergence. Performance falls when testing prompts differ from training prompts. Two-dimensional methods suit slab-like images and coarse targets, while three-dimensional context helps with large or irregular shapes. General models such as SAM2 also degrade on poor contrast and complex shapes.
arxiv-2510-09599:
Sondos Mahmoud Bsharat and Zhiqiang Shen present a cheap way to manufacture reasoning training data in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large language models reason better after fine-tuning on chains of thought, but curating large reasoning datasets is laborious and expensive. Their method, Prompting Test-Time Scaling, starts from only ninety hand-picked reasoning examples.

The trick is to vary prompting intensity at inference time, asking the model to scale its reasoning up or down. Each variation synthesises a different trajectory around the same seed problems, producing diverse training contexts from a tiny pool. Fine-tuned Qwen models of two sizes then beat strong one-thousand-example baselines such as S1 and S1.1. On the AIME 2024 contest the gains reached thirty percentage points for the smaller model, with comparable or better results on other maths and science benchmarks. The approach also improved zero-shot generalisation to out-of-domain reasoning tests.
arxiv-2510-09999:
Bai, Feng Xiong, and Xueheng Kuang compute material properties with random states on quantum computers in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classical computation of electronic properties in large materials is expensive. Quantum computers promise smaller memory footprints and better scaling, but practical algorithms for real materials are still scarce.

The authors propose and implement random-state quantum algorithms for electronic-structure properties. Random states stand in for the full quantum state of a material, cutting the cost of the calculation. They run the method on real materials rather than toy models, which tests whether the savings survive contact with realistic chemistry. The work is a step toward quantum tools that materials scientists could actually use.
arxiv-2510-10299:
Bordenave surveys sparse graphs and their local limits in this 2025 arXiv lecture-style paper in probability and combinatorics. Sparse graphs have bounded average degree, few edges per vertex, yet their local geometry strongly shapes their global behavior. Benjamini-Schramm convergence describes the asymptotic local structure of such graphs.

The note tours the spectral side of that convergence: how eigenvalue distributions behave as graphs grow while local views stabilize. Applications run through random Schreier graphs and covering graphs, two families built from group actions. Spectra govern expansion, mixing, and random walks, so a spectral view of local limits ties combinatorics to dynamics. The survey gives researchers a map of this active borderland.
arxiv-2510-10399:
Kaushik, Roshni Anna Jacob, Souma Chowdhury, and Jie Zhang plan power grid restoration with many agents in this 2025 arXiv paper on infrastructure resilience. Restoring distribution networks after events like tornadoes is a hard coordination problem. Several repair crews must be routed under uncertainty, with strict sequencing rules.

The setting couples the power grid with the transportation network, since crews travel on damaged roads to reach damaged lines. Interdependent failures across the two networks compound the difficulty. The authors model multi-agent restoration that respects those coupled constraints. Better restoration plans shorten blackouts after extreme weather, a growing need as storms strain grids built for milder conditions.
arxiv-2510-10699:
Murat Can Karakoc and three co-authors review quantum radar from an engineering standpoint, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum radar uses entanglement and quantum correlations to detect objects better than classical radar in noisy, lossy settings. Entangled microwaves come from superconducting devices like Josephson parametric amplifiers and traveling wave amplifiers. In theory, these systems promise sharper sensitivity, lower error rates, and robustness against thermal noise and jamming.

The review starts from the theory of quantum illumination, the core protocol. It then examines the subsystems a practical radar needs: entanglement sources, transducers, amplification chains, and receivers. The authors survey recent lab systems, covering proof of principle demos and the slow move from concepts to hardware. Their verdict: quantum radar is evolving into a practical technology, though engineering hurdles remain.
arxiv-2510-10899:
Andrew Huang and Vinod Vaikuntanathan make one shot signatures practical, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A one shot signature is a quantum cryptographic tool: from a public reference string, anyone creates a verification key and a quantum signing state. The state can sign exactly one message, never two. A 2025 breakthrough built such signatures, but inefficiently: it signed messages bit by bit, needing signing keys with quartic size in the security parameter and cubic size signatures.

The new scheme is simple, direct, and far leaner. It signs messages of any polynomial length with keys and signatures that are only quadratic in the security parameter, with matching runtime savings, in both the oracle model and the plain model. Unlike the earlier construction, it achieves perfect correctness: honest signatures always verify. It also achieves strong signature incompressibility. That property yields public key quantum money with perfect correctness, fixing an error in a recent work.
arxiv-2510-11499:
Learning from a fixed dataset of past behavior, offline reinforcement learning needs policies expressive enough to capture multi-modal strategies, and generative models supply it at a price. Xinsong Feng, Leshu Tang, Chenan Wang, and Haipeng Chen attack the price in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Diffusion policies are strong but slow, needing many iterative steps; consistency policies are fast but weaker. The authors argue both are views of one object.

Their unifying perspective treats diffusion, flow matching, and consistency models as instances of learning a continuous-time generative trajectory governed by an ordinary differential equation. On that foundation they propose Generative Trajectory Policies, which learn the entire solution map of the equation, plus two principled adaptations for offline reinforcement learning. On D4RL benchmarks it beat earlier generative policies significantly, earning perfect scores on several hard AntMaze tasks.
arxiv-2510-11599:
A scientific field is too big to hold in your head, so researchers map it with embeddings, but ordinary ones blur every aspect of a paper into one opaque point. Marc Brinner and Sina Zarrieß propose SemCSE-Multi, an unsupervised framework for multifaceted embeddings of paper abstracts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Each one captures one specifiable aspect of a paper, enabling similarity judgments that respect a chosen facet.

The pipeline first generates aspect-specific summary sentences without supervision and trains models to place semantically related summaries near each other. Those skills are distilled into one model predicting all aspect vectors in a single pass. A decoding pipeline turns the vectors back into natural language descriptions of their aspects, and the decoding still works for unoccupied regions of low-dimensional maps. Evaluated in invasion biology and medicine, it supports controllable, interpretable domain maps.
arxiv-2510-11799:
A. Gkini leads a large team hunting for shells of gas thrown off by stars just before they exploded. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies twenty-one hydrogen-poor superluminous supernovae, among the brightest stellar explosions known. If a star sheds material months before exploding, the blast light later leaves broad absorption marks in that shell. The team took ultraviolet spectra with the X-shooter instrument.

Five of the twenty-one supernovae show the broad magnesium absorption that betrays a shell. Three were known before; two shells, around DES15S2nr and DES16C3ggu, are new discoveries. The shells rush outward at roughly four thousand eight hundred kilometers per second. Their distances imply they were expelled only about two and three months before the explosions. Such late, violent shedding matches eruptions of luminous blue variables or pulsational pair-instability events.
arxiv-2510-11899:
Chenliang Li and six colleagues present AdaRL, a kinder way to make reinforcement learning robust. Agents trained in one environment often fail when the real world's dynamics differ slightly. Classic robust methods guard against the worst case through nested min-max optimization, which is expensive and produces timid policies. Their 2025 arXiv paper instead ties a policy's complexity to the task's intrinsic dimension.

AdaRL works on two levels. Below, it optimizes a policy whose parameters are constrained to a low-rank structure, while dynamics vary inside a Wasserstein ball, a neighborhood of plausible worlds around a central model. Above, it adapts the rank itself, trading bias against variance as learning proceeds. On MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks, AdaRL consistently beat fixed-rank baselines like SAC and leading robust methods like RNAC. Its chosen ranks also converged toward each task's intrinsic rank, evidence the adaptation finds the right size on its own.
arxiv-2510-12299:
Li and co-authors systematically compare ways of feeding video into multimodal language models for question answering, in a 2025 arXiv paper. These models can process images, text, and audio together, but it is unclear which video representation serves them best. The choice matters because accuracy and computing cost pull in opposite directions.

The study evaluates single modality inputs, including the question alone, subtitles, visual frames, and audio, plus combinations of them. Tests ran on two popular benchmarks, VideoMME and LongVideoBench. Visual frames raised accuracy greatly but demanded heavy graphics memory and slow inference. Subtitles proved a lightweight yet effective alternative, especially for long videos where frame processing costs grow fastest. The authors frame the results as practical guidance for building resource aware video question answering systems, where designers must balance answer quality against the hardware and latency they can afford.
arxiv-2510-12399:
Ge and a large team survey vibe coding, the practice of building software by directing language models and judging outcomes rather than reading code closely, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The survey is billed as the first full review of this emergent method. The authors analyze over one thousand research papers covering the whole ecosystem, from coding models and agents to environments and feedback mechanisms.

They formalize vibe coding as a constrained Markov decision process which captures the three way relationship among human developers, software projects, plus coding agents. Existing practice is sorted into five development models, from unconstrained automation through iterative conversational collaboration to test driven, planning driven, and context enhanced models. The analysis finds success depends less on raw agent capability than on systematic context engineering, solid environments, and the collaboration model chosen. Challenges in infrastructure, security, and human centered design are mapped as a roadmap for the field.
arxiv-2510-12599:
Deffner asks what resource lets a quantum heat engine genuinely outperform a classical style one, and finds the answer in nonlinearity rather than correlations alone, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum Otto engines cycle a working medium through heating, expansion, cooling, and compression. He develops a full thermodynamic description of nonlinear qubits, computing units whose energy levels are not evenly spaced, starting from the correct equilibrium state.

For ideal cycles, and also at maximum power, the nonlinear engine's efficiency is greatly higher than the linear engine's. Nonlinear dynamics can be read as an effective description of one correlated, complex many body system. The findings therefore support the common wisdom that correlations power quantum advantage, while pointing to a concrete new design: build the working medium from nonlinear qubits. The paper offers both a thermodynamic framework for such qubits and a practical direction for more efficient quantum engines.
arxiv-2510-12699:
Yu and colleagues measure how large a space of different answers a language model entertains for a prompt, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Open ended tasks need different amounts of diversity: creative writing should vary, factual answers should not. Current models are miscalibrated both ways, collapsing to samey outputs on creative tasks and hallucinating varied but wrong answers on factual ones.

The authors unify these failures under the effective generation space size, the set of outputs distinct in meaning that the model considers. Their benchmark, GSSBench, uses prompt pairs with known size relationships to test metrics and locate where models diverge from desired behavior. Hallucination detection metrics, above all one called EigenScore, beat standard diversity and uncertainty measures while using only model internals. They show three applications. These are detecting ambiguous prompts and predicting clarification questions, reading overthinking and underthinking in reasoning models, and steering models toward diverse, high quality outputs.
arxiv-2510-12899:
Wei and colleagues build a large corpus of teacher-student dialogues in this 2025 arXiv paper, aiming to benchmark how well language models can teach. Intelligent education needs models that follow instructional context over many turns and give personalized guidance, but dedicated multi-turn classroom data were scarce.

Their dataset, EduDial, covers several hundred core knowledge points and holds tens of thousands of dialogue sessions generated by teacher and student agents. Its design follows Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives and uses ten questioning strategies, including metacognitive questioning that prompts reflection. Teaching strategies differ by student cognitive level. The team also trained a thirty-two-billion-parameter model on the corpus and built an eleven-dimension evaluation framework. Testing seventeen mainstream models, most struggled in student-centered scenarios, while their trained model beat all baselines across every metric.
arxiv-2510-13099:
Chen and Hong prove curvature obstruction theorems for manifolds with boundary in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Intermediate curvatures sit between the scalar and sectional kinds. A line of results going back to the Geroch conjecture shows that certain manifolds admit no metric making them positive. Those results treated closed manifolds, leaving the boundary case open. The paper is pure theory.

For dimensions up to seven, the authors show that such a space carries no metric of positive intermediate curvature when its boundary meets a matching convexity condition. Rigidity holds when the curvature is merely nonnegative. This absence persists after taking connected sums with arbitrary spaces. Gluing on extra topology cannot evade the obstruction. The theorems extend recent work by Brendle, Hirsch, and Johne and by several other groups to the boundary setting.
arxiv-2510-13199:
Kim and Xin speed up three-dimensional chemotaxis simulation with a neural particle method in this 2025 arXiv paper. Chemotaxis systems model cells chasing chemical signals, as when tumor cells move toward blood vessels during angiogenesis, the growth of new vessels that feeds tumors. Solving their equations in 3D is expensive because solutions develop steep gradients at unknown locations.

Starting from a regularized version of a parabolic-hyperbolic Keller-Segel system, the authors derive a mesh-free algorithm. In it, cell density is carried by interacting particles. The chemical field is represented by a convolutional neural network trained on cheap synthetic data. The method preserves total mass and non-negativity of the density, two properties naive schemes often break. On three-dimensional multi-bump solutions it captured the dynamics much faster than classical finite difference and earlier particle-field methods.
arxiv-2510-13299:
Kanungo, Mishra, and Molica Bisci prove bifurcation and multiplicity results for a critical Choquard problem in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. The equation pairs the Grushin operator, a degenerate diffusion operator whose strength varies across space, with a nonlocal Choquard term. In that term, each point couples to the whole domain through a singular kernel. The nonlinearity sits exactly at the Sobolev critical exponent, the threshold where compactness is lost.

Working in the Brézis-Nirenberg style, the authors prove that solutions bifurcate from every eigenvalue of the Grushin operator under zero boundary conditions. Near each eigenvalue, solution branches split off from the trivial solution. Also, just left of any eigenvalue, the problem admits at least twice as many nontrivial solutions. The results extend point theory into this setting.
arxiv-2510-13499:
Li and co-authors introduce ConsintBench, a benchmark for testing how well language models grasp consumer intent. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets real public discussions about products, which mix many voices at once. Such threads carry conflicting views, hidden assumptions, and shifting concerns. No large benchmark existed for this kind of intent reading, the authors note.

ConsintBench is dynamic and live, updating over time through an automated curation pipeline. That design blocks data contamination, since test items keep changing. The team evaluated twenty language models, both open and closed, on the benchmark. Scoring covers four dimensions of intent understanding: depth, breadth, informativeness, and correctness. The benchmark aims to push models toward expert-level reasoning about messy human discourse. It is the largest and most diverse resource of its kind, they report.
arxiv-2510-13599:
Wang and co-authors present PlanarMesh, a system that builds compact 3D maps from LiDAR scans in real time. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves robots that must map spaces online without drowning in raw point data. Fixed-resolution meshes either blur fine detail or balloon in size. Their representation mixes flat plane modelling with ordinary meshing.

The mesh resolution adapts locally, guided by surface curvature and by free-space evidence from the sensor. Updates arrive incrementally as new measurements stream in, so the map stays current. A multi-threaded design with a bounding volume hierarchy keeps storage and search fast. Experiments match or beat leading methods, including signed distance and voxel approaches, on accuracy. Output files came out ten times smaller than the raw input and over five times smaller than rival mesh outputs in their tests, at roughly two updates per second.
arxiv-2510-13899:
Leibetseder, Schoeffmann, and the Kecksteins present a system that flags endometriosis implants inside keyhole surgery videos. Their 2025 arXiv demo paper helps doctors treating a condition with wildly varied look. Dark endometrial implants are one frequent visual form of the disease. Missing lesions during surgery risks incomplete treatment and lasting symptoms.

The system is trained to mark exactly those dark implant regions in video frames. Found areas receive multi-coloured marks directly on the surgery footage. A summary list helps doctors browse long videos for the flagged moments. The tool targets support: specialists confirm what the marks suggest, and it does not take their place. The camera exam already informs care, and software marking could align how findings get recorded. Complete lesion records matter for scoring systems that grade how bad the disease is. The demo shows the system running on real operation videos.
arxiv-2510-13999:
Mike Lasby and co-authors show that pruning, not merging, is the better way to compress mixture-of-experts language models in a single pass, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These models route each input to a few specialist sub-networks called experts, which keeps computation cheap but demands memory for the experts. Recent work favored merging experts, at least on classification-style tests.

The authors prove merging causes an irreducible error: it collapses the router's independent, input-dependent control over experts, a failure they name functional subspace collapse. Their method, REAP, scores experts using the router's gate values and how strongly each expert activates, then deletes the weakest. Across models from twenty billion to a trillion parameters, REAP beat merging and pruning methods on generative tasks, especially at half compression. On code generation and tool calling with large models, it stayed nearly lossless after removing half the experts.
arxiv-2510-14099:
Cesar Amaral and co-authors review quantum machine learning and quantum-inspired methods for computational fluid dynamics, the simulation of flow that supports engineering, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classical simulation becomes too expensive for high-dimensional, multiscale, and turbulent problems. That motivates the search for quantum shortcuts.

The review surveys variational quantum algorithms, quantum-classical solvers that can handle nonlinear effects through processing units, and neural networks. Some variants are physics-informed, baking the governing equations into training. These show gains in parameter savings and accuracy on benchmarks. It covers tensor network methods from many-body physics, usable on classical hardware. Reported gains reach orders of magnitude in memory and runtime, with accuracy preserved. The authors conclude that quantum fluid dynamics remains out of reach in the noisy era. But quantum-inspired tensor networks pay off. Hybrid approaches are the best near-term strategy.
arxiv-2510-14299:
Nam Le and co-authors present TED++, a detector for backdoor attacks on neural networks that watches whether an input's activations stay inside the neighborhood of its class, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Backdoored models behave normally until a hidden trigger appears. Many defenses fail when attackers exploit subtle distance anomalies, or when only a few clean examples are available for calibration.

TED++ builds a tubular neighborhood around each class's hidden-feature manifold, estimating its local thickness from a handful of clean activations. It then ranks each layer's activations with an adaptive scheme that flags any drift outside the admissible tube. Aggregating these rankings across all layers captures how faithfully an input follows the class shapes, and inputs whose ranking patterns deviate are flagged as backdoored. Experiments show state-of-the-art detection under adaptive attacks and limited data; with five held-out examples per class, detection stayed near perfect.
arxiv-2510-14499:
Keshab Chandra Bakshi, Satyajit Guin, and Guruprasad study what happens where two subfactors built from complex Hadamard matrices meet, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Subfactors sit inside operator algebras, and their relative position encodes deep structure. Hadamard matrices, square arrays with orthogonal rows of unit-modulus entries, build sets of them through Fourier matrices.

Take two distinct complex Hadamard matrices from the same class, generated by tensor products of Fourier matrices. If their subfactors are conjugate, their intersection is again a factor. It has finite Jones index, a measure of the inclusion's size. They compute that index and find the intersection's relative commutant, the algebra commuting with it. They characterize when these give vertex model subfactors, building on their earlier results. They derive a formula for the Connes-Størmer relative entropy of them. This reveals how their algebra governs their entropy.
arxiv-2510-14599:
Konopa, Fesl, and Beránek propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a new way to schedule work on graphics processors that can be split into separate instances. Modern workloads vary a lot over time, and central schedulers struggle to keep up. Earlier work on scheduler-driven job atomization broke jobs into pieces. This paper pushes the idea further, toward a negotiation between jobs and the scheduler.

Under their algorithm, JASDA, the scheduler announces execution windows. Jobs then generate and score feasible sub-jobs that fit those windows. The scheduler clears the offers using policies that balance utilization, fairness, and responsiveness. Feedback, calibration, and safety checks are built into the loop itself. The design borrows from auction theory and online optimization. The authors present it as a scalable base for fair, market-aware resource management on multi-instance GPUs, with uses ranging from artificial intelligence to smart farming.
arxiv-2510-14699:
Akshay and co-authors work, in a 2025 arXiv paper, on verifying timed systems, such as controllers that must react within deadlines. Properties are written in Metric Interval Temporal Logic, a language that can say a response must come within a stated time window. The logic becomes much more expressive when it can refer to the past as well as the future, but tools handle that combination poorly.

The authors develop a new translation under pointwise semantics, where time is a sequence of events. The past fragment of the logic converts, in linear time, into synchronous networks of deterministic timed automata, machines whose behavior leaves no ambiguity. Determinism survives even when top-level future requirements are added. For the full logic, they translate into generalized timed automata with future clocks and give a liveness algorithm to analyze them. A prototype tool beat the state of the art in their benchmark experiments.
arxiv-2510-14999:
Mirzaei and co-authors reach, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the sharpest possible spectrum for a single molecule stuck to a surface. Gas-phase spectroscopy is exquisite. But molecules adsorbed on surfaces have always fallen short of the ultimate limit, where a transition's linewidth is set only by the excited state's lifetime. Here that width is just nano-electronvolts. The team's new deposition approach closes that gap.

They adsorbed single dibenzoterrylene molecules onto an anthracene crystal's surface and examined them at liquid helium temperature, combining spectral measurements with super-resolution microscopy. The electronic transitions they measured were Fourier-limited, meaning lifetime-limited, the sharpest nature allows. Along the way the work revealed several properties of the adsorbed species. The authors present the work as opening a class of surface science studies that unite pinpoint spatial detail with the sharpest spectra.
arxiv-2510-15099:
Ravin Kumar proposes a fresh way to write numbers inside digital computers in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. His Adaptive Base Representation theorem describes a number system meant as a structured alternative to the familiar binary system. Kumar argues that each decimal number can be represented uniquely while using the same count of bits that binary encoding would need.

The paper lays out the theory and the formulas behind the system, showing it can cover the same range of whole numbers as binary. Kumar also reports that the scheme works alongside standard data compression methods such as Huffman coding and arithmetic coding. It likewise fits error detection and correction tools like Hamming codes. As a practical illustration, he discusses digital steganography, the hiding of information inside other data, and suggests the system could inspire new designs for digital encoding.
arxiv-2510-15599:
T. V. Pavlova and V. M. Shevlyuga trace how single phosphorus atoms wander across a silicon surface, a step that matters for atom-precise electronics. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses scanning tunneling microscopy at seventy-seven and three hundred kelvin to watch the motion. The phosphorus came from PBr3 molecules, which split apart completely on the Si(100) surface at the lower temperature.

Phosphorus atoms moved both along and across the rows of silicon dimers that pattern the surface. Calculations with density functional theory supplied the activation energies behind each observed pathway. At low temperature, journeys mostly started or ended at bridge positions between atoms. At room temperature, atoms hopped mainly between end-bridge positions, and nearby bromine atoms, left over from the source molecule, clearly restricted their motion. Phosphorus also drifted toward an oxygen atom left by stray water, because the site beside it is more stable.
arxiv-2510-15999:
D. Mondal leads twenty-two co-authors in a search for a faint neutrino interaction using sapphire detectors beside a small research reactor. The target process, coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, is a standard model prediction long hard to see because the recoil energy is tiny. The MINER setup sits near the one-megawatt TRIGA reactor at Texas A and M University.

A primary detector of only tens of grams ran cold with fine energy resolution, gathering reactor-on and reactor-off exposures for background subtraction at low energies. A GEANT4 simulation of reactor-linked background matches the observations. After that background is rejected with the simulation's help, the fitted signal rate is far below the standard model prediction with very low significance, which the team attributes to high low-energy background. A planned move to a stronger reactor with better shielding should reach a firm detection.
arxiv-2510-16099:
Theodore B. Smith leads twenty-one co-authors in timing the light echoes of a quasar's coronal line region. Coronal lines are emission lines needing very high ionisation energy, so they trace vigorous activity near a black hole. Their home region's size was known only from spatial imaging, which cannot resolve the innermost zones of an active nucleus.

Reverberation mapping of the neon coronal line in the quasar COS168 gives an optimal emission radius of a few hundred light-days, with a modest error range quoted in the study. That places the coronal region outside the dusty torus, whose size follows from a radius and luminosity relation. The virial product for the coronal line matches that of a hydrogen line within errors, which suggests the gas orbits under the black hole's gravity. Coronal lines could therefore weigh black holes, the team argues.
arxiv-2510-16199:
Menglong Zhao and ten co-authors built a huge library of plasma simulations to help control a fusion machine. The machine is KSTAR, a Korean tokamak where hot plasma must be kept from scorching the walls. One key state is detachment, where the plasma cools just before it hits the wall plates.

Their library holds nearly seventy thousand steady runs, sweeping gas density, heating power, current, and added impurities. One signal proves sturdy: the wall strike point cools to about three or four electron volts when detachment starts, whatever the settings. The two wall sides behave unlike those in a US machine, a quirk controllers must respect. Tests with gas puffs show delays of a few dozen milliseconds, well matched by simple control models. The library now feeds stand-in models for live control.
arxiv-2510-16299:
Zi-Xuan Xu and four co-authors model how charm quarks turn into D mesons inside the fireball of a nuclear collision. That fireball, the quark-gluon plasma, is matter so hot that quarks roam free before cooling into particles. The order in which charm finds partners shapes what detectors finally see.

Their model has charm quarks drift through the plasma, then join partners in sequence. The strange partner meson, Ds, forms first, and the plain D0 forms later. Because of that order, the Ds flows less sideways than the D0, matching fresh ALICE data well. The model also predicts a peak in the Ds to D0 yield ratio at low momentum. Future collisions can test that peak and, with it, the whole sequence picture.
arxiv-2510-16499:
Michelle Yuan leads seven co-authors in a 2025 study on how to build AI agent teams well. A system must pick agents, tools, and models that fit the job and the budget. Past picks rely on fixed word search, which misses true skill and cost. Their frame casts the pick as a knapsack task. A knapsack task asks what fits best in a fixed budget.

A composer agent tests parts live and weighs skill, cost, and fit. Tests with Claude 3.5 Sonnet span five data sets. The composer hit the best trade-off curve of skill versus cost. Gains in success rate reached up to about 32 percent for solo setups. In team setups, success rose from 37 to 87 percent.
arxiv-2510-17199:
Nirai Hayakawa and five co-authors predict round wins in a pro shooter game from video in this 2025 paper. Past work leaned on match logs and plain stats. The team instead reads the small map shown in match films. That map holds troop spots and key in-round events.

A video model learns from map films plus tags for tactic events. Tagged training lifted hit rates a lot in mid and late round play. The best model called about four in five rounds right. Plain map films alone gave far worse scores. The work shows rich tactic tags help a lot for live game reads.
arxiv-2510-17299:
Longer training is usually assumed to help a learning model, but Siran Dai and four co-authors report the opposite for detailed prediction tasks. In self-supervised learning, where models learn from unlabelled data, extra training hurt tasks like marking each pixel of an image by class. The team names this effect self-supervised dense degradation and finds it across many leading methods.

To spot the problem without labels, Dai and her co-authors build an estimator from two measures: how relevant hidden units are to classes, and how many useful directions the representation really uses. Picking models by that score raised accuracy by about three points on average. A training penalty based on the same score also eased the decline.
arxiv-2510-17399:
Set theory studies the foundations of mathematics itself, and one old question asks whether certain large collections of almost disjoint sets, called MAD families, must exist. Jialiang He, Jintao Luo, and Shuguo Zhang tackle a conjecture on that question first made by A R D Mathias in nineteen seventy-seven. The setting is a class of sets where a regularity condition known as the Ramsey property holds.

He and his co-authors argue that when the Ramsey property holds in such a class, no MAD family can exist there, which would settle the conjecture. The short paper rests on a proof technique the team expects to serve in other problems as well. They also announce four related theorems, with proofs promised in a follow up paper.
arxiv-2510-17499:
TianQin is a planned space mission that will listen for gravitational waves using three satellites flying in formation around Earth, linked by laser beams. Yuzhou Fang and seven co-authors study one stubborn noise source for that observatory: tilt to length coupling, where slight tilts of the optics leak into the distance readings. This noise is expected to rank third among TianQin error sources, after laser and clock noise, and it must be subtracted for the mission to hit its precision target.

Using realistic closed loop simulations of the satellite steering and pointing controls, Fang and his co-authors test how well the coupling can be measured and removed. Rotating only one optical assembly, rather than two in mirror fashion, gave cleaner estimates. Two further tricks, alternate signal combinations and deliberate small manoeuvres, improved the accuracy again.
arxiv-2510-17899:
Floris-Jan Willemsen, Niki van Stein, and Ben van Werkhoven let large language models write the tuning algorithms for fast programs. Hand tuning is slow because the search spaces are huge and uneven. Their system prompts a model with the problem and its search space, then tests and refines the code it writes.

The made algorithms ran on four real tuning tasks across six hardware platforms. Adding task and search-space detail at the writing stage improved average results against strong existing tuners. The paper shows a new division of labor: models draft the optimizer, and benchmarks decide whether it stays.
arxiv-2510-17999:
Ghazal Danaee and three co-authors check whether brain scan tools treat demographic groups unevenly. The task is outlining a small deep brain region tied to reward, in MRI images from four groups split by race and sex. Three deep learning systems are compared with a classic atlas-based method, using hand-drawn outlines as truth.

One part of the study scores outline quality for each group. A second part checks the volumes the tools report, where bias could distort later research. Medical imaging readers get a direct audit of fairness in a task where small errors and group gaps can quietly shape findings.
arxiv-2510-18099:
Arindam Fadikar, with five co-authors, upgrades Bayesian optimization so it learns from single simulation runs, not just their averages. Pricey simulators are often judged by summary numbers over many runs, which throws away how each run unfolds. Their method feeds both settings and random seeds into a shared surrogate model.

That trick allows direct inference at the level of one trajectory. A common-seed scheme defines a likelihood over individual paths. For scientists tuning costly models, the gain is sharper guidance from the same runs, especially when the path itself, not the average, is what the study cares about.
arxiv-2510-18199:
Jinyu Hu and Chen Wu sharpen predictions of alpha decay by adding a nonlocal effect and machine learning tuning. Alpha particles do not behave as purely local objects inside the nucleus, and folding that fact into a two-potential model already improved results in earlier work. Here three classic learning models optimize the extended approach against reference data.

Decision tree and gradient boosting models agreed best with the data. Their spread dropped by over half against the plain two-potential model without nonlocality. The random forest variant lagged behind. Nuclear theorists get a ranked sense of which simple learners best polish a physics-based decay model.
arxiv-2510-18399:
Mikito Kohno and his fifteen co-authors report two molecular clouds that appear to be falling toward the disk of the Milky Way. Using survey data from the Mopra radio telescope, they found cloud shapes stretched like heads with tails, pointing across the plane of the galaxy. Distance estimates from Gaia star data place the clouds roughly two and a half kiloparsecs away, and their fall speed exceeds thirty-five kilometers per second.

Gas temperatures inside the clouds run from thirty to fifty kelvin, far warmer than the ten kelvin typical of such clouds, even though no nearby heat source was found. The heads are warmest, which the team reads as heating from a shock where the clouds strike gas in the disk. They suggest the clouds began as faster-moving atomic gas that was squeezed by the shock into molecular form, a first clear case of its kind.
arxiv-2510-18499:
Hyewon Lee and her four co-authors report on the search system their DILAB team built for an Alibaba competition on multilingual online shopping search. Shoppers type queries in many languages, and the system must match them to the right product categories and items. The team's entry finished fifth on the final leaderboard, with steady, strong scores across the evaluation measures.

Their pipeline worked in stages. First, careful data cleaning improved consistency and category coverage, while language tagging and noise removal raised input quality. Then several model designs and fine-tuning plans were tried, with settings tuned on curated validation sets to balance the query-category and query-item tasks. The authors credit the system's robustness across languages and product areas to disciplined data curation and repeated evaluation rather than to any single model, and they released the code publicly.
arxiv-2510-18999:
Zhirui Dai and three co-authors present OREN, a network for building signed distance maps from point clouds in real time. Such maps tell a robot how far it is from the nearest surface at any point, which supports location tracking, planning, and control.

Pure neural methods give smooth maps but can forget, run slowly, and struggle in large spaces, while grid methods are fast but rough. OREN joins an octree-based starting estimate with a neural correction. The hybrid aims for maps that stay smooth and usable for calculus-based planning while updating fast enough for robots working online.
arxiv-2510-19299:
Philipp J Schneider, Lin Tian, and Marian-Andrei Rizoiu ask whether language model agents can learn to form social ties the way people do online. Human networks grow through likeness, mutual exchange, and social approval, and it is unclear which memory and learning mechanisms let artificial agents reproduce those patterns.

Their simulation lets agents interact repeatedly, judge each other, and adapt through in-context learning sped by a coaching signal. Reward functions mirror real motives such as seeking information, self-presentation, coordination, and emotional support. Watching network structures emerge from those rewards helps researchers study online behavior without experimenting on real users.
arxiv-2510-19599:
Haozhe Luo and four co-authors introduce XBench, a benchmark that tests whether vision-language models actually look at the right place in a chest X-ray. Such models answer questions about medical images, but their grounding, the match between words and image regions, is rarely measured. Reliable grounding matters before any clinical use.

The benchmark evaluates seven CLIP-style models, generating explanation maps from cross-attention and similarity methods and comparing them with radiologist annotations across diseases. All models localized large, clear findings reasonably well but degraded on small or diffuse lesions. Models pretrained on chest X-rays aligned better than general-domain ones, and recognition skill and grounding skill were strongly linked.
arxiv-2510-19699:
Jorge L. Rodríguez-Monteverde, Santiago Jaraba, and Juan García-Bellido simulate what happens when two black holes fly at each other and are captured into a merger by their own gravity. Dynamical captures probe the strongest gravitational fields, and their signals differ from ordinary inspiraling binaries. The team ran numerical relativity simulations of equal-mass, nonspinning pairs across a range of momenta and incidence angles.

They measured the emitted gravitational-wave signal and the masses and spins before and after merger, and built a simple analytical model that fits the wave emission well. The delay between capture and merger follows a first-order divergent pattern in the incidence angle, marking the boundary between a capture and a flyby scattering.
arxiv-2510-19899:
Parth Nayak, Michael Walther, and Daniel Gruen test whether deep learning can extract cosmological information from noisy Lyman-alpha forest spectra. These spectra are the absorption patterns quasars stamp on their light as it crosses intergalactic gas. Their network squeezes each spectrum into a summary tuned to one thing: the temperature-density relation of the gas. Real observations are noisy, which earlier field-level methods had not faced.

Training used simulated spectra with varied noise levels. The pipeline pairs its learned summary with a mixture-model surrogate for likelihood-free inference. Against two classic human-designed summaries, precision improved by roughly two-thirds at moderate noise. At low noise it more than doubled. Deep learning, the authors conclude, stays powerful on realistic, imperfect data.
arxiv-2510-19999:
Yixiao Wang and three co-authors speed up elastic net penalized linear models with an enhanced cyclic coordinate descent framework. Coordinate descent is a workhorse for these models, but nonlinear steps in its gradient work slow training down. The team uses a Taylor expansion around the current point to avoid those costly operations.

That change lets them unroll the vector recurrences into batched computations controlled by a tunable parameter. Settings above one improve speed without harming convergence, while the lowest setting recovers the original method. Unlike block methods, their approach avoids convergence delay and numerical instability. Tests show average speed gains of about three times over leading solvers.
arxiv-2510-20199:
Jane H. Lee and four co-authors build a risk-aware frame for reinforcement learning with limits on more than one goal. Most such work states goals as mean gains over time. That view skips rare but dire tail events. For high-stakes use, those tail risks can be the whole point. Their frame uses tuned certainty scores to gain strength at each step in both gain and time.

In a strong dual form, the risk-aware task matches the first task in an exact way, if set terms hold. The steps then wrap around stock solvers such as PPO with no deep change. The team proves the steps meet in the limit, in the plain case. Tests with numbers back the risk-aware traits they claim.
arxiv-2510-20299:
Saraf Anzum Shreya, MD. Abu Ismail Siddique, and Sharaf Tasnim propose DB-FGA-Net, a network for classifying brain tumors in medical images across several classes. Early, precise diagnosis matters for treatment, yet many deep learning systems lean on heavy data augmentation, which can hurt generalization and clinician trust. Their design joins two backbones, VGG16 and Xception, with a frequency-gated attention block that captures local and global features together.

Grad-CAM visualizations show the tumor regions behind each prediction, linking model output to clinical reading. Without augmentation, the model reaches accuracy above ninety-nine percent on one dataset in the four-class setting and generalizes at nearly ninety-six percent on an independent dataset. A graphical interface provides real-time classification with tumor localization for clinical use.
arxiv-2510-20499:
Akif Çördük, Piotr Sielski, Alice Boucher, and Kumar Aatish combine several graphics-processor-accelerated primal heuristics for mixed integer programming. Graphics acceleration allows larger search regions and faster iterations when hunting for good feasible solutions. A GPU version of a primal-dual linear method serves as an approximate linear programming solver, while a new probing cache speeds up roundings and detects infeasibility early.

Well-known heuristics including Feasibility Pump, Feasibility Jump, and Fix-and-Propagate are further accelerated and enhanced on the graphics hardware. On the MIPLIB2017 benchmark over a presolved dataset, the combined approach finds two hundred twenty-one feasible solutions and reaches a twenty-two percent objective gap. The authors report significant gains over existing methods in both solution count and objective quality.
arxiv-2510-20699:
Yaxuan Kong and five co-authors built M2VN, a deep learning system that forecasts market volatility by joining price data with the story content of news. Price swings drive risk calls, yet numbers alone miss the mood and events that news text carries.

A core risk in finance models is peeking at future news, so the team uses time stamped news summaries from a model built to respect the clock. An extra alignment loss helps the numeric and text streams blend inside the network rather than clash. Across wide tests the system beats prior baselines again and again, suggesting joined news and market signals give a firmer base for risk and trading choices.
arxiv-2510-20799:
Wei-Chen Lin, Dong-han Yeom, and Dejan Stojkovic ask whether time slices in quantum gravity may safely cross a black hole horizon. Accounts that keep evolution unitary usually slice only the outside region, but the ban on crossing slices needed a direct test.

Solving the Wheeler DeWitt equation for slices that cover both sides, the team finds an outside wave packet can be built, yet the wave function must vanish near the horizon itself. No single smooth classical state can then cover a crossing slice, so the interior must be a blend of several such states. That blend implies horizon scale uncertainty and recasts the black hole as a deeply quantum large object, with fresh light on the information loss puzzle.
arxiv-2510-20999: Ilmar Gahramanov leads two co-authors in building new Bailey pairs for the pentagon identity obeyed by the tetrahedron index, expressed through q-series. The tetrahedron index sits beneath shape based values of three dimensional manifolds and related knot quantities, so rules it obeys ripple outward into geometry. Bailey pairs are paired sequences that generate families of such rules. New pairs for this index may yield a fresh framework for deriving knot values through the Bailey chain, extending classic summation methods into modern shape based territory.
arxiv-2510-21099:
Alvaro Alvarez-Parrilla leads two co-authors on tessellations determined by rational complex functions and a converse through the Riemann existence theorem. A rational function of degree above one, with its critical values in cyclic order, tiles its Riemann surface with twice the degree many alternating colored polygons.

That tiling gives a simple visual picture of the function. Conversely, a suitably labeled alternating tiling, even a non homogeneous one with varied polygon sizes, guarantees a rational function realizing it. The two way bridge between pictures and functions aids the study of dessins and branched coverings.
arxiv-2510-21199:
Yang Zhong and four co-authors describe their entry to a Kaggle recognition challenge on fine-grained food images, held with an ICCV workshop. Sorting foods into close categories, such as similar dishes, matters for later health-related analysis of what people eat and how diets affect the body.

The team found that pairing ArcFace loss with Circle loss improved accuracy over either method used on its own. Models were trained with carefully tuned settings and then combined into an ensemble for the final predictions. That recipe earned the team third place in the contest. The short report centers on the loss pairing, the tuning choices, and the ensemble step rather than on a new network design.
arxiv-2510-21299:
Shengkang Chen and five co-authors send images over wireless links at extremely low rates, where normal compression leaves pictures badly damaged. Their answer is to rebuild a picture that keeps the meaning of the scene, instead of chasing an exact copy of every pixel in the original.

The sender compresses the image with a learned joint source-channel code and also sends a short text prompt describing the scene. At the receiver, the damaged signal and the prompt are fused and passed to a Stable Diffusion model steered by ControlNet, which rebuilds a convincing image. Across varied channel conditions, tests beat both classic coding schemes and deep learning baselines on how good the resulting pictures look.
arxiv-2510-21399:
Svetoslav Zahariev builds continuum limits for a family of lattice gauge theories, simplified versions of the forces described by quantum field theory. The theories are Abelian and polyhedral, living on grids that can sit in any number of space-time dimensions, and the goal is a rigorous passage from the grid to smooth space.

He gives two routes. One rests on projective systems of heat kernel measures, families of probability rules that agree across grid refinements. The other defines a single heat kernel measure on an infinite-dimensional space built as a projective limit of Hilbert spaces. As a special case, the construction yields a gauge theory on the endless cubical lattice that, unlike the standard version, stays massless for every value of the coupling strength.
arxiv-2510-21599:
Reda Marzouk, Shahaf Bassan, and Guy Katz compute SHAP explanations for tensor networks, models that factor large arrays into chained smaller ones and underlie many compressed neural networks. SHAP values fairly split a prediction among the input features, but for expressive models they are usually hard to compute exactly, right where explanations matter most.

For general tensor networks the authors give a framework that produces provably exact SHAP values whatever the network's shape. When the network is a tensor train, a linear chain, the computation runs in poly-logarithmic parallel time, an unusually strong guarantee. Because trains can encode decision trees, ensembles, linear models, and linear recurrent networks, the speed result tightens what was known for all of them. They also show that binarized neural networks become tractable when their width is fixed, fingering width, not depth, as the true bottleneck.
arxiv-2510-21799:
Vinícius Pereira da Silva Oliveira, Danilo da Silva Borges, and Erick de Moraes Franklin run experiments on a nuisance in fluidized beds, tubes where rising fluid keeps particles floating. In liquid beds, grains often stick together into clumps, shrinking the contact area with the fluid and spoiling the floating state. The team asks how the clump's shape drives that breakdown.

Trios of spheres were glued at set angles and floated in water inside a narrow tube while flow speed varied. Depending on angle and speed, the bed showed clean floating, plugs, clogging, glass-like frozen structures, or settled packing. A bonding angle of ninety degrees floated best at a given speed, and the authors chart a regime map linking angle and flow so operators can keep beds running.
arxiv-2510-21899:
Eyad H. Al-Samra offers a self-contained introduction to de Sitter space and cosmic inflation, written for readers meeting the subjects for the first time. De Sitter space describes a universe expanding at an ever-quickening pace, and inflation borrows that geometry to explain a burst of growth in the universe's first moments.

With teaching figures throughout, the overview shows how the space can be pictured as a curved surface inside a higher-dimensional flat space. Works out its symmetry motions in two coordinate systems, tracing their paths on a Penrose diagram. Al-Samra then quantizes the inflaton field, the driver of inflation, in its standard vacuum and computes the two- and three-point patterns it leaves behind. Those patterns connect to the tiny temperature ripples seen in the cosmic microwave background.
arxiv-2510-22099:
Xuanming Zhang studies the split personality of large language models, which sometimes reason in general patterns and sometimes recite memorized training text word for word. That unpredictability is dangerous in high-stakes settings. Zhang builds a framework to tell the two modes apart while a model is running and to lean it toward the safer one.

The theory comes from the information bottleneck principle: generalizing means keeping a compressed, task-relevant picture, while memorizing means failing to compress. On that foundation, a small probe reads the model's state and estimates how much it is leaning on memory right now. A steering mechanism then nudges its activity toward circuits linked with generalization. Zhang frames the pairing as the model contrasting against itself during decoding, and reports experiments on reasoning tasks and factual questions.
arxiv-2510-22199:
Kunal Bhosikar, Siddharth Katageri, Vivek Madhavaram, Kai Han, and Charu Sharma close a gap between two kinds of motion generation. Systems that animate a full body walking through a three-dimensional room rarely handle the fingers well enough to grasp. Systems that craft precise grasps ignore the room entirely, leaving the reach floating in a void.

Their dataset, MOGRAS, records the missing middle: full-body walking motions that lead into a final grasp, staged inside richly annotated indoor scenes. With that resource they benchmark existing full-body grasping methods and expose where scene awareness breaks down, then offer a simple adaptation that lets current approaches operate inside real scenes. The dataset serves robotics, virtual reality, and interface research, anywhere a digital human has to walk up to something and actually pick it up.
arxiv-2510-22299:
Matthias J. Ehrhardt, Davide Murari, and Ferdia Sherry survey a design philosophy for neural networks. It treats a network as a dynamical system unfolding in time. The motivation is stability. Networks that a tiny crafted input change can fool are untrustworthy. One active school of defense borrows the mathematics of continuous dynamics and optimal control.

The paper gives a bird's-eye map of that school. The fundamental concepts most of the literature shares are named. It then slows down for one concrete approach to stable networks. The theory is laid out, and the implementation is described. Working code accompanies the text. A notebook shows a small adversarial robustness example for image classification. It runs on an ordinary computer. The discussion walks through the toy example so readers can feel the stability mechanism.
arxiv-2510-22599:
