How much a shape bends is called curvature. That bend can reveal hidden traits in data. Yasharth Yadav and Kelin Xia wrote a 2025 review on this theme. It covers the use of curvature in data work and in learning. The data types span graphs, point clouds, and cell complexes.

The review lays out the math base for each model. It also lays out how to compute with them. Uses span group finding in networks and deep learning on shapes. The pair view curvature from two angles of geometry. They set out a clear pipeline for such work. Work from the top groups is summed up at the end. Open paths for the field close the review.
arxiv-2510-22699:
Spacecraft that inspect large orbital targets must maneuver precisely while models of their motion stay imperfect. Matteo El-Hariry, Andrej Orsula, Matthieu Geist, and Miguel Olivares-Mendez introduce RL-AVIST in 2025, a reinforcement learning framework for autonomous visual inspection of space targets.

Using a high fidelity robotics simulator, they train agents with a model based method called DreamerV3 and compare two model free baselines. Tasks involve three dimensional proximity flight around targets such as the Lunar Gateway. Both general agents trained on varied velocities and specialist agents following fixed inspection paths are tested. Model based learning shows promise in path accuracy and sample efficiency across spacecraft shapes.
arxiv-2510-22799:
Recommender systems often fail when users and items are all new. Florian Grotschla, Elia Trachsel, Luca A Lanzendorfer, and Roger Wattenhofer address that limit in 2025. Their model is called NBF-Rec. It is a graph based recommender. It supports transfer across disjoint datasets.

Older embedding methods need retraining per domain. NBF-Rec computes embeddings live at inference time. Message passing runs over interaction links. Tests span seven real datasets. Domains include movies, music, shopping, and check ins. Zero shot results stay competitive. Light fine tuning improves them further. The work shows graph transfer needs no aligned users or items.
arxiv-2510-22899:
A model that makes new data may favor some trends over others. Andreas Floros wrote a 2025 paper on that bias. His co-authors are Seyed-Mohsen Moosavi-Dezfooli and Pier Luigi Dragotti. The models are score based. A score is a slope field that guides how new data is made.

The team name the key trends Score Anisotropy Directions. In short, they call them SADs. Each network has its own set of SADs. The SADs seem to form a base that fits the network shape. That fit may hint at how well a model will learn. It can be read before training starts. Tests on fake data and on image sets back this claim. SADs also track with downstream scores.
arxiv-2510-23199:
Junpei Komiyama, Kyoungseok Jang, and Junya Honda design rate-optimal methods for finding the best arm among many options under a sampling budget. The problem models A/B testing, where each arm has an unknown average reward and samples are limited. Their framework covers algorithms that are minimax optimal up to a constant factor, generalizing fixed-budget work limited to one risk measure.

They propose Almost Tracking, a closed-form algorithm with a provable guarantee for anytime identification. Users need not fix the budget in advance to trust the answer. The results give testers a principled way to stop early with known error risk.
arxiv-2510-23499:
Yiqi Huang and Xinrui Zhao study how surfaces evolve under mean curvature flow near a cylinder, the standard model for a common kind of singularity. The flow moves each point of a surface in the direction that shrinks area fastest, and rescaled views near a pinch often look like a round cylinder. The question is how fast a nearly cylindrical flow must settle down before it is forced to be the cylinder itself.

They prove a rescaled flow drawn as a global graph over the cylinder must coincide with the cylinder exactly, if it settles faster than any exponential rate. It is a first result of its kind. Then they show the global assumption is essential. For local graphs they build counterexamples settling at any such rate, whole families of Tikhonov-type exceptions. Their constructions even produce flows whose singular sets form prescribed flat shapes at chosen speeds.
arxiv-2510-23699:
Jan Boruch and three co-authors construct new saddle-point solutions in five-dimensional supergravity: families of Euclidean multi-black-hole, black ring, black Saturn, and black lens configurations. These exotic geometries feed into the gravitational supersymmetric index, a protected count that physicists compute either in flat space or in a curved AdS setting. All the solutions are supersymmetric, carry finite temperature, and spin just so that fermions stay periodic around the thermal circle.

Each saddle's action is independent of temperature, as a protected index demands, and equals the entropy of the matching extremal black object. The construction lifts four-dimensional saddles that look singular but smooth out in five dimensions. A surprise follows, which the authors call an index enigma: less symmetric black ring saddles can outweigh plain black holes in the flat-space index. That inversion, unseen in earlier Lorentzian examples, may reshape how index computations are assembled.
arxiv-2510-24199:
Loek van Everdingen and eight co-authors cooled a tiny beam that bends and vibrates to about six thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Beams like this can sense very small forces. If they stay in balance with their cold surroundings, they may keep a clean motion for longer. The beam hums near seven hundred times per second and weighs about one and a half billionths of a gram.

The team cooled it with no active fridge on the device. They used a method based on nuclear spin loss of heat. They then tracked the beam's tiny heat driven motion with a lock in tool. Even at the coldest point, that motion stood out from the noise. It also matched the spread that heat theory predicts. The work opens a path to cool such beams below one thousandth of a degree.
arxiv-2510-24399:
Toan Van Nguyen and three co-authors introduce GenTrack, a hybrid method for multi-object tracking in video. Its first contribution is mixing stochastic and deterministic tracking to handle unknown, time varying numbers of targets while preserving identity consistency under nonlinear dynamics. This balance aims to avoid the identity switches that plague purely probabilistic trackers.

Second, particle swarm optimization guides the stochastic particles toward their target distributions using new fitness measures, enabling tracking even with weak, noisy detectors. Third, the method integrates social interactions among targets to improve the guided particles and to update both matched and unmatched tracks. The paper presents GenTrack as a new generation baseline for multi-object tracking.
arxiv-2510-24499:
Y. M. Oviedo-Torres and two co-authors explore whether ultra peripheral heavy ion collisions at the LHC can reveal a new charged vector boson. In the Vector Scotogenic Model, this boson decays into heavy neutral leptons. The authors study lead ion collisions where the nuclei miss each other but exchange intense electromagnetic fields, producing clean signals.

They show the ATLAS experiment, searching for dilepton plus missing energy final states, can probe boson and lepton masses from five to one hundred five gigaelectron volts. Their analysis finds parameter regions where the signal stands out with high significance and where ATLAS could exclude the boson at ninety five percent confidence.
arxiv-2510-24599:
Harsha Kokel leads a team of seven authors on finding joinable columns. Two table columns are joinable if their values can link the tables. Automated analysis needs such links found without human help. Past methods used value overlap or meaning similarity alone. Which method wins for which data was poorly understood.

The team compare syntactic and semantic methods on seven benchmarks. The benchmarks span relational databases and loose data lakes. Six criteria are tested, from shared values to metadata meaning. Ensemble ranking, a blend of criteria, beat single-criterion methods. Meaning of values and metadata mattered most for data lakes. Size-based criteria mattered more for relational databases. The study gives builders clear rules for choosing a method.
arxiv-2510-25199:
Manisha More leads a team with six co-authors who built an AI frame to catch three grave ills early, from shots and sounds. Early finds lift cure odds and cut costs, yet top tests are dear, harsh, or far from poor zones. Their frame joins shot reads, heat shots, and sound reads in one kit.

A tuned phone grade net sorts skin spots for cancer, trained on a known large set, with high right rates. A classic tool reads heat shots for blood clots in veins. For heart and lung, sound traits feed a woods based tool. Each arm is cheap and can run with no cut or probe.
arxiv-2510-25399:
Alexander V Savin and Artem P Klinov simulate slits in graphite. Their 2025 physics paper studies multilayer graphite crystals. A linear cavity sits on a flat crystal surface. A multilayer graphene sheet covers that cavity. Sometimes an open slit forms under the sheet. Other times the sheet fills the cavity completely.

They use a two-dimensional coarse-grained chain model. An open slit forms only below a critical width. That critical width grows with covering sheet layers. For single-layer cavities, the limit stays under three nanometers. For deeper cavities, maximum width grows without bound. Inside the crystal, open slits can stay stable widely. Thermal oscillations were also simulated for stability checks. Two-layer open slits under fifteen nanometers stayed stable. Wider slits closed when temperature exceeded four hundred kelvin. Three-layer open slits stayed stable against thermal oscillations.
arxiv-2510-25499:
Usama Syed Aqeel, Clare Burrage, Oliver Gould, and Paul M Saffin study bubble nucleation. Their 2025 physics paper uses the asymmetron scalar-tensor theory. That theory couples universally to matter in cosmology. It also has explicit symmetry breaking built in. Matter density distributions affect thin-wall bubble formation. Screening inside dense objects changes the picture.

Screening induces a surface tension at object edges. That yields richer bubble answers than standard nucleation. Standard Coleman-Callan bulk nucleation is the comparison case. Edge tensions modify the Nambu-Goto action for instantons. Euclidean actions are computed for several surface geometries. Flat planes and cylindrical surfaces are considered here. Smallest action occurs at concave spherical edges. Edge nucleation beats bulk nucleation within their approximation. Weak asymmetron couplings largely explain that preference. Uses include cosmic void curvature limits in cosmology. Domain wall nucleation preferentially occurs at void edges. Homogeneous gas around substrates reduces the maximum radius.
arxiv-2510-25699:
Charles Hyde led ten co-authors building tessellated lookup tables. Mitch Kerver, Christos Tsolakis, and Polykarpos Thomadakis helped. Spiros Tsalikis, Kevin Garner, and Angelos Angelopoulos joined. Wirawan Purwanto, Gagik Gavalian, and Christian Weiss joined. Nikos Chrisochoides closes the eleven-author team. Their 2025 paper approximates Compton form factors faster.

Irregular tetrahedra tile 3D space in tessellation. Arbitrary functions are approximated to desired precision by interpolation. Nuclear femtography uses Compton form factors for runs. Tessellations reached only one percent mean interpolation error. Monte Carlo event generation sped up dramatically with tables. Speedups reached about twenty-three times for ten million events. Extrapolation suggests far larger gains for bigger samples. Lookup tables trade memory for computation time. Nuclear physics runs benefit from faster form factors.
arxiv-2510-26099:
Nick Masi and Randall Balestriero argue that AI weather models should be judged place by place, not only by a global average. Standard scoring averages loss over all test points, which in weather means averaging over the whole Earth at once. That hides gaps tied to uneven human development and geography, since a model can excel in data rich regions and fail elsewhere.

Their package, SAFE, stratifies forecast scores by territory, subregion, income, and land cover, using linked data domains for each grid point. Applied to a zoo of leading AI weather models, it finds disparities across every attribute for all models. The authors use the tool to seed a fairness benchmark across lead times and climate variables.
arxiv-2510-26299:
Sofiene Kammoun, Xavier Alameda-Pineda, and Simon Leglaive compare ways to train speech enhancement models inside the latent space of a neural audio codec. A codec compresses speech into a compact latent form, either continuous vectors or discrete tokens. Speech enhancement aims to clean a noisy recording, and working in the codec latent space may be more efficient than working on raw waveforms.

Kammoun and the team test autoregressive and non autoregressive models based on the Conformer architecture, plus a baseline that fine tunes the codec encoder itself. Predicting continuous latents consistently beat discrete token prediction. Autoregressive models gave higher quality but lower intelligibility and efficiency, while encoder fine tuning gave the strongest enhancement scores at the cost of worse codec reconstruction.
arxiv-2510-26399:
Gabriella G Damas, with four co-authors, designs a way to control quantum states held in coupled oscillators. These devices, called Kerr nonlinear oscillators, shift their tones as they fill with energy. When two are linked, their tones can crowd together, so picking out one change without touching others gets hard.

Damas and her co-authors trace the crowding to simple ratios between the two shifts, then set the ratio to a complex value that acts like a number with no clean fraction form. That move clears the clashes. They work out the full rules for the device, with all small shifts counted, and test the plan in simulation. It built paired states and four-photon states with fidelity above ninety-nine point nine percent, and it held up under loss and heat.
arxiv-2510-26999:
Adithya Neelakantan, Pratik Satpute, Prerna Shinde, and Tejas Devang describe a smart classroom system that joins artificial intelligence with connected devices. Schools face proxy attendance, weak personal support, disengaged students, and wasted energy. Their platform attacks all four problems in one design built for live classroom use.

Attendance uses two checks, an RFID card scan plus WiFi confirmation, to block fraud. A context-aware tutor answers from teacher materials and makes quizzes, while a test generator eases assessment work. A campus module adjusts lights, air quality, and heat from sensor readings. Simulated tests suggest the system monitors well in real time, supports wider engagement, and can scale to larger settings.
arxiv-2510-27299:
Leilei Liu, Jieheng Zeng, and Hu Zhao build a theory of noncommutative Poisson extensions in this 2025 paper. Noncommutative algebra studies systems where the order of operations matters, so swapping factors changes results. A Poisson bracket is a rule that pairs two quantities and measures how they interact. Their work uses a doubled, shifted form of that rule.

They show the doubled rule turns a certain homology, a way of counting holes in algebra, into a graded Lie algebra, a structured set of brackets. The extension also fits with Hamiltonian reduction, a way of shrinking a system by its symmetries. The structures do not depend on which clean stand-in for the algebra is chosen. They also induce matching structures on spaces of representations, the concrete forms an algebra can take.
arxiv-2510-27499:
Michaël De San Féliciano, Christophe Adessi, and five other co-authors probe how heat crosses metal-silicon borders, in a 2025 study. Chips keep shrinking, and heat stuck at the border between metal and silicon can choke them. A second heat channel may exist there, carried by electrons handing energy to phonons, the lattice's vibrations. Decades on, its existence is still disputed.

The team computes the crossing from first principles paired with a Green's function method for out-of-balance flow. They correct that method for how carriers stray from equilibrium near the border; the fix can reach fifteen percent. Checked against lab data for gold, platinum, and aluminum on silicon, the results split. At gold-silicon borders, phonon-to-phonon flow rules and the electron channel is negligible. For aluminum on silicon, the contrast points the other way.
arxiv-2511-00499:
Yoav Simhon, Alex Segal, Ofer Amrani, and Erez Etzion improve small particle detectors built from a prism-shaped scintillator with silicon sensors at the corners. Light from a passing particle spreads through the prism, and earlier analytic methods read that pattern to estimate where the particle hit and how much energy it left, with moderate accuracy. The team replaces the analytic step with machine learning.

Simulated cosmic muons and energetic oxygen ions, generated with the GEANT4 toolkit, trained gradient boosting models such as XGBoost and LightGBM. Both beat the analytic baseline at position and energy estimation. Hybrid strategies were tested too: plain hybrid boosting added little, but a probing strategy gave measurable gains, including for energy transfer estimates. The results suit compact detectors for physics, tomography, and space missions.
arxiv-2511-00699:
Sophie Li and six co-authors trim the cost of careful reasoning at inference time. Language models reason better when they generate several candidate solutions, but the standard best-of-N approach pays full price for every branch, including hopeless ones. An earlier fix, self-truncation, cuts weak paths early yet judges them by consistency habits rather than by quality directly.

Their method, KAPPA, scores branches with a principled mix of three latent signals: divergence from the pack, confidence, and entropy. Exploration keeps diversity early, then low-scoring branches are pruned step by step. On grade-school and competition math benchmarks, with two mid-size models, KAPPA held accuracy while cutting peak memory by about sixty percent and total token generation by about ninety percent against best-of-N. Smaller models also ran more stably.
arxiv-2511-01099:
Zhenqiao Cheng, Chongjun Ouyang, and Nicola Marchetti analyze a new antenna technology for wireless links. In a pinching antenna system, small active elements can be repositioned along dielectric waveguides, reshaping the radiation pattern to fight path loss. The paper combines that idea with hybrid digital and analog beamforming.

The authors characterize the channel capacity of the combined, tri-hybrid system. They derive the best beamformer in both the digital and analog domains, and the best placement of the pinching antennas. They then obtain closed form upper and lower bounds on capacity. That yields a scaling law in the number of antennas. Numerical results confirm the bounds are tight and show a notable gain over conventional hybrid beamforming with the same number of radio chains.
arxiv-2511-01599:
M. Ertug Pihtili and six colleagues work on integrated sensing and communication, the 6G idea of making one radio system double as a radar. A bistatic setup, with transmitter and receiver apart, must estimate both the angle and the Doppler shift of targets, but reflections from static surroundings, called clutter, can swamp the sensing signal.

The team proposes a clutter suppression method built on two-dimensional root-MUSIC, an algorithm that extracts angle and Doppler jointly. Simulations show the method suppresses strong background clutter effectively, estimates target parameters accurately, and improves the signal-to-clutter-and-noise ratio, outperforming the prior benchmark methods. The result is a step toward reliable sensing in the denser, higher-frequency networks planned for 6G.
arxiv-2511-01799:
John Joseph Carrasco and Suna Zekioglu rebuild quantum field theory actions from scattering data. Standard Lagrangian forms prize compactness and off-shell symmetry. That can hide the structure of what experiments actually measure. Their framework treats gauge-invariant scattering amplitudes as the defining data of a theory. Effective field theories count too.

The focus is double-copy theories, where gravity amplitudes factor into gauge theory parts. The authors promote color-dual amplitude numerators to quantum operators. This exposes new local operator content at each multiplicity, step by step. It also yields actions that fit the double copy. Applied to the tree-level double copy between Einstein gravity and Yang-Mills theory, the method rebuilds the Einstein-Hilbert action's operator expansion from gauge parts. Color-kinematics duality thus extends from amplitudes to actions and states.
arxiv-2511-01899:
Krishna Kingkar Pathak uses a matched pair of wells to watch how swapping hydrogen for its heavier isotope deuterium changes quantum tunneling across hydrogen bonds. Isotope substitution is a sharp probe of tunneling. Tunneling itself shapes structure and dynamics in chemistry, biology, and solid-state physics. Yet many treatments hide the physics inside purely numerical tools.

His model combines a Cornell-type potential with a double-well Schrödinger approach, producing semi-analytical wavefunctions and tunneling splittings that display the isotope dependence openly. The study maps how splittings scale with isotope mass and how barrier width and curvature move them, then compares the trends with typical experimental and computational results. The framework is offered as a general method for double-well tunneling, with applications from spectroscopy to enzyme catalysis and materials.
arxiv-2511-02199:
Seong-ho Lee and Yongho Jeon propose a disarmingly simple way to spot outliers in data with very many dimensions, a setting where classical detectors break down. Traditional methods lean on behaviour that only emerges when the sample is large relative to a fixed dimension. The authors instead exploit the geometry of high-dimensional space itself, turning the usual curse of dimensionality into an asset.

They define two statistics from each point's pattern of distances, or inner products, to every other point. Theory shows that as dimension grows, these statistics open a persistent gap between outliers and ordinary points. Practical procedures follow, including a simple clustering algorithm and a distribution-free test based on random rotations. Simulations and real data tests showed a better balance of detection power and false positive control than existing methods.
arxiv-2511-02299:
Srijeet Bhattacharjee, Eknath Ghate, Shivansh Pandey, and Sriram Veerapaneni solve two linked problems about representations of a matrix group over a finite field, studied modulo a prime. The group is GL2 over the field with q elements. The first problem asks how the tensor product of two of its modular representations breaks into pieces, a Clebsch-Gordan type decomposition. It is familiar from classical representation theory but much harder in the modular world.

The authors prove that decomposition theorem in full. They then apply it to predict the structure of quotients of symmetric power representations by submodules in the theta filtration. They give a direct proof of that structure as well, showing the quotients are built from principal series representations. The pair of results gives the modular theory of this group a firmer algebraic skeleton.
arxiv-2511-02599:
Max Norris, Kobi Gal, and Sahan Bulathwela predict what a student will do next by treating their learning history as a sentence to complete. Knowledge tracing asks how well a student knows each skill, given their past answers, to personalise teaching. Standard models consume correctness, skill tags, and timestamps but throw away the actual text of the questions. That text carries real pedagogical information about what is being asked and how hard it is.

Their method rewrites both the student's history and the question content as text sequences. It lets a pretrained large language model, with all its reading ability, forecast the next response as next-token prediction. Experiments showed notable gains over leading neural knowledge tracing models. Generalisation was notably better to questions and students the system had never seen, the cold-start cases where tutoring systems are usually weakest.
arxiv-2511-02899:
Siyu Zhu, Arthur Ramirez, and Sergey Syzranov use entropy to read the hidden states of frustrated magnets. In such materials, the atoms' magnetic moments cannot all settle at once, and cooling releases entropy in a low-temperature peak. That peak reflects spin states tied to the ground states of classical models on the same lattice. Their 2025 paper simulates the entropy for higher-spin layered triangular systems and for SCGO lattices.

They then compare measured entropy in three strongly frustrated compounds with values the classical models allow. The match suggests the lowest states of the layered compounds act like doublet states on single sites. The work shows how a bulk heat measure can reveal fine state structure, and calls for sharper thermodynamic measurements in these materials.
arxiv-2511-03299:
A R Shelke and a multi-author team probe why electrons in the layered metal cobalt telluride behave less sluggishly than expected. The material hosts topological band features, yet its cobalt bands lack the narrowing that strong electron repulsion causes in a sister oxide. Hard X-ray and related spectroscopies let the team measure that repulsion directly.

They find the on-site repulsion is notably smaller in the telluride than in the oxide. Cluster simulations tie the gap to charge transfer that runs in the opposite, negative direction. In plain terms, electrons spill between cobalt and tellurium in a way that softens their mutual push. Linking transfer sign to repulsion strength helps explain how chemistry tunes correlation in topological metals.
arxiv-2511-03399:
Andrea Cremaschi, Manuele Leonelli, and Gherardo Varando estimate cause and effect for category data with a fully Bayesian staged tree method. Staged trees are graph models that can show uneven, context-bound links which simpler graphs miss. Their method places flexible prior beliefs over both tree shape and its numbers.

Some priors favor lean trees, one new prior favors readable dependence patterns, and an extension lets continuous measures join the learning. Sampling runs with split-and-merge moves yield many plausible trees, from which average treatment effects and their uncertainty follow. Tests on artificial and real data check whether the effects come out right. The approach suits health and social data where categories dominate and symmetry cannot be assumed.
arxiv-2511-03499:
Gabriel Spadon, Vaishnav Vaidheeswaran, and Claudio DiBacco couple port climate likeness with ship movement to forecast where marine invaders may spread. Shipping carries species worldwide in ballast and on hulls, with heavy ecological and economic costs. Classic risk checks need ballast and traffic records that often stay incomplete, leaving blind spots.

Climate profiles describe each port's marine conditions, while tracking data map vessel flows between ports. Clustering and metric learning find climate twins and gauge survival odds along each route. A time-aware link model projects how routes themselves may shift. Together, the coupled predictors promise global coverage even where detailed ballast records are missing.
arxiv-2511-03699:
Francesco Corso, Francesco Pierri, and Gianmarco De Francisci Morales probe whether language models lean toward conspiracy thinking. Conspiracy beliefs fuel misinformation and institutional distrust, and models used as stand-ins for human groups could import those leanings into studies. Validated mindset surveys, adapted from psychology, were given to several models under varied prompts.

The team also checks whether leanings shift with the persona a model is asked to play, and how easily prompting can push a model into a conspiratorial stance. Results map which models carry a baseline tendency and which bend under light pressure. Such audits matter before models are trusted to simulate public opinion or to moderate charged topics.
arxiv-2511-03799:
Tatiana S Parlanti and Carlos A Catania review how intrusion detection systems handle time, arguing that most still spot attacks only after serious damage is done. Their framework sorts network detection methods by how they treat time, from static checks on single flows to models that follow sequences across many windows.

Drawing on more than forty studies from 2020 to 2025, the pair find that sequential and window-based methods cover the widest range of attack stages, from reconnaissance through impact. Widely used datasets, they show, over-represent late-stage attacks and hold back early detection. The taxonomy is offered as groundwork for systems that anticipate threats rather than only react.
arxiv-2511-04699:
Haneen Al-Homoud leads eight authors building Cross-Lingual SynthDocs, a synthetic corpus for Arabic OCR. Arabic documents lack the large training sets that document AI needs. Their corpus holds over two and a half million samples in total.

It includes one and a half million text samples and two hundred seventy thousand annotated tables. Hundreds of thousands of charts drawn from real data join them. Authentic scanned backgrounds, bilingual layouts, and diacritic-aware fonts mimic real Arabic pages. Fine-tuning Qwen-2.5-VL on the corpus improved word and character error rates across several public Arabic benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-05099:
Mrinal Kanti Roychowdhury offers a beginner-friendly tour of optimal quantization for measures that live on spheres and on sphere curves. Quantization sums up a spread of values with a small set of points, chosen to lose as little as one can.

The study builds the needed geometry first: great and small circles, geodesic distance, sphere triangles, and Voronoi cells on a sphere. It then gives clear models for both smooth curves and finite point sets on the sphere. Worked forms for quantization error and dimension help new readers enter a niche field with firm ground.
arxiv-2511-05299:
Zhenyu Yang and co-authors present LiveStar, a live streaming assistant that watches video as it flows and replies at the right moments. Offline video models can scan a whole clip first, but a live aid must act frame by frame and choose when to speak.

LiveStar uses adaptive streaming decoding to stay always on and proactive. A training plan aligns video and language step by step, so replies stay in sync with events. The design targets live help where late or off-beat replies fail, such as guided tasks and live event support.
arxiv-2511-05399:
Shubhr Singh and co-authors make audio fingerprinting tougher against the warped, squeezed clips that flood platforms like TikTok. A fingerprint should name the source track even after heavy edits, so rights and credit can be traced.

Their method uses a pretrained music foundation model as its backbone, a fresh base for this task. They also widen data augmentation in training, so the model learns from many kinds of damage at once. Tests gauge how the new fingerprints hold up when clips are sped, pitched, or mixed, next to past neural methods.
arxiv-2511-05699:
Thuy Ngoc Nguyen, Jeffrey Flagg, and Cleotilde Gonzalez study how reading other minds shapes play in rock-paper-scissors. Theory of mind, the skill of tracking others' beliefs and aims, matters when people face off against people or machines. How its parts interact during such contests was unclear.

Players took standard theory-of-mind tests, then played repeated games against bots and humans. The team measured how reasoning, spatial skill, and emotion reading related to performance. People did spot patterns in opponents' moves. Yet most single test scores failed to predict who played well. Recursive thinking, thinking about what the other thinks, was the one moderate predictor. Modeling split the influences into two hidden factors with opposite effects.
arxiv-2511-05799:
Venus Keus and Stephen King revive an old idea for the early universe in light of new telescope data. Chaotic inflation with a simple mass term predicts the right tilt in the cosmic microwave background but too many gravitational waves. Quantum corrections change the picture, adding a field that can also serve as today's dark energy.

Their model, called RIDE, couples the field to gravity in a non-standard way, which lowers the wave signal enough to fit the older Planck data. Adding a small quartic term then raises both the tilt and the wave signal. With the coupling set near one, the authors find a good fit to the new Atacama Cosmology Telescope results.
arxiv-2511-05999:
Chennan Wang leads a team probing a layered kagome superconductor with muons, particles used as tiny local magnets. The material, a titanium-doped cesium vanadium antimonide, is notable for lacking both static magnetism and long-range charge order. The team asks what excitations actually dominate inside it.

Muon spin tests show the local response is ruled by orbital effects with a split energy level. Electrons stay mobile and weakly magnetic down to low heat and high fields, proof that no fixed magnetism sits there. Below a set point the nuclear field spread widens, which the authors tie to small local strains in the lattice, perhaps orbital ordering. They conclude the orbital effects are built into this kagome lattice, with spin-orbit coupling steering how the lattice moves.
arxiv-2511-06099:
A Mirjalili and co-authors test whether a universal rule governs how atomic nuclei alter the quarks inside paired nucleons. When nucleons bind in a nucleus, their internal structure functions shift, a puzzle known as the EMC effect. Short-range correlated pairs, two nucleons briefly close together, are thought to drive much of that shift.

The team builds a modified universal function from pair distributions and applies it to a nonsinglet structure function measured in neutrino-nucleus scattering. Calculations inside a standard parton framework confirm the ratio for this function behaves universally, as earlier shown for another structure function. They then rewrite the EMC weight function in those terms. That yields the nuclear structure function they set out to extract.
arxiv-2511-06399:
G. J. M. Luna, A. Dobrotka, and M. Orio mine archival observations from the TESS space telescope for three nova systems after their eruptions. The team searched for orbital periods and white dwarf spin periods, and for changes in those periods over time. Novae are stellar explosions on accreting white dwarfs, and their clocks reveal how the systems evolve afterward.

One nova showed a spin period near one hundred seventeen seconds that is lengthening at one of the fastest rates ever recorded, hinting at a magnetic propeller state. The team measured a new orbital period for a second nova and confirmed both known periods in a third, an intermediate polar. The results stress what steady, high-cadence monitoring can uncover.
arxiv-2511-06599:
Siddharth Agarwal, Maria Rodriguez, and Rajkumar Buyya present Saarthi, a platform that tunes serverless cloud functions to each incoming request. Function-as-a-service computing bills only for execution, yet cold starts, fixed configurations, and workload-blind scheduling cause uneven performance and surprise costs. Static sizing wastes resources on small requests and starves large ones.

Saarthi reads the request payload to anticipate resource needs, sizes functions accordingly, and orchestrates requests across configurations. A redundancy mechanism guards against faults, while an integer linear program keeps the number of running functions near optimal for throughput and cost. Built on OpenFaaS, it raised throughput, cut costs, and held service targets with small added delay.
arxiv-2511-06799:
Guanxi Li works in intersection theory, a branch of algebraic geometry that counts and classifies how geometric objects meet. The paper generalizes Fulton's Residual Intersection Theorem for the Segre class, an invariant that measures how a scheme sits inside its surroundings. The setting is schemes whose parts are regularly embedded, a well-behaved class of pieces.

Li expresses the Segre classes of such schemes through the Chern classes of the normal bundles of the parts and their intersections. Formulas are given for two cases: when the parts meet transversely. When the ideal sheaf of the scheme, after blowing up along one part, factors into the exceptional divisor part and the residual scheme part. The results give geometers concrete tools for computing these invariants.
arxiv-2511-06899:
Haofeng Wang and Yu Zhang argue that judging vision-language models only by their final answers misses whether the reasoning was sound. A model can reach the right answer through flawed steps. Their metric, the Reasoning Process Tree Score, organizes a model's reasoning steps into a tree and scores the faithfulness of each step using the tree's structure.

Weights adjust dynamically, so the metric grades the whole chain and pinpoints where it breaks. To test it, the authors built RPTS-Eval, a benchmark of 374 images and 390 reasoning instances with reliable visual and textual clues as leaf nodes. Evaluating models such as GPT-4o and LLaVA-Next exposed weaknesses in multimodal reasoning and gaps between open-source and commercial systems.
arxiv-2511-06999:
Jessica Renz, Frederik Witt, and Iain G Johnston bring algebra to evolutionary accumulation models, which learn and predict the order in which evolutionary features, such as mutations or traits, accumulate over time. Inference in this field is usually done by numerical optimization. The authors instead exploit the polynomial structure built into the evolutionary process itself, a route they present as complementary to the standard statistical machinery.

Their method first constructs a semi-algebraic set of all parameter values consistent with a given dataset, and only then maximizes the likelihood within that set. Worked examples show the approach agrees with the solutions of several established statistical accumulation models. They also discuss the extra information the algebraic description carries beyond those models, since the full feasible set, not just one best fit, becomes visible.
arxiv-2511-07399:
Tianrui Feng and thirteen co-authors rebuild streaming diffusion for live video rather than offline rendering. Image-based streaming generators powered early live products but could not hold temporal consistency. Video diffusion models fix consistency yet are built for batched throughput, the opposite of live streaming's strict deadlines: minimal time to first frame and a hard per-frame budget with low jitter. StreamDiffusionV2 is a training-free pipeline built around those service-level objectives.

Its pieces include a deadline-aware batching scheduler, a block scheduler, a rolling key-value cache guided by sink tokens. A motion-aware noise controller, all orchestrated to parallelize diffusion across steps and layers over multiple GPUs. Without TensorRT or quantization, it renders a first frame within half a second and streams at about fifty-eight frames per second with a fourteen-billion-parameter model on four H100 GPUs.
arxiv-2511-07499:
Kwanyoung Kim seeks firmer ground for guidance methods that sharpen diffusion model outputs. Popular guidance improves a target result by deliberately worsening another, using hand-designed distortions. That trick works in practice but lacks a principled basis and can misfire.

Adversarial Sinkhorn Attention Guidance reframes attention scores through optimal transport, the math of moving mass at least cost. The Sinkhorn algorithm then disrupts that transport cost on purpose to steer sampling. Guidance becomes a defined operation rather than folklore. The aim is reliable sampling with fewer artifacts, giving practitioners a method they can reason about and tune with confidence.
arxiv-2511-07599:
The CHROMA Collaboration with Kord Valeshabadi and Rezaie test how well theory predicts photon pairs from proton collisions. Prompt diphoton production at the Large Hadron Collider probes proton structure. Within transverse-momentum factorization, predictions hinge on unintegrated parton distributions that track partons sideways motion.

Three distribution models face ATLAS data at thirteen tera-electronvolts across many observables, from photon momenta to pair mass. Several partonic channels, including a loop-driven gluon route, enter the comparison. Some models track data better in certain ranges. The verdict helps collider physicists pick distribution sets and sharpens searches that use photon pairs as background or signal.
arxiv-2511-07699:
David Autor, Andrew Caplin, and Daniel Martin show a well-meant training habit that backfires. In high-stakes tasks, missing a real case costs far more than a false alarm, so models are often trained with lopsided losses matching human trade-offs. That standard alignment practice can still misfire.

In two focal applications, training the model as if errors cost equally, then adjusting its predictions afterward to honor the real trade-offs, beats baking the asymmetry into training. Human objectives belong at the decision stage, not always in the loss. The result reshapes how teams should align diagnostic and screening systems with expert judgment.
arxiv-2511-07799:
Renyong Guan and Yuxi Hu prove stability for planar viscous shock waves in relaxed compressible fluid flow. The setting is three dimensional, and a Maxwell type rule replaces the classic Newtonian stress relation. A shock wave here is a sharp traveling front, allowed to shift from its starting position.

With small shock strength and small starting disturbances, the shifted wave is shown to be nonlinearly stable over time. The proof uses weighted relative entropy, contraction with shifts, and higher order energy estimates. As the relaxation value tends to zero, solutions converge globally to those of the classical Navier Stokes system.
arxiv-2511-07899:
Ihab Tabbara, Yuxuan Yang, and Hussein Sibai certify safety for learned controllers with statistics instead of blind trust. Reachability analysis can verify safety and synthesize safe controllers, but computing its value function grows brutally expensive in high dimensions. Learned approximations dodge the cost yet lose guarantees.

Ensembles of safety filters, checked with conformal prediction, restore statistical assurance. The method quantifies how much to trust a learned value function state by state. Autonomous systems in cars, robots, and aircraft need exactly this middle path: learning for scale, statistics for honesty about the risk that remains.
arxiv-2511-08099: Marija Bliznac Trebjesanin and Pavao Radic study whether certain number pairs with the D4 property can grow into larger sets. A D4 pair has the feature that the product of its two elements, plus four, is a perfect square. They focus on pairs where the second element is a fixed multiple of the first, for multipliers seven, eight, ten, eleven, twelve, and thirteen.
arxiv-2511-08699:
Nishita Jadoo, David Brown, and Charles Evans simulate what happens when a small elastic body swings past a black hole on a nearly unbound orbit. The body is modeled as a hyperelastic sphere, a rubber-like object whose parts pull on each other while curved spacetime pulls on all of them.

The calculation uses a general relativistic finite element scheme that follows many mass elements at once in Schwarzschild coordinates. Afterward the team measures how the body's center of mass drifts from its starting orbit, how orbital and spin angular momentum shift, and how much orbital energy sinks into internal elastic motion. The multipolar equations of motion match the simulation through quadrupole order. In one sample run the encounter captures the body into an extremely eccentric bound orbit.
arxiv-2511-08899:
Howard Ho, Ebenezer Essel, and Pierre Edwardson simulate a circular synthetic jet blowing into a crossflow, the kind of actuator engineers use to keep airflow attached to wings and blades. Three knobs are varied one at a time across nine cases: blowing ratio, stroke ratio, and the height of the incoming boundary layer relative to the nozzle.

The three-dimensional unsteady simulations freeze the free-stream speed while sweeping jet velocity, actuation frequency between two hundred and four hundred hertz, and boundary-layer Reynolds number. Low frequencies shed tilted vortex rings with trailing pairs, while high frequencies expel tightly packed structures, and the thickest boundary layer spawns hairpin vortices. Jets under thin to moderate boundary layers keep near-wall momentum farthest downstream, marking them as the best candidates for separation control. Tertiary vortices near the wall drive downwash and raise skin friction.
arxiv-2511-09299:
Helena Monke and four co-authors turn neural networks into exact decision trees, so their reasoning can be read off exactly. Explanation tools like LIME and SHAP often misdescribe what a network actually computed. Tree conversions promise faithful explanations, but earlier versions lacked exactness, scalability, or clarity.

Their algorithm, RENTT, computes an exactly matching decision tree while staying lean in time and memory. The extension covers convolutional and recurrent networks, non-ReLU activations, and bias terms, all with rigorous proofs. From the tree they derive ground-truth feature weights for whole models, input regions, or single choices. Tests show only RENTT recovers the true explanations, unlike the usual approximations.
arxiv-2511-09399:
Slimane Zaim and two co-authors examine a Schwarzschild anti-de Sitter black hole. They ask how noncommutative geometry changes its thermodynamics. Noncommutative geometry blurs points at tiny scales, adding a dial that gauges the blur. They ask how that dial reshapes the black hole's temperature, entropy, and stability.

The thermodynamic functions depend critically on the noncommutativity dial while still obeying the first law of thermodynamics. Stability analysis reveals a phase transition at a critical point, and the overall behavior resembles a van der Waals fluid. Noncommutativity also adds a correction term to the surface temperature. The authors place the parameter near the Planck scale and treat it as a new thermodynamic variable.
arxiv-2511-09799:
Lyes Smaili and Soulaimane Berkane design a feedback controller that steers an autonomous agent safely through unknown, obstacle-filled spaces using only local sensing. Their controller starts from an unconstrained penalty formulation and adjusts any nominal input through a closed-form rule. The result blends the nominal command with its projection onto the obstacle boundary, keeping a user-set safety margin intact by construction.

The law needs only the distance and bearing to obstacles, with no map, switching logic, or set construction. When the nominal input follows the gradient of a navigation potential, the authors prove almost global convergence to the goal, and unwanted equilibria are unstable under a mild curvature condition. Simulations in complex two- and three-dimensional scenes show safe, smooth navigation at low computational cost.
arxiv-2511-09899:
Chen Li, Ryan Requist, and E. K. U. Gross formulate a density functional theory for electrons and nuclei moving as one, going beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation that freezes nuclear motion apart from electronic motion. Coupled motion matters for processes such as proton transfer, where the standard separation misses real effects. The authors identify a small set of densities that carry the full dynamics.

They prove that the nuclear probability density, the conditional electronic density, and the current density jointly determine the full time-evolving electron-nuclear wave function. A Kohn-Sham scheme built on those quantities reproduces the exact densities, leaving the search for good approximations as the remaining task. A driven proton transfer model shows an adiabatic extension of a beyond-Born-Oppenheimer version capturing the main nonadiabatic effects under slow driving.
arxiv-2511-09999:
Saket S. Chaturvedi, Gaurav Bagwe, Lan Zhang, Pan He, and Xiaoyong Yuan introduce MOBA, a backdoor attack on LiDAR-based 3D object detection that is designed to work in the physical world. Backdoors hide malicious behavior in a model during training, but digital triggers often fail outdoors because they ignore how real materials reflect LiDAR pulses. Physically built triggers, in turn, are often unoptimized.

MOBA models the trigger's material directly, selecting titanium dioxide for its strong diffuse reflectivity and weather resilience. A simulation pipeline approximates a standard reflectance model in an angle-independent way and scales by distance so the digital trigger mimics the physical one. Across leading LiDAR and camera-LiDAR fusion detectors, the attack succeeded at a rate above ninety-three percent, beating prior methods by over forty points.
arxiv-2511-10299:
Laurent Loosveldt, Yassine Nachit, Ivan Nourdin, and Ciprian Tudor study the smoothness of probability densities for the Rosenblatt process, a non-Gaussian process arising from long-range dependence. Working inside Malliavin calculus, they prove that finite-dimensional vectors of the process are nondegenerate in the Malliavin sense. As a consequence, their densities are Schwartz functions: smooth and rapidly decreasing at infinity.

The proof establishes that the determinant of the Malliavin matrix has finite moments of every negative order, exploiting the special structure of variables in the second Wiener chaos. The authors also derive exponential-type upper bounds for the partial derivatives of these densities. Smooth density results of this kind underpin limit theorems and statistical procedures for strongly dependent data.
arxiv-2511-10699:
Hongchao Shu and eight co-authors present DualVision ArthroNav, a navigation system for arthroscopic surgery, where a camera inside a joint gives surgeons a narrow, disorienting view. Optical tracking systems help but constrain the workspace and disrupt workflow, while systems relying only on the arthroscope camera suffer drift, scale ambiguity, and failures under fast motion or occlusion.

Their design rigidly mounts an external camera on the arthroscope. The external view supplies stable visual odometry and absolute localization. The internal video supports dense scene reconstruction. Together they cancel the drift and scale problems of monocular methods. Experiments gave an average trajectory error of about one millimeter and a target registration error of about two millimeters, which the authors call practical and cost-efficient for clinical use.
arxiv-2511-10799:
Manish Dhakal, Venkat R. Dasari, Rajshekhar Sunderraman, and Yi Ding propose Graph Feature Tuning, a leaner way to adapt transformer models to point cloud data. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning updates only a small slice of a model's weights, cutting cost and memory, but generic recipes underperform on point clouds, and earlier point-cloud-specific versions still tune more than necessary.

Their method learns a dynamic graph from the model's tokenized input using a lightweight graph convolution network, then feeds those graph features into deeper layers through skip connections and efficient cross-attention. Only this small machinery trains. Across object classification and segmentation benchmarks, Graph Feature Tuning rivaled existing methods while reducing the number of trainable parameters further. The code is publicly available.
arxiv-2511-10899:
Farima Fatahi Bayat, Pouya Pezeshkpour, and Estevam Hruschka show that giving a language model a code interpreter can make its answers better and its reasoning worse. Even when the tool is chosen and run correctly, models tend to treat its output as a substitute for thinking. They present solutions that look right but lack coherent justification, a failure the authors name tool-induced myopia.

They study the effect on PYMATH, a benchmark of 1,679 competition-level problems where Python helps but does not suffice. Tool-equipped models gained up to about nineteen points of final-answer accuracy, yet lost reasoning comparisons against their tool-free counterparts far more often, and heavier tool use meant shallower reasoning. Errors shifted from arithmetic slips to global failures of logic and assumptions. A preference-optimization fix that treats tool output as evidence improved both accuracy and depth.
arxiv-2511-11099:
Vicenç Méndez and Rosa Flaquer-Galmés study how long a wandering particle spends in each region of a patchy material, and whether those shares settle to steady values over time. When they do not, the motion is called non-ergodic, and time averages mislead. The authors use the Feynman-Kac frame, which links such timing questions to a solvable equation.

They treat two cases where spread speed varies in space: a step-wise profile and a power-law profile. Each gives named spread shapes for the timing shares, some of which signal broken ergodicity. As a key exponent varies, both models cross from broken to steady behavior, and simulations match the math.
arxiv-2511-11399:
Rosario Napoli, Antonio Celesti, and their colleagues propose adding a knowledge completion phase to graph machine learning systems that run on graph databases. Such systems learn from interconnected data, but they usually train on graphs that look incomplete even though hidden knowledge sits inside them. Training on a fragmented view can distort what the model concludes from the data.

Their architecture completes the knowledge graph first, using scalable transitive relationships: links that carry information across many nodes under a decay rule, so influence fades with distance. Experiments show completion reshapes both the graph's topology and its overall dynamics, which the authors argue makes the added phase essential for trustworthy results.
arxiv-2511-11899:
Xi Li and thirteen co-authors build Frame-to-Outcome, an end-to-end surgical video system. It reads operation video and recognizes the surgeon's gestures. It then tests if those gestures predict how patients recover. Fine-grained study of what happens inside an operation has long resisted automation.

Transformer models classify frame by frame through one step of robot-assisted prostate surgery. That step is the nerve-sparing step. Short gestures of about two seconds are detected with solid accuracy. Features from gesture counts, durations, and transitions predict outcomes about as well as human notes. Effect directions agree across shared features. Objective skill signals, with no manual coding, could feed training and quality review.
arxiv-2511-11999:
Zeyu Lu and seven co-authors make predictive mutation testing cheaper and broader with WITNESS. Mutation testing grades a test suite by seeding bugs. It checks if the tests catch them. Predictive versions guess mutant outcomes to skip costly runs. Deep learning predictors cost so much they defeat that purpose.

They also handle only mutants inside methods. Real tools generate mutants outside methods too. A lightweight approach replaces the heavy models. It covers outside-method mutants as well, restoring real-world use. Fine-grained prediction at each mutant location keeps the feedback developers use. Test quality tooling helps only if teams can afford to run it.
arxiv-2511-12799:
Rylan Malarchick asks a practical question for quantum hardware teams: when does numerically optimizing control pulses actually beat textbook recipes? The GRAPE algorithm can, in principle, shape microwave pulses that erase all coherent error in a qubit gate. Malarchick compares Gaussian, DRAG, and GRAPE pulses on a three-level transmon model matched to IQM Garnet hardware, separating the error budget into coherent error, relaxation, dephasing. Control noise, and testing robustness to the frequency errors that plague real calibration.

The answer is often that the simple recipe suffices. Properly calibrated DRAG already sits near the decoherence floor at twenty-nanosecond gates. It proved hardier than GRAPE against frequency detuning, while GRAPE won on amplitude robustness and at very short gate times. The paper turns those findings into calibration guidance for three regimes and ships an open-source framework, QubitPulseOpt, so labs can rerun the comparison on their own hardware numbers.
arxiv-2511-12999:
Harrison H. Li and four co-authors estimate crop yields from photographs, carefully enough for insurance decisions. The trusted method, cutting and weighing sample plots at harvest, is slow and expensive, so zones get few measurements. Their approach trains a vision model to predict yields from field photos, then uses prediction-powered inference: the photos multiply the data. A smaller set of real crop cuts, recalibrated through a control function that uses field coordinates, keeps the estimates honest. The method was trained on nearly twenty thousand real crop cuts and photos of rice and maize fields in sub-Saharan Africa.

The resulting zone averages are provably unbiased and never worse than crop cuts alone. In practice, even zones with twenty fields gained effective sample size, up to seventy-three percent more for rice, with shorter confidence intervals.
arxiv-2511-13099:
Doanh C. Bui and five co-authors teach pathology models new cancer tasks without forgetting old ones. Whole slide images are gigabytes each, so retraining a unified model per task is expensive. MergeSlide treats lifelong learning as model merging: each new task is defined with class-aware prompts, fine-tuned briefly on a vision-language pathology foundation model. It is then merged into the shared model, limiting interference between tasks.

At test time the system may not know which task an image belongs to. Their prompt-aligned inference first identifies the likely task from task-level prompts, then applies that task's class prompts for the final call. Across a stream of six cancer datasets from TCGA, MergeSlide beat rehearsal-based continual learning and zero-shot vision-language baselines. It targets hospital pipelines where new tasks arrive over time.
arxiv-2511-13299:
David Muñoz-Lahoz and Pedro Tradacete construct the free Banach f-algebra generated by a Banach space. An f-algebra mixes multiplication with lattice order, so the free object must honor both structures at once. Their work extends recent results on free Banach lattices to this richer setting.

Starting from a concrete model inside functions on a dual space, they prove a structure theorem that identifies the kernel of a key seminorm. That yields a faithful picture of the free normed algebra inside continuous functions on a ball. They prove the completed algebra is semiprime in key cases and use the tools to extend lattice-algebra maps from subalgebras to larger algebras.
arxiv-2511-13499:
Anil Alan and Bart De Schutter prove feasibility guarantees for safety filters built from smoothed backup control barrier functions. Safe sets are often defined by the lowest of several smooth functions, which creates a nonsmooth edge. Replacing that minimum with a soft log-sum-exp smoothing is common, but the smoothed version needs proof that it still works as a barrier.

Under a strict safety condition, they show the smooth function qualifies as a barrier for a range of smoothing values and give an explicit lower bound for compact sets. Tail conditions extend the result to unbounded sets. Applied to backup methods, safety of the backup set and its boundary behavior suffice for feasibility.
arxiv-2511-13599:
James Tian builds a unified kernel model for repeated application of completely positive maps. Each operator-valued kernel is placed inside one Hilbert space, where composing maps becomes a matter of applying bounded creation operators to feature vectors. Keeping all iterates in a single space makes their comparison far more direct than tracking separate spaces.

From that setup Tian derives a direct formula for every iterated kernel. Main results include an explicit limit kernel for unital maps, a Stein-type decomposition, and a Radon-Nikodym form under a subunital condition. A growth law for random compositions rounds out the picture, turning limit, contractive, and domination questions into standard operator facts.
arxiv-2511-13999:
Michael Menart and Aleksandar Nikolov pin down how much work privacy costs in optimization. They study differentially private risk minimization, where an algorithm must learn from data without leaking individual records. The cost is counted in calls to a gradient oracle, and in one setting that oracle itself may only send private messages about small batches.

For non-smooth losses the authors prove lower bounds on the number of oracle calls any private method needs, and show a standard private algorithm matches them in high dimensions. For smooth losses they bound the calls under privacy alone and again find near-matching algorithms. The message is a precise price tag: private optimizers provably pay extra queries.
arxiv-2511-14099:
Jingren Liu, Shuning Xu, Qirui Yang, and three co-authors build one image restoration system that handles many kinds of damage. Photos may be blurred, noisy, dark, or compressed, and older unified methods rely on rigid task designs that adapt poorly to mixed real-world damage. Their framework, FAPE-IR, splits the job into planning and execution along frequency lines.

A frozen multimodal language model inspects each damaged image and writes a short frequency-aware restoration plan. That plan steers a diffusion executor whose mixture-of-experts module picks high or low frequency specialists. Adversarial training and a frequency loss cut artifacts. Tests across seven restoration tasks reached state-of-the-art results, with strong zero-shot handling of mixed damage.
arxiv-2511-14299:
Xiaochuan Liu, Yuanfeng Song, Xiaoming Yin, and one co-author present DataSage, a team of language model agents that mines data sets for useful findings. Automated insight discovery often fails through shallow analysis, unused domain knowledge, and buggy generated code. DataSage attacks all three weaknesses with separate mechanisms inside one multi-agent framework.

External knowledge retrieval enriches the context before analysis begins. A multi-role debate, in which agents argue from different analytical viewpoints, deepens the reasoning. Multi-path reasoning checks results along several routes to catch code and logic errors. On the InsightBench benchmark the system beat existing data insight agents at every difficulty level.
arxiv-2511-14899:
Daniel Gilo and Or Litany address editing a scene consistently from only a few input views. Given sparse photos and a text instruction, the edit must agree across all viewpoints. Past methods based on neural fields or temporal attention often create artifacts here. Their framework distills a two dimensional diffusion editor into a pretrained multi view diffusion model.

The multi view student replaces the usual neural field consolidator in score distillation. New adaptations include incremental student updates, a teacher noise schedule that prevents degeneration, and an attention change for consistency. The data driven three dimensional prior helps keep edits coherent. The method targets sparse view editing where geometry cues are limited but consistency is essential.
arxiv-2511-14999:
Fahad Alrasheedi and Hesham Ali map how United States counties resemble each other in the traits that drive electric vehicle adoption. Cutting transport emissions needs more drivers in electric cars, yet adoption varies sharply by region. State-level studies blur those local differences and can mislead policy meant for a specific county.

The authors average feature importance scores from several predictive models and use them as weights in a similarity measure between counties. Counties are then linked into a network of near twins, found through a mutual nearest-neighbor procedure. Planners can borrow playbooks from a county's network twins instead of copying distant states whose conditions do not match.
arxiv-2511-15099:
Ethan Ashby, Dean Follmann, and six co-authors fix a subtle bias in measuring how vaccine protection fades over time. Standard time-varying estimates from Cox regression can be distorted by hidden differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated people and by selection effects. The team instead uses infections that the vaccine cannot affect as a built-in control signal.

Under stated assumptions, those irrelevant infections reveal the hidden bias and let the true hazard-based effect be identified. Two estimator styles are developed, with options for monotone shapes and for several viral variants at once. As a case study, the authors revisit data modeled on a pivotal phase three COVID-19 vaccine trial.
arxiv-2511-15299:
Jialong Sun, Hongguang Zhu, and four co-authors generate synthetic X-ray security images to train detectors that spot banned items in luggage. Real scans of prohibited objects are scarce and costly to label, so data runs short. Older synthesis pipelines first cut out item foregrounds by hand, then pasted them into scenes, a slow two-stage chore that still looked artificial.

Their one-stage pipeline, Xsyn, builds whole scans from text prompts with a generative image model. A cross-attention refinement step uses the model's own attention maps to sharpen where items land and how they blend. The aim is training data that teaches detectors the real look of threats without the manual compositing bill.
arxiv-2511-15399:
Malek Telfah and Abdalla Obeidat solve the 1D Ising chain exactly when a magnetic field hits every k-th site periodically. The Ising model is a core part of statistical physics. A symmetrized transfer matrix approach yields a compact closed form for the system eigenvalues at arbitrary period. Free energy follows directly from those eigenvalues.

Exact formulas are derived for magnetization and zero field susceptibility. Explicit results cover periods one, two, and three, with the last described as novel. Spin correlations yield the correlation length and position dependent strengths. Wider impurity spacing suppresses thermodynamic response in a simple scaling law. The solution serves as a benchmark for diluted and quasiperiodic magnetic systems.
arxiv-2511-15499:
Ruiqing Yang, Kaixin Zhang, and three co-authors propose a new order for building images with models that predict one piece at a time. Such models work like language models, which write one word at a time. Old orders are slow, building token by token, or use many scales at once, which is hard to run.

Their method, called Expanding Autoregressive Representation, copies how human sight moves from the center outward. Image tokens appear in a spiral that starts at the center and grows, keeping near areas together and letting steps run in parallel. A flexible rule changes how many tokens are made at each step. On ImageNet tests, the method gave a strong mix of image quality and speed.
arxiv-2511-15999:
Andrey O. Leonov and Kaito Nakamura introduce skyrmionium meta-matter, a magnetic crystal mixing two kinds of swirling spin textures. Skyrmions are stable whirlpool-like spin patterns with a topological charge, while skyrmioniums are ring-shaped textures with zero charge. Arranged in periodic lattices, the mixture mimics the compositional richness of atomic materials.

Pure skyrmionium lattices prove unstable and relax into spirals, but a small fraction of skyrmions pins the mixed crystals into stable forms. Compositions host several metastable arrangements with distinct symmetries, switchable by changing lattice spacing through pressure or strain. Collective spin dynamics shows extra resonant modes beyond those of ordinary skyrmion lattices, including hybrid motions where breathing rings drive confined skyrmions in circles.
arxiv-2511-16299:
Idris Delsol, Omar Fawzi, Li Gao, and Mizanur Rahaman work out the best possible rates for emulating one quantum channel with another when both channels are idempotent. Idempotent here means each channel leaves its own output range unchanged. They consider three settings: no help, shared classical randomness, and unlimited shared entanglement.

For the first two settings the capacity has a single-letter formula set by the channels' shape vectors, shared randomness adds nothing, and emulation cannot be reversed. An efficient algorithm approximates the capacity to any precision, and a strong converse holds. With entanglement, the smallest error at every finite block length is fixed exactly by one number, the length of the shape vector. Emulation becomes reversible, and exact emulation needs only finitely many maximally entangled states.
arxiv-2511-16499:
Zahra Basiri and four co-authors build a tunable semiconductor laser whose external mirror is a resonant electro-optic metasurface, removing the moving parts that limit ordinary tunable lasers. Fast, stable wavelength control matters for optical communication, sensing, and spectroscopy, while temperature or current tuning is slow or tangles frequency with intensity.

The metasurface gives narrowband feedback, supporting single-mode operation with voltage-controlled tuning over a wide current range. The team demonstrates mode-hop-free linear frequency tuning at rates up to 70 terahertz per second, with excursions reaching well over a hundred megahertz under a modest radio-frequency drive. Run near threshold, the same device modulates intensity with efficiency above one hundred percent at low voltage, suiting it to ranging and free-space links.
arxiv-2511-16599:
Lukas Billera, Hedwig Nora Nordlinder, and Ben Murrell write a clarifying note on the theory of flow matching and diffusion models, the engines behind much of modern generative AI. Practitioners often reweight the training loss by time to stabilize learning, and this note asks whether that habit is actually justified.

Within Generator Matching, a framework covering many flow and diffusion schemes, the authors show the loss and the generator's linear parameterization can each depend on the current state and on time. The time average in the loss can then be taken against a broad class of time distributions. The same freedom holds for Edit Flows, which sit outside that framework. Time-dependent weighting is therefore legitimate, and the result also simplifies building certain predictor schemes.
arxiv-2511-16699:
Juan Cadile investigates empathy in action in large language models as a steerable direction in activation space. Empathy in action means sacrificing task efficiency to meet human needs. Contrastive prompts from a dedicated benchmark probe three models of different training styles. Detection of the empathy direction is near perfect at optimal layers in all models tested.

An uncensored model matches safety trained models, suggesting empathy encoding arises independently of safety training. Probe scores correlate strongly with behavioral empathy scores in one model. Agreement across models is limited, implying architecture specific implementations. Steering succeeds bidirectionally in two models while keeping output coherent, even at strong interventions. A third model shows asymmetric steering behavior worth further study.
arxiv-2511-16799:
Emily H. Dickey and Noah A. Rosenberg count labeled histories for evolutionary trees that allow multifurcation, where one ancestor can split into several lineages at once. A labeled history records the order in which labeled lineages coalesce, and the count depends on the tree's shape.

For trees whose internal nodes have between two and r offspring, the authors enumerate all labeled histories and the histories of any specific topology. They then show a shape result. The unlabeled topology whose labelings carry the most histories, the maximally probable shape, is the same with multifurcation allowed as in the strictly bifurcating case. A parallel treatment covers simultaneous branchings, with a conjecture for the optimal shape there. The combinatorics connect to precedence-constrained scheduling and to real processes where multifurcation occurs.
arxiv-2511-16899:
Yoshiki Chazono shows theoretically that the Maris polarization effect, a workhorse for reading nuclear structure from proton knockout reactions, also appears when the knocked-out cluster is a deuteron. In the Maris effect, absorption and spin-orbit coupling inside the nucleus give the struck particle an effective polarization whose sign reveals the orbit's total angular momentum.

Chazono first computes the spin correlation of proton-deuteron elastic scattering to find favorable kinematics. He then calculates the vector analyzing power for proton-induced deuteron knockout at 250 MeV from orbits of angular momentum one, two, and three. The signs separate cleanly: positive for the highest orbit, negative for the lowest, with the middle case explained by knockout near the poles. The pattern barely depends on the deuteron's internal state or the interaction chosen, and it motivates a new notion of deuteron-cluster orbit.
arxiv-2511-16999:
Tanmoy Biswas, Chandan Datta, and Luis Pedro García-Pintos ask whether a purely quantum kind of correlation can help cool a system. Cooling matters because quantum computers must reset their parts to a clean state before each run, and that reset is tied to removing heat. The correlation they study is steering, where measuring one particle can guide the state of a distant partner.

The team designs a cooling task where steerable correlations always remove more heat than any setup lacking steering. Better still, the largest possible gain connects directly to a geometric measure of how steerable the correlations are. The advantage also grows in some higher-dimensional examples. Their result turns a cooling edge into a practical witness that steering is present.
arxiv-2511-17299:
Tomáš Musil, Matěj Petrlík, and Martin Saska present MonoSpheres, a system that lets a drone explore unknown spaces with a single camera and no range sensors. Monocular exploration is largely unsolved at scale because one camera yields sparse, uncertain depth. MonoSpheres is built around the quirks of its sparse monocular mapping front end, designing both mapping and planning to respect what that front end can and cannot see.

The mapper oversamples free space where textures are sparse and tracks uncertainty in obstacle positions. The planner replans rapidly and steers the camera's heading to gather the views it needs. The authors show frontier-based exploration still works from sparse depth if parallax and textureless surfaces are handled. Tests in real and simulated indoor and outdoor environments, including the first real-world outdoor demonstrations of this kind, support the design. Code is open-sourced.
arxiv-2511-17499:
David Machado and three co-authors develop a method for predicting the fate of ecosystems modeled on sparse, asymmetric interaction networks. Real food webs and microbial communities are exactly that: most species pairs never interact, and influence rarely runs equally both ways. The generalized Lotka-Volterra model captures such communities, but its stochastic dynamics on sparse graphs resisted standard analysis. The authors derive local Fokker-Planck equations for each species and close the system with a mean-field approximation.

Stationary states then become cheap to compute for both symmetric and asymmetric interactions. The team validates the method against direct integration of the dynamics and against known results, and produces the first phase diagram for sparse asymmetric networks. The framework also transfers to other fields with similar network dynamics, such as economics and evolutionary game theory.
arxiv-2511-17599:
Jianbing Dong and Jianbin Chang propose a leaner way to train large language models at the final output step. Standard training first projects the model's inner states into scores for every word in its vocabulary, then compares those scores with the target word. That score table is huge, scaling with batch, length, and vocabulary, and it must sit in graphics memory even though only one target word per spot is ever used.

Their method folds projection and loss into a single operation, computing the loss straight from the inner states and the target words. Skipping the full score table cuts memory use and data movement, which should lift training speed and allow larger runs. The paper targets a quiet bottleneck that grows worse as vocabularies and models expand.
arxiv-2511-18299:
Steven Oh, Tai Inui, Magdeline Kuan, and Jia-Yeu Lin turn an ordinary Bluetooth pin microphone into a cheap touch sensor for robot hands. Manipulation is rich in contact, yet imitation learning leans on vision, which misses stiffness, roughness, and slip. Dedicated touch sensors tend to be costly, fragile, or hard to fit. MicCheck instead clips the microphone into a printed gripper insert and streams its audio through a standard receiver, with no custom electronics.

Even so, the sound of contact carries real information. On a ten-class material test across tapping, knocking, pressing, and dragging, the sensor sorts materials with high accuracy. Plugged into an imitation learning pipeline, it also improves manipulation. The appeal is practical: a sensor anyone can buy and clip on.
arxiv-2511-18499: Tyler Shoemaker argues, in a position paper, that literary scholars must engage with research on large language model interpretability, the study of how such models work inside. He accepts that the engagement will involve ideological struggle and a measure of complicity. His claim is that the narrow, instrumental standards of current interpretability work cannot be the only measure of what interpretation with these models means. He suggests the red team, the group tasked with probing a model's failures, as one site where that struggle could productively take place.
arxiv-2511-18599:
Eric A. Bai, Minling Zhou, Ricardo Henao, Kyle M. Schwing, and Lawrence Carin measure story lines in a huge text corpus in a way readers can inspect. Narratives steer human acts and lie at the core of geopolitics, yet they have dodged counts that track their overlap and shift over time. Full model reads of a vast corpus cost too much and stay opaque.

Their model joins a word count topic code with a question and answer story model built on a language model. Both share one latent kernel space. Gradient steps for the fit stay readable and echo the self attention of transformers in form. A context based trick forecasts question outcomes for unasked texts. The mix aims at cheap, clear narrative gauges at corpus scale.
arxiv-2511-18699:
Jiarui Xue, Dongjian Yang, Ye Sun, and Gang Liu design a convolution operation modelled on the dendrites of real neurons, aiming at image recognition that survives heavy noise. Most anti-noise work adjusts networks or training recipes, and progress there has stalled.
