The team instead rebuilds the basic operation: dendrites in biology interact with neighbours and preprocess signals with XOR-like logic, and their convolution copies that behaviour through nonlinear interactions between input features.

In a standard convolution, noise flows straight into feature extraction and corrupts it early. The dendritic design processes the neighbourhood jointly, which the authors argue filters interference at the point of entry rather than downstream. The paper presents the operation as a new mathematical basis for feature extraction in noisy settings, from street cameras to medical scanners.
arxiv-2511-18799:
Chengyu Wu, Yushan Xue, and Jiaqing Yang prove a first well-posedness result for elastic waves scattered by a locally rough interface. Most of the boundary is flat, with roughness in a bounded zone. Prior theory left this mixed shape open in both flat and solid settings.

A Helmholtz split of the field yields a key identity for the stress vector. It links the generalized stress to the Lamé constants and to surface operators. Two limit facts for surface integrals follow, and with them the first uniqueness proof for the direct problem at all frequencies. A steepest descent study then builds the two layer Green's tensor in closed form for unit transmission. Existence of solutions caps the work.
arxiv-2511-19199:
Teodora Popordanoska, Jiameng Li, and Matthew B. Blaschko introduce CLASH, a benchmark that tests whether vision-language models notice when an image and its caption disagree. Real inputs often conflict across modes, yet most benchmarks assume consistency. CLASH pairs COCO photos with captions altered at the object or attribute level to create controlled contradictions.

Questions come in multiple-choice and open-ended forms, backed by a large fine-tuning set and a smaller human-checked diagnostic set. Leading models show clear limits, with biases toward one mode and weak spots in certain categories. Fine-tuning on CLASH sharply improves conflict detection, showing the skill can be taught.
arxiv-2511-19399:
Rulin Shao and twenty co-authors train an open model for deep research, the kind of agent that searches many sources and writes a long, sourced answer. Most open agents learn on short questions with checkable answers, which does not prepare them for open-ended reports. Their method lets grading rubrics evolve during training.

As the model explores, the rubrics absorb new facts from search and from contrasting answers, giving sharper feedback and better fact checking. The resulting model, DR Tulu-8B, is presented as the first fully open one trained directly for long-form research. On four benchmarks it beats other open agents and rivals closed ones at lower cost.
arxiv-2511-19699:
Charles Fleming, Luca Muscariello, Vijoy Pandey, and Ramana Kompella propose two new protocol layers for an Internet of Agents. Language model agents now act through tool protocols such as MCP, but their context windows cap memory and computing power. Collaboration across agents is the way to scale, much as memory tiers scale computers.

Classic network stacks move data between hosts, not meaning between agents. An Agent Communication Layer would formalize how agents address and exchange messages, while an Agent Semantic Layer would carry shared meaning on top. The proposal sketches the stack that agent collaboration needs, beyond what the present internet layers provide.
arxiv-2511-19799:
C. R. Das surveys the hunt for strangelets, stable clusters of strange quark matter, across the sky. Strange quark matter may be the true ground state of dense matter, and odd objects hint at it: one light neutron star remnant fits a strange star well. Events such as a major neutron star merger could also forge strangelets.

Such clusters might reveal themselves by annihilating into narrow gamma-ray lines. Using data from current gamma-ray observatories, the study sets limits on those spectral features and fluxes. Sharper instruments will be needed for a detection, tying the search to multimessenger astronomy and dense matter theory.
arxiv-2511-19999: Anton Lyubinin extends a known result called the Popularity Bias Memorization theorem in several directions. The extension covers arbitrary degree distributions, beyond the cases treated before. Lyubinin also proves both upper and lower estimates for the alignment with the top-k singular hyperspace. The work thus widens the theorem's reach. It also pins down the size of the alignment from both sides.
arxiv-2511-20599:
Ramachandran, Jensen, and Alhassid compute the heat bookkeeping of a flat Fermi gas. Their 2025 paper studies cold atoms in two dimensions. As attraction strengthens, loose Cooper pairs morph into tight molecules. That BCS-to-BEC crossover is murkiest at strong coupling. Quantum Monte Carlo supplies precision numbers there.

Monte Carlo ran on lattices with controlled errors. Time and lattice limits were taken to clean the numbers. The team measured condensate fraction and spin susceptibility. Tan's contact and the energy equation of state came out too. A free energy staggering gap was computed alongside. Signs of a pseudogap regime appear in two observables. Spin response stays suppressed well above the superfluid transition. Pairing seems to linger without full condensation there in that window. Their numbers benchmark future cold-atom experiments directly. Energy values at low temperature undercut an earlier reference notably.
arxiv-2511-20899:
Zhanxiang Hua, Christina Karamperidou, and Zilu Meng run in 2025 the first Pacific pacemaker experiment inside a deep-learning climate model. Pacemaker runs nudge tropical Pacific sea temperatures to observed values, isolating how the atmosphere answers El Nino and La Nina. The emulator, DLESyM, couples a learned atmosphere to a simple learned ocean, but its own ENSO swings are too weak to test far-field links directly. Forcing it with real Pacific temperatures bypasses that flaw.

It reproduced its own internal weather variability realistically. Its forced response to ENSO, though, came out significantly amplified compared with reality. That overshoot distorted extremes: blocking events occurred too often and lasted too long, while peak intensity came out too weak. The authors warn that learned climate models need the same physical validation as traditional ones before their ENSO teleconnections can be trusted.
arxiv-2511-21099:
Chandra Chekuri, Pooja Kulkarni, Ruta Mehta, and Jan Vondrák extend in 2025 a fair-division tool to pickier tastes. Dividing indivisible goods among agents is easier when values add up item by item: then a cycle-cancelling lemma tidies fractional allocations without hurting anyone. Valuations are often submodular, showing diminishing returns, and the lemma failed there. The authors prove the analogue: cycles can be stripped from a fractional allocation's support graph while no agent's value, measured by the multilinear extension, ever decreases.

The lemma powers approximation algorithms for three objectives. For Nash social welfare under submodular values they obtain a one-fifth approximation. For maximin share they reach one half of (1 minus 1 over e), through simple algorithms. The Santa Claus max-min problem also benefits. In special cases, small-valued goods or constantly many agents, their algorithms are tight or best-known, all within the value-oracle model.
arxiv-2511-21199:
Alessia Andò and colleagues model in 2025 how behaviour alone can make an epidemic pulse in waves. During an outbreak's early phase, before susceptibles run out, people react to news of new cases by cutting contacts, then relax as headlines fade. Earlier models captured this with a fixed delay or a simple memory shape. Andò lets memory be distributed: an information index averages past incidence through a memory kernel, a weighting over the past.

Using a pseudospectral method, a numerical technique for delay equations, they handle gamma-distribution kernels with any shape parameter, beyond what the linear chain trick allows. Their analysis confirms earlier findings: behavioural adaptation alone produces sustained infection waves, with no need for seasonality, waning immunity, or population turnover. They show how the kernel's shape sets the waves' period and peak height. The minimal contact level people keep also decides whether the behaviour-driven equilibrium stays stable.
arxiv-2511-21299:
Cyprien Bone and seven coauthors teach a generative model to design crystal materials to order in 2025. Their base system, CrystaLLM, writes out crystal structures as text. Asking it for a target property was clumsy, though. Properties had to be chopped into tokens. Fine-tuning also risked catastrophic forgetting, where new training erases old knowledge. Their upgrade, CrystaLLM-pi, injects continuous property values straight into the transformer's attention mechanism.

Bone and his coauthors present two injection designs, Property-Key-Value prefix attention and a residual variant. On structure recovery, the model reads messy X-ray diffraction patterns and rebuilds the matching crystal with accuracy rivaling specialized tools, even distinguishing polymorphs, same-composition crystals with different layouts. Fine-tuned on a photovoltaic dataset, it also generated novel, stable candidate materials aimed at solar-cell properties, showing one framework can both recover and invent.
arxiv-2511-21399:
Joshua Fonseca Rivera shows that a language model can be taught to notice thoughts planted inside it, in a 2025 machine learning study. The work follows Lindsey's 2025 introspection experiments, where models sometimes reported injected activation patterns, thoughts inserted directly into their internals, but succeeded only about 20 percent of the time at best. Fonseca Rivera asks whether that flicker of self-detection can be trained directly instead of awaited at larger scales.

Fine-tuning a 7-billion-parameter model on fleeting single-token injections transformed its performance. Accuracy on held-out concepts jumped from 0.4 percent to 85 percent, while false positives fell from 6.7 percent to zero across 60 control trials. The model reported injected content it had never seen in training, with only a 7.5 point gap on unseen concept vectors, suggesting a transferable skill. It met Lindsey's accuracy, grounding, and internality criteria.
arxiv-2511-21499:
Wenkang Xin and Andrew Mummery build one machine for computing tidal forces around any spinning compact object, in 2025. Tidal accelerations, the stretching an orbiting body feels, encode the spacetime it moves through. Existing derivations are cumbersome case-by-case crafts. The authors give a unified analytic method for any stationary, axisymmetric spacetime, built on the frame of zero-angular-momentum observers.

Xin and Mummery validate the method on the four classic black hole solutions, Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordström, Kerr, and Kerr-Newman, plus a wormhole metric. As a showcase application, they revisit the Hills mass, the largest black hole mass that can still shred a star outside its horizon and flare observably. They extend that limit to naked singularity spacetimes, objects with no horizon at all. Such rare disruption events become tests of exotic gravity.
arxiv-2511-21599:
Baptiste Bermond, Lucila Peralta Gavensky, Anaïs Defossez, and Nathan Goldman find a new experimental handle on two elusive material properties, in 2025. Orbital magnetization and heat magnetization describe how a material's ground state circulates charge and heat internally, yet both are very hard to measure directly. The team connects them to excitation spectra, values experiments can record, through thermoelectric probes and sum rules.

Starting from zero-temperature transport data and Kramers–Kronig relations, Bermond and his coauthors derive spectral formulas for both quantities. Excitation rates under chiral thermoelectric drives, heating patterns with a handedness, then serve as direct probes, putting both quantities on truly equal footing with the topological Chern number. The framework also splits each one into a hierarchy of distinct physical parts and yields real-space markers. Recipes using modulated strain fields in quantum-engineered platforms are proposed, making measurements a practical route to ground-state properties.
arxiv-2511-21699:
Zhiyao Ma, In Gim, and Lin Zhong accelerate language model inference with nothing but a cache, in 2025. Speculative decoding speeds generation by having a cheap drafter propose tokens that the big model verifies in one pass. Drafters are usually smaller neural networks. Cacheback's drafter is radically simpler: least-recently-used cache tables of token n-grams, exploiting the locality of language, the tendency of nearby text to repeat patterns.

The method needs no training and works with any model. Despite its minimalism, Cacheback reaches state-of-the-art performance among comparable training-free, model-agnostic methods, and integrates easily into existing systems. Its drafts form a tree, so other methods' predictions can be grafted in as extra branches for further speedup. The idea has pedigree: cache language models cut perplexity by 38 to 50 percent in 1990s speech recognition. Cacheback also adapts quickly to new domains, since its tables absorb fresh text.
arxiv-2511-22299:
Bathula, Krishnakumar, and Jena, radio astronomers, test a pipeline for un-smearing pulsar signals. Pulsars make superb cosmic clocks, but their radio pulses are broadened and delayed by scattering in the interstellar medium, blurring the intrinsic profile that precision timing needs. The team studies a CLEAN-based deconvolution algorithm in the tradition of Bhat and colleagues. It peels the scattering tail off an observed profile to recover the pulse shape the pulsar emitted, along with the scattering parameters themselves.

They validate the pipeline on simulated profiles, single and multi-component Gaussians mimicking real pulsar shapes, injecting known dispersion measures, scattering times, and frequency scaling, then checking what the recovery returns. The comparison quantifies the method's efficiency and limitations across profile types. Such validation is the due diligence pulsar timing programs need before trusting deconvolved profiles in gravitational-wave searches.
arxiv-2511-22499:
Nakada and Kubota ask a practical question about erasing text from document images: what shape should the mask be? Inpainting tools fill whatever a mask covers, and most text-removal research targets sparse text in outdoor photos. The authors built a benchmark of dense, realistic documents, including folded, crumpled, and handwritten pages, and found removal quality surprisingly sensitive to small changes in mask shape.

They model flexible mask outlines and tune them with Bayesian optimisation, judging results by FID score. The winning masks were character-wise, chunked per character rather than covering whole words or lines, and slightly larger than the text itself. The tightest cover of a text region was not optimal, and the optimised masks suppressed the brick-like traces removal often leaves. The guideline is simple: mask character by character, with a little margin, whether from OCR boxes or drawn by hand.
arxiv-2511-22699:
The Z-Image Team at Alibaba Group argues that top-tier image generation does not require giant models. Leading open image models carry 20 to 80 billion parameters, impractical on consumer hardware. Z-Image is a 6 billion parameter foundation model built on a single-stream diffusion transformer. It was trained end to end in about 314 thousand H800 GPU hours, roughly 630 thousand dollars, through curated data infrastructure and a streamlined curriculum.

A few-step distillation scheme with reward post-training produces Z-Image-Turbo, generating in under a second on an enterprise GPU and fitting consumer hardware with under 16 gigabytes of video memory. An omni-pre-training paradigm also yields Z-Image-Edit, an editing variant with strong instruction following. Across evaluations, the family performs comparably to or better than leading competitors, with standout strength in photorealistic generation and bilingual text rendering rivalling top commercial systems. Code, weights, and demos are publicly released.
arxiv-2511-22899:
Liu, Deng, and Cohen model what Earth's inner core is made of, using silicon-bearing iron alloys. Seismology shows the inner core bends shear waves by direction, up to 15 percent or more, yet pure iron's likely hexagonal phase is nearly isotropic, a long-standing mismatch. Silicon is a probable major light element, so the team computed Gibbs free energies of four alloy structures with first-principles molecular dynamics and built the phase diagram at inner-core pressures and temperatures.

A miscibility gap emerged: hexagonal and ordered B2 phases coexist across 6 to 11 weight percent silicon at 6000 kelvin. The B2 alloy shows strong shear anisotropy, 22.9 percent at 6000 kelvin, against the hexagonal phase's 0.6 percent, and its shear wave velocity of 3.73 kilometres per second and Poisson's ratio match seismological observations. The inner core likely hosts multiple phases whose texture shapes its seismic signature and thermal history.
arxiv-2511-22999:
Liu classifies a family of seven-dimensional shapes: the total spaces of bundles whose fiber is a 3-sphere over the complex projective plane, a standard four-dimensional space. Two such shapes can look alike to algebra yet differ smoothly. Earlier work by Escher sorted them up to homeomorphism, meaning continuous deformation. The coarser question of homotopy equivalence, which ignores more detail, was only partly answered.

The classification proceeds in two steps, first computing Kreck-Stolz invariants, numerical fingerprints built from characteristic classes, to sort the spaces up to PL-homeomorphism, a piecewise-linear form of sameness. It then applies surgery theory to pass to homotopy equivalence. The result is a complete homotopy classification of these bundle spaces, obtained without relying on Kruggel's earlier partial analysis. And the same classification turns out to hold for the pairs formed by each space together with its embedded 3-sphere.
arxiv-2511-23099:
Čertík and colleagues turn to cores of ordered graphs, the minimal representatives of a graph under order-preserving homomorphisms, maps that preserve edges and vertex order. A core is a graph that cannot be shrunk onto a proper subgraph of itself. And every ordered graph has a unique core. So cores are the natural atoms for comparing graphs up to homomorphism.

Their complexity results split in a surprising direction: deciding whether a graph retracts onto a given subgraph, the key subroutine, is solvable in polynomial time. That is unlike the unordered setting, where retraction is hard. Yet deciding whether an ordered graph is itself a core is NP-hard. It is even NP-hard to tell graphs that are their own core from graphs whose core is as small as theory allows. There is W[1]-hardness in that smallest size, and only exponential-in-the-parameter algorithms are known.
arxiv-2511-23199:
Tan and colleagues scale Brownian Bridge models, generative models that travel directly from an input to an output instead of starting from noise. They scale them up to transformer size for image and video translation jobs. Diffusion models waste effort erasing a starting image that already resembles the target, while earlier bridge models stayed small. So the team built the Vision Bridge Transformer at 20 billion parameters for images and 1.3 billion parameters for video.

Training at that scale needed a fix, because the conventional objective is numerically unstable. So they propose a variance-stabilized velocity-matching objective that keeps learning robust throughout the bridge trajectory. In experiments the framework consistently outperformed existing baselines on instruction-based image editing and complex video translation. Its formulation also promises cheaper inference than conditional diffusion transformers, since no auxiliary conditioning branches or extra tokens are needed to inject the source.
arxiv-2511-23399:
Swain and colleagues test whether a fundamental three-way complementarity relation among coherence, predictability. And entanglement survives contact with noise, in qubit and qutrit systems sent through two- and three-slit interferometers. The triality relation says the squares of visibility, path predictability, and system-path entanglement sum exactly to one for a pure isolated system. And the team derives closed-form expressions for all three quantities in the system-path framework for both setups.

Passing the systems through amplitude damping and phase damping channels, they find the relation is never violated. Since amplitude damping merely redistributes coherence and population imbalance while phase damping lowers coherence but leaves predictability untouched. The persistence of the exact trade-off in open, decohering systems shows complementarity is robust rather than a fragile idealization. Giving real noisy quantum interferometry in small systems a unified analytical footing in practice.
arxiv-2512-00799:
Taha Anwar wrote a 2025 teaching review on the roots of the Standard Model of particle physics. That model rests on local gauge symmetry, the idea that physics stays the same when certain internal labels are twisted from place to place. It is one of the great achievements of modern science.

Yet its main equation, the Lagrangian, is usually taught to students who already have deep training. Anwar builds a gentler bridge aimed at advanced undergraduates. The path runs through quantum electrodynamics, the theory of light and electrons, as the worked example. A clearer on-ramp could bring more students into modern particle theory.
arxiv-2512-00899:
Raka Dabhade, Jebraan Mudholkar, Siddhesh Durgude, and Arpit Kottur propose a first filter for promising planets in a 2025 paper. The hunt for habitable exoplanets, worlds around other stars, is a central goal of modern astrophysics. Missions like Kepler and TESS have found vast numbers of candidates.

No team can study every candidate in depth. Follow-up time on big telescopes is scarce, so targets must be ranked. The authors offer a first-order filter, a quick screen that flags the most promising candidates for detailed characterization. A good early screen keeps rare, Earth-like worlds from being lost in the pile.
arxiv-2512-01099:
Daria Smirnova, Hamid Nasiri, Marta Adamska, Zhengxin Yu, and Peter Garraghan study the energy cost of choosing models in a 2025 paper. Modern AI systems can call many tools and models to do complex tasks. Large language models often orchestrate those choices, deciding which model handles each step, based on written descriptions of what each model does.

That qualitative approach ignores energy use, which varies widely between models. The authors propose energy-aware, data-driven model selection inside LLM-orchestrated systems. Picking models by measured performance and energy, not just description, could cut the power bill of compound AI systems substantially.
arxiv-2512-01399:
Martin Thummler and co-authors model bright light made by quantum dots under strong fields. When a strong laser hits a dot, it can emit light at many times the laser tone. That effect is called high-order harmonic generation. Tests show it fades for small dots at long laser tones.

No model could yet match that fade for tiny dots. The team built one based on a real-space tight-binding view. Their model tracks electrons on a grid of sites in the dot. It aims to match the size trend seen in tests. A sound model guides new light sources based on dots.
arxiv-2512-01499:
Over a decade past its discovery, the Higgs boson still anchors particle physics. Its links to heavy particles and gauge bosons are now well gauged. Much else is not. The shape of its self-interaction is still weakly known. Its links to light fermions are also loose.

An overview lays out Higgs theory in the Standard Model and in its effective extension. That extension adds new terms that new physics could fill. The review maps what is known and what is open. It gives scope teams a shared base for the next round of Higgs tests at colliders.
arxiv-2512-01699:
Fadhila Chehami and co-authors report self-organized freeform waveguiding inspired by nature. Butterfly wings gain iridescent hues from complex photonic forms. Those forms grow from local rules, with no central plan. They still yield advanced optical traits like band gaps.

The team shows waveguides that form by like self-organization. No in-situ tuning or top-down design is used. Local rules alone set the final path for light. Self-formed guides could cut fabrication cost for photonic chips and sensors. Freeform guides bend in curves set by growth rules, which suits implants and wearable optics where straight channels waste precious space.
arxiv-2512-02299:
Asked a health question, a language model may get several documents that disagree, and which one it trusts decides whether its answer helps or harms. Boya Zhang and four co-authors build HealthContradict in 2025, an expert-verified dataset for testing how models reason over long, conflicting biomedical material.

Each of its nine hundred twenty cases pairs a health question with a factual answer backed by scientific evidence, plus documents in conflict. The study asks how models use context and how contradictions bend their responses. As medical chatbots spread, measuring their behavior under conflicting evidence is a basic safety exercise.
arxiv-2512-02999:
Dhimiter Canko and Mattia Pozzoli compute a full set of three loop Feynman integrals for collider physics. Producing two vector bosons at hadron colliders is a key process at the Large Hadron Collider. Precision predictions for it need next to next to next to leading order corrections in quantum chromodynamics.

The authors compute all planar three loop master integrals for the leading color part of those corrections. The integrals fall into nine four point families with massless internal lines and two massive external legs. Such integrals are reusable bricks for many precision predictions at current and future colliders. Bricks of this sort get used for years. Each new rate that needs them can stack on the set in place and skip months of fresh work.
arxiv-2512-03099:
Graph neural networks can sort and predict, but they rarely explain why. Haribandhu Jena, Jyotirmaya Shivottam, and Subhankar Mishra tackle that gap in this 2025 work. These networks are now used in drug research, social network study, and recommendation tools.

One fair way to explain a result is the Shapley value, which scores each part's share. But exact scores need a huge number of checks, far too many for real graphs. The authors use quantum methods to speed that task, in a tool called QGShap. Fast, faithful reasons could help experts trust network outputs. For practitioners, faster Shapley scores could bring explanations to graphs with millions of links.
arxiv-2512-03199:
Face recognition works worse on tilted or blocked faces. Justin Norman and Hany Farid test a fix in this 2025 work. Real-world photos often have poor quality, non-frontal poses, and objects hiding part of the face.

The authors ask whether AI-driven pose correction and image restoration lift accuracy. Their study checks if straightening a head pose helps the model name the person. The answer matters for security and photo tools that rely on faces. It also warns where such fixes might fail or mislead. The study also shows the risk that restored faces might fool systems in harmful ways.
arxiv-2512-03299:
Some curves hide groups that are hard to compute. Justin Chen, Heidi Goodson, Rezwan Hoque, and Sabeeha Malikah study one family in this 2025 work. They look at hyperelliptic curves given by a simple prime-power equation.

A variety is called degenerate when its Hodge ring is not built from divisor classes. Degeneracy makes Sato-Tate groups, which describe statistical patterns of the curve, hard to find. Few examples and techniques exist in the literature. The authors add both, aiding number theory and cryptography research. New examples of degenerate curves help map where Sato-Tate computations break down.
arxiv-2512-03399:
Aligning one AI system is not enough for good outcomes. Joe Edelman and a large team argue for full-stack alignment in this 2025 work. Even a system perfectly aligned to its operator can cause harm if the operator's goals clash with others.

Institutions, not just models, need alignment with shared values. The authors use thick models of value, rich accounts of what people hold dear. Co-aligning AI and institutions could prevent perverse outcomes at scale. The work speaks to policy makers as much as to model builders. Thick value models resist thin metrics that miss what communities actually care about.
arxiv-2512-03699: Mark Pollicott and Richard Sharp, both specialists in dynamical systems, published this short mathematics preprint in 2025. It concerns Anosov flows, a class of chaotic systems that stretch and fold points as they move. A recent theorem by Gogolev and Rodriguez Hertz tied certain periodic orbits of such flows to a cohomology condition. The authors show the same conclusion survives when attention is restricted to orbits that lift trivially to any regular cover on which the lifted flow remains transitive.
arxiv-2512-03799:
Physical networks that learn, such as grids of adjustable resistors, forget old tasks when trained on new ones. Purba Chatterjee, Marcelo Guzman, and Andrea J. Liu study that forgetting in a 2025 preprint on disordered systems and soft matter. The problem mirrors catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks, but here the student is a piece of tunable matter.

Their remedy is a hard threshold in the learning rule: only connections receiving a strong training signal are allowed to change. Thresholding keeps each task's adjustments near its inputs and outputs, so the network splits into weakly overlapping regions, one per task. Simulations of tunable resistor networks show several tasks can then be remembered in sequence. The strategy also uses fewer connections and lowers the overall cost of tuning. The authors suggest constrained training as a simple, local route past forgetting.
arxiv-2512-03899:
UMAP, a popular tool for flattening high-dimensional data into pictures, is built on fuzzy simplicial sets, objects from algebraic topology. Janis Keck and colleagues give those objects a probabilistic meaning in a 2025 machine learning preprint. Without one, they argue, the theory floats free of the statistical frameworks data scientists normally use.

Their framework presents those fuzzy sets as shadows of probability measures on ordinary simplicial sets. Under that lens, UMAP's fuzzy weights become cumulative distribution functions of pairwise distances, sampled through a generative process over filtrations. The viewpoint clarifies how divergence scores relate to fuzzy cross-entropy, and recovers fuzzy logic rules from set rules. To show the approach can create as well as explain, the authors derive a generalised embedding method using Cech ones and triplet sampling.
arxiv-2512-04399:
Haoqi Han and five co-authors describe a bionic hand with fifteen joints that copies the size and motion range of a human hand. Robotic hands face a hard trade: many motors make a hand bulky, while few motors limit its grip. Their 2025 arXiv paper seeks human-like dexterity with far fewer drivers, taking cues from how muscles are laid out in the arm and palm.

A cable-driven design runs the fingers on tendons, cutting motor counts versus older tendon rigs. Five motors sit in the forearm and supply strong gripping force. Ten small motors in the palm handle fine finger work. The paper details the frame, the joint sensors, and the drive electronics as one system. Tests of grip and motion show the layout works in practice. Such hands could serve prosthetics and service robots that must handle daily objects.
arxiv-2512-04799:
Gianluca Barmina, Nathalie Norman, Peter Schneider-Kamp, and co-authors present DaLA, a benchmark that grades language models on judging whether Danish sentences are acceptable. Acceptability tests probe whether a model truly knows a language's grammar, beyond fluent chatter. The team first studied the errors real writers make in Danish. Their 2025 arXiv paper turns those findings into a tougher test than prior Danish benchmarks.

Fourteen corruption functions take correct Danish sentences and inject the common error kinds, one at a time. Manual and automatic checks confirm each corruption is a genuine error of its kind. Models must then flag the broken sentences. Scores fell compared with older benchmarks, showing the new test bites harder. A broader spread of error types gives a fuller picture of grammatical knowledge. Such benchmarks help track whether models serve smaller languages with real care.
arxiv-2512-05099:
Roger Romani, Maya Beleznay, Alexei Filippenko, Thomas Brink, and WeiKang Zheng tighten the mass measurement of the heaviest known neutron star, the pulsar PSR J0952-0607. This dense stellar corpse spins extremely fast and carries an unusually weak magnetic field, signs of an odd life history tied to its great mass. Weighing it precisely matters: the heaviest neutron star sets a floor under the maximum mass such stars can reach, constraining how stiff dense matter can be.

The team gathered new light curves at the orbit's faintest phase and refit the companion star's radial velocities. The neutron star comes out at well over twice the Sun's mass, clearly heavier than the record holder among pulsars with white dwarf companions. That pushes the allowed maximum mass upward and sharpens bounds on matter at extreme density. The authors also flag remaining uncertainties and how future observations could shrink them.
arxiv-2512-05199:
Yang-Ting Chien and Sonny Mantry propose a new measurement for probing how quarks behave inside the proton and how they dress into visible particles. The observable is the electric charge of a jet region, defined within a global event shape, a whole-event measure of energy flow. The setup records the jet's charge and the event's overall pattern together. They develop the idea for deep inelastic scattering, where an electron strikes a proton, at past and future colliders.

Binning by jet charge sharpens quark-flavour separation in the proton's structure; binning the other way probes flavour dynamics during hadronization. The authors prove a factorization theorem that organizes the calculation in the relevant regime and introduces a new universal charged jet function, extractable from electron-positron collider data. Simulations show genuine sensitivity to quark flavour dynamics, making it a promising tool for the future Electron-Ion Collider.
arxiv-2512-05399:
Sepanta Zeighami, Shreya Shankar, and Aditya Parameswaran cut the cost of semantic joins. A semantic join is the database operation that pairs rows from two tables when a language model must judge each pair against a plain-language condition. Done naively, that means a model call for every pair in the cross product — ruinous at scale. Shortcuts filter pairs by embedding similarity first, but similarity often fails to predict the join's outcome, so the savings disappoint.

Their method, Featurized-Decomposition Join, instead extracts informative features from the text records and composes them into a logical formula that cheaply rules out most non-matching pairs, reserving the model for the survivors. Using language models to propose features while keeping statistical guarantees on the output is the technical crux, given how features depend on one another. On real datasets the method cuts cost by up to tenfold at the same quality guarantees.
arxiv-2512-05799:
Alessandro Veneri, Francesco Quintavalle, Thierry Valet, and Roberto Raimondi study how electric current creates spin polarization in Rashba materials. Spin-orbit coupling ties spin to motion in these materials, so a charge current can generate a spin density. Textbook treatments assume in-plane symmetry. Real crystals often break it, turning the spectrum anisotropic. The team studies the two main lowered symmetry patterns.

In the first pattern, the answer depends on the balance of spin-orbit strength along the two main axes. The induced spin density can swing well away from the neat right angle to the field that the symmetric case predicts. In the second pattern, cubic warping leaves the right angle intact but scales the conversion. The calculations include disorder through vertex corrections, checked two independent ways. Those corrections prove essential: simpler approximations miss the details. For spintronics, crystal orientation becomes a design variable.
arxiv-2512-05899:
The Euclid Collaboration reports what its first quick data release taught the hunt for strong gravitational lenses. Such lenses are rare and precious. Euclid's first release covered sixty three square degrees, and a combined effort of machine learning, citizen scientists, and expert eyes found five hundred lens candidates in it. Machine learning does the heavy lifting, but models train on simulations, since known real lenses are few.

Real data exposes the simulation gap brutally. A network trained only on simulations recovered up to ninety two percent of simulated lenses at perfect purity. On real Euclid images it found only half the lenses, and most of its picks were wrong. Mixing real lenses and false alarms into training changed the outlook: expected yields rose by a quarter to a third. Simulations give breadth; a pinch of reality makes a finder trustworthy.
arxiv-2512-05999:
Leonard Storcks and Tobias Buck put the student inside the simulator. Astrophysical fluid simulations are usually fixed codes. A differentiable simulator lets a model learn inside it. The authors present two demonstrations. Simulating wind blown bubbles at low resolution converges painfully slowly. A learned cooling function, trained in the loop, recovers high resolution dynamics at low resolution cost.

The second case trains a convolutional network to correct two dimensional magnetohydrodynamics simulations of a blast wave, patching the errors a coarse grid makes. Together the demos argue a point. The usual approach fits outputs after the fact. Training inside a differentiable solver ties the learning to the equations, so corrections respect the physics by construction and generalize with it. The code is open source. The pattern could become standard inside serious simulation codes.
arxiv-2512-06099:
Khondakar Ashik Shahriar makes the case, with data, that the body's signals refuse to be read with straight lines. A wrist wearable streams heart, sweat, temperature, and motion data; from them, software hopes to recognize cognitive load, stress, and exercise. Shahriar evaluates all three tasks across three public Empatica datasets. The honest test is leave one subject out: facing a person never seen.

Nonlinear models win everywhere. Linear baselines lag far behind. Cross person performance drops, but the advantage survives. Skin conductance, temperature, and acceleration carry special weight, for sensible reasons. The unified benchmark is the deliverable, and the lesson is simple: physiology is nonlinear.
arxiv-2512-06299:
Nakisa Ghanbarian and Stanislav Jabuka study how many band moves it takes to untie a knot. In knot theory, a band move is one kind of local change that can loosen a tangled loop. The band unknotting number counts the fewest such moves that turn a given knot into a plain round loop. A natural guess is that joining two knots into one, by a connected sum, adds their counts together.

The authors show that guess fails, and fails often. They find endless pairs of knots whose joined knot needs fewer moves than the sum of the two counts. Even more striking, some joined knots need fewer moves than either knot alone. Their work follows a recent surprise of the same kind for the classic unknotting number. They also prove fresh upper and lower bounds for two genus measures of a knot, in both the rough and smooth senses.
arxiv-2512-07399:
Pascal Auscher, Sebastian Bechtel, and Luca Haardt wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on function spaces. Function spaces are sets of functions sorted by how rough or smooth they are. The authors build a new scale of such spaces that matches a well-known family called the homogeneous Besov spaces.

Their new spaces complete earlier work by Ullrich on the same problem. They also contain spaces that Barton and Mayboroda introduced for boundary value problems. Amenta later studied those spaces under the name weighted Z-spaces. The new scale links to tent spaces built with Whitney averages, arising as their real interpolants. The authors then map out basic traits: completeness, duality, and how the spaces sit inside each other. They also work out both real and complex interpolation between them.
arxiv-2512-07599:
Hanshi Wang, Zijian Cai, Jin Gao, Yiwei Zhang, Weiming Hu, Ke Wang, and Zhipeng Zhang wrote this 2025 computer vision paper. Robots need to pick out objects in three dimensions, live, as they move through a space. Most current systems treat each moment separately and miss the flow of time.

Their method, AutoSeg3D, reframes the task as tracking objects across frames. Set object queries carry identity and features forward through time. Long-term links keep each object's picture coherent as views change. Short-term updates fold in fresh details from the newest frame. It helps when only part of an object is visible. A spatial consistency step also repairs the patchy output of vision foundation models. The sparse queries keep the computing cost far below dense point-cloud methods. On standard indoor scan datasets, the method sets a new best score.
arxiv-2512-07699:
Mostafa Shibl, Sharan Srinivasan, Harsha Honnappa, and Vijay Gupta wrote this 2025 control theory paper. The classic linear quadratic Gaussian framework steers systems buffeted by noise. It assumes that noise is Brownian, the smooth random walk of textbooks.

Real noise can be far rougher than that classic picture. It may remember its past and lack the tidy structure calculus expects. Such non-Markovian, non-semimartingale noise breaks the standard Itô tools. The authors solve the control problem anyway, for both process and measurement noise. Rough path theory supplies the replacement mathematics for the task. Signature representations turn the noise's shape into usable data. Controlled rough paths then guide the system's evolution through it. From that machinery, they derive the best possible estimation strategy. The matching optimal control strategy comes from the same derivation. The result widens optimal control to a rougher, more honest noise world.
arxiv-2512-07799:
Roozbeh Bostandoost, Adam Lechowicz, Walid Hanafy, Prashant Shenoy, and Mohammad Hajiesmaili wrote this 2025 computing paper. Data centers can cut carbon by running flexible work when electricity is cleanest. Most carbon-aware schedulers treat each job as one solid block.

Real jobs are often webs of smaller tasks with dependencies between them. Video encoding and offline inference both have that tangled structure. Knowing the structure opens room for deeper carbon savings. The authors model the problem as flexible job-shop scheduling. An offline solver then computes the best savings anyone could achieve. Dependency-aware schedules cut carbon sharply against a makespan-only baseline. Total completion time need not grow to earn those savings. On mixed server fleets, carbon-optimal schedules can still burn extra energy. Doubling the allowed makespan nearly doubles the carbon benefit in their tests. Job structure and server count strongly shape what is achievable.
arxiv-2512-08199:
Zhanqiang Bai, William Q Erickson, Markus Hunziker, and Jing Jiang, mathematicians in representation theory, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is highest weight Harish Chandra modules for a real Lie group of Hermitian type. A central question is which of these modules are unitary, carrying an inner product that fits the group action.

The authors build a one to one match between two sets that look unrelated. On one side sit the connected Dynkin subdiagrams containing the noncompact simple root. On the other side sit a special family of unitary highest weight modules built from Weyl group elements. Their main result: such a module is unitary exactly when the matching Schubert variety is smooth. They also count how many unitary modules of this family lie in each Kazhdan Lusztig right cell. The link turns a hard question into a geometric smoothness check.
arxiv-2512-08299:
Aman Kumar and Ankit Chaudhary, computer scientists in India, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about hiding audio inside images. Steganography conceals the very existence of secret data, which can protect sensitive multimedia messages better than encryption alone. Their method embeds sound files into picture pixels using the least significant bit technique.

The twist is how the hiding spots are chosen. An optimization algorithm inspired by the hunting behavior of Harris hawks searches for the best pixel positions for embedding. The team judges the results with standard image quality measures that track distortion and similarity. Their hawk guided method beat existing approaches on image quality, robustness, and how much audio an image can carry. The study offers a nature inspired way to make hidden data both safer and harder to spot.
arxiv-2512-08499:
Waleed Razzaq and Yun Bo Zhao, engineers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about industrial prognostics: predicting how much useful life remains in machines such as rolling bearings. A good forecaster must also know when it is guessing, especially when inputs drift away from anything seen in training, a weakness of many published models.

The authors build two probabilistic frameworks that are both physics constrained and distance aware. Spectral normalization keeps the network internal geometry honest, so distance from the training data stays meaningful in its hidden space. One version ends in a Gaussian process whose uncertainty grows with that distance. The other predicts the parameters of a distribution designed for the same purpose. A dynamic weighting balances data fit against physical consistency. On three public bearing datasets, both frameworks beat baselines on accuracy and uncertainty calibration, holding up under strong adversarial perturbations.
arxiv-2512-09099:
Suman Baral and coauthors calculate system energies for families of pentaquarks using a Thomas Fermi statistical quark model. A pentaquark here is a five quark system with two light up quarks, one down quark, a charm quark, and an anticharm quark. Families are built from a single pentaquark up to many units, reaching seventy quarks in total.

The model assumes spherical symmetry, with particles distributed continuously at varying density inside a boundary. Particles interact through Coulomb like forces, and a break in the light quark density profile is found to be energetically favored. Total energies are computed for each multiquark system and compared to judge stability across the family. A striking pattern appears: combinations made of multiples of four pentaquarks are especially stable. The authors call such a unit an icosaquark, and its first case has the lowest energy per quark, suggesting a preferred stable configuration for these exotic systems.
arxiv-2512-09199:
Yasaman Esfandiari and four co-authors test whether large language models can help design analog electronic circuits. Analog design is demanding work. A model must respect physical limits and produce designs in a strict structured form, not just plausible text. The team studies AI help in which a human designer stays in the loop.

They compare small models such as T5 and GPT-2 with larger ones such as Mistral-7B and GPT-oss-20B, under different training setups. They also test how the way circuit data is written down changes what the models do. The results expose weak points: answers shift with data format, generated designs can be unstable, and models struggle with circuit layouts they have not seen. The paper maps both the promise and the current limits of language models in real engineering work.
arxiv-2512-09299:
Daili Hua and ten co-authors introduce VABench, a benchmark for judging models that generate video together with synchronized sound. Recent generators make striking silent video, and some now add audio, but existing benchmarks mostly grade picture quality alone. A model can look good while its sound drifts out of sync or fails to match the scene.

VABench covers three task types: generating audio and video from text, from a still image, and in stereo. Its two evaluation modules span fifteen dimensions, including how well text, video, and audio match each other, lip-speech consistency, and question-answering checks on both sound and picture. Content spans seven categories, from animals and music to complex scenes and virtual worlds. The authors analyze and visualize results across models, aiming to set a standard for audio-video generation and push the field toward sound and picture that truly belong together.
arxiv-2512-10399:
Lucas English and co-authors connect two fields that rarely meet in exact formulas: quantum error correction and the Ising model of statistical mechanics. Big quantum computers need codes that suppress errors, and their performance is usually mapped by heavy simulation. The authors find a case where simulation can be replaced by a closed-form answer.

A toric code suffering bit-flip noise, filtered to keep only error-free syndrome cases, maps exactly onto the two-dimensional Ising model on a torus, a doughnut shape. Because that model is solvable, they derive the logical failure rate across all physical error rates, in four plain regimes from below threshold to above it. They also propose formulas for ordinary codes, including a tension model and a new near-threshold scaling form, giving code designers tools beyond brute-force simulation.
arxiv-2512-10699:
Gregory Galloway and Eric Ling simplify the proof of a cosmological singularity theorem, a result about whether the universe can be extended into the past without end. Their earlier theorem concerns four-dimensional spacetimes obeying the null energy condition with a positive cosmological constant. If such a spacetime has a compact slice that is expanding in all directions, it must be past-incomplete, unless that slice has the topology of a spherical space form.

The original proof leaned on the positive solution of the surface subgroup conjecture, heavy machinery from geometric group theory. This short note shows that a less famous result, the positive solution of the virtual positive first Betti number conjecture, gives a more streamlined and unified route to the same theorem. The authors show the statement with examples and probe its rigidity, asking how firmly the result holds when a spacetime is complete after all.
arxiv-2512-10799:
Karolina Gorna and co-authors hunt bugs in Go programs without running every path. Go powers critical infrastructure, but symbolic execution tools struggle with compiled Go binaries because the runtime is complex and the path count explodes. Their framework, Zorya, runs concolic execution, mixing concrete runs with symbolic reasoning, by translating Go binaries into Ghidra's P-Code intermediate representation.

Two additions sharpen the search. Zorya now detects bugs hiding on paths the concrete run did not take. And a multi-layer filter gates the symbolic effort onto paths that can actually reach a panic, Go's crash state. On five known vulnerabilities, the gating cut the branch load by a third to two thirds and ran several times faster. While Zorya found every panic and rival tools found at most two. Starting analysis at the function of interest, rather than at main, proved essential for larger programs.
arxiv-2512-11099:
Weitai Kang and colleagues present VGent, a system that finds the object a text description refers to inside an image. Existing approaches either let a large multimodal model spell out box coordinates slowly, risking invented answers, or retrain the model with special tokens, which can damage its reasoning. VGent instead splits reasoning and box prediction into separate modules.

A frozen multimodal model does the high level reasoning, untouched. A decoder then takes candidate boxes from ordinary detectors and picks the right ones by attending to the reasoner's internal states. Extra training improves multi target reasoning, labels resolve confusion between detection and segmentation, and a global recognition step checks all targets. On multi target benchmarks the system set new best scores while keeping fast, constant inference time.
arxiv-2512-11399:
Galann Pennec and fellow authors summarise long videos by first choosing the few clips that matter most. Vision language models can ingest ever longer footage, yet key visual details get lost in the flood, and processing everything is expensive. Their method targets the moments a good multimodal summary in fact needs.

The video is chopped into short clips, each described in compact words by a lightweight captioning model. A large language model then reads those descriptions and picks the clips carrying the most relevant visual information. Reference clips derived from human written screenplays and summaries of films provided the test bed. Clips amounting to a small fraction of a film sufficed to rebuild a complete summary. The automatic choice performed close to those reference clips, while capturing far more relevant content than random choice. Cheap captioning keeps the whole process affordable.
arxiv-2512-11699:
Roberta De Viti and co-authors map the crowded world of Multi-Party Computation, or MPC, protocols. MPC lets groups compute on shared data while keeping each input private. In practice it stays rare: costs run high, most of all with dishonest players, and builders lack clear guidance on which protocol fits which job.

The team lists the theory and practice factors that drive MPC speed, then runs broad tests across many tasks. Their study weighs trade offs between protocol families and matches tools to use cases. It ends with direct advice for developers and open problems for researchers. The goal is to close the gap between MPC promise and daily use.
arxiv-2512-12399:
Takahiro S Yamamoto, Kipp Cannon, Hayato Motohashi, and Hiroaki W H Tahara mix matched filtering with neural networks to hunt gravitational waves in a 2025 paper. Matched filtering is the standard search tool, comparing data against known wave shapes. Their network instead reads a whole SNR map, a stack of signal to noise time series from many templates.

Trained to say whether a wave is present, the system was tested on stellar mass black hole merger signals placed in steady Gaussian noise. It matched the standard pipeline and the machine learning entries in the MLGWSC-1 mock data challenge. It also reached fair sensitivity with practical computing resources, as a proof of concept.
arxiv-2512-12699:
Anrafel Fernandes Pereira and eleven co-authors identify attributes that help frame practical research problems in software engineering in a 2025 paper. A well framed problem is key to research that industry can use, yet early guidance is scarce. The team draws seven attributes from the literature: practical problem, context, impacts, practitioners, evidence, objective, and research questions.

At the ISERN 2024 meeting, 42 senior researchers discussed the attributes in a workshop, using a Problem Vision board with a worked example, then rated importance and completeness by survey. Results confirmed all seven matter for industry oriented problems. Feedback suggested adding financial criteria like return on investment under impacts, and feasibility and constraints under evidence.
arxiv-2512-12999:
Leonardo Bohach presents a universal design for quantum random access memory, a device that would let a quantum computer look up data coherently. Critics note that a single lookup can hide routing depth and control costs. Any honest design must state its hardware assumptions clearly.

In his design, the memory register itself takes part in the lookup as a quantum control, so one fixed operation works for all stored data. He gives an exact Hamiltonian, a total energy rule, that performs the lookup in one evolution. Its parts are built from projectors that commute with each other. A one-hot form of the address makes each part simple and local.
arxiv-2512-13599:
Angela Stallone and Ilaria Spassiani fix a flaw in tests of earthquake magnitude data. Above a completeness threshold, magnitudes are modeled with an exponential law. In practice, catalogs record magnitudes in bins, which makes the data discrete rather than smooth.

A common fix adds uniform noise to binned values before testing, but the authors show that fix fails. It creates a piecewise-constant form whose gap from the exponential law grows with catalog size or bin width. That bias can push the completeness estimate up by more than one magnitude unit. They derive the exact noise law, a truncated exponential in each bin, that restores the right form. Their tests confirm the fix across bin widths and catalog sizes.
arxiv-2512-13799:
Partha Konar and Sudipta Show argue that freeze-in dark matter comes with a hidden era of matter domination. Freeze-in models make dark matter through very feeble interactions, matching the lack of direct detections. Past work studied a heavy mediator's decay into dark matter but ignored the mediator's own role in the early universe.

The authors stress that the mediator can dominate the energy budget while it decays, forcing an early matter-dominated phase. Dark matter is then made in both radiation and matter phases, and entropy from the decay dilutes its abundance. The phase also boosts the gravitational wave signal from graviton emission during decay. That boost could make the signal visible to future high-frequency gravitational wave experiments.
arxiv-2512-13899:
Charlie Becker and co-authors build a machine learning method to diagnose winter precipitation type with honest uncertainty. Telling rain, snow, freezing rain, and ice pellets apart drives high-impact decisions, yet thermodynamically ambiguous cases defeat many methods. Most methods also give no uncertainty from a single model run.

Their evidential neural network predicts calibrated probabilities for all four types plus epistemic uncertainty, at standard network cost. Training pairs crowd-sourced mPING reports with NOAA Rapid Refresh profiles, after strict physical quality control. On held-out data from June 2020 to June 2022, it beat area-based methods on success ratio for freezing rain and ice pellets. Two Midwest storm case studies show its physical consistency in practice.
arxiv-2512-13999:
Arohee Bhoja presents a verified implementation of the Misra and Gries edge coloring algorithm in the Lean theorem prover. Vizing's theorem says every simple undirected graph can be edge-colored with at most one more color than its maximum degree. The Misra and Gries method is a modified, polynomial-time version of Vizing's original procedure.

Verified means the code is machine-checked to maintain the invariants the algorithm needs, rather than merely tested. The focus of the work is building libraries for the relevant mathematical objects in Lean. Invariants are rigorously maintained as the partial coloring is extended step by step until complete. The result is a formally trustworthy version of a classic graph algorithm.
arxiv-2512-14299:
Youngwoo Choi, Woojin Kwon, Leslie Looney, and John Tobin report a bridge between two young stellar systems in a 2025 paper. Most stars are born in clusters, where close passes between young stars with planet forming disks should be common, yet direct evidence is rare.

Millimeter observations show a clear bridge of tidally stripped material between L1448 IRS3A and L1448 IRS3B. Spiral arms on both disks support the same story: the systems are in a dynamical flyby. Hydrodynamical simulations reproduce the features and place the closest approach about 15,000 years ago. The case gives rare insight into how stellar encounters reshape disks and shape young multiple star systems.
arxiv-2512-14499:
Jia Guo and twenty-three co-authors introduce ReVision, an AI model for reading retinal photographs that learned from real clinical work instead of curated research sets. Its training data came from a decade-long telemedicine program in China, pairing nearly half a million eye photographs with the diagnostic reports doctors wrote for them across 162 institutions.

Because the model absorbed real practice, it deploys with little local effort. With no retraining at all it detected eye disease strongly across public benchmarks and hospital cohorts. Light adaptation matched heavily tuned rivals using far fewer labeled examples. When thirty-three eye doctors used its help in a trial, their diagnostic accuracy rose by roughly fifteen percent.
arxiv-2512-14599:
Jimi E. Harrold and eight co-authors ask how the population of quiescent galaxies, ones that have largely stopped forming stars, was built up at cosmic noon. They study the question with a mock lightcone from the L-Galaxies semi-analytic model, matched closely to observations from the UKIDSS Ultra Deep Survey.

Within that sample they track merging, rejuvenation, and how long each phase stays visible, across star-forming, quiescent, and post-starburst galaxies. The aim is to judge how much mergers and restarts contribute to the passive galaxy mass function. The work helps observers read real survey data through a model's lens.
arxiv-2512-14899:
J. Sumaya-Martinez studies tiny light based sensors and asks a surprising question: does a sharper resonance always mean a better sensor, even at the quantum limit? The sensors are resonant nanophotonic devices built from subwavelength slit cavities, which trap light at set frequencies. Classical theory already used Fisher information to judge their precision.

Sumaya-Martinez builds a quantum version of that framework, modeling the sensing step as a phase and loss channel inside an interferometer. The quantum Fisher information shows precision is set by how strongly the target shifts the phase, not by the cavity quality factor Q. So the best working point often sits away from the sharpest resonance. Quantum probes still boost sensitivity, but they do not change which sensor shape is best, a clear design rule for future devices.
arxiv-2512-14999:
Yiding Wang and three coauthors study how the storage capacity of a quantum battery splits among its parts. A quantum battery stores energy in quantum states, and its capacity says how much work can be drawn out. For a two qubit system, they find a trade off: the sum of the parts' capacities is governed by the capacity of the whole.

The trade off holds for a class of models including Ising, XX, XXZ, and XXX chains. Building on it, the authors define a leftover, or residual, capacity and split each part's capacity into coherent and incoherent pieces. They give a protocol that picks unitary operations to boost a chosen part's capacity, with a condition that guarantees a gain, and find the shortest time such a boost can take. Parallel results cover three qubit systems, and numeric examples check the protocol works.
arxiv-2512-15199:
Lemieux Wang and three coauthors show how several parties can share one quantum resource in turn: the uncertainty between two quantum states that are not orthogonal. Indistinguishability of such states powers uses like cryptography and randomness generation. Their scheme lets a single party's generated uncertainty, measured by max relative entropy, be passed along a chain.

The method rests on maximum confidence measurements and weak measurements gentle enough to leave the system usable for the next party. Each party in sequence performs state discrimination on the same quantum system. The authors review known sequential discrimination results, then walk through examples with and without symmetries in the state ensembles. The work probes the ultimate limits of pulling information from one system in sequence, and guides how quantum resources might be shared in such settings.
arxiv-2512-15599:
Tobias Kirschstein, Simon Giebenhain, and Matthias Niessner present FlexAvatar for building complete 3D head avatars from one image in a 2025 paper. Training from monocular video tends to leave the back and sides of the head incomplete. The team traces that flaw to entanglement between the driving signal and the target viewpoint.

Their transformer based animation model uses learnable data source tokens, called bias sinks, so monocular and multi view data can train together. Inference then combines the broad generalization of monocular data with the full 3D completeness of multi view supervision. The smooth latent space also supports identity blending and fitting to a few input views.
arxiv-2512-15899:
Bruno Le Floch, Gela Patashuri, and Emilio Trevisani revisit dimensional reduction in Parisi Sourlas theory in a 2025 paper. Such supersymmetric models are known to behave like models in two fewer dimensions, a striking simplification. Existing proofs of that reduction are revisited and reframed through the cohomology of a supercharge Q.

Three results follow. The recent decoupling picture of reduction is explained naturally by Q exactness. A new proof uses localization. Cardy's blending proof, much like localization but without saddle point methods, is shown to follow from deforming the action by a Q exact term. That last form extends beyond scalar models to any such theory.
arxiv-2512-15999:
Dan M Watson leads a large team reporting James Webb Space Telescope results in a paper posted to arXiv in 2025. They studied IRAS 16253-2429, a very young, low-mass protostar still gathering material. Its mid-infrared light shows bright lines from hydroxide molecules, called OH, plus carbon dioxide lines, but oddly no water lines to match.

The team shows the OH glow is fluorescence: ultraviolet light breaks water apart, and the freed OH then cascades down through its energy levels. That lets them use the OH spectrum to measure the star's ultraviolet output directly. They find a disk-to-star growth rate of 3 times 10 to the minus 10 solar masses per year. Most of the system's light comes from the star itself, not from infalling gas.
arxiv-2512-16199:
Jerrin Bright and six co-authors present a synthetic data factory in an arXiv paper posted in 2025. Pose estimation, tracking human body positions, needs lots of labeled motion data, which is costly to collect for special fields like sports. Avatar4D generates custom 4D human motion data, meaning 3D bodies moving over time, without any manual labeling.

Users control pose, appearance, camera angle, and setting. To prove its worth, the team built Syn2Sport, a large synthetic data set covering baseball and ice hockey, sports with unusual motions that challenge trackers. They benchmarked leading pose models on it and tested supervised training, zero-shot transfer to real footage, and generalization across sports. The results show synthetic humans can train and test real systems when domain-specific real data is scarce.
arxiv-2512-16699:
J. Berteaud and a large team report two new millisecond pulsars found toward the bulge of the Milky Way. A hidden crowd of such fast-spinning pulsars could explain the Galactic Center Excess, a glow of gamma rays with no clear source.

Guided by a new way to pick candidates, the team ran deep radio searches with MeerKAT, Murriyang, and Green Bank toward nine X-ray sources in the inner Galaxy. Two pulsars turned up, one a black widow candidate, named PSRs J1740-2805 and J1740-28. The finds double the count of such pulsars known within the innermost two degrees of the center, proof the hunt method works.
arxiv-2512-16999:
Patrick D. Bolton, Jernej F. Kamenik, and Martín Novoa-Brunet explain a Belle II excess in B meson decays with missing energy. The data fit a two-body decay with a light unseen particle near 2.1 GeV, and the team builds a full model around a Higgsed U(1) prime gauge force.

A light Z prime boson plus a vector-like top partner can lift the needed decay rate. The plain version fails, though: loop effects force the Z prime to decay to muons, which LHCb searches rule out. Adding one light charged singlet fermion lets the boson decay mostly invisibly. The fixed model dodges collider and Higgs limits and can also yield the observed dark matter share by resonant freeze-out.
arxiv-2512-17299:
Abdullah M Zyarah and Dhireesha Kudithipudi design a chip that lets small edge devices keep learning over time without draining power. Recurrent networks, which handle sequences, normally need costly training and constant data shuttling. That load is too heavy for tiny embedded hardware that must adapt on the spot.

Their design, M2RU, mixes analog memristor circuits with digital control and runs a compact recurrent unit on the chip itself. Two tricks help: inputs stream in bit by bit without pricey converters, and a replay store steadies learning when the data shifts. The chip hits 312 billion operations per watt, uses 29 times less energy than a standard digital design, and should last about 12.2 years.
arxiv-2512-17399:
Simon Marionnet answers an open question about how to arrange weights around a ring-shaped matrix to make it as tame as possible. The matrix has zeros everywhere except one ring of slots, filled with a fixed set of growing weights in some order. Its numerical radius, a measure of how far the matrix can stretch a vector's shadow, swings with the chosen order.

Earlier work by Gau and by Chang and Wang had settled which order makes the radius largest. Chien and co-authors then asked the reverse: which order makes it smallest, for rings of six or more? Marionnet's note gives that minimizing arrangement. The result closes a small but nagging gap in the study of these cyclic matrices.
arxiv-2512-18199:
Devang Dhanuka and Nidhi Rastogi at the Rochester Institute of Technology build PROVEX, an explainability layer for intrusion detection in security operations centers. Modern detectors use graph neural networks on system provenance data, but their alerts arrive as black box verdicts that analysts struggle to trust. PROVEX sits on top of KAIROS, a leading temporal graph based detector. Its design can adapt to other temporal graph detectors with little change.

The framework adds explanations after detection, showing why an alert fired by naming the key causal subgraphs and events. Three explanation methods, GraphMask, GNNExplainer, and a temporal variant, are adapted to provenance graphs. On the DARPA CADETS Engagement 3 dataset, the explainers preserve the detector's decisions with high fidelity. They surface telling edges such as malicious file interactions and anomalous network flows. Each explanation costs only 3 to 5 seconds per event. The goal is faster triage and justified trust in automated alerts.
arxiv-2512-18299:
Amir Eskandari-asl and Adolfo Avella study how germanium, a key chip material, soaks up ultra short laser flashes. A flash can lift electrons into excited states in a flash of time far below a trillionth of a second. Their computing method tracks where those electrons and holes land and how much energy the crystal keeps, at low cost in machine time.

Sorting the response by how many light particles act at once shows that two particle hits do most of the work. One and three particle paths matter only for select flash lengths, strengths, and colors. Knowing which path rules lets engineers tune flashes for fast optical switches and sensors built on such crystals.
arxiv-2512-18499:
Sara Ditsch, Johannes M. Henn, and Prashanth Raman find new ways to compute Feynman integrals, the notoriously hard integrals behind particle physics predictions. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and accepted by JHEP, exploits two hidden properties of these integrals: complete monotonicity, where every derivative keeps one sign, and the stronger Stieltjes property.

The first method pairs monotonicity with the differential equations the integrals obey, building a numerical bootstrap that pins values down tightly; they test it on multi-loop integrals with internal masses. The second proves the integrals are Stieltjes functions in a parameter range, so Pade approximants describe them well even in physical scattering regions. With only a Taylor expansion near a soft limit, they approximate a 20-loop banana-type integral. The work opens fresh routes to precision calculations.
arxiv-2512-18799:
Xiao Yang, Qiyao Peng, and Sander C. Hille study a diffusion model with a twist: something senses the spreading substance from afar but acts only at one point. Mathematically, the reaction term is a Dirac source or sink at the origin, a stripped-down picture of a control system that monitors at a distance and intervenes centrally. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in the Journal of Differential Equations, asks when solutions stay positive.

Positivity, meaning concentrations never go negative, fails for some parameter choices. The authors find the regime, plus monotonicity and symmetry conditions on the starting state, that keep solutions positive for all time. They also give conditions for the system to settle to a constant steady state away from the observed region. Laplace transform arguments carry the proofs, tools reusable for other singular control models.
arxiv-2512-19399:
Sandro Andric uses human brain activity as a coordinate system for reading language model states. Most interpretability tools carve directions from text labels alone, which can float free of any outside ground truth. Andric instead builds a word-level brain atlas from MEG recordings in the SMN4Lang dataset, using phase-locking patterns.

Independent component analysis pulls latent axes from the atlas, checked against outside word lists and labels. Lightweight adapters then map a model's hidden states onto those axes, with the model itself frozen. Steering along one axis shifted word-frequency behavior robustly in a small model, at matched perplexity. A function-versus-content axis steered consistently across three model families.
arxiv-2512-19899:
Paúl Cumba-Armijos, Diego Riofrío-Luzcando, Verónica Rodríguez-Arboleda, and Joe Carrión-Jumbo train a neural network to spot cyberbullying written in Spanish. Their starting point is that harmful exchanges on social networks and messaging apps leave textual traces that machines might learn to flag, protecting the most vulnerable users. Most detection research targets English, so Spanish material needed its own groundwork.

The team consolidated and prepared a corpus of Spanish bullying expressions harvested from Twitter, then trained a convolutional neural network on it with deep learning techniques. The resulting predictive model recognizes categories of abuse including insults, racism, and homophobic attacks. The work appeared in the International Journal of Data Mining, Modelling and Management, and is preserved here as the authors' original manuscript.
arxiv-2512-19999:
Kexin Nie, Xin Tang, Mengyao Guo, and Ze Gao describe a workshop on creating with AI. The setting is visual storytelling education in human-computer interaction. The method is their gap-and-fill approach. Students must keep creative agency while they use AI help with care. The philosophy draws on Eastern ideas of planned emptiness. It cites Chinese negative-space traditions and the Japanese concept of ma. Design minimalism of today joins the same line.

The session runs in three phases. First, a human-led narrative base is built. Then the class marks strategic gaps. Last, AI help fills just those gaps. Storyboards and sequential art carry the hands-on work. The tasks stress how to show interactive concepts and access fixes. This run builds on past ones at ACM C&C 2025. It addresses the needs of the Chinese HCI community.
arxiv-2512-20399:
Corey Adams, Rishikesh Ranade, Ram Cherukuri, and Sanjay Choudhry present GeoTransolver, a Transformer that learns physics on awkward, irregular engineering domains. Computer-aided design work needs fast stand-ins for runs such as airflow over cars. Their model extends the Transolver design with geometry-aware attention, branded GALE.

GALE pairs physics-aware self-attention on learned state slices with cross-attention to shared geometry and global context, gathered by multi-scale ball queries and reused in every block. Released inside NVIDIA's PhysicsNeMo, the model is benchmarked on automotive and wing data sets against strong benchmarks. It also handles crash-dynamics problems for bumper beams and full vehicle bodies. Accuracy, toughness to geometry shifts, and data thrift all improve over the comparison models.
arxiv-2512-20499:
Cho Win Aung and co-authors compute how a magnetic field changes the stickiness of electron fluids. Without a field, one shear viscosity coefficient describes the flow. A field breaks the symmetry, and five independent coefficients appear, sorting into components perpendicular, parallel, and Hall-like relative to the field direction.

The kinetic theory maths, done in the relaxation time shortcut, extends earlier zero-field work on graphene. When the scattering time matches the cyclotron time, the perpendicular viscosity drops by about eighty percent and the parallel one by half, while the Hall response peaks. The field needed is modest for graphene, larger for ordinary charged fluids, and hugely large for quark fluids. Three very different systems thus share one magnetic fingerprint.
arxiv-2512-20999:
Verene Einwalter, Eric Hooper, and three co-authors clean up a radio-astronomy catalog whose images are salted with fakes. The Very Large Array Sky Survey's Quick Look products come from a simplified imaging pipeline that leaves widespread artifacts. The catalog of double radio sources tied to active galactic nuclei inherits that contamination. Each catalog entry has two or three components, any of which might be an artifact rather than a real source.

Random forest classifiers learn to count how many components of each entry are spurious, handling the dataset's class imbalance through careful training-set selection. The best model reaches a weighted F1 score near ninety-seven percent. Its classifications yield a cleaned catalog. From it, researchers can extract a sample that is nearly complete and almost entirely artifact-free, ready for studies of double-lobed galaxies.
arxiv-2512-21099:
Jaeseong Lee, Jaegul Choo, and two co-authors make digital heads that survive extreme expressions. Photorealistic three-dimensional Gaussian avatars break down when rigged by purely analytic rules or purely learned deformation fields, and texel-space methods waste the underlying face mesh. TexAvatars splits the job along a clean seam. Convolutional networks predict local geometric attributes in the mesh's texture space. The actual three-dimensional deformation runs through mesh-aware Jacobians, keeping motion smooth and meaningful across triangle boundaries.
