arxiv-2602-00899: Mritunjay Pandey casts content-based recommendation as recommendation-as-retrieval, where an intent signal retrieves the top-K relevant items via semantic similarity. Sparse keyword matching like BM25 breaks under vocabulary mismatch when intent barely overlaps product metadata. His two-tower bi-encoder, fine-tuned on Amazon Reviews 2023 Fashion, trains on 50,000 sampled interactions. FAISS HNSW indexing plus an ONNX Runtime pipeline with INT8 quantization serves results efficiently. Over 826,402 catalog items, a review-to-title benchmark shows Recall@10 more than doubles over BM25, meeting practical latency needs.
arxiv-2602-01299: Gianluca Curzi and Graham E. Leigh prove cut removal for endless proof systems built for induction and coinduction. In such systems, soundness leans on global rules like progressivity, and keeping those rules alive through endless cut removal stayed a hard core problem. The team gives two cut-removal proofs for endless muMALL, a linear logic slice with fixed points, via Tait and Girard's reducibility-candidate toolkit. In both proofs, progressivity holds follow straight from the candidates' own defining traits.
arxiv-2602-01399: Fabian Fumagalli and co-authors ground paired sampling for Shapley estimation. Shapley values attribute credit across feature importance, data valuation, and causal inference, but exact computation is intractable. The team proves the value hinges only on the odd part of the set function, and paired sampling drops the even part from the regression task. From that insight comes OddSHAP, an estimator running polynomial regression on the odd subspace, isolated via a Fourier basis, with a proxy model flagging interactions. In benchmarks, OddSHAP reaches top accuracy at larger sampling budgets.
arxiv-2602-01499: Caleb McFarland introduces totally Δ-modular treewidth, a tree-decomposition parameter for matrices with two nonzero entries in each row. He shows integer programs with bounded TDM-treewidth matrices can be solved in polynomial time for bounded-domain variables. That extends earlier graph-based parameters for two-entry-per-row matrices to entries outside minus one, zero, and one. He also gives a Grid Theorem analogue for bounded TDM-treewidth matrices in the language of rooted signed graphs.
arxiv-2602-01599: Israel Adewuyi and colleagues test the simplest use of redundancy in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: train only a picked slice of parameters, leaving the rest frozen. Training just one percent of parameters matches or beats full tuning across three models and two domains. Different random masks barely overlap yet all succeed, suggesting pretrained models hold many workable sparse subnetworks, not one privileged set. The authors name this the Multiple Ticket Hypothesis, explaining it through the KL limit in training, which confines updates to a low dimensional space.
arxiv-2602-01799: Ido Faran and colleagues track satellite image series in landscapes, where Mediterranean patterns, season change and multi decade shifts mix. Their Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Long Term Forecasting joins space and time, processing patches with sequences up to twenty years. Training with masked space, masked time and sampled horizons learns from decades of unlabeled Landsat imagery, while direct prediction of future points avoids error accumulation. Tests on Landsat data from 1984 to 2024 beat statistical, convolutional, LSTM and standard transformer baselines for next year forecasts, and the design handles irregular sampling.
arxiv-2602-01999: Yanrui Du and colleagues trace reflection in R1 style models, reading activation paths with the logit lens. Three stages emerge: latent control layers holding thinking budget in a linear direction; pivot layers where turning point and summary cues rule; and behavior overt layers where reflection likelihood rises. Interventions reveal a chain: prompt semantics shift latent control projections, inducing rivalry between turning point and summary cues, regulating reflection sampling in overt layers. The findings suggest a human like process from monitoring to reflection.
arxiv-2602-02199: Aryan Sood and colleagues present LASER-KV, a cache compression framework challenging the assumption that attention scores alone reveal which tokens matter. Language models claim long context windows, but cache memory grows linearly and pruning trades semantic recall for savings. The team replaces the fixed summary size with block-wise accumulation under a budget governed by a protection divisor. That isolates compression effects from sliding-window artifacts. On the Babilong benchmark, earlier methods degrade sharply while LASER-KV holds performance and leads by a margin at the longest context tested.
arxiv-2602-02399:
Utsab Dey and 1 co-author compute predictions for rare decays of the Bc meson within the Standard Model, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The decays turn a Bc meson into a Ds meson plus either charged leptons or neutrinos. Form factors, which encode how quarks rearrange inside the mesons, are the key inputs.

The authors use perturbative QCD form factors tied to meson wave functions. Lattice QCD results for related transitions fix the shape parameters and values at zero momentum transfer. Heavy-quark spin symmetry plus a fitting scheme then extends the factors across the full allowed range. With those inputs they predict branching ratios and observables sensitive to lepton flavor. A detailed angular analysis of a cascade decay, where the excited Ds meson decays further, completes the predictions.
arxiv-2602-02599:
Jihao Xin and 4 co-authors shrink the key-value cache of long-context language models without breaking their sense of position, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The cache dominates memory and compute at long contexts. Pruning the least useful projection channels is a direct fix, but rotary position embeddings rotate feature dimensions in pairs. Deleting single channels corrupts those pairs and the pruned model becomes unusable.

Their method, RoPE-aligned pruning, removes whole aligned pairs instead, keeping every rotation intact. Across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models from three to fourteen billion parameters, accuracy held at thirty percent cache compression. The method far outperformed position-blind channel pruning. It stayed near the strongest low-rank method at lower attention cost. It also composes with orthogonal techniques such as quantization, so savings can stack.
arxiv-2602-02799:
Wasu Top Piriyakulkij and 3 co-authors teach agents composable skills and a world model at the same time, so each makes the other cheaper to learn, in a 2026 paper. Building new skills by composing old ones is a long-standing goal. Model-free hierarchical reinforcement learning can do it, but only with large amounts of data.

Their agent jointly learns an abstract world model, compressed across both states and time, and a set of hierarchical neural options, reusable skill units. Learning proceeds sample-efficiently because the model guides skill acquisition while skills structure the model. On a subset of object-centric Atari games, the method learned more skills from less data than baselines. It also showed learning and generalization capabilities the baselines lacked entirely. The authors frame joint learning, not bigger hierarchies, as the route to agents that accumulate skills like people do.
arxiv-2602-03699:
A cosmological simulation normally grows a random universe, so it can only be compared with ours statistically. Aurélien Valade and 6 co-authors present Hamlet-PM in a 2026 paper, a method for constraining simulations to reproduce the actual local universe. That matters for rare or well-studied nearby objects that live in one specific environment.

The method forward-models the early density field from sparse, noisy measurements of late-time galaxy velocities, integrating gravity with a particle-mesh solver. Applied to the Cosmicflows-4 velocity compilation, it generates initial conditions that are rerun with a precision N-body code. A suite of one hundred constrained simulations follows, with twelve prominent nearby clusters matched by mass and separation to their real counterparts.
arxiv-2602-03799:
A controller for a system nobody has modeled exactly cannot lean on the usual safety proofs. Xinhang Ma and 3 co-authors combine conformal prediction with reachability analysis in a 2026 paper to certify safety anyway. Conformal prediction supplies valid uncertainty intervals for the unknown dynamics at each step, from data alone.

Reachability analysis then checks whether safety holds throughout those uncertainty bounds. The authors also give an algorithm that trains control policies to earn high reward while stretching the horizon over which the probabilistic guarantee holds. Seven test settings across four domains, from cartpole to drones, cover affine and nonlinear safety rules. Their policies achieve the strongest provable safety guarantees while keeping average reward high.
arxiv-2602-03899:
A few bad actors should not be able to poison shared machine learning. Gilles Bareilles and 3 co-authors study MultiKrum, a rule that filters worker updates before averaging them, in a 2026 paper. MultiKrum is popular in practice, yet until now it lacked any proof of robustness.

The authors supply that proof and bound how accurate the rule stays under attack. They introduce a sharper measure of robustness for judging such rules in general. MultiKrum's bounds turn out never worse than the older Krum rule, and better in realistic conditions. Experiments check how tight the new lower bound is.
arxiv-2602-03999:
Anming Gu and 2 co-authors generalize a powerful sampling construction. Eldan's stochastic localization gradually reveals a random draw from a distribution, and it has driven breakthroughs in high-dimensional geometry. Their 2026 paper rebuilds the process for non-Euclidean geometry, motivated by mirror descent in optimization.

Gaussian smoothing is replaced by a broader family of regularizers built from log-Laplace transforms. The authors bound the mixing time of the resulting Markov chain under a functional Poincaré inequality. Applied to private convex optimization in certain norms, the framework improves known query costs. The work extends a central modern tool to geometries where it could not go before.
arxiv-2602-04199:
Acceleration warps quantum resources, and Saveetha Harikrishnan and 2 co-authors map exactly how. Their 2026 paper studies static quantum resource theories under noninertial motion. The Unruh effect, where an accelerating observer sees particles in empty space, is the physical driver.

They first show noninertial effects equal a well-defined quantum channel, specifically a bosonic amplifier. Then they trace that channel through a resource theory's three ingredients: free states, free operations, and resource measures. General statements emerge about what motion preserves and destroys. The results matter for relativistic quantum information, where satellites and detectors rarely sit still in inertial frames.
arxiv-2602-04599:
Nikola Milosevic and 5 co-authors rethink safety limits in reinforcement learning in a 2026 paper on stochastic decision horizons. Instead of treating each rule violation as spending from a fixed budget, their framework shortens the agent's effective planning horizon when violations occur.

That change cuts both present reward credit and reliance on future estimates. The authors show it represents a survival-style constraint and derive two algorithms compatible with replayed experience. One ends the episode after violations; the other stops reward credit while play continues. Tests included a highly muscled simulated humanoid and standard safety tasks. One algorithm reached strong gait quality far earlier than its reference and trained more stably.
arxiv-2602-04899:
Data poisoning slips crafted examples into training data so a model learns a hidden behavior, and defenders usually answer by cleaning the data. It is the work of Andrew Draganov and 3 co-authors. Poisoning means slipping crafted examples into training data so the model learns a hidden behavior. Defenders usually respond by cleaning the data. The authors argue that one attack survives even perfect knowledge of how the poison was placed.

The attack, named Phantom Transfer, adapts a technique called subliminal learning to real-world settings. It works no matter which model made the data, which model trains on it, or what behavior is targeted. It survived 11 tested defenses, including rewriting every sample with another model, and it can plant behaviors triggered by a password. The authors recommend adding white-box checks and audits of the trained model, not just data cleaning.
arxiv-2602-04999:
Giacomo Bartolucci and Fabrizio Olmeda wrote this 2026 soft matter paper on blends of many liquid parts. Such blends split into drops of varied makeup, a trick cells use to sort their insides. With many parts that interact, the split can stall in long-lived states instead of settling fast.

Mixing math with computer runs, the authors first show how two coexisting phases can break up into many phases at once. They then look again at Ostwald ripening, the classic pattern where drop size grows with a cube-root law in time. In messy blends that growth can be held back a lot. The holdup comes from glass-like slow easing and short-lived states marked by varied wetting angles. The results link phase split physics with the slow, sticky motion seen in cell condensates.
arxiv-2602-05099:
Platforms A/B test a handful of incentive levels, then must guess how untested levels would work for each kind of user. Zhiqi Zhang and 3 co-authors build a scheme for just that leap in this 2026 econometrics paper. The setup is a continuous choice, such as a price or a creator incentive, seen only at a few discrete test values.

Their scheme, deep learning for policy targeting, estimates each user's policy value and then learns a personalized continuous policy from the discrete test. The authors prove their value estimates are asymptotically unbiased and consistent, and that the learned policy's regret shrinks at the root-n rate. In work with a major social media platform, the method tuned incentives for content creation. It beat current benchmarks at both valuing policies per user group and finding the best personalized policy.
arxiv-2602-05299:
Freelancers now often work in short-lived teams, yet AI tools are built for lone output inside stable companies. Kashif Imteyaz and 3 co-authors co-designed alternatives with freelancers in this 2026 human-computer interaction paper. Twenty-seven freelancers joined design sessions to imagine joint AI that fits platform work rather than fighting it.

A central fear surfaced: AI that generates content freely could erode creative agency and expert identity. That risk grows if it reproduces work without attribution, blurring what makes each collaborator's input distinctive. People proposed helper AI instead, human-guided tools that support agency and allow freelancer-led teamwork with productive friction kept in. Reading the results through Marcuse's idea of tech logic, the authors argue freelancers are resisting one-dimensional, speed-only AI. The paper ends with design advice for joint tools that protect collective creative agency.
arxiv-2602-05599:
Languages with very little labeled data, such as Mizo and Khasi, lag far behind rich-resource languages in language technology. Subhadip Maji and Arnab Bhattacharya study how to transfer knowledge from high-resource languages to extreme low-resource ones, where labeled examples number only in the hundreds. They work on sentence-level and word-level tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, sentiment classification, and named entity recognition.

Their new method, GETR, builds token representations with a graph neural network to carry knowledge across languages. Two baselines are tested beside it: augmentation inside hidden layers, and token embedding transfer through translation. GETR beat existing multilingual and cross-lingual methods by clear margins on the truly low-resource languages, and by larger ones on simulated low-resource versions of Marathi, Bangla, and Malayalam. The authors also analyze which factors make transfer succeed. The work targets builders of language tools for underserved communities.
arxiv-2602-05699:
The number of steps a solver needs on a polyhedron lower bounds how fast whole families of algorithms can run. Daniel Dadush, Stefan Kober, and Zhuan Khye Koh study two such measures. One is circuit diameter, the longest shortest circuit walk between vertices. The other is straight line complexity, a newer measure tied to interior point methods. Straight line complexity counts the fewest pieces of a piecewise linear curve that can track a neighborhood of the central path.

The authors show the circuit diameter is bounded above by the straight line complexity, up to a polynomial factor in the dimension. That yields a strongly polynomial bound for polyhedra whose constraints each involve at most two variables. They also give a circuit augmentation algorithm whose iteration count matches the bound. The paper links two lines of research that grew up apart.
arxiv-2602-05899:
Fisher zeros, the points where a partition function vanishes in the complex plane, can reveal phases of matter that ordinary measurements blur. Songtai Lv, Yang Liu, Erhai Zhao, Haiyuan Zou, and Tao Xiang use them to probe the quantum XY chain in an external field. Their approach works with complex valued inverse temperature and leans on thermofield dynamics to characterize quantum and thermal fluctuations.

Oscillatory gap behavior shows up as oscillations in the long time dynamics of a spectral form factor. Near the gapless limit, the authors find giant bubbles: large closed loops of Fisher zeros. Those bubbles set an energy scale that seems to contradict the standard low energy theory of a featureless Luttinger liquid. Tracking the bubbles as the field varies ties their motion to spectral weight moving from high to low energies. The short paper links zeros, dynamics, and excitations in strongly correlated systems.
arxiv-2602-05999:
In reinforcement learning, compute and parameter count are usually tangled: bigger nets both hold more and compute more. Raj Ghugare and three co-authors untangle them by formalising policies with a hard compute budget. They prove that a policy allowed more compute can solve tasks and stretch to longer horizons that a cheaper policy cannot reach, even when parameter counts stay fixed.

They build a minimal variable-compute architecture from earlier work on algorithmic learning and model-free planning. Across thirty-one tasks, online and offline, more compute alone lifts performance, and long-horizon generalisation beats feedforward and deep residual nets with up to five times more parameters. The paper argues that how much a policy thinks, not just how big it is, sets what it can learn.
arxiv-2602-06299:
Air and water flowing past a moving plate shed swirling vortices, and engineers would love a cheap model that predicts the forces. Yu Jun Loo and Silas Alben compare an idealized vortex sheet model, which ignores viscosity, against full Navier-Stokes simulations. They test roughly seventy motions of translating and rotating plates at moderate flow speed.

When the plate's own motion drives the flow, the ideal model matched force histories and vortex patterns well. When the flow sheds vortices on its own rhythm, agreement stayed good but weakened at low attack angles. The comparison maps where the cheap model can be trusted for force prediction and physical insight, and where it cannot.
arxiv-2602-06399:
A smart surface that can amplify and steer radio waves may rescue both communication and sensing where direct paths are blocked. Xin Jin and 4 co-authors design such a system, joining an active reconfigurable intelligent surface with rate-splitting access and integrated sensing and communication. The fairness bottleneck is the weakest target's echo getting drowned out.

They jointly tune the transmitter, the surface, and the rate split to lift the worst echo quality, under user rate and power limits. The hard optimization splits into three subproblems solved in turn with standard relaxation methods. Simulations beat rival access schemes and plain passive surfaces, closing in on the sensing-only upper bound. The design targets settings like blocked city canyons.
arxiv-2602-06599:
Ariyan Bighashdel, Thiago D. Simão, and Frans A. Oliehoek work on computer agents that learn strategies by playing against growing sets of rival strategies. Their setting is a framework that slowly expands a pool of strategies and trains best replies to them. Training a separate reply for each agent is costly, so the authors look for a cheaper path.

Their method collects game records once under the current mix of strategies, then reuses that shared data to compute a best reply for every agent at the same time. Because learning from stored data can drift off course, they add three fixes, including a variant that adds extra exploration during data collection. In benchmark tests the explored version gave the best balance of accuracy and cost, while a hybrid version nearly matched the original method for a fraction of the data.
arxiv-2602-06699:
Alessio Pecilli and Matteo Rosati build a quantum version of self-attention, the operation at the heart of transformer models and large language models. Attention predicts what comes next in a sequence by blending past elements, weighted by how much they overlap. Their design gets the needed nonlinearity from interference between quantum states rather than from classical arithmetic.

The method scores its predictions with an entropy-based loss read from just two measurements, and it can learn how input data is embedded so that state overlaps mirror real similarity. The authors derive its training cost and show cases where it beats the fairest classical rival, chiefly when sequences are long. In simulations the quantum transformer learned to predict both ordinary classical data and the behavior of a many-body quantum magnet model.
arxiv-2602-06799:
Shamik Bhattacharya and five co-authors take on words that can mean more than one thing. A word like "bank" can point to a river edge or a place for money, and text alone may not settle it. Their fix pairs each word sense with pictures, using the CLIP model to place words and images in one shared space.

Two kinds of text hints enrich the word side: hints about meaning, and hints about photos, plus near words from WordNet. On the image side, the team tweaks each picture at test time, then picks the picture that lines up best with the text. On a 2023 test set, the enriched hints lifted the main score from about 0.72 to 0.76. Extra word lists and hints in many tongues, by contrast, tended to blur meaning.
arxiv-2602-06899:
Ameya Rathod and four co-authors ask how much data it takes to pin down a cause-and-effect graph when the world itself shifts over time. From observations alone, many different cause graphs can fit the same data, so the graph is not fixed without extra structure. Past work leaned on either time patterns or on data from many settings, but not on both at once.

The team joins the two kinds of variation and works out shared rules for when the graph can be fixed at all. Time structure, they show, can stand in for missing setting variety. Then they price the job: under heavy-tailed noise, the shape rules stay the same, yet the data needed grows far beyond the bell-curve case. Sharp theory bounds mark the limits of covariance-based recovery for real shifting systems.
arxiv-2602-07299:
Keeping drinking water safe means holding chlorine residuals steady across a large, messy spread network, where flows are non-linear and noisy.  Rivaaj Monsia and three co-authors tackle the control problem with surrogate-assisted neuroevolution.

Neural controllers evolved with NEAT decide where and when to inject chlorine, optimized with NSGA-II across four goals: less total chlorine, even concentrations, safe maximum levels, and regular injection timing.  Each candidate is scored against a fast surrogate model instead of a full simulation.  Water utilities get a multi-objective control design that balances safety, cost, and uniformity in networks too complex for classic controllers.
arxiv-2602-07399:
Vision-language-action models can propose plausible robot trajectories yet fail on fine shape, where near-miss actions diverge under scarce supervision.  Changhua Xu and three co-authors tackle few-shot adaptation from a generation-choice angle with VGAS, value-guided action-chunk choice.

A fine-tuned vision-language-action model generates many candidate action chunks, and a geometrically grounded critic, the Q-Chunk-Former, selects the chunk that is both semantically faithful and geometrically precise at inference time.  The best-of-N choice resolves ambiguities that training alone cannot.  Robot learning teams get an inference-time fix for the last-millimeter failures of few-shot policies.  The critic judges chunks on shape the generator alone cannot resolve, which is why choice beats generating a single trajectory.
arxiv-2602-07799:
Reward models trained on human preferences can absorb demographic skews and pass them into aligned language models. Ching Lam Choi and four co-authors offer Faro, a training method that builds fairness constraints directly into reward modeling rather than patching bias before or after.

Faro supports demographic parity, equalized odds, and counterfactual fairness. The paper proves fairness certificates with controllable slack, shows fairness carries from reward to policy under standard fine-tuning, and shows that a genuine accuracy-fairness frontier exists. Across models and benchmarks, Faro cuts bias and harmful outputs while holding or improving quality. Alignment teams gain both theory and a usable in-training method.
arxiv-2602-08099:
Making multi-sense models can be reused as coding readers, but for video they trail built video base models. Issar Tzachor and two co-authors analyze multi-sense language models layer by layer and find that middle ready layers already encode large task-apt information for video-text search.

Mixing those middle codes with a tuned model head yields strong zero-shot search without any training. A lightweight text-only match step, mapping dense video captions to short digests, then enables task-related coding learning without visual guidance, beating current methods often by wide margins. Video search teams gain a reminder that useful representations may already sit inside making models, waiting to be read out correctly.
arxiv-2602-08199:
AI agents that explore multiple solution paths need to try changes, keep the winner, and discard the rest, including file and process state. Cong Wang and Yusheng Zheng introduce branch contexts, a new operating-system abstraction for exactly that lifecycle: fork, explore, commit or abort.

Each branch gets copy-on-write isolation with its own filesystem view and process group, first-commit-wins resolution that invalidates siblings, and nesting for hierarchical exploration. The Linux implementation pairs BranchFS, a filesystem with constant-time branch creation and atomic commit without root privileges, with process-state support. Systems researchers building agent infrastructure gain primitives that make exploration safe, atomic, and cheap.
arxiv-2602-08299:
Educational data offer rich opportunities for learning analytics, but privacy concerns block secondary research use, and private synthesis work has focused on large, low-dimensional open datasets. Hibiki Ito and two co-authors propose Cyclic Adaptive Private Synthesis, a method for sharing real-world educational data that is typically high-dimensional and small-sampled.

Because educational practice is iterative, data sharing is continual rather than one-off, and the method shares data in cycles, adapting as new data arrive. Evaluated on authentic real-world data, it supports open science while protecting privacy through differential privacy. Learning-analytics teams gain a synthesis approach fitted to education's actual data shape and sharing rhythm, not borrowed from settings where data are plentiful and simple.
arxiv-2602-08499:
Training reasoning models with verifiable rewards wastes much of its data: responses of mixed quality are treated alike, and past rollouts are thrown away after one use. Xiaodong Lu and nine co-authors reframe rollout scheduling as a contextual bandit problem, letting a scheduler pick the most valuable rollouts throughout training. Their arXiv paper targets noisy supervision and poor sample efficiency.

Each rollout acts as an arm whose reward is the performance gain it drives between optimization steps. The scheduler supports noise-aware selection within prompt groups and adaptive reuse of historical rollouts in one framework. Theory gives sublinear regret bounds and shows larger buffers raise the achievable ceiling. Tests on six math benchmarks show consistent gains in accuracy and efficiency. Readers get a principled way to spend rollout budgets.
arxiv-2602-08899:
Jiaqi Huang studies economic models where hidden individual traits enter the equations as fixed effects. Estimating those traits first and plugging them in can bias the main results, a problem known as generated regressors. His paper builds orthogonal moment conditions that wipe out that first-order bias when the traits come from a side panel regression.

Machine learning and empirical Bayes methods can sharpen the nuisance estimates inside those moments. A central limit theorem follows without assuming the panel errors are unrelated to the main equations, and simulations show smaller bias when that assumption fails. An application to experimental site selection shows the method handling nonlinear moments in practice.
arxiv-2602-08999:
Robots that help at home must know when a request is ambiguous and ask, rather than guess wrong. Mouad Abrini and one co-author present CLUE, a system that turns a vision-language model's cross-modal attention into an explicit signal for when to clarify. Text-to-image attention maps feed a small convolutional network that detects referential ambiguity, while a fine-tuned decoder carries the dialogue and emits grounding locations.

Trained on a real interactive grounding data set, CLUE beats a state-of-the-art method using only InViG supervision plus parameter-efficient tuning. Its ambiguity detector also tops prior baselines. Code and data are public, offering a practical route to robots that ask at the right moment.
arxiv-2602-09199:
Khagendra Katuwal and one co-author examine the magnetic polarity beneath 70 equatorial coronal holes, using photospheric field measurements from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager. Skewness of the field distributions shows strong asymmetry: about 88 percent of holes have skewness between 0.20 and 0.40 in magnitude, with flux imbalance from 20 to 45 percent. Quiet-Sun regions, by contrast, look symmetric, with skewness under 0.11 and imbalance under 11 percent.

Tracking one hole across the disk shows its field distribution barely evolves over half a solar rotation. Flux imbalance correlates moderately, at 0.60, with the speed of associated high-speed solar wind streams, suggesting imbalance favors plasma acceleration through more open field structures, though other factors clearly matter too.
arxiv-2602-09899:
Algebraists study modules over rings the way geometers study spaces, asking when a complicated object is secretly simple. A 2026 paper by Mohsen Asgharzadeh and Elham Mahdavi treats modules with finite projective dimension over Noetherian local rings. Its central question is when such a module must be free, meaning it behaves like a plain coordinate space, and when it must be reflexive, a weaker form of self-consistency.

The authors show that freeness or reflexivity of certain tensor products forces strong structure on the module itself, often making it free. Their results extend classical theorems of Auslander beyond regular rings. A second part bounds the size of Ext modules at key degrees. It links the findings to the grade conjecture, to a question of Jorgensen, and to prime ideals in rings that lack chain conditions.
arxiv-2602-10099:
Representation encoders offer efficient, high-quality generation, yet standard diffusion transformers fail to settle on their representations at all. A 2026 paper by Amandeep Kumar and Vishal M. Patel traces the failure to shape, not capacity. Standard Euclidean flow matching pushes probability paths through the sparse interior of the encoders' hyperspherical feature space instead of hugging the manifold surface.

The authors call that failure Geometric Interference and answer with Riemannian Flow Matching plus Jacobi Regularization. Holding generation to manifold geodesics and fixing curvature-driven error lets standard architectures settle without costly width scaling. A standard mid-size model then settles nicely, reaching a strong image quality score where prior methods failed to settle at all.
arxiv-2602-11299:
Pairing in nuclei may be less collective than textbook pictures suggest. Chong Qi and two co-authors critically reexamine pairing rotations and gauge-space moments of inertia drawn from test binding energies. They study like-nucleon pairing, neutron-proton pairing, and alpha-type links.

Alpha separation energies and binding-energy differences along fixed-isospin chains reveal a smooth, near-universal residual alpha link energy with parabolic trends of collective spin. Yet the standard gauge-space moment for like-nucleon pairing is dominated by macroscopic Coulomb and symmetry terms. Once removed, it turns negative, suggesting Pauli blocking eats link energy. Alpha links, by contrast, look like a genuine collective quartetting mode.
arxiv-2602-12099:
Vision-language-action models that predict action chunks straight from observations often understand scenes shallowly and anticipate the future weakly. The GigaBrain Team instead trains a robot model with reinforcement learning guided by a video world model, which reasons about space and time and predicts what comes next.

Their model, called GigaBrain-0.5M, builds on a predecessor trained on over 10,000 hours of robot manipulation data, then adds world-model-based reinforcement learning through a method called RAMP. Tests report gains of about 30 percent over a baseline on hard tasks such as laundry folding, box packing, and espresso preparation, with reliable long-horizon execution shown in real-world deployment videos.
arxiv-2602-12299:
Room acoustics shape classrooms, clinics, and studios, yet tools that pair rigorous maths with clear visuals are scarce. Mandip Goswami works alone here, presenting AcoustiVision Pro, an open-source web platform for room impulse response analysis. From uploaded or data-set responses, it computes twelve acoustic parameters, including reverberation, clarity, and speech transmission measures.

Interactive three-dimensional views show early reflections, waterfall plots trace decay by frequency, and checks test compliance with ANSI S12.60 and ISO 3382. Two new data sets, RIRMega and RIRMega Speech, supply thousands of simulated responses with full metadata. Real-time auralisation, PDF reports, and CSV export round out a tool tested on classrooms, healthcare spaces, and recording studios.
arxiv-2602-12399:
Shadowing asks whether near-orbits of a dynamical system are tracked by true orbits, and periodic shadowing asks for periodic trackers. M. C. Oliveira works alone here, studying those properties for set-valued maps, where each point can map to a set of points. The paper links the periodic case to expansivity, which separates nearby orbits, and to chain transitivity, which links states by near-orbits.

For positively expansive set-valued maps on compact metric spaces, ordinary tracking implies periodic tracking. For chain transitive maps, periodic tracking implies both ordinary tracking and topological transitivity. A general construction builds set-valued maps with tracking from single-valued systems with an isometric involution. Examples from symbolic dynamics illustrate the theory, giving readers a compact map of how these tracking notions imply each other.
arxiv-2602-12499:
Mamba and other selective state space models have worked well in tests without attention, yet their theory lags behind. Mugunthan Shandirasegaran led this work with four co-authors, looking at a simple but typical Mamba block. It is a single-layer, single-head picking state space model with input-tied gating, then a two-layer MLP trained by gradient descent. Data include key and off-topic token patterns under token-level noise.

Two cases are studied, most-vote and nearness-ordered series, and the model is proven to extend with limit sample cost and settling bounds that improve as signal rises and noise falls. The gating vector lines up with key traits while skipping off-topic ones, stating a choice role similar to focus but through picking loops. Made-up tests support the theory, showing when and why Mamba-style models learn well.
arxiv-2602-12599:
Local string breaking models of hadron making are memory-free by build, yet final states feel global constraints across the whole breaking path. Tony Menzo works alone here, recasts hadron making as a tuned random spread process, fixing that tension. Keeping laws induce non-memory links between free breaking steps.

Those links fold into a retuning of local motion via a Doob h-transform. The frame covers a quark-anti-quark string in the chiral limit, where along factoring of the Lund kernel is exact, allowing stepwise counting and clean UV-IR split. Motion sorts into a tower of working theories by left string mass. It spans a UV fixed point with scale-free transport, a middle regime with set running, and an IR edge layer where non-local effects enter first. That structure includes beta functions, odd sizes, and matching rules.
arxiv-2602-12999:
Since Federer's 1959 work, submanifolds of class C^{1,1} are known to have positive reach, a measure of how far a tubular neighbourhood extends without self-overlap. Vincent Borrelli, Jean-Baptiste Follet, and Boris Thibert extend that property to rougher submanifolds using mu-reach, a notion from the 2000s. They first show every compact C^1 submanifold of Euclidean space has positive mu-reach for all mu below one.

For intermediate regularity C^{1,alpha}, the authors give quantitative bounds on the generalised gradient of the distance function, with an exponent 2alpha/(1-alpha) controlling how fast the gradient norm approaches one near the submanifold. Finally, they prove that exponent is sharp: no better rate holds in general. The results fill a gap between smooth geometry and the minimal regularity where tubular neighbourhoods still behave.
arxiv-2602-13099:
How closely can a finite set of quantum states mimic Haar randomness? Riccardo Castellano and four co-authors attack the question geometrically through Welch bounds, inequalities that exactly describe k-designs, ensembles reproducing the k-th Haar moment. They derive stronger Welch bounds giving a number-based, operationally meaningful characterisation of approximate k-designs.

The new bounds are often tight, identifying optimal approximate designs even for small ensembles. A notable example: complete sets of mutually unbiased bases are optimal approximate 3-designs within 1-designs of the same size. That result suggests a varying approach to the existence of complete mutually unbiased bases, explored numerically in dimension six. Links to shadow tomography, through the shadow norm, and extensions to toric and unitary designs round out the paper, with a full spectrum computation as a key technical ingredient.
arxiv-2602-13299:
Children born with hydronephrosis, a swelling of the kidney from blocked urine flow, are imaged with magnetic resonance urography, which shows the renal pelvis and calyces through water contrast. Turning those scans into meshes for flow simulation usually takes heavy post-processing, since voxel segmentations capture shape but not a mesh surface. KidMesh skips that step, rebuilding a kidney mesh directly from the scan with deep networks.

It samples feature points from the scan, then deforms a template mesh to match, trained without exact mesh labels, which are hard to obtain from sparse slices. Meshes emerged in 0.4 seconds on average, clean of self-intersections, with a Dice score of 0.86 against hand-drawn masks, and they fed urine flow simulations for clinical use. Haoran Sun leads the work with nine co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13799:
Voltage power spectral density measured around the ambient plasma frequency in space is unaffected by spacecraft perturbations that impact old plasma analyzers. That makes quasi-thermal noise spectroscopy a strong tool for measuring in situ plasma properties. The lower-frequency spectrum, set by parallel antenna resistance due to electric currents, instead depends on the spacecraft's local environment. A recent study wrongly estimated this resistance from Parker Solar Probe data. This paper presents a theoretical calculation of it, setting shot noise and receiver gain at low frequencies, with a first comparison to Parker Solar Probe FIELDS data.

The calculation also shows that this resistance can change receiver gain in the frequency range used for quasi-thermal noise spectroscopy during Parker Solar Probe inner orbits. Correcting the resistance estimate thus matters for reading low-frequency measurements from the mission's closest solar approaches. Nicole Meyer-Vernet leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14099:
Anas Al Shikh Khalil and two co-authors describe a 2026 arXiv system that lets robots sense what they hold. As robots join everyday tasks, they need to feel both shape and material while handling objects. The paper extends the NeuralFeels framework with semantic labels from vision and touch.

High-resolution Digit tactile readings feed a fine-tuned EfficientNet-B0 network that predicts local materials. Those predictions join an augmented signed distance field that predicts shape and material regions together. Tests show strong agreement between predicted and true materials on single- and multi-material objects. On one multi-material object, mean matching accuracy reached 79.87% across trials.
arxiv-2602-14399:
In Chong Choi and three co-authors attack a 2026 arXiv safety problem in vision-language models. Multi-turn jailbreaks work well against text-only models by gradually introducing malicious content, but extending them to vision-language models is underexplored. Naively adding visual inputs can backfire: overly malicious images trigger defenses, yielding more conservative responses.

Their multi-turn adaptive prompting attack, MAPA, alternates text and vision attack actions each turn to elicit the most malicious response, and adjusts the attack trajectory across turns through iterative refinement. That two-level design consistently beat state-of-the-art methods, lifting attack success rates by 15 to 30% on recent benchmarks against LLaVA, Qwen2.5-VL, and Llama-3.2-Vision models. The result exposes a gap in multimodal safety alignment.
arxiv-2602-14699:
Muzhi Chen and coauthors sketch Qute, a quantum database that treats quantum computation as a first-class execution option rather than a simulation trick. Qute compiles an extended form of SQL into gate-efficient quantum circuits. It uses a hybrid optimiser to choose between quantum and classical plans on the fly, adds selective quantum indexing, and designs fidelity-preserving storage to soften current qubit limits.

A three-stage roadmap charts the path toward a fully quantum-native database, and the team deploys Qute on a real quantum processor, Origin Wukong, to test its ideas in practice. The paper envisions databases that plan, store, and run across both kinds of hardware at once.
arxiv-2602-14799:
Javier Gonzalez Villasmil plans paths for many robots at once with QUBO, a binary maths that dodges the blast in joint states when one brain plans all. His robot-first plan trims vars by over ninety-five percent with breadth-first pre-work, fines crashes and rule breaks with tuned weights, and splits time into windows that fit today's gear.

Grid runs with up to four robots show the plan at work. Team robots thus gain a plan built for many movers, not one brain choking on all of them.
arxiv-2602-15099:
Lohmann and colleagues use intracluster globular clusters to trace Hydra I assembly. Hierarchical assembly predicts faint stellar substructures and intracluster light tracing the global potential. Globular clusters serve as brighter stand-ins, since such features are extremely faint. Deep VLT FORS imaging supplies the sample, split by color into blue and red groups.

A clear spatial split emerges. Red clusters crowd around the massive central galaxies NGC 3311 and NGC 3309. Blue clusters spread wider and sit offset from the center, matching a secondary peak of X-ray gas. Near the center, young metal-rich clusters spread wider, possibly from ram-pressure stripping, while old metal-poor clusters hug the center, possibly from disrupted dwarfs. Red clusters follow galaxy light closely, while blue clusters trace the global potential instead. The team also derives a method to constrain the past faint-end slope of the luminosity function from cluster frequencies and colors.
arxiv-2602-15299:
Burgin and colleagues study a Cantor set of whole numbers with limited figures mod a base, where zero is one of the limited figures. They show a certain multiple-intersection average has positive lower limit. That builds on the IP Ergodic Theorem of Furstenberg and Katznelson, and partly builds on recent work of Kra and Shalom.

Notably, for any part of whole numbers of positive upper Banach density, there is a set of whole numbers of positive lower Banach density. The part then contains an ℓ+1 term run with step size given by a Cantor set element. This adds to recent work of Kra and Shalom, for IP sets of whole numbers, and Burgin, on Sarkozy's Theorem for Primes with limited figures.
arxiv-2602-15399:
Hannukainen and colleagues study using low sets tools in link to total change smoothing in electric block scanning, though similar tricks can also be used for other flipped oval edge cases. It is shown that turning to low sets can speed up a rebuild routine based on joining the slow spread routine with stepwise linear steps and primed LSQR loops.

This comes without any big loss of rebuild grade or of the edge-boosting trait of total change smoothing. The tricks are tried in numbers in three spaces on messy set piece grids with both fake and lab data. That gives live rebuild times of only a few moments on a plain notebook machine.
arxiv-2602-15799:
Springer and colleagues show fine-tuning aligned language models on benign tasks weakens safety guardrails without warning. That holds even with harmless training data and no hostile intent. The common story says fine-tuning updates should sit at right angles to safety-critical paths. That story offers false comfort: right-angle structure is unstable and fails under gradient descent.

The team solves the puzzle through shape analysis. Alignment pools in small spaces with sharp bend, which first-order methods cannot detect or defend. Early updates may avoid those spaces, but loss bend steers paths into alignment-sensitive regions. As the Alignment Instability Condition, three shape traits as one produce safety decay. Alignment loss grows as the fourth power of training time, ruled by shape sharpness and bend coupling. That weakness is built into gradient descent on curved shapes, motivating bend-aware methods and a shift to forward checks.
arxiv-2602-15899:
Gelencsér-Horváth and colleagues built SceneVGGT, a 3D scene system that joins SLAM with semantic maps for self-guided and assistive navigation. Built on VGGT, it handles long video streams through a sliding window. Local submaps line up through camera-pose shifts, so maps stay true in shape while saving memory and time.

Sense data rise from 2D instance masks to 3D objects through the VGGT tracking head. Object tags stay stable over time, which aids change spotting. As a proof of concept, object spots are cast onto a flat floor map for assistive navigation. Memory use stays under 17 GB at any stream length. Point-cloud scores on ScanNet++ match top rivals, and the pace suits live assistive use with audio feedback.
arxiv-2602-15999:
Adkins and Jentschura work out how a nucleus tensor polarizability shifts bound state energies. Their general formula covers two body systems, and its headline effect is mixing: states of different orbital angular momentum, normally kept apart, bleed into each other through the tensor response.

The paper then applies the formula to muonic deuterium, where a heavy muon orbits close to the nucleus and feels its structure keenly. There they evaluate the shift for hyperfine components of P states and for S and D state mixing. The result matters for precision spectroscopy, where tiny nuclear structure effects must be accounted for before fundamental constants or tests of theory can be read off the lines.
arxiv-2602-16299:
Mathias Vast and coauthors bridge two approaches to faster cross-encoder ranking in information retrieval. Cross-encoder models deliver state-of-the-art ranking quality but carry high inference cost, limiting them to second-stage re-rankers. Prior work attacked that bottleneck from two largely separate directions. One accelerates cross-encoder running through attention sparsification. The other improves first-stage search quality with more complex models such as late-interaction models.

The authors bridge those paths through an in-depth analysis of cross-encoder internal mechanisms. By identifying and removing extra interactions, they derive MICE, Minimal Cross-Encoders, a new design that retains quality while reducing compute overhead. Evaluations show MICE retaining most of its rivals scores in-domain and matching or even exceeding it out-of-domain, while cutting floating-point operations down to two and a half times.
arxiv-2602-16399:
Michael Neri and Tuomas Virtanen propose acoustic maps as a new spatial feature for detecting replayed speech from multi-channel recordings. Replay attacks remain a critical weakness for automatic speaker verification systems, especially in real-time voice assistant applications. These maps are derived from standard beamforming over discrete azimuth and elevation grids, and they encode directional energy patterns.

Those patterns capture physical differences between how humans radiate speech and how loudspeakers replay it. A lightweight convolutional neural network built to work on these maps reaches competitive results on the ReMASC dataset with about six thousand trainable parameters. Experiments show the maps give a compact, physically clear feature space for replay attack detection across different devices and recording environments.
arxiv-2602-16599:
Eduard Looijenga relates level structures on cyclic covers of projective space to the homology of Fermat hypersurfaces. Let a smooth hypersurface of degree greater than one be given, with a cyclic cover totally ramified along it. The paper links full level structures on the primitive cohomology of the hypersurface with those on the primitive cohomology of the cover.

In the special case of degree and dimension both three, a marking of a smooth cubic surface determines a level structure on the associated cubic threefold. That answers a question posed by Beauville. The author expects many more applications, and algebraic geometers get a precise bridge between two classical objects that should unlock further results.
arxiv-2602-16699:
Wenxuan Ding, Nicholas Tomlin, and Greg Durrett study cost-aware exploration by language model agents. Agents that act in the world must weigh the cost of gathering info against the risk of acting too soon. On a coding task, writing and running a test costs something, but less than running buggy code. The paper shows agents can be led to reason plainly about such cost-uncertainty trade-offs and then act more wisely.

Tasks such as retrieval-augmented question answering and file-reading coding are cast as sequential choices under uncertainty, with hidden environment states shaping success. The Calibrate-Then-Act frame hands the agent an inferred prior about that state, changing behavior in ways standard reinforcement learning training does not teach. Tests on synthetic, question answering, and file-reading tasks show explicit cost-benefit reasoning pays off.
arxiv-2602-16899:
Y. Oubaid and co-authors probe the ground state of BaFe2S3, a ladder compound, through lattice and spin dynamics. They join infrared spectra, density functional theory, and neutron scattering to study how lattice symmetry, phonons, and magnetism interact. Lattice study finds symmetry lower than previously proposed, consistent with a P1 space group at low temperature.

Several phonon modes show marked anomalies at the structural shift near one hundred thirty kelvin and the Néel temperature near ninety-five kelvin. Modes affected at the structural shift mainly involve moves that modulate magnetic exchange pathways. Neutron scattering shows order below the Néel temperature is three-dimensional, long-ranged, and static, while between the two temperatures short-range dynamic magnetic links appear that vanish above the structural shift. Those links thus suffice to drive a static structural instability.
arxiv-2602-17299:
Nirvana Coppola led a three-author paper on when local agreement implies global agreement for twists of arithmetic objects. The work studies a local-global principle for finite twists of objects carrying a continuous action of the absolute Galois group of a number field, including abelian varieties, modular forms, and Galois representations. The question is when twists given locally by characters of some order arise from a single global character of that order.

The authors define and study a Tate-Shafarevich cohomology set that governs the obstruction to the principle for such twists, and they prove that set is finite. Applying the machinery yields several instances of the local-global principle across varied examples. The paper thus maps both the obstruction and the cases where local data successfully determines global twists.
arxiv-2602-17499:
Giordano Felicioni led a large team measuring UV slopes of starforming galaxies in strong lensing fields at the Epoch of Reionization with JWST. Low and middle redshift work finds slow reddening and steeper slopes for faint galaxies, but JWST work shows that trend flattening past redshift seven. The team gauges slopes past redshift seven point five, using massive-cluster lensing to reach faint, far galaxies.

Faint galaxies matter most as reionization's likely prime drivers. From NIRCam and NIRSpec data across MEGASCIENCE, UNCOVER, Silver Bullet, JUMPS, Technicolor, and CANUCS, the team nets three hundred seventy-eight galaxies, forty-five with spectra. Mean slope is near minus two point three at mean redshift eight point five, with no clear drift. Slope links weakly to ultraviolet brightness. For fourteen galaxies, mean escape share is about zero point two six, above the redshift-six need, though a low-redshift model may overstate it.
arxiv-2602-17799:
Jose Sosa and team ask how far training-free text-based remote sensing segmentation can go with existing foundation models alone. Most current approaches still rely on added trainable components, limiting generalization and practical use. Their approach integrates contrastive and generative vision-language models with the Segment Anything Model, enabling a fully training-free or lightweight LoRA-tuned pipeline.

The contrastive route uses CLIP as mask selector for SAM's grid-based proposals, reaching state-of-the-art open-vocabulary semantic segmentation in a fully zero-shot setting. The generative route enables reasoning and referring segmentation by generating click prompts for SAM with GPT-5 in a zero-shot setting and a LoRA-tuned Qwen-VL model, with the latter scoring best. Tests across nineteen remote sensing benchmarks, spanning open-vocabulary, referring and reasoning tasks, demonstrate strong capabilities, with code slated for release.
arxiv-2602-18199:
Gahyeon Shim and two co-authors built a fixer for motion made from text prompts. Their 2026 paper notes that text-to-motion systems have grown fast, yet their outputs still float, sink, or otherwise break physics while matching the words. The Distortion-aware Motion Calibrator, or DMC, is a plug-in module that repairs such flaws after generation.

DMC learns on its own, from deliberately warped motions paired with their texts, so it needs no heavy physics engine. Applied to several generators, it cut a standard quality gap by about forty-three percent on one system and thirteen percent on another, while topping a text-match score. On a strong model it also cut body-surface overlap by a third and pulled floating feet toward the true reference. The module offers any text-to-motion system a cheap physics polish that keeps meaning intact.
arxiv-2602-18699:
Word meanings drift over time, but the many signals of that drift have lacked one shared account. Stephen Russell, writing alone in 2026, proposes Semantic Substrate Dynamics Theory, an operator-theoretic frame that treats embedding shifts, neighbour changes, and unstable trajectories as views of one time-indexed substrate.

The substrate separates everyday churn inside a meaning basin from true crossings between basins, and from instability caused by recursive generation. Coarse Ricci curvature describes basin and bridge geometry in bulk, while bridge mass picks out the rare nodes that truly link basins. Predictions are stated in falsifiable form, with tests promised later; the work itself gives the formal model, assumptions, and test contracts.
arxiv-2602-18899:
Speech models encode rich phonetic information, but how is that information organised? Kwanghee Choi, with four co-authors, studies that question across ninety-six languages in 2026. The focus is on phonological vectors inside self-supervised speech models.

Linear directions in representation space correspond to phonological features. The size of those vectors tracks how strongly a feature is realised in sound, in a continuous way. The classic example is voicing. The difference between two sounds yields a voicing vector. Adding it to one sound produces its voiced counterpart. Scaling it gives a continuum of voicing. Together, the findings show speech models encode phonology with interpretable, compositional vectors, a form of phonological vector arithmetic.
arxiv-2602-18999:
Strong matrix traits describe generic rules under which spectral and pattern changes interact nicely to cover an area. Minerva Catral, with three co-authors, introduces a new such trait in 2026. It is the strong spectral property for weighted Laplacian matrices.

Instead of the space of symmetric matrix forms, the new trait uses the ambient space spanned by all weighted Laplacian matrix forms. Supergraph and Bifurcation lemmas are established for it. A detailed comparison of the Jacobian Method with strong traits gives a full account of how the two techniques relate. Those tools find potential boundaries of spectral regions for weighted cases of connected graphs on four vertices, extending earlier work. They also find absolute algebraic connectivity for small ordered graphs, and establish strong weighted cases for several graph families.
arxiv-2602-19199:
On Ethereum, digital tokens today sit at two extremes: ordinary tokens can move freely, while soulbound tokens cannot move at all. No common standard covers the middle ground, where a token may change hands a set number of times and then stop. Qin Wang and three colleagues close that gap with a design for counted transfers.

Their proposal, ERC-7634, adds a transfer counter and a programmable cap to each token while staying compatible with the usual ERC-721 standard. Ownership can therefore evolve under a finite transfer budget, set in advance by the token's rules. The paper lays out the minimal interface for this idea, so builders can add bounded mobility without inventing a whole new token system.
arxiv-2602-19499:
AV3Sb5 metals are kagome metals and superconductors where multiple quantum states meet. Charles Menil and four co-authors study electric and heat transport in CsV3Sb5. They find it to be a metallic Fermi liquid showing middling electronic correlations and a strong electron-phonon collision cross-section. Inelastic resistivity parts dominate in distinct T windows.

The prefactor of the T-squared term matches Kadowaki-Woods scaling, the pattern for a Fermi liquid with middling correlation. Heat conductivity readings at zero and finite magnetic field separate electronic and lattice parts. The Wiedemann-Franz law holds at zero T, while a downward deviation reflects mismatched prefactors of electrical and thermal T-squared resistivities.
arxiv-2602-19699:
Robot control can be planned by trajectory optimization, which is fast but can get stuck, or learned by reinforcement learning, which is robust but slow. A 2026 arXiv paper by Elisa Alboni and three co-authors builds on a hybrid called CACTO, which learns a warm-start policy to guide the optimizer toward low-cost paths.

Their new version, CACTO-BIC, samples starting states in a biased way that exploits a property of the value function, and it runs the optimization on graphics hardware. Tests show better use of data and faster computation than the earlier method, with results matching a standard baseline in less time. Trials on a four-legged AlienGO robot show the approach can handle high-dimensional systems and suit real-time use.
arxiv-2602-19799:
Rescaling the weights of a ReLU network can leave the function it computes unchanged while changing how training behaves, yet sound ways to exploit that freedom have been scarce. A 2026 arXiv paper by Arthur Lebeurrier and two co-authors offers one, building on the path-lifting framework that breaks ReLU networks down compactly.

The authors introduce a geometric criterion for rescaling parameters, whose minimization yields a tuning strategy: it aligns a kernel in path-lifting space with a chosen reference. They derive an efficient algorithm for that alignment and analyze how design and starting scale jointly shape its output at random initialization. Numerical tests suggest the approach can speed up training, giving practitioners a sound handle on rescaling symmetry.
arxiv-2602-20399:
Physics simulation usually needs costly high-fidelity training data to scale neural simulators, and training on static geometry alone can hurt performance on physics tasks. Haixu Wu and six co-authors answer with GeoPT, a pre-trained model for general physics simulation. Its core idea, lifted geometric pre-training, adds synthetic dynamics to geometry, giving dynamics-aware self-supervision without physics labels.

Pre-trained on over a million samples, GeoPT improves industrial-fidelity benchmarks in fluid mechanics for cars, aircraft, and ships, and in solid mechanics for crash simulation. It cuts labeled data needs by twenty to sixty percent and doubles convergence speed. The work shows that lifting geometry with synthetic dynamics bridges the gap between shape and physics, opening a scalable path for neural simulation. Code is openly available.
arxiv-2602-20499:
Quantum machine learning sits between quantum computing and classical machine learning, promising new ways to process complex data. Lirandë Pira and Patrick Rebentrost introduce its fundamentals in this chapter, building a shared conceptual foundation for readers from both communities. They connect the worst-case, adversarial view from theoretical computer science with the physics of quantum systems, showing how superposition, entanglement, and measurement collapse shape learning and robustness.

Special attention goes to adversarial robustness: the ability of quantum models to resist inputs designed to make them fail. The authors motivate studying quantum learning under attack, drawing distinctions between classical and quantum data and computation when the adversary is central. The chapter serves as a starting point for adversarial and robust quantum machine learning in later chapters.
arxiv-2602-20799:
Guangsheng Ou and eleven co-authors address a blind spot of language models: newly released software frameworks leave models guessing and hallucinating, because training never covered them. Prompt-time retrieval helps only partly, since it cannot teach the model how parts of a codebase relate and combine.

Their UCD-Training method first parses source code into a code graph. It then runs dependency-preserving continued pretraining, followed by graph-grounded fine-tuning on three kinds of reasoning data: single-hop relations, compositional API reasoning, and codebase use. They also release UnseenCodeBench, a benchmark for code generation on unseen codebases.
arxiv-2602-21099:
Language models know a lot about items and users, but turning that knowledge into tip vectors is awkward. Junjie Meng and eight co-authors bridge the gap in this 2026 arXiv paper using Topology-Augmented Graph Collaborative Filtering. The setup uses language models to infer contact intents and causal links from user-item pairs, coding them as trait nodes in a rich user-trait-item graph.

A tunable link-weighted graph conv then learns how much each link type matters, using link-own guessing nets. Tests across trials and joint-sifting bases show steady gains, including cold-start cases where new items lack past use. The work turns meaning knowledge into graph shape rather than bolting text traits onto vectors.
arxiv-2602-21199:
Shape-based Green's function zeros have drawn notice in condensed matter, and Floquet systems add a twist. Elio J. König and Aditi Mitra study those zeros in shape-based Floquet systems in this 2026 arXiv paper, with a focus on linked Kitaev-like chains and their transverse-field Ising circuit twins. They present Floquet Green's-function shape invariants for symmetry class BDI.

Near key points of the free-fermion phase map, with links giving a Floquet form of symmetric mass making, edge and bulk Green's functions are worked out by hand. Shape bands of zeros can feed the invariant, as in steady time, but Floquet functions can also have zeros with no links. A digital mimic circuit and its key readouts are presented.
arxiv-2602-21299:
Random-matrix shared rule orders complex quantum spectra, but does it rule real molecules? Zhen Tao and Victor Galitski test that question with ab initio methods in this 2026 arXiv paper, working out orbital levels and jumps for benzene, alanine, phenylethylamine, methyloxirane, and helicene chains. Generic low-pattern shapes show Wigner-Dyson stats of the square set.

Long helicene chains bound to bound valence jumps below the ion point still show the same stats, placing the shared rule among real states. Charge and magnet field tie is also tried: charge-bend spread is called non-analytic in magnet field, and a shift to the unitary set appears only at fields far beyond lab reach. Random-matrix theory thus frames ab initio calls for linked charge spectra.
arxiv-2602-21399:
Alina Devkota and four co-authors propose FedVG, a gradient-guided way to combine models in federated learning, where clients train together without sharing private data. Data differences across clients cause client drift, which hurts generalization, and standard weighting by dataset size can overemphasize weak clients.

FedVG instead scores each client from a global validation set built from public data: layerwise gradient norms show how much each client model still needs to adjust to generalize well. Those scores drive adaptive aggregation, weighting clients by need rather than by size. Tests on natural and medical image benchmarks across varied architectures show steady gains, above all in highly mixed settings, and FedVG plugs into other leading federated methods to improve them further.
arxiv-2602-21599:
Weisheng Xu and nine co-authors offer round-by-round closed-loop motion synthesis to scale human-like control skills. Physics-based human-like control trains on motion data sets with varied spreads, but fixed hardness spreads cap trained control rules. Getting high-quality data via studio motion capture costs heavily, blocking large-scale scale-up.

Their closed-loop auto motion making and round design makes high-quality motion data with rich action meanings, including martial arts, dance, combat, sports, gym work, and more. The design steps up rule and data hardness through physics metrics and goal tests, letting the trained tracker break old hardness limits. On the PHC single-primitive tracker, using only about one-tenth the AMASS data size, average test failure rate falls 45 percent versus baseline across 2201 clips. Wide knockout and side-by-side tests highlight the design's sense and gains.
arxiv-2602-21799:
A pen-like tool lets people drag drawings from one model to another and land on exact spots. Yang Liu and six co-authors explore how teleportation can join stylus interaction without disrupting common stylus use. Their design rests on two central concepts: turning the pen over to switch intuitively between sketching and teleporting, and letting eye direction set facing while pen placement sets position.

A user study with a teleport-and-orient task evaluates six teleportation techniques, covering two mode-switching methods, Button and Flip, and three orientation approaches, StylusRoll, StylusPoint, and GazePoint. Results offer new insights into the relative merits and limits of each technique. Beyond the comparison itself, the study advances understanding of moving instantly through virtual spaces and closes an open need: blending that movement smoothly with pen-based interaction in three dimensions.
arxiv-2602-21999:
A chemostat is a tank where microbes grow on a single limiting food, and engineers can steer the mix by controlling the feed. Claudia Alvarez-Latuz and two co-authors study how to drive such a trait-structured population, with mutation included, to a chosen target in the least possible time. The target picks out microbes with a low average half-saturation constant, meaning strains that thrive on scarce food.

The paper first proves the control problem is well posed, so that each feeding plan leads to one definite outcome. It then shows that feedback rules holding food level steady, called auxostat controls, steer the tank toward a fixed state, and that the target can indeed be reached. Finally the authors prove a fastest possible plan exists, backed by computer simulations that show the theory in action.
arxiv-2602-22399:
The cosmic microwave background cools as the universe expands, so its heat at earlier times tests cosmic history directly. Tatsuya Kotani and two co-authors measure that heat at redshift zero point six eight, using molecular absorption lines toward a distant quasar observed with ALMA. They analyze rotational transitions of hydrogen cyanide, formylium, hydrogen isocyanide, and their isotopologues.

For the three main species, two distinct line components appear in both transitions, while isotopologue spectra show one component each. Excitation levels from line strengths, with error bars carried through Monte Carlo sampling and fixes for uneven column density, yield the background heat. The measurement offers a clean molecular gauge for the early universe's afterglow.
arxiv-2602-22499:
How much energy, money, and emissions can smarter heating and cooling control save in real buildings? Arash Khabbazi and Kevin Kircher note that researchers sometimes control a few thermal zones inside a larger building, then report savings for those zones only. That approach can overstate savings by ignoring heat flow between controlled zones and their neighbors. The paper characterizes that overstatement error mathematically for linear dynamics and linear objectives, as usually holds when optimizing energy, cost, or emissions.

The errors can be large even in seemingly harmless cases: controlling only interior zones with no direct outdoor contact makes all perceived savings fictitious. The authors offer an alternative estimation method based on temperature readings from controlled and adjacent zones. It needs no estimate of what the building would have used at baseline, removing a hard measurement and verification burden.
arxiv-2602-22599:
Km Akanksha Dubey and one co-author study high harmonic generation, the burst of high-frequency light thrown off when intense laser pulses hit matter, in gas-phase fullerenes from C20 to C60. Tight energy spacing in these carbon cages means many orbitals join the action at once, causing strong spectral interference.

Cutoff and plateau ranges stayed fairly similar across sizes, but electron correlations mattered deeply: the independent-particle picture, which ignores dynamic electron interaction, failed almost everywhere except the cutoff energy. Correlations lowered yields and sharpened emission peaks. Larger fullerenes also lost angular sensitivity and, except for C60, shed yield faster with laser ellipticity, marking fullerenes as a prime testbed for multi-electron strong-field physics.
arxiv-2602-22899:
Maria Manuel Clementino and one co-author study ordered systems through two kind notions: lax proto-modular and Ord-Mal'tsev kinds. The work lifts both ideas to the level of tidy families of pre-ordered systems, setting them beside earlier plain work.

Families that are colax proto-modular or Ord-Mal'tsev are pinned down by ops whose arities come from ordered sets, plus order rules among them. New cases of colax proto-modular non-flat Ord-kinds appear here. For Ord-Mal'tsev families, the order of systems turns out flat, meaning two-way. Hence the classic link from proto-modular to Mal'tsev fails in the ordered world, though non-tidy families can still host non-flat order.
arxiv-2602-23099:
Lukas Litzba and three co-authors study coupling-energy driven pumping through quantum dots, zeroing in on off-matching hopping and links. Two charge-pump setups are studied where lowest-order hopping steps are blocked and the pump runs only on shifts of the coupling energy. One flips dot-lead couplings on and off, while the other uses readings of the dot fill.

The authors work out exact answers for any strong tunnel couplings without Coulomb push-pull. They pin down setting regimes with best pumping currents or best energy use, and discuss links between both pumping tricks. The work shows how link effects shape pumping when direct hopping is blocked.
arxiv-2602-23299:
Chengchao Yuan and two co-authors explain the longest gamma-ray burst on record, GRB 250702B, as a white dwarf torn apart by an intermediate-mass black hole. Its prompt emission lasted about 25,000 seconds, challenging the standard collapsar model. Other oddities include a huge X-ray flare about 1.3 days after detection, a late shift from steep to shallow decay in the X-ray afterglow, and hard spectra spanning keV to MeV energies.

The team models a relativistic jet powered by repeated partial tidal disruptions of the white dwarf, with the final complete disruption driving the flare. External forward and reverse shocks account for the long-term X-ray, near-infrared, and radio afterglow, while the flare comes from internal dissipation as fast and slow relativistic ejecta collide. The fit establishes white-dwarf disruptions by intermediate-mass black holes as a viable engine for ultra-long gamma-ray bursts.
arxiv-2602-23599:
Dang Sy Duy and three co-authors test scaling and startup plans for graph neural networks in blockchain anomaly spotting. Graph neural networks learn jointly from node traits and trade graph shape for money fraud spotting, yet their success on real-world anti-money laundering benchmarks depends deeply on training habits that remain little-studied.

The team runs a full cut-out test of startup and scaling plans across three designs, GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE, on the Elliptic Bitcoin data set. Results show the plans vary by design: GraphSAGE performs strongest with Xavier startup alone, GAT gains most from mixing GraphNorm with Xavier startup, while GCN shows limited response to these changes. The findings offer usable, design-specific guidance for deploying graph neural networks in anti-money laundering flows with severe class skew. A shared method with time splits, seeded runs, and full cut-out results is shared.
arxiv-2602-23899:
Pramit Saha and three co-authors present BUSD-Agent, a cascaded multi-agent framework for breast ultrasound screening and diagnosis that aims to cut needless biopsy referrals. The 2026 paper models the workflow in two stages. A light screening clinic filters out low-risk benign and normal cases. A diagnostic clinic handles higher-risk cases with richer perception and radiology tools.

Past pathology-confirmed cases, with images, predictions, and agent actions, are stored as decision trajectories. For each new case the system retrieves similar past cases to adjust trust and escalation thresholds on the fly, without retraining. Tests across ten breast ultrasound datasets show a large drop in diagnostic escalation and in biopsy referrals versus the same architecture without trajectory conditioning, while screening specificity improves. The design shows how memory of past decisions can make triage both safer and less invasive.
arxiv-2603-00299: Acharya extends Remling's theorem to vector-valued discrete Schrödinger operators, which model quantum particles hopping on a lattice with several components at each site. In plain terms, the limiting potentials let waves pass without reflection across the continuous part of the spectrum, with every channel behaving this way. Formally, shifting the matrix potentials to their limit points leaves them reflectionless across the absolutely continuous spectrum, at full multiplicity.
arxiv-2603-00599: Sun and seven colleagues make hypergraph neural nets work where linked nodes often differ and long range dependence matters. Standard message passing assumes similar neighbours and struggles at narrow choke points, a problem they link to oversquashing under Riemannian manifold heat flow. Their adaptive local heat exchanger tunes choke points per subgroup, capturing long range links through a Robin condition while preserving distinct representations via source terms. The design yields message passing that ignores heterophily, with theoretical guarantees.
arxiv-2603-00699: Shao and five colleagues review deep learning based multimodal data fusion in astronomy, where sky surveys now pour out optical, infrared, gravitational wave, and other mixed data. Single mode analysis gives only limited insight into such massive mixed data, while fusion promises deeper understanding by combining modes. The review covers motivations, data sources, major modes, and representative deep learning models for fusion. A timely synthesis, it maps how artificial intelligence accelerates astronomy research across modes.
