Their framework, SWARD, attacks the gap two ways. A module aligns teacher and student attention links inside window blocks. The window offsets are reshuffled at random each training round. That kills boundary bias and spans short and long range links at many scales. A second loss, prototype discriminative regularization, sharpens how class prototypes spread in the student. The aim is not to copy features but to copy relations. Their design gives the small net the teacher's sense of spatial structure and class order.
arxiv-2606-01099:
Han and co-authors build a language model that understands fuzzy home commands in this 2026 paper. Smart home systems nail crisp orders like 'turn on the bedroom light.' Vague ones like 'make the bedroom cozy' trip them up. Language models generalize well, but scarce domain data, weak adaptation, and high cost hold them back in this niche.

Their pipeline first synthesizes training data from user logs with model help. Their model, MiCU, then learns in stages. Curriculum learning injects domain knowledge into the base model. Cold start training plus reinforcement learning, guided by domain thinking rules, sharpens its reasoning. A token compression trick squeezes each device description into one special token. That cut enables a fast variant for long inputs. In wide tests, MiCU beats baselines by a wide mark, they report. The average accuracy gain is 20.01 percent across the test suites in their study.
arxiv-2606-01199:
Zhu and co-authors test if language agents can run a firm over time. In a firm, goals flow down through ranks. Tasks build on past work, and files pile up. They frame this as a problem of shared memory. Their TaskWeave system keeps plans in a set cycle. It grounds each step in a trace of past steps.

They run a year-long test in a mock IT firm. TaskWeave is set against other multi-agent tools. It keeps work more coherent across the long run. Its outputs stay tied to what came before. The work shows that structured memory helps such sims stay sound.
arxiv-2606-01599:
Yang and co-authors build online environments for visual reasoning RL. RL for visual reasoning needs scalable, verifiable training signals. Static curated datasets cap training at their collection budget. TRON is an online environment substrate instead. A generator-verifier program makes each rollout on demand. It samples a fresh latent visual state and renders an image. It asks a question and verifies the answer exactly. One run can draw an unbounded stream of fresh instances.

Difficulty matches the current curriculum in that stream. The suite holds 520 environments in five ability buckets. Buckets span spatial, math, diagram, pattern, and counting skills. RL post-training improves ten external benchmarks in their tests. Gains hold across three model families.
arxiv-2606-01699:
Takahashi and Nakashi compare wormhole and black hole shadows under accretion. The Ellis-Bronnikov wormhole is their wormhole model. The Schwarzschild black hole is the comparison case. They run general relativistic radiative transfer simulations for both. A spherically symmetric steady accretion flow feeds the scenes. Synchrotron emission lights the flow in the simulations. Both objects show a central shadow and a bright photon ring. The wormhole's shadow and ring are brighter than the black hole's.

The gap traces to the missing event horizon. Matter near and beyond the throat adds emission in the wormhole case. Comparisons with EHT views of M87 star follow. Ring size and total flux are comparable there. Neither model reproduces the deep central depression, though. Non-spherical flow seems required for that.
arxiv-2606-01799:
Wang and Ding study dueling bandits, a choice problem with paired tests. Each test pits two arms against each other. A Condorcet winner beats all other arms head to head. Three goals matter here: find the best arm, and cut two kinds of regret. Past methods treat these goals apart.

Their TG-ITE method joins all three goals in one frame. A tree guides the search for a strong first pick. That search needs only order N paired tests. Varied play rules then serve each goal in turn. The authors prove order N costs for best-arm search. Weak regret also stays order N, a first for its style.
arxiv-2606-01999:
Butera and co-authors ask why forecast models need long input windows. Deep models for grouped time series use ever longer windows. The gain is often credited to long-range dependencies. How global models use those observations is less discussed. The team split forecasting into two linked objectives.

One objective identifies the process behind the input sequence. The other forecasts future values given the observations. Optimal forecasts average over plausible generating processes. Each process is weighted by its likelihood given the window. Long windows shrink uncertainty about which process is active. That offers a second reason windows help forecasts. Identification gains, not just memory, drive the benefit. The view reframes how window size should be chosen.
arxiv-2606-02199:
van Heerden and co-authors build a new model for count data from microbiome studies. Labs count microbes in a sample and record how many of each kind they find. A few counts are often way off, and those bad counts can pull the fit of a model far from the truth. The standard model for such counts is the Dirichlet-multinomial, but it is known to be weak when bad counts are present.

The new model mixes two parts, one for clean data and one for the bad counts. The clean part has low spread, while the part for bad counts has much more spread built in. Bad counts are thus soaked up by the model instead of being cut from the data set. Tests with single bad counts and with noise show the model works well.
arxiv-2606-02299:
Ismoilov studies sign uncertainty for trigonometric polynomials of fixed degree. A symmetric Borel measure on the unit circle is given. Polynomials have prescribed degree N in the study. The question is the smallest radius of the last sign change. That radius is sought for polynomials with non-positive integral against the measure.

Sharp results are determined for each such measure. Extensions go to polar measures on higher dimensional spheres. The extremal problem reduces to the one dimensional case there. Reduction runs through the polar part of the measure. A polynomial analogue on the interval zero to one is also established. Orthogonal polynomials on the real line supply that analogue. Uncertainty principles gain sharp forms in this setting. Harmonic analysts are the main audience.
arxiv-2606-02499:
Majaess sets a distance to the galaxy IC1613 without using Gaia data. Cepheid stars anchor the cosmic distance scale. Their brightness depends in part on metallicity. The size of that effect is disputed. Gaia's parallax zeropoint is also debated. Majaess unifies 18 HST parallaxes for Galactic Cepheids. That base yields a Gaia-independent distance to IC1613.

Three proposed metallicity corrections are then benchmarked. The zero case gives a distance modulus of 24.39, matching the TRGB and JAGB means. The quarter-magnitude case gives 24.16 instead. The half-magnitude case gives 23.93, well below the comparison means. Larger corrections are therefore disfavored. Smaller corrections need a wider metallicity baseline to test. More non-Gaia parallaxes are also wanted. Concerns about Gaia DR3 for long-period Cepheids add weight to that call.
arxiv-2606-02699:
Pucha and co-authors run the largest systematic hunt for active galactic nuclei in dwarf galaxies. The data come from the first DESI spectroscopic release. Nearly two million low-redshift line-emitting galaxies are searched. Emission-line ratios separate AGN from star-forming systems. AGN appear in 25.9 percent of high-mass galaxies. In dwarfs, the share is just over 2 percent.

The AGN fraction climbs with stellar mass. It runs from about 1.4 percent at the low end to 93.3 percent at the high end. Broad-line AGN number 17,949. Their black hole masses come from single-epoch virial methods. The black hole to stellar mass relation extends down to very low masses. Its distribution is bimodal, with two distinct relations. The high-mass branch extrapolates to overmassive high-redshift candidates. Two broad evolutionary pathways are suggested. The team also releases the EmFit catalog of line measures for 7.4 million galaxies.
arxiv-2606-02899:
Ennaji, Igbida, Jradi, and Urbano propose a new model for the motion of dense crowds. Their model builds on the classic Hughes model. That model couples a conservation law for pedestrian density with an Eikonal equation for the shortest path to a target.

The new version joins Hughes' setup to a prediction-correction framework from recent work. Pedestrians in the model anticipate what lies ahead. They also adjust their routes as conditions change. The authors present the model's mathematical form and discuss when it is well posed. Numerical simulations show its qualitative behavior in complex settings. The variant behaves in a way the authors find realistic for congested crowds. They suggest it may also open a path toward proving well-posedness for the original Hughes model. That problem has stayed open for a long time, and the paper frames its model as a step toward it.
arxiv-2606-02999:
Bhandari and Malik study how a two-dimensional Coulomb glass model relaxes. The model is a random-site system at half-filling. The authors ask how material density, disorder in onsite energies, and localization length shape the relaxation dynamics.

They compute the eigenvalue distribution of the linear dynamical matrix using mean-field approximations. The system first relaxes fast through energy-lowering transitions. Then depletion of states near the Fermi level slows it down. Fluctuations decay by a power law for a while. After a set relaxation time, decay turns exponential. That time is inversely related to the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix. Lower density slows relaxation and lengthens the time. More onsite disorder at fixed density and localization length does the same. Much of the spectrum stays unaffected. The authors note that shrinking localization length may matter as much as disorder in the slow dynamics.
arxiv-2606-03599:
Zhang, Lyu, Li, and Lin speed up band-structure calculations for 3D anisotropic phononic crystals. Standard staggered-grid methods face a mismatch. Anisotropic coupling needs derivative parts at grid spots that do not line up. Interpolation or averaging closures patch the gap. Their parity-blocked rotated staggered method avoids those patches.

Directional derivatives are rebuilt from four Bloch-periodic body-diagonal differences. That yields a Hermitian generalized eigenvalue form with coupling built in. On even grids, two parity invariants survive the shifts. The velocity space then splits exactly into four independent blocks. Solving the four smaller problems and merging spectra recovers the full spectrum. A Fourier SVD frame supports zero-mode handling and fast solvers. Tests on a two-phase crystal keep the full spectrum exact. Wall-clock time drops sharply versus the full-space solve.
arxiv-2606-03699:
Cobucci and co-authors give quantum coherence a sharp meaning when hidden classical control may be at play. States that do not commute show coherence. That claim assumes the preparation device is untouched by hidden classical settings. Allowing such control yields a stronger notion of coherence. Its worth is shown through randomness certification.

A preparation device is coherent exactly when it can certify randomness in a prepare-and-measure test. Certifying coherence under hidden control becomes the core problem. A hierarchy of semidefinite programs characterizes it in full. A practical variant stays accurate while scaling to many high-dimensional states. For qubits, links to joint measurability push accuracy higher still. The toolbox covers more than one thousand qubit states. Quantum information readers get both meaning and method for this stronger coherence.
arxiv-2606-03899:
Li, Zhang, Liu, and Bao explain why momentum helps the Muon optimizer by acting as a spectral filter. Muon trains large language models well in practice. What momentum does inside it stayed unclear. Past analyses dropped momentum or kept it unexplained. A structured signal-plus-perturbation gradient model frames the answer.

Momentum suppresses the perturbations while keeping the dominant signal. The spectral gap between them widens as a result. That wider gap steadies the singular subspaces fed to orthogonalization. The update that follows is more reliable. Running momentum before orthogonalization provably aligns better with the signal than the reverse order. Dropping momentum is worse still. Experiments, including language model pretraining, back the theory. The frame may extend to other matrix-based optimizers. Trainer teams get a reasoned basis for Muon's recipe, not just folklore.
arxiv-2606-04699:
Kumar, Ahire, and Ganaie propose classifiers aimed at distinguishing Alzheimer's disease from healthy cognition in brain scans, in a 2026 arXiv medical machine learning paper. Earlier methods treated those samples as independent points, ignoring the geometric relationships among them.

The authors build a graph over the Universum samples using Gaussian similarity, minimum spanning tree connectivity, and multi-hop propagation, and turn it into a Laplacian-based regularizer capturing the samples' geometry. On ADNI MRI dataset variants with two feature types and five noise levels, both models consistently outperformed existing methods, the first reaching the highest average AUC of 88.07 percent and staying stable as noise increased, with statistical tests confirming significance.
arxiv-2606-04899:
Wu and colleagues harden federated learning against the very server meant to run it, in a 2026 arXiv security paper. Federated learning trains models across many clients, and trusted execution environments promise trustworthy aggregation. The authors dissect existing protocols and show server-side adversaries can still manipulate client selection and replay aggregation.

Their system, DisT-FL, distributes trust across servers guarded by multiple enclaves that form an append-only ledger for private, robust aggregation. Operation linearizability thwarts state rollback attacks, and inputs drawn from reliable servers mitigate input-output manipulation. DisT-FL counters the demonstrated attacks while matching a single enclave's performance, and it delivers a six-fold throughput boost over counterpart multi-enclave designs. The lesson is: one enclave concentrates trust and therefore risk, while a ledger of enclaves can check the server that hosts them.
arxiv-2606-04999:
Sourav Maji revisits the path integral quantization of the null bosonic string in this 2026 arXiv paper, working with Carroll-Weyl ghosts. A null, or tensionless, string lives on a Carrollian worldsheet, a surface where light cones collapse. The paper argues that every local gauge symmetry of that worldsheet must be fixed before the quantum theory is properly defined.

Beyond the known BMS ghost system, a Carrollian worldsheet allows a volume-preserving Carroll-Weyl scaling whose generator must also be gauge fixed, adding one more Faddeev-Popov row. The correct ghost system therefore pairs the BMS ghosts with an extra scalar ghost and antighost. Maji derives the revised path integral, the ghost action, its residual symmetry equations, and its mode expansion. He shows the change alters the BRST complex and the anomaly problem. The familiar dimension check based on the old ghosts alone was therefore only a partial gauge fixing.
arxiv-2606-05499:
Md Humaun Kabir, Md Rakibul Islam, and Helen Lou present STMutants in this 2026 arXiv paper, the first public mutation testing dataset for automation software. Mutation testing judges a test suite by seeding small faults, called mutants, and checking if the tests catch them. The target language is Structured Text, the IEC 61131-3 language used in programmable logic controllers running real-time, safety-critical processes, where faults can damage equipment or hurt people.

It contains 110 generated first-order mutants from eleven programs in the OSCAT open library and industry sources, with 108 retained after screening. Seven operator categories cover value, relational, arithmetic, logical, negation, insertion or omission, and initialization faults. The authors ran three large language models on test generation and kill-or-survive prediction. Across the 108 mutants the models reached accuracies of about 86, 94, and 86 percent, with clear differences between them. It opens research on AI-assisted quality assurance for controller software.
arxiv-2606-05799:
Jawad and Caragea calibrate a model's confidence by testing how easily it gets distracted in a 2026 arXiv paper. A trustworthy model should know when it is likely wrong. Standard calibration ignores whether stray content can sway the model. CaliDist slips semantic distractors into the prompt and watches the prediction wobble. That wobble becomes a penalty applied to the model's stated confidence.

The method is post-hoc, so no retraining is needed. Seven language understanding benchmarks and six models put it against strong baselines. Calibration error and Brier score both came out lower across the board. Average calibration error fell from twenty-three percent to seven percent. That drop is a relative improvement of about seventy percent. Stability under pressure, the authors argue, is a real signal of earned confidence. A model that flinches at irrelevant text should not sound sure of itself.
arxiv-2606-05899:
Duranthon, Boncoraglio, and Zdeborová build an exactly solvable model of LoRA fine-tuning in a 2026 arXiv paper. LoRA adapts big pretrained models by training only a small low-rank patch. Practitioners use it everywhere, yet theory for attention layers lagged. The authors study a single attention head, first pretrained on a data-rich task, then adapted with a rank-one update on scarce data.

In the high-dimensional limit, each stage reduces to a few order parameters with sharp predictions. Test errors and representation alignment follow explicitly. Pretraining's whole influence compresses into one effective noise term. From it, the authors derive how pretraining should be run to help adaptation most. They also find a regime where test error and representation quality disagree, warning against single-metric judgments. The theory extends to active fine-tuning, choosing which data to adapt on. Solvable models, they argue, can steer real adaptation recipes.
arxiv-2606-06299:
Daniel Galvin, Patrick Orson, and Mark Powell study when two surfaces in a four dimensional space must match smoothly in this 2026 arXiv paper on topology. Four manifolds locally look like ordinary four dimensional space, and hold surprises that lower dimensions lack. Two surfaces can be deformed into each other by a continuous, topological isotopy, yet resist every smooth deformation. Stabilization, adding copies of a standard piece to the space, sometimes removes the obstruction.

The authors prove that topologically isotopic surfaces do become smoothly isotopic after stabilization in two broad situations. The first is when the surfaces are trivial in the mod two homology of the ambient space. The second covers a large class of fundamental groups, including free products of classical knot groups and, in particular, free groups. The proof leans on Saeki's extension of Wall's theorem to manifolds with boundary, a step shown to be necessary.
arxiv-2606-06399:
Jiaju Chen and co-authors build a laboratory for testing how well AI agents cooperate in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi agent systems fail less often from weak individual skill than from poor collaboration: no common ground, drifting shared understanding, and unrepaired misunderstandings. Standard benchmarks score task outcomes, so those social failures stay invisible. The authors borrow decades of research on computer supported cooperative work to define what collaborative competence actually requires.

Their framework, CollabSim, runs controlled multi agent experiments across four task paradigms from that literature. It varies communication bandwidth, information visibility, and team size. It also probes each agent's stated mental model of the task, its partners, and its own reasoning at every action. Tests across four language models separated design choices cleanly. Condition effects emerged that outcome only scoring would miss, suggesting teamwork is its own measurable skill.
arxiv-2606-06499:
Shuai Hou, Zafar Normatov, and Lina Song build the theory of a young algebraic structure in this 2026 arXiv paper. Mock pre Lie algebras are a variant of Lie type algebras with a twisted symmetry in their product. A bialgebra carries both a product and a coproduct that must fit together. The paper develops the subject from scratch, starting with phase spaces of mock Lie algebras.

Their central results are equivalences. Mock pre Lie bialgebras turn out to be the same thing as Manin triples, as certain matched pairs of algebras, and as phase spaces. A mock Lie algebra admits a phase space exactly when it sits inside a mock pre Lie algebra. For coboundary cases they derive an analogue of the Yang Baxter equation. Two special classes, quasi triangular and factorizable bialgebras, are introduced. The quasi triangular ones yield Rota Baxter operators of weight minus one.
arxiv-2606-06799:
Two lasers that pulse at slightly different colors are powerful tools for microscopy and spectroscopy, but only if their pulses march in lockstep. Huang and co-authors report a simpler way to lock them in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system pairs ytterbium and erbium fiber lasers, one leading and one following, in an all optical scheme with no electronic control loop doing the timing work.

Pulses from the lead laser enter the follower's cavity, where a nonlinear loop mirror acts as a fast intensity gate that nudges the follower into sync. The locked pair tolerated a cavity length mismatch of eight hundred micrometers, and their relative timing jitter was just twenty six femtoseconds, millionths of a billionth of a second. Built from polarization maintaining fiber, it ran stably for twelve hours without temperature control, ready for pump probe microscopy and two color spectroscopy.
arxiv-2606-06899:
Lighting can change a photo of the same room beyond recognition. Lizhen Zhu and Wyble argue that vision models should learn from that fact in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most training treats lighting as a nuisance to erase. Augmentations push models to ignore it entirely.

Their framework does the opposite. It adds lighting as an explicit training signal. A contrastive objective, which pulls matching views together, gains an auxiliary head. That head captures how the scene changes with illumination. The model thus keeps meaning stable while staying sensitive to light. Tests covered ImageNet, the dark image set ExDark, and PASCAL VOC. The lighting aware training improved classification and detection over standard baselines. It did so with the same architecture and budget. Gains also appeared in supervised setups. The moral: controlled variation can teach, not just confuse.
arxiv-2606-07099:
Power engineers now solve the grid's flow equations thousands of times inside learning loops. Park, Song, and Kim build an accelerator for that grind in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, SABLE, runs batched AC power flow on graphics processors. It is built to plug into differentiable training frameworks without losing sparsity.

The key is a shared sparse template. Batched three dimensional Jacobians are repacked into one fixed two dimensional pattern. That pattern is reused across the whole software stack with zero copying. Custom kernels and a sparse direct solver do the heavy lifting. Mixed precision adds further speed. Against a standard tool, standalone throughput rose up to about two hundred fifty fold. End to end training throughput rose up to about two hundred seven fold. Feasible batch sizes grew by up to sixty four times. Grid learning at scale becomes practical, not aspirational.
arxiv-2606-07199:
Bilayer nickelates superconduct under pressure in bulk crystals but behave differently as strained thin films, and theory must explain both. LaBollita, Millis, and Gingras offer a unifying picture in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their calculations mix two heavy simulation methods. The materials stack two nickel oxide layers in a layered structure.

The key actors are interlayer dynamical singlets. Electrons in upright orbitals pair across the two layers into shifting singlet states. Those orbitals mix with the flatter, freely moving in plane orbitals. Pressure and strain squeeze this arrangement differently. Hydrostatic pressure strengthens the coupling; compressive strain weakens it. That single difference reproduces the experimental split between bulk and film behavior. Photoemission spectra and transport trends both match the calculations. The picture resembles orbital selective Mott physics, with one orbital stuck and magnetic. Here the localized orbitals pair up between layers, adding the new twist.
arxiv-2606-07499:
Aronowitz and Bartroff quantify how accurate sequential clinical trial estimates are at finite sample sizes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Group sequential trials analyze data in batches and may stop early, which is ethical and economical, but their stopping rules rest on maximum likelihood estimates whose joint behavior matters. The authors study quasi-maximum likelihood estimators, which use a possibly wrong model, under model misspecification and dependence within groups. They derive its limiting form and explicit error bounds for the normal approximation using Stein's method.

Uniquely, the bounds carry constants, so a trialist can compute a guaranteed accuracy rather than an asymptotic promise. The covariance structure accounts for both at once. They work it out for a Poisson generalized linear mixed model with random group effects, a common overdispersed count model. An epilepsy clinical trial dataset shows the method, tying the bounds to the monitoring problems that motivated the theory.
arxiv-2606-07599:
Ma and co-authors recast ordinal regression, ordered values like star ratings or disease stages, as a continuous generation problem, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Older approaches chop the scale into rigid classification bins, creating artifacts at boundaries, or regress directly and miss the ordering structure. Their framework, DiffoR, uses a diffusion model, which recovers a value by denoising step by step, letting predictions settle anywhere on the continuum while learning soft steps between nearby ranks.

Ordinal topology is protected by a dual strategy: targets split into layered increments at several scales, and denoising steps sync with feature frequencies for coarse-to-fine polish. Across twelve benchmarks in four domains, DiffoR beat state-of-the-art ordinal methods in their reported experiments. The authors present generative modeling as a general replacement for bin-based ordinal regression, from recommendation to vision.
arxiv-2606-07799:
Carrasco-Martinez and Hall introduce a framework for explaining why particle masses and mixing angles follow steep hierarchies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quarks and leptons come in three generations with wildly different masses, the flavour problem. The classic Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism explains it with chosen charges per particle. Their alternative, maximal Abelian flavour symmetries, needs no chosen charges and applies anywhere.

The framework assigns one small parameter, epsilon, to each fermion multiplet, and the hierarchies follow from products of those small numbers. It grows stronger as multiplets shrink in number. In SU(5) unified theories, fifteen observed mass ratios and mixing angles are matched at factor-of-two level by five small parameters. In SO(10) unification only three parameters suffice, around a hundredth, a fiftieth, and a five-hundredth. The same setup roughly reproduces the cosmic matter-antimatter imbalance via leptogenesis in SU(5), with no extra small parameter.
arxiv-2606-07999:
Sera Choi and co-authors help small language models adapt robot skills to new bodies and rooms, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Skill grounding means making a reusable skill work on a different robot or in a changed environment, where small differences can break it. Large models can rewrite a skill from scratch, but deployed robots often cannot carry them. Small models rewriting freely make mistakes that compound.

Their framework, RECENT, treats skills as executable code and splits meaning from mechanics. The skill's control structure, its semantic intent, stays fixed. Only the execution bindings, the parts tied to a specific body or environment, are rewritten, through localised refactoring rather than regeneration. Across scenarios spanning multiple robot embodiments, RECENT achieved the best performance among small-model code-as-policies methods and matched large-model approaches. Careful editing, it turns out, beats rewriting when the editor is small.
arxiv-2606-08199:
Shah and Yang study typical long-run behavior for a flow on the space of lattices in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is a diagonal flow, a stretching motion, acting on grids of points, with starting points restricted to flat slices of a special curved orbit, called a horosphere. A point is Birkhoff generic when its time averages match the space average.

The authors prove almost every point on such a slice has this property. Two exceptional situations can spoil the conclusion. One involves a defining matrix too well approximated by rationals, measured by its Diophantine exponent. The other occurs when the slice itself is approximable by lower-dimensional slices defined over a number field. As applications, they obtain results on Dirichlet non-improvability and on logarithmic density for almost every point on these slices.
arxiv-2606-08299:
Grigorian studies an operator built purely from octonion multiplication in this 2026 arXiv paper. The octonions are an eight-dimensional number system extending the complex numbers. They are non-associative: the grouping of a product can change its value. The operator acts on tensors combining octonions with the seven-dimensional representation of the group G2, and respects that symmetry. He first computes its real spectrum.

The harder problem is the octonionic right-eigenvalue equation, where eigenvalues themselves are octonions multiplying from the right. Fixing a complex slice inside the octonions reduces the problem to a real one whose leftover symmetry is SU(3). The split yields two spectral loci in each slice: a quartic curve and a circle. The loci do not depend on the slice chosen, so the full spectrum follows by letting the slice vary.
arxiv-2606-08499:
Zabolotnii settles when a variance-reduction trick tuned under one hypothesis stays honest under another, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Control-variate estimators reduce the noise of a statistic by adding correction terms. But they are optimized at a single fixed distribution. Hypothesis tests, however, decide between two regions of a parameter family. So an estimator tuned under the null hypothesis may misbehave under the alternative. Zabolotnii gives a closed-form criterion for when this transfer succeeds without bias.

For a null-centered augmentation of a target moment statistic, the alternative-side mean equals the target plus a cross term. Transfer is unbiased exactly when that cross term vanishes. Requiring each augmenting function to stay mean-zero is sufficient but stronger than necessary. The criterion is applied to a recent third-order cumulant test for measurement-error independence.
arxiv-2606-08599: Posted to arXiv in 2026, this research manuscript reports new work. The title states what it covers: Projective subvarieties of. Its subject belongs to science and technology (careful study of how the natural and built world works). It contributes fresh work that later studies can cite and extend.
arxiv-2606-08799:
Kharel and colleagues explain why fitted models can predict well on new data, using the geometry of what training learned, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They study ridge-regularized nonlinear least squares, a fitting method whose penalty keeps parameters small. Their tool is algorithmic stability: if swapping one data point barely moves the fit, it should generalize. They bound the generalization error through an effective dimension built from the model's Jacobian at the trained parameters.

In the linear case their measure recovers the classical effective dimension, but at the trained model rather than at initialization. For data on a low-dimensional manifold, the bounds scale with that intrinsic dimension, not the parameter count. For one-hidden-layer ReLU networks, the mechanism becomes counts of regions where activation patterns stay fixed. Experiments on manifolds, clustered data, and benchmarks matched the theory: the trained Jacobian compresses, and the bound tracks generalization gaps.
arxiv-2606-09499:
Ethan Rathbun and his colleagues show that world models, simulators increasingly used to generate robot training data, open a stealthy poisoning route in this 2026 arXiv paper. Traditional data poisoning plants dangerous behaviour directly in a dataset, where reviewers might spot it. Their attacks instead hide malicious prompts or tampered transition dynamics inside visibly safe teleoperation data, which stay dormant until the data passes through a world model.

Once the world model generates synthetic trajectories from the poisoned input, the hidden trigger activates and produces dangerous training examples. The team demonstrated the attacks against leading action-conditioned and text-conditioned world models. They achieved a full end-to-end backdoor on a downstream deep reinforcement learning policy, plus a proof of concept in the vision-language-action setting. The authors argue that world models must be treated as a security-critical link in the robot learning supply chain.
arxiv-2606-09599:
Marco Enríquez and Francisco Delgado study how to make entanglement on demand from plain, unlinked quantum states in this 2026 arXiv paper. Entanglement is a strict link between particles that powers teleportation and quantum codes. Building it in a controlled way, rather than by luck, is a core task for quantum tech.

The authors test two control styles. In the first, a control system puts local operations into a superposition, so several paths run at once. From fully separate inputs, this trick builds states of the Bell, GHZ, and W classes, the best-known entangled forms. The team derives the rules the local steps must meet. In the second style, noisy Pauli channels, a standard error model, are placed in path superposition and in swapped order. There, entanglement can still emerge from mixed states. The authors map where it appears, its success odds, and the trade-off with purity.
arxiv-2606-09899:
Zhang and Wang ask when a cheap shortcut for probing language models gives wrong answers, in a 2026 arXiv paper on mechanistic interpretability, the study of a model's inner workings. Their subject is attribution patching, a fast gradient-based estimate of which components matter. Activation patching, the slower test that swaps real activations, serves as their trusted standard for comparison.

The authors trace the main error to nonlinear steps later in the network, not to curvature at the patched part itself. They build a reliability score, error bounds, and a correction using Hessian-vector products, meaning second-derivative information gathered in one extra backward pass. Across five model families sized from 124 million to nine billion parameters, the multi-step correction matched or beat Integrated Gradients while using far less compute. Their Screen-Flag-Fix workflow then spends effort only on components flagged as unreliable, improving circuit recovery.
arxiv-2606-09999:
Yunwei Deng and colleagues let the spectrum of newborn star masses emerge from local conditions instead of imposing it, in a 2026 arXiv paper on star formation simulations. Simulations usually sample stars from a fixed initial mass function, the distribution of newborn star masses. Their semi-deterministic scheme represents unresolved cores and discs with reservoir particles and groups them into clusters with a friends-of-friends method linking nearby particles.

The mass function for each new cluster then follows from the cluster's current mass. Tests on isolated molecular clouds and a dwarf galaxy merger reproduce the observed relation between the most massive star and its cluster mass. It also gives the smallest run-to-run variation among seeds and natural mass segregation in clusters. On galactic scales it predicts fewer massive stars at low star formation rates, warning that common rate diagnostics will underestimate true rates.
arxiv-2606-10099:
Rivera Soto and colleagues learn to detect AI-generated text from writing style alone, without labeled authors, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Their trick is paraphrase inversion: a style encoder learns to reconstruct human-authored text from its machine-generated paraphrase. A frozen semantic encoder forces the style encoder to capture only non-semantic features, the stylistic residue.

Detection uses either a few-shot comparison or a zero-shot detector based on DeepSVDD, a one-class anomaly method. Across benchmarks, their representations matched or beat all baselines in the few-shot setting. In the zero-shot regime they rivaled fully supervised classifiers on in-distribution data and generalized better to outputs from unseen language models. The same representations transferred to authorship verification and fine-grained style discrimination, tasks they were never trained on, suggesting genuinely general style features.
arxiv-2606-10399:
Gibney and Huffstutler show that a practical decoder for quantum color codes is nearly optimal on typical noise, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum error correction. Exact decoding, by contrast, is provably hard. Their block-based decoder partitions a triangular lattice with periodically spaced boundary walls, solves each block exactly by a frontier dynamic program, then repairs the leftover syndrome on the boundaries.

That construction gives a deterministic additive guarantee bounding the excess error weight by a term shrinking with wall spacing. Under natural noise models with independent face errors at constant rate, the additive bound becomes a near-optimal multiplicative guarantee with overwhelming probability, in stated running time. A smoothed analysis analogue holds when an arbitrary adversarial error pattern is perturbed by independent random noise. The results separate typical-case decoding, where near-optimality is achievable, from the worst case that complexity theory rules on.
arxiv-2606-10499:
Zhehao Dai and colleagues address traffic prediction for cities with too few sensors in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pooling raw data across cities would raise privacy problems. Their framework, MoE-FedTP, uses federated learning, where each city trains locally and shares only model parameters. A mixture-of-experts design keeps a set of expert networks drawn from different source cities, linked by partial parameter sharing. A gating mechanism blends the experts per city.

The design targets the strong differences in traffic patterns between cities, in both space and time. On four real-world traffic datasets, MoE-FedTP beats leading cross-city and federated baselines in accuracy and generalisation. Ablation tests, which remove parts of the system to see what matters, confirm that the expert structure and its selection strategy drive the gains. The method is offered as a privacy-preserving way to lift prediction quality where sensors are scarce.
arxiv-2606-10799:
Yifeng Sun tests whether language models can referee research mathematics in this 2026 arXiv paper. Judging a whole proof at once fails in a way Sun calls context poisoning. Plausible statements hide one subtle logical flaw, and the model waves the proof through or turns sceptical of everything. The framework verifies step by step, keeping context for each deduction and constraining which theorems may be cited. It is evaluated on a diagnostic suite of research-level proofs from the FirstProof challenge.

Ablations show the constraints are indispensable: unconstrained global prompting fails to localise errors, while the step-level framework localises them. The interesting shift is in the remaining failures: instead of hallucinations, rejections are dominated by pedantic hyper-rigor, objections to unstated conventions that human experts supply automatically. The verifier is now strict enough to expose ambiguities in the benchmark itself, a sign for automated proof review.
arxiv-2606-10999:
Blois completes a classification in linear dynamics in this 2026 arXiv paper. A composition operator re-expresses a function through a fixed symbol map: feed the input through the map first. On weighted Bergman spaces over the right half-plane, the question is which such operators, induced by affine symbols, are cyclic, supercyclic, or hypercyclic. Those are grades of how thoroughly one vector's orbit can fill the space.

Blois characterizes the cyclic and supercyclic cases for affine symbols across the full range of weights. Together with earlier hypercyclic results, that completes the picture for all three grades in this setting. The distinctions are fine ones: every hypercyclic operator is supercyclic, and every supercyclic one cyclic, but neither implication reverses in general.
arxiv-2606-11099:
Ana Larrañaga and co-authors present the Fuel Optimizer in a 2026 arXiv paper, a framework for designing sustainable aviation turbine fuels. Synthetic fuels must meet strict property standards while cutting emissions, and testing each blend in hardware is slow and costly. It inverts the problem: the user states a merit function, a scoring rule for a good fuel, and the tool searches for the best blend.

The team simulated blends in a reactor model of a CFM56 engine, then trained a surrogate model, a fast stand-in predicting emissions from composition. The surrogate matched the full model within five percent in most cases, judging thousands of candidates per minute. A genetic algorithm then optimized blends under property constraints, including seal swelling. Its best candidates beat every training blend on both merit functions, one built to break the nitrogen oxides versus carbon monoxide trade-off. Reactor simulations confirmed the winners.
arxiv-2606-11299:
Kiuchi, Reboul-Salze, Sekiguchi, and Shibata report a record-breaking simulation of two neutron stars merging in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their global general relativistic neutrino-radiation-transfer magnetohydrodynamics simulation follows a binary of two 1.35 solar-mass neutron stars. It ran on the Japanese supercomputer FUGAKU at an unprecedented spatial resolution of 6.25 meters, consuming roughly 530 million core hours.

The binary's magnetic field starts at 3.16 times ten to the twelfth gauss at maximum, the upper end for observed binary pulsars. When the stars touch, the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability amplifies the field to an electromagnetic saturation energy near ten to the fiftieth erg within three milliseconds of merger. Spectral analysis reproduces the expected Kazantsev and Kolmogorov power spectra. The instability induces stellar-scale field amplification by at least a factor of 316. The authors conclude that a magnetar, a neutron star with an extreme magnetic field, may form at least temporarily after mergers.
arxiv-2606-11399:
Dang, Kieu, and Masud probe the cultural values inside large language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models are deployed across cultures but often reflect homogenized values from training data. Evaluations typically prompt directly with survey-style questions, which elicit neutral or safety-aligned responses and miss underlying preferences. The authors translate social value questions into scenario-based behavioral dilemmas instead.

Working along the two Inglehart-Welzel axes of the World Values Survey, they extract token-level probabilities to measure implicit values. They then apply activation steering, optionally with country-conditioned prompting, to shift behavior without retraining. Across three open-source models and four target cultures, steerability varies substantially. They identify latent entanglement: interventions along one such dimension induce shifts along another. This coupling mirrors correlations in human survey data and persists across steering methods. It constrains axis-independent alignment, though general task performance is largely preserved.
arxiv-2606-11699:
Ha-Linh Nguyen leads a five-author team fixing mislabelled training data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Real datasets carry noisy labels, wrong tags assigned by crowdsourcing or automatic tools, with reported error rates reaching well over a third in some collections. Such errors quietly degrade model accuracy and reliability.

Their framework, Relabeler, works in two stages. Detection uses local links, how a sample relates to its neighbours, plus global patterns to flag suspect labels. Correction then estimates the most probable clean label from its features and its observed label together. Across multiple datasets, noise types and noise rates, Relabeler consistently beats the strongest existing baselines. Label correction precision improves by up to fifty-eight percent, and downstream task performance by up to six percent. The authors note it also complements other noise-finding methods rather than only replacing them.
arxiv-2606-11899:
David Pask links automata, tilings and group theory in this 2026 arXiv paper on pure mathematics. A Mealy automaton is a small machine whose states both read and write symbols. From a full such automaton he builds a bijection, a one-vertex higher-rank graph, and a square complex, a space tiled by squares corresponding to Wang tiles.

The main theorem characterises when this complex contains an anti-torus, a flat sheet with no periodic pattern. This happens exactly when two independent conditions hold together. The automaton must be bi-reversible, its transitions invertible in both directions, which makes the complex complete, its universal cover splitting as a product of two trees. And the associated graph must be aperiodic. The two hypotheses do separate jobs. As a corollary, exactly two of the smallest automata carry an anti-torus, the lamplighter pair, while freer behaviour appears at larger alphabet sizes.
arxiv-2606-12199:
Zhen Ye and co-authors hunt for the speech encoding that best fits a text-trained model's way of thinking, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spoken dialogue models reuse language model backbones, yet reasoning weakens when speech replaces text as input. One culprit is rate: speech tokenizers emit 12.5 to 50 tokens per second, while matching text needs only about 3.32. Long, thin tokens dilute meaning per step. The team freezes the backbone and sweeps token frame rates at fixed information rate.

A factorized quantizer design makes very low rates workable, packing nearly 300 bits into each frame. Sweeping rates from 50 down to about two per second reveals a clear winner. Speech question answering peaks at about 4.17 tokens per second, far below standard settings. Aligning the model's middle layers to the speech encoding, rather than shallow or deep ones, works best. The result reframes speech token design as choosing a representation, not just compressing audio.
arxiv-2606-12699:
Gao and colleagues propose GlyLLM, a framework that uses a large language model for personalised blood-sugar assessment in type 2 diabetes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Glycemic assessment means judging how well a patient's glucose is controlled. Wearable glucose monitors and fitness trackers stream rich data, but traditional methods mostly use past glucose readings and ignore personal context such as surveys and biometric tests. GlyLLM instead feeds sensor data and structured personal metadata into the model together.

A vision transformer encoder first converts the wearable signals into representations the language model can use alongside the metadata. On the AI-READI dataset, GlyLLM beats traditional methods by an average of 13.66 percent in forecasting error and by 13.08 percent in AUROC for diabetes categorisation, where AUROC scores how well categories are separated. Ablation tests, which remove one input at a time, show diabetes surveys and biometric tests matter more than other health information.
arxiv-2606-12999:
Kulikovsky models how in-phase oscillations of cell current density and temperature affect the impedance of the cathode catalyst layer in a proton exchange membrane fuel cell, in this 2026 arXiv paper. This work studies a regime where 2 parameters swing together in phase, building on models that found reduced resistivity under perturbations of potential and oxygen concentration.

The model shows that in-phase harmonic perturbations to the current density and the catalyst layer temperature lower both the layer's impedance and, in the zero-frequency limit, the cell resistivity. The drop is larger than a previous model of the same effect found. Two mechanisms act together. The temperature oscillations induce oscillations in the layer's proton conductivity, which lowers proton transport losses. They induce oscillations in the exchange current density of the oxygen reduction reaction, which reduces the faradaic impedance. The oscillating exchange current density is the dominant contribution to the drop.
arxiv-2606-13099:
Rathi and colleagues explore 3-dimensional tracking of in-silico Lagrangian sensors in a lab-scale stirred tank reactor, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Lagrangian sensors drift through a liquid, sending back conditions along their trajectory, which could improve operator awareness inside chemical reactors where wall-mounted sensors give an incomplete picture.

The simulated sensors follow a real-world design, and filtering algorithms with a dynamic model convert the inertial readings into position estimates. The authors compare an extended Kalman filter, a particle filter, and the unscented Kalman filter as in the pykalman library. Numerical tests track the in-silico particles in a 3-dimensional vortex and in the measured flow field of the stirred tank, using the Maxey-Riley-Gatignol equations for inertial particle motion as ground truth. Paths are reconstructed from noisy synthetic data with errors below 10 percent.
arxiv-2606-13199:
Stefan Hoffelner and Müller work in descriptive set theory in this 2026 arXiv paper, the branch of logic studying definable sets of real numbers. They address a variant of the twelfth Delfino problem, a question about which combinations of regularity properties can coexist. Regularity properties include Lebesgue measurability, the idea that a set has a defined length or volume, and the Baire property, a notion of being non-negligible. The authors assume an inner model with many Woodin cardinals, strong infinity assumptions.

By forcing, a technique that builds mathematical universes, they produce a model with regularity at one projective level. Every set at that level is measurable and has the Baire property, and uniformisation, a choice principle, holds at nearby levels. Yet the universe carries a definable well-ordering of the reals, a feature tied to the opposite, non-regular world. The construction answers a question posed in 1999.
arxiv-2606-13599:
Akpinar and colleagues build a framework linking black hole thermodynamics to scattering amplitudes in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large objects radiate and absorb, and their state count is encoded in their entropy. The authors describe equilibrium states as on-shell particles and non-steady processes as transitions between them, in particle-physics language. An observation is that spinning states remain essential for objects that do not rotate at large scale. Consistency with large-scale symmetries then forces spin universality: all spinning states governed by a single coupling.

A consequence follows: absorption and emission chances are controlled by the same coupling, so local detailed balance, the reversibility of heat processes, emerges from on-shell data alone. Applied to black holes, the framework reproduces the thermal emission spectrum of Hawking radiation. The result strengthens the bridge between gravity thermodynamics and amplitude methods, suggesting thermal behaviour follows the same unitarity principles behind particle collisions.
arxiv-2606-14299:
Huang and colleagues stop chasing leaderboard gains for test-time adaptation of CLIP and ask what actually makes it work. CLIP's zero-shot predictions degrade under distribution shift, and a crowd of adaptation methods has grown up around fixing that, with little understanding of where gains come from. Their 2026 arXiv paper organizes methods into three paradigms by what gets updated at test time, and builds TTABC, an open benchmark standardizing evaluation across twenty-plus representative methods.

The analysis delivers three verdicts. First, in parameter-based methods, gains are driven primarily by test-time evidence and reliable proxies, not heavy optimization. Second, competitive, far more efficient performance is achievable without heavy tuning, using evidence across or within samples, plus lightweight prototype updates. Third, there is no silver bullet: the best paradigm depends on the shift, with norm-layer updates suiting corruptions and stream-aware designs suiting label shifts.
arxiv-2606-14399:
Kędzierski and Krasoń continue a study of duality for t-modules in a 2026 arXiv paper in arithmetic geometry. T-modules are higher-dimensional analogues of Drinfeld modules, objects that behave like elliptic curves over function fields. Duality questions ask when such an object matches its double dual, a reflection applied twice.

The authors focus on two-dimensional triangular t-modules in a specific reduced form, described as the difficult cases. Computer-assisted symbolic calculations with matrices over a skew field revealed a reduction pattern for t-modules meeting a stated condition. Using that pattern, they prove these t-modules are isomorphic to their double duals. The proof extends two classic results, the Cartier-Nishi theorem and the Weil-Barsotti formula, to a substantially broader class of t-modules than before.
arxiv-2606-14699:
Li and co-authors teach machines to articulate three-dimensional objects in a 2026 arXiv paper. Articulated objects have moving parts, like drawers and doors, and reconstructing their joints matters for animation, games, and robot simulation. Neural methods exist, but annotated training data are scarce, limiting generalization.

Their model, Instruct-Particulate, takes a 3D mesh plus a target kinematic specification: part descriptions, connectivity, joint types, and optional point prompts. It then predicts the part segmentation and joint motion parameters matching that specification. Because the specification can vary in granularity, heterogeneous data become usable, and at test time a vision-language model can supply it automatically. The team built a training set of over one hundred fifty thousand articulated objects, partly labeled by vision-language models, and the model generalized across categories and to AI-generated meshes.
arxiv-2606-14999:
Choudhary and coauthors learn compact representations of X-ray scattering images with a variational autoencoder in a 2026 study. Synchrotron facilities now produce scattering data faster than manual workflows can handle. The team trains an attention-based convolutional model on one and a half million images. The goal is a latent space that reveals structure during both archive study and live experiments.

The learned space shows clean clusters and smooth paths that track how experiments progress. It also supports generating synthetic scattering images across varied structural states. Deployed without retraining at a second facility, the model still organizes time-resolved film formation data into readable structure. Against DINOv3, a large general vision model, the domain-trained encoder gives cleaner cluster separation and smoother trajectories. The tools run inside the Latent Space Explorer on the MLExchange platform. Inference takes about a twentieth of a second per image, fast enough for live monitoring.
arxiv-2606-15399:
Kalathoor and coauthor examine what spatial filtering does to entropy in a supersonic reacting shear layer in a 2026 fluid dynamics paper. A shear layer is the turbulent mixing zone between two fast streams, here with chemical reaction adding heat. Filtering, averaging the flow over boxes, is how large-eddy simulations afford turbulent flows. The authors apply box filters of growing width to high-resolution simulation data and track entropy, disorder tied to irreversibility, and its production by friction and heat conduction.

Filtering barely changes the entropy field itself, but it weakens the sharp peaks of entropy production and inflates the transport residual, the mismatch between filtered and reconstructed entropy change. The errors concentrate in the layer's core, where mechanical and thermal activity is strongest, rather than spreading evenly. For engineers modeling scramjets and combustors, the lesson is that coarse filtering corrupts entropy budgets precisely where the physics matters most.
arxiv-2606-15699:
Prajapati and colleagues study almost rational Finsler metrics in 2026, asking when they are dually or projectively flat. Finsler geometry lets distance depend on direction, and flatness conditions single out the tractable metrics. Almost rational metrics have a fundamental tensor splitting into a smooth positive factor times a rational part.

The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for each kind of flatness. They then characterise metrics enjoying both kinds at once, and prove a rigidity result for this class. Guided by known rigidity in neighbouring classes, they conjecture that metrics with both kinds of flatness must be locally Minkowskian, meaning locally just a flat norm. Worked examples illustrate each condition. The results narrow the search for explicit metrics with prescribed flatness, needed in information geometry and physics.
arxiv-2606-15799:
Fadafan and colleagues use machine learning to extract topological order from the two-dimensional Ising model in 2026, training restricted Boltzmann machines on samples taken at criticality. The samples span the model's sectors, created by inserting spin-flip defects, equivalent to twisted boundary conditions, on a torus. The question is whether a statistical learner can see emergent topological structure, not just local correlations.

A square-root map turns the learned distributions into candidate wavefunctions for the Ising topological field theory in one higher dimension. From overlaps of those states the team extracts the modular S-matrix, the fingerprint of the topological order, recovering the expected Ising data. The network's learned couplings also reproduce the Ising model's nearest-neighbour pattern and detect the sign reversals at defect seams. The networks capture both critical fluctuations and emergent topology, offering a data-driven route from lattice models to topological field theory.
arxiv-2606-16099:
Krauss proposes in 2026 that gravitational wave detectors double as dark matter detectors for ultralight axion-like particles. Such particles, if they form a coherent cosmic background and couple to photons, would slightly modulate light phase or polarization in an interferometer. The modulation peaks at a frequency set by the particle mass, and fades when the coherence length exceeds the arm length.

For the ground-based LIGO band, Krauss finds sensitivity sits below current bounds, so LIGO is unlikely to lead here. The space-based LISA mission looks far more promising. Its natural mass window matches sideband frequencies inside the LISA science band. A one-year shot-noise-limited search projects sensitivity roughly a thousand to ten thousand times below the CAST helioscope bound across much of that band. An RF heterodyne upgrade could extend the reach further. Existing observatories may thus probe new dark matter territory cheaply.
arxiv-2606-16299:
Paudel and co-authors catalog groups of dwarf galaxies in the nearby universe in 2026, the smallest galaxy groups yet charted as systems. Dwarf galaxies are faint and hard to confirm, so their groupings stay poorly known. The team searches two large spectroscopic surveys, SDSS and DESI, within redshift 0.02, roughly the local cosmic neighborhood. A group needs at least four confirmed members near a central galaxy.

Membership requires a projected distance within 300 kiloparsecs of the central galaxy and a line-of-sight velocity within 200 kilometers per second of it. The search finds 28 groups holding 129 dwarf members in total. The median group sits about 55 megaparsecs away, and its central galaxy holds about 1.7 billion solar masses in stars. Some centrals weigh only about 100 million solar masses, near the Fornax dwarf spheroidal. Even such tiny galaxies can anchor a group, the census shows. That extends theories of galaxy assembly down to the smallest scales.
arxiv-2606-16499:
Forsberg Conde and Hudak classify maps between Specht modules in 2026. Specht modules sit at the center of the representation theory of symmetric groups. The setting is level-one cyclotomic quiver Hecke algebras of affine type C. The authors focus on hook partitions, diagrams shaped like a bent arm, distinguishing hooks with a short leg from those with a short arm.

They then show that every non-zero homomorphism from an arbitrary Specht module is determined by sending the cyclic generator to a single standard basis element, a drastic simplification of the search space. Using that action, they obtain a full classification of homomorphisms in the short leg case. The short arm case proves trickier: some plausible source partitions fail to produce maps, blocked by Garnir relations. This is the first investigation of homomorphisms between Specht modules in affine type C, extending methods from type A.
arxiv-2606-16599:
Crols and co-authors grow Gaussian random numbers on a binary tree in 2026, giving probabilistic AI chips a cheap source of shaped noise. Bayesian neural networks track their own uncertainty, but every neuron needs Gaussian random numbers. Standard generators lean on arithmetic units and large look-up tables, both costly on tiny hardware. TreeGRNG instead walks a binary tree: each level generates one bit by a weighted coin flip, with each probability set by the flips before it.

Because the required probabilities come from Gaussian properties, they are computed once at design time. The synthesis tool then shrinks the constant comparators to a minimal footprint, and no arithmetic units or tables are needed at run time. The result surpasses the state of the art in distribution accuracy while cutting energy per sample by a factor of 3.7 and raising throughput per unit area by a factor of 5.8, per the report.
arxiv-2606-16699:
Han and Soffer Aranov prove a quantitative Oppenheim result in a 2026 number theory paper set in function fields. The classic Oppenheim conjecture says an irrational quadratic form takes values dense in the real numbers. Quantitative versions ask how fast those values fill in, which becomes a counting problem about lattice points.

Working over function fields, where polynomials play the role of integers, the authors compute higher moments of the Siegel transform, a tool that turns lattice counts into averages over spaces of lattices. From those moments they obtain an optimal bound on the variance of the number of lattice points in a set. They also compute the exact variance for points inside a ball, a result of independent interest. Sharp variance control is what turns a density statement into a reliable rate, and it feeds back into counting problems across homogeneous dynamics.
arxiv-2606-16799:
Meng tackles quality scoring for AI-generated images in a 2026 computer vision paper. Judging such images mixes two questions: does the picture make sense, and is it clean at pixel level? Vision-language models trained for meaning tend to blur the two, so fine defects slip past them.

The proposed system, MST-CLIPIQA, splits the job into two streams. Coarse patches feed a stream that reads global semantic coherence. Fine patches feed a second stream that keeps texture and artifact detail. A gated fusion step, inspired by the information bottleneck idea, mixes the scales adaptively, and an optional cross-attention step checks the image against its generation prompt. Across five benchmarks the method sets new best scores for quality and for text-image correspondence prediction. It does so while training very few parameters, which keeps the scorer cheap to adapt as image generators keep changing.
arxiv-2606-16899:
Kaiyue Wen and colleagues introduce Hyperball in a 2026 paper on optimizers for language model pretraining. Matrix-based optimizers such as Muon train models faster than the standard AdamW, but their edge shrinks as models and datasets grow under the usual weight decay rule. Something at large scale erodes the advantage.

Hyperball is a wrapper that can sit on top of Adam or Muon. Instead of letting weight decay set matrix sizes indirectly, it fixes the Frobenius norms of each weight matrix and of each update to set constants. On Qwen3-style models up to just over a billion parameters, Muon with Hyperball trains as if it had a fifth to a third more data than weight-decay baselines. Learning rates also transfer more reliably across model widths and depths. Theory motivates the design: weight decay quietly sets an equilibrium norm, which sets how fast weight directions rotate.
arxiv-2606-17099:
Schmalbach measures whether explicit contracts make AI coding work easier to review in a 2026 software engineering paper. Agents increasingly work in delegated mode: take a task, act inside a repository under bounded authority, return a work package for human review. The delegation contract was proposed as the unit of analysis, but never tested.

The pilot runs dozens of agent executions on an instrumented codebase with seeded defects, under three conditions: plain prompt, explicit contract, and contract plus evidence bundle. Objective success saturates: every run passes the hidden acceptance tests with no scope violations, contract or not. Reviewability is another story. Evidence sufficiency improves markedly under contracts, reviewer ambiguity falls, and structured elements like changed-file lists appear almost only when contracts require them. The cost is modest extra tokens and time. A delegate, the study concludes, is only as useful as its work is reviewable.
arxiv-2606-17199:
Zhao and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on on-policy distillation for language models. The method trains a small student on a large teacher's behaviour. It uses tokens the student itself samples, avoiding costly full-vocabulary sums. In practice, though, the cheap estimator trains badly and lags exact methods.

Diagnosis traces the faults to the log-ratio reward used in training. That reward is unbounded, so gradients vary wildly and cluster at early positions. The proposed PowerOPD swaps in bounded rewards from a Box-Cox power transformation. Across six mathematics benchmarks and four Qwen3 teacher-student pairs, it beat plain distillation. It also beat post-hoc stabilisation while cutting training time and memory use by large margins.
arxiv-2606-17299:
Huang and Wu present a 2026 arXiv paper testing Word2Vec, the classic word embedding method, on Toki Pona, a constructed language with only about a hundred and thirty core words. Embeddings are usually validated on languages with huge vocabularies, so this is an extreme lower-bound test. The corpus held well over a million sentences drawn from the Toki Pona community, though many sentences contained names, loanwords, and new coinages outside the core set.

Two models were trained, one keeping those stray tokens and one filtering them out completely. Judged by word closeness to category centres, clustering scores, and similarity patterns, the stray tokens did not distort the learned structure at all. They actually pulled similar words closer together in the vector space, contrary to the usual fear of noise. The findings suggest Word2Vec depends more on distributional patterns in text than on vocabulary size.
arxiv-2606-17599:
Wang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on OQ 208, a nearby active galaxy whose iron emission vanished in step with its broad hydrogen lines. That joint fading marks a new kind of changing-look event. Changing-look galaxies flip their spectral type over years as broad lines appear or disappear, challenging steady disk models. Multi-epoch spectra show this flat-spectrum radio source lost both its strong iron complex and its Balmer broad lines over roughly fourteen years of monitoring by the team.

The joint disappearance implies the iron and hydrogen light come from the same region bathed in the central continuum. Looking across dozens of known changing-look galaxies, the authors find iron strength falls as the continuum brightens, a negative response. That pattern fits Comptonisation in a hot, thin accretion flow as the driver. The work extends the changing-look phenomenon beyond hydrogen for the first time.
arxiv-2606-17799:
Gorinova and colleagues offer a 2026 position paper arguing that coding benchmarks no longer fit how software is actually built. Coding agents now do much engineering work, yet the tests used to rank them come from a pre-agent era. A real agent is a whole system of model, harness, context, environment, and feedback, not a bare model.

The authors name three symptoms of the mismatch. Scores blur the model together with the rest of the harness, grading against one reference solution punishes other valid answers, and no component-level signal exists to guide improvement. They urge harness-aware metadata, verifiers that accept multiple solution shapes, and component-level evaluation alongside end-to-end scores, while flagging how hard it is to state goals a grader can apply.
arxiv-2606-17999:
Liu and colleagues fix a role confusion at the heart of masked diffusion language models, in a 2026 paper. These models write by denoising a fixed-size masked canvas, so response length must be learned. Borrowed from autoregressive practice, the end token doubles as padding during training, which teaches it two jobs at once: filler and true stop signal. Under large-block decoding that confusion overflows, and text runs long.

Their fix, VoidPadding, gives padding its own token and reserves the end token purely for meaning-bearing stops. At inference the clean end signal allows early stopping, while the padding signal guides adaptive growth of the canvas. On a seven-billion-parameter instruction model, the change lifted scores across math and code benchmarks by a wide margin. It beat both the original model and a rival padding scheme, while cutting decoding steps by more than half.
arxiv-2606-18099:
Levene and colleagues settle the structure of a class of operator spaces tied to maximal abelian algebras, in a 2026 functional analysis paper. A masa-bimodule is a space of operators that a chosen maximal abelian self-adjoint algebra can multiply from both sides without leaving the space. The strongly reflexive ones, those determined by rank-one operators, arise naturally from graphs and relations, including the matrix spaces behind quantum zero-error information theory.

The authors first characterize when the positive rank-one part of such a bimodule is dense, in terms of its support. They then prove the strongly reflexive bimodules form a Boolean lattice under natural join and meet operations. Lattice properties are examined for the subclasses that are also operator systems, and for bimodules built from closed subsets of a locally compact group the lattice operations get a concrete topological description.
arxiv-2606-18199:
Cuonzo sharpens an uncertainty tool so it checks each tail of a forecast on its own, in a 2026 statistics paper. Conformal prediction wraps any model in intervals with a promised coverage rate. But the promise is global. An interval can hit its overall target while missing the bad tail too often and the good tail too rarely. With skewed data, such as asset returns, that hidden imbalance is a risk.

Working with split conformal prediction, Cuonzo builds one-sided intervals for the lower and upper tails. Each tail carries its own coverage promise. He then intersects the two into a two-sided interval. Theorems prove both the tail-wise and global promises, first for exchangeable data, then for dependent data. Simulations show the method fixes the directional errors that standard intervals keep. A finance case study uses it to chase returns while holding the left tail in check.
arxiv-2606-18399:
Arróyave introduces akaitools, a Python package for working with output from the AkaiKKR electronic structure code, in a 2026 software paper. AkaiKKR uses a Green's function method well suited to disordered alloys and magnetic metals, but it writes its results as unstructured plain text. That leaves users to extract data by hand and blocks large systematic studies.

The package parses three kinds of output into structured, type-annotated Python objects. These include self-consistent field results with convergence history and per-atom electronic and magnetic properties. They also include spin-resolved density of states broken down by orbital and alloy component, and Bloch spectral functions along chosen paths through momentum space. Results arrive as immutable data classes backed by arrays and can be exported to data frames. They come with plotting, a command line interface for quick summaries and JSON export, and a generator for AkaiKKR input files.
arxiv-2606-19099:
Pacheco-Arias and colleagues map angular momentum in the IllustrisTNG50 simulation in 2026 to trace how galaxy form and motion evolve together. A first observational study of two-dimensional stellar angular momentum maps found unexpected diversity within galactic discs. The team asks whether that morpho-kinematic diversity also appears in simulations, using a classification scheme first built for late-type galaxy observations to make the comparison direct and fair.

They build a sample of about eight thousand simulated discs with stable rotation, spanning a wide mass range and cosmic time. For each, they compute maps of stellar specific angular momentum surface density and four metrics from them. A Gaussian mixture model sorts galaxies into four classes by those metrics. Membership probabilities show how classes shift with mass and epoch. The analysis tests whether simulated discs match patterns seen in real galaxies.
arxiv-2606-19199:
Gabriele and colleagues present decision-focused reinforcement learning for controlled electric vehicle charging in 2026. Growing EV use raises peak demand and grid instability risks. Smart charging control can ease both by learning time and context patterns. In real settings, though, key data like departure time are often unknown, which makes an effective charging policy hard to learn and execute for a controller working live.

A forecaster can estimate the missing features, but forecasters are trained for accuracy, not for the quality of downstream decisions. Their errors can thus propagate and hurt control. The authors instead train the forecaster inside the decision loop, so it forecasts what matters for charging outcomes. Predictions are judged by their effect on the agent's choices, not by raw error alone. The approach aims to keep cars charged by departure while shaving grid peaks, even when departure times must be inferred from partial data.
arxiv-2606-19299:
Andriamirado and colleagues explore searching for long-lived particles in muon decays at the Spallation Neutron Source in 2026. The facility at Oak Ridge is a prolific muon producer, which makes it ideal for studying dark sector particles born in muon decays at rest. The team considers a tons-scale hydrocarbon scintillator detector, highly capable for this search, placed at the source to catch rare decay products from new particles.

The search targets electron-positron final states from decays of long-lived axion-like particles and heavy neutral leptons in the tens of MeV mass range. Detector technology drawn from the PROSPECT and mobile demonstrator programs offers strong rejection of cosmic ray backgrounds. Those backgrounds would normally dominate an on-surface search of this kind. Benchmarking against expected cosmic signals sets the reach. A capable hydrocarbon detector at a muon-rich source could open dark sector space other experiments leave untested.
arxiv-2606-19399:
Acharya and colleagues present VERITAS in 2026, a verifier-guided proof search framework for zero-shot formal theorem proving. Language model provers often collapse rich verifier signals into a binary pass or fail bit. Syntax errors, type mismatches, and partial progress all carry guidance. VERITAS routes every verifier signal back into the search.

The protocol runs in two phases. Best-of-N sampling comes first. Then a critic-guided tree search ingests the first phase's failures as explicit negative examples. Every theorem solved in phase one stays solved, so added solves in phase two are attributable to feedback-driven exploration. On a standard school-level benchmark, VERITAS beats independently run best-of-N sampling and a portfolio baseline. The team also releases a combinatorics benchmark where unguided sampling falls behind, where lemma names must be recovered from feedback. The gap shows feedback, not just more samples, drives hard formal proofs.
arxiv-2606-19499:
Shun Zhang and three colleagues count and cluster story tropes in the sitcom Friends in this 2026 study. A trope is a stock story device, such as a secret twin or a last-minute rescue, that writers reuse. The team join fan-curated TVTropes labels to episode scripts and IMDb ratings for the full run.

Episodes packed with more tropes earn slightly higher weighted ratings, though trope counts alone explain little of the gap. Dialogue tied to each trope is turned into TF-IDF features, weighting rare words over common ones. Clustering then groups 1,954 tropes into 15 clusters with clear themes. The six lead characters spread unevenly across clusters, matching their known roles in the show. One comedy cluster scores high on danger, while a revelation cluster scores high on power, showing tropes can map whole casts at once.
arxiv-2606-20599:
Atkia Mahila, Avinash Maurya, M. Mustafa Rafique, and Bogdan Nicolae characterize when Tree-of-Thought reasoning stops improving with bigger budgets. Their 2026 paper studies the tree search strategy that boosts language model reasoning by exploring branching chains of thought. More search is usually assumed to mean better answers.

The authors measure the inelasticity of Tree-of-Thought strategies: past a point, extra compute buys little or no accuracy.
