Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of problems, including belly fat, high blood sugar, and high blood pressure, that raise the risk of diabetes and heart disease. Extra body fat fuels both inflammation and oxidative stress, which then damage tissue over time.

The review traces the chemical steps by which that stress builds and spreads harm. It links the process to each part of the syndrome. It also surveys treatments that target the stress itself. Those include drugs and lifestyle change.
europmc-pmc10320099:
Kolberg and co-authors described the 2023 update of g:Profiler, a free web tool for gene list studies. A gene list study asks what shared jobs a set of genes does. The tool links gene lists to large data banks on gene roles, cell paths, and gene control.

The tool now works for 849 species, from humans to plants, fungi, and pests. Users can also upload data for any other species. Kolberg added a new filter that picks out the gene terms that drive a result. New graphs show how those terms connect to each other. Old data banks stay saved back to 2015, so past work can be checked again.
europmc-pmc10391899:
Marassi and Fadini reviewed in 2023 how three chronic diseases drive each other. The three are type 2 diabetes, heart and vessel disease, and chronic kidney disease. Each is common, and they often strike the same person. Doctors have coined one shared name for the linked trio: cardio-renal-metabolic disease.

High blood sugar can damage the heart and kidneys in well-known ways. Marassi notes that the heart and kidneys also harm each other directly. Less clear is how heart or kidney disease then worsens blood sugar control. The review gathers proof for each link in the chain. It builds the case for care plans that treat the trio as one illness, not three.
europmc-pmc10457199:
Zhao led a gene study of blood proteins tied to inflammation in 2023, with the Estonian Biobank Research Team among the partners. The team measured 91 such proteins in 14,824 people. It then searched each genome for spots that raise or lower a protein level. Such spots are called protein quantitative trait loci.

The search found 180 spots, 59 near the protein's own gene and 121 far away. Zhao merged these with disease gene data to test which proteins cause illness. One protein, lymphotoxin-alpha, stood out in multiple sclerosis. A second, CD40, raised risk for one joint disease yet lowered it for two others. One more, CXCL5, was tied to ulcerative colitis and ran high in patient guts.
europmc-pmc10499599:
Takeuchi and a large team linked gut microbe sugar use to insulin resistance in 2023. Insulin resistance is the core fault behind metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes. In it, body cells respond weakly to insulin, the hormone that lowers blood sugar. Gut microbes help digest food, and their sugar use may feed the fault.

The team joined stool chemistry, microbe gene reads, and blood data in humans. Stools of resistant people held more simple sugars that the body can absorb. Takeuchi tied that surplus to microbe sugar paths and to swelling signals. Some gut bacteria tracked with resistance, others with healthy response. The healthy-response set eased the fault when fed to mice.
europmc-pmc10667099:
Wadden led the SURMOUNT-3 trial in 2023 on a weight drug given after a lifestyle program. Adults with obesity first spent 12 weeks on strict diet and activity coaching. Those who lost at least 5% of body weight moved to the drug phase. In all, 579 people got tirzepatide or a dummy shot once a week for 72 weeks.

The drug arm lost far more weight, Wadden reports. Mean extra change was a loss of 18.4% on the drug, versus a gain of 2.5% on the dummy. A further loss of 5% or more hit 87.5% on the drug and 16.5% on the dummy. Gut side effects were the most common harm, mostly mild or moderate.
europmc-pmc10767899:
Zdrazil and co-authors described the ChEMBL database in 2023, a free store of drug-like compounds and their test results. Staff curate each entry by hand for quality. The bank has grown in size and in data types since its 2009 launch. Past reports ran in 2012, 2014, 2017, and 2019.

Deposited data now slightly outweigh data mined from papers, Zdrazil reports. Chemical probe data flow in on a set schedule through a European consortium. Screens for anti-Covid compounds were added in release 27, with patent data close behind. New flags mark natural products and chemical probes. About 270,000 test records now carry a note on how the compound acts.
europmc-pmc11031399:
Barthélemy and a large team test a precise blood measure for Alzheimer disease against spinal fluid tests in this 2024 study. New Alzheimer treatments that slow the disease make it vital to spot who can benefit. Spinal fluid tests are approved but need a spinal tap. The team measured a blood ratio of a tau protein form, called plasma percent p-tau217, in two patient groups.

The groups held 1,422 people in Sweden and 337 in the US, the authors report. Brain scans served as the truth standard for amyloid plaques and tau tangles. The blood test matched approved spinal fluid tests at sorting plaque status, with accuracy scores from 0.95 up to 0.97 for plaques. For tangles it scored from 0.95 up to 0.98 and generally beat the fluid tests. The main checks focused on people with mild memory impairment.
europmc-pmc11093599:
Ju and a large team show that a protein-building enzyme doubles as a lactate tagger in stomach cancer in this 2024 study. Lactylation is a chemical tag that lactate, a sugar breakdown product, adds to proteins. The known tagger was doubted, since its fuel is about a thousand times scarcer than a rival fuel. The team tested an enzyme called AARS1, which normally helps build proteins.

AARS1 used lactate and ATP, the cell's energy currency, to attach the tag directly, they found. It sensed lactate levels, moved into the nucleus, and tagged a growth complex called YAP-TEAD, switching it on. That complex in turn raises AARS1 levels, forming a positive feedback loop. AARS1 was higher in stomach tumours, and high levels tracked with poor patient outlook. Blocking the loop slowed cancer cell growth in their tests.
europmc-pmc1621099:
Social forces decide who gets sick and who gets care. Farmer and co-authors developed that claim in 2006 under the name structural violence: the harm done by social structures themselves. They drew on work with HIV patients in the US and Rwanda.

Racism, poverty, gender inequality, and war shape illness far upstream of the clinic. Yet medical training seldom links that analysis to daily practice, since the field prizes molecular answers. Farmer calls such inquiry desocialized. He urges biosocial thinking: treating disease as a joint product of bodies and society, built into clinical frameworks, not left as bedside intuition.
europmc-pmc1665399:
Nanoparticles slip into fish eggs, organs, and even brains. Kashiwada tracked them in 2006 using see-through medaka, a small fish whose body is transparent. Fluorescent latex particles of many sizes floated in the water.

Particles stuck to the egg shell and pooled in oil droplets. Mid-sized particles, 474 nanometers, entered eggs best. The smallest, about 39 nanometers, reached the yolk and gallbladder as embryos grew. In adults they lodged mainly in gills and gut, but also brain, liver, testis, and blood. Kashiwada concludes particles can cross the blood-brain barrier, and toxicity rose with water salinity.
europmc-pmc1779499:
Sheridan and co-authors examined in 2006 a small group of breast cancer cells marked CD44 positive and CD24 negative. Such cells had been reported to act like stem cells, which can grow and renew themselves. The team asked whether these cells can invade tissue and travel to new sites.

The researchers checked 13 breast cancer cell lines and found five where over 30 percent of cells carried the mark. Those lines made more of several invasion-linked genes, such as interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and urokinase plasminogen activator. In lab invasion tests the marked lines invaded more strongly than other lines. Yet only some of them could settle and grow in mouse lungs. The mark alone did not predict spread to the lungs.
europmc-pmc1936999:
McCarney and colleagues ran in 2007 what they describe as the first randomized trial of the Hawthorne Effect itself. The effect is the claim that people in studies change or improve simply because they are being watched closely. It threatens how well trial results transfer to routine care, yet it had never been quantified.

Inside a trial of Ginkgo biloba against placebo for mild to moderate dementia, 176 participants were randomized again. One arm got intensive follow-up with full assessments at baseline and at two, four, and six months. The other got a short baseline check and one full assessment at six months. At six months, the intensive group scored better on the cognitive test used, by about two points, and on participant-rated quality of life. The effect was significant for cognition in the main model.
europmc-pmc2125099:
J. H. Musser and Edward B. Krumbhaar, of the University of Pennsylvania's Musser department, charted the blood after spleen removal in 1913, the sixth paper of the spleen series. Dogs were counted over months. Anemia is, they say, inevitable after the operation, and so, later, is some degree of repair.

The anemia develops quickly and peaks in three to six weeks. The picture then improves slowly, nearing normal at three to four months, with full return somewhere between five and ten months. Some animals break the schedule, sinking slowly into slight anemia or repairing late. Their tables follow red counts in the millions as they fall and climb back. Readers get the timetable of recovery from losing an organ the blood cannot do without, and then does without.
europmc-pmc2125499:
Harold L. Amoss and Alan M. Chesney reported the serum treatment of twenty-six cases of epidemic poliomyelitis in 1917. The serum came from recently recovered cases, judged probably the best source. Prepared sterile, free of corpuscles and hemoglobin, and run in slowly by gravity with the usual cautions, it could be given, they state, without danger.

Their rules are practical. Give it both into the spinal canal and into the blood, the latter directly or under the skin. Give it early; the earlier, the more promise. Expect it to arrest paralysis more reliably than to reverse it. Decide from the examination backed by the spinal fluid's microscopy and chemistry. Repeated injections remain an open question. Readers get an emergency therapy's protocol and its score, good and bad together.
europmc-pmc2128199:
Theobald Smith, of the Rockefeller Institute's animal pathology department at Princeton, tied a calf bronchopneumonia outbreak to one minute bacillus. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1921. The disease struck calves in their early months in a large dairy herd. Smith names the germ Bacillus actinoides and argues it is the definite cause.

Other germs, including Bacillus pyogenes and Bacillus bovisepticus, may appear later in the diseased lungs, but as followers rather than starters. Injections of actinoides cultures under the skin produced large hard swellings that ended in dead tissue. Injections into the windpipe produced bounded areas of dead lung tissue. Smith notes that his earlier publication described the germ's culture habits and shapes in full, with illustrations. Anyone attempting to isolate it from a herd outbreak can follow that account.
europmc-pmc2128399:
Carl F. Schmidt and W. Benson Harer opened a drug series with the morphine family's action on breathing. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923. They recorded chest pressure in cats without opening the chest, made the animals breathe out actively with a steady carbon dioxide mixture, and then dosed them.

Morphine and heroine (heroin) pressed selectively on the central mechanism that drives breathing out. Breathing slowed while its depth stayed much the same, partly because the lungs emptied more slowly. Codeine had no depressant effect in cats with the brain's upper part removed. Once breathing out had gone passive, even larger morphine doses did no more harm unless the circulation failed. Breathing failure, they conclude, followed circulation failure rather than causing it. Strong doses also stirred the spinal cord, making expiration active again and speeding the rate.
europmc-pmc2131299:
Ida Pritchett published part twelve of her mouse typhoid studies in 1927, on diet and host resistance. White mice were fed a bread and milk diet, plain or with added fats, then infected by mouth with the paratyphoid bacillus. The base diet alone could keep a healthy stock breeding for years, so any gain would show the added food at work.

Adding butter fat or cod liver oil, at five percent of the diet, clearly raised the mice's resistance to infection. A complete McCollum diet worked even without butter fat, and milk treated with a mercury vapor lamp helped too. An inactive fat such as Crisco gave muddy results. The improved diets also steadied the death rate across the seasons at a lower level.
europmc-pmc2131499:
Landsteiner and Philip Levine studied the inheritance of two blood traits in a 1928 paper at The Rockefeller Institute. Beyond the known blood groups, immune sera reveal two further clumping structures in human red cells, called M and N. The pair collected family data to learn how M and N pass from parents to children.

They examined one hundred sixty-six families. The pattern fit Mendelian inheritance: a trait absent in both parents did not appear in the children, a point backed by ten families with forty-six children. The work shows that blood traits beyond the standard groups can be traced in families. The authors note a forensic use in disputed paternity cases, with care and further study still needed.
europmc-pmc2131599:
Rivers and Eldridge opened their two-part study of varicella and herpes zoster with statistics in 1929, at the Hospital of The Rockefeller Institute. Chicken-pox and shingles look alike blister by blister, yet the whole picture of each differs. If one virus caused both, their patterns in age and season should track together. The pair assembled the case records to test that.

Chicken-pox falls mostly on children under ten years old. Zoster, as a rule, falls on people past that age. Chicken-pox cases swing with the seasons in a markedly constant pattern year after year. Zoster cases swing irregularly, and their pattern does not parallel the chicken-pox curve. The plain numbers thus argue against a single shared cause, before any laboratory test is made.
europmc-pmc2140499:
Edwin Powers studied fish breathing and water acidity in a 1922 paper in The Journal of General Physiology. Marine fish draw oxygen from sea water, sometimes at low oxygen tension. Powers asked how the hydrogen ion level of the water changes that uptake, and whether a fish's tolerance for acidity swings matches where it lives.

The ability to absorb oxygen at low tension depends in part on the water's acidity. Fish that shrug off wide acidity swings range widely in habitat, while fish that tolerate little swing live restricted lives. In the herring, the water condition best for oxygen uptake matches the condition the fish choose and where they gather most thickly. Powers suggests each fish's alkaline reserve in the blood sets its personal limit.
europmc-pmc2270899:
Outeiro and co-workers visualised toxic alpha-synuclein oligomers in living cells in 2008. In Parkinson's disease, this protein misfolds and clumps; its fibrils fill Lewy bodies, the disease's hallmark inclusions. Growing evidence instead blames small prefibrillar clusters, called oligomers, as the toxic species. They had never been identified in living cells. The team used bimolecular fluorescence complementation, a method where two protein halves glow only when they meet, to watch oligomers form.

Stabilising the oligomers through the assay increased cell toxicity. Adding the protective chaperone Hsp70 rescued the cells and reduced oligomer formation. Parkinson's-linked mutations did not change how many oligomers formed. Their biochemical properties, however, differed from normal alpha-synuclein oligomers. The assay gives researchers a direct tool to test candidate therapeutics for these synuclein disorders.
europmc-pmc2516199:
Homer and colleagues showed in 2008 that a person's DNA can be picked out of a mixed sample using dense gene-chip data. Their tool was a microarray that reads hundreds of thousands of SNPs, the single-letter DNA differences that vary between people. The question was whether someone contributing only a trace to a mixture could still be identified.

The team built the statistical theory, tested its limits in simulations, and then ran real mixtures in the laboratory. They correctly detected specific people even when a person supplied less than 0.1 percent of the total DNA in the mix. The result matters for forensics, where samples are often contaminated. It also means summary statistics from large genetic studies do not fully hide who took part.
europmc-pmc2556099:
Dowd and colleagues catalogued the bacteria living in chronic diabetic foot ulcers in this 2008 study. Such ulcers often end in amputation, and the microbe communities inside them, growing as biofilms, were poorly understood. Culture methods grow only easy species, so the team used a DNA sequencing method called bTEFAP to census 40 ulcers from different patients.

The commonest genus was Corynebacterium, ahead of the usual suspects like Staphylococcus and Streptococcus. Oxygen-hating bacteria such as Bacteroides, Peptoniphilus, and Anaerococcus appeared in nearly every ulcer and made up much of each community. The authors propose that distinct bacteria form groups they call functional equivalent pathogroups. Alone, each member is harmless. Together they act like one consortium, as damaging as a classic pathogen. That would explain why these infections persist.
europmc-pmc2570799:
Knopp and colleagues tested in 2008 how well standard stool examinations find intestinal worms in Zanzibar schoolchildren. These soil-transmitted helminths infect the poorest communities, and control programmes giving deworming drugs need accurate counts. But repeated mass treatment had lowered worm burdens, making infections easy to miss. The team collected three stool samples from each of 342 children on Unguja Island and applied three laboratory techniques.

A single sample missed much. Sensitivity ranged from 20.7 percent for one method detecting Strongyloides to 84.2 percent for another detecting Ascaris. Examining three samples raised the observed hookworm prevalence by 161 percent under one technique. Combining different techniques on multiple samples came closest to the true prevalence predicted by a mathematical model. After three samples, whipworm prevalence stood at 47.9 percent.
europmc-pmc261899:
Stein and a large consortium sequenced in 2003 the genome of the soil worm Caenorhabditis briggsae and compared it with its famous relative C. elegans. The two species split about 100 million years ago yet look nearly identical and share chromosome number, genome size, and habitat. The comparison aimed to expose which features evolution has conserved.

The draft genome holds roughly 19,500 protein-coding genes, about the same as C. elegans. Clear counterparts exist for 12,200 of them, and about 800 genes have no detectable match. Gene order is extensively shared, and operons, the worm's clustered gene units, kept their arrangement in 96 percent of cases. Genome size differences came almost entirely from repetitive DNA, which makes up 22.4 percent of the C. briggsae genome. The comparison also revealed 1,300 new C. elegans genes.
europmc-pmc2627899:
Ramagopalan and colleagues showed in 2009 that vitamin D directly switches on the main gene behind multiple sclerosis risk. Multiple sclerosis clusters in sunny-poor regions, and the strongest genetic factor is a variant of the immune gene HLA-DRB1, the *1501 type. The team searched that gene's control region for a vitamin D response element, a DNA switch the vitamin's receptor can grip.

Sequencing over 1,000 chromosomes showed the switch perfectly conserved on the risk-carrying *15 haplotypes but variable on others. Binding tests confirmed the vitamin D receptor docks there. In cell experiments, adding active vitamin D raised expression from the *15 promoter, an effect lost when the switch was deleted or swapped for a non-risk version. Cell-surface protein rose only in *15-bearing cells. The authors frame this as a direct gene-environment interaction.
europmc-pmc2631699:
Maki and Tambyah reviewed in 2001 how to engineer away urinary catheter infections, the most common hospital-acquired infection. More than a million patients in American hospitals and care facilities catch one each year. Risk runs at 5 percent per day of catheter use. These infections are also the second most common cause of hospital bloodstream infection and are tied to higher death rates.

The review examines catheters redesigned to fight infection at the surface. Catheters impregnated with the antibiotics nitrofurazone or minocycline plus rifampin show anti-infective activity. So do catheters carrying a silver alloy hydrogel coating. Both significantly cut infection risk for short-term use up to two or three weeks. Silent infections trigger needless antibiotic treatment. They also breed resistant organisms. So the authors argue prevention by design beats treatment after the fact.
europmc-pmc2700099:
Le Guilloux, Schmidtke, and Tuffery released in 2009 Fpocket, a free program that finds the pockets on a protein's surface where drug molecules might sit. Structure-based drug hunting starts by docking thousands of candidate compounds into such a pocket, so spotting the right pocket comes first. Many proteins' pockets were still found by eye or by luck.

Fpocket builds a geometric mesh of the protein and marks hollow spheres that nestle against its surface, clustering them into pockets. On proteins with known bound drugs, the true pocket sat in its top three guesses 94 percent of the time. For empty proteins the figure was 92 percent. It beat the field's standard tools while running faster. The package includes benchmarking and descriptor tools, and its open code invites others to build better scoring on top.
europmc-pmc2707599:
Moher, Liberati, Tetzlaff, Altman, and the PRISMA Group issued the PRISMA statement in 2009, a guide for reporting systematic reviews and pooled analyses in health care. Clinicians and guideline writers rely on such reviews to stay current. Yet early checks showed review reports often missed basic facts about methods and quality checks.

PRISMA replaces the older QUOROM guide and reflects new ideas in how reviews should be done and described. It sets out what authors should state about their search, study choice, bias checks, and combined results. Clearer reports, the authors argue, let readers judge for themselves whether a review can be trusted and used in care.
europmc-pmc2719799:
Sequeira and co-authors scanned gene activity across many brain regions in 2009 for changes tied to suicide and major depression. Most prior work focused on serotonin, one brain messenger, yet other messenger systems likely play a part too. They sampled seventeen cortical and deeper regions from suicide cases, with and without depression, and from controls.

Suicide-linked changes clustered most in prefrontal cortex, the front planning area, and in the hippocampus, a memory area. Two messenger systems stood out as broadly altered: glutamate, the main excitatory signal, and GABA, the main calming signal. Follow-up tests on receptor subunit genes, the parts that receive those signals, matched the scan results in independent samples.
europmc-pmc2791199:
Gao and colleagues hunted for the exact protein changes that let H5N1 bird flu pass between mammals, using guinea pigs as hosts in 2009. Since 2003 the virus had caused over four hundred known human cases, most after close contact with poultry, and over sixty percent of those patients died.

Of six virus strains tested, only two spread from infected animals to healthy cage mates. Changing single building blocks in two proteins showed what made the difference. One change in the PB2 protein, at position seven hundred one, was required for spread. A second change in the HA protein removed a sugar attachment and let the virus grip cell surfaces found in mammal airways.
europmc-pmc2851599:
Parchman, Geist, Grahnen, Benkman, and Buerkle sequenced the working genes of lodgepole pine in 2010, building a genomic toolkit for a tree whose huge genome blocks whole-genome sequencing. Lodgepole pine anchors mountain forests across western North America and varies strikingly across its range. Using a high-throughput sequencer on copied gene messages, the team gathered nearly six hundred thousand reads.

Assembly produced over sixty thousand gene clusters representing roughly seventeen thousand distinct genes, plus a surprising haul of active retrotransposons, jumping genes that copy themselves around the genome. The collection yielded thousands of simple repeat and single-letter variants as ready markers, with working lab primers for many. The authors present the set as a foundation for population and adaptation studies in pines.
europmc-pmc2873499:
Harte and colleagues found in 2010 that a bacterial toxin leaking from the gut runs high in people with fatty liver disease not caused by alcohol. The toxin, endotoxin, comes from gut germ walls and can stir body-wide inflammation tied to insulin resistance. They measured it in one hundred fifty-five patients with biopsy-confirmed fatty liver and in healthy controls.

Toxin levels in patients ran nearly three times the control levels on average. Having diabetes on top of fatty liver did not push levels higher, and the toxin level tracked how insulin-resistant a patient was. Companion markers of toxin response also rose. A small follow-up group treated with diet or diet plus a fat-blocking drug let the team probe whether levels fall as the liver improves.
europmc-pmc2887799:
Harteveld and Higgs reviewed in 2010 alpha-thalassaemia, likely the most common single-gene disorder in the world. The condition cuts production of alpha-globin, one chain of the hemoglobin that carries oxygen in red cells. It clusters around the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia, and migration has raised its frequency in northern Europe and North America.

Healthy people carry four working alpha-globin genes, and losing one, two, three, or all four explains the range of severity. Losing three causes HbH disease, a moderate to severe anemia, while losing all four is lethal before birth. Most cases come from deleted genes rather than spelling errors. Because blood tests alone can mislead, DNA analysis usually confirms the exact form, which matters for family counseling.
europmc-pmc2954799:
Williams and co-authors isolated a progenitor cell group living inside normal adult human joint cartilage in a 2010 study. Cartilage repairs itself poorly, and lab-grown cartilage cells lose their character, yielding patch tissue weaker than the original.

Using a sticking test on the protein fibronectin, they pulled out clones that multiplied through many doublings while keeping normal chromosome counts. The cells showed strong activity of telomerase, an enzyme that guards chromosome ends, and in three-dimensional pellets they formed cartilage-like tissue with limited range. Such resident progenitors could give repair therapies a better starting cell than borrowed marrow cells.
europmc-pmc3038199:
Amano, Nakayama, and Kaibuchi reviewed in 2010 a protein switch that helps cells keep their shape, grip, and direction. The switch, called ROCK in short, is turned on by a small partner protein and belongs to a wider family of such control proteins. Once active, it tunes the cell's inner scaffolding, the network of fibers that lets cells contract, crawl, and divide.

Drug studies link this switch to blood vessel spasm, lung blood pressure problems, nerve injury, and glaucoma. That spread makes it an attractive drug target across several fields. The review covers the switch's structure, how it is switched on, and what it acts on inside cells. It gathers the case for blocking or tuning it in treatment. Readers get a compact map of a pathway found in nearly every tissue.
europmc-pmc3040199:
Nacke and colleagues surveyed in 2011 how land use shapes the bacteria living in German soils. They sampled nine forest and nine grassland sites covering six management styles in one region, and read a marker gene from nearly six hundred thousand bacterial sequences. Soil bacteria drive nutrient cycles and soil quality, yet how farming and forestry steer them was poorly known.

Grassland soils held a richer spread of bacterial groups than forest soils, and several major groups differed clearly between the two land uses. Beech and spruce forest soils also hosted distinct communities. Soil acidity tracked many of the shifts, while management style itself showed weak links once acidity was considered. The authors conclude that land use matters mainly through the soil conditions and trees it creates. Their dataset sets a scale few earlier soil surveys could reach.
europmc-pmc3091299:
Bell and coauthors asked in 2011 how much of the variation in DNA methylation between people is written in their DNA sequence itself. Methylation, a chemical tag on DNA, helps regulate genes and differs from person to person for unclear reasons. The team measured tags at more than twenty thousand sites in cell lines from seventy seven donors of African ancestry, alongside full genotypes and gene activity data.

Nearly two hundred tag sites tracked with nearby DNA variants, showing local genetic control is common. One variant inside a gene previously suspected of shaping methylation tracked with the genome wide pattern as a whole, though such long range effects were rare overall. Tags near gene starts generally went with lower gene activity, as expected. Many variants affected both tagging and activity of the same gene. The work shows methylation is partly inherited through the sequence, not purely environmental.
europmc-pmc3108599:
David Johnston-Monje and Manish Raizada published a 2011 study in PLoS ONE on microbes that live inside maize seeds without causing disease. They compared seed bacteria across wild relatives of maize and farmed varieties, from Mexico to Canada, to see which microbes survived domestication. Samples were grown in the lab and also read by DNA fingerprint methods.

Most seed microbes found in the wild ancestor still occur in modern maize, and a small shared core appeared in every plant type tested. Cultured microbes came from many groups, and several could help plants by freeing phosphate or making growth signals. One strain strongly boosted potato shoot growth in tests. The work suggests seeds carry a lasting microbial inheritance worth protecting in breeding.
europmc-pmc3141799:
Sarah Crowe and colleagues made the case for case study research in health services in a 2011 paper in BMC Medical Research Methodology. The approach, standard in business, law, and policy, lets researchers study a complex issue closely in its real setting. Health research has used it less, despite its fit for tangled service questions.

Drawing on their own health case studies, the authors sort the main designs, the questions each suits, and the records, interviews, and observations typically used. Strengths include depth and context; risks include weak theory and cherry-picked cases. The paper closes with design pointers and a checklist for judging case study reports, aiming to raise both use and quality of the method in health research.
europmc-pmc3170599:
Nadine Genet and colleagues reviewed the scientific literature on home care across Europe in a 2011 paper in BMC Health Services Research. Care delivered at home is growing as populations age and family carers become scarcer, yet cross-country knowledge was patchy. The team screened thousands of papers from a decade, keeping seventy-four that described whole home care systems.

The surviving studies covered eighteen countries and dwelt mostly on who receives care and how services are organised. Unequal regional access, market pressures, quality, and joining health with social care recurred as themes. Systems differed sharply between and even within countries, comparative studies were rare, and financing and Eastern Europe were barely covered. The authors call for uniform frameworks so countries can finally be compared like with like.
europmc-pmc3219299:
Cornelis de Jager and colleagues tested whether simple blood-count ratios predict bloodstream infection in emergency patients, in this 2010 paper in Critical Care. Doctors usually rely on markers such as C-reactive protein and white cell counts, which perform imperfectly. The team compared these with the lymphocyte count and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio in patients suspected of community-acquired bacteremia.

They matched ninety-two patients with positive blood cultures against ninety-two with negative cultures. The groups differed clearly in C-reactive protein, lymphocyte count, and the ratio, but not in total white cell or neutrophil counts. The ratio gave the best overall test performance, closely followed by the lymphocyte count, and both beat the conventional markers. Because the values come free with a routine blood count, the authors suggest using them in daily practice.
europmc-pmc3224599:
Ryan Dowling, Pamela Goodwin, and Vuk Stambolic reviewed the case for the diabetes drug metformin as a cancer treatment in this 2011 article in BMC Medicine. Metformin is the most widely prescribed drug of its class for type 2 diabetes. Population, laboratory, and early clinical evidence had begun to suggest it might also fight cancer.

The authors set out two routes by which the drug could help. By lowering circulating insulin, it may starve cancers that thrive on high insulin, such as breast and colon tumors. It may also act directly on cancer cells by blocking the mTOR signaling pathway, which controls protein production and growth. The review weighs the supporting evidence and the molecular mechanisms, framing metformin as a promising repurposed therapy.
europmc-pmc3257299:
Angela Bruex and colleagues built a gene regulatory network for root skin cell development in the model plant Arabidopsis, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Genetics. The root epidermis makes just two cell types, hair cells and non-hair cells, making it a clean system for studying how fate is decided. The team wanted a systems-level view of the whole differentiation program.

The team used mutants that produce only one cell type, plus cell sorting to isolate the epidermis. They found over fifteen hundred genes differing between the two fates. About two hundred formed a core set. They then perturbed the system with seventeen mutants and two hormone treatments. Watching each core gene respond let them arrange the genes into a network. Timing data and statistical modeling helped place the genes. A family of regulatory proteins called bHLH emerged as stage-specific organizers.
europmc-pmc3285199:
Kresten Lindorff-Larsen and colleagues put eight protein force fields through a systematic trial in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Molecular dynamics simulations animate proteins atom by atom, but their accuracy rests entirely on the force field, the equations approximating atomic forces. With simulations now reaching previously inaccessible timescales, the team compared the fields against hard experimental data.

They checked how well each field reproduced the structures and wobbles of folded proteins measured by NMR. They tested whether simulations of small peptides were biased toward helices or sheets. And they asked whether two small proteins folded correctly from scratch, one helical and one sheet-based. Force fields have clearly improved with each generation. The newest versions, while imperfect, describe many structural and dynamical properties of proteins accurately, a verdict modelers can build on.
europmc-pmc3291999:
Pópulo, Lopes, and Soares reviewed a cell growth control system called mTOR and its role in cancer in 2012. The system sits at the center of signals that tell cells when to grow, divide, and survive. It works in two distinct protein complexes, one that responds to food, energy, and growth signals, and one that helps organize the cell's inner skeleton.

Many cancers carry faults in this system or in the pathways feeding into it, and the authors note especially strong effects in melanoma. Because of that, drugs that block mTOR have entered trials for many tumor types. Two related drugs had recently won approval for kidney cancer and certain other tumors, and the review also covers newer drugs that block the system in other ways.
europmc-pmc3320399:
Brug and colleagues surveyed how people in the Netherlands perceived the SARS threat during the 2003 outbreak, reporting in 2004. The Netherlands never recorded a case, yet the disease dominated news coverage for months. Public health officials wanted to know whether people in an untouched country would panic, take needless precautions, or tune out entirely.

An internet panel of several hundred adults answered questions about their knowledge of SARS, how risky it felt, what precautions they took, and where they got their information. Awareness of the outbreak was high, but worry stayed modest and people took few unnecessary actions. The authors draw lessons for future outbreaks, stressing that clear information through trusted channels keeps risk perception realistic even when an epidemic is far away.
europmc-pmc3375299:
Nazzi and colleagues traced in 2012 how a parasitic mite can help a virus destroy honeybee colonies. Colony losses threaten bees and, through pollination, world crop production. The team combined colony-level tracking with molecular tests on bees infested by the mite Varroa destructor.

The mite, they show, unsettles the bees' hold on deformed wing virus, turning a quiet, hidden infection into a fast-growing killer late in the season. That shift came with a shutdown of the immune factor NF-kB, a hub for many stress responses. Because different stresses converge on the same hub, the model may explain losses with many triggers.
europmc-pmc3534499:
Smartphone apps for health grew fast, and Abu Saleh Mohammad Mosa, Illhoi Yoo, and Lincoln Sheets sort the early literature in 2012. Searching MEDLINE in April 2011, they sift 2,894 articles down to 55 papers that describe 83 apps for clinicians, students, or patients.

Most apps, 57, serve health professionals. Diagnosis aids lead with 21, then drug references, medical calculators, and literature search tools; hospital system access and team messaging appear too. The rest target students and patients. Each class is summed up with the platforms it runs on. The review freezes a moment when app stores were new and proof still trailed invention.
europmc-pmc3541399:
Alcohol rewrites the gut microbiome on the way to liver disease, and Lara Bull-Otterson leads a fifteen-author mouse study documenting the rewrite in 2013. Mice drink a liquid diet with 5 percent alcohol for six weeks; some then receive the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG for two more weeks while gut leakiness and liver injury are tracked.

Chronic alcohol shrinks the two dominant phyla, Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes, while Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria expand. Alcaligenes and Corynebacterium-like genera grow the most. The shifts track rising gut pH, permeability, and bacterial leakage into the body. Probiotic treatment mitigates the changes. The paper pairs the census with a candidate remedy tested in the same animals.
europmc-pmc3553399:
Neutrophils cast nets that can injure the lungs they defend, and Olivia Z. Cheng and Nades Palaniyar review this balance problem in 2013. Neutrophil extracellular traps, webs of DNA, histones, and enzymes, catch invading microbes. Yet diseased airways fill with neutrophils, and traps have turned up in cystic fibrosis, acute lung injury, and allergic asthma.

Different triggers spark different routes to trap release, but the products share toxic, immune-provoking parts that damage host tissue when they linger. Lung collectins such as surfactant protein D bind the traps and aid clearance of dying cells and DNA. Health, the review argues, depends on forming traps fast and clearing them completely.
europmc-pmc3580499:
David Kelley and John Rinn studied jumping genes inside noncoding RNAs in Genome Biology in 2012. Long intergenic noncoding RNAs, or lincRNAs, are RNA strands that regulate genes without coding for proteins. Transposable elements are DNA chunks that copy themselves around the genome. The pair asked how much of the lincRNA world is built from them, and whether those pieces shape what lincRNAs do.

Across 9,241 human lincRNAs, eighty-three percent contained a transposable element, and such pieces made up forty-two percent of lincRNA sequence, a sharp contrast with protein-coding genes. Some element families were scarce inside lincRNAs while virus-derived ones clustered near their start points. One family, HERVH, matched closely with lincRNAs switched on only in stem cells. Strands free of elements were expressed more strongly everywhere. Borrowed viral switches, the authors suggest, helped give lincRNAs their tissue-specific voices.
europmc-pmc3586699:
Jasper Akerboom and a large team of collaborators built red calcium sensors for brain imaging in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience in 2013. Genetically encoded calcium indicators glow as nerve cells fire, since firing lets calcium flood in. Green versions ruled the field, but a red sensor would free the green channel for a second signal and pair with blue-light tools that switch cells on. Their sensors, called RCaMPs, were engineered from a heat-stable red protein named mRuby.

Crystal structures of the parent protein and of a finished sensor showed how calcium binding reshapes the glowing core. The sensors performed in worms, fly larvae, and young zebrafish. Two-color imaging tracked calcium in two compartments of one cell, and in neurons beside their support cells. Paired with a light-activated channel, stimulation and recording ran at once in crawling worms, each in its own color channel.
europmc-pmc3627099:
Robert Reiner and a large team of collaborators took a forty-year census of mosquito disease models in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface in 2013. Mathematical models of mosquito-borne transmission began with malaria theory in the early nineteen hundreds, and the Ross-Macdonald framework set their foundations by 1970. Since then models have multiplied as control programs lean on them. The team compiled 325 publications from 1970 to 2010 holding 388 distinct models, then scored each against a seventy-nine-part questionnaire on its biological assumptions.

A summary score measured how closely each model hugged fifteen core Ross-Macdonald assumptions. Later models did absorb more geography, ecology, and epidemic detail, the census found, yet most still sat close to the classical frame. The authors name the frontiers worth expanding: uneven mosquito biting, poorly mixed encounters between mosquitoes and hosts, and variation across space and time. Modelers get a map of their own habits.
europmc-pmc3644299:
Bony fishes get a new family tree in a 2013 PLoS Currents study by Betancur-R and a large team of co-authors. Past trees, built on body form, left the spiny-finned fishes in a tangle that had vexed fish experts for over a century. Gene data were pouring in and shifting old groupings, yet no tree yet covered all major lineages of bony fishes at once.

The team read 21 gene markers in 1,410 bony fish kinds, plus a few land and shark outgroups, spanning 1,093 genera and 369 families. Their tree settled the spiny-finned mass into nine well-backed higher groups. The vast order Perciformes, long called a waste-basket group, came out as one true branch for the first time. A new naming scheme and a time tree set by 60 fossils follow from the work.
europmc-pmc3675899:
The cell's power plants carry their own small genome, and its faults cause a growing list of diseases, Chinnery and Hudson review in a 2013 British Medical Bulletin article. Power plants, called mitochondria in the text, make cell energy and also handle calcium signals, blood pigment building and cell death. Two genomes must cooperate to run them: the plant's own DNA and the cell nucleus DNA. Faults in either break energy supply.

The review introduces both genomes and the clinical troubles that follow when their talk breaks down. How the plant genome is inherited remains hotly debated, and the authors mark the open points. Public data banks of plant genome variation are woven through the piece. A growing strand covers lab methods to alter the plant genome, which might one day end the passing-on of the worst faults.
europmc-pmc3682299:
Too much fluid at the start of kidney replacement marks high risk, Vaara and a large Finnish study group report in a 2012 Critical Care study. The prospective study ran in 17 Finnish intensive care units over five months and enrolled 296 critically ill patients on kidney replacement therapy. Fluid overload was set as fluid gain over ten percent of starting body weight by the time replacement began. Complete balance data existed for 283 patients.

Seventy-six patients, about 27 percent, met the overload mark. Their crude 90-day death rate was about 59 percent against about 31 percent in the rest. After adjustment for illness severity, timing, treatment kind and sepsis, overload still carried over double the odds of death. About a fifth of survivors with data still needed replacement at 90 days. Fluid state at start deserves a place in risk checks.
europmc-pmc3686699:
Stirman and colleagues built a framework and coding system for describing the changes people make to evidence-based treatments when they put them into routine practice. Programs are often adjusted to fit a new population or setting, but without a shared vocabulary nobody could say whether such changes help or harm.

The team coded 258 modifications reported in 32 published articles. They found twelve kinds of content change, five kinds of contextual change, and recorded who made each change and at what level, from a single clinician to a hospital network. The scheme proved reliable between raters, giving fidelity research a way to track adaptation instead of treating every change as drift.
europmc-pmc3701999:
Bonjour and colleagues estimated how many households cook with solid fuels, country by country, from 1980 to 2010. Smoke from wood, dung, charcoal, and coal burned in simple stoves is a major health risk, and tracking its use guides disease burden estimates and policy.

Using a multilevel model fitted to national surveys, they found the share of households relying mainly on solid fuels fell from about sixty-two percent to forty-one percent over the thirty years. Population growth cancelled the gain: the number of people exposed stayed near 2.8 billion. Use remains highest in Africa and Southeast Asia, above sixty percent of households.
europmc-pmc3734499:
Amy Pruden and co-authors published a review in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2013 on cutting the release of antibiotics and resistance genes into the environment. Polluted soil and water may help resistance spread, shortening the useful life of lifesaving drugs. The team set out to find practical management options and the incentives behind them.

They focused on farm sources, wastewater from homes, hospitals, and industry, and fish farming. Options include better handling of manure and nutrients, runoff control, and upgraded treatment plants. A Swedish case study shows how clear communication brought stakeholders on board. Many steps cost little or nothing, and some serve other policy goals too. The authors stress checking that measures truly work once in place.
europmc-pmc3758299:
Samantha Eaton and co-authors reported a methods study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on a flaw in quantitative Western blotting. Western blotting measures how much of a protein a sample holds. For fair comparison, results are scaled to a loading control protein assumed to be steady, such as actin or tubulin.

The team showed that those controls are not steady. In spinal cord from a mouse model of spinal muscular atrophy, beta-actin fell by about 19 percent, which would skew every scaled result by about 20 percent. The problem appeared across many tissues, and even between parts of the same tissue. As a fix, they show that scaling to total protein, measured with a stain such as Coomassie blue on a parallel sample, is more robust.
europmc-pmc3769299:
Bhanu Priya Ganesh, Robert Klopfleisch, Gunnar Loh, and Michael Blaut reported a mouse study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on a gut bacterium that eats mucus. Akkermansia muciniphila lives in the gut's mucus layer. Too much mucus breakdown could open the barrier to gut contents and feed bowel inflammation. The team used mice raised with a defined set of eight bacterial species.

Adding Akkermansia to mice infected with Salmonella Typhimurium made gut inflammation worse. Tissue damage scores and inflammatory signals rose, Salmonella counts in lymph nodes were ten times higher, and mucus-filled goblet cells fell two to threefold. The microbe mix also flipped: a normally dominant species nearly vanished while Salmonella took over. The authors conclude the mucus eater worsens Salmonella inflammation by disturbing mucus balance.
europmc-pmc3780999:
Stephen Burgess and Simon Thompson wrote a methods study in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2013 on allele scores in Mendelian randomization. That technique uses genetic variants as natural experiments to estimate whether a risk factor truly causes an outcome. An allele score sums all of a person's risk-raising variants into one number, weighted or not.

Using simulated data, the authors tested how scores behave when using many variants one by one would bias results. A correctly built score gave unbiased causal estimates with proper coverage. Weighted scores were slightly more powerful than unweighted ones when variant effects were similar. But choosing which variants to include, or their weights, from the same data being analyzed caused large biases. Violations of the instrument assumptions also broke the estimates, even when most variants were valid.
europmc-pmc3787199:
Diana Gaspar, A. Salomé Veiga, and Miguel Castanho wrote a review in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2013 on turning antimicrobial peptides into anticancer peptides. Antimicrobial peptides are small defense molecules found across living things. Since cancer still kills heavily worldwide and new, selective drugs are needed, researchers have asked whether these peptides can kill tumor cells while sparing normal ones.

The review covers the peptides' structures, modes of action, selectivity, and efficacy against solid tumors and blood cancers. Some peptides break tumor cell membranes, others act on targets inside the cell, and several modes can coexist in one cancer type. Predicting anticancer power from structure is not yet possible. The authors also discuss design strategies for raising selectivity and lowering toxicity.
europmc-pmc3791399:
Graeme Gowans, Simon Hawley, Fiona Ross, and D. Grahame Hardie reported a study in Cell Metabolism in 2013 on AMP-activated protein kinase, or AMPK. AMPK senses a cell's energy state and restores balance by switching on fuel-making paths and switching off fuel-using ones. A dispute had arisen over which molecule truly controls it in living cells, AMP or its relative ADP.

The team found that AMP is about ten times stronger than ADP at protecting the kinase's key activation site from being stripped. Only AMP boosted the site's phosphorylation by its upstream kinase, and AMP alone could raise activity more than tenfold at levels far below those of ATP. They also showed allosteric activation raising downstream targets in intact cells. The authors conclude AMP is the true physiological regulator.
europmc-pmc3895799:
Tatyana A. Shtam, Roman A. Kovalev, Elena Yu Varfolomeeva, Evgeny M. Makarov, Yury V. Kil, and Michael V. Filatov test exosomes as RNA carriers in Cell Communication and Signaling in 2013. Exosomes are tiny vesicles cells shed to send RNA to each other. Silencing RNA, siRNA, can switch off a chosen gene, but bare siRNA breaks down fast and crosses cell walls poorly.

The team loaded labeled siRNA into human exosomes from several sources by varied methods. Microscope and flow tests showed the vesicles handed the cargo to target cells. Two siRNAs aimed at DNA repair genes silenced their targets once delivered. One broke down its target protein and curbed cell growth as hoped. The study gives early proof that natural vesicles can ferry therapy RNA.
europmc-pmc3904699:
Christopher M. Shea, Sara R. Jacobs, Denise A. Esserman, Kerry Bruce, and Bryan J. Weiner test a readiness scale in Implementation Science, with the record dated 2014. Hospitals often fail to land new practices, and how ready an organization is for change is a prime suspect. No brief, sound measure of that readiness existed.

Their scale, ORIC, rests on a theory that splits readiness into commitment to a change and belief that the group can pull it off. Four studies check the scale: expert rating of its items, a lab simulation for structure and reliability, a group-level version built from pooled replies, and a small field test. The items held together as two clean factors. The authors offer the scale to leaders who need a readiness read before a rollout.
europmc-pmc3930499:
Francesca D. Frentiu and colleagues test virus-blocking mosquitoes caught in the field. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2014. Dengue is a widespread virus disease carried by the mosquito Aedes aegypti. That insect is hard to control by standard means. Mosquitoes that carry Wolbachia germs copy the virus poorly. Such mosquitoes were let loose in Cairns, Australia, as a living control tool.

The team caught some back and fed them blood with three dengue types. Field-caught carriers showed far lower rates of body infection than clean controls. Virus growth in them was low, and spread to the head was rare. The rates matched the first lab line of carriers. The germs sat in the same body tissues as in lab insects. The result backs the release plan.
europmc-pmc4114799:
Lindsay E. Nicolle, writing alone, reviewed urinary tract infections caused by indwelling catheters. Her review appeared in Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control in 2014. These infections are among the most common that patients pick up in health care facilities.

A slimy biofilm eventually forms on every catheter, so the main driver of bacteria in the urine is simply how long the device stays in. Few such cases become symptomatic, but catheter use is so frequent that the total burden is large. These infections source about a fifth of hospital-acquired bloodstream infections in acute care and over half in long-term care. The strongest defences are limiting catheter use and removing devices promptly. Lasting prevention, Nicolle argues, needs catheter materials that resist biofilm.
europmc-pmc4132299:
Tracy L. Tylka and colleagues compared two philosophies of care: judging health mainly by weight, or treating well-being as many-sided and fighting weight stigma. Their review appeared in the Journal of Obesity. The weight-normative approach centres weight loss; the weight-inclusive approach, seen in Health at Every Size models, targets health habits and access.

Data show weight-loss efforts fail for most people over time, and repeated regain cycles link to worse physical and mental health. A heavy focus on weight also fosters stigma, itself tied to harm. Inclusive programmes instead improved blood pressure, binge eating, and depression, and their messages were more acceptable. Judged ethically, the authors argue the inclusive approach does good and avoids harm, while the normative one does neither reliably.
europmc-pmc4141699:
Calum C. Bain and Allan McI. Mowat reviewed macrophages in the intestine, the body's largest pool of these immune cells. Their review appeared in Immunological Reviews in 2014. Gut macrophages keep peace with resident microbes and renewing tissue, yet they also fight infection and drive inflammatory bowel disease.

Sorting out their jobs was long hampered by the difficulty of telling similar cell populations apart. The authors explain how combined markers separate functionally distinct groups. Unlike most tissue macrophages, gut macrophages break the self-renewing embryo-derived pattern: blood monocytes constantly enter the mucosa and the local environment decides what they become. Knowing what drives their development in calm and inflamed states could open treatments, they argue.
europmc-pmc4179699:
Rachael D. Rubin, Neal J. Cohen, and two co-authors made a wide case for the hippocampus in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014. The hippocampus is best known for forming memories. The authors argue its real job is broader: building flexible mental maps of how things, places, and people relate to each other.

They gather evidence that hippocampal damage stiffens thinking across many tasks, from finding one's way and imagining new scenes to judging character, holding a conversation, and keeping social bonds. Standard tests tuned to the frontal lobes can miss these problems, yet real life constantly demands flexible use of what one knows. The review urges clinicians to test for such deficits in patients with hippocampal harm, since the costs show up most in daily life.
europmc-pmc4214299:
Suzanne Bialek-Davenet, Sylvain Brisse, and ten co-authors defined dangerous Klebsiella lineages by genome in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2014. Klebsiella pneumoniae causes hospital infections and, in some forms, severe liver abscesses caught in the community. Other forms resist nearly all antibiotics, and the fear is a strain that does both.

Older typing by seven housekeeping genes blurred the borders between lineages. Using whole genomes, the team drew sharp boundaries for the clonal groups, separating the highly virulent groups from the multidrug-resistant ones. They also built a free web database that pulls type, virulence, and resistance facts straight from a submitted genome sequence. The tool lets hospitals spot a high-risk clone fast and track its spread.
europmc-pmc4251899:
Martin C. Tammemägi, Christine D. Berg, and seven co-authors worked out who should get lung cancer screening in PLoS Medicine in 2014. CT screening cuts lung cancer deaths in heavy smokers, but programs picked candidates by simple age and smoking cut-offs, or by broader task force rules. A risk model might choose better, if a fair threshold could be set.

Applying the PLCOm2012 risk model to two large trial cohorts, the team found benefit was consistent above a six-year risk of about 1.5 percent. That rule screened 8.8 percent fewer people than the task force criteria yet caught 12.4 percent more cancers, with fewer false alarms. For never-smokers, no one in the large cohort crossed the threshold, so the authors advise against screening them for now.
europmc-pmc4300399:
Roberto Cecere, Geraint Rees, and Vincenzo Romei linked a classic sight and sound illusion to the speed of each person's brain waves. Their study appeared in Current Biology in 2015. When one flash comes with two quick beeps, people often see a second flash that never happened, because the senses bind events that fall close in time.

The brain's alpha rhythm cycles at a personal rate, and the authors reasoned that this rate sets the width of the binding window. Listeners with faster alpha fell for the illusion across a narrower span of beep timings. The result ties a basic feature of perception, how the brain fuses the senses into one moment, to a measurable rhythm that differs between people.
europmc-pmc4313599:
Patrick R Hannon and Jodi A Flaws review what phthalates, chemicals that soften plastic, do to the ovary. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology in 2015. Phthalates fill consumer goods, medical gear, and personal care products, so exposure through food, air, and skin is nearly universal, and several are classed as hormone disruptors.

Effects on male reproduction are better charted than on female reproduction, a gap the review works to close. Animal and cell studies show phthalates can disturb follicle growth, hormone output, and egg quality at several life stages, and women often carry higher exposure than men. The authors set out what is known, what is contested, and which studies are most needed.
europmc-pmc4316799:
Brian Tjaden presents Rockhopper 2, software that assembles bacterial transcriptomes from RNA sequencing reads without a reference genome. The paper appeared in Genome Biology in 2015, and Tjaden writes as sole author. Many bacteria have never had their genomes read, so their RNA data cannot be mapped onto a known template and must be pieced together from scratch.

The algorithms respect bacterial gene structure, which differs from the spliced genes of larger organisms that older assemblers assume. In tests the system beat other de novo assemblers on accuracy and speed for bacterial data. Released as open source, it also handles downstream steps such as finding transcript boundaries. The tool serves microbiologists working on unsequenced species.
europmc-pmc4320099:
Frank Szulzewsky and a large team profiled the immune cells that gather inside gliomas, the most aggressive brain tumors. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Microglia and macrophages flood these tumors yet fail to attack them and even help them grow, and glioblastoma patients survive only about a year on average.

Cells sorted from tumor bearing mouse brains had about a thousand genes turned up or down versus normal brain immune cells. Their profile matched neither the classic attack mode nor the classic repair mode of macrophages, but something in between with its own markers, notably high Gpnmb and Spp1. Naming this distinct state matters for therapies that hope to reprogram tumor immune cells.
europmc-pmc4369099:
Moran Cabili and colleagues mapped where long non-coding RNAs sit inside single human cells, in Genome Biology in 2015. These RNAs do not code for proteins, and many are thought to act in the cell nucleus, but few had been located directly. The team used a method that lights up single RNA molecules under a microscope. They measured 61 such RNAs in three cell types, counting each molecule and its position.

Patterns ranged from bright spots inside the nucleus to almost fully cytoplasmic spread. Low average levels did not come from a few jackpot cells expressing a lot; most cells held few copies. Nuclear spots dissolved during cell division and scattered, arguing against a bookmarking role. Sister RNAs read from the same DNA stretch as a partner gene did not always track that gene's output.
europmc-pmc4382699:
Hao Bin Wu, Bao Yu Xia, Le Yu, Xin-Yao Yu, and Xiong Wen Lou made a hydrogen-making catalyst inside a molecular scaffold, in Nature Communications in 2015. Splitting water with electricity is a clean route to hydrogen fuel, but the catalysts that speed the hydrogen side are often costly. Metal-organic frameworks are porous crystals with tunable structure that can serve as molds. The team grew a copper framework holding molybdenum-rich clusters, then heated it so carbon fused with the molybdenum in place.

The product was porous octahedron-shaped particles of molybdenum carbide, built from ultrafine crystals. As a catalyst it drove hydrogen production strongly from both acidic and alkaline solutions. Because the scaffold confines the reaction, particle size and shape stay controlled. The study offers design rules for making other nanostructured catalysts the same confined way.
europmc-pmc4383899:
Nikolay Kolesnikov and colleagues reported an ArrayExpress update focused on easier submissions, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. ArrayExpress, at the European Bioinformatics Institute, archives functional genomics data behind published studies, and most journals recommend it. By then it held data from more than 7,000 sequencing studies and 42,000 array studies, over 1.5 million assays in all. Sequencing submissions had doubled in 18 months, while array submissions still grew slowly.

All data use one tabular format that links cleanly to analysis tools. The headline change was Annotare, a new submission tool that cut average submission time almost threefold, soon to become the sole route in. Planned work included automating data flows and joining ArrayExpress more tightly with sister resources, so multi-layer studies can be stored and read as one.
europmc-pmc4399399:
Rong Kong and co-authors studied a long non-coding RNA in stomach cancer, in Molecular Cancer in 2015. Such RNAs regulate genes without making proteins, and PVT1 had been tied to cancer biology in other tissues. Its role in gastric cancer was largely unknown. The team measured PVT1 in 80 tumor samples and in cell lines, then lowered its level in cancer cells and in mice to watch the effects on growth.

Tumors with more PVT1 had invaded deeper and reached more advanced stages, and high PVT1 independently predicted shorter survival. Silencing PVT1 slowed cancer cell growth in dishes and in mice, partly by pausing the cell cycle. PVT1 partners with a silencing enzyme, EZH2, and that pairing is needed to shut down two brake genes, p15 and p16. PVT1 thus both marks poor outlook and drives growth.
europmc-pmc4410499:
Paul von Hippel exposed a bias in a popular meta-analysis statistic, in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2015. Meta-analyses pool studies whose effects differ partly by chance and partly by real heterogeneity. The statistic I-squared states what fraction of the spread is real. Small meta-analyses are common: the median Cochrane review has seven or fewer studies. Using exact calculations, von Hippel worked out the bias of I-squared when study counts are small.

The bias flips sign with the truth. With seven studies and no real heterogeneity, I-squared overstates it by about 12 percentage points on average. With 80 percent true heterogeneity, it understates by about 28 points. Those are large errors next to the median reported value of 21 percent. His advice is plain: in small meta-analyses, report a confidence interval rather than trusting the point estimate.
europmc-pmc4465199:
Swati Nigudkar and Alexei Demchenko surveyed progress in making sugar chains with exact shapes in Chemical Science in 2015. Sugars are the most abundant natural compounds and, attached to proteins, lipids, and drugs, they mediate immunity, fertilization, infection, cancer spread, and cell signaling. To study them, chemists must build sugar chains in the lab with the right link at each joint, including the tricky bent form called 1,2-cis.

The past decade brought new ways to control which shape forms when two sugars join, the step called glycosylation. The review gathers those methods, from specially designed donor sugars and catalysts to conditions that steer the reaction. Reliable control of this one link, the authors argue, has driven the wider field of synthetic carbohydrate chemistry and opened access to sugar structures once too hard to make.
europmc-pmc4469799:
Jack Bowden, George Davey Smith, and Stephen Burgess adapted a bias test for Mendelian randomization in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2015. The method uses gene variants as instruments to infer cause, and studies now use many variants at once for precision. Some variants, though, affect the outcome through other traits as well, a flaw called pleiotropy, which breaks their validity.

Viewing the variants as a small meta-analysis opens a fix. Bias from pleiotropy resembles the small-study bias familiar in meta-analysis, which Egger regression was built to detect, and a funnel plot can reveal it visually. The adapted Egger test still gives a valid check of no causal effect. Its slope estimates the true effect, even when every variant is invalid. That holds provided each variant's strength is independent of its side effect.
europmc-pmc4529699:
Serena Rubina Baglio leads an eleven-author team cataloging the small RNAs that human stem cells export, in Stem Cell Research & Therapy in 2015. Mesenchymal stem cells, found in bone marrow and fat, show promise for immune and degenerative diseases. Much of their healing effect seems to come from what they release, including exosomes, tiny sacs carrying small RNA pieces.

The team isolated exosomes from fat and marrow stem cells and read their full small RNA cargo by sequencing, checking cells and sacs side by side in repeat samples. The two cell sources carried highly similar profiles. The sacs were enriched in select microRNAs and transfer RNA pieces, a signature that could itself become a cell-free therapy.
europmc-pmc4557299:
Haotian Wang and seven co-authors forge better water-splitting catalysts from cheap metals, in Nature Communications in 2015. Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs catalysts for both halves of the reaction, ideally earth-abundant ones working in the same bath. Noble metals do the job but cost too much for scale.

Starting from iron, cobalt, and nickel oxide grains about 20 nanometers wide, the team used a lithium-driven conversion to shatter them into particles just 2 to 5 nanometers across, still wired together. The tiny nickel-iron oxide version drove full water splitting at 10 milliamps per square centimeter with only 1.51 volts, holding steady for over 200 hours. That beat the standard iridium-plus-platinum pairing.
europmc-pmc4618999:
Pavan K. Gupta and colleagues brought out a 2015 study identifying CD39 as a marker of worn-out killer T cells. In long-term viral infections, CD8 T cells gradually lose their fighting ability, a state called exhaustion. Clear markers would help find and maybe revive these cells. The work appeared in PLOS Pathogens and covered hepatitis C, HIV, and a mouse virus model.

T cells targeting hepatitis C or HIV carried high CD39, while those targeting two other viruses did not. CD39 sat alongside the known exhaustion marker PD-1 and matched the exhaustion gene pattern. Its level tracked viral load in patients. In mice, the highest CD39 group held the most deeply exhausted cells. The finding adds a tool for staging immune failure in chronic infection.
europmc-pmc4624599:
Marija Bogic, Anthony Njoku, and Stefan Priebe published a 2015 systematic review of long-term mental health in war refugees. Millions of displaced people stay in host countries for years, yet most research covers the early period. The review covered adults at least five years after displacement. Searches ran across five databases up to October 2014. The work appeared in the International Journal of Mental Health Systems.

Twenty-nine studies with 16,010 refugees qualified. Rates varied enormously between studies: depression from 2.3 to 80 percent, and post-traumatic stress from 4.4 to 86 percent, though most estimates sat at twenty percent or higher. Better-quality studies tended to report lower rates. The authors also examined factors before and after migration linked to illness, and they stress that study methods explain much of the spread.
europmc-pmc4643399:
Andrew D. Doyle and colleagues' 2015 study centres on how the local three-dimensional matrix around a cell steers its migration. Cells move through scaffolds of collagen fibres in the body. Two-dimensional lab surfaces miss much of that setting. The team built collagen gels with different fibre layouts. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

Gels with bundled fibres felt stiffer at adhesion sites and held adhesions steady. Loose, net-like gels let adhesions slip and retract. Migration needed the cell's pulling machinery matched to local stiffness; shutting down the motor protein myosin II stalled movement in all gels. Force was not needed to cluster adhesion receptors on natural collagen. Efficient movement, the authors argue, balances pulling strength against local matrix stiffness.
europmc-pmc4656699:
A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis by Melanie Lesinski and colleagues deals with balance training in healthy older adults. Balance practice improves posture control, but the dose needed for the best effect was unknown. They searched PubMed and Web of Science for randomised trials from 1985 to early 2015. The work appeared in Sports Medicine.

Of 345 articles screened, twenty-three trials in community-dwelling adults aged sixty-five or older met the rules. The authors pooled changes in balance test outcomes against passive controls. They also charted how training period, frequency, and session volume related to improvement. The resulting dose-response picture helps practitioners design balance programs that give older adults the largest safe gains in stability.
europmc-pmc4700099:
Dianne S. Schwarz and Michael D. Blower reviewed the endoplasmic reticulum in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2016. The ER is the cell's largest internal structure, a shifting network of tubes and sheets plus the envelope around the nucleus. It stores calcium, builds lipids, and makes and folds proteins. Distinct regions of the network handle distinct jobs. How those regions form, and how the whole structure reshapes itself when the cell's state changes, is the review's central puzzle.

The authors gather the proteins known to bend, join, and anchor ER membranes. They weigh what is understood about shape changes across the cell cycle, between cell types, and during development. Open questions get as much space as settled facts. Readers come away seeing the ER not as fixed furniture but as a responsive organelle whose form is itself a kind of regulation.
europmc-pmc4702899:
Robert Hubley, Robert D. Finn, Jody Clements, and five colleagues expanded the Dfam database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Much of many genomes is repetitive DNA, largely left by transposable elements, mobile sequences that copy themselves around. Dfam catalogs repeat families, each stored as an alignment plus a statistical profile model that can spot distant relatives of the family in new genomes. Better spotting matters because old copies fade as mutations pile up.

The new release holds 4,150 families, up from a human-only start, adding full known sets for mouse, zebrafish, fly, and nematode. Coverage improved and false hits were trimmed. The profile library plugs into the standard RepeatMasker tool, where it has already added large amounts of annotation to the human genome. Seed alignments and hit lists are free to download. The update strengthens the base layer on which genome annotation stands.
europmc-pmc4729899:
Nataliya Petryk, Malik Kahli, Yves d'Aubenton-Carafa, and six colleagues mapped where human DNA replication starts and stops, in Nature Communications in 2016. Each cell cycle, copying must begin at many origins and end cleanly between them, yet origin maps from earlier methods disagreed wildly. The team purified Okazaki fragments, the short pieces made on one strand during copying, from two cell types and sequenced them deeply. Strand counts revealed which direction forks traveled everywhere in the genome.

Copying starts at random points inside broad zones, often beside active genes and open chromatin, and ends scattered between zones. Forks mostly travel the same way genes are read, avoiding head-on collisions. Start zones frequently touch chromosome folding domains and carry marks of gene enhancers. The map gives the clearest genome-wide picture yet of a process every cell performs, and shows how chromatin and transcription choreograph it.
europmc-pmc4807699:
Philip C. Haycock and five co-authors lay out best practice for Mendelian randomization studies in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2016. The method uses genes as natural experiments: since gene variants are dealt at conception, they escape the reversed cause and tangled factors that plague diet and lifestyle studies. Done well, it can test whether a risk factor truly causes a disease.

Done poorly, it misleads, and the authors stress its assumptions and failure modes. New two-sample designs, in which exposure and outcome come from separate groups, plus open data from huge gene consortia, are making the method routine. The paper walks through design, analysis, and honest reading of results. It closes by rating the method a cheap way to rank targets for prevention trials.
europmc-pmc4832199:
Jie-Zhi Cheng leads nine authors in Scientific Reports in 2016 testing deep learning for medical image diagnosis. Computer aids that judge whether a lump is cancer usually chain hand-built image steps, and errors in outlining the lump or in the chosen features drag accuracy down. The team instead fed images to a stacked denoising auto-encoder, a deep network that learns its own features and shrugs off noise.

They tested it on two jobs: breast lumps in ultrasound and lung nodules in CT scans. Against two leading conventional systems, in repeated cross-checks, the deep system won by a clear margin on both. The authors argue the result could change how diagnosis aids are built: learn the features from data rather than hand-design them for each scan type.
europmc-pmc4863499:
Sarmiza V. Bădescu and co-authors reviewed the two-way link between diabetes and depression in 2016. Depression occurs two to three times more often in people with diabetes than in others, and most cases go undiagnosed. Shared roots may include long stress, hormone axis strain, and inflammation, which feed both the mood disorder and blood sugar failure.

Each illness worsens the other: depression erodes self-care, while diabetes burden deepens low mood. Screening diabetic patients for depression, with standard scales, is the review's central plea. Treating both together improves outcomes for each. Diabetes specialists who know the overlap, the review argues, can catch hidden cases early.
europmc-pmc4876999:
Kylie Anderson, Oliver Burford, and Lynne Emmerton studied how people use health apps for self-care in 2016, through interviews in Perth, Australia. Adults are living longer with chronic illness, and self-care apps multiply fast. Yet little was known about how users actually engage with self-monitoring apps. Adults who used any health or fitness app for tracking were interviewed in depth.

Users valued easy logging, clear feedback, and a sense of control over their health. Clunky entry, poor fit with daily life, and weak links to care staff dulled use. Suggested fixes include simpler design and better tailoring. Hearing users first, the study argues, is how apps earn a lasting place in self-care.
europmc-pmc4880799:
Anton Goloborodko, John F. Marko, and Leonid A. Mirny tested in 2016 whether chromosomes pack by active loop extrusion. At cell division, chromosomes shorten more than a hundredfold into stacked loops of about 100,000 DNA letters each. The packing machine was unknown. The team modeled protein factors that grab DNA and reel it in, growing a loop as they go.
