Simulations plus an exact math model found two stable states. In the sparse state, loops churn fast and pack little. In the dense state, loops hold steady and length crashes down, matching real chromosomes. How many machines load, and how long they stay, picks the state. The model gives experiments a sharp target to test.
europmc-pmc4886099:
Lisa Whitehead and Philip Seaton reviewed phone and tablet apps for self-care of long-term illness in 2016. Chronic disease burdens patients and health systems, and guidelines urge self-management programs, yet research programs often fail to stick in routine care. Cheap, handy apps might carry such programs into daily life. The review searched major databases for trials of symptom self-care apps.

Proof so far is early and mixed, with small studies and short follow-ups, but apps show real promise for better symptom control. Design quality and fit with care teams vary widely. Stronger, longer trials are the clear next step. The review maps a young field at the point where hope must meet hard testing.
europmc-pmc4951199:
Nicholas J. Sofroniew, Daniel Flickinger, Jonathan King, and Karel Svoboda build a two-photon mesoscope that images wide brain areas at single cell sharpness. Their paper appeared in eLife in 2016. Standard microscopes that resolve single cells see less than a millimeter at a time. Wide field microscopes cover more ground but blur cells, above all in depth. Their instrument, the 2p-RAM, scans a volume 5 millimeters wide and 1 millimeter deep, spanning several brain areas at once.

Resolution stays near the diffraction limit across that volume. A fast three dimensional scanner samples chosen spots efficiently, skipping empty space. The team used it in living mice that express calcium sensors in neurons. They recorded activity in several separate brain areas at the same time in the same animal. The authors offer the design for studies of how distant brain regions act together, a question small view tools cannot reach.
europmc-pmc4967299:
Martin Prince and five co-authors review global trends in dementia rates and survival. Their systematic review appeared in Alzheimer's Research and Therapy in 2016. Forecasts of a dementia epidemic assume that age specific rates stay flat and population aging alone drives growth. The team searched for studies since 1980 that tracked prevalence, incidence, or death among people with dementia over time.

They found nine prevalence studies, eight incidence studies, and four mortality studies. Incidence may be falling in high income countries, the evidence moderately suggests. Prevalence findings clashed across studies with no clear overall direction. Longer survival could offset falling incidence, but death trends were barely studied. Rising prevalence in East Asia stood out. The authors advise policymakers to treat forecasts with caution and not to lean on single studies.
europmc-pmc4989499:
Li-Fang Chu and nine co-authors use single cell RNA sequencing to find regulators of early human development. Their study appeared in Genome Biology in 2016. Human embryonic stem cells can become any cell type, but how single cells leave the pluripotent state was murky. The team sequenced RNA from more than seventeen hundred single cells. The set held stem cells, their lineage specific descendants, and cells caught mid transition toward definitive endoderm. That layer later forms gut and liver.

They found a gene signature for definitive endoderm and a time window when low oxygen boosts its formation. Two new tools traced stage specific genes and rebuilt the path from pluripotency through mesendoderm to endoderm. Cells on the way could be spotted by their markers. New regulators found in that window changed differentiation when tested. The authors offer the map as a guide to steering stem cells.
europmc-pmc4991899:
Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs, and Ron Milo recount the cells in a human body, human and bacterial. Their study appeared in PLoS Biology in 2016. Textbook claims put bacteria at ten times the human cell count, a ratio traced to a rough old estimate. The team rebuilt both counts from current data for a reference man of seventy kilograms. Blood cells dominate the human side, making up about ninety percent of the total.

Their revised counts land near three times ten to the thirteenth power for each side: bacteria and human cells are roughly equal in number. Together the bacteria weigh only about a fifth of a kilogram. The authors show each step of the arithmetic so others can update it. They present the one to one ratio as a better starting fact for microbiome science than the famous ten to one slogan.
europmc-pmc5082599:
Paula Mulvenna and a large trial team report the QUARTZ trial in The Lancet in 2016, on brain metastases from lung cancer. Whole brain radiotherapy plus the steroid dexamethasone was standard for patients unfit for surgery or focused radiation, yet no trial had shown it lengthens life or improves its quality. Across 69 UK and three Australian centres, patients were randomized to supportive care with dexamethasone, with or without whole brain radiotherapy.

The main measure was quality-adjusted life-years, built from survival and weekly patient questionnaires. Quality of life showed no evidence of difference between the two strategies, and detailed symptom records found only small gaps, with radiotherapy adding drowsiness, hair loss, nausea, and scalp irritation. For this frail group, the results question routine whole brain radiotherapy. The authors note their quality-of-life tool was general rather than brain-specific, a stated limit of the trial.
europmc-pmc509299:
Rick S. Mitchell and seven co-authors compared where three retroviruses insert their DNA into human cells, reporting in PLoS Biology in 2004. They gathered 3,127 insertion sites for viruses drawn from HIV, a bird virus called ASLV, and a mouse virus called MLV, and matched the sites against gene activity in the infected cells.

HIV-based inserts strongly favored active genes, and the pattern shifted a little with the type of cell, following which genes that tissue had switched on. MLV inserts clustered near the start points of genes, while ASLV showed only a faint pull toward active genes. The team reads the contrast as a sign that each virus's own machinery reads different marks on the host's chromosomes when it picks a landing spot.
europmc-pmc5183899:
A review in The British and Foreign Medico-Chirurgical Review, dated 1865 in the hosted text, compares two books on spinal curvature. One holds William Adams's lectures, delivered in 1860-61 and published in 1865. The other is Bernard Brodhurst's Curvatures of the Spine, a rewritten second edition of 1864. Both men worked at the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital.

The reviewer treats Brodhurst first: his 93-page sketch is clear and interesting but, unusually, too short; thirty-one illustrations leave little reading, though doubling the book would have helped. It opens with the spine's normal curves, then treats forward, backward, and lateral curvatures, the lateral by far the fullest. Adams's 334 pages get the longer discussion the reviewer promises, and both authors are credited with spreading sound views in a young surgical specialty.
europmc-pmc518999:
Paul D. N. Hebert, Mark Y. Stoeckle, Tyler S. Zemlak, and Charles M. Francis test DNA barcoding on birds. Their marker is a 648-base-pair stretch of the mitochondrial gene cytochrome c oxidase I, known as COI. They built barcodes for 260 species of North American birds, a group that is large and well studied. Every species carried a distinct barcode. Differences between close relatives averaged 18 times the differences found within a species.

The results also flagged four probable new species hiding inside named ones. The authors propose a screening threshold of ten times the average within-species difference to speed the discovery of unrecognized species. They argue for a public library of barcodes tied to named specimens. As sequencing grows faster and cheaper, they suggest, such a library could become a master key for identifying animal species.
europmc-pmc520599:
Teresa A. Venezia and six co-authors chart the gene activity of blood stem cells as they wake and rest again. Adult hematopoietic stem cells sit mostly quiescent, yet one cell can rebuild the blood of many recipients. The team pushed stem cells to proliferate in living animals, then let them return to rest, measuring gene expression across the cycle. They compared these profiles with the natural contrast between dividing fetal stem cells and quiet adult ones.

The signatures resolve into stages: a poised readiness, a preparative phase, early and late proliferation, then a return marked by changes in migration molecules. Two genes rose in both message and protein during activation, offering candidate markers for dividing stem cells. The authors offer their model of the activation cycle as a guide for expanding stem cells for therapy, and note its possible echo in cancer stem cells.
europmc-pmc5263899:
Alexander Goodall read a case of acute myelocythaemia in an infant to the Edinburgh Medico-Chirurgical Society on May 1, 1912, printed in the Edinburgh Medical Journal. The patient, a girl of ten weeks admitted to the Royal Hospital for Sick Children on March 12, 1912, came in with nose bleeding and diarrhoea. She was the seventh child of healthy parents, breastfed, and well until three weeks before, when her colour worsened and bleeding began.

On admission she looked like a baby of four weeks: pale, wasted, with blood oozing thinly from her nostrils and from raw patches on her buttocks. Spots of bleeding dotted her trunk and limbs, small ulcers marked her tongue, and her liver was enlarged, while vomiting of blood had started two days earlier. The title's unusual features join the blood disease to hardening of bone, osteosclerosis, remarkable in so young a child.
europmc-pmc5394399:
Pedro M. Aponte and Andrés Caicedo review stemness in cancer in a 2017 paper in Stem Cells International. Stemness is the power of a cell to keep its line going, make mature cell types, and swap rest for growth as its setting demands. Normal adult stem cells use that power to keep tissues sound. The authors argue that a small set of cancer stem cells uses the same power for harm.

Cancer stem cells can drive tumor growth, work with their surroundings to find survival factors, and live through treatment to restart the disease. The review maps the niche that shelters them, including support cells that feed the niche. It ends with treatment ideas that strike these stem traits and with new lab tools for studying them.
europmc-pmc5487399:
Bi and Tian present a review in Frontiers in Immunology on natural killer cell exhaustion. NK cells are front-line immune killers of tumors and infected cells. In cancers and long infections, they often lose their punch. Output of key signals drops, and killing power fades. Several suppressive routes drive that decline.

Faulty receptor signals on the NK cells play a part. So do regulatory cells and soluble factors around them. The review maps the traits that mark an exhausted NK cell. It also covers attempts to reverse the state. Restoring NK vigor could open fresh immunotherapy targets, they argue.
europmc-pmc5487899:
Siliakus, van der Oost, and Kengen present a review in Extremophiles on microbe membranes in harsh settings. Bacteria and archaea shield their cells with lipid membranes. Heat, acidity, and pressure can all damage that shield. Each group must adjust its membrane lipids fast to survive. Their core lipids differ sharply in chemical structure.

The review compares the tricks each domain uses to retune fluidity. Some tricks are unique to one domain, while others are shared. Shared tricks cluster near the growth limits of bacteria, they note. Membrane-spanning ether lipids and methyl branches track those limits closely. The survey links membrane chemistry to the edges of life.
europmc-pmc5488299:
Lämke and Bäurle present a review in Genome Biology on plant stress memory. Plants face repeated drought, heat, and attack during their lives. Past stress can prime a faster, stronger response next time. Chemical marks on chromatin and DNA may store that memory. The authors review the evidence in the model plant Arabidopsis.

Marks covered include DNA methylation, histone changes, and nucleosome shifts. The review separates memory within one plant's life from memory passed to offspring. Some marks fade fast, while others persist across generations. The authors stress that hard molecular proof is still rare. Tapping this memory could help breed tougher crops, they suggest.
europmc-pmc5506099:
Gæde and co-authors report a long follow-up study in Diabetologia. It extends the Steno-2 trial in type 2 diabetes. The trial enrolled 160 patients who also leaked protein in their urine. Half got intensive care aimed at many risk factors at once. The rest got standard care for about eight years. All were then tracked for over 21 years in total.

Deaths numbered 38 in the intensive group against 55 on standard care, they report. Intensive patients lived a median of 7.9 years longer. Their first heart or vessel event came 8.1 years later too. Most small-vessel complications also fell. The gains matched the extra years free of heart disease.
europmc-pmc5517399:
Herr, Bode, and Duerschmied present a review in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine on serotonin in immune cells. Serotonin is famed as a brain signal, but most of it rides in blood platelets. Platelets dump it at clots and inflamed sites. Nearly every immune cell carries some serotonin machinery. That reach gives the chemical a hand in immune control.

In macrophages, serotonin tunes which cytokines get released, they report. It can damp output of two strong inflammatory signals. It also helps recruit neutrophils and activate T cells. The review sorts these effects by cell type and receptor. Platelet serotonin looks like the main immune source.
europmc-pmc5529999:
Hayashi presents a review in Chemical Science on pot economy in organic synthesis. Making a target molecule usually takes many separate steps. Each step needs its own vessel, workup, and purification. One-pot synthesis runs several steps in a single vessel instead. Waste drops, time shrinks, and handling simplifies. Robinson's tropinone synthesis showed the trick a century ago.

The review sorts the vocabulary: domino, cascade, and tandem reactions. It sets pot economy beside atom, step, and redox economy as design ideals. Organocatalysts shine in this format, the author argues. Worked examples from his own lab show the criteria for success.
europmc-pmc5542299:
Deslouches and Di review antimicrobial peptides as possible cancer drugs in Oncotarget. Cancer drugs often fail two ways. Tumors learn to resist them, and they poison healthy fast-growing cells. Peptides that kill bacteria may dodge both flaws.

These peptides carry a positive charge and a split water-loving, water-hating shape. They stick to negatively charged cell surfaces. Bacterial surfaces carry such charges in plenty. Cancer cells expose more of one charged lipid than normal cells do. That gap could let the peptides hit tumors while sparing healthy tissue. Since binding needs no exact receptor, resistance may be slow to arise. The review centers on how these peptides kill. Readers get the case for a cheap, selective drug class.
europmc-pmc5549999:
Eastman and co-authors present a software article in PLOS Computational Biology. They describe OpenMM 7, a toolkit for molecular dynamics. Such software simulates how molecules move over time. Most rival packages are hard to extend with new methods.

OpenMM was built so users can add features with ease. New forces or step methods can be stated as math, with little code. Added features then run on both CPUs and graphics cards without extra work. They need no change to OpenMM itself and can be shared on their own. Readers learn how the design speeds method research and spreads new tools fast.
europmc-pmc5597799:
D'Agostino and co-authors report a consensus project in RMD Open. Ultrasound can spot joint inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis better than a physical exam. Yet experts scored scans in clashing ways. The EULAR-OMERACT task force set out to build one shared system.

First, they measured how much sonographers agreed at baseline. Agreement swung widely, above all on live patient scans. Grey-scale scoring varied more than power Doppler scoring. A Delphi round then settled shared definitions. Synovitis now needs both pale tissue growth and a Doppler signal. Severity blends the signal amount with the tissue volume and look. The parts can also be scored on their own. More testing must come before trial use. Readers get the agreed yardstick itself.
europmc-pmc5742599:
Bousfiha and co-authors present the 2017 IUIS phenotypic classification for primary immunodeficiencies. These inborn errors of immunity now number 320 single gene faults. Their effects range from infection to allergy and autoimmunity. A full catalog exists, but it is hard to use at the bedside.

This version sorts disorders by how they show up in patients. Nine main groups each get an algorithm and a color code. Disease names, genes, and inheritance patterns are shown in a set format. The scheme builds on the companion 2017 IUIS report. It aims to help clinicians match a patient to a likely fault.
europmc-pmc5758799:
Larraufie and co-authors study how gut fatty acids affect a hunger hormone in human gut cells. Short chain fatty acids form when gut bacteria ferment fiber. Peptide YY, or PYY, curbs food intake and is made low in the gut. The team used a human cell line and primary gut cultures.

Propionate and butyrate strongly raised PYY output, they report. The same acids did not raise the related gene GCG. Most of the effect came from blocking histone deacetylases. A smaller part came through the FFA2 receptor. Mouse cultures showed no such effect, a species gap the authors stress.
europmc-pmc5758899:
Cheng and co-authors review molecular testing for BRAF mutations in melanoma care. About half of advanced melanomas carry a BRAF mutation. The V600E form is the most common one. Drugs that block BRAF and MEK help those patients a lot.

The review sets out the main test methods in use. DNA based companion tests and lab built DNA and protein tests all get weighed. Tumors can differ between the first site and spread sites. Resistance to paired BRAF and MEK drugs also grows over time. The authors aim to help doctors read test results in that full context.
europmc-pmc5802499:
Bunea and co-authors pool studies on early hardship and stress hormones. Hardship in childhood raises the risk of later mental illness. One proposed link is a changed stress system. The team tests how cortisol reacts to social stress.

Their meta-analysis covers 30 data sets and 4,292 people of varied ages. Overall, early hardship linked to a blunted cortisol response. The effect was larger at peak and during recovery. It was also stronger for maltreatment and for adults. Readers get firm evidence that early stress can dull the body's stress signal for life.
europmc-pmc5844999:
Agostini and co-authors probe how remdesivir defeats coronaviruses, and how the viruses fight back. Their study appeared in mBio. No approved drug yet targets this virus family. Remdesivir blocks the viral polymerase that copies its genome.

The drug held potency against SARS, MERS, and a mouse coronavirus. Forced evolution bred resistant mutants in the polymerase gene. Resistance topped out near sixfold and cost the virus dearly. Resistant SARS virus sickened mice less. Viruses missing their proofreading enzyme fell even harder. Higher, still safe doses overcame the resistance in tests.
europmc-pmc5849599:
George and co-authors sort large-cell neuroendocrine lung tumors into two molecular families. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. These aggressive cancers resemble small cell lung cancer yet respond worse to its drugs. The team profiled the genes and transcripts of 75 tumors.

One family pairs broken TP53 with STK11 or KEAP1 damage. The other knocks out TP53 and RB1 together. Both families cluster apart from other lung cancers on gene activity. The second family dims its neuroendocrine markers and stirs immune pathways. Splitting the disease this way could guide targeted treatment.
europmc-pmc5850899:
Phi and co-authors review cancer stem cells, the stubborn minority blamed for drug resistance and relapse. Their review appeared in Stem Cells International. These cells renew themselves like true stem cells. They also spawn the varied cell types of a tumor.

Ordinary chemotherapy kills dividing cells in bulk. Stem-like cells slip through by lying dormant. They pump drugs out and ride survival pathways. Stress responses like epithelial-mesenchymal transition harden them further. Relapse then grows from the survivors left behind. The authors survey therapies aimed squarely at this root population.
europmc-pmc5872399:
Fan and Fan review how alveolar macrophage death drives lung inflammation. Their article appeared in Respiratory Research. These macrophages form about 95 percent of airspace immune cells. Acute lung injury can follow sepsis, trauma, or major surgery. Lung and body-wide inflammation feed each other in a cycle. Dying macrophages influence other immune cells around them. That influence can push inflammation toward severe disease.

The review covers forms of regulated cell death. Apoptosis stays quiet, while pyroptosis and necroptosis inflame tissue. The authors explain signals that control each pathway. They also trace how cell death worsens lung injury. Drugs that steer macrophage death could treat these syndromes. That prospect anchors the review's closing outlook.
europmc-pmc5919599:
Baio and co-authors report autism prevalence among eight-year-olds in the United States for 2014. Their surveillance report appeared in MMWR Surveillance Summaries. The monitoring network covered 11 sites across the country. Trained staff reviewed health and school records in depth. Clinicians then judged each case against standard criteria. The method has run for years in the same network.

Prevalence reached 16.8 per 1,000 children, they report. That equals about one in 59 children. The figure was higher than earlier network estimates. Rates and traits varied across the sites studied. The report gives a baseline for services and policy. It also notes that newer diagnostic rules had just changed.
europmc-pmc5923499:
Moye and co-authors review bacteriophage use in food production and processing. Their review appeared in Viruses. Foodborne illness still causes vast harm worldwide. Standard cleaning methods can damage taste or gear. They also kill helpful bacteria along with harmful ones. Phages offer a targeted, natural alternative.

Lytic phages attack only their target bacteria, the authors report. Studies cover deli meats, fruit, and vegetables. Approved phage products for food safety are growing in number. Challenges remain in coverage and public acceptance. The method spares the normal food flora. Readers get a survey of results and products.
europmc-pmc5934999:
Mandolesi and co-authors review the effects of physical exercise on cognition and wellbeing. Their concise review appeared in Frontiers in Psychology. Exercise acts as a strong gene modulator, the authors note. It brings structural and functional changes in the brain. It also protects against neurodegeneration. How that protection works is still not fully clear.

The review covers work in animals and humans on brain plasticity. It also covers epigenetic mechanisms behind the gains. Biological and psychological effects are treated together, since they shape each other. The authors explain how to gain the most from exercise. They also warn about harm, as in exercise addiction.
europmc-pmc5948099:
Kivimäki and a large team of co-authors examine body mass index and dementia risk across many cohorts. Their analysis appeared in Alzheimer's & Dementia. Higher midlife BMI is often said to raise dementia risk. But weight loss before diagnosis can mask such effects. The team pooled individual data from 39 cohort studies. In all, 1,349,857 dementia-free participants were included.

Higher BMI looked protective when measured within ten years of diagnosis, they report. The hazard ratio per five-unit BMI rise was 0.71 there. Measured over twenty years before diagnosis, higher BMI raised risk instead. The ratio then reached 1.16. Two processes seem to mix: real harm and reverse causation.
europmc-pmc5972399:
Li and co-authors expand base editing in rice and wheat with a Cas9-adenosine deaminase fusion. Their study appeared in Genome Biology. Plant base editors could only convert cytosine to thymine before. The new editor swaps adenine-thymine pairs to guanine-cytosine. It joins an evolved tRNA adenosine deaminase to a Cas9 nickase. Rates reached 7.5 percent in protoplasts, they report.

In regenerated rice and wheat plants, rates reached 59.1 percent. The team also edited an endogenous gene directly. A gain-of-function point change made a herbicide-tolerant rice plant. All base pairs can now be edited precisely in plants. That widens the toolbox for crop research.
europmc-pmc5975699:
Wittich and co-authors test whether location and date can shortlist plant taxa for field identification. Their study appeared in BMC Bioinformatics. Naming a plant is slowed by the huge number of candidates. A ranked shortlist of likely taxa could speed the task. The team used Germany as a case study. They drew on 7.62 million records for 2,700 plant taxa.

They compared presence-absence data with single occurrence records. Flickr images with labels served as an independent test set. Presence data alone gave an average recall of 82 percent. Both sources together reached 96 percent, they report. Candidate lists shrank by 62 percent on average.
europmc-pmc5993799:
Blancon and a large team of co-authors set out a scaling law for excitons in two-dimensional perovskite quantum wells. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. These layered halide perovskites are tuned by changing layer thickness. Whether their light resonances are excitons or free carriers was debated. Exciton mass and binding energy across thicknesses were also unknown. The team used optical spectroscopy and 60-tesla magneto-absorption. Modelling backed the measurements.

The resonances come from tightly bound excitons, they show. Exciton binding energy fell from 470 to 125 millielectronvolts as layers thickened. Reduced mass fell as well over the same range. Their scaling law predicts binding energy for any thickness.
europmc-pmc6048199:
Salem and co-authors review the gut microbiome as a regulator of skin health. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Gut and skin share immune and nerve roles. Evidence now links gut health to skin balance. Gut microbes may shape several skin diseases.

The review explains how gut microbes talk to skin. They influence skin growth and surface protein formation. They also tune immune responses in the skin. Three common disorders get detailed coverage. Acne, atopic dermatitis, and psoriasis all appear. Probiotic supplements are weighed as a control route. Readers get a tour of the gut-skin axis. It offers a fresh angle on stubborn skin conditions.
europmc-pmc6137099:
Ruytinx and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Immunology on chemokines and macrophage forms. Macrophages are immune cells that shift shape and role with their setting. Old labels split them into M1 and M2 types. That split is now seen as too simple. Real cells fall along a spectrum between the two.

The review focuses on chemokines, signals that guide immune cells. It asks how these signals push macrophages toward each form. Cases include obesity, cancer, and clogged arteries. In tumors, shifted macrophages can help the cancer grow. Readers get a nuanced view of cell types that resist neat labels.
europmc-pmc6152299:
Mokoena wrote a mini-review in Molecules on lactic acid bacteria and the antimicrobial proteins they make, called bacteriocins. Such bacteria are already used to preserve food, partly because they kill other microbes. Urinary tract infections are a global problem, mainly for women and people with diabetes. Many urinary pathogens now resist common antibiotics.

The review sorts bacteriocins by class and explains how they are built. It then reviews studies of lactic acid bacteria against uropathogens. Mokoena stresses that candidate strains must be chosen with care and delivered the right way. The work weighs a possible antibiotic alternative for a very common infection.
europmc-pmc6223899:
Sirelkhatim and co-authors review zinc oxide nanoparticles against bacteria. These tiny particles draw wide interest. Their small size gives a large surface area. That raises surface reactivity and antibacterial power. The review appeared in Nano-Micro Letters.

The authors cover test methods for antibacterial action. They review the impact of UV light. Particle size, dose, shape, and defects all matter. Surface changes also alter the effect. A key mechanism is release of reactive oxygen species. These species damage bacterial cell walls. They raise membrane leakiness and let particles inside. Dissolved zinc ions add toxicity. Together these effects stop growth and kill cells. Safety limits are also discussed.
europmc-pmc6269599:
Parker and co-authors ran the STAMPEDE trial on prostate radiation in spread prostate cancer. Their trial report appeared in The Lancet. Standard care was hormone therapy for life. The trial asked whether adding radiation to the prostate itself helped men live longer. Benefit was expected to be largest in men with a low spread burden. The trial ran at 117 hospitals in the United Kingdom and Switzerland.

Over 2,000 men were assigned at random to standard care alone or with radiation. Radiation clearly lengthened the time before treatment failed. It did not lengthen overall life in the full group. Side effects were modest, with severe events in about five percent during treatment. Groups had similar rates of severe events overall. The results guide which men should get prostate radiation after spread. Subgroup tests by spread burden were built into the design.
europmc-pmc6306799:
Herold and co-authors review brain imaging methods in exercise and cognition research. Their systematic review appeared in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. The tool under study is functional near-infrared spectroscopy, or fNIRS. It tracks oxygen levels in the brain without surgery. Active brains need steady oxygen and blood flow. Exercise can change both.

The team examined methods in 35 relevant papers. Practices varied widely across the field. No standard routine exists for setup or analysis. The review sets out clear recommendations. These cover how to run, process, and report fNIRS studies. Cleaner methods should sharpen future exercise-cognition work.
europmc-pmc6331599:
Chen and co-authors show how a hormone-like signal lets nerves govern bone growth. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The signal is prostaglandin E2, made by bone-forming cells. When bone density drops, its output rises. The team asked whether sensory nerves read that change. Those nerves carry a receptor for the signal, EP4.

Removing EP4 from sensory nerves lowered bone volume in mice. Cutting the nerves harmed the skeleton as well. Blocking the signal's source in bone cells did the same. The path runs through the brain to the sympathetic system. Lower sympathetic tone then lets bone formation rise. A drug that raised local levels boosted bone growth. That boost vanished without nerve EP4. The loop suggests new routes to treat bone loss.
europmc-pmc6332599:
Jeong and co-authors review calcium phosphate materials for bone repair. Their review appeared in Biomaterials Research. Bone rebuilds through complex, staged biology. Calcium phosphates occur naturally in bone itself. That makes them natural candidates for repair materials. Studies use them alone and with other materials.

These materials can guide new bone along their surface. Some forms can even spark bone formation directly. They release calcium and phosphorus ions as they sit. Those ions switch bone-building and bone-eating cells on. Surface texture and pore design matter as well. They steer cell attachment and mineral growth. Types such as HAP and TCP differ in solubility and strength. Mixing types lets designers balance those traits. The review maps uses across bone regeneration.
europmc-pmc6341099:
Kang and co-authors probe how lignin grips plant wall sugars. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Lignin is a tough aromatic polymer in wood. It stiffens cell walls and seals water channels. Removing it is key to paper and biofuel making. Yet how it touches other wall parts was unclear.

The team used solid-state NMR on intact maize stems. A signal-boosting method sharpened the data. They found lignin clumps into hydrophobic nanodomains. Those domains pressed widely against xylan, a wall sugar. Lignin favored xylans with a loose helical shape. Those xylans sit away from cellulose fibers. The contacts are partly electrostatic in nature. Knowing them may help re-engineer wood for easier use.
europmc-pmc6375899:
Liu and co-authors review NMDA receptors in Alzheimer's disease, writing in Frontiers in Neuroscience. These receptors help brain cells talk at synapses and support memory. Early in the disease, clumps of amyloid-beta protein disturb them.

Too much receptor activity can depress synapses and remove their spines. The drug memantine blocks the receptor lightly and treats moderate to severe cases. The review covers changes in receptor subunits and odd modes of receptor action. It also weighs how receptor failure links to memory loss. Clearer proof of these links could guide better drugs.
europmc-pmc6392299:
Kato and co-authors report a mouse study in PLoS ONE on a paired cancer treatment. Lenvatinib blocks signals that feed tumor blood vessels. The team asked whether it also changes the immune setting inside tumors, helping PD-1 blockade work better.

Given together, the drugs raised CD8 T cell activity in tumors. Tumor-linked macrophages, which calm immune attack, became fewer. Interferon pathways, which drive immune attack, switched on. Single-cell and tissue tests backed those shifts. The authors present the pair as more than the sum of its parts. The work supports trials of the combination in patients.
europmc-pmc6433899:
Degenhardt and co-authors compare methods for selecting variables in random forest models built on omics data, where measured features dwarf the number of patients. A study may want the smallest set that predicts well, or every variable truly involved so pathways can be traced. Those goals call for different selection tools.

Six procedures, including the Boruta algorithm, the Vita method, and recursive feature elimination, faced simulated data plus real methylation and gene expression sets. Boruta proved most powerful, with Vita close behind and sturdier when no real signal existed. Vita also ran much faster and held up slightly better on real data, making it the pick for very large sets.
europmc-pmc6450999:
Smits and co-authors grow midbrain-like organoids to model Parkinson's disease in 3D form, a step up from flat cell dishes that miss tissue layout. Starting from self-copying starter cells of the midbrain floor plate, the organoids form neurons that make and release dopamine, much like the human midbrain zone the disease destroys.

Organoids grown from patients with the LRRK2-G2019S mutation showed fewer and simpler dopamine neurons under machine image checks. The marker FOXA2, needed to build those neurons, rose in patient organoids, hinting at an early growth defect behind the loss. A steady protocol gives researchers human tissue in a dish for testing causes and candidate drugs.
europmc-pmc6461899:
Rosado and co-authors test whether dosing corals with beneficial native bacteria can blunt bleaching, the heat-driven collapse devastating reefs. No field treatment existed for bleaching or coral disease, so the team borrowed the probiotic idea from human and plant health. Their consortium came from the coral Pocillopora damicornis and its surrounding seawater: five Pseudoalteromonas strains plus Halomonas and Cobetia relatives.

Aquarium corals faced 26 or 30 degrees, with or without a Vibrio pathogen. Dosed corals bleached significantly less, keeping more photopigment and higher photosynthetic efficiency, especially under pathogen challenge. Their microbiomes shifted in step, with Cobetia marking the protected state. Field trials are the implied next step.
europmc-pmc6465999:
Basnet and co-authors review zebrafish larvae as a high-throughput behavioral model for screening neuroactive drugs. Larvae develop a swim bladder by four days after fertilization and settle into clear swimming patterns that differ between light and dark. Automated tracking can now catch subtle changes that human observers miss.

The fish bring practical gifts: external fertilization, transparency, small size, and low cost, with 84 percent of human disease-linked genes having zebrafish counterparts. The light-dark locomotion test anchors the review, with drug examples from stimulants to metal nanoparticles that shifted activity in condition-specific ways. Anxiety, learning, and social repertoires widen the model's reach into psychiatric research.
europmc-pmc6482399:
Zhou and co-authors build and validate the MAUQ, a questionnaire for judging whether a mobile health app is actually usable. General instruments like the SUS and PSSUQ were not written for health apps, and home-made questionnaires litter the field unvalidated. The team drafted items from existing tools and tested them against two real apps, one interactive and one standalone.

Responses from 128 participants resolved into three subscales, ease of use and satisfaction, system information arrangement, and usefulness, across 21 items with an overall reliability coefficient of 0.932. Scores tracked the older instruments closely where they should. Four versions cover patient and provider users of each app type, distributed through a project website.
europmc-pmc6546699:
Pellin and co-authors chart the first fate choices of human blood stem cells, writing in Nature Communications. These progenitors in bone marrow must stock every blood cell type for life, but their early branching order is disputed. The team read the RNA of thousands of single marrow cells to draw the map.

Their map of 6,011 stem-marker cells shows a tree-like order, not a loose cloud. Wider sampling of less mature cells recovered a missing early branch that leads to basophils, a rare white cell type. The human tree closely matched the mouse one in shape and gene use. The authors also name CD164 as a marker of the earliest branches, which could help design better transplant cell products.
europmc-pmc6612399:
Steven and co-authors review how inflammation and oxidative stress drive cardiovascular disease. Their article appears in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Heart and vessel disease remains a leading cause of death worldwide. Chronic inflammation now ranks among its proven risks. Immune cells can add to the oxidative load inside vessel walls.

The review links low-grade inflammation with endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis. Missing antioxidant defenses worsen the picture in study models. So does excess output from enzymes that make reactive oxygen species. Older anti-inflammatory drugs often protect vessels as a side benefit. New trials show targeted antibody therapy cuts deaths in atherosclerosis. Modern diabetes drugs share calming, antioxidant effects. The authors frame redox balance as a shared goal of therapy.
europmc-pmc6721499:
Fu and co-authors reviewed how mesenchymal stem cells move and repair tissue. These stem cells can renew themselves and turn into several cell types. Bone marrow stem cells are the type used most in cell therapy. To heal damage, they must leave the marrow, ride the blood, and enter injured tissue.

The review covers the chemical and physical signals that steer this migration. It then covers two repair roles: turning into replacement cells, and releasing helpful signals to nearby cells. Knowing how movement and repair connect could guide better clinical use. Therapies could then call more stem cells to where they are needed.
europmc-pmc6795799:
Fyhrquist and co-authors compared skin microbes and skin gene patterns in two skin diseases. Atopic dermatitis and psoriasis both inflame the skin, but their microbe stories were unclear. The team sequenced skin microbes in patients and in healthy volunteers. They also measured which genes were switched on in skin samples. Then they joined the two data sets to sort each disease.

One microbe, Staphylococcus aureus, dominated the dermatitis skin. It came with host gene patterns tied to the skin barrier and to immune response. The sicker the skin, the fewer kinds of microbes it held. Psoriasis skin held mixed microbe groups instead, with weak links to gene patterns. The contrast may guide tests and targeted care.
europmc-pmc7012599:
Sampson and co-authors show that a bacterial protein from the gut worsens brain disease in mice. Their study appeared in eLife. Parkinson's disease involves clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein. Amyloid proteins seed each other's clumping, prion-style. Gut bacteria make their own amyloids, notably curli, a surface fibre of certain E. coli.

Mice bred to overproduce human alpha-synuclein were colonised with curli-making bacteria. Their gut and brain pathology worsened, and movement and gut function declined. Without curli, the bacteria lost the effect. Purified curli sped alpha-synuclein clumping in test tubes. A gut-only amyloid blocker given by mouth prevented the worsening. Curli alone did not harm normal mice, so the microbial trigger needs a susceptible host. The work links gut microbes to synuclein disease through a concrete molecule. It also hints that blocking amyloid formation in the gut might slow such diseases.
europmc-pmc7034599:
Riddell examines Dr. George Cheyne and the so-called English Malady in the Annals of Medical History, writing as sole author. Nations have a habit of naming diseases after foreigners they dislike, and Riddell opens with a string of examples, from the French pox to the Spanish flu. Against that backdrop he turns to Cheyne, the Scottish physician who wrote about nervous disorders among the English.

Cheyne treated what his age called the English Malady: a cluster of spleen, vapours, and low spirits blamed on English wealth, diet, and climate. Riddell recounts Cheyne's views and prescriptions, including bleeding in small amounts, alterative medicines such as calomel, and plant-based remedies. The essay preserves an early attempt to explain why a prosperous nation seemed prone to nervous illness, written when such complaints were only beginning to be studied as medical problems.
europmc-pmc7052699:
Jiao and co-authors rebuild the maize reference genome in Nature. Maize is the world's most grown crop and a key model for genetics. The first reference assembly, published in 2009 from Sanger sequencing, held more than 100,000 small bits, many placed in a random order. That patchwork made study of single genes hard, and study of the regions between them harder still.

Using single-molecule sequencing at 65-fold coverage plus optical mapping, the team produced a far more joined-up assembly. The new genome lets researchers study structural change and repeat-rich regions that the old assembly scrambled. Comparisons found expansions of transposable element families unique to maize. The authors also sized the structural gaps between maize lines. A cleaner reference sharpens every use that follows, from tracing trait genes to guiding breeding for higher yields.
europmc-pmc7099199:
Parapouli and co-authors review the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and its industrial uses, in AIMS Microbiology. This single-celled fungus is the best studied eukaryote in basic research. It is also easy to change genetically. The same species has served bakers and brewers for thousands of years.

The review covers the yeast's work in food, drink, and biofuel production. Wine making gets close attention, alone and beside other microbes. The authors explain the traits behind its value, such as strong fermentation and tolerance of low pH. They also weigh wild strains as a fresh source of useful types. Readers get a tour of one microbe that links the lab bench to the bakery, the winery, and the fuel tank.
europmc-pmc7163299:
Erdel and co-authors test whether HP1 protein droplets drive the packing of silent chromatin in mouse cells, in Molecular Cell. Heterochromatin is the tightly packed, switched-off part of the genome. It gathers the protein HP1, which can form liquid droplets in a test tube. Whether real chromatin foci work that way was unsettled.

Four findings argue against the droplet model in living cells. HP1 formed droplets only weakly. Focus size and packing did not depend on HP1. No separate liquid HP1 pool existed inside the foci. And packing flipped between two fixed states when a strong gene switch was present. The authors liken the foci to collapsed polymer globules soaked through with the same nuclear fluid as open chromatin.
europmc-pmc7183199:
Moghadas and co-authors project hospital demand from COVID-19 in the United States. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team built an age-based model of virus spread. They fed it United States population data and early outbreak estimates. The model tracked who would need a hospital bed. It also tracked who would need intensive care.

The authors report that the outbreak would likely swamp current hospital capacity. In their base case, infection could reach most of the population. Older adults faced the highest rates of intensive care need. Self-isolation by sick people eased some pressure in the model. Still, intensive care beds fell short in each scenario. The authors call for rapid expansion of hospital capacity. They also urge support for voluntary isolation of cases.
europmc-pmc7236499:
Bauer and co-authors pool studies to pin down death rates in sepsis and septic shock across three regions. Their meta-analysis appeared in Critical Care. Sepsis is a runaway response to infection that fills intensive care units. Published mortality figures swing widely, from 15 to 56 percent. The team reviewed studies from Europe, North America, and Australia between 2009 and 2019.

They separated 30-day and 90-day deaths for sepsis and for the graver septic shock. In Europe, 46 studies with 19,667 participants put 30-day septic shock mortality near a third. North American figures were similar, while Australian data ran lower. Rates also rose with organ failure scores. Solid numbers help hospitals benchmark their care. The authors stress that the syndrome's variety still clouds comparisons.
europmc-pmc7275199:
Nazir and co-authors map gum disease worldwide and find that its tracking is poor. Their ecological study appeared in The Scientific World Journal. Periodontal disease damages the tissues holding teeth in place. It is linked with wider health problems, yet its global distribution is not fully charted.

Using World Health Organization databank figures based on a standard periodontal index, they compared adolescents, adults, and older people across income groups. Deep periodontal pockets were most common in older persons, while surface problems such as calculus appeared often in adolescents. Among adults, periodontitis rates differed sharply by country income, reaching 43.7% in high-income countries. Disease burden grows with age, the authors conclude, and surveillance remains too weak to guide policy well.
europmc-pmc7292499:
Broggi and co-authors show that a class of antiviral signal, type III interferons, can damage the lung lining it is meant to protect. Their study appeared in Science. Interferons switch on antiviral defenses after a virus is detected. Type III interferons act mainly at mucosal surfaces and were thought to protect without the damaging inflammation of other types, making them candidates for COVID-19 treatment.

In COVID-19 patients, worse illness tracked with high levels of type I and III interferons in the lung. In mice, type III interferon released by lung dendritic cells after exposure to synthetic viral RNA injured the airway lining. That damage raised susceptibility to lethal bacterial infections on top of the virus. The findings complicate plans to use these interferons as straightforward therapy.
europmc-pmc7360599:
Vivanti and co-authors document a case of COVID-19 passing from mother to baby before birth, in Nature Communications. Whether the virus could cross the placenta was unknown early in the pandemic. The mother was infected in the last trimester, and her newborn showed neurological problems.

Tests built a chain of evidence. Virus was found in the mother's blood, then in the placenta at very high load, with inflammation visible under the microscope. The baby's blood carried virus after birth, following the placental infection. Brain imaging and follow-up tracked the newborn's course. The authors present the case as confirmed transplacental transmission, with symptoms in the baby resembling those seen in adults.
europmc-pmc7410499:
Garvin and co-authors propose a bradykinin storm model of COVID-19 in eLife. Neither the disease mechanism nor treatments were known, so the team reanalyzed gene activity in lung wash fluid from patients. The virus enters through ACE2, part of the blood-pressure control system called RAS.

Patient samples showed an atypical RAS pattern: less ACE, more ACE2, renin, and the enzymes that activate bradykinin, plus both bradykinin receptors. Bradykinin widens vessels and lowers pressure, and the pattern predicts its levels climbing in many tissues. A bradykinin storm, rather than only a cytokine storm, could explain leaky vessels and odd symptoms. Existing approved drugs touch several points in the chain, giving the model immediate, testable treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc7458899:
Bento and co-authors describe an open source pipeline that cleans chemical structures for databases. The ChEMBL database gathers drug activity data from many sources. Incoming compounds often break shared format rules.

Built with the RDKit toolkit, the pipeline has three parts. A Checker tests each structure and flags grave errors. A Standardizer formats compounds to set rules. A GetParent step strips salts and solvents to leave the parent form. The team ran it on ChEMBL and on raw sets from elsewhere. It handled the nearly 2 million compounds in ChEMBL well. The code is free on GitHub and through ChEMBL web services. Other teams can adapt it for their own collections.
europmc-pmc7486399:
Yang and co-authors probe how the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds the ACE2 receptor at the single-molecule level. They used atomic force microscopy on model surfaces and living cells. Binding strength and timing were the targets.

The receptor binding domain of the spike forms the contact face with ACE2. The team pulled out the kinetic and thermodynamic traits of this binding pocket. Their picture shows how the grip forms and holds on real cells. They then tested inhibitor peptides that aim at the early attachment stage. Such peptides could block entry before infection starts. The results add hard numbers to a key step of infection. They also open new routes for treatment design against COVID-19.
europmc-pmc7488299:
Giano, Wheeler, and Hubach update how common adverse childhood experiences are in the United States. Harm in childhood can echo across a whole life. The team used survey data with broad reach.

Data covered 211,376 adults across 34 states from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System in this study. The survey spans 8 domains, from abuse to household illness and jail. Most adults, 57.8 percent, reported at least one adverse experience in the weighted results of this large sample. About one in five reported three or more. Women scored higher than men on average. Multiracial adults and the 25-to-34 age group scored highest among their peers. Higher income and schooling linked with lower scores. The authors urge focus on at-risk groups.
europmc-pmc7493799:
Nivette and co-authors study why some Swiss young adults broke COVID-19 public health rules. Young people were flagged worldwide as a low-compliance group. Most past work checked same-time traits, not earlier risk factors.

The team used a Zurich cohort with data from before and during the pandemic. The cohort held 737 participants, with rule-following measured at age 22. Most young adults followed the measures well. Hygiene steps, such as cleaning phones and keeping distance, were skipped most. Non-compliance ran higher in males and in those with more schooling or higher status. Past antisocial traits, such as low self-control and delinquent peers, predicted more rule-breaking. Low trust in authorities did the same. Campaigns, the authors say, should build trust and duty.
europmc-pmc7536299:
Niederberger and Spranger map how the Delphi technique is used in health sciences. The method gathers expert judgment across rounds. It is used when knowledge is incomplete or uncertain.

Their map rests on 12 systematic reviews of Delphi work. Studies often ran two to three rounds. Panels were chosen with care by design. Many variants of the method now exist. Reporting quality showed clear weaknesses across reviews. The authors call for clearer method standards. They also want criteria for judging execution and reporting. Readers get a broad view of where Delphi methods help and where they fall short.
europmc-pmc7583499:
Rossen, Branum, Ahmad, Sutton and Anderson estimate excess deaths linked to COVID-19 in the United States. Official COVID-19 death counts may miss part of the impact. Excess deaths offer a fuller measure of pandemic harm.

The study covers January 26 to October 3 in that year. An estimated 299,028 excess deaths occurred in that span. Two thirds of them were attributed to COVID-19. The largest percentage rises hit adults aged 25–44 years. Hispanic or Latino persons also saw large rises. Data came from national vital statistics records. Models accounted for seasonal patterns in deaths. Results can guide efforts to cut direct and indirect pandemic deaths.
europmc-pmc7588399:
Van Overwalle and co-authors present a consensus paper on the cerebellum and social cognition. The cerebellum was long seen as a motor structure. Recent work shows it also supports thought and feeling.

Its social role became clear only in recent years. One part mirrors goal-directed actions of others. Another part helps read intentions, beliefs and traits. The rear cerebellum supports most of this mentalizing work. The lead idea is that it predicts social sequences. Good prediction smooths interaction and cooperation with others. The paper covers findings in ataxia and autism. It also covers brain stimulation as a possible therapy. Human circuit methods are reviewed for future studies.
europmc-pmc7591699:
Sharma, Sultan, Ding and Triggle review progress and hurdles in COVID-19 vaccine work. The virus was first detected in Wuhan in December 2019. By late August it had hit over 24 million people.

More than 800,000 deaths were reported worldwide then. At that time 30 vaccines were in clinical trials. Over 200 more were in earlier development stages. The review focuses on eight early phase 1 candidates. Named examples include AZD1222, mRNA-1273 and CoronaVac. Platforms, trial stages and immune needs are covered. Ethics, coverage and production limits are discussed. The authors stress global teamwork for vaccine success.
europmc-pmc7745099:
Kasi and co-authors compare two treatment orders for locally advanced rectal cancer. The new order, total neoadjuvant therapy, gives all chemo and radiation before surgery. The standard order gives radiation with chemo, then surgery, then more chemo. The question was which order clears the tumor better.

The pool held 7 studies with 2416 patients. The new order gave a higher rate of complete tumor clearance in tissue after treatment. It also gave better disease-free survival. Rates of sphincter-saving surgery and stoma need did not differ. The authors say front-loading therapy may help curb distant spread, the main cause of death here.
europmc-pmc7778599:
Zhao and co-authors trace how reactive oxygen in mitochondria drives kidney injury after blood flow returns. This injury, from ischemia and reperfusion, is marked by energy failure and inflammation. The team studied mice and kidney tubule cells. They focused on TFAM, a protein that keeps mitochondrial DNA in good shape.

Cutting mitochondrial reactive oxygen eased kidney damage in mice. In cells, this stress lowered TFAM and mitochondrial DNA counts. It both cut TFAM making and sped its breakdown by a shredding enzyme. Silencing TFAM erased the rescue from an antioxidant drug. Kidney samples from injured mice and patients showed the same TFAM loss. The authors name it a repair target.
europmc-pmc7788999:
Liu and co-authors review natural killer cell therapy for cancer, from basic biology to clinical work. NK cells are immune cells that attack abnormal cells. They do not need antigen processing to switch on. Receptor contact with a target cell governs their response.

That simple trigger drew wide interest in cancer therapy. Many teams now build or engineer NK cell treatments. The authors cover NK cell biology first. They then survey pre-clinical and clinical development. Progress, setbacks, and open challenges are weighed. Future paths for NK cell products close the review.
europmc-pmc7792099:
Yi and co-authors review how PD-L1 levels are controlled inside the tumor microenvironment. PD-L1 on cancer cells binds PD-1 on immune cells. That contact helps tumors escape immune attack. Blocking the pair can revive tired T cells.

Only some PD-L1-positive patients gain from these blocking drugs. PD-L1 levels are set by many factors, so a positive test can mean different things. The authors sort the controls by level. Gene transcription is one level. RNA handling, protein change, and protein removal are others. They close with ways this knowledge could sharpen patient choice and drug effect in the clinic.
europmc-pmc7819999:
Koelsche and co-authors show that DNA methylation patterns can classify sarcomas. Sarcomas are cancers of soft tissue and bone. They affect adults and children alike. Types blur into each other under the microscope. Experts often disagree on the diagnosis.

The team trained a machine learning classifier on methylation data. The training set held 1,077 well-checked tumor profiles. It covered 62 tumor classes across the age range. A test set of 428 tumors followed. The classifier named 322 of those cases. Error rates from human review are a known burden in this field. The authors argue methylation typing can support research now. It may enter routine diagnosis in time.
europmc-pmc7857399:
Laxminarayan and co-authors chart COVID-19 spread in two Indian states. India had logged several million cases by August 2020. Its cases skewed younger than in rich countries. The team used rich contact and testing data. Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh supplied the records.

Both states built strong contact tracing systems. Their data show who passed the virus to whom. Children and young adults played a large spread role. Most traced contacts never caught the virus, though. A small share of cases drove most transmission. Household and close contacts carried the highest risk. The authors say such data can aim control at the true hot spots.
europmc-pmc7864599:
Lee and co-authors test empagliflozin in patients with weak hearts and diabetes or prediabetes. The trial is called SUGAR-DM-HF. Drugs of this class already improve heart failure outcomes. How they change heart size was less clear. Left ventricular volumes were the main measure.

Patients had heart failure with reduced pumping power. They also had type 2 diabetes or prediabetes. Heart scans tracked chamber volumes over treatment. The team compared drug and placebo arms. Remodeling of the heart wall was a key interest. Such volume shifts predict later health. The trial adds hard imaging proof to the class's record.
europmc-pmc7977499:
Brownson and co-authors present a paper arguing that implementation science should give health equity a higher place. Implementation science studies how proven care reaches real settings. Equity reframes the goal in a positive way: not what society does badly, but what it can achieve. Health gaps often mirror social injustice, the authors note. The tools of their field could act on that at once.

They set out a vision and ten action steps. The steps link social conditions to health outcomes and build equity into all policies. They call for metrics that can see equity, and for study of what communities already do. Models, strategies, and training all need equity inside them, not bolted on. Links beyond the health sector matter too. The paper is a programme for change in U.S. research and practice.
europmc-pmc7994399:
Duan and Luo present a review of targeting macrophages in cancer immunotherapy. Immunotherapy is held to be the most hopeful path in cancer care. Its forms range from cell transfers and vaccines to checkpoint blockers and small molecules. Macrophages, the eating cells first described by Metchnikoff, thread through all of them. Their help or harm can decide whether a therapy works.

The review first sorts macrophages by origin, growth, type, markers, and jobs. It then sums up their part in each current therapy. Plans that rest on macrophages, or pair them with other drugs, could lift results, the authors argue. Tumour macrophages often shield the cancer instead. Flipping that stance is a live goal. The authors gather the research progress in one place for labs that want to use these cells well.
europmc-pmc8026399:
Buchfink and co-authors upgrade DIAMOND for protein searches at the scale of the whole tree of life. A genomic revolution plans to sequence all known species within the decade. Comparing those genomes demands alignment that is both fast and sensitive. BLASTP sets the sensitivity standard but crawls at this scale. The team estimated one database search would take over 2 months on a large supercomputer.

The new DIAMOND finishes the same search in several hours. It matches BLASTP sensitivity while doing so. Gains came from double indexing, multiple spaced seeds, and a tuned supercomputing framework. Two new modes, very-sensitive and ultra-sensitive, serve data-heavy studies. The aim is tree-of-life tracing of protein evolution. The software is open source under a GPL3 license.
europmc-pmc8075899:
Jebb and co-authors build reference-quality genomes for six bat species and read bat evolution in them. Bats fly, echolocate, live long, and shrug off viruses that kill other mammals. Past genomes were too rough to explain those gifts. The team used long-read sequencing and careful scaffolding. Six species got the full treatment, from horseshoe bat to free-tailed bat.

Gene checks placed bats at a basal spot within their mammal branch. Hearing genes showed signs of selection on the ancestral bat line. That supports echolocation as an early bat trait, not a late add-on. Immune genes showed both losses and sharp expansions. The antiviral APOBEC3 family grew notably large. Old virus DNA sits frozen inside the genomes as a record. Bat-specific microRNA changes were tested and confirmed in the lab.
europmc-pmc8131399:
Godoy-Gallardo and co-authors review metal ions and nanoparticles as antibacterial weapons for engineered tissue. Infected implants can fail catastrophically, even years after surgery. Drug-resistant bacteria make that risk harder to treat. Metals have fought microbes since long before antibiotics. Nanoscale forms sharpen and tune that old power. The review explains the accepted killing mechanisms first.

Oxidative stress, ion leakage, and biomolecule disruption do most of the work. Exact pathways for each metal stay partly murky. Silver, zinc, copper, iron, and gold each get a chapter. Their modes of action differ in useful ways. Mixing ions or decorating particle surfaces can create synergy. It can also soften harm to the patient's own cells. The survey ends inside real scaffold designs. Tissue engineers gain a menu of tested options. Infection-proof implants remain the field's shared prize.
europmc-pmc8150999:
Raziyeva and co-authors trace the immune side of wound healing, acute and chronic. Skin wounds place a heavy load on health systems. Immune cells start the clean-up and repair of fresh wounds.

When immune control fails, wounds stall in lasting inflammation. Chronic wounds hold many pro-inflammatory macrophages and high levels of signals such as TNF-α and IL-1β. Enzyme activity and reactive oxygen species also run high there. The review contrasts the orderly steps of acute healing with this stalled state. It points to immune targets that might restart repair. That contrast frames the search for better wound care.
europmc-pmc8238499:
Hao and co-authors present a method for joint analysis of multimodal single-cell data. New tools can measure several data types in one cell at once. Methods must weigh those types to define cell states well.

Their weighted-nearest neighbor approach learns each data type's value per cell. They applied it to CITE-seq data from 211,000 human blood cells. Panels reached 228 antibodies per cell. The result is a reference atlas of the circulating immune system. Multimodal reading resolved cell states far better than single types. New rare cell groups came into view and were validated.
europmc-pmc8304699:
Salvi and Cowles review butyrate and the gut lining in health and disease. Butyrate is made by gut microbes and feeds the intestinal wall. Transporters MCT1 and SMCT1 carry it into epithelial cells.

Inside, the molecule burns fast as fuel. Not all gut cells use it alike, though. Stem cells at the crypt base prefer glucose instead. That split drives the so-called butyrate paradox. Butyrate can push growth in one cell and halt it in another. The review ties this to inflammation control. Homeostasis and disease states get separate treatment.
europmc-pmc8336499:
Song and co-authors test plant flavonoids against multidrug-resistant bacteria. Resistant pathogens spread fast and strain the hunt for antibiotics. Natural products supply many prized antibacterial scaffolds.

Two flavonoids stood out: α-mangostin and isobavachalcone. A prenyl group tuned their activity, structure analysis showed. Both killed Gram-positive bacteria quickly. They also restored colistin's power against Gram-negative pathogens. Binding studies traced how they act on the cells. Such compounds could revive failing drugs. They may also seed new ones. The work joins chemistry to microbiology tightly. Structure and activity were linked compound by compound. The point is not just to name the size of the risk, but to show where wells, pipes, and plans can cut it down for the towns that need help most.
europmc-pmc8363499:
Kustin and co-authors test whether variants of concern break through BNT162b2 vaccination more often than the older strain. The vaccine works very well against SARS-CoV-2 in trials and in practice. Lab work, though, showed weaker neutralisation of the Alpha and Beta variants by vaccine sera.

The team read 813 viral genome sequences from a large Israeli health service. They compared the variant shares found in vaccinated and unvaccinated cases. If a variant dodged the vaccine, its share should swell among breakthrough cases. Sequences came from nose and throat swabs taken from patients. The pattern differed by variant and by time since dosing. Such checks tell health systems whether vaccine updates are due.
europmc-pmc8441299:
Atkins and co-authors search the genome for roots of the frailty index in ageing. Frailty is a common syndrome of later life tied to disability, hospital stays, and death. The index counts health deficits built up over a lifetime. Its biology is still poorly known.

The genome-wide study pooled UK Biobank and Swedish TwinGene data, over 175,000 people in all. The team found 14 loci tied to the frailty index. Many loci link to known traits like body mass, smoking, depression, and heart disease. One locus looked new. Gene enrichment pointed to brain pathways. The authors say these finds may help delay or prevent frailty.
europmc-pmc8602399:
Wang and co-authors compare two widely used single-cell RNA sequencing methods on the same samples. The droplet-based 10X method can profile many cells at once. The plate-based Smart-seq2 method reads full-length transcripts from fewer cells. Few direct tests had weighed their trade-offs.

Smart-seq2 found more genes per cell, plus more low-level and splice-form transcripts. Its pooled data also matched bulk data more closely. The 10X data had more noise for low-level genes and more dropouts. Yet 10X could find rare cell types due to its scale. Each method found gene sets the other missed. The study helps labs pick a method by goal, not by habit.
europmc-pmc8629999:
Uxa and co-authors describe how the cell cycle controls the gene that makes Ki-67, a widely used cancer marker. Gene activity and protein levels peak in the G2 phase and in cell division. The team traced which DNA sites and protein groups switch the gene on and off. They used binding tests and knockout cell models.

Two DNA elements and one nearby site guide the control. A repressor group called DREAM binds there and quiets the gene in resting cells. From S phase on, other groups switch it on. The tumor suppressors RB and p53 also feed into this control. p53 acts through the p21 protein. The work maps a key growth marker in fine detail.
europmc-pmc8796199:
Capaldo, Ravelli, and Fagnoni survey direct photocatalyzed hydrogen atom transfer for building on aliphatic carbon-hydrogen bonds. In this method, a photocatalyst uses light energy to break such bonds in a controlled way. Careful choice of the hydrogen taker gives selectivity. Additives can tune the result further.

Many catalyst classes now serve this role. They span aromatic ketones, dyes, metal salts, and newer charged species. Most reactions run under mild conditions with visible light. Carbon-carbon bond formation is the most common use. The review gathers the synthetic applications in one place. It aims to be a full guide to this growing method.
europmc-pmc8821599:
Jin and co-authors survey new forms of therapeutic antibodies for cancer care. Standard monoclonal antibodies already help the immune system attack tumors. More than 100 have won approval for human disease. Newer designs shrink the antibody or give it extra jobs. The review covers these formats and their clinical progress.

The authors walk through antibody-drug conjugates first. They then cover multispecific antibodies that grip two targets at once. Antibody-cytokine fusions and small antibody fragments follow. Non-antibody scaffold proteins close the survey. For each form, they explain how it works and why it might help. They also note trial results and open problems. The review maps a fast-moving field for cancer researchers.
europmc-pmc8991999:
Marek and co-authors show that brain-wide association studies need far larger samples than the field has used. Such studies link brain scans to traits like cognition and mental health. The typical study enrolls about 25 people. The team pooled three of the largest scan datasets. Together they held around 50,000 people. They measured how effect sizes and repeatability change with sample size. The answer was stark.

True brain-trait links proved much smaller than thought. Small studies thus miss them or inflate them. Failed replications follow as a matter of course. As samples grew into the thousands, replication improved. Inflated effects shrank toward honest sizes. Functional scans beat structural ones for sturdy effects. Cognitive tests beat mental health surveys. The authors still value small studies for other designs. Lesion and within-person work can use them well.
europmc-pmc9146299:
Shawky and co-authors give a comprehensive overview of globally approved JAK inhibitors. JAK enzymes pass cytokine signals into cells through the JAK-STAT pathway. That pathway shapes inflammation, immunity, and some cancers. Blocking JAK enzymes has proved useful against several diseases.

The overview covers eleven approved drugs, from abrocitinib to upadacitinib. For each drug it gives synthesis routes and strength against different kinases. It also covers medical uses, crystal structures, and binding modes in detail. Metabolic paths and breakdown products are shown as well. The data should help chemists design new JAK drugs. Readers get chemical and medical facts on a whole drug family in one place.
europmc-pmc9365699:
Erickson and co-authors read cancer family history directly from tissue maps. They inferred DNA copy number changes from spatial gene activity data. Over 120,000 tissue regions were covered across several organs. The prostate got an organ-wide deep look, in both benign and malignant areas.

Copy number patterns split tumors into clear clone groups. Nearby benign tissue held clonal patches of its own. The pattern suggests genome instability starts before tissue looks cancerous. That challenges treatment plans that target only visible tumor spots. The method matches DNA-based family trees built from the same samples. It avoids the bias of picking a few regions by eye. The authors say spatial genome maps can sharpen early cancer detection. Benign tissue, in this view, may already carry the seeds of change.
europmc-pmc9452299:
Tsui and co-authors trace how the factor MYB shapes T cell exhaustion in chronic infection. Worn-out CD8 T cells bear brakes such as PD-1 and make few cytokines. A small pool of precursor cells keeps that response alive over time. Those precursors renew themselves and feed the worn-out pool.

The team found a distinct CD62L positive precursor group with stem-like traits. This group held the long-term growth and repopulation power. MYB proved key to building and keeping that group. It also drove the loss of effector function, which guards against lethal tissue damage. The burst of growth after PD-1 blockade came only from these cells. That burst also needed MYB. The work names a core cell type behind lasting antiviral defense.
europmc-pmc9679999:
Bojar and co-authors create a guide to lectin binding, with machine learning notes on 57 lectin specificities. Lectins are proteins that grip sugar chains called glycans. Most glycan knowledge rests on what these probes bind. Their exact tastes were poorly defined for years.

The team used a large glycan microarray data set as their base. The arrays tested trade lectins against hundreds of glycans. They blended 68 hand-set glycan features with machine learning rules. Expert notes then joined the model output for each lectin. The guide sorts the 57 lectins by their lead binding taste. Mannose binders and complex N-glycan binders lead the groups. Fucose, sialic acid, and GalNAc binders follow in turn. The authors say the guide shows how tangled lectin tastes can be. Labs can now pick probes with clearer eyes.
europmc-pmc9820499:
Rochette and co-authors review lipid peroxidation and iron metabolism as the two cornerstones of ferroptosis control. Ferroptosis is a rust driven form of regulated cell death. Reactive oxygen species attack the fats in cell membranes. That attack builds the peroxides that execute the cell.

Two events sit at the center of the death cascade. Iron piles up inside the cell beyond safe levels. Membrane fats peroxidize faster than they can be cleared. Glutathione is the main shield against that buildup. It feeds the guard enzyme GPX4 that disarms peroxides. A membrane transport pair supplies the shield's raw material. Storage iron can be freed by a self-eating route. That route, ferritinophagy, feeds the iron pool on demand. Organelles like mitochondria help tune the balance. Broken control links ferroptosis to many diseases. Drugs on both sides of the switch are surveyed.
europmc-pmc9876799:
de Vries and co-authors investigate γδ T cells in cancers that lack HLA class I presentation. The study focuses on mismatch repair-deficient cancers, which respond well to immune checkpoint blockade. Most such cancers stayed responsive even when B2M was lost. The team found 20 of 21 B2M-inactivated cancers still responded.

B2M loss was linked to greater infiltration by γδ T cells, mainly Vδ1 and Vδ3 types. These cells carried PD-1 and other activation and cytotoxic markers. In lab tests they reacted strongly to tumor cells lacking HLA class I. Checkpoint blockade raised their frequency further in B2M-deficient tumors. The findings point to γδ T cells as real effectors in this setting.
europmc-pmc9952099:
Olufunmilayo and co-authors review oxidative stress and antioxidants in neurodegenerative disorders. Such disorders form a large share of neurological disease. Their course involves complex general and disease-specific factors. Oxidative stress arises when reactive oxygen and nitrogen species outpace antioxidant defenses.

The review covers broad effects of oxidative stress on the central nervous system. It then traces routes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease. Mitochondrial dysfunction appears as a shared thread across these conditions. The authors discuss how easing oxidative stress might slow disease progression. Such steps could bring clinical gains if they work in patients. Readers get a linked view of stress, cell damage, and therapy ideas.
europmc-pmc9982699:
Tu and co-authors estimate the burden of stroke in China in 2020. Their cross-sectional study used a nationally representative sample. It covered both rural and urban populations. Stroke is a leading cause of death in China, and prevalence keeps rising.

China holds the highest estimated lifetime stroke risk worldwide. Risk factors such as diabetes, obesity, hypertension, and inactivity have all trended upward. The team set out to update prevalence, incidence, and mortality figures. Older national data from 2013 gave a baseline for comparison. Global Burden of Disease work showed falls in age-standardized rates over past decades. Fresh 2020 numbers let planners judge current need. The study frames stroke as a growing national health task.
freeman-jamesons-1899:
Freeman tried comedy in The Jamesons, issued in 1899 with pictures. Chapter one, They Arrive, stresses that the village had never taken boarders before. No rich family lived there, yet folk were proud to keep their homes shut to strangers.

That proud custom breaks when the Jamesons, among the best-off locals, take in paying guests. The new family then sets out to improve the village to city tastes. A village narrator watches their schemes fail with dry delight. Yankee common sense quietly beats city airs, and the satire lands sharp though the tone stays lighter than Freeman's usual work.
frus-1861-d199:
