Cassius Clay wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 June 1861. The dispatch is document 199 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The printed order sets Clay's June report after Seward's July letter. By date, Clay wrote first, from a Russia bright with goodwill. His page adds a northern light to a file elsewhere full of doubt and care. Northern light was rare that summer, which makes Clay's June page shine in the file. Northern light in a dark summer was a thing the cabinet learned to prize. Northern light was rare and prized that summer.
frus-1861-d299:
Another report crossed the ocean to Seward, this one from Mr. Crosby on 1 June 1861. It stands as Document 299 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d99:
On 16 October 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister at the capital. The letter is document 99 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The Lyons file swells in October, as trade and blockade claims piled up. Seward's mid month note keeps the tone even and the terms precise. Formal care in such letters was not mere style; it was how two governments avoided a second war. Each precise term in such notes could later be quoted back as a pledge. Quoted back as pledges, such terms bound the men who had penned them.
frus-1862-d199:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent Lord Lyons a note on 7 January 1862, printed as Document 199 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, was Seward's daily counterpart for British business in the capital.

The first week of January saw the Trent affair close, with the seized envoys freed and sailing for Europe. Both governments wanted the quarrel buried. Seward's notes to Lyons in this period, this one among them. Belong to the repair work that followed, when each side tested how normal dealings might resume. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d299:
On 4 August 1862 William L. Dayton sent another report to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 299 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Dayton reports under that date.

Two reports in one mail let Dayton separate audiences and subjects. A habit that suited Paris, where court talk and ministry business ran on different tracks. Early August found France urging Britain toward joint action on the war. Dayton's paired letters that week are part of the evidence for how that push looked from inside the French capital. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d399:
On 23 January 1862, nine days after his last instruction to the same post, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Horace J. Perry in Madrid. The dispatch is Document 399 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record sent to Congress.

Madrid mattered to the Union because Spain ruled Cuba and Puerto Rico and had joined the armed move into Mexico. Seward's steady stream of orders kept the Madrid legation pressing Spain to stay neutral and to keep Confederate agents at arm's length. Single letters look small, but together they formed the daily pressure that kept Spain out of the American war.
frus-1862-d499:
On 9 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. The instruction is Document 499 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

May 1862 found McClellan creeping toward Richmond and the Union's stock high in Europe. Seward's orders in that season pressed ministers to convert goodwill into firm neutrality rulings and public statements. The Dutch file shows the routine side of that work: no crisis, just steady pressure and exact reporting. An instruction to a small post in a quiet month may look minor. Yet the sum of such letters was the Union's European policy in daily practice.
frus-1862-d599:
Spain's minister of state sent this circular on 20 December 1861 to the Spanish ambassador in Paris and the Spanish minister in London. It is Document 599 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, among the appended Spanish papers.

The writers and readers here are all Spanish. Madrid was briefing its own envoys at the two allied capitals. The subject was the Mexican expedition then under way. Such a circular fixed the line those envoys were to take with the French and British governments. For American readers of the printed volume, it was evidence of how the three allies coordinated, and of where their aims already differed. The document is Spanish statecraft in its own words, preserved in an American record.
frus-1862-d699: A Mr. Yrisarri dated this dispatch 9 September 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 699 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, part of a short back-and-forth between the two men that fall. The record names the writer and the date but not his post or topic, so this note stays within those bounds.
frus-1862-d99:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 12 July 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 99 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d199:
Writing from London on 14 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 199 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In 1863 the great question in London was whether Britain would treat the Confederacy as a real nation. Adams's reports helped Washington judge that risk week by week. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d299:
Washington's orders to London on 26 September 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 299 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Seward wrote in a firm tone but had to avoid pushing Britain into the war on the Southern side. His instructions walked that line again and again. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d399:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 February 1863. His note is document 399 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Seward kept every note, and the State Department printed the exchange for Congress. Reading Lyons's side shows how the crisis looked from the other desk. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d499:
Writing on 8 May 1863, Secretary William H. Seward addressed Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington in an official letter. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d599:
Dated 3 August 1863, document 599 is a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the late summer of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d99:
William H. Seward addressed this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 March 1863, the third of twelve to him dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 99 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A secretary who writes twelve letters to one post in a day is putting his house in order. Seward's batch gave Adams a fresh sheet for each live point in the British file. This one is the third of the run. On its own it is a plain note of orders. In its row, it shows the scale of the London brief in the spring of 1863.
frus-1899:
The 1899 volume opens onto a wider American map. Belgium's file now touches the Philippine Islands. Neutral vessels coasting there raise a legal question. Austria-Hungary still pursues the Lattimer killings. Its military service cases run on by name. Admiral Dewey's reception at Trieste adds ceremony. Bolivia prints a revolution and a jailed captain. British interests there rest under American protection.

The mid-volume wires watch a Gulf port. Inspectors crowd New Orleans landings and depots. About 116 alleged filibusters arrive from Kansas City. Most are turned back; the rest stay watched. Such telegrams show neutrality enforced at home. Argentina and Chile still dispute their boundary. Trademark theft in Buenos Aires joins the list. Empire has widened the beat. The century closes on a global watch.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d199:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius sent President Roosevelt a memorandum on 8 November 1943 summing up oil concessions in the Middle East. Roosevelt had asked for the two-page brief at their Friday meeting, saying he wanted the whole picture with him before the coming conferences.

The enclosure maps who owned what. Four big firms each held 23.75 percent of the Iraq Petroleum Company, with Gulbenkian keeping five percent. Anglo-Iranian ran Iran's fields and the Abadan refinery, American firms held Bahrain and the vast Saudi fields, and Kuwait's proved reserves sat idle. It closes with open questions: where to build new refineries, and whether Washington should buy shares in the firms or options on oil in the ground.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d299:
Memoranda by the Chinese government, submitted at Cairo on 24 November 1943, set out China's design for the postwar order. The papers cover a four-power council, security during the transition after the war, European questions, and Far East machinery.

Pending a full Council of the United Nations, the four Moscow powers should form a Four-Power Council at once. It would have a standing committee in Washington. Its charge would be building the larger body, in which the Big Four would act as a presidium. An inter-Allied military commission would handle security, backed by international naval and air bases at agreed points. China also asks to be told of all European discussions, to share in decisions on Germany's surrender, and to build a Far Eastern Committee and a unified Far East command.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d399:
The Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent the American Legation in Iran an aide-mémoire at Tehran on 1 December 1943, while the three Allied leaders met in the capital. Written in formal, grateful language, it sets out what Iran hopes to gain from hosting the conference.

Iran, the note says, has cooperated fully under the Tripartite Pact, declared war on Germany, and borne economic hardship beyond her power in the Allied cause. In return she expects two things from the Allies. They should weigh the troubles and damage the war has inflicted on her. And they should make a special effort to hand back the vital threads of the country's affairs now in their hands, leaving security to Iran's own forces. The written promises of Iran's integrity and full independence, it urges, should be strengthened by moral and material help in every field.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d499:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff presented this formal report to President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill on December 6, 1943, closing the military work of the Second Cairo Conference. It gathered the chiefs' joint conclusions for the two leaders' approval. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

A final report of this kind is the summit's military bottom line: the strategy both staffs could jointly recommend after weeks of argument at Tehran and Cairo. Roosevelt and Churchill governed the war through papers like this one. For readers, it is one of the key documents of the conference, stating where the alliance agreed to strike, and in what order, in the decisive year ahead.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d99: A second message from Churchill to Roosevelt dated November 6, 1943 stands as Document 99 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Same-day pairs run all through this correspondence, and this one falls in the last week before Roosevelt sailed aboard the Iowa. The catalog record gives no topic for the note. It is kept in the Foreign Relations series, in the thick of the pre-summit traffic.
frus-1944-quebec-d199: An editors' note records that no account survives of the discussion at this luncheon meeting either. The time of the lunch and the names of its participants come from the President's Log. The Log's evidence is confirmed by Sir Alexander Cadogan's diary, cited by page. Beyond attendance and timing, the conversation at this table left no trace in the records the editors could find.
frus-1944-quebec-d299: Roosevelt and Churchill both put their initials to this aide-mémoire, dated 19 September 1944, days after their Quebec meetings ended. An aide-mémoire is a short written summary left behind to fix what was agreed. Filed as document 299 in the Foreign Relations volume on the conference, it carries unusual weight because both leaders personally marked the text as accepted.
frus-1944-quebec-d99:
Ambassador Winant wrote to Secretary Hull on August 25, 1944. John Gilbert Winant served as America's ambassador in London. The State Department printed his message in the Quebec 1944 volume. Paris was liberated on the day he wrote.

An ambassador's reports gave Washington the view from the allied capital. Winant enjoyed unusual trust among British leaders. His letters carried both facts and a sense of British feeling. For readers, the message shows London speaking into summit preparation. The Quebec Conference opened less than three weeks later. Reports like Winant's helped shape the American brief.
frus-1945-50-intel-d199:
A memorandum from the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) reached the National Intelligence Authority on 30 July 1946. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 199 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d299:
On 19 August 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 18th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. It is document 299 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

After key talks, an aide would write up what was said for the file. The result is close to the room itself. Later memos cite such notes the way lawyers cite a witness: as the best proof of words once spoken. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d399:
Willis Machle, the CIA's assistant director for scientific intelligence, wrote to Director Roscoe Hillenkoetter on 29 September 1949. The memo is document 399 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Scientific intelligence tracked foreign advances in weapons, above all the atomic bomb. The Soviet Union had tested its first bomb just weeks before, in late August 1949. Machle's office had to judge what the test meant and how fast the Soviets would move. His memo puts that tense moment in front of the agency's director. His memo came at a moment when each fresh fact about Soviet arms could shift budgets and plans.
frus-1945-50-intel-d99:
Magruder wrote to McCloy once more on 15 November 1945. Three Magruder letters to the same patron within seven weeks trace the SSU's autumn in miniature. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

November found the unit still alive, still funded, and still unsure of its place in the coming central system. Magruder's steady letters were part of why: no crisis found the War Department uninformed or the unit undefended. Readers closing the SSU thread for 1945 can see the method plainly. Survival, for a leftover agency, is a correspondence conducted on time, every time, with the right man reading it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d199:
Leave some heavy weapons behind: that is Churchill's parting idea in this excerpt of 27 November 1944. His message number 834 to Roosevelt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It closes, for the moment, the argument over arming France.

Churchill agrees the point has not yet come, and that the allies should gather a good many arms from the Germans. Still, he presses one practical thought. When the American divisions start for home, there would be a strong case for their leaving part of their heavy weapons and equipment behind. The French could then take over the job in western Germany with tools already on the ground.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d299:
A morning walk is all that survives of this Malta meeting, as the editorial note in the volume frankly states. No record of the substance of the talk has been found, the editors write. What follows is gathered from Stettinius's own account, at pages 60, 62, and 63 of his book.

Stettinius and Eden were both quartered aboard H. M. S. Sirius in Grand Harbor during the Malta days. In the early part of the morning they went ashore together and took a walk. In its course, it seems, they “discussed some of the problems to be raised at Yalta.” Nothing more is known. The note preserves the outline of a conversation between the two foreign ministers on the eve of the great conference, and no more than the outline.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d399:
America answered Molotov on Poland in a formal proposal of February 8, 1945. On frontiers, Washington raised no objection to the Soviet first point. Poland's eastern boundary would follow the Curzon line, with changes in Poland's favor of five to eight kilometers in some areas. On payment for that loss, the paper agrees in part.

Poland should gain at Germany's expense: East Prussia south of the Koenigsberg line, Upper Silesia, and land up to the Oder. But the paper sees little justification for pushing Poland's western boundary to the Western Neisse River. Here the Oder-Neisse dispute, which ran for decades, enters the record in careful language.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d499:
Stalin agreed at once, in this letter to Roosevelt of February 11, 1945, given here in translation. He had received the President's letter of February 10. Soviet votes would rise to three once Ukraine and White Russia joined the Assembly. Stalin entirely agreed: the number of votes for the United States should also be increased.

The American total might rise to three, he wrote, as in the Soviet case with its two basic republics. If necessary, he was prepared to support the proposal officially. With sincere respects, the letter closes. In the event, the United States never took the extra votes. The exchange survives as a measure of how far Stalin would go, that week, to keep Roosevelt content.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d99:
Three stopgap plans for the peace are summed up side by side in this paper from the Division of International Security and Organization. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Each plan tries to fill the gap before a world body can start work.

Senator Vandenberg proposed an allied treaty to keep Germany and Japan disarmed for good, with instant power for the President to act. Senator Connally proposed an interim United Nations council of eleven states, to advise on disputes until the Charter took force. The third plan, an Emergency High Commission for Liberated Europe, would seat the three allies and France. It would help freed and former satellite states build popular, stable rule and meet urgent needs.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d199:
Edwin Pauley pressed for reparations to rank high on the agenda in a telegram extract dated July 7, 1945. The extract is document 199 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Pauley, the American member of the reparations commission in Moscow, sent the message to Secretary Byrnes as he traveled to Berlin.

Pauley considers it most important, he writes, that the conference agenda provide for the reparations matters deadlocked in Moscow. He adds the question of including France in the reparations commission. These are questions of high policy that must be determined, he argues, and he asks Byrnes to see that they are given a high place on the agenda. The full text appears later in the volume, where Pauley's dispute with the Soviet negotiator Maisky over the size of Germany's bill is set out.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d299:
General Schuyler, the American military chief on Rumania's Allied Control Commission, warned the War Department on June 28, 1945, against an early peace with Rumania. His top secret message answered British proposals for a quick treaty. Schuyler had seen the Rumanian government up close from Bucharest.

Joining peace talks with the present government, he argued, would in effect recognize it. Yet that government spoke for only a small share of Rumanians. Schuyler's warning put the military view plainly before Washington: a fast treaty could lock in a regime the United States did not trust, weeks before Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d399:
The Ruhr's disposition is argued in a briefing book paper dated June 27, 1945. Its recommendation is plain: the United States should oppose separating the Ruhr from Germany. That bar covers internationalization, a separate Ruhr state, and annexation by one or more neighboring states alike. No route to separation is acceptable.

Proposals for the Ruhr, the discussion says, should be judged by two tests. They must serve long-range security, and they must allow the full use of the region's resources to restore European production and living standards. Security measures in turn must be effective, cheap in effort, and durable. A Germany stripped of soldiers and arsenals, it notes, could not launch a new war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d499:
Truman bends to Churchill's difficulty in an extract of his top secret reply of July 3, 1945. He has just received the Prime Minister's message, he writes, and in view of the reasons given, he concurs with the suggestion that recognition of the new Polish government be delayed temporarily. Churchill's proposed twenty-four hour delay, though, lands on an awkward date.

That delay would mean according recognition on Independence Day. Truman therefore suggests, and hopes Churchill will concur, that recognition be postponed for forty-eight hours instead. The new time would be 7 p.m., Eastern War Time, on July 5. The brief extract shows the President trading speed for allied unity.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d599:
The United States Chiefs of Staff laid out the Pacific campaign plan in a top secret memo of June 29, 1945. It is document 599 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its stated aim was Japan's unconditional surrender at the earliest date.

The plan works in three steps. First, forces based on Okinawa, Iwo Jima, the Marianas, and the Philippines will tighten the blockade and step up bombing. Next comes an assault on Kyushu, to destroy major enemy forces there. Last comes the decisive invasion of Japan's industrial heart through the Tokyo Plain. The chiefs also cut side operations in the Ryukyus, dropping landings on two islands for good. The men and gear saved would speed the build-up on Okinawa instead.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d699:
Ambassador Kirk relayed a British report on Soviet military moves in Rumania from Caserta on July 5, 1945. His secret wire is document 699 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The source was Air Vice Marshal Stevenson, head of the British team on Rumania's control commission.

Stevenson put Rumania's planned peacetime army at fifteen or sixteen infantry divisions plus one armored division. Russia would supply its arms and gear under a treaty then being prepared. Four pontoon bridges now crossed the Danube, and night truck movements ran south toward Constanta. That port's center had been emptied to house Russian troops, and its hotels seized for staffs. Marshal Tolbukhin's headquarters, Stevenson judged, would almost surely sit at Constanta. With reports from Hungary, Bulgaria, and Allied headquarters, he read a broad Soviet build-up in the making.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d99:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew recorded a complaint from the French ambassador in a memorandum dated June 25, 1945. The extracts form document 99 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Ambassador Henri Bonnet came, without instructions, to warn that relations between France and the United States were drifting the wrong way.

Among his points is France's exclusion from the coming Big Three meeting. Despite all France had suffered, and her stake in the occupation of Germany and Austria, reparations, and the Far East, she had not been invited, and the snub hurt deeply at home. Grew listened, gave no assurances, and promised to pass the points to the President. The memo shows the resentment the closed Big Three system stirred among shut-out allies.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1099:
On 24 July 1945, midway through the Potsdam Conference, the Soviet team put a formal proposal on the table. It appears as Document 1099 in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. The talks in Germany brought Truman, Stalin, and Churchill together to set the terms of the postwar order.

Written proposals were how each side stated its terms so the others could accept, reject, or trade against them. The Soviet Union had lost more of its people in the war than any other ally. Its team pressed its case hard at Potsdam, and a paper of this kind fixes the stand Moscow took at that stage of the bargaining.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1199:
Truman wrote to Churchill on 23 July 1945, two days before the British leader's last day at the summit. The president kept up his direct exchange with the prime minister through the final Churchill week. Neither man yet knew the count's result, though both could guess.

Their letters show the British-American partnership working at the top, in the men's own hands. A note between them could clear a point faster than a day of staff talks. This one belongs to the closing days of the Churchill era at Potsdam. It is part of the last set of letters the two wartime partners exchanged as leaders.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1299:
Baruch, the American ambassador in Portugal, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 21 July 1945. Portugal was neutral, but its capital was a crossroads of the war's quiet traffic: trade, spies, and the Atlantic air route through the Azores.

An envoy in Lisbon reported a scene unlike any other post's. Both sides courted Portugal, and both watched it. Baruch's dispatch fed that odd picture into Washington during the summit. It is the Lisbon end of the Potsdam web. The peace was shaped by neutral ground as well as by battlefields and tables.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1399:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, wrote to Georges Bidault, the French foreign minister, on 1 August 1945. The volume prints six Caffery letters to Bidault from the turn of August 1945. Three letters from Caffery to Bidault bear that single date in the volume.

A third letter in a day points to business that kept generating paper: drafts answered, points clarified, positions nudged. Caffery was an old hand in the foreign service, and Bidault a resistance leader turned minister; their styles met on paper with care. For readers, the cluster of August letters shows how much of the peace was made outside the famous rooms. The Potsdam three decided the frame; men like these two fitted France into it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-99: Standing in the run of unnumbered items after document 710, this editorial note belongs to the apparatus of the Potsdam volume. Foreign Relations editors wrote notes like this to fill small holes in the story the papers tell. The note may cite a source file or a related text in another volume. It helps readers trust the order and completeness of what surrounds it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d799:
Schoenfeld reported again from Hungary on July 17, 1945, in document 799. The representative in Budapest sent two letters as the conference opened. This one went to the Acting Secretary of State. It joined the second Potsdam volume beside his other reports.

Two letters on opening day suggest a post with much to say. Hungary's politics moved fast under the armistice. Readers can watch Schoenfeld sorting the urgent from the routine. The document extends the volume's Hungary file at its start. It shows a mission determined to be heard while the great decisions were still open.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d899:
Members of the American reparations delegation in Moscow answered Edwin Pauley's request in this secret telegram of July 18, 1945. Pauley had asked for figures on German capital assets and output. The reply gives estimates for the Soviet zone and for land east of the Oder-Neisse line.

About 40 percent of Germany's prewar movable and fixed capital assets lay in the Russian zone, Berlin included. Movable assets east of the Oder-Neisse were worth about 6 billion Reichsmarks in 1938. That area produced about 7 percent of German industrial and mining output. The senders warn that losing this land may cut Germany's power to pay by more than the raw shares suggest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d999:
Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled George Kennan in Moscow on July 30, 1945. The message ties back to the American note just delivered to the Soviets on German assets in Spain. It passes on a report from the military attaché in Stockholm.

A Russian delegation there has surveyed interned German planes in Sweden. The planes are to be flown out as war booty, and newspapers have aired the plan. The papers also state that neither the United States nor Britain has asked about the remaining aircraft. The cable is short, and it asks Kennan for nothing beyond noting the report.
gao-gaoreports-b-296099:
Gold Cross Safety protested a Marine Corps purchase order for a vehicle safety drive in GAO decision B-296099, dated June 13, 2005. The order went to Driven2Dare. The drive was set for Camp Lejeune. The firm said its quote was cut on price alone. No one had scored its tech plan.

GAO denied the protest. The firm's price was 20 times the winner's price. GAO said that gap made the price not fair or sound. The agency could cut the quote on that ground. No tech review was due first. The case shows when a huge price gap can end a quote at once.
gao-gaoreports-b-296699:
BAE Technical Services protested an Air Force award for test range work in GAO decision B-296699, dated October 5, 2005. The winner was InDyne. The site was the Eglin Test and Training Complex in Florida. Firms had to back plans to cut staff counts. Proof for such cuts was a key test.

GAO sustained the protest. The agency used a strict test for the firm's proof. It used a lax test for the winner's proof. That split was unfair. Like bids must face the same bar for proof. When the bar shifts by firm, the marks fall. The case is a clean guide on even proof tests.
gao-gaoreports-b-297099:
Europe Displays protested a sole-source award for a show pavilion in GAO decision B-297099, dated December 5, 2005. The holder was Connexion. The buyer was the Federal Transit Administration. The show was a transit fair in Rome, Italy. The agency thought the fair host required that firm be used.

GAO sustained the protest. That belief was wrong and not sound. A sole-source pick under short-form rules needs a true base. A false belief in a host rule is not such a base. The firm sought bid costs as well. GAO would not back those costs. A note of skill and will to bid is not a bid or a priced plan.
gao-gaoreports-b-299599:
Beck's Spray Service protested an Interior Department award to Thomas Helicopters. The contract covered aerial spraying of herbicide on land near Boise, Idaho. The Bureau of Land Management ran the buy. GAO ruled in B-299599 on June 18, 2007.

The firm's technical bid earned less than half the points on offer. It lacked facts on past work with the required navigation system. Most of its past refs had thin links to the job. One ref said it would hire the firm again with hesitation. GAO found the low score fair. The mark was a scored call, not a fitness bar. No referral duty arose from it. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-199:
Catastrophe Risk, GAO-05-199 of February 28, 2005, compares how the United States and Europe insure against huge storms and terror attacks. Such events can swamp insurers with claims. Rates then spike and cover shrinks. The 2004 hurricanes gave the test a live case. Lawmakers asked how the trade could hold more risk.

GAO sizes the trade's room to pay for storm losses. It weighs two tools: bonds that spread risk to investors, and tax-free reserves set aside for bad years. It then shows how six European states handle the same risk. Their paths frame the U.S. choice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-299:
Military Personnel, GAO-05-299 of February 23, 2005, tries to price a policy that drove gay troops out of the ranks. From fiscal year 1994 through fiscal year 2003, the services cut about 9,500 troops for gay conduct. That was about 0.40 percent of 2.37 million cuts for all causes. Since the 2001 attacks, fears rose that scarce skills left with them, such as Arabic speech.

GAO adds up the yearly cost to hire and train new troops in their place. It counts how many cut troops held key jobs or rare tongues. Full sums elude reach, the title warns, since key facts were never kept.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-399:
HHS, GAO-05-399 of March 31, 2005, traces a birth aid gel that may aid the very ill it was hoped to block. Nonoxynol-9, a sperm killer in many birth aids, showed vow in mid-1980s tests as a shield vs HIV. Fresh tests then found it may raise the risk of the virus for some who use it. The swing put firms and the state in a hard spot.

GAO tells what federal arms and gel makers did to test the gel's safety and worth. It tells what word they gave the public on both points. Health arms such as the disease and drug chiefs share the tale.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-399:
Firms owned by Alaska Native corporations won a fast-growing share of federal contracts. GAO wrote GAO-06-399 on April 27, 2006, about special 8(a) provisions for those firms. Most of their 8(a) dollars came through sole-source contracts. Agencies saw such awards as quick and as help toward small business goals. The firms used the program to raise revenue and fund benefits.

GAO found required notices and subcontract checks were not always done. It judged the Small Business Administration's oversight not adequate. Gaps included tracking side lines of business and collecting program data. GAO called for oversight tailored to this growth. Readers see benefits, risks, and fixes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-799:
Two charity tools under tax scrutiny fill GAO-06-799, released on July 27, 2006. Donor-advised funds let donors suggest grants from accounts held by a sponsor. Supporting organizations back the work of other charities. Congress and the Internal Revenue Service saw room for abuse in both forms. GAO gathered facts on the laws that govern them and how they compare with private foundations.

GAO found that tax law treats the three giving vehicles in different ways. Donors to advised funds and supporting groups keep less control than foundation founders do. They also face lower administrative burdens. That mix of ease and tax benefit drew the compliance concern. GAO said collecting more data on both forms could help the tax agency spot abuse. The report maps a fast-growing corner of philanthropy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-99:
Mercury waste rules need sharper lines, GAO concludes in report GAO-06-99, dated December 16, 2005. The Environmental Protection Agency guards hazardous waste under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. Mercury waste must meet set treatment norms before burial. Bulky debris waste can use other norms, with more varied treatment choices.

GAO traced how the agency tracks mercury debris and how much of it exists. It asked if the agency, states, and firms share one view of which mercury waste counts as debris. It checked the controls that watch for rule breaches. The agency must clear up which waste types fit, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-299:
Airport screeners must be at the right checkpoints when crowds surge. GAO tested the staffing model in GAO-07-299, issued February 28, 2007. The transport security agency hired about 55,000 screeners after 2001. Law has capped screening staff at 45,000 full-time slots since August 2002. A computer model now splits staff across over 400 airports. GAO checked how the model guards staffing levels. It also reviewed how local managers deploy the staff assigned.

The model aims for waits of 10 minutes or less on peak weeks, GAO found. It assumes an 80-to-20 blend of full-time and part-time staff. Local security directors can ask to adjust the inputs. The agency granted some requests in the model's first 2 years. A 2006 review changed several assumptions for fiscal year 2007. But reviews cover chosen assumptions each year. GAO urged a systematic recheck of all key assumptions. Stale inputs could leave some airports short.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-399:
Securities markets have grown far harder to knock out since the September 11 attacks, and GAO-07-399, a GAO report issued March 29, 2007, measures that progress. It is GAO's third review of market security and resiliency since the attacks. GAO checked steps taken to prevent attacks and speed recovery. It also weighed work to shore up phone and data networks.

GAO found that big exchanges and clearing groups had added strong physical and system safeguards. Regulators had also pressed firms to plan for wide-scale disruption. Gaps remained, though. Pandemic planning lagged, and some backup plans rested on thin testing. The report is a benchmark for how well U.S. markets could keep trading through a crisis.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-699:
Payments to Iraqi and Afghan civilians harmed in combat fill GAO-07-699, a report dated May 23, 2007. The Defense Department makes two kinds of such payments. Solatia payments follow local custom. Condolence payments voice sympathy for death, injury, or property loss. Neither kind admits legal fault. From fiscal years 2003 to 2006, the department paid about $1.9 million in solatia. It paid more than $29 million in condolence funds.

Commanders pay the funds from accounts set up for that use. GAO found the department had guidance on how to make and log the payments. One record it checked held a small error of about $30. Records from other units could not be matched, though. No single central source holds the data needed for checks. GAO's recommendations target that record gap. The report also notes aid that State and the U.S. Agency for International Development give to harmed civilians.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-99:
Shortcut environmental reviews in the national forests are counted in GAO-07-99, dated October 10, 2006. The Forest Service manages over 192 million acres. Federal law requires impact studies for major projects. Set categories of routine work skip those studies. One such exclusion existed as of 2003. It covered timber stand and habitat improvement work. Four more exclusions were added after 2003. Little was known about their use in the field. GAO surveyed officials from all 155 national forests. It counted vegetation projects for calendar years 2003 through 2005.

The survey maps which exclusions offices actually used. It also counts projects approved with and without full studies. Where offices avoided the shortcuts, GAO asked why. Workload, court risk, and habit all shape local choices. The service broadly agreed with the findings. No recommendations headline the report. The value lies in the first full census of the practice. Oversight of the exclusions can now rest on data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-399:
Joint ventures between the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and other health providers are what GAO takes up in report GAO-08-399, released March 28, 2008. VA runs eight joint ventures with the Department of Defense, sharing or building medical facilities. GAO visited all existing and proposed venture sites.

Officials named gains such as better access to care, lower costs, and richer training. They also named risks: clashing missions and cultures, loss of control, staffing doubts, and money risks. But neither the sites nor VA itself used performance measures to track results, so no one could show how far the gains were real. GAO recommended department-level measures and sharper tests for new proposals. VA generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-599:
In GAO report GAO-08-599, dated June 3, 2008, GAO looks at mail recycling at the Postal Service. In 2006, the service discarded about 317,000 tons of undeliverable advertising mail. The Postal Accountability and Enhancement Act prompted this look at recycling work and untried chances.

The service aims to lift recycling revenue from $7.5 million in fiscal year 2007 to $40 million by fiscal year 2010. Those goals omit disposal savings, so they understate the gain. A New York City pilot may teach lessons, but no rule yet forces other sites to copy them. Mailing groups run their own drives; one association's members send about 80 percent of Standard Mail. GAO listed five more steps the service could take. It agreed with most of the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-99:
How taxes are held back on U.S. income paid to investors abroad is the subject of GAO-08-99, a report dated December 19, 2007. Foreign banks that sign up as qualified intermediaries agree to hold back tax and report payments to the Internal Revenue Service. The aim is to stop tax dodging through offshore accounts.

For tax year 2003, GAO found, only about 12.5 percent of $293 billion in such income passed through these banks. The rest moved through U.S. agents who may accept an owner's word on who they are. Billions went to unknown owners, yet tax was held back at well below the 30 percent rate. GAO urges the tax agency to use its data with more care and to tighten the checks.
garland-prairie-folks-1899:
Prairie Folks bears rights dates of 1892 and a Chicago imprint of F. J. Schulte from 1893. Garland opens with the same pioneer verses used in his later farm book. Settlers, he writes, face a dazzling sky, blue and clear as steel in winter.

Farmers, schoolteachers, and small-town dreamers people these Middle West tales. The tone runs gentler than the angry realism of Main-Travelled Roads. Character studies warmed by fondness replace protest here. Readers still get the full range of prairie life, from comedy to pathos. No writer knew that world better, and the 1899 gathering shows his affection at its clearest.
geneva-bible-new-testament-1599:
English exiles at Geneva printed a Bible in 1560 that became the household Bible of Protestant England. The 1599 edition of its New Testament is the text here, with the famous Geneva study notes kept in place. William Whittingham led the team of translators.

The notes in the margins explain hard verses, name the lessons for church and state, and sometimes scold kings and bishops. Readers know it as the Bible of Shakespeare, Milton, and Bunyan, and the one the Pilgrims carried to America. Its plain, direct English shaped the language of faith for a century. The King James version later took its place but kept much of its wording.
guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-complete:
Guy Mannering, or The Astrologer, by Sir Walter Scott, is his second novel, presented complete with two volumes of illustrations. Scott's front matter lists etchings of Ellangowan Castle and the departure of the gypsies. Cruikshank contributes original etchings, including Dominie Sampson in the library and the advocate Pleydell enthroned as king of a tavern night.

The story follows Harry Bertram, heir of Ellangowan, stolen as a small child when a smuggler was murdered before his eyes. Grown up in India as Vanbeest Brown, he returns unknown while the lawyer Glossin, who profited by his loss, schemes to secure the estate. The gypsy Meg Merrilies, the pedantic Dominie Sampson, and the sporting farmer Dandie Dinmont guard the truth. Smugglers attack, and Dirk Hatteraick is captured on the Solway shore. An old prophecy about the lost heir runs under every chapter.
harsnett-discovery-fraudulent-practises-:
Samuel Harsnett opened England's possession controversy with his Discovery of the Fraudulent Practises of John Darrell in 1599. Darrell, a Puritan minister, had made his name casting out devils. Harsnett denounces the famous dispossessions as outright counterfeit, staged by Darrell and coached into his patients.

He reconstructs how fits were rehearsed and symptoms suggested. The attack aims to disgrace Puritan exorcism and to defend the established church's ban on it. Darrell's party answered in print the next year. The pamphlet war that followed filled shelves. This Discovery is its opening shot, and it still reads like a prosecution speech.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol2-1899:
Volume Two of Hastings's Dictionary of the Bible appeared in 1899, covering entries from Feign to Kinsman. James Hastings kept his team of scholars to a high, even standard. The dictionary was meant to serve study, preaching, and teaching alike.

Articles explain hard words, trace customs, and set out the theology of the Old and New Testaments. Archaeology, then a young science, adds fresh finds from Egypt and Palestine. The tone stays reverent but honest about hard questions. For a generation, this was the first place English readers turned when a Bible name or place puzzled them.
hertz-principles-of-mechanics-1899:
Heinrich Hertz's Principles of Mechanics Presented in a New Form appeared in English in 1899, translated by D E Jones and J T Walley. Hertz wrote the work in German near the end of his short life; it appeared after his death in 1894. It was his last book and his boldest.

Hertz tried to rebuild mechanics without the concept of force, which he found murky. In its place he put masses linked by rigid connections, some of them hidden, moving by the straightest paths. The scheme influenced Wittgenstein's picture theory of language and later philosophy of science. The book is hard, strange, and admired: a great experimenter's attempt to make physics rest on images the mind can fully grasp.
history-japanese-literature-aston-1899:
W. G. Aston wrote A History of Japanese Literature in 1899, the first such history in English. Aston, translator of the Nihongi chronicles, knew the sources at first hand from years in Japan. His survey runs from the oldest songs and chronicles through the great age of the novel and drama to his own century.

Poetry, prose, theater, and popular fiction each get their place in the long arc. Aston writes with a diplomat's clarity and a scholar's love for his subject. Later histories have added much, but his remains the foundation, the first map of a whole literature for Western readers.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1598-9:
Chapters thirty-six and thirty-seven of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands pair commerce with war in 1598 and 1599. Commercial prospects of Holland come first, with the travels of John Huygen van Linschoten. His stolen Portuguese sea-knowledge opened the East Indies to Dutch ships. The republic's future sails in this chapter.

Military operations follow: Orsoy besieged, Rheinberg advanced upon, and Spanish outrages in peaceful provinces. Albert and Isabella arrive at Brussels as the new sovereigns. Van der Does leads a naval expedition against Spain's coasts. Motley balances the ledgers of a state becoming an empire while still fighting for its life. Trade pays for the war; the war guards the trade. Few chapters show his republic's double nature, counting house and camp, so clearly.
holmes-auriferous-gravel-man-1899:
William Henry Holmes, a geologist with the United States survey, took up the California gold gravel claims in 1899. Men had claimed stone tools and a skull from deep gold beds as proof of old man in the west. Holmes had dug in those fields and knew the ground well.

He goes through the famed finds one by one, the Calaveras skull first of all. Each, he shows, is a hoax, a plant, or a late thing sunk in old beds by chance. His paper shut the case for deep age man in the gold state for good.
inge-christian-mysticism-1899:
William Ralph Inge, later famous as the gloomy Dean of Saint Paul's in London, gave the Bampton Lectures printed in 1899 as Christian Mysticism. The lectures survey the mystical tradition from the church fathers to the moderns. Inge writes as a scholar who also practiced the life he describes.

He traces Plotinus's influence on Christian prayer, the medieval mystics, and the quiet teachers of the inner way. Inge defends mysticism as the vital core of religion rather than a fringe oddity for specialists. The book made his name and remains a landmark history of Christian mysticism in English.
ireland-bewitching-relation-1699:
Ireland left few witchcraft prints, which makes Daniel Higgs's 1699 relation the more prized. The Wonderfull and True Relation tells of a young girl in Ireland said to be bewitched. It even prints a receipt, or cure, meant to free her from the spell.

Accusation and remedy sit side by side in the text, charge first and folk cure after. Readers see both the fear a strange illness raised and the means a household used against it. Irish cases rarely reached print at all in this period. The small pamphlet thus holds an outsized place in the record.
jackson-zoroaster-1899:
Abraham Valentine Williams Jackson, a Columbia professor, gave the lectures printed in 1899 as Zoroaster, the Prophet of Ancient Iran. Jackson had traveled in Persia and India to study the faith at its sources. The book helped found Iranian studies in America.

He rebuilds the prophet's life from the hymns of the Avesta, the scriptures that bear Zoroaster's name, and from Greek reports. The lectures weigh legend against history with a scholar's care and a traveler's eye. For English readers, Jackson's life of Zoroaster long stood as the classic account of the prophet. He writes for students, but his book reached travelers and teachers far beyond Columbia.
james-talks-to-teachers-1899:
Talks to Teachers, published in 1899, gathers James's lectures to teachers on psychology, joined with addresses to students on some of life's ideals. James had lectured to teachers for years and wrote down his counsel with a practitioner's warmth.

He warns teachers against turning psychology into rigid rules, and urges attention to habit, interest, and the child's own native impulses. The student addresses praise ideals like tolerance and the strenuous mood, life lived with effort and faith. The book shaped American teaching talk for a generation. Its humanity, more than its science, has kept it in print.
jenner-further-observations-variolae-179:
One year after his first Inquiry, Edward Jenner issued Further Observations on the Variolae Vaccinae in 1799. The London sequel adds fresh cases of cowpox vaccination to the record. Early critics had raised doubts and reported failures. Jenner answers them point by point with new evidence.

He sorts true cowpox from other sores that could mislead a doctor. Careful rules for taking and using the matter run through the pages. The aim was to make the new practice safe in other hands. Together with the Inquiry, the sequel built trust in vaccination. Readers see a claim being tested in public. The tone stays modest and exact.
jewett-queens-twin-1899:
Houghton Mifflin issued The Queen's Twin and Other Stories at Boston in 1899. Jewett dedicated the book to Susan Burley Cabot. Contents list A Dunnet Shepherdess, Martha's Lady, and The Night Before Thanksgiving beside the title tale.

The title story concerns a Maine woman sure she is Queen Victoria's twin, born in the same hour. Her whole village kindly humors the fond belief. Other tales treat aging, loneliness, and the odd dignity of country folk. The opening pages note how Maine's busy fleet once bound its coast to foreign shores. The book reads as a late, mellow harvest from a fond observer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdima-called-a: Abdima is a name borne by several Palestinian amoraim, also known in Babylonia. It appears in like forms as Abdimi, Abudma, and Abudmi. One bearer is named in the Palestinian Talmud simply as R. Abdimi, with no added surname. He flourished in the fourth century. His peers were R. Jose II, who outlived him, and R. Eliezer II. More men of the name stand in the Palestinian Talmud and in midrashic writing. The entry notes that some of them are treated under the name Dimi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abulafia-abraha:
Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia was one of the first cabalists. He was born in 1240 at Saragossa, in Aragon. He died some time after 1291. His parents took him young to Tudela, in Navarre. There his father taught him Bible and Talmud. His father died when Abraham was eighteen. Two years later he began a life of travel that never stopped.

He went first toward Palestine, hoping to find the fabled river Sambation and the lost Ten Tribes. War damage stopped him at Acre. At Capua he studied the works of Maimonides under a doctor named Hillel. Back in Spain he had visions. At thirty-one he took up the book "Yeẓirah" at Barcelona. Letters, numbers, and vowel points became signs of being for him. He taught that men could rise, by rites and strict practice, to the rank of prophets. Many pupils took up his path.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adhan-799: Adhan is a family name of north Africa. Its first form was Aldahhan. In old Arabic that means an oil merchant. In the Arabic of Morocco it means a painter. Moses Adhan is known from a legal call he put out in Iyyar, 1732. A script holds a lament by him for the Ninth of Ab. Jacob Adhan wrote a hymn in Hebrew and Arabic both. In it Israel speaks to God as a bride to her love. It asks for new help in hard times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agla-899: Agla is a cabalistic sign used as a charm. It is built from the first letters of four Hebrew words. Those words open the second blessing of the Shemoneh 'Esreh. They mean Thou art mighty for ever, O Lord. Isaac Luria tied its letter count to thirty-five. Other cabalists link the name to thirty-five angel princes of the Torah. The four letters sat on wooden dishes in Christian homes too. There they were held to guard against fire, with a German sense read into the letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahmed-pasha-999:
Ahmed Pasha was a Turkish vizier and viceroy of Egypt under Solyman the Magnificent. His posts were rewards for valor at the conquest of Rhodes in 1523. He had hoped for the grand vizier's place instead. In his disappointment he plotted to make Egypt his own kingdom.

He pressed the Jewish mint farmer Abraham de Castro to put his name on the coins. De Castro carried the signed order to Constantinople and exposed the plot. Ahmed then turned on the Jews of Cairo. He held twelve leading Jews hostage for a vast payment, under threat of death to all. As the deadline neared, in March 1524, conspirators attacked him in his bath. He was later captured and beheaded. Egyptian Jews long kept the date as the Cairo Purim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alnaqua-1299:
Alnaqua was a leading family of Spanish Jews. First word of the family comes late in the twelfth century. Its members spread to North Africa and Turkey. Two of the first named men died by court slander. That was at Toledo about the year 1200. Three brothers of the next age all died young.

Ephraim ben Israel gets the fullest tale. He founded the Jewish group at Tlemçen in North Africa. Tale says he fled Spain on a lion. He cured a king's daughter when others had failed. He asked no gold as his fee. He asked that Jews near Tlemçen be joined in one group. He died in 1442.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amigo-abraham-1: Abraham Amigo was a noted rabbi of Palestine. He worked about the middle of the seventeenth century. His peers held him in high regard. They prized both his piety and his learning. He wrote a book called New Fruit. It treats one part of the Shulhan Aruk. The part runs from the laws of Passover to the end. That book has been lost, the entry says. A large book of his responsa also existed. Azulai saw that work and noted it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-andrade-velosin:
Jacob de Andrade Velosino was a physician born in Pernambuco in 1657, to Portuguese parents. Like many Maranos, his family had fled to Brazil while it was a Dutch colony. When Portugal retook Brazil, he moved to Holland and practiced medicine at The Hague, then later at Antwerp.

Andrade wrote a polemic against Spinoza's philosophy. He also turned Saul Morteira's Torat Mosheh into Portuguese. His largest work, a six-volume defense of Judaism against Isaac Jaquelot's book on the Messiah, stayed in manuscript. The entry presents him as a doctor who spent much of his pen on religious debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antipater-1599:
Antipater was the eldest son of Herod the Great and his Idumean wife Doris. Born about 38 B.C., he was executed in 4 B.C. His mother was cast off soon after his birth, and he grew up in obscurity and want.

Herod's brother and sister, fearing the sons of Mariamne, brought mother and son back to the palace. From that day, the entry says, Antipater's life was one long bid to supplant every rival in his father's favor. At Rome he fed Herod lies about Alexander and Aristobulus and their wish to avenge their mother. The entry follows his schemes to their end, a plot against Herod's own life and the throne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aram-geshur-169: Aram-Geshur was an Aramean district and small kingdom near Maachah. Second Samuel, chapter 15, verse 8, and Joshua, chapter 13, verse 13, link the two lands. David married a daughter of its king, as Second Samuel, chapter 3, verse 3, records. She became the mother of Absalom. When Absalom killed his brother Amnon, he fled to Geshur for shelter, the entry adds from Second Samuel, chapter 13, verse 38. It gives no size, capital, or later history for the little kingdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arnon-1799:
Eastern Palestine's river Arnon, now the Wady Mojib, runs about 45 miles from the desert to the Dead Sea. Its name may mean noisy, fitting the lower course. The stream spreads to 100 feet wide in places, yet stays narrow for most of its length. Shallow in summer, it runs 8 or 10 feet deep in winter. Near its mouth it drops through a steep, narrow gorge between high limestone hills, then widens into an estuary nearly 100 feet across.

As a boundary the Arnon mattered for centuries. It parted Moabites from Amorites, then Moab from the tribes of Reuben and Gad. King Mesha's inscription says he drove Israel from Ataroth and built a road along the river. Ruins of bridges and forts near its banks, and a mention of its fords in Isaiah, mark its old weight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascoli-david-d-:
David Ascoli, an Italian writer of about the middle of the sixteenth century, wrote the Apologia Hebraeorum, printed at Strasburg in 1559. In it he protested a decree of Pius IV. The decree ordered all Jews in Catholic lands to dress in orange or yellow, so that they could be told apart from Christians at sight.

Free words cost him dearly. Both Ascoli and Cinelli, who praised the book in his Bibliotheca Volante, suffered a long term of imprisonment. Their offense was open criticism of the church authorities. The entry is brief, and its facts are stark: a printed defense of the Jews, a badge decree, praise from one fellow writer, and prison for both men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-attorney-2099:
Attorney here means a legal agent who acts for another in court. The entry opens with a flat point: attorneys at law are unknown in Jewish law. Judges questioned the witnesses themselves. In criminal cases the judges had to guard the prisoner's rights. Agents in fact, though, could appear and run a suit, within set limits.

Talmudic law let an agent receive property from a trustee when no one disputed it. Contested cases were barred at first. The Geonim later opened them, and by the eleventh century agents could act in all cases. The power had to be written, in set words. The entry then covers pay, expenses, who may act, and how the power ends. Women, slaves, and even non-Jews could serve as agents for Jewish claimants, with limits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azariah-2199:
Azariah, in this entry, was a Palestinian scholar of the fourth generation of the amoraim, in the fourth century. He is often quoted beside R. Aḥa, R. Judan, and R. Judah b. Simon. A few rulings on points of law carry his name. The entry doubts they are truly his, and assigns them rather to R. Ezra.

Azariah's real field was the Haggadah, the lore and story side of rabbinic teaching. He passes on sayings of earlier masters and quotes men of his own day. The entry works to fix his true century, against scholars who made him a pupil of R. Mana the Second. His fancy could build a teaching out of single letters. From the word eshel, the tamarisk Abraham planted at Beersheba, he drew three duties of welcome: meat for the guest, drink, and an escort on the road.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacharach-abrah:
Abraham Samuel Bacharach was a rabbi. He was born about 1575 and died at Gernsheim on May 26, 1615. He seems to have come from Worms. At Prague in 1600 he married Eva, granddaughter of the chief rabbi Löwe ben Bezalel. He served as rabbi in Turbin, Kolin, and Pohrlitz. Then he was called to the great congregation of Worms.

Guild-fed riots against the Jews drove Bacharach from Worms. He died in exile and was buried at Alsbach. He was honored for learning and piety. He stood firm against the Frankfort rabbis, who claimed rank above all other German rabbis. His grandson later printed some of his legal answers. He also wrote on the Jewish calendar, against Christianity, and in verse for the liturgy. Some works survive only in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barzillai-2599:
Barzillai was a wealthy noble of Rogelim in Gilead. When David fled from Absalom, Barzillai met him at Mahanaim with two other chiefs. They brought food for the king and his tired men.

After Absalom died, Barzillai escorted David across the Jordan. David invited him to live at court, but the old man chose to stay home and sent his son Chimham instead. On his deathbed David asked Solomon to care for Barzillai's sons. The entry also notes a priestly clan later called Children of Barzillai in the census lists of Ezra and Nehemiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bebai-b-abba-r-:
Bebai ben Abba was a Palestinian teller of traditions, rarely cited and of uncertain date. His name also appears as Bebai Rabbah and in other spellings across editions. The entry centers on one teaching of his that entered prayer.

Bebai praised a form of confession for the Day of Atonement, part of which the evening ritual still uses. It asks pardon for sins, wrongs, and errors, and vows not to repeat them. The entry then weighs whether he is the same man as Bebai ben Abin. That confession rests on a verse from Isaiah about the wicked man leaving his way and his thoughts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belasco-david-2:
David Belasco was an American dramatist born in San Francisco in 1858, of English parents. He began stage work as a boy and by 1878 managed a San Francisco theater. He also directed touring companies while learning to write and adapt plays.

In New York from 1880, Belasco won his first clear success with a play of 1884. He then directed at the Lyceum and wrote hit plays with partners. Later works named here include Zaza and Madame Butterfly. The entry ranks him at the head of American stage authors of his day. A later play set in Maryland, staged in the middle 1890s, added fresh strength to his growing name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benary-franz-fe:
Franz Benary was a German scholar of the East, born at Cassel on March 22, 1805. He died at Berlin on Feb. 7, 1880. He studied at Bonn and at Halle, where the teacher Gesenius first turned him toward the tongues of the East. At Berlin he heard Hegel and Schleiermacher, and he sat under Bopp for Sanskrit.

From 1829 to 1831 he taught the tongues of the East at Berlin. In 1830 he brought out the old Hindu poem Nalodaya. In 1831 he rose to a post in the school of theology there. His talks dealt with the Bible, with Semitic tongues, and with old scripts. A work on Hebrew levirate law won him a degree from Halle in 1835.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ze-eb-:
Benjamin Ze'eb of Slonim was a Russian Talmudist of the late eighteenth century, said to be a pupil of Elijah of Wilna. Letters under his name, printed as Purifier of the Ritual, stage his slow turn toward Ḥasidism. A friend answers his doubts, and a dialogue with a Ḥasid meets nineteen objections one by one.

The entry then shows the letters are a made-up work. They cite a book not printed until 1819 and speak of Elijah as dead years before his death. The piece stands as a clever defense of Ḥasidism in letter form, and its true author stays unknown.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berliner-abraha:
Abraham Berliner, a German theologian and historian, was born on May 2, 1833, at Obersitzko, in Posen. He took a doctorate at Leipsic and served as preacher and teacher at Arnswalde. In 1865 Berlin called him to run a religious school, and in 1873 he became professor of Jewish history at the new rabbinical seminary.

His edition of Rashi's commentary in 1866 first made his name. Work in the archives of Italy fed a stream of historical books. He edited a scholarly journal for two decades and revived a society that printed old Jewish texts. He also answered attacks on Jewish scholars in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bet-hillel-and-:
Bet Hillel and Bet Shammai were rival schools in Palestine. They flourished in the first century. Both schools shaped the oral law more than any others. Their founders had few disputes between them. Their disciples had very many. The Talmud preserves 316 controversies between the schools. They cover laws, interpretations, and guard-rules.

The entry draws a clear contrast in character. The Hillelites were mild and peace-loving. The Shammaites were stern and unbending. Only rarely did the Shammaites take the lenient side. The entry also links Shammaite views to the Zealots. That link sharpened conflict in Jerusalem's last days. It even split public worship between the schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-aven-3199: Beth-Aven was a city on the border of Benjamin. It stood east of Bethel and west of Michmash. Joshua places it in the wilderness there. The entry recalls a battle at the site. Saul's forces defeated the Philistines near it. That fight is told in First Samuel. Hosea uses the name Beth-Aven several times. The entry says it is probably a disguise there. In Hosea it stands for Beth-el. Its calves are named as objects of idolatry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bilhah-3299: Bilhah here is a locality in southern Judea. First Chronicles names it in chapter four. The entry identifies it with two other names. It is evidently the same as Balah in Joshua. It also matches Ba'alah in the same book. The entry is only two lines long. It gives no events tied to the place. No modern site is proposed for it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-moses-339: Moses Bloch was a German rabbi. He was born at Gailingen, Baden, in 1805. He died at Buchau on March 3, 1841. He studied Talmud at Endingen, Manheim, and Carlsruhe. Then he entered the University of Heidelberg. In 1829 he became assistant rabbi at Oberdorf. In 1834 he became rabbi at Buchau. He belonged to the liberal religious party. Besides sermons, he published one essay. It treated Jewish fasts in Geiger's journal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonan-david-349: David Bonan was rabbi of the Livornian community of Tunis. He died there in 1850. After his death his family paid to print his works. They include two books of responsa, a work on ritual divorce, and notes on Solomon Adret. With Judah Levy of Gibraltar he wrote on women's hair covering and on the treatise Sanhedrin. He also edited works by his father and by others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brichany-3699: Brichany is a town in the government of Bessarabia, Russia. In 1898 it had 7,303 Jewish inhabitants in a total population of 8,094. Its Jewish artisans number 972, most of them furriers. They export fur overcoats and caps to the extent of 25,000 per annum, as the entry phrases it. About twenty-five families work in tobacco culture and gardening. About 700 Jews are day laborers there. They earn from 10 to 30 copecks per day, the count closes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-budinger-moses-: Moses Israel Büdinger, son of Isaac, taught at Metz around the turn of the nineteenth century. He gave himself to Hebrew grammar and literature and trained many grammarians and fine Hebrew writers. All his listed works appeared at Metz. They include a Hebrew reading manual and a shorter extract, both in 1816, plus an essay on Purim with the roll of Esther. His festival prayer commentary ran to nine volumes in 1817. Later works covered a bar mitzvah lecture and the penitential prayers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cahen-isidore-3:
Isidore Cahen was a French scholar and journalist born at Paris in 1826. He shone at the Collége Charlemagne and entered the Ecole Normale in philosophy. Classmates included Taine and Sarcey. He took his teaching degree in 1849 and won a philosophy post the next year. A clerical press campaign soon cost him that chair.

Cahen turned down other posts the government offered and chose journalism. He wrote for the Journal des Débats and served for years on Le Temps. At his father's death he took over the Archives Israélites and ran it until his own death in 1902. He also lectured on history and literature at the Paris Jewish seminary from 1859 to 1878. His books plead for liberty of conscience and treat the soul's immortality among Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caper-berry-tra: Caper berry is the right rendering of a Hebrew word in Ecclesiastes, the entry argues, not desire. Old versions in Greek, Latin, and Syriac all give caper berry. Talmud passages back them and sort the berry from the plant's shoots and flower cases. The plant is a woody, trailing shrub that grows on old walls and in rock cracks around the Mediterranean. Its big white flowers carry many long lilac stamens. The pickled caper of trade is the flower bud, not the berry. The berries themselves were eaten.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-casimir-iv-jage:
Casimir IV Jagellon, grand duke of Lithuania and king of Poland, was born in 1427 and died at Grodno in 1492. He took the grand duchy in 1440 and the Polish throne in 1447. For much of his reign, Jews in Poland and Lithuania fared well, as under Casimir the Great.

At Troki he granted Jews the Magdeburg law, with a Jewish bailiff elected by the community. When fire at Posen burned the old privilege document, he renewed those rights and added new ones. Clerical pressure led him to abolish the privileges in 1454. Riots at Cracow followed in 1464, killing about thirty Jews. The Diet confirmed Jewish rights again in 1467. The entry notes that Casimir died owing Jews unpaid debts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chenstochov-pol:
Chenstochov, in Polish Czenstochowa, is a city in Russian Poland. In 1897 it held 12,500 Jews in a total of 45,130 people. Most Jews were merchants, and 2,155 were artisans. Tailors led, at 801, then shoemakers at 228. Jews owned seven estates nearby and, in 1898, 57 factories with 397 workers.

Jewish factories first made medallions with pictures of the Virgin for pilgrims to the city. When that trade was barred to Jews, they turned to toy making. Fifteen factories took it up, with Jews as 80 per cent of the workers. A liquor monopoly left eighty families without work. Passover aid requests rose year by year, reaching 708 families in 1898. In September 1902 the city saw a Jewish uprising, soon put down by the authorities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ciudad-real-for:
Ciudad Real, once Villa Real, capital of La Mancha in New Castile, was founded in 1255 by Alfonso X of Castile. Jews from nearby Alarcos were among its first settlers. By 1290 its Jewry paid 26,486 maravedis in taxes, more than all other townsfolk together, and it held its own quarter apart from the Christians.

The entry maps that Jewry street by street, from the Great Synagogue to the cemetery of about 3,000 square feet. Peace held under Pedro I, and service to Henry II brought grants paid from Jewish taxes. Then came the persecution of 1391, which struck the city hard in June of that year. Inquisition work began there in April, 1483.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-moses-ben: Moses ben Eliezer Cohen was a moralist who lived in Germany, probably at Coblenz, in the later fourteenth century. He wrote an ethical work called Sefer Hasidim, or Book of the Pious. The entry dates its writing to 1473 and its printing to Warsaw in 1866. The book also bears the title Sefer ha-Maskil. It gives a short picture of Jewish piety as then understood. The entry calls it a useful source for the history of Jewish culture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-darda-4899: Darda is one of the wise men whose wisdom Solomon surpassed. First Kings names him with Ethan, Heman, and Chalcol, as a son of Mahol. Chronicles calls him Dara, a son of Zerah. Rabbinic fancy matched each sage to a great figure of old. Darda stands for the generation of knowledge, the wilderness generation. Ethan is Abraham in that reading. Heman is Moses, and Chalcol is Joseph. The entry is short. It rests on the two Bible verses and on Rashi's note to Kings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davis-frederick: Frederick Davis was an archeologist born at Cheltenham in 1843 who died in London on July 14, 1900. He was the eldest son of John Davis of Derby and was educated at the Derby and Belper schools. He first worked in engineering, as a partner in a Derby foundry, then turned to archeology. He sat on the council of the Society of Antiquaries and on the Silchester Excavation Committee. He wrote on the finds at the Roman British city of Silchester, and on Derbyshire place names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-derceto-5099:
Derceto was a goddess of the Syrians, better known under her fuller name Atargatis. The entry is mostly a study of that name. Second Maccabees mentions her sanctuary indirectly. Diodorus and Lucian use the short form Derceto, and the Talmud has a form that may match it once a letter's sound is allowed for.

A bilingual inscription from Palmyra, dated to the year 140, proves the name in both languages. Coins of the Syrian city Hierapolis carry it too. The entry breaks the name into two parts: Athtar, a goddess of fertility and wells in South Arabian inscriptions, and a second part probably meaning time. It weighs Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic evidence for each step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dillon-maria-lv: Maria Lvovna Dillon was a Russian sculptress born at St. Petersburg in 1859. She entered the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts there in 1875. She graduated in 1888 with a gold medal for her statue "Andromeda." She then studied in Paris and Italy. Of her works shown since 1888, the entry names "Nyega," "The Slave," "Tatyana," and "Ophelia." Emperor Nicholas II bought her Bacchante "Lily." In a contest of twenty-eight sculptors she won first prize for a design marking 200 years since St. Petersburg was founded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drabkin-abraham:
Abraham Drabkin was chief rabbi of St. Petersburg, born at Mohilev on the Dnieper in 1844. He came from an old-established family and studied Talmud from boyhood. He also learned Cabala from Hasidic rabbis. After graduating at the Wilna rabbinical institute, he taught there.

A scholarship took Drabkin to Breslau in 1871, where he studied under Grätz and Frankel. He took his doctorate in 1875 and became chief rabbi at St. Petersburg in 1876. During the anti-Jewish riots of 1882 he pressed Count Ignatiev in person. He also preached against anti-Semitism in Russian, a first among rabbis there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-easter-from-eos:
Easter is the Anglo-Saxon name for the Christian Passover, the feast of the Resurrection. The word comes from Eostre, a Teuton goddess of the rising day. Acts wrongly uses Easter for the Jewish Passover, the entry notes. At first Christians simply kept Pascha on the fourteenth of Nisan.

Churches in East and West drifted apart on the date. Some stressed Friday, the day of the Crucifixion. Others held to the Jewish fourteenth of Nisan. Holders of that date, the Quatrodecimani, were condemned as heretics. The Nicene Council settled the Christian Passover in 325.
