Easter became a solar feast, while Passover stayed lunar, so the two rarely share a day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-the-ast: Eliezer the Astronomer was a German scholar. He lived in the sixteenth century. His book Ge Hizzayon gathers star lore from three tongues. Hebrew, Arabic, and Latin sources all feed into it. He quotes a long list of older star experts. Copernicus may stand among them, one writer holds. In his preface he tells of a great work on the stars. One chapter of it treats Ibn Ezra at length. Two more works bear the plain name Eliezer. The entry cannot say if they are his as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elloji-shahir-e: Elloji Shahir was a Beni-Israel poet and singer. He lived at Bombay in India in the eighteenth century. His birth name was Elloji Nagawkar, the entry says. He came of a class allowed a plume in the turban. Men said he made up songs on the spot as he sang. His ballads treat faith and morals in two tongues. He sang them in Mahrati and in Hindustani. Some of those songs are still in hand today. The Peshwa's court at Poona called him to perform there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-ben-jac: Ephraim ben Jacob ha-Kohen was a Lithuanian Talmudist. He was born at Wilna in the year 1616. He died at Ofen in Hungary on June 3, 1678. The Chmielnicki attacks drove him from his home town. He had served as a judge in Wilna till then. Moravia took him in as a refugee from the storm. He held pulpits at Trebitsch and then at Ofen. His responsa were printed after his death at Sulzbach. A second work on the Pentateuch stayed in handwriting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ettlinger-jacob:
Jacob Ettlinger was a German rabbi and a leader of modern Orthodoxy, born at Carlsruhe on March 17, 1798. He died at Altona on December 7, 1871. His father taught him first, then Abraham Bing at Wurzburg, where he also attended the university. In 1836 he became chief rabbi of Altona, serving until his death.

Ettlinger stood for joining secular learning with strict hold on tradition. He led the protest of 173 rabbis against the Brunswick Conference of 1844. In 1845 he founded the first Orthodox journal, Der Zionswachter, with a Hebrew supplement. His pupils included Samson Raphael Hirsch and Israel Hildesheimer. He was also the last German rabbi to act as a civil judge, a right Denmark ended in 1863.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fall-of-man-599:
The fall of man is the doctrine that humankind dropped from a blameless, happy state through Adam and Eve's disobedience in Eden. As the entry sets it out, the first pair were made perfect and sinless. Their wants were met, and they felt no shame. Had they obeyed, they would never have known guilt or death.

By eating the forbidden fruit they fell under a curse of labor and pain. Joy, innocence, and deathlessness were lost for good. Their descendants share the taint, the doctrine holds, so none escapes death or sin. The entry then sets Genesis beside like tales from other peoples. A Zoroastrian story of Yima, cast from paradise after sin, is named as a close match.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-florida-6199:
Florida is the most southern state of the United States, washed by the Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico. Little is known of its early Jewish history. A London plan of 1825 to send Jews there as colonists came to nothing. Two Florida Jews are named for the Civil War. One served in the Milton Artillery. The other was captured and died at Elmira, New York.

A congregation named Beth El was founded at Pensacola in 1874. A second, Ahavath Chesed, followed at Jacksonville in 1882. Aid societies formed at Jacksonville and Ocala, and religious bodies at Tampa and Key West. Morris Dzialinsky was twice elected mayor of Jacksonville. The entry puts the Jewish population at about 3,000. The state's whole population in 1890 was 391,422.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-frankel:
Simon Wolf Fränkel-Spira headed the Jewish community of Prague for two decades from May 20, 1724. He died on June 9, 1745. He was a firm defender of his oppressed fellow Jews. Wealth came to him by inheritance, and wide business brought him into contact with the great of the land. He founded an orphan asylum. He also raised the level of the Jewish schools.

Fränkel loved display, the entry admits, and was not free of ambition. For the birth of Archduke Joseph in 1741 he staged a costly festival at his own expense. He rode in a carriage drawn by six horses. The show roused envy, and the mob later looted the Jewry. Jews were murdered and many more wounded. Then came Maria Theresia's order expelling all Jews from Bohemia. Broken by insult and slander, he died days after signing a plea for aid to the Jews of London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frizzi-benedett:
Benedetto Frizzi, also named Benzion Raphael Kohen, was an Italian physician and writer born at Ostiano in 1756. He died there on May 30, 1844. Taught by Jesuits at Mantua, he was the first Jew to attend a public school there. He took his medical degree at Pavia and later settled as a doctor in Triest in 1789.

His largest work runs to six volumes on Mosaic law. It treats food rules, marriage, birth, sickness, mourning, and town life. An early defense of the Jews against an attack on them led him toward wider study of Jewish life and law. He also wrote notes on the Talmud and works on medicine, mathematics, and music.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gamaliel-vi-649: Gamaliel VI was the last patriarch. A decree of October 17, 415, by Honorius and Theodosius II stripped him of his high honors and of the patriarchate itself. The charge was that he had flouted the special laws against Jews. He had built new synagogues and judged cases between Jews and Christians. At his death the office ended. A decree of 426 sent the patriarch tax to the state chest. He also seems to have worked as a physician.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-girgashites-659: The Girgashites were one of the nations holding the land of Canaan before the Israelite conquest. In Hebrew the name appears only in the singular, with the definite article. Genesis x. 16 and I Chronicles i. 14 call "the Girgashite" the fifth son of Canaan, while other passages use the name for the whole tribe. Their exact territory was never located, though it lay west of the Jordan. Josephus, the entry notes, said that in his time nothing was known of them beyond the name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-glaser-eduard-6:
Eduard Glaser was an Austrian traveler and Arabist born March 15, 1855, at Deutsch-Rust, Bohemia. He studied mathematics and geodesy at the Prague polytechnical school while learning Arabic on his own. After stays in Vienna and Tunis, he reached South Arabia in 1883 and crossed it in several directions.

On later journeys in 1885-86 and 1887-88 he pushed on to Marib, the ancient Saba, collecting more than 1,000 Himyaritic and Sabean inscriptions. A fourth trip in 1892 took him from Aden toward Mecca; he mapped the country, gathered about 800 more inscriptions, and recorded dialects such as Mahra. His books cover Arabia's history and geography up to Muhammad's time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grozovski-judah: Judah Löb Grozovski was a Russian Hebraist. He was born at Pogosti, in the Minsk government, in 1861. He studied at Volozhin's yeshibah. He then learned teaching method at Wilna's Institute for Hebrew Teachers. At twenty-seven he went to Palestine. He taught Hebrew in many places there. In 1896 the Jaffa agricultural school hired him as Hebrew teacher. In 1899 he moved to the Miḳweh Yisrael colony in the same post. His textbooks include graded Hebrew courses of 1895-97. His "Millon" of 1900 is a Hebrew-Russian-German dictionary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hadad-6999:
Hadad was the name of an Aramaic storm and weather god, and perhaps of an Edomite one too. The name comes from a root meaning to make a loud noise, like thunder. It lives inside personal names such as Hadadezer and Benhadad. In Assyrian records the same god appears as Hadad-idri, and he may be the same as Rimmon.

Much of the entry turns on Hadadrimmon in Zechariah xii. 11, a byword for deep grief. Older readers took it as a place near Megiddo tied to mourning for a fallen king, most often Josiah. Later scholars read it as mourning for the god himself, akin to Tammuz. The entry weighs those views, notes the god's links to Moloch rites, and leaves the hard case open.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halle-aaron-ben:
Aaron ben Wolf Halle, also called Wolfsohn, was a translator and commentator of the Bible. Born at Halle in 1754, he died at Fürth on March 20, 1835. He followed Moses Mendelssohn. From 1792 to 1807 he taught at the Königliche Wilhelmsschule at Breslau, and in 1797 he edited the periodical "Ha-Meassef." He helped found the Gesellschaft der Freunde in Berlin in 1792.

With Joel Löwe he edited Mendelssohn's German Song of Solomon in 1788. His own versions of Lamentations, Ruth, and Esther came out that year. He also rendered Kings, Job with a Hebrew commentary, the Hafṭarot with friends, and part of Habakkuk. His "Abtalion" is a Hebrew primer often reprinted. He also wrote "Jeschurun," a defense of Judaism, and a three-act family play.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hasan-ben-mashi:
Hasan ben Mashiah was a Karaite teacher of the ninth or tenth century. One account says he argued in public with Saadia and later wrote against him. Another account places him in Bagdad, debating a Christian doctor. The entry notes that the second account's date does not fit his lifetime.

A piece of his attack on Saadia survives. It deals with how old the Jewish calendar is. Other writers quote his view on inheritance law. Ibn Ezra names him among the leading Karaite Bible explainers. Some books on law and belief were wrongly put under his name, the entry warns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilprin-louis-: Louis Heilprin, born in Hungary on July 2, 1851, was an American encyclopedist and a son of Michael Heilprin. The family came to the United States in 1856. He was educated in private. He wrote for the second edition of the "American Cyclopaedia," where his father had served as an editor. His "Historical Reference Book" came out in 1884 and reached a sixth edition by 1899. In 1902 he joined the "New International Encyclopedia." He also worked with his brother Angelo on a new gazetteer of the world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herod-ii-7599: Herod II was king of Chalcis, a son of Aristobulus and Berenice, and a grandson of Herod I. He was brother of Agrippa I and Herodias. He died in 48-49 C.E. His two marriages, to Mariamne and then to Berenice, and his sons are named. In 41 C.E. Claudius granted him Chalcis at Agrippa's request. After Agrippa died, he oversaw the Temple and named two high priests during four years in that role.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hillel-ii-7699:
Hillel II was patriarch from 330 to 365, son and successor of Judah III. He is quoted only twice on laws, the entry notes. Tradition credits him with a calendar enactment of lasting benefit. It let Jews everywhere keep festivals on the fixed days.

Calendar meetings had been banned under Constantius, putting distant congregations at risk. A coded Talmud letter shows the strain of secret intercalation. Hillel chose to issue an authorized calendar for all time, though it loosened Diaspora ties to Palestine. Emperor Julian honored him and wrote in friendship, the entry adds. Julian also promised better terms for Jews and burned their tax rolls, by his own letter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hodaviah-7799: Hodaviah is a name the entry gives to two men, in numbered order. The first was a son of Elioenai, among the last members of Judah's royal line, in First Chronicles. The second was a Levite who founded a key family of Levites, in Ezra. A parallel list in Nehemiah writes the name in a variant form, the entry notes. The entry is only a few lines long. It gives no deeds, dates, or sayings for either man beyond those two identifications and their verse sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hoshaiah-ze-era: Hoshaiah Ze'era de-min Habraya was a Palestinian teacher of the third period of amoraim who died about 350. His surname Ze'era, meaning the minor or junior, set him apart from Hoshaiah the Elder. Habraya may name his birthplace, as the Tosafot claim. Rashi instead reads it as a society of colleagues. He belonged to the rabbis of southern Galilee. He may be the Hoshaiah who was brother of Hanina. Only one legal ruling is told in his name, in tractate Niddah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-incense-8099:
Incense, the aromatic spice and gum burned in worship, filled Eastern life: garments, beds and honored guests were perfumed, and censers passed after meals. Egyptian kings are pictured censer in hand, and Herodotus reports 1,000 talents burned at Bel's yearly feast. In Israel, though, altar incense appears late in the Bible and seldom in the historic and prophetic books.

The Temple mixture grew from four named ingredients to eleven or thirteen. Three hundred and sixty-eight minas were prepared once a year, one for each day and three extra for the Day of Atonement, with a quarter kab of Sodom salt. Later tradition read the incense chapter as a guard against plague and death in the house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-melch:
Isaac ben Melchizedek of Siponto was an Italian rabbi and Talmudist who lived about 1110 to 1170. He was born in Siponto, a seaport of Apulia and an old seat of Jewish learning, where his father was a noted Talmudist. For reasons the entry does not give, he moved to Salerno. There the traveler Benjamin of Tudela met him and later called him the great rabbi. Isaac put a legal question to R. Tam and wrote to the rabbis of Rome about a hard mishnah.

His chief work was a commentary on the Mishnah, probably covering the whole of it. Only the part on Seder Zera'im survives in full, printed in the Wilna Talmud of 1890. His comments are concise and clear, close to Rashi's manner, and draw on Greek, Arabic, and Italian word likenesses. The entry credits him with opening the way for Talmud study in Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-of-corbei: Jacob of Corbeil, called the Saint, was a French tosafist of the twelfth century, brother of Judah of Corbeil, who wrote tosafot to many tractates. He is at times mixed up with Jacob ha-Levi, the Pious, of Marvège. Aaron ben Hayyim ha-Kohen praised him highly in a commentary on the prayer book. Jacob wrote tosafot to several Talmudic treatises, and the received Tosafot quote him often. The Memorbuch of Mayence lists him among the martyrs of Corbeil. The entry gives no dates for his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jagel-abraham-b:
Abraham ben Hananiah dei Galicchi Jagel was an Italian teacher of religion, thinker, and cabalist who lived in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Born at Monselice, he lived in turn at Luzzara, Venice, Ferrara, and Sassuolo. Older writers wrongly said he had become a Christian censor named Camillo, a claim later scholars disproved.

In 1615 bandits seized Jagel near Luzzara while he sought ransom for a rich companion, and rabbis of Modena helped free them both. His best known book is a catechism printed at Venice in 1587, shaped in part on clergy models yet Jewish in content. He also wrote on prayer against plague, on a wife's duties, and a four-part work on Cabala and nature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeroboam-8599:
Jeroboam is the name of two kings of Israel, and the entry treats the first at length. Jeroboam son of Nebat was an Ephraimite who won Solomon's favor by hard work on the city wall. The prophet Ahijah met him, tore a new cloak into twelve pieces, and told him to take ten, a sign that he would rule ten tribes after Solomon.

When Solomon sought his life, Jeroboam fled to Egypt. After Solomon died, the northern tribes rejected Rehoboam's harsh answer at Shechem and crowned Jeroboam instead. So he became founder of the separate kingdom of Israel. The entry follows his reign and that of his later namesake in the divided kingdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jochebed-8699:
Jochebed was the wife and aunt of Amram and the mother of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. A daughter of Levi, she was born in Egypt. In the birth story of Moses she is not named at first, only called a daughter of Levi. From those spare facts the entry builds its Bible notice, then turns to rabbinic tradition.

The rabbis match Jochebed with Shiphrah, a midwife who defied Pharaoh's order to kill newborn boys. They also call her the thirty-third child in a count that seems to give only thirty-two. By their reckoning she was 130 years old when Moses was born, and a wit in the Midrash calls Moses worth 600,000 Israelites, so that she bore a nation at one birth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-b-nehorai-: Jose b. Nehorai was a Palestinian amora of the first generation whose legal rulings were passed on by Johanan. His best-known teaching reads a verse in Ecclesiastes to mean that God always helps the persecuted. Even when a good man pursues a bad one, he said, God sides with the one being chased. He also held that rites taught to children serve to train them rather than bind them. On taxes, he said collectors should not deal harshly, except for school taxes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-zadd: Joseph ben Zaddik was a rabbi in Arevalo, Spain, during the fifteenth century. His book Zeker Zaddik treats ritual matters in fifty chapters and survives only in manuscript. The last chapter is a chronicle of Jewish worthies from the Creation down to his own day. Its final entry is dated 1487. Events near his own time get fuller treatment, while the rest is names and dates, often much distorted. Neubauer printed that chapter and found its facts mostly shared with Abraham Zacuto's Yuhasin, from a common source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-justus-dr-pseud:
Dr. Justus was the pen name of Aaron Briman, a convert to Christianity who wrote against the Jews. He was born at Costinasti in Rumania about 1860. After study in Berlin, where he posed as strictly Orthodox, he turned Protestant, then Catholic at Paderborn. In 1883 his Judenspiegel set out 100 laws from the Shulhan Aruk, bent to show Jewish spite toward Christians.

When a paper that printed extracts was sued, Briman secretly helped the court's own expert attack and defend the book at once. Back in Austria he fed Rohling matter for his libels. In March 1885 he was jailed for fraud and then cast out of Austria. He went on to study medicine in Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaplan-abraham-:
Abraham Kaplan was a Russian Hebrew writer. He was born at Wilke on July 25, 1839. He died at Vienna on Feb. 2, 1897. He won a name at home as a good Hebrew writer. Then he moved to Vienna. He worked there as a publicist for the rest of his life.

The entry lists Kaplan's books one by one. He turned a German novel on Jewish secrets into Hebrew. He wrote a life of the Hebrew writer Abraham Mapu. He also put the third volume of Grätz's history of the Jews into Hebrew. Two satirical poems and a piece on the sun are named as well. He wrote often for the Hebrew press. His defense of Smolenskin drew a fierce pamphlet attack on him in 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kholm-chelm-929:
Kholm, also called Chelm, is a Russian district town in the government of Lublin. Its Jews appear in papers from 1550 to 1569. On Easter Day of 1580 an armed crowd fell on the synagogue during service. They stoned the windows and shot into the building. Many in the congregation were hurt. The loss was put at 2,000 gold ducats.

In the Cossack rising of 1648-49 most of the town's people were killed. About 400 of the dead were Jews. By 1897 the town held 19,236 people, and about 12,500 were Jews. Nearly all its trade lay in Jewish hands, the entry says. A long list of the town's rabbis closes the article. It runs from the late sixteenth century to the nineteenth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kraus-adolf-949: Adolf Kraus, an American lawyer born at Blowitz in Bohemia on Feb. 26, 1850, came to the United States at age fifteen. He worked on a farm, in a factory, and in a store. In 1871 he moved to Chicago and read law while in trade. He was admitted to the bar in 1877. City posts followed: the board of education from 1881 to 1887, corporation counsel in 1893, and civil service work in 1897. He also led Isaiah Temple and held high office in a Jewish fraternal order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lamp-perpetual-: Perpetual Lamp is the light kept burning in synagogues before the Holy Ark. A glass vessel holds a wick in olive oil, hung in a metal holder from the ceiling. The custom descends from the Temple, where a western light on the candlestick was said never to go out. Lighting this lamp is a chief act when a synagogue is dedicated. Rabbis read the light as a sign of God's presence in Israel. Others read it as the light of God's Law, which Israel must keep alive in the world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lebert-lewy-her: Hermann Lebert, born Lewy, was a German physician born at Breslau on June 9, 1813. He died at Bex in Switzerland on Aug. 1, 1878. Medicine at Berlin and Zurich ended in a degree in 1834. A year of Swiss botany travel and Paris study followed. He settled at Bex in 1838, then Paris in 1846. Zurich made him professor in 1853; Breslau called six years later. He quit in 1874. His many books advanced knowledge of disease and of spiders. He took the name Lebert on adopting Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levetus-celia-c:
Celia Levetus, born Celia Moss, was an English writer. She was born at Portsea in 1819 and died at Birmingham in 1873. She was a daughter of Joseph and Amelia Moss. At eighteen she and her sister Marion printed a book of poems, "Early Efforts," in 1838.

The sisters then issued a "Romance of Jewish History" in 1840 and "Tales of Jewish History" in 1843. Both books came out by subscription, with names like Bulwer Lytton and Lord Palmerston on the list. The sisters taught in London and started "The Sabbath Journal" in 1855, though it soon folded. Celia later married Lewis Levetus of Birmingham. Her last book, "The King's Physician," came out in 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-maurice-98:
Maurice Lévy, a French engineer, was born at Ribeauville, Alsace, on Feb. 28, 1838. He studied at the Ecole Polytechnique and the school of bridges and roads. He became an engineer in 1863. In the war of 1870-71 the state gave him charge of part of the artillery.

Lévy taught at the Ecole Centrale from 1875 and at the Collège de France from 1885. He also served on the geodetic survey commission. In 1888 he set up a boat-towing system that used overhead cables and steam power. The trial line ran at four kilometers an hour, but the system proved a failure. His books treat graphic statics and the energy principle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-linen-9999:
Linen, cloth made of flax, is covered here through its Hebrew names and its uses in the Bible. The entry gives the terms bad, shesh, and buz, with their Greek renderings. It notes linen in the Tabernacle covers, screens, and veil, and in the priests' garments.

Much of the entry weighs whether the three Hebrew terms name the same cloth or close forms of it. It cites the Septuagint, Josephus, Philo, and the Talmud. It also notes the rule that garments use only one kind of stuff, and that Levites were later allowed to wear linen garments too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-london-committe:
London Board of Deputies is a body formed to guard the interests of British Jews as a religious community. Its roots reach to a committee set up in 1745 to watch a naturalization bill in the Irish Parliament. In 1760 deputies of the Portuguese Jews attended court to pledge loyalty to George III.

German Jews joined in time, and by 1812 they sat on the board as full members. The board watched laws on marriage and labor, aided the fight for equal rights, and acted in the Damascus Affair. Sir Moses Montefiore led it from 1835 until his death. Elections in May, 1904, chose sixty-five deputies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luxemburg-10199:
Luxemburg, the small grand duchy of central Europe, is surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The article admits the sources do not show when Jews first settled there. The first record of a Jew in the duchy comes from a document of 1276. Through the Middle Ages its Jews lived in a ghetto with a gate, cemetery, and synagogue.

The entry traces a cycle of protection and attack. As chamber-serfs of the emperor, the Jews were taxed but also guarded by local princes. Charles IV ordered their safety kept during the Black Death in 1350. Yet in 1370 they were swept up in an expulsion from Brabant. In 1470 a mob plundered their houses and drove them to shelter in the castle. The article also notes a striking fact from 1644. The famous citadel of Luxemburg was built by a Jewish engineer, Isaac de Traybac.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maimon-maimun-b:
Maimon ben Joseph, father of Moses Maimonides, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Spanish exegete and moralist born about 1110, he studied under Joseph ibn Migash at Lucena. He rose to serve as a dayyan, a judge in Jewish law. His own writing was done in Arabic.

The article weighs what survives of his work. His commentary on the Pentateuch is lost except for fragments quoted by his grandson Abraham. He also wrote on the laws of ritual and festivals. Maimonides appears to quote him in his Mishnah commentary and in his great code. His one whole surviving work is a letter of consolation, long credited to his son. It was written at Fez in 1160, during years of forced conversion. The family left Fez in 1165 and reached Jerusalem that October. The entry restores a father long hidden by his son's fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marcuse-adolf-1:
Adolf Marcuse, a German astronomer, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Magdeburg on November 17, 1860, he studied at Strasburg and Berlin, taking his doctorate in 1884. Before graduating he joined the German expedition to South Carolina. That 1882 mission observed the transit of Venus.

The article follows his work on the wandering pole. After study at Pulkova, he ran Chile's national observatory at Santiago for two years. Back in Berlin he spent years measuring the periodic shifts of latitude. In 1891 he led an astronomical-geodetic expedition to Hawaii for the same problem. His observations greatly advanced the study of latitude change. He later built a large photographic zenith telescope in Berlin. His lectures treated the fixing of places by astronomy, for geographers and sailors alike. The entry preserves a specialist who chased the Earth's wobble across three oceans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mauschberger-le: Leopold Mauschberger, a biblical scholar of the eighteenth century, is recorded in a brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906, contributed by Crawford Howell Toy. Nothing of his life is given: no birthplace, no dates, and no teachers. His name survives only through his books. He wrote commentaries on the Pentateuch and the Earlier Prophets, printed at Olmütz in 1757, and a second set, printed there a year later, covering Chronicles, Ezra, Tobit, and Judith. The entry points readers to Fürst's Bibliotheca Judaica.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melbourne-10599:
Melbourne, capital of the British colony of Victoria, receives a communal history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Joseph Jacobs and D. I. Freedman wrote it. Jews tried holding services in private houses in 1839 and 1841. In 1844 they formed a congregation. They built a synagogue on government-granted land in 1847 and called the Rev. Moses Rintel from Sydney as their first minister.

In 1858 the community split over a trifle: Rintel had attended a funeral without his canonical robes and quarreled with the president. He led a secession that became the East Melbourne congregation, and the entry treats the rivalry as healthy, spurring both sides. It follows the Bourke Street mother congregation through its ministers to Joseph Abrahams, incumbent in 1904. He was president of the United Jewish Education Board and of the bet din of Victoria. The entry is a compact record of how a colonial congregation grew, quarreled, and organized itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-middleman-judah:
Judah Middleman was an English rabbi of the first half of the nineteenth century, remembered for one unfinished book. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote in Hebrew, answering a Christian critic of the Talmud, and reached English readers the same year through a translator.

His Netibot Emet defended the traditions of the Talmud against Alexander McCaul's Old Paths, a well-known attack of the day. Only the first part ever appeared, published in 1847 as Paths of Truth in M. H. Breslau's English version. The bibliography points to Jacobs and Wolf's Bibliotheca Anglo-Judaica for what little more is recorded of him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moabite-stone-1:
The Moabite Stone is the only surviving inscribed monument of ancient Moab, and Joseph Jacobs and J. Frederic McCurdy tell its dramatic rescue in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Found at Dhiban in 1868 — a black basalt slab three and a half feet long — it was smashed by local Arabs who feared losing their talisman. A squeeze taken beforehand saved the text.

Clermont-Ganneau recovered most fragments and pieced the stone together; it stands in the Louvre beside the squeeze. The inscription runs thirty-four lines in old Hebrew characters, cut about 860 B.C. for Mesha, king of Moab, who boasts that Chemosh delivered him from all his attackers. The article prints a translation of its first two-thirds — a king's own voice from Israel's world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ju:
Mordecai ben Judah Aryeh Löb Ashkenazi was a Dutch ritualist of Amsterdam in the early seventeenth century, noticed by Joseph Jacobs and S. J. Levinson in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a disciple of the cabalist Abraham Rovigo, and his service to his master was editorial: he arranged and corrected Rovigo's commentary on the Zohar, the Eshel Abraham.

The commentary was printed with the text at Fürth in 1701, his preface to it a year earlier. His own book is humbler and more practical: Miḳweh Yisrael, a treatise on circumcision in Judæo-German, published in 1710 with David of Lida's Sod Adonai appended. Between the Zohar and a circumciser's handbook, his short bibliography maps the two poles of his world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-issac:
Moses ben Issachar was rabbi at Aussee in Moravia in the second half of the seventeenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was a nephew of Mordecai Jaffe, the well-known codifier. Only two works of his are recorded.

The first, Holek be-Derek Tamim, printed at Frankfort on the Oder in 1680, explains the long Psalm one hundred nineteen. The second, Pene Mosheh, printed at Lublin in 1681, comments on the first seder of Genesis. Nothing more of his life is given. The notice is a small tile in the map of Moravian rabbinic writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muhlfeld-lucien:
Lucien Mühlfeld was a French novelist and dramatic critic born in Paris on August 4, 1870. Isidore Singer and Edouard André wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied at the Lycée Condorcet and took degrees in literature and law at the University of Paris. For five years he worked as assistant librarian there, then quit for literature.

Mühlfeld wrote dramatic criticism for the Revue Blanche, the Echo de Paris, and other periodicals. His three novels, from Le Mauvais Desir to L'Associée, all deal with Parisian life. His two critical books never became popular, a fact the entry states flatly. He died in Paris in 1902, aged thirty-two, with one one-act play also to his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nail-11299:
Nail, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, covers both the nails of the body and the metal pin. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the article. For nail parings the rabbis grade a man by his disposal. Burn them, and he is pious; bury them, and he is righteous; throw them away, and he is wicked. A pregnant woman stepping on them was feared to miscarry.

Customs cluster around the nails: hands washed after cutting, nails viewed at the Saturday-evening Habdalah, white spots read as luck. The metal nail runs from David's iron for the Temple to Solomon's gold nails of fifty shekels. Jael's tent peg and the hangman's nail, worn as a cure, close the article's survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-year-11499:
The Hebrew year first began in autumn, not spring. Isidore Singer, J. F. McLaughlin, Wilhelm Bacher, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The farm year opened with seed sowing then. Festivals followed the crops: barley, harvest, then ingathering. Semites in general kept this autumn start.

Kings' regnal years were reckoned the same way. Later law made Nisan, in spring, the first month. Babylon's sacred year likely shaped that change. Yet the New-Year feast stayed in autumn, in Tishri. That day was set for the blowing of trumpets. No servile work was done, and sacrifices were offered. The rabbis in time counted four new years. Each served a different purpose in law and life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nose-ring-11599:
The nose-ring was an ornament worn by women only. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One Hebrew word serves for earrings and nose-rings alike. Context or an added word tells them apart. Genesis shows Eliezer giving Rebekah such a ring.

Hers was gold, and weighed half a shekel. That gold is named hints at baser metals too. Proverbs turns the jewel into a sharp reproach. A fair woman lacking discretion, it says, compares. She is a gold ring in a swine's snout. Talmudic women still wore nose-rings in public life. Law barred them outdoors on the Sabbath day. The Mishnah counts them among vessels liable to uncleanness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-note-for-topics:
The Chazars were a Turkish people of South Russia. Herman Rosenthal wrote their entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Their kingdom stood firm before Russia's monarchy began. Jews had lived by the Black Sea for centuries. The Chazar home lay toward the Ural region.

Armenian writers record their raids from the third century. Rome and Persia fought across their battle-ground Armenia. Alliance with Byzantium guarded them against Persia. They marched for Attila and fought at Châlons. Westward they spread to the Don and the Volga. Forty thousand of them helped Heraclius beat Persia. Their king and grandees then embraced Judaism. King Bulan, King Joseph's letter says, chose after debate. Envoys of emperor and calif had argued in vain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paraclete-or-11:
Paraclete is a word for one who pleads for a man. Kaufmann Kohler wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is a rabbis' word, took from the Greek tongue. In Greek it means a pleader or a go-between. The Aramaic texts use it for a word in Job.

One good deed wins a man one such pleader, men taught. One bad deed wins a man one who speaks against him. A man on trial for his life needs strong pleaders. His own turn from sin and good deeds plead for him. Nine hundred foes may speak, and one friend may save him. Good works by Israel plead for the folk in heaven. The sin gift at the altar is such a pleader too. It speaks for man and is marked by a thanks gift.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pen-11999:
The pen came late to Israel; the style came first. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Old Hebrew words for writing mean to cut or to scratch. That tells how early writing was actually done. The article traces tools from stone to ink.

Writers cut letters into stone, clay, and wax. Iron styles did the cutting work for them. Ink is named only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah. Yet Egypt wrote with color long before Israel settled. Clay tablets from Tell el-Amarna show the older local habit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philipp-isidor-:
Isidor Philipp was a Hungarian pianist who made Paris his home. He was born at Budapest on September 2, 1863. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He arrived in Paris at sixteen to study.

Philipp won the Conservatoire's first piano prize in 1883. He then polished his art under Saint-Saëns and others. He played with the great Paris orchestras of his day. He also toured to London, Brussels, and Barcelona. With two partners he founded chamber concerts at Salle Erard. His own pieces include a Suite Fantastique for orchestra.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-place-names-121:
Palestine's place-names keep the land's deep past inside them. Joseph Jacobs wrote this survey for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Most names predate the Israelite conquest itself. Joppa, Gaza, and Jerusalem run back three thousand years. Some names end in dual or plural forms.

Many names honor the gods of old shrines. Beth-shemesh recalls the sun, Beth-dagon the god Dagon. Others come from plants that grew nearby. Beth-tappuah means house of the apple tree. Still others come from beasts of the field. En-gedi recalls the kid, Akrabbim the scorpions. Jerusalem's own form hints at twin hills.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posen-11799:
Posen is a province of Prussia that once belonged to Poland. Gotthard Deutsch and Louis Lewin wrote its long article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Prussia took the land in the partitions of 1772 and 1793. Germans crossed into the region in the thirteenth century. Many Jews seem to have come in with them.

Jews lived in Great Poland before that time as well. They are named at Deutsch-Krone in the eleventh century. They are named at Gnesen in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Traces of them appear at Meseritz too. The article follows the province town by town. It gives a full picture of Jewish life under Polish and Prussian rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-proverbs-12399:
Proverbs, meaning short wise sayings, are gathered from many Jewish sources. Joseph Jacobs, M. Grunwald, Marcus Jastrow, and Louis Lewin wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A proverb is wise, witty, and brief, they say. Jewish sayings of this kind come from five streams. Each stream has its own age and flavor.

First come the sayings held in the canon of the Bible. Next come those in books left out of the canon. The Talmud forms the third great store. A fourth store grew in Spain under Moorish rule. Loose works of many kinds form the last. The article draws choice sayings from each stream in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbinowicz-isr:
Israel Michel Rabbinowicz was a Russian-born French author and translator. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Horodetz near Kobrin in 1818. He died in London in 1893. His father and grandfather were both rabbis of his home town.

The boy had the usual rabbinical schooling of his place. In 1828 his father became rabbi of nearby Antopol. There the son grew up and won note as a keen Talmudist. His later life took him far from that small world. The entry follows his move to France and his work in French. His name rests on his renderings of Jewish books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ravenna-12599:
Ravenna is an Italian city, capital of its province. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A Jewish community lived there from very early times. In 519 a crowd burned its synagogues.

The article says King Theodoric ordered the city to rebuild them. Those who could not pay the fine faced the lash. Later rulers both harmed and protected Ravenna's Jews. Frederick II defended one Jew against unjust demands in 1226. Under Venice from 1441, Jews could stay and lend money. Set rates applied to local borrowers and to strangers. The entry shows a community kept under close, shifting rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rethy-moriz-126:
Moriz Réthy was a Hungarian mathematician born on November 3, 1846. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Nagy-Körös. He studied at Budapest, Vienna, Göttingen, and Heidelberg.

The article says he taught mathematics and theoretical physics at Klausenburg. He held that chair from 1874 to 1886. He then moved to Budapest's School of Technology. Since 1891 he lectured there on analytic mechanics. In 1878 he joined the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. That academy asked him to edit Bólyai's Tentamen. The edition appeared in 1897. He also wrote many articles for technical journals. One lexicon entry is the cited source. The record is compact but complete in outline.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rodrigues-olind:
Olinde Rodrigues was a French economist and reformer born on October 16, 1794. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Bordeaux. He died at Paris on December 26, 1850.

The article says he excelled in mathematics at the École Normale. He later assisted at the École Polytechnique. In 1823 Saint-Simon converted him to his doctrines. At Saint-Simon's funeral he gathered the disciples together. They launched a journal called Le Producteur under him. He organized the followers into a sect in 1829. A rupture with Enfantin followed in 1831. He then entered banking and helped build early French railroads. In 1848 he backed the republic and workers' rights. His last years built mutual aid societies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rossiena-rossie:
Rossiena, or Rossieny, is a district city in the Kovno region of Russia. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its Jewish community prospered in the first half of the nineteenth century.

Rossiena was then a center of Haskalah, the movement for modern Jewish learning. The novelist Abraham Mapu lived there from 1837 to 1844 among kindred spirits. A great fire in 1865 nearly destroyed the city and began its decline. In 1866 it counted 8,290 Jews among 10,579 residents in all. By 1897 the whole population had shrunk to 7,455, mostly Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-haeem-13:
Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Haeem Samuel. He was an Indian communal worker, born at Alibag, near Bombay, in 1830. He was educated at the Robert Money School in Bombay. In 1851 he entered government service. He rose to second assistant to the inspector-general of ordnance at Puna, and retired on a pension in 1878.

In service, Samuel won European rates of batta, or field pay, for Beni-Israel soldiers. In 1853 he founded the Bombay Beni-Israel Benevolent Society. In 1881 he founded the Israelite High School of the Anglo-Jewish Association. He ran that school for twenty-four years. He also opened a prayer hall in 1888. The three Beni-Israel synagogues of Bombay excommunicated him for that step. He also wrote a sketch of Beni-Israel history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saraval-13199:
Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Saraval family. The Saravals were a family of scholars. Abraham ben Judah Löb Saraval flourished in the sixteenth century. He wrote a commentary on the Ma'amadot. A second edition of it is dated 1617.

Jacob Raphael ben Simḥah Saraval was a rabbi at Venice. Born about 1708, he died there in April 1782. He answered a lawyer's treatise on Jewish religion and oaths. He also wrote a lament for sixty-five Jews killed together in an accident. Judah Löb Saraval, another Venetian rabbi, died in 1617. He translated Saadia's commentary on Canticles into Hebrew. Leon Vita Saraval of Triest was a noted book collector. The Breslau seminary bought his whole library in 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schonerer-georg:
Joseph Jacobs and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Georg von Schönerer. He was an Austrian politician and anti-Semitic agitator. Schönerer was born at Vienna on July 17, 1842. He worked in agriculture before politics. In 1873 he entered the Austrian Diet. There he backed the German-National party and the anti-Semitic movement.

In 1888 Schönerer forced his way into the office of the Neues Wiener Tageblatt. He called that paper a Judenblatt for pleading the Jews' cause. On May 5, 1888, he was sentenced to four months in prison. He also lost his nobility and his Diet immunity. He later regained his status. He spread his views in his paper Unverfälschte Deutsche Worte. In 1895 he retired from public life. He kept attacking the Christian-Social party and its leaders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-selden-john-133:
Lewis N. Dembitz and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on John Selden. He was an English jurist and Orientalist. Selden was born on December 16, 1584, at Salvington, in Sussex. He died at Whitefriars, London, on November 30, 1654. He studied at Oxford and entered the Inner Temple in 1612. Sir Robert Cotton's library fed his antiquarian research.

Selden's vast writings quote rabbinic opinions throughout. His History of Tythes of 1617 rests on rabbinic authorities. Other works treat Jewish succession law and the Jewish civil year. His Uxor Ebraica covers Jewish marriage and divorce. His De Synedriis studies the ancient Sanhedrins at length. He argued there that priests should hold no judicial power. Ordinary judges, like the rabbis, should judge all cases. Selden also dealt early with Karaite views.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shneor-zalman-b:
Shneor Zalman ben Baruch, called Zalman Ladier, led the rational Hasidim known as Habad. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born at Liozna in 1747. Poor parents raised a boy who shone at Talmud study.

Marriage into a wealthy Vitebsk family freed him to learn full time. He gained mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Cabala as well. Luria's mystic system drew his dreamy, searching mind. He admired Baer of Meseritz, then its leading voice. For twelve years he lived in Baer's house. He helped spread Hasidic teaching across the region. Habad's name joins Hebrew words for wisdom, understanding, and knowledge. He died in 1812 while fleeing war, far from home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slaves-and-slav:
The Hebrew word ebed is often rendered servant in the English Bible. Wilhelm Bacher, Lewis N Dembitz, Gotthard Deutsch, and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. At times the word means a real slave. At times it means a courtier or a servant of the Lord. Hebrew bondmen held a status well above slavery.

The Law put the care of Hebrew servants near its head. That rule came right after the Ten Commandments in Exodus. A Hebrew servant could be kept only for a limited time. Jeremiah called lifelong holding of Hebrews a grave national sin. He warned that Judah would fall into ruin for that wrong. The article weighs these texts and their tensions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ibn-ya-:
Solomon ibn Ya'ish ben Abraham was a Spanish scholar and physician. Wilhelm Bacher and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Seville in May 1345, a tombstone says. That stone credits him with many works on medicine and science. None of those works has survived to the present day.

He likely wrote a supercommentary on Ibn Ezra's Pentateuch commentary. A part on the ephod survives in another author's collection. A fragment explains a geometrical calculation in that commentary. A second, younger Solomon ibn Ya'ish also commented on Ibn Ezra. His full supercommentary sits in the Bodleian Library today. Scholars debate which man wrote the Arabic original text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spain-also-the-:
Spain held Jewish communities from very early times onward. Richard Gottheil, Meyer Kayserling, and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Legends link Spain to Solomon's treasurer and to Toledo Jews. Those tales cannot be credited as history, the article warns. Paul still meant to visit the Jews living in Spain.

Jewish coins from ancient Tarragona prove an early settlement there. The oldest Jewish tombstone in Spain dates to the third century. It was found at Adra and marks a Jewish girl's grave. Under the Arian Visigoths, Jews lived as equals of others. They traded, farmed, and even held judicial offices at times. The Council of Elvira first barred close contact in 303.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-suchostaver-mor:
Mordecai Suchostaver was a Galician follower of the Haskalah movement. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He was born near Brody in 1790. As a youth he studied under Nachman Krochmal. He died at Jitomir on July 29, 1880.

Suchostaver worked in Odessa as secretary and tutor in a baron's household. He settled for a time at Kamenetz-Podolsk. When the Jitomir rabbinical seminary opened, he joined its staff. He taught philosophy there until the school closed in 1873. In 1829 he published an introduction to Maimonides' Guide. It framed the medieval classic for modern readers. A later treatise studies the law of conspiring witnesses. The entry joins Enlightenment ideals with seminary teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-timbrel-or-tabr:
The timbrel, or hand-drum, was the oldest percussion instrument in Hebrew music. Immanuel Benzinger wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Rhythm mattered more than melody in that music. A skin stretched over a hoop made the drum. Metal bits on the rim jingled when shaken.

Women usually played it among the Hebrews. They beat it while dancing and singing at joyful events. Miriam's song after the sea crossing used timbrels. Weddings, banquets, and homecoming feasts all featured the drum. It never suited mourning, the article notes. Nor did it join the Temple orchestra. Only cymbals appear in that list of percussion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-urbino-14599:
Urbino, an Italian city once capital of its own duchy, had Jews from the 1200s. Gotthard Deutsch and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Abraham Abulafia sojourned there in the thirteenth century. Documents first name a Maestro Daniele from Viterbo. He opened a loan office in the next century.

His son Isaac received privileges from Count Antonio. Lending rights stayed reserved to Daniele's descendants for generations. Outsiders paid those families 500 scudi yearly for entry. Other Jews worked as physicians or in humble trades. They could own real estate anywhere in town. They also employed Christian servants before 1500. A Monte di Pietà arose against them in 1468. Popular persecution grew around 1500 despite ducal favor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vienna-14699:
Vienna is the capital of Austria Hungary. Joseph Jacobs, Meyer Kayserling, Gotthard Deutsch, and Theodor Lieben wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Legend claims Jews settled there in ancient times. Toll rules for Jewish merchants date to 905. Under the Babenberg dukes, Jews fared better than elsewhere in Germany.

One early figure stands out in the account. In 1194 Duke Leopold placed a Jew named Shlom over the mint. Crusaders later stormed Shlom's house and killed him. They also murdered fifteen other Jews. The duke executed two of the ringleaders. The long entry follows the community through favor, attack, and expulsion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wax-hebr-donag-:
Wax appears rarely in the Bible, mostly in comparisons. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew word is donag. Psalms use wax melting as a picture of weakness. It stands for quick fading, soft yielding, and fear.

The Talmud knows wax as a fuel for light. It probably burned in the form of candles. Today wax candles serve where olive oil is scarce at Hanukkah. Large wax candles burn in synagogues on Yom Kippur eve. They also burn on the anniversary of a death. A braided wax taper serves in the Habdalah rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-west-indies-129:
The West Indies are islands in the North Atlantic near Mexico's gulf. Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Columbus thought he had reached India by sailing west. Jews link to the islands from that first voyage. Luis de Torres, who sailed with Columbus, settled in Cuba.

Spanish rule barred Jews for centuries there. Hidden Jews still lived in Cuba for four hundred years. The Inquisition claimed Cuban victims as late as 1783. Dutch and British tolerance changed the islands' fate. Refugees from Brazil enriched Curaçao after 1654. Full legal rights came only after the Spanish American war. The entry maps community after community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-bar-jose:
Yizhak bar Joseph was a scholar of Palestine in the 300s and 400s. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a pupil of Abbahu and of Johanan. He passed on the words of Johanan most of all.

One tale says a spirit once came near to kill him. A cedar tree saved his life at that hard hour. He is tied to a grim rule on the Samaritans. He once went to their land to buy wine there. An old man told him that no one kept the law. He brought that word back to Abbahu at once. Abbahu and two peers then ruled them a heathen folk. Yizhak was a chief link of lore to Babylon as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-book-:
Book of Zechariah is a book of prophecies in fourteen parts. Emil G. Hirsch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands as the eleventh of the twelve small prophets. It comes after Haggai and before Malachi in that set.

The first eight parts hold three works of the seer. First comes a head note that calls the folk to turn. That note leans on the fate of the sires of old. Next comes a set of eight dreams in one night. Those dreams show horse men, horns, and smiths in turn. They show a town of peace and a priest with Satan. They show a lamp stand, a scroll, and a maid in a bin. They show carts of the four winds of the sky. A last note tells of a crown and a word of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zunz-leopold-he:
Leopold Zunz was the founder of the modern science of Judaism. Isidore Singer and Emil G. Hirsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Detmold on August 10, 1794, he died at Berlin on March 18, 1886. His family line runs back three centuries, with roots in the Jewish community of Frankfort-on-the-Main.

Zunz pioneered the study of Jewish literature, religious poetry, and synagogue ritual. Poverty and illness marked his childhood; both parents died while he was young. A free scholarship took him to the Samson school at Wolfenbüttel, where his gift for mathematics stood out. There a new director, Ehrenberg, set his studies in order. The entry follows the making of the scholar who would put Jewish learning on a modern footing.
kamaratna-1899: Kāmaratna is a Sanskrit work by Nityanātha, son of Gaurī, printed at Bombay in 1899. The publisher named in the catalog record is Khemarāja Śrīkr̥ṣṇadāsa. The scanned sample is heavily garbled, mixing broken type and stray marks. Its title page still shows the work's name and its author's name in Sanskrit script. Beyond that, the sample's text cannot be read with confidence. This notice stays at the level of the title page and the catalog record.
kamaratnam-1899: Kāmaratnam is another printed form of Nityanātha's Sanskrit Kāmaratna, issued at Bombay in 1899. The sample's title page names a commentary by Pandit Jvālāprasāda Miśra of Moradabad. It also names the Venkateśvara press, where the publisher had the book printed. The scan is badly garbled, so the commentary's contents cannot be checked from this sample. This notice therefore records only what the title page and catalog entry plainly give.
kingsley-west-african-studies-1899:
Mary Kingsley turned her travels into system in West African Studies, published in 1899. Where her earlier book wandered, this one argues: fetishism, ancestor worship, and the sacred logic of native custom get sustained treatment. Kingsley defends African law and religion as coherent systems, against the scorn of her age.

Her years in French Congo and the Cameroons stand behind every claim, and traders and chiefs speak in her evidence. The book became the most influential Victorian account of West African religion and law. Readers still meet in Kingsley a mind that respected what she saw, even when it startled her.
kropotkin-memoirs-revolutionist-1899:
Peter Kropotkin published Memoirs of a Revolutionist in 1899, first in English in a leading American magazine. The memoir tells how a Russian prince and army officer became the leading theorist of anarchism. Kropotkin wrote it in exile, looking back over a dramatic life.

He recalled boyhood at the Tsar's court, geographic work in Siberia, and the slow turn against the state he served. Prison in Russia, a daring escape, and years among European socialists followed. The book mixes adventure with the growth of an idea, anarchist communism, in one man's mind. It remains a classic of radical autobiography, valued for its candor and its picture of nineteenth-century Russia.
leadbeater-clairvoyance-1899:
C. W. Leadbeater taught fans how hid sight works in Clairvoyance, his hand book of 1899. Leadbeater claimed he could see the glow round folk, past lives, and far places at will. He sorts sight by kind: sight of the near glow, sight through space, and sight through time and past ages.

Drills and warns fill the last parts of the guide. He tells the pupil to test each sight with care and calm. Groups took the book as their chief text on the theme. Its scheme still shapes how the occult talks of sight.
leland-aradia-1899:
Charles Godfrey Leland put out Aradia in 1899. He said a Tuscan witch named Maddalena gave him the core of the text. The book claims to be the gospel of the witches of Italy. Diana, the moon queen, stands at its heart.

Spells, chants, and tales tell how Diana sent her child Aradia to Earth. Aradia was to teach witch craft to the poor and help them fight the rich. Some doubt how much of the text is old lore. The book still lit the spark of the new witch faith of our day.
leo-astrology-for-all-1899:
Alan Leo made star lore a trade and a craze in Britain. His Astrology for All came out in 1899. Leo wrote for the plain reader, not the math adept. He ran a press that sold charts and books by post to all.

The book teaches the signs, planets, and houses in short, clear steps. A reader can cast a rough chart and read its main traits at home. Leo drops much of the old doom talk for a bright, keen tone. The book marks the birth of the new, mass star lore of our age.
marx-value-price-profit-aveling-1899:
Marx addressed the General Council of the International in 1865, and the speech became Value, Price and Profit. His daughter Eleanor Marx Aveling edited the first English edition in 1899. Fellow council members had claimed that wage rises were useless. Marx answers them with his full theory of value in brief.

He explains surplus value, the source of profit in his system, with plain examples. Wages, prices, and profit fall into one connected account. He closes on the limits of trade union struggle under capitalism. Many readers find this his clearest short statement of his economics. It bridges his lectures and the vast Capital. The speech form keeps it lively.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s:
Lewis Goldsmith's St. Cloud letters appear here in a complete set. A publishers' note promises facts on Napoleon found in no other book. The letters run from a gentleman at Paris to a lord in London.

The writer, said to be Stewarton, knew Josephine in her glad days. He gives lives of near all Napoleon's ministers and generals. Anecdotes of Talleyrand and Fouche fill many of the pages. Stark tales tell of folk who vanished after crossing the Emperor. A grand dinner and Cardinal Fesch stand in the picture list. The complete set keeps the letters' mix of praise and sharp blame.
mungo-park-travels-interior-districts-af:
Mungo Park, a Scottish surgeon, was sent by the African Association in 1795 to find the course of the Niger river. His Travels in the Interior Districts of Africa, published in 1799 in the Bulmer first edition, tells that journey. Rennell's geographical appendix follows the narrative.

Park crossed from the Gambia toward Segu, was robbed and held prisoner by a Moorish chief, escaped, and at last saw the Niger flowing east. Fever and hardship cut the journey short before he could follow the river to its end. His plain, brave telling made the book a classic of exploration. It fixed the Niger question that his second, fatal journey tried to close.
nash-leaders-in-homoeopathic-therapeutic:
E. B. Nash wrote for the busy prescriber, and Leaders in Homoeopathic Therapeutics, from 1899, became his best loved book. Nash had spent years in country practice, testing remedies on real patients. He gathered the drugs he reached for most and set down how he told them apart.

Each chapter takes a leading remedy and gives its strongest signs in plain, lively words. Nash compares near neighbors side by side, so a reader can spot the small point that decides a case. The handbook was likely the most used of its kind in its era, carried in many a doctor's bag.
nelson-eskimo-bering-strait-1899:
Edward William Nelson, a naturalist with the Signal Corps, spent years near Bering Strait in Alaska, and his great report came out in 1899. The Bureau of American Ethnology in Washington issued the work. It deals with the Yupik peoples of that coast. Few white men of his time knew that shore as well as he did.

Nelson set down homes, tools, dress, hunts, and feasts in fine detail. He gave long care to rites, masks, and the work of shamans in Yupik life. The book still stands as the main 19th century record of that coast and its ways.
norris-mcteague-1899:
Frank Norris published McTeague in 1899, after years of study in Paris and at Harvard. Norris set the novel on Polk Street in San Francisco, where he watched the city's dentists, saloons, and rooming houses. He worked in the naturalist manner of Zola, treating character as a product of heredity and habit.

McTeague, a huge, slow dentist with no license, marries Trina, who wins a lottery and turns miserly over her gold. Greed, jealousy, and drink grind the couple down from comfort to a squalid room. The story ends in Death Valley, with murder and handcuffs in the sand. Critics rank McTeague as the masterpiece of American naturalism, and its force has not faded.
openalex-w1957266799:
The CMS and LHCb collaborations jointly reported this result. It appeared in the journal Nature in the year 2015. A strange B meson can decay into two muons. The standard model predicts this decay is extremely rare. Only about four occur per billion such mesons.

Combined LHC data gave the first clear observation, they report. The signal passed six standard deviations in strength. A sister decay also showed evidence at three deviations. Both rates matched standard model predictions closely, they found. Tight matches limit theories that extend the model. Later LHC runs should sharpen these crucial tests.
openalex-w1994677299:
José Argüello, Daniel Raimunda, and Teresita Padilla-Benavides wrote this review. It appeared in a microbiology journal in November 2013. Copper helps enzymes work as a redox co-factor. Free copper is also a hazard from its reactivity. Bacteria must therefore control copper with great care.

The review traces how bacteria handle copper traffic. Entry, exit, and internal routing all stay tightly managed. Transport proteins move copper ions across cell membranes. Sensing systems switch those movers on and off. Balance lets bacteria use copper without being poisoned. The mechanisms matter for infection and for biotechnology.
openalex-w2010581199:
Thomas Koellner, Laura de Baan, Tabea Beck and colleagues wrote a guideline on land use in product life cycle studies. Their paper appeared in 2013. Land serves many uses at once. So judging land use impacts needs several impact paths. The guideline came from the UNEP-SETAC Life Cycle Initiative.

The authors set shared rules for modelling those impacts. They covered harm to biodiversity and ecosystem services. They addressed whether impacts can reverse over time. They also covered where and when impacts occur. The paper tells method builders what they must state clearly. Shared rules make studies from different teams comparable. That helps firms and policy makers trust the results.
openalex-w2061420699:
Paul Mahaffy, Christopher Webster, Michel Cabane and colleagues described the Sample Analysis at Mars instrument suite. Their paper appeared in Space Science Reviews in 2012. The suite flew on the Mars Science Laboratory rover. It analyses the air of Mars. It also studies gases drawn from solid samples.

The instruments measure chemical makeup in fine detail. They also measure isotope ratios in gases. Such data bear on whether Mars could support life. They also trace the planet's climate history. The paper details each instrument in the suite. It explains how samples move through the system. Design choices balanced weight, power and precision. The suite was built for years of work on Mars.
openalex-w2507689999:
Emma L. Wakeling, Frédéric Brioude, and Oluwakemi Lokulo-Sodipe led a large expert group behind this 2016 consensus statement in Nature Reviews Endocrinology. It is the first international statement on diagnosing and managing Silver-Russell syndrome. The syndrome is an imprinting disorder, a fault in how certain genes are switched on or off. It slows growth before and after birth.

Diagnosis rests mainly on clinical signs, though genetic testing can confirm it and identify the subtype. A normal test result does not rule the syndrome out. Care needs an experienced team covering feeding problems, low blood sugar, body asymmetry, and scoliosis. The statement backs growth hormone treatment, which can add height and improve appetite and body composition. It also warns that fast weight gain after birth may raise later metabolic risks.
openalex-w2575296699:
Oriol Mitjà, Michael Marks, and Laia Bertran lead this 2017 policy paper in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. It argues for handling neglected tropical skin diseases together rather than one by one. These diseases thrive in poverty and affect over a billion people in tropical countries. Many cause lasting disfigurement and disability, from Buruli ulcer to leprosy and yaws.

A single skin check can spot several of these conditions in one visit, the authors note. That makes joint screening in villages and schools cheaper and wider-reaching than separate programs. The World Health Organization's disease control department plans to promote exactly this integrated strategy. The approach also creates a platform for treating common skin problems. Combining care this way could stretch limited health budgets across more patients.
openalex-w2792992299: Scott A. Thomson, Richard L. Pyle, and Shane T. Ahyong lead a very long list of signatories on this 2018 formal comment in PLOS Biology. Its title states the claim plainly: taxonomy based on science is necessary for global conservation. The preserved sample contains only the citation header and the hundreds of author names. No argument text survives in the sample. The comment's reasoning and examples therefore cannot be described from the evidence kept here.
openalex-w2905571899:
Ana Beatriz Amaral, Marcondes Viana da Silva, and Suzana Caetano da Silva Lannes reviewed lipid oxidation in meat. Their review appeared in Food Science and Technology in 2018. When polyunsaturated fats in meat meet reactive oxygen species, oxidation cascades begin. The endpoint is rancidity: off flavors, lost nutrients, and rejected products. Oxidation is thus a chief enemy of meat quality and consumer acceptance.

The review explains the oxidation mechanisms step by step. It then surveys ways to protect meat at every stage. Feeding animals antioxidant supplements is one lever; adding antioxidants to products is another. Vacuum and modified-atmosphere packaging slow oxygen's access. Combining steps together protects best, the authors find. They caution that controls must not harm other sensory qualities or food safety. For processors, this is the reference map of a costly, constant problem.
openalex-w2972599699:
G. Aad, B. Abbott, D. Abbott, and colleagues of the ATLAS collaboration published this search paper in The European Physical Journal C in 2020. Using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, they hunted for two kinds of predicted particles, charginos and sleptons. These come from supersymmetry, a theory that partners every known particle with a heavier twin.

The team looked for collisions that produce two electrons or muons plus missing energy, the sign of an invisible particle escaping. They tested three scenarios in which the lightest such twin is stable and unseen. No clear excess over Standard Model expectations appeared. The authors therefore set firm limits on how heavy these particles could be in each scenario.

G. Aad, B. Abbott, D. Abbott, and colleagues of the ATLAS collaboration published this measurement paper in Physical Review D in 2020. It combines many ATLAS analyses of the Higgs boson into single, sharper results. The Higgs is the particle tied to how other particles gain mass.

The combination covers the main ways the Higgs is made and the main ways it decays, including decays to photons, to pairs of other bosons, and to quarks and leptons. It also folds in searches for invisible decays and for off-shell Higgs production. By merging the separate studies, the team obtains tighter measures of production rates and decay shares. These combined values test the Standard Model of particle physics as a whole.
openalex-w3004480399:
Ludmil Alexandrov, Jaegil Kim, Nicholas Haradhvala, and colleagues published this study in Nature in 2020. It catalogs mutational signatures in human cancer, the distinct patterns that different damaging processes stamp into DNA. The work comes from the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes consortium.

Earlier studies had named more than thirty signatures for single-letter DNA changes, some from known causes and many from unknown ones. Far less work had covered other mutation classes, such as rearrangements of the genome. This study widens the repertoire across those classes. It also estimates how many mutations in each tumor each signature explains. The catalog helps link a cancer's DNA scars to the processes that produced them.

Carlos Duarte, Susana Agustí, Edward Barbier, and colleagues published this review in Nature in 2020. It assesses the state of life in the oceans and asks how much of it can be rebuilt. The paper appeared as marine protection was gaining urgency in global policy debates.

Oceans have lost wildlife to fishing, pollution, coastal development, and warming. The authors review evidence on those losses alongside cases where species and habitats have recovered. Their survey weighs what recovery requires, from cutting pressures to active restoration. The conclusion they build toward is hopeful but conditional: marine life can rebound within decades if the main pressures are eased. The paper gives leaders a science-based case for acting.
openalex-w3164581399:
Naschla Gasaly, Paul de Vos, and Marcela Hermoso review how chemicals made by gut bacteria affect the gut wall and immunity. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology in 2021. The gut lining must let food through while keeping harmful microbes out. Bacteria living there release small molecules, called metabolites, that help run that balance.

The authors sum up what is known about these metabolites in health and in gut inflammation. They focus on inflammatory bowel disease and celiac disease, where the balance breaks down. Diet, including fibre, shapes which metabolites bacteria produce. The review weighs whether such compounds could one day support new treatments for intestinal inflammation.
openalex-w4405626299:
Kecheng Liu, Takeshi Suzuki, Yigui Zhong, and colleagues probe a charge density wave material called LaTe3. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. In such materials the electron density settles into a regular ripple. Laser pulses can shake that ripple, creating a vibration called an amplitude mode.

The team uses ultrafast laser pulses with time- and angle-resolved photoemission. That method watches electrons and the crystal lattice separately as the vibration evolves. They compare pulses tuned to the energy gap with pulses tuned away from it. Separating charge effects from lattice effects helps explain how these ordered states form and melt.
openalex-w4414590999:
Lisa Force, Jonathan Kocarnik, Miranda May, and the GBD 2023 Cancer Collaborators estimate the global burden of cancer. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet in 2025. Many countries lack current cancer surveillance data. Policy still needs accurate numbers.

The team modelled forty-seven cancer types across two hundred four countries, from 1990 to 2023. In 2023 there were about eighteen and a half million new cases and over ten million deaths. Cancer ranked second only to cardiovascular disease as a cause of death. Most cases and deaths fell in poorer countries. About two fifths of deaths traced to known risk factors. The study also forecasts the burden through 2050.
openalex-w7212063499:
Caroline Santos de Oliveira leads a team weighing two ways to take out risky lower wisdom teeth. When a tooth sits close to the jaw nerve, full removal can harm the nerve and numb the lip. Coronectomy is the safer-looking rival: the crown is cut off, and the roots are left in place on purpose. The team read trials and reviews from four large databases, most from 2021 to 2026.

The review sets the two paths side by side on one key harm: nerve injury. It also tracks the wider results that count for patients, such as pain, healing, and later trouble from roots left behind. Classic older studies anchor the tale, back to a key trial from 2005. For oral surgeons, the value is a clear frame for a hard choice. High risk to the nerve calls for proof, not habit.
openalex-w7212439899:
Adriana Giarola Ferraz Figueiredo leads a team that reads the 2025 ENADE test for Brazil's would-be teachers. ENADE is the state test given to those who leave college. In 2025 it took a new shape for teaching degrees. The team read the test in two parts: Portuguese and words, and shared teaching craft. Their hunch was that the new test prizes skills in use, not facts held still.

The test, they find, asks the taker to act like a teacher. Tasks pose class scenes and call for a wise move. Deep lore on the tongue still counts, but in use. New aims run through the whole: many kinds of text, and themes that cross all fields. For schools that train teachers, the read is a map. It shows the skills their grads will now be judged on.

Ernélia Isabel António Gove, Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva, and Hildeberto Arcanjo Filho wrote a 2026 library article on formal and non-formal education in the development of children and young people. Formal education happens in schools with structured programs and defined goals. Non-formal education happens in community, cultural, sports, and social spaces, and current studies treat it as a main support rather than an extra.

Formal education, the reviewed authors show, feeds mainly thinking growth and learning to live with others. Non-formal education sparks socioemotional skills, autonomy, and citizenship. Joining the two strengthens learning and gives a broader, more critical, and more human formation, fitting the person to play a real role in society. The article's value lies in denying the hierarchy that counts only schooling as education, and in giving learning outside school a grounded place beside the classroom.

João Victor Ferreira da Paz led a 2026 report on an integrated, auditable management system for Crea Júnior in Alagoas, Brazil. The program links engineering and geoscience students to Brazil's engineering council system. But it historically ran on manual controls: emails, parallel spreadsheets, web forms, and informal checks, with no auditable record of decisions. The team designed it on design science principles around a single database.

Three integrated portals now cover the program's whole cycle. A public portal handles registration and verification of members and certificates. A member portal offers a digital card, event registration, history, and downloads. An administrative panel covers approvals, selection processes, events, and audit. Every administrative action is logged with its author, date, and network origin, and certificates go out through QR-code credentialing. Fragmented manual controls gave way to one traceable flow in real use, with larger quantitative evaluation still to come.

Janine Cecília Gonçalves Peixoto and Lázara Cristina da Silva propose a new planning tool for accessibility in higher education, in a 2026 article. Building on the individualized education plans used in schools, they design an Academic Accessibility Plan meant to follow a student with a disability through a whole degree.

The plan names barriers, agrees on reasonable adaptations, assigns duties, and schedules review at least once a semester. A shared-responsibility chart links the student, teachers, course coordinators, the accessibility office, and the institution. The authors also warn, through a Foucauldian lens, that individual plans can normalize and bureaucratize. Used with that caution, they argue, the plan protects student autonomy and legal security alike.
philippine-constitution-1899:
The Malolos Congress adopted the first Philippine constitution in January 1899, founding the First Philippine Republic. Filipino revolutionaries had thrown off Spanish rule and proclaimed independence at Kawit the summer before. At Malolos they built Asia's first republic, weeks before war with the United States began.

The charter creates a republic with an assembly holding strong power over the president, and it separates church and state. It promises the rights of citizens in the liberal style of its age, drawn from European and American models. The republic lived only months before the American war crushed it, and the constitution was never fully put into practice. The founding law of a republic the great powers would not let stand remains a proud document in Philippine memory. It proves the revolution had a state in mind, not only an army.
phrenology-essays-and-studies-1899: Hosted here, the sample shows only the Google Books digital-copy notice pages that precede this scan, with no page of the work itself visible. The catalogue record names the book Phrenology: Essays and Studies and dates it 1899. It gives the author's name in a garbled double form, Stackpool Edward O'Dell and Geelossapuss E. O'Dell, which looks like two catalogue entries for the same man fused into one line.
plaw-106-032-1999:
Public Law 106-32 deals with an old canal in Richmond, Virginia: the James River and Kanawha Canal. Congress found that the canal had helped build Virginia's economy but stopped carrying commerce in the late 1800s. A federal court had already found parts of it nonnavigable, yet its old legal status as a navigable waterway lingered.
