The act declares the canal stretch between the Great Ship Lock and Richmond's western city limits a nonnavigable waterway under federal maritime law. The restored canal was meant for entertainment and education downtown, not general public boating. Congress said keeping a status based on traffic that ended more than a century earlier served no public interest and was not needed for safety.
plaw-106-1-1999:
The District of Columbia Management Restoration Act of 1999, Public Law 106-1, gave management and personnel authority back to the mayor of Washington, D.C. Congress had earlier put a financial control authority over the city to restore stability. By 1999 it found the District had performed far better than expected.

Sharing power among the mayor, the council, and the control authority had blurred who was accountable for city services, Congress said. With Mayor Anthony Williams taking office, the authority had begun handing daily operations back to city agencies. The act completes that return, restoring the home rule arrangement that existed before the control period.
plaw-106-10-1999: North Carolina's federal courthouse in Winston-Salem received a person's name under Public Law 106-10. The building at 251 North Main Street became the Hiram H. Ward Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Congress passed the act early in the 106th Congress, it was approved on April 5, 1999, and its references section carries the Ward name into every federal law, map, and record.
plaw-106-100-1999: Public Law 106-100 opened the House of Representatives Child Care Center to a wider group of children in 1999. Enrollment at the center had been tied to the legislative branch. The amendment lets children of employees of other federal offices, departments, and agencies enroll, but only when places remain after every eligible legislative branch child has been admitted. It applies to children admitted on or after the act took effect.
plaw-106-101-1999:
Missouri and Nebraska needed a fixed border, and Public Law 106-101 gave Congress's consent to their boundary compact. The Missouri River forms the line between the two states, but the river has shifted course over time. Those shifts left real and possible disputes over where the boundary actually runs, including court cases and criminal proceedings.

Under the compact, the border follows the river's main channel as mapped by the two states' surveyors, with maps filed in both states. The states aimed for a firm compromise line that would not disturb private property rights or titles. They also wanted one clear authority over taxation, courts, and police powers instead of overlapping claims.
plaw-106-102-1999:
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, Public Law 106-102, remade the rules for American finance in 1999. Congress said its goal was stronger competition among financial firms, under a careful framework for linking them. Banks, securities firms, insurance companies, and other providers could now affiliate in ways older law had kept apart.

Its first title repeals parts of the Glass-Steagall Act, the Depression-era law separating banking from securities work. It sets conditions for bank holding companies that become financial holding companies and limits those that do not. The act also protects deposit funds against firms seen as too big to fail, and orders a study of how the changes affect loans to small businesses and farms.
plaw-106-103-1999:
Civil defense and emergency management workers gained a planned monument under Public Law 106-103, passed in 1999. Congress gave a private nonprofit group, the United States National Civil Defense Monument Commission, the right to build it. The commission was formed under Pennsylvania law.

The monument would stand on federal land run by the Federal Emergency Management Agency at Emmitsburg, Maryland. Both its site and its design need the okay of the agency's director. Private gifts, not federal money, pay the building costs. The building power lapses after seven years unless the needed permits are in hand and work has begun by then.
plaw-106-104-1999: Public Law 106-104 made two small changes to immigration law in 1999. It stretched the admission period for the S category of nonimmigrant visa holders by two more years, changing five years to seven in the statute. Congress also urged wider use of that visa in alien smuggling cases. Separately, the act authorized refugee assistance funding for the years 2000 through 2002.
plaw-106-105-1999: Keeping the federal government funded for one more day was the whole job of Public Law 106-105. The joint resolution amended an earlier continuing appropriations law, moving its cutoff from November 17, 1999, to November 18, 1999. A second funding law received the same one-day change. Both the House and the Senate passed the measure on November 17, and it was approved the next day.
plaw-106-106-1999: Public Law 106-106 bought the government about two more weeks of funding in the fall of 1999. The joint resolution pushed the continuing appropriations cutoff from November 18 to December 2, 1999, in two earlier laws. It also raised one stated funding figure from about three hundred forty-six million dollars to about seven hundred fifty-six million dollars. Congress passed it on November 18, 1999, and it was approved the next day.
plaw-106-107-1999:
More than six hundred federal financial assistance programs served domestic policy in 1999, and Congress said their paperwork had grown tangled. The Federal Financial Assistance Management Improvement Act of 1999, Public Law 106-107, answered that complaint. Its findings call some federal requirements duplicative, burdensome, or conflicting, which slowed services at the local level.

The act's stated purposes are threefold: make federal assistance programs work better, simplify how people apply for aid and report on it, and improve the services the public receives. State, local, and tribal governments and nonprofit groups deliver much of that help. Streamlining the rules, Congress argued, would let those partners spend less effort on procedure and more on the problems themselves.
plaw-106-108-1999:
Too many geese, not too few, drove the Arctic Tundra Habitat Emergency Conservation Act, Public Law 106-108. Mid-continent light geese numbered about eight hundred thousand in 1969, Congress found, but had grown past five million birds by 1999. The flock was still expanding by more than five percent a year.

All that grazing was tearing up the salt-marsh country around Hudson Bay in Canada, land many migrating birds depend on. Congress blamed farm grain, sanctuaries along the flyways, and falling harvest rates for the boom. The act directs the Secretary of the Interior to put rules in place that reduce the overabundant goose population and protect the wider ecosystem.
plaw-106-109-1999:
Public Law 106-109 is a fix-it law, passed in 1999 to make technical corrections to the Water Resources Development Act of 1999. Most of its opening sections adjust an older environmental infrastructure program. The changes reach water and sewer projects in several named states and cities.

In Jackson County, Mississippi, funding rises from ten million dollars to twenty million, with new language on an alternative water supply and combined sewer overflows. Manchester, New Hampshire, receives the same ten-to-twenty million dollar increase. For Atlanta, Georgia, and for Paterson and the Passaic Valley in New Jersey, the act strikes stated funding amounts from the older text instead.
plaw-106-11-1999: Billings, Montana, is home to the courthouse renamed by Public Law 106-11 in 1999. The United States courthouse at 316 North 26th Street became the James F. Battin United States Courthouse under the act. Approved on April 5, 1999, the short law also provides that any reference to the courthouse in a federal law, map, or other record means the Battin courthouse.
plaw-106-110-1999: Railroad police officers could attend the FBI National Academy under Public Law 106-110, passed in 1999. The act amends the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 to add rail carriers and their police officers to the federal law enforcement training program. One limit applies to the new students: no federal funds may pay a railroad officer's travel, transportation, or living expenses for the training.
plaw-106-111-1999: Three Philadelphia postal buildings received names in a single act, Public Law 106-111, approved on November 29, 1999. The building at 2601 North 16th Street became the Roxanne H. Jones Post Office Building. The one at 5300 West Jefferson Street became the Freeman Hankins Post Office Building. And the building at 2037 Chestnut Street became the Max Weiner Post Office Building. Each designation carries a references clause, so federal records mentioning any of the three buildings use its new name.
plaw-106-112-1999: Garden City, Kansas, is where Public Law 106-112 applies. Approved on November 29, 1999, the act designates the Postal Service facility at 410 North 6th Street as the Clifford R. Hope Post Office. Its second section provides that references to the facility in any federal law, regulation, map, or other record are to be considered references to the Clifford R. Hope Post Office.
plaw-106-113-1999:
Money for much of the federal government for fiscal year 2000 came through Public Law 106-113, a consolidated appropriations act passed in late 1999. The act appropriates sums from the Treasury for the several departments, agencies, corporations, and other units of government. Its fiscal year ran through September 30, 2000.

Division A covers the District of Columbia. One early item gives the District seventeen million dollars for a resident tuition support program, run by the mayor once Congress authorized it. The program would pay the gap between in-state and out-of-state tuition for eligible residents. Awards could favor academic merit, and the District could add its own money on top.
plaw-106-114-1999:
Public Law 106-114 moves a federal site in New Mexico into county hands. Within one year, the Secretary of the Interior had to convey the Old Coyote Administrative Site to Rio Arriba County. The land, about half a mile east of the village of Coyote on State Road 96, covers two tracts of roughly one hundred thirty and two hundred seventy-seven acres.

The county pays a price set under the government pricing program of the Recreation and Public Purposes Act. It also agrees to shield the United States from liability arising from the property. The land must stay in public use; if that use ends, the United States may take it back. Old land withdrawals on the site end when the transfer closes.
plaw-106-115-1999:
South Dakota gained a Cold War historic site under the Minuteman Missile National Historic Site Establishment Act of 1999, Public Law 106-115. Congress called the Delta 1 launch control facility and the Delta 9 launch facility the best preserved examples of how missile work actually ran during the Cold War. No unit of the National Park System then told that story.

The site preserves and interprets the Minuteman II missile system and the crews, called missileers, who staffed remote posts across the upper Great Plains. Congress saw the two Delta facilities as a rare chance to explain the arms race and missile development. The Air Force crews' dedication and readiness form part of that story.
plaw-106-116-1999: Map paper, not coastline, is the subject of Public Law 106-116. The act replaces seven maps for the Cape Hatteras and Hatteras Island units of the Coastal Barrier Resources System in Dare County, North Carolina. Fourteen newer maps, dated October 18, 1999, take their place. The Secretary of the Interior must keep the new maps on file, open for public inspection under the Coastal Barrier Resources Act. Congress approved the swap on November 29, 1999.
plaw-106-117-1999:
Veterans' health care and benefits were overhauled by the Veterans Millennium Health Care and Benefits Act, Public Law 106-117, in 1999. The act amends title 38 of the United States Code. Its stated aims include a program of extended care services for veterans and improvements across the Department of Veterans Affairs, from compensation and housing to memorial affairs.

The opening title deals with access to care. It requires extended care services and sets up pilot programs on long-term care and assisted living. Other sections cover emergency treatment in non-department hospitals, care for combat-injured veterans, and access for military retirees under TRICARE. Counseling for veterans who experienced sexual trauma also appears in the contents.
plaw-106-118-1999:
For the second time in this era, Congress wrote a veterans' pay raise straight into the rate table, this time in the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 1999, Public Law 106-118. The act again amends title 38. It raises disability compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities. Survivors' dependency and indemnity compensation rises on the same terms.

The increases pick up where the 1997 raise left off. The lowest rate moves from ninety-five dollars to ninety-eight dollars a month. A mid-range rate goes from five hundred sixty-nine dollars to five hundred eighty-nine dollars. Higher ratings climb as well, one from a little over a thousand dollars to a slightly larger figure. The act was approved on November 30, 1999.
plaw-106-119-1999:
Visitors to the Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River were promised a proper welcome center by Public Law 106-119, passed in 1999. Its formal name is the Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River Mongaup Visitor Center Act. The act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to build and run the center on land owned by New York State.

Congress traced the plan to a 1987 river management plan, which called for a main visitor facility at the corridor's southern end, run by the National Park Service. New York had authorized a ninety-nine-year lease for the preferred site near Mongaup, in the town of Deerpark, Orange County. Federal land-buying limits inside the corridor made the lease arrangement necessary.
plaw-106-12-1999: El Paso's federal building took a new name under Public Law 106-12 in the spring of 1999. The building at 700 East San Antonio Street became the Richard C. White Federal Building. Approved on April 5, 1999, the act adds the usual references rule: mentions of the building in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are treated as mentions of the Richard C. White Federal Building.
plaw-106-120-1999:
Spy agencies got their yearly funding authority from the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2000, Public Law 106-120. The act authorizes appropriations for intelligence and intelligence-related work across the government. It also funds the Community Management Account and the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Much of the detail sits in a classified schedule of authorizations, named in the contents but not printed for the public. The visible sections allow personnel ceiling adjustments and an emergency supplemental for fiscal year 1999. General provisions follow, covering matters such as diplomatic intelligence support centers. Another section protects the identity of retired covert agents.
plaw-106-121-1999: A hydroelectric project called Mt. Hope received more time under Public Law 106-121. The act extends the construction deadline for Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Project No. 9401, the Mt. Hope Waterpower Project. Despite the usual time limits in the Federal Power Act, the commission may push the start of construction to August 3, 2002, if the licensee asks. Good faith, due diligence, and the public interest still govern the extension. The act was approved on December 6, 1999.
plaw-106-122-1999: One sentence of the Federal Reserve Act changes under Public Law 106-122, approved on December 6, 1999. The amendment widens the kinds of discount window loans that can serve as collateral for Federal Reserve notes. Where the older text pointed only to acceptances acquired under one section of the act, the new text reaches acceptances acquired under four sections. The change is small in length but touches the paper backing of the nation's currency.
plaw-106-123-1999: Chicago gained four named post office buildings under Public Law 106-123, approved on December 6, 1999. The facility at 433 West Harrison Street became the Cardiss Collins Post Office Building, and the one at 2302 South Pulaski Street became the Otis Grant Collins Post Office Building. The act also names the building at 4222 West Madison Street for Mary Alice (Ma) Henry and the facility on West Division Street for Robert LeFlore, Jr. Each name comes with a references clause for federal records.
plaw-106-124-1999: Public Law 106-124 concerns a postal building in Sandy, Utah. The building at 8850 South 700 East became the Noal Cushing Bateman Post Office Building under the act, approved on December 6, 1999. Its second section handles references. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record counts as a mention of the Bateman building.
plaw-106-125-1999: Out on the Oregon coast, Public Law 106-125 renamed a post office in 1999. The Postal Service building at 34480 Highway 101 South in Cloverdale became the Maurine B. Neuberger United States Post Office. Congress approved the designation on December 6, 1999. As with other naming acts, any mention of the building in federal laws, maps, or records is read as a mention of it under the Neuberger name.
plaw-106-126-1999:
Leif Ericson's voyage to the New World, a thousand years earlier, was marked with a coin program under Public Law 106-126 in 1999. Congress directed the Treasury Secretary to mint one-dollar silver coins alongside a matching issue by the Republic of Iceland. The American coins were capped at five hundred thousand pieces.

Each coin weighs a stated amount and runs ninety percent silver and ten percent copper. The coins count as legal tender and as numismatic items, meaning items struck for collectors. The Treasury could draw silver from any available source, including government stockpiles. Design rules for the coins follow in the act's next section.
plaw-106-127-1999: Setting Congress's own return date was the business of Public Law 106-127, a joint resolution approved on December 6, 1999. It appoints noon on Monday, January 24, 2000, as the start of the second regular session of the 106th Congress. A second section covers an emergency return: if the House Speaker and the Senate Majority Leader jointly decide the public interest requires it, members can be called back earlier. Congress would then reassemble at noon two days after members are notified.
plaw-106-128-1999: Delaware's Cape Henlopen map needed fixing, and Public Law 106-128 ordered the fix within thirty days. The Secretary of the Interior had to move a Coastal Barrier Resources System boundary so it matched the Cape Henlopen State Park boundary. The shift removes leased private property held by the Barcroft Company and Cape Shores Associates from the protected area. It adds the park's northwestern corner, seaward of the Lewes and Rehoboth Canal, into that area. The map in question dates from 1990, as revised in 1992.
plaw-106-129-1999:
Health care research got a renamed and rebuilt federal agency under the Healthcare Research and Quality Act of 1999, Public Law 106-129. The act rewrites title IX of the Public Health Service Act. The older Agency for Healthcare Policy and Research gives way to the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, led by a director.

The new agency's mission is to raise the quality, fit, and effectiveness of health services, and to widen access to them. It works by building a broad base of scientific research and by promoting better practice in clinics and health systems. Its research covers care outcomes and costs, and ways to help patients take part in their own care and share decisions with their doctors.
plaw-106-13-1999: Oakland, California, is the city named in Public Law 106-13, a federal building designation from 1999. The building at 1301 Clay Street became the Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building under the act. It was approved on April 5, 1999, after passing the House in February and the Senate in March. The references section makes the Dellums name the official one in every federal law, map, regulation, and record.
plaw-106-130-1999: Federal court can sit in Natchez, Mississippi, on the same footing as Vicksburg under Public Law 106-130, approved on December 6, 1999. The act strikes limiting language from title 28 of the United States Code to make that change. A second, unrelated section adds Wheaton, Illinois, alongside Chicago as a place for holding court. The measure passed the Senate in November 1999, was amended and passed by the House, and the Senate then agreed to the House change.
plaw-106-131-1999:
Philadelphia's Independence National Historical Park was slated for a new front door by the Gateway Visitor Center Authorization Act of 1999, Public Law 106-131. Congress found that the park's 1997 general management plan called for revitalizing Independence Mall. A new Gateway Visitor Center stood at the center of that plan.

The center would replace the park's existing visitor center and orient visitors to the park and to city and regional attractions. A nonprofit body, the Gateway Visitor Center Corporation, was formed to raise funds and work with the Secretary of the Interior. Together they would design, develop, and build the center. The Park Service had already finished a design project and master plan for the mall.
plaw-106-132-1999: Miller Field, on Staten Island, received a veterans' name under Public Law 106-132 in 1999. The act designates that part of the Gateway National Recreation Area as World War Veterans Park at Miller Field. It does so by amending the law that created the recreation area. Any reference to Miller Field in a federal law, regulation, map, or record is treated as a reference to World War Veterans Park at Miller Field. The act was approved on December 7, 1999.
plaw-106-133-1999:
Arizona's permanent trust funds were the concern of Public Law 106-133, the Arizona Statehood and Enabling Act Amendments of 1999. Congress aimed to protect the funds from erosion by inflation and to change how distributions from them are made. The act amends the 1910 law that set the terms of Arizona statehood.

The trust funds, including interest, dividends, and gains in value, must now be invested prudently for total return. Distributions follow article 10, section 7 of Arizona's own constitution. Matching changes replace older income-only language elsewhere in the 1910 act. One more change lets the Miners' Hospital Endowment Fund be used for the benefit of the Arizona Pioneers' Home.
plaw-106-134-1999: One small wording change is all Public Law 106-134 makes, in the law for Keweenaw National Historical Park in Michigan. The park has an Advisory Commission whose members the Secretary of the Interior picks. Before, the law said the picks came from names put forth by local groups. Now it says the secretary picks only after weighing those names. The change became law on December 7, 1999. The park itself dates to a 1992 act.
plaw-106-135-1999:
The route of Britain's 1812 invasion of Maryland and Washington was marked for possible trail status by the Star-Spangled Banner National Historic Trail Study Act of 1999, Public Law 106-135. Congress called that invasion a defining period, the only time a foreign power has invaded the United States. The act amends the National Trails System Act.

The route runs from the British fleet's arrival in the Patuxent River through the landing at Benedict and the American defeat at Bladensburg. It covers the burning of the Capitol and the White House, then follows American troops to Baltimore. It ends at Fort McHenry, where Francis Scott Key wrote his famous words on September 14, 1814. The act designates the route for study toward joining the national trails system.
plaw-106-136-1999:
Rural water for a South Dakota county is the project behind the Perkins County Rural Water System Act of 1999, Public Law 106-136. The act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to help Perkins County Rural Water System, Inc. build water supply facilities in Perkins County. The corporation is a nonprofit organized under South Dakota law.

Congress traced the system to a 1977 North Dakota study of water service for the southwest area, which included part of Perkins County. Later federal law made the Southwest Pipeline an eligible project for federal cost sharing. State agencies, the Interior Department, and Congress had all kept recognizing the county system as a piece of that pipeline project.
plaw-106-137-1999:
Taiwan's place in world health work drew Congress's attention in Public Law 106-137, an act concerning Taiwan's participation in the World Health Organization. The findings open with a broad claim: good health is a basic right, and direct participation in international health forums is crucial. That matters more, Congress said, as diseases cross borders more easily.

The act builds its case from Taiwan's record. Its twenty-one million people outnumber most member states' populations, and its health results rival Western countries. When an enterovirus outbreak in 1998 killed seventy Taiwanese children, the organization could not assist Taiwan. Congress also noted Taiwan's stated willingness to give money and technical help to international health aid.
plaw-106-138-1999:
Public Law 106-138, the Terry Peak Land Transfer Act of 1999, clears federal land at a South Dakota ski area for sale to its operator. The land sits in the Black Hills National Forest in Lawrence County. Congress found the federal parcel made up only ten percent of the Terry Peak Ski Area.

The rest of the ski area already stands on private land owned by the operator. Ski lifts, trails, and a base lodge parking lot crowd onto the federal ten percent too. Selling it, Congress reasoned, would unify management and end federal permitting costs. Money from the sale could then help buy small private inholdings inside the forest from willing sellers.
plaw-106-139-1999: Keeping adopted siblings together in immigration law is the point of Public Law 106-139, approved on December 7, 1999. The act amends the Immigration and Nationality Act. An adopted person under eighteen can now count as a child under the act when adopted with, or after, a natural sibling who already qualifies as one. The same adoptive parents must adopt both children. Matching changes for naturalization follow in the act's second part.
plaw-106-14-1999: A seat on the Smithsonian Institution's Board of Regents was refilled by Public Law 106-14, a joint resolution from April 1999. Barber B. Conable, Jr. of New York had served in the citizen class of regents, those who are not members of Congress. His term expired on April 11, 1999. The resolution reappoints him for six more years, effective April 12, 1999. Congress acted under an old Revised Statutes provision governing such appointments.
plaw-106-140-1999: Utah's big federal water project received flexible money under Public Law 106-140, a one-section amendment to the Central Utah Project Completion Act. The secretary may use unexpended budget authority, up to sixty million dollars, plus commission funds for fish and wildlife. The money carries a sixty-five percent federal share. It can buy water and water rights, including flows left in streams, finish project facilities, and fund water conservation. It can also design and build the Hatchtown Dam in Garfield County and facilities to deliver its water.
plaw-106-141-1999:
Budget paperwork about state mandates is the subject of the State Flexibility Clarification Act, Public Law 106-141. The act amends the Congressional Budget Act of 1974. It targets bills that cut a federal payment to states while expecting states to make up ground through flexibility.

When such a bill moves, the reporting committee must state how it intends states to carry out the reduction. It must also say how much new flexibility, if any, the bill gives to offset the cut. The Congressional Budget Office must add matching analysis to its cost estimates. Its statement covers whether states can offset the reduction under existing law, and whether added flexibility would save enough to do so.
plaw-106-142-1999:
Veterans of one of World War II's hardest battles were honored by Public Law 106-142, a joint resolution commending those who fought in the Battle of the Bulge. The battle ran from December 16, 1944, to January 25, 1945, in the Ardennes forest of Belgium and Luxembourg. Germany's surprise offensive aimed to split the Allied armies and cut their fuel lines.

Six hundred thousand American troops fought in the battle, joined by fifty-five thousand British soldiers. American casualties reached about eighty-one thousand, including roughly nineteen thousand killed. The resolution recalls the Malmedy Massacre, where eighty-six unarmed American prisoners were gunned down. It also recalls the 101st Airborne holding Bastogne, a stand that helped block the drive on Antwerp and set up Germany's defeat months later.
plaw-106-143-1999:
Only one spot in the United States joins four state corners, and Public Law 106-143 authorizes an interpretive center there. The Four Corners Interpretive Center Act covers the Four Corners Monument Tribal Park, where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah meet. Boundary lines drawn between 1868 and 1875 created the point, and a monument went up in 1899.

About two hundred fifty thousand people visit each year, yet the park had no permanent facilities or utilities. The whole park lies within the Navajo Nation and Ute Mountain Ute Tribe reservations. The two tribes had agreed on planning its development together. The act authorizes an interpretive center and related visitor facilities inside the tribal park.
plaw-106-144-1999:
A missing sewer system in a small Oregon city led to Public Law 106-144, approved on December 7, 1999. Congress found that Sisters, Oregon, faced a public health threat from possible disease outbreaks because it had no sewer system. Groundwater and surface water stood at risk as well. Federal forest land surrounds the city, leaving no suitable private parcel for a treatment plant.

The act directs the Secretary of Agriculture to convey federal land to the city for a sewage treatment facility and treated effluent disposal. The parcel would run one hundred sixty or two hundred forty acres, as much as reasonably needed and no more. The transfer was due within one hundred eighty days, once environmental review documents were complete.
plaw-106-145-1999:
California's Otay Mountain, hard against the Mexican border, became protected wilderness under Public Law 106-145 in 1999. Congress called the public lands there among the last pristine places in western San Diego County. The rugged area is known worldwide for its variety of unusual and sensitive plants. It also plays a key part in San Diego's multi-species conservation plan.

Roughly eighteen thousand five hundred acres, managed by the Bureau of Land Management, were designated as the Otay Mountain Wilderness. The land joins the National Wilderness Preservation System. Congress noted two pressures on the area beside its wildlife value. Border enforcement work focuses there, and illegal crossing traffic plus steep ground make fire management unusually hard.
plaw-106-146-1999:
The home of a leading American landscape painter gained park status through the Thomas Cole National Historic Site Act, Public Law 106-146. The act establishes the Thomas Cole National Historic Site in New York as an affiliated area of the National Park System. Its definitions tie the site to the Hudson River school of landscape painting.

The Greene County Historical Society owns Cole's home, studio, and the rest of the site property. The act's contents show the society keeping ownership and management of the historic site. The Secretary of the Interior administers the site's federal side, and a general management plan is provided for. Authorization of appropriations closes the act.
plaw-106-147-1999: Hyde Park, New York, is where Public Law 106-147 does its work. The act lets the Secretary of the Interior transfer control of up to one acre inside the Home of Franklin D. Roosevelt National Historic Site to the Archivist of the United States. The archivist would build a visitor center there, jointly serving the Roosevelt home site and the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library. The transfer costs nothing, rests on a protective agreement, and the land reverts to Interior if the archivist's use ends.
plaw-106-148-1999:
Knowing the rocks beneath the country is the long project renewed by the National Geologic Mapping Reauthorization Act of 1999, Public Law 106-148. The act reauthorizes and amends the National Geologic Mapping Act of 1992. Its new findings stress why geologic maps matter more than before.

Map information, Congress said, is required for balanced development of energy, minerals, land, water, and living resources. Digital technology and geographic information systems have turned map databases into decision tools for land and resource managers. The amendments also add definitions for parts of the mapping program, including its education component and its federal component.
plaw-106-149-1999: New England's Quinebaug and Shetucket Rivers Valley corridor grows under Public Law 106-149, a 1999 reauthorization act. The act amends the corridor's 1994 law to expand its boundaries. Again and again its changes insert the Commonwealth of Massachusetts alongside the State of Connecticut, in the findings and in the corridor's establishment. One findings edit also adds New Haven to a list of places. The corridor's stated purpose remains helping the states involved, now two instead of one.
plaw-106-15-1999: Public Law 106-15 is a short joint resolution about the Smithsonian Institution's governing board. Dr. Hanna H. Gray of Illinois served as a citizen regent, in the class of regents who are not members of Congress. Her term was set to expire on April 11, 1999. The resolution reappoints her for a six-year term effective April 12, 1999. It was approved on April 6, 1999, after quick passage in both chambers in late March.
plaw-106-150-1999: How the Park Service may gather land for a Virginia Civil War battlefield changes under Public Law 106-150. The Wilderness Battlefield addition had been authorized earlier, but one parcel group could effectively come only in limited ways. The act removes a condition from the earlier law. Three mapped parcels may now be acquired by donation, purchase from willing sellers, or exchange, while a fourth stays donation-only. The act also fixes a spelling error in the older statute, changing Spotslyvania to Spotsylvania. It was approved on December 9, 1999.
plaw-106-151-1999: Who counts as a fire protection worker for overtime pay is made clearer by Public Law 106-151, which amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. The new term covers firefighters, paramedics, emergency medical technicians, rescue workers, ambulance staff, and hazardous materials workers. Each must be trained to fight fires, hold the legal right to do so, and work for a city, county, fire district, or state fire department. A safeguard adds that the change cannot cut pay standards won through union contracts.
plaw-106-152-1999:
Making or selling images of cruelty to animals became a federal crime under Public Law 106-152, passed in 1999. The act adds a new section to title 18 of the United States Code. It targets depictions, from photographs and films to electronic images and sound recordings. The conduct shown must be illegal where the depiction is made, sold, or held.

Whoever knowingly creates, sells, or possesses such a depiction, intending to place it in interstate or foreign commerce for commercial gain, faces a fine or up to five years in prison. An exception protects depictions with serious religious, political, scientific, educational, journalistic, historical, or artistic value. The definition covers an animal intentionally maimed, tortured, wounded, or killed.
plaw-106-153-1999:
Father Theodore M. Hesburgh received Congress's gold medal authorization under Public Law 106-153 in 1999. Congress praised his lasting work in civil rights, higher education, the Catholic Church, and public life at home and abroad. The act authorizes the President to present the medal on Congress's behalf.

The findings sketch a long career. Hesburgh was a charter member of the United States Commission on Civil Rights in 1957 and chaired it from 1969 to 1972. He led the University of Notre Dame as president from 1952 to 1987, then as president emeritus. He collected more than one hundred thirty honorary degrees. He also co-chaired the Knight Commission on college athletics and chaired Harvard's Board of Overseers in the mid-1990s.
plaw-106-154-1999:
Atlanta's growth pressed on a river corridor, and Public Law 106-154 answers with stronger protection for the Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area in Georgia. Congress called the area a nationally significant resource, already hurt by land use changes inside and outside its borders. Chances to protect the river's scenery and nature shrink as the metro area spreads north.

The zone of concern runs two thousand feet from each bank along a forty-eight-mile stretch of the river. Georgia had already passed its own river protection law for that corridor. Visitor use had shifted from boats toward land-based activity. The act supports a cooperative plan, joining federal, state, local, and private money, to link the recreation area's separate units with linear corridors.
plaw-106-155-1999: More time and more money for a Holocaust assets inquiry came from Public Law 106-155, the U.S. Holocaust Assets Commission Extension Act of 1999. The act pushes the commission's final report deadline from December 31, 1999, to December 31, 2000. It also raises the commission's authorized funding from three and a half million dollars to six million dollars. The funding years stretch through 2001. Congress approved the extension on December 9, 1999.
plaw-106-156-1999:
Alabama gained a new wilderness area when Public Law 106-156 designated the Dugger Mountain Wilderness in 1999. The land lies in the Talladega National Forest and covers roughly nine thousand two hundred acres. A map dated July 2, 1999, shows its boundaries. The designation adds the area to the National Wilderness Preservation System.

The Secretary of Agriculture manages the wilderness under the Wilderness Act, subject to existing valid rights. The secretary also had to send Congress a map and boundary description with legal force, open to public inspection at Forest Service offices. One special section deals with the treatment of the Dugger Mountain fire tower inside the new wilderness.
plaw-106-157-1999: Illinois received a piece of the Lewis and Clark trail corridor under Public Law 106-157, approved on December 9, 1999. The Secretary of the Interior may convey, free of charge, roughly thirty-nine acres of federal land in Madison County to the state. Illinois, through its Historic Preservation Agency, must use the land as an historic site and interpretive center for the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail. The governor had two years to produce a development plan, with public review, and the state pays the survey and transfer costs.
plaw-106-158-1999:
Two export agencies were renewed by the Export Enhancement Act of 1999, Public Law 106-158. The act reauthorizes the Overseas Private Investment Corporation and the Trade and Development Agency. For the investment corporation, it extends issuing authority from 1999 to 2003.

New environmental rules come with the renewal. The corporation's board may not approve an action likely to cause significant, sensitive, and unusual environmental harm unless an impact study has been ready for at least sixty days. That study, comparing the action with alternatives, must reach the board, the American public, affected local groups, and host country civic organizations before the vote.
plaw-106-159-1999:
Truck and bus safety gained its own federal agency through the Motor Carrier Safety Improvement Act of 1999, Public Law 106-159. The act amends title 49 of the United States Code to establish the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. Its contents promise added money for the motor carrier safety grant program and a written safety strategy.

A second title turns to commercial vehicles and drivers. It covers disqualifications, state participation and noncompliance, and checks before driver's licenses are issued. Registration enforcement, unpaid penalties, and imminent hazards all get sections. An advisory committee on commercial motor vehicle safety is also created under the first title.
plaw-106-16-1999: Another Smithsonian regent kept his seat through Public Law 106-16, a joint resolution approved on April 6, 1999. Wesley S. Williams, Jr. of the District of Columbia served in the citizen class of the Board of Regents, apart from the members of Congress. With his term expiring on April 11, 1999, the resolution reappoints him for six years starting April 12. The House and Senate each passed it within two days in March.
plaw-106-160-1999: Copyright owners won higher statutory damages under the Digital Theft Deterrence and Copyright Damages Improvement Act of 1999, Public Law 106-160. The standard range in title 17 rises from five hundred to seven hundred fifty dollars at the low end, and from twenty thousand to thirty thousand at the top. The cap for willful infringement climbs from one hundred thousand to one hundred fifty thousand dollars. The act also orders the Sentencing Commission to issue emergency guideline changes within one hundred twenty days, carrying out the No Electronic Theft Act.
plaw-106-161-1999:
Honorary veteran status, granted only once before to Bob Hope, went to Zachary Fisher under Public Law 106-161 in 1999. Fisher was not a veteran; a medical condition kept him out when he tried to enlist during World War II. Congress called the honor extraordinary and said it should stay rare.

What Fisher did instead was give, on a large scale, to service members and their families. The resolution credits him with preserving the carrier Intrepid as a museum in New York harbor. It also names the Fisher House program, lodging for relatives of critically ill service members, and scholarships for families who lost someone in service. He had already received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
plaw-106-162-1999: Washington's headquarters of the Department of Housing and Urban Development was named by Public Law 106-162, approved on December 9, 1999. The building at 451 Seventh Street, Southwest, became the Robert C. Weaver Federal Building. The act states the reason plainly: the name honors the department's first secretary. Its references section then carries the Weaver name into every federal law, map, regulation, and record mentioning the headquarters.
plaw-106-163-1999:
Water rights for a Montana tribe were settled, rather than litigated, under Public Law 106-163 in 1999. Its long title names the Chippewa Cree Tribe of the Rocky Boy's Reservation. Congress stated a policy of settling tribal water claims without lengthy and costly court fights, as part of its trust duty to tribes.

The reservation serves as the tribe's homeland, in a water-short part of Montana. Congress found that dependable water underpins the tribe's sovereignty and its economy. Building the works to use that water well was necessary, the act says, for a viable reservation economy. The settlement also carries out the water rights compact reached between the tribe and Montana.
plaw-106-164-1999:
An Ohio battlefield from the 1790s gained a national historic site under Public Law 106-164, passed in 1999. The Fallen Timbers Battlefield covers one hundred eighty-five acres. There, in 1794, General Anthony Wayne fought a confederation of Native American tribes led by Little Turtle and Blue Jacket. Nearby Fort Miamis hosted Wayne's legion from 1796 to 1798.

The act establishes the combined Fallen Timbers Battlefield and Fort Miamis National Historic Site. Management falls to the Metropolitan Park District of the Toledo Area, named as the management entity. The Secretary of the Interior supplies technical assistance, meaning guidance and advice rather than money. A general management plan is required for the site.
plaw-106-165-1999:
Women's business centers faced tighter review under the Women's Business Centers Sustainability Act of 1999, Public Law 106-165. The act amends the women's business center program in the Small Business Act. It spells out that the private organizations running centers must be nonprofit, in the tax code's sense.

Oversight grows in the act's third section. The Small Business Administration must examine every center each year, on both program and money. Each center reports an itemized breakdown of the prior year's spending. It also documents how much matching help it drew from non-federal sources. Congress framed the added scrutiny as the path to keeping the centers sustainable.
plaw-106-166-1999: Phoenix's federal courthouse received a famous Arizonan's name under Public Law 106-166. The courthouse at 401 West Washington Street became the Sandra Day O'Connor United States Courthouse. The Senate passed the naming act in October 1999 and the House followed in November; it was approved on December 9, 1999. Federal laws, maps, and records that mention the courthouse are read as using the O'Connor name.
plaw-106-167-1999:
A whole coastal protection system took a senator's name under Public Law 106-167 in 1999. The act redesignates the Coastal Barrier Resources System as the John H. Chafee Coastal Barrier Resources System. Congress used the findings to explain why Chafee, of Rhode Island, fit the honor.

For two decades, the findings say, Chafee led on environmental protection, serving twenty-two years on the Senate's Environment and Public Works Committee. He fought for clean air, clean water, and toxic waste cleanup. In 1982 he authored the Coastal Barrier Resources Act itself. That law aimed to cut loss of life, wasteful federal spending, and damage to wildlife along Atlantic and Gulf coast barriers.
plaw-106-168-1999:
Sweepstakes mail that tricks readers drew a crackdown in Public Law 106-168, headed Deceptive Mail Prevention and Enforcement. The act amends the postal laws to make certain deceptive matter nonmailable. Its first title restricts mailings that use misleading references to the United States government. It also restricts deceptive sweepstakes mailings directly.

The Postal Service gains orders to stop such mailings, backed by temporary restraining orders and civil penalties. Administrative subpoenas support the enforcement work. Promoters of skill contests and sweepstakes face their own requirements, and state law is not pushed aside. Later titles in the same act turn to Federal Reserve retirement portability and federal property matters.
plaw-106-169-1999:
Young people aging out of foster care were the focus of the Foster Care Independence Act of 1999, Public Law 106-169. The act amends the Social Security Act to give states more money and more flexibility. The goal is programs that help children move from foster care to self-sufficiency.

Its first title builds an improved independent living program. Nearby sections raise the assets a foster child may hold and address preparing foster parents for children's needs. A Medicaid change lets states cover adolescents leaving foster care. Adoption incentive payments appear in the contents as well, rewarding states for moving children into permanent homes.
plaw-106-17-1999: Money rules for women's business centers changed under Public Law 106-17, the Women's Business Center Amendments Act of 1999. In a center's third, fourth, and fifth years, the match became one non-federal dollar for each federal dollar. The act also raised the program's authorization from eight million dollars to eleven million dollars. The new conditions apply from October 1, 1998, before the act itself passed. It was approved on April 6, 1999.
plaw-106-170-1999:
Working while disabled became less risky under the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999, Public Law 106-170. The act amends the Social Security Act in two directions. It widens health care coverage for working people with disabilities. It also builds a Ticket to Work and Self-Sufficiency Program inside the Social Security Administration.

The ticket program aims to give people with disabilities real chances to work. Other sections attack the rules that punished trying: how work activity counts in disability reviews, and faster reinstatement of benefits when a job attempt fails. Planning help and outreach grants to states round out the first title, before a second title expands health care services.
plaw-106-18-1999: New Jersey's Coastal Heritage Trail Route received a larger authorization under Public Law 106-18, approved on April 8, 1999. The act amends an earlier law, Public Law 100-515, in two places. One change raises the authorized appropriation from one million dollars to four million dollars. The other replaces the number five with ten in a related subsection of that law. The House passed the bill in February 1999 and the Senate followed in March.
plaw-106-19-1999: House mail reports are the narrow subject of Public Law 106-19, approved on April 8, 1999. The act makes technical corrections to the monthly reports the Postmaster General submits on official mail of the House of Representatives. Its amendment sharpens which allocation holders the report language covers, splitting one reference into two subparagraphs. The corrected rule applies to January 1999 and every month after. The underlying provision sits in the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act of 1991.
plaw-106-2-1999: Beginning farmers and ranchers were the intended winners of Public Law 106-2, approved on March 15, 1999. The act nullifies a reservation of fiscal year 1999 funds for guaranteed loans under the Consolidated Farm and Rural Development Act. That reservation had set money aside in a way the act wipes out. Loan money flows without regard to it. A second section tells the Secretary of Agriculture to give qualified beginning farmers and ranchers priority, where practical, when making guaranteed loans from 1999 supplemental funds.
plaw-106-20-1999:
Three Massachusetts rivers joined the national protected list under the Sudbury, Assabet, and Concord Wild and Scenic River Act, Public Law 106-20, in 1999. An earlier study act had marked twenty-nine river miles for review. A study committee advised the Secretary of the Interior through that review.

The study found segments eligible for their free-flowing state and their scenery, recreation, wildlife, culture, and history. The Sudbury River segment runs sixteen and six-tenths miles, from the Danforth Street Bridge in Framingham to where it meets the Assabet. An Assabet segment of four and four-tenths miles follows in the findings. The act designates the chosen stretches as scenic and recreational rivers in the national system.
plaw-106-21-1999:
American troops serving around Kosovo in 1999 received combat zone tax treatment under Public Law 106-21. The act extends tax benefits tied to combat zones to service in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, meaning Serbia and Montenegro, and nearby areas. Congress called the covered zone a qualified hazardous duty area, linked to Operation Allied Force.

Treated as a combat zone, the area triggers a list of tax code provisions. They include the exclusion for combat pay and rules on taxes when a service member dies. Withholding on wages, taxes on phone service from the zone, and filing deadlines all follow combat rules. The zone also covers Albania, the Adriatic Sea, and the northern Ionian Sea above the thirty-ninth parallel, while members there drew special pay.
plaw-106-22-1999: Small business microloans were retuned by the Microloan Program Technical Corrections Act of 1999, Public Law 106-22. The act rewrites the allocation rules in the Small Business Act. Each state, plus the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Guam, and American Samoa, gets a minimum share of new loan funds. That floor is the lesser of eight hundred thousand dollars or one fifty-fifth of the year's total loan funds, plus any extra the administration assigns. Left-over state amounts face redistribution starting in the fiscal year's third quarter.
plaw-106-23-1999: Raleigh's federal building received its name from Public Law 106-23, approved on April 27, 1999. The building at 310 New Bern Avenue became the Terry Sanford Federal Building. The House passed the bill on April 12 and the Senate on April 15. Its references section deems every mention of the building in a federal law, map, or record a mention of the Terry Sanford Federal Building.
plaw-106-24-1999:
Preparing small businesses before disaster strikes, rather than only paying after, is the idea in Public Law 106-24. The act authorizes a disaster mitigation pilot program inside the Small Business Administration. It amends the Small Business Act's loan provisions for fiscal years 2000 through 2004.

The program makes loans, directly or through banks, so small businesses can use mitigation techniques tied to a Federal Emergency Management Agency mitigation program. A business must show it cannot otherwise get credit for the work. Congress authorized fifteen million dollars of program loans for each of the five years. The administrator also owed the House and Senate small business committees an effectiveness report on January 31, 2003.
plaw-106-25-1999:
States chafing under federal school rules were offered waivers by the Education Flexibility Partnership Act of 1999, Public Law 106-25. Congress found that states differ widely in students, school governance, and funding. Rules that help schools improve in one state may fail in another. Some federal requirements, the findings say, block local reform.

Waivers of federal rules can remove those blocks and raise achievement for all children, Congress argued. State education agencies sit closer to local schools and run statewide reforms, so they are often best placed to grant the waivers. An earlier demonstration act allowed only twelve states to qualify for such flexibility. The 1999 act builds education flexibility partnerships beyond that narrow start.
plaw-106-26-1999:
Rosa Parks, called the first lady of civil rights, was voted a congressional gold medal under Public Law 106-26 in 1999. Parks was born on February 4, 1913, in Tuskegee, Alabama. Congress honored her quiet dignity and her lifetime of contributions to the nation.

On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Parks refused to give up her bus seat to a white man and was arrested. About forty-two thousand African Americans then boycotted Montgomery's buses for three hundred eighty-one days. The Supreme Court ruled the segregation law unconstitutional in November 1956, and the buses were ordered desegregated that December. Congress links her stand to the movement that produced the Civil Rights Act of 1964. She had already received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
plaw-106-27-1999: Alaska's capital gained a named federal building under Public Law 106-27, approved on May 13, 1999. The building at 709 West 9th Street in Juneau became the Hurff A. Saunders Federal Building. The Senate passed the bill in March 1999 and the House in May. Its references section deems any mention of the building in a federal law, map, or record a mention of the Saunders building.
plaw-106-28-1999: South Bend, Indiana, is the city in Public Law 106-28, a courthouse naming approved on May 13, 1999. The courthouse at 401 South Michigan Street became the Robert K. Rodibaugh United States Bankruptcy Courthouse. The longer name makes the building's specialty part of its title. The Senate passed the act in March 1999 and the House in May. Federal references to the courthouse now use the Rodibaugh name.
plaw-106-29-1999: A Florida study center took a congressman's name under Public Law 106-29, approved on May 21, 1999. The educational institution in Florida known as the North/South Center became the Dante B. Fascell North-South Center. The act edits the center's authorizing section in an earlier foreign relations law. Even that law's short title gains the Fascell name. References in any other law, to the center or to its act, are read as references to the renamed institution.
plaw-106-3-1999: Two small Montana school districts were rescued from a filing deadline by Public Law 106-3, approved on March 23, 1999. Their applications for fiscal year 1999 Impact Aid payments under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act were at risk. The Secretary of Education must treat the applications as filed on time and process them for payment. The relief covers the Dodson Elementary School District and the Dodson High School District. To qualify, each application had to reach the secretary within thirty days after the act passed.
plaw-106-30-1999:
Peace Corps funding for four years was authorized by Public Law 106-30, approved on May 21, 1999. The act amends the Peace Corps Act. Authorized amounts rise year by year: two hundred seventy million dollars for fiscal year 2000, then two hundred ninety-eight million, three hundred twenty-seven million, and three hundred sixty-five million for 2003.

Money for a year stays available for that year and the one after it. Other amendments touch how the corps moves people around the world. Peace Corps employees, volunteers, their dependents, and baggage may travel on foreign air carriers between two places outside the United States. A technical edit replaces the old Civil Service Commission with the Office of Personnel Management in the act's text.
plaw-106-31-1999:
Emergency money for the 1999 fiscal year flowed through Public Law 106-31, the 1999 Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act. Title I opens in the Department of Agriculture. Its first item is emergency grants to help low-income migrant and seasonal farmworkers.

Twenty million dollars is provided for those grants, gated by budget rules. The money flows only when an official presidential budget request labels the full amount an emergency requirement. Congress adds its own matching emergency designation under the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act. Next, the Agricultural Marketing Service receives an additional one hundred forty-five million dollars for a fund supporting farm markets, income, and supply. The same emergency request conditions guard that sum.
plaw-106-33-1999: A Georgia federal building receives a name in Public Law 106-33, approved June 7, 1999. The federal building and United States courthouse at 18 Greenville Street in Newnan becomes the Lewis R. Morgan Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Section two says references to that building in federal laws, maps, regulations, or records mean the Morgan building. The act is a designation only.
plaw-106-34-1999:
Bolts, screws, and other fasteners are regulated under Public Law 106-34, approved June 8, 1999. Called the Fastener Quality Act Amendments Act of 1999, it amends the Fastener Quality Act. Congress said its aims were stronger protection against mismarked, misrepresented, and counterfeit fasteners, and removal of needless requirements.

The findings note that the American fastener industry employs thousands of workers and that billions of fasteners are used each year. They also say modern manufacturing has made nearly all fasteners meet the standards for their use. Still, a small number of bad fasteners enter commerce. The amendments respond to that narrow problem while easing rules the findings no longer support.
plaw-106-35-1999:
Public Law 106-35, approved June 15, 1999, bears the name Western Hemisphere Drug Elimination Technical Corrections Act. For all its broad name, the act makes one small fix to a large 1999 funds law. That fix deals with aid to help other lands fight the drug trade.

The act adds a new part to the 1999 law. The new part lets Congress set aside such sums as may be needed for the State Department in fiscal year 1999. The money is for work under section 481 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. The act makes clear that this money comes on top of funds under any other law. A like fix to the act's own text follows.
plaw-106-36-1999:
Many small fixes to trade law fill Public Law 106-36, approved June 25, 1999. The Miscellaneous Trade and Technical Corrections Act of 1999 makes miscellaneous and technical changes to various trade laws. Its first title lists clerical amendments, removal of obsolete references to GATT, and tariff classification for thirteen-inch televisions.

A second title covers temporary duty suspensions and reductions, plus other trade provisions. Its duty chapter names single chemicals and products one by one, from compounds with long technical names to certain snowboard boots. The act is a housekeeping package: each item corrects, suspends, or reduces a narrow duty or reference rather than setting broad trade policy.
plaw-106-37-1999:
Lawsuits over the year 2000 computer problem are governed by Public Law 106-37, approved July 20, 1999. Called the Y2K Act, it sets procedures for civil actions for damages tied to a device or system failing to handle the change from 1999 to 2000.

Its sections cover limits on punitive damages, proportionate liability, prelitigation notice, and pleading requirements. Other sections address the duty to mitigate, contract limits on damages, tort damages, and class actions. It also covers special masters for Y2K actions, the role of state law, and suspension of penalties for certain year 2000 failures by small businesses. The act channels a feared wave of cases into set rules.
plaw-106-38-1999:
Public Law 106-38, approved July 22, 1999, declares a national missile defense policy. The National Missile Defense Act of 1999 states that the United States will deploy a national missile defense. Its policy section gives the terms of that commitment.

It is United States policy to deploy, as soon as technologically possible, an effective system able to defend United States territory against limited ballistic missile attack. That includes accidental, unauthorized, or deliberate attacks. Funding remains subject to annual authorization and appropriation. A separate section states a second policy: seeking continued negotiated reductions in Russian nuclear forces alongside the defense plan.
plaw-106-39-1999: Public Law 106-39, approved July 28, 1999, corrects two funding figures for highway safety programs. It fixes errors in authorizations for programs run by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. For motor vehicle safety, a figure in title 49 is struck and a higher figure, ninety-eight million dollars and more, is inserted. For motor vehicle information, a six million dollar figure is replaced with one over nine million dollars. The act consists only of those two substitutions, raising the authorized amounts for both programs.
plaw-106-4-1999:
Nursing home residents gain protection when a home leaves Medicaid, under Public Law 106-4, approved March 25, 1999. The Nursing Home Resident Protection Amendments of 1999 amend title XIX of the Social Security Act. The law bars transfers or discharges of residents because a facility voluntarily withdraws from Medicaid.

New language says that when a facility withdraws but keeps providing nursing services, the withdrawal is not an acceptable basis for moving out residents. The protection covers people who were living in the facility the day before the withdrawal took effect. The amendment defends residents' continuing rights at a moment when their home changes its payment status, not its care business.
plaw-106-40-1999:
Propane and other fuels are eased out of a chemical safety list by Public Law 106-40, approved August 5, 1999. The Chemical Safety Information, Site Security and Fuels Regulatory Relief Act amends the Clean Air Act. It removes flammable fuels from the substances covered by reporting and other duties under the risk management plan program.

Section two is headed removal of propane sold by retailers and other flammable fuels from the risk management list. The amendment restructures how the Administrator weighs listing criteria. It bars listing a flammable substance when it is used as a fuel, or held for sale as fuel at a retail facility, under the conditions stated in the text.
plaw-106-41-1999:
A Georgia land swap is ordered completed by Public Law 106-41, approved August 5, 1999. The Lake Oconee Land Exchange Act directs the Secretary of Agriculture to complete a land exchange with Georgia Power Company. The company is a division of the Southern Company, a Georgia corporation, or its successors.

The exchange rests on papers already on file: a boundary description dated September 6, 1996, prepared by the Forest Service, and an exchange agreement dated December 26, 1996, amended August 17, 1998. When Georgia Power conveys its land to the Secretary, the Secretary conveys federal land to the company at the same time. The law finishes a negotiated swap rather than starting one.
plaw-106-42-1999: Patent office funding is authorized by Public Law 106-42, approved August 5, 1999. The Patent Fee Integrity and Innovation Protection Act of 1999 authorizes funds for salaries and expenses of the Patent and Trademark Office. For fiscal year 2000, one hundred sixteen million dollars is made available from fees collected in fiscal years 1999 and 2000 under patent and trademark law. The Commissioner may not charge fees to cover accrued indirect personnel costs for post-retirement health and life insurance, beyond what those laws allow. The act takes effect October 1, 1999.
plaw-106-43-1999:
Big brand names gain a clear path to fight weak copies in Public Law 106-43, approved August 5, 1999. The Trademark Amendments Act of 1999 amends the Trademark Act of 1946. The point at issue is dilution, the slow loss of a famed mark's punch when like marks crowd in on it.

Part two bears the name of that fight. New text says a mark that would cause dilution may be kept off the rolls only by a case brought under section 13. A mark on the rolls that would cause dilution may be struck off by a case under section 14 or section 24. The act adds the word dilution to the part on claims against new marks as well. The rules set the road, not the right itself.
plaw-106-44-1999:
Small slips in the copyright code are mended by Public Law 106-44, approved August 5, 1999. The act makes what it calls technical corrections in title 17 of the code, and in other laws as well. It fixes counts and cross-ties in the text. It does not set new policy for books, songs, or films.

In one part, on when a show or display is free of the owner's rights, two lettered clauses gain new marks. In the next, on short-lived tapes and discs, ten parts are re-counted as nine. Each cross-tie in that part is then changed to match the new count. A reader gains no new right from these edits. Their worth is that the code points each reader to the right words.
plaw-106-45-1999:
The old highway called Route 66 gets federal preservation help in Public Law 106-45, approved August 10, 1999. The law aims to preserve the cultural resources of the Route 66 corridor. It authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to provide assistance for that work.

Definitions set the scope. The corridor covers structures and other cultural resources near the portions of highway once designated United States Route 66. It includes federal, state, and local land nearby, plus private land whose owners are willing to take part. Cultural resource programs are those run by the National Park Service to support preservation of the corridor, directly or indirectly. Participation by private owners is voluntary.
plaw-106-46-1999: Public Law 106-46, approved August 11, 1999, clarifies who can act for the Export-Import Bank when its board is short-handed. It rewrites the quorum rule in the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945: a quorum of the Board of Directors shall consist of at least three members. An exception covers July 21 through October 1, 1999. If fewer than three people hold board office in that period, the entire membership then serving counts as a quorum until the period ends. The act is a governance fix for a temporary vacancy problem.
plaw-106-47-1999:
Tobacco data may be shared under set limits by Public Law 106-47, approved August 13, 1999. It amends the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938 to release, and protect the release of, tobacco production and marketing information.

A new section lets the Secretary release marketing information submitted by growers and sellers to state trusts or similar organizations. Those organizations distribute national trust funds to tobacco producers and others with interests in tobacco production. Release is allowed only as far as the Secretary finds it in the interest of tobacco producers. It also must go to an organization created or charged with distributing such funds, as the limits continue in the text.
plaw-106-48-1999:
Two names are bestowed in Spokane by Public Law 106-48, approved August 17, 1999. The federal building and courthouse at 920 West Riverside Avenue becomes the Thomas S. Foley United States Courthouse. References to it in federal laws, maps, and records are deemed references to the Foley courthouse.

The plaza at the south entrance of the same building receives its own designation. It becomes the Walter F. Horan Plaza, with the same references rule for the plaza. Few naming laws in this set name two features at once. The act gives a courthouse and its entrance plaza separate honored names in one statute.
plaw-106-49-1999:
Workers on federal building jobs gain stronger payment protection from Public Law 106-49, approved August 17, 1999. The Construction Industry Payment Protection Act of 1999 amends the Miller Act. That act covers payment protection for people providing labor and materials for federal construction projects.

The payment bond amount must equal the total amount payable under the contract. A contracting officer may set a different amount only with a written finding, backed by specific facts, that the full amount is impractical. In no case may the payment bond be less than the performance bond. A second change modernizes delivery of notice, replacing registered mail wording in the Miller Act, as the sample shows.
plaw-106-5-1999: Public Law 106-5, approved March 30, 1999, extends a bankruptcy chapter for six more months. It extends the period for which chapter 12 of title 11, the bankruptcy code, is reenacted. Amendments to a 1998 law strike April 1, 1999, and insert October 1, 1999, in each place. Other dates shift as well: September 30, 1998, becomes March 31, 1999, and October 1, 1998, becomes April 1, 1999. One subsection is struck entirely. The changes take effect April 1, 1999. The brief act keeps chapter 12 alive by moving its dates rather than rewriting the chapter itself.
plaw-106-50-1999:
Small firms owned by men and women who served in war gain aid from Public Law 106-50. Congress approved the Veterans Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development Act of 1999 on August 17 of that year. The act gives skill aid, funds aid, and aid in bids for work to such firms, and it sets up the groups that run that aid.

The act's own list of parts shows how wide the aid runs. One title deals with a growth plan for such firms in the Small Business Administration. It sets up a body for the whole land to push that growth, and a board to give views on it. A next title deals with skill aid, through a corps of past chiefs who coach new firms, and through help for firms owned by those called back to duty.
plaw-106-51-1999:
Emergency loan guarantees for hard-hit industries are funded by Public Law 106-51, approved August 17, 1999. The Emergency Steel Loan Guarantee and Emergency Oil and Gas Guaranteed Loan Act of 1999 gives emergency authority for guaranteeing loans. Qualified steel and iron ore companies, and qualified oil and gas companies, are the borrowers named.

Chapter one is the Emergency Steel Loan Guarantee Act of 1999. Congress found the steel industry was badly harmed by a record surge of more than forty million tons of steel imports in 1998, caused by the world financial crisis. That surge cost more than ten thousand steel jobs that year. It was the imminent cause of three bankruptcies by medium-sized firms, named as Acme Steel, Laclede Steel, and Geneva Steel.
plaw-106-52-1999:
Military building and housing money is appropriated by Public Law 106-52, approved August 17, 1999. The Military Construction Appropriations Act, 2000, covers military construction, family housing, and base realignment and closure for the Department of Defense. It covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2000.

The first account, Military Construction, Army, provides more than one billion dollars, in figures stated in the sample, for building and equipping Army installations and real property. Money stays available until September 30, 2004. A capped portion may fund study, planning, design, architect and engineer services, and host nation support. Service-by-service accounts follow in the full appropriations text, which, unlike incorporated acts, prints its sums directly.
plaw-106-53-1999:
Rivers and harbors projects are authorized across the country by Public Law 106-53, approved August 17, 1999. The Water Resources Development Act of 1999 provides for conservation and development of water and related resources. It authorizes the Army Corps of Engineers to build projects improving the nation's rivers and harbors.

Title I lists project authorizations, then small-project categories: flood control, bank stabilization, navigation, environmental quality improvement, and aquatic ecosystem restoration. Title II holds general provisions, including small flood control authority, use of non-federal funds for flood information, and state and local contributions. A sediment topic begins as the sample ends. These biennial-style acts are the Corps of Engineers' main project charter.
plaw-106-54-1999:
Three firms end old claims on the United States in Public Law 106-54, approved August 17, 1999. The head line speaks of claims and fines tied to the spread of facts on bombs. The act is for the relief of three named firms, Global Exploration and Development Corporation, Kerr-McGee Corporation, and Kerr-McGee Chemical, LLC.

The Treasury must pay set sums from funds not yet set aside. One firm, a Florida firm set up in Delaware, is to get a sum in the high single-digit millions. A second firm, an Oklahoma firm set up in Delaware, is to get ten million dollars in full. The third firm, a Delaware firm of a kind that caps the loss of its owners, is listed at a sum of zero. The first firm's pay ends all of its claims, as a court set out.
plaw-106-55-1999:
Public Law 106-55, approved August 17, 1999, amends the International Religious Freedom Act of 1998, the statute under which the United States tracks religious persecution abroad. Its subject is housekeeping for the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom, the body that the 1998 act created to advise on that issue.

The amendments grant the commission additional administrative authorities and settle its calendar. Each member's two-year term is treated as running on fixed dates in May, whatever the actual appointment date. A member who fills a vacancy serves only until that term ends. Administrative support comes from the Administrator of General Services, on a reimbursable basis unless waived. The remaining sections make technical corrections to the 1998 act.
plaw-106-56-1999:
Federal workers who donate an organ get more time off under the Organ Donor Leave Act, Public Law 106-56, approved September 24, 1999. The short statute amends title 5 of the United States Code, the part of federal law that governs leave for government employees.

The act sets the leave an employee may use in any calendar year. The cap is seven days to serve as a bone-marrow donor and thirty days to serve as an organ donor. A technical amendment cleans up a numbering collision in the same chapter. It redesignates the second section 6327, which covers absence for funerals of fellow federal law enforcement officers, as section 6328.
plaw-106-57-1999:
Congress pays its own bills in the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 2000, Public Law 106-57, approved September 29, 1999. The act appropriates money for the legislative branch for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2000, out of funds in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated.

Title I, styled the Congressional Operations Appropriations Act, begins with small personal allowances. There is ten thousand dollars each for the Vice President, the President Pro Tempore of the Senate, and the Senate's majority and minority leaders. Lesser sums go to the whips and conference chairmen. It then funds salaries, officers, and employees of the Senate at close to ninety million dollars, including agency contributions. The lines that follow repeat the pattern across Congress, office by office and dollar by dollar.
plaw-106-58-1999:
The Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 2000, Public Law 106-58, approved September 29, 1999, funds a cluster of federal operations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2000. The money covers the Treasury Department, the United States Postal Service, the Executive Office of the President, and certain independent agencies.

Title I covers the Treasury Department itself. It provides about 134 million dollars for the departmental offices, including operation of the Treasury Building and Annex, and official travel. A small sum covers unforeseen emergencies of a confidential nature, spent on the Secretary's certificate alone. A separate account supplies roughly 44 million dollars for department-wide systems and capital investments, funding data processing equipment, software, and services, with the money available until expended.
plaw-106-59-1999: Public Law 106-59, approved September 29, 1999, stretches certain expiring Federal Aviation Administration authorizations through the end of fiscal year 1999. It raises the Airport Improvement Program authorization to about 2.4 billion dollars for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1999, and moves the program's obligation deadline from August 6 to September 30. A third change removes a hold that a 1999 transportation spending act had placed on obligating airport grant funds until Congress extended the program's contract authorization.
plaw-106-6-1999: Two months of breathing room for airport funding is what the Interim Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act, Public Law 106-6, supplied. The 106th Congress passed it, and it was approved March 31, 1999. It sets Airport Improvement Program funding at about 1.6 billion dollars for the eight-month period beginning October 1, 1998, and extends obligation authority into May. It also authorizes about 2.1 billion dollars for the airway facilities improvement program for fiscal year 1999 and about 5.6 billion dollars for Federal Aviation Administration operations that year.
