The study tested whether a language's prestige shapes how much a translation borrows features from its source text, comparing translations in both directions. The notice fixes a broken data link and replaces a series of sentences across the introduction, background, and methods sections.

Among the corrections, the notice restates how earlier scholars defined translation universals and the laws of interference and growing standardization, and clarifies the wording of the prestige hypothesis itself. Anyone reusing the study's data or quoting its framing should follow this corrected version, which points to the proper open-data record for the underlying corpus.
plos-pone-0356999:
Ramon Eduardo Cortina and colleagues built UROREC, a compact, low-cost instrument that records bladder pressure and sphincter muscle activity at the same time in rats, the standard animals for bladder research. Their 2026 paper describes the electronics, validates them on the bench, and proves the system in living rats, healthy and with chemically irritated, overactive bladders.

Bench tests showed clean, faithful signals, and the live recordings captured eighteen standard bladder measures matching published values. The device sharply registered the disease model's signature changes, including much shorter gaps between contractions. Commercial rigs for this work are pricey and bulky; a validated, affordable alternative could widen who can run careful bladder studies and how easily results get reproduced.
plos-pone-0357099:
Kathryn L. Campbell and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on viruses living in iron-oxidizing microbial mats at deep-sea hydrothermal vents on the East Pacific Rise. These rust-colored mats coat seafloor vents where warm, iron-rich water meets cold seawater, and their microbes run cycles the whole vent ecosystem depends on. Viruses infect everything there, but their ecological role was nearly unmapped. The team sequenced viral communities from several mats and linked viruses to hosts.

Each site held a distinctive viral community, although about two fifths of viral types appeared everywhere, in shifting abundances. Viruses carried auxiliary genes for carbon and sulfur chemistry, differing by site, meaning an infection can rewrite what its host does for a living. Different viruses preyed on different mat members. Viruses, they argue, shape these communities by killing hosts and reprogramming survivors' metabolism, a real force in deep-ocean food webs.
plos-pone-0357499:
Seon-Hye Won and coauthors published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on something rarely researched in cancer care: the clothing colors women choose after breast cancer. Fourteen patients and survivors at a Korean hospital sat for hour-long interviews with an art therapist, talking about their usual colors, attached memories, and whether diagnosis changed their choices.

Every woman had meaningful color memories. Four themes organized their reasons. Color served social life first: managing how others see them and easing interaction. Next came self-image, including colors and shapes that conceal a changed body. Colors also summoned positive feelings directly. And a smaller theme recorded real shifts in preference after diagnosis, toward or away from certain shades as identity shifted. Clothing color, they suggest, is a small but genuine recovery resource, and color-based interventions deserve testing for mood and social confidence in oncology care.
plos-pone-0357599:
Jiayu Zhu and Anding Liu ask why young buyers keep wearing slow fashion, clothing made to last rather than chase fast trends. Their 2026 survey study builds a model in which a person's sense of style acts as a trigger, inner values respond, and continued use is the outcome. Several hundred young Chinese consumers answered scaled questions about taste, values, and buying intent.

Personal style sense linked directly to staying with slow fashion, and social and green values carried part of the effect of shared style awareness. Looks and warm feelings, by contrast, did not carry the effect. Zhu and Liu advise brands to stress shared meaning and care for the planet, since those values seem to hold young buyers over time.
plos-pone-0357799:
Marco Zanchi led a team of seven authors using machine learning to judge young sport horses, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Picking a future elite show jumper is an expensive gamble usually made on gut feeling and pedigree. The team tested whether data gathered early can predict which horses reach elite level.

Zanchi's models help breeders and buyers spot genuine talent before prices explode and years of training are spent. Early prediction also spares horses unlikely to thrive at elite level from harsh campaigns. Horse selection has resisted data for a long time, relying on expert eyes. A model that adds to that judgment, tested on real outcomes, gives buyers a second, cooler opinion.
plos-pone-0357899:
Nemanja Đorđević and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on metabolic syndrome in people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, where the syndrome is common and inflammation a suspected driver. At two Serbian centers, just over one hundred patients were classified by standard criteria, genotyped for a variant in a hypoxia-response gene, and tested for inflammation markers.

Two ordinary blood markers, C-reactive protein and fibrinogen, ran significantly higher in patients with the syndrome, and threshold analysis suggested cut-off levels at which each could flag it. Both markers also tracked the syndrome's ingredients, high blood pressure and unhealthy triglycerides among them, and age correlated with inflammation. The genetic variant added a twist: carriers with the syndrome showed higher levels of another inflammatory signal, interleukin-6. The two cheap markers, they propose, could complement the standard checklist for spotting patients at rising risk of heart disease and diabetes.
plos-pone-0357999:
Agustina Serafino led a team of eight authors studying bacterial RNA inside tumors, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. They found that bacterial RNA can lower a surface marker called MHC-I on tumor cells. That sounds like it would hide tumors, yet the change instead promoted attack by natural killer cells and delayed tumor growth in their tests.

Serafino's counterintuitive result works because natural killer cells attack cells that lack MHC-I, the very flag lowered here. Hiding one flag raises a louder alarm for a different defender. The mechanism suggests a fresh immunotherapy angle: use bacterial signals to make tumors visible to killer cells. Much work remains, but the direction is genuinely new.
plos-pone-0358199:
Ruigang Zhang and seven co-authors published a geology methods study in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their test site was a fossil-rich rock section in Chongqing, China, formed in the early Silurian period. The work deals with a basic field task: reading how rock layers tilt and how thick each layer truly is.

Rather than rely only on tape and compass work on the cliff face, Zhang's team built the measures from detailed three-dimensional scans of the real outcrop. Their steps let a reader work out layer tilt and true thickness from the model itself. A digital route like this can make field measures faster, safer, and easier to check again later.
plos-pone-0358599:
Oluchi Joan Kanma-Okafor and eight colleagues wrote this study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It lays out a planned systematic review about flu. The question is whether joining participatory surveillance programs, where the public reports its own symptoms, is linked to more people getting the flu vaccine.

A systematic review gathers all past studies on a question and weighs them together. Programs that ask people to report flu-like illness each week might also nudge them toward vaccination, or they might simply attract the already willing. Public health planners designing such programs will use the eventual review to judge what participation can and cannot do.
plos-pone-0358699: Ghadimi and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for an ongoing review on eye disease. Geographic atrophy is an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration that slowly destroys central vision. The plan sets out a living review that compares treatments and updates as new trials appear. A network method lets treatments be ranked even without head-to-head trials. Patients and eye doctors need that ranking.
plos-pone-0358999: Roest and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on fast heart screening in the community. Their Healthy Heart approach aimed to find people at high risk of serious heart events in a single quick round. Finding high-risk people outside hospitals matters because many first learn of their risk from a heart attack. Quick screening can push prevention toward those who need it most.
pmc-10320099:
Kolberg and co-authors present the 2023 update of g:Profiler, a free web service used in gene research. The service helps users read long gene lists and work out what those genes do together. It also converts gene names between the many naming systems used across labs and databases.

Inside, the update links gene lists to large shared sources such as Gene Ontology, KEGG, and TRANSFAC. Users can draw on many kinds of evidence and many kinds of gene names, across many species. For bench scientists, the value is speed and trust: one current tool turns raw gene lists into clear clues about cell roles.
pmc-10652699:
An expert panel of the European Food Safety Authority reviews renewing approval for a beech and oak smoke flavoring, in work from twenty twenty-three. The product, proFagus Smoke R709, flavors food by wood pyrolysis. Renewal needed fresh checks on makeup, exposure, and gene damage risk.

The panel found the composition data adequate. Modeled intake at top use levels ranged widely across consumers. Three named components raised a possible gene damage concern, and the uncharacterized part of the mix raised another. One component showed gene damage in live animals after oral dosing, at exposures above the safety threshold for such compounds. The panel concluded the product raises a genotoxicity concern.
pmc-10654299:
Atsuhiro Kitaura and co-authors report a case where breathing support failed during surgery because of a hidden crack in the anaesthesia mask, in work published in 2023. The patient was a 72-year-old man set for chest surgery. The machine and circuit had been checked for leaks before the case began.

After drugs were given, the breathing trace looked wrong and then vanished, and blood oxygen fell sharply. Staff added an airway tube in the mouth, but venting grew harder and help was called. A second doctor felt an odd sensation in the hand holding the mask and found the crack. A fresh mask restored normal breathing at once. The authors stress that mask checks must be part of every equipment check before anaesthesia.
pmc-10656499:
Marlies Cortés and co-authors trace how immune guard cells shift from attack mode to calm mode, in work from two thousand twenty-three. That shift decides whether swelling fades or turns long-term. A factor in the cells proved key to both starting and ending the attack.

The factor cuts the making of proteins inside the cell's energy units and boosts cell cleanup. A common diabetes drug copies much of the same shift. Tests used mice that lack the factor in these cells, plus human samples. Blocking amino acid intake lies near the core of the change. The work points to new ways to calm harmful swelling.
pmc-10656899:
Yisen Hou and co-authors review research on bile acid metabolism and type two diabetes, in work from twenty twenty-three. Bile acids are steroid molecules made in the liver from cholesterol. Long seen as fat digestion aids, they also steer glucose and energy balance through many receptors.

Through those receptors, bile acids lower blood glucose, boost insulin release, raise insulin sensitivity, and lift energy burn. Gut flora, cell stress, and bitter taste receptors add more paths. The review maps the main routes in detail for diabetes care. It also weighs current limits in the evidence. Therapeutic ideas based on bile acid signals close the piece.
pmc-10672599:
Tina Deyhim and co-authors review drug clearance in inflammatory bowel disease in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Biologic drugs work well for moderate to severe disease, but many patients never respond or lose response over time. Often the cause is that the body clears the drug too fast, leaving levels too low.

The review covers what speeds clearance, including body weight, low blood albumin, and immune reactions to the drug. It gathers evidence linking clearance to treatment outcomes. It also explains dosing dashboards that use clearance to set personal doses aimed at a target level. The authors note that the role of clearance checks in daily practice is still unsettled.
pmc-10684299:
Angela Juby and colleagues published a pilot study in 2023. They tested cheap body scanners against a reference scan. Sarcopenia means dangerous loss of muscle with aging. It raises illness and death risk in older adults. Muscle function is easy to test in clinics. Muscle mass normally needs an expensive DXA scan. Two consumer bioimpedance scales were compared with DXA. Fifty mobile older adults joined the pilot. Most participants had high body fat levels. Standard cutoffs classified low muscle mass for each tool.

Office scales could flag many low-muscle cases cheaply. Agreement with DXA was imperfect but potentially useful. Hand sensors on one scale changed its readings. Obesity can hide muscle loss from simple checks. A cheap first screen could trigger full testing. Clinics without DXA access gain an option here. Larger validation studies should follow this pilot.
pmc-10686599:
Hairong Gong, Taoyuan Zhang, Hailong Dong, Chong Lei, and Jing Ni present a retrospective cohort study from two thousand twenty-three. It examines whether cardiopulmonary bypass during coronary artery bypass grafting raises the risk of acute kidney injury afterward.

The authors reviewed patients who had elective bypass surgery at Xijing Hospital over about a year. They compared on-pump surgery, which uses the bypass machine, with off-pump surgery. Kidney injury was judged by the standard KDIGO definition, based on creatinine levels and urine output. Records covered patient health, medications, and anesthesia details, giving readers a careful test of a disputed surgical risk factor.
pmc-10693599:
Sida Kang, Xilin Hou, Yuhan Hu, and Hongyu Liu modeled investor sentiment as a contagious process that regulators might isolate. Market moods spread through society and move economies. Their stochastic model tracks positive and negative sentiment groups, adding watching and isolation steps plus random shocks. The team proved positive solutions exist across the board. They derived the terms under which sentiment dies out or settles into a steady spread.

A best control plan was then built for the model. Computer runs backed the theory, and checks against a fixed version showed what randomness changes. The positive and negative strains compete, the authors find. Stronger social guidance boosts the positive strain. Timely supervisory action curbs contagion overall. The 2023 paper treats market psychology with the math of epidemics and quarantine.
pmc-10693799:
Xijian Ke, Yinzhu Wu, and Hua Zheng report a case where a nerve block ended persistent hiccups after abdominal surgery. Lingering hiccups seriously slow recovery, and drugs and physical maneuvers do not always work. Blocking the phrenic nerve is a recommended fallback. The nerve is thin and varies anatomically, so locating it precisely is hard. The twenty twenty-three report pairs the block with a literature review.

The clinicians combined real-time ultrasound with a nerve stimulator to find and block the nerve in one patient. The ongoing hiccups stopped immediately, with no adverse effects. No recurrence appeared during two weeks of follow-up. The authors conclude the combined guidance technique looks effective, while calling for further studies of its safety and wider use.
pmc-10696799:
Xiaonan Chen, Jie Gu, and Yanyan Huang used a large United States health survey in a 2023 study. They asked whether eating more unsaturated fats, as a share of all fats, links to better handling of insulin. Poor insulin response raises the risk of diabetes and other illness.

The study drew on thousands of adults from survey years before and during 2020. People with a high share of these fats had lower scores on two common insulin measures. The link grew stronger once the share passed a certain level. The pattern held across many subgroups split by age, sex, body size, and other traits. The authors treat diet makeup, not just total fat, as worth attention.
pmc-10700499:
Gar-Wing Truong and colleagues reported a 2023 optics breakthrough: mirrors for mid-infrared light far more reflective than any before them. Mirrors that trap light between them let scientists detect faint traces of gases, but the mid-infrared range, prized for sensing, had lagged far behind visible light in mirror quality.

The team grew single-crystal coatings and transferred them onto mirror substrates, cutting light loss to a few parts per million. Their light-trapping chambers reached performance levels previously seen only at shorter wavelengths, and a test instrument set a record for detecting absorption. Better mirrors promise sharper tools for air monitoring, breath analysis, and hunting industrial leaks.
pmc-10704299:
Dong-Peng Li and co-authors make a new dye that can tell apart two hazards by its glow, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. One hazard is hydrazine, a toxic chemical, and the other is very strong acid. The dye joins a coumarin base with a sulfur ring part, and its glow shifts in clear ways for each hazard.

At normal body acidity the glow moved from one color band to another when hydrazine was added. That shift let the team spot hydrazine vapor and hydrazine inside live cells. At very low pH the glow grew much stronger, which marks strong acid. Readers get a single probe that flags two distinct risks by distinct signals.
pmc-10708399:
Lauren Williams leads a team on asking Indigenous families what they need. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with child weight in Australia. Indigenous children face higher overweight rates than peers.

Culturally safe nutrition programs are needed for this group. A participatory approach shaped the early research design. A steering group with First Australian members led governance. They chose yarning circles for community consultation. Trained members gathered data in their own communities. Interviews added depth to the circle talks. Lessons cover how to ask needs the right way.  Steering members trained in data collection.
pmc-10714899:
Reid and Pillemer open a theme set on pain in late life and its care in this twenty twenty-three piece. Pain hits old folks at high rates, with half in some counts in pain most days. Its roots span joint ills, nerve ills, cancer, and late heart and lung ills.

Inside, the pair maps the toll pain takes past the ache, from falls to lone life. Kin and town ties strain as pain grinds on year by year. Care has swung from drug-first plans to mind and move cures in late years. Gaps in how pain is gauged and what drives it still bar good care. The set gathers work on those gaps for old folks in full.
pmc-10716499:
Leila Satari and her team turn a stock lab ice tool into a place to find new small life. Their 2023 study sets out a thick film of life that grows in the drain pipes of more than one lab ice tool. It sets out the group that lives there, in a cold, scant-food place.

Growth of the life gave twenty-five named strains. DNA reads showed two germ groups at the top. A fungus with no name yet led the fungus side. Checks next to like cold and man-made places showed scant same traits. That fact marks the tool as a place of its own kind. Gene sets built back from the group showed a rate of new kinds that struck the team as high. Work set-outs of what the life does found proteins for face films and for parts that stick to a face.
pmc-10717999:
Susanna Pusa, Rebecca Baxter, and Anna Sandgren published this study in 2023 on talks about serious illness. A set program helps doctors hold earlier, better chats with very ill patients about goals and values. Such chats improve end-of-life care, but programs fail if staff will not carry them. The team ran four group talks with fourteen doctors at a hospital adopting the program.

Three themes came out. Doctors hovered between feeling ready and unready for the chats. They felt the work changed them, and knew it changed patients' care. Some picked just pieces of the program, while others took the whole thing on board. The authors sort what helps or blocks uptake: the doctor, the team, the patient, and the bosses' backing. Training plans can use the map.
pmc-10723599:
Andrea Sauer and four colleagues published a proof-of-concept study in two thousand twenty-three on pain during commercial spaceflight. Two astronauts on a seventeen-day mission to the International Space Station reported their pain and underwent sensory testing before, during, and after flight.

Both developed musculoskeletal pain in flight and right after landing, managed with anti-inflammatory drugs and stretching. Pain returned to baseline by three months. Questionnaires showed heightened pain experience in flight, though their fit for space is uncertain. Sensory tests shifted in several ways after flight, including touch thresholds and pain summation, but inconsistently. Interviews added personal detail. The authors call for bigger studies of sensory change in space.
pmc-10735599:
Christina Miyawaki, Kim Nguyen, Angela McClellan, and Tuong-Vi Ho describe building a dementia education program with the Vietnamese American community. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. Health data on older Vietnamese refugees in the United States are scarce. The team first ran a survey of older adults in Houston, Texas. The survey found much poor health, including a high rate of memory problems.

Fourteen key informants from the community then rated how much people knew about dementia. In focus groups, the team studied local views of the illness. Many saw dementia as a normal part of aging. The group made a one-page sheet in plain words, in both languages, with warning signs. The sheet urges readers to see a doctor for memory checks. Next steps include sharing it on local ethnic social media and at health fairs.
pmc-10736799:
Louay Almidani and four co-authors study vision loss and mental and social health in older adults in a 2023 paper. Using a national survey of Medicare beneficiaries aged sixty five and over, they compared people with and without measured vision impairment. Depression and anxiety were assessed with a short standard questionnaire, and social isolation from living and contact patterns.

Symptoms and isolation were more common in adults with any measured impairment. After adjustment, measured vision did not predict depression or anxiety, but self reported vision trouble strongly did. Worse measured acuity and contrast did predict severe social isolation. The authors note perceived and measured vision tell different parts of the story.
pmc-10737799:
Shraddha Shende and Raksha Mudar compare, in a 2023 study, what older adults with age-related hearing loss say about their daily difficulties and what objective tests show. Most people with this kind of hearing loss struggle to follow speech in noise. Evidence also points to changes in cognitive ability in this group, so the pair examined both hearing and cognition in two ways.

They tested 15 adults with mild-to-moderate untreated sensorineural hearing loss in both ears and 15 matched peers with normal hearing. The hearing loss group reported more hearing handicap and rated their own cognition worse. They also performed worse on speech-in-noise tests and on cognitive screening tests, including memory scores. The pair argue that hearing care for older adults should assess cognition both by self-report and by objective testing.
pmc-10742399:
Jeena Deka and seven colleagues reviewed ultrasound scans of nerve sheath tumors to check a classic imaging sign. Schwannomas and neurofibromas are benign tumors growing on nerves. On MRI, a rim of split fat around them hints at their position between or inside muscles. Whether high-resolution ultrasound shows the same sign was barely documented. The retrospective analysis covered ten tumors and two post-traumatic neuromas scanned with a high-frequency probe.

The tumors appeared mostly dark on ultrasound, oval or spindle-shaped. Entering and exiting nerve tails were visible in six cases. The team assessed fatty tissue deposition around the lesions and surrounding blood flow. Confirming the split fat sign on ultrasound would let a cheap bedside scan do diagnostic work now reserved for MRI. The twenty twenty-three series adds cases to that evidence base.
pmc-10743799:
Pergola and a large team of colleagues review mixed scan use in late heart failure in this twenty twenty-three paper. Late failure is a hard mix of finds, care, and fate calls for a ward team. No one scan type can show the whole heart tale on its own.

Inside, sound, magnet, glow, and beam scans each take a set part of the work. For pump-aid rigs they guide pick, place, and watch of the gear in the chest. For heart swaps they check graft health and spot cell snub or vein ills early. Wave-track sound adds a fine read on graft strain past plain scans. The team frames the mix as the base of sharp care in this field.
pmc-10744899:
Falei Zhang and five co-authors wake a silent gene set in a sea fungus to make fresh forms of a plant-like compound class. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. The gene set was moved into a host fungus that could run it. That waking path is a known way to mine fungus gene wealth for new goods.

Thirteen compounds came out, five of them new to science. Their builds were read by mass and magnet tools plus light tests. One new form has a rare cut ring and a lost acid group, a first for its class. Three enzymes did the key trim steps, like burn, cut, and cap. Most forms spared cells, and two curbed drug-proof germs.
pmc-10749199:
Osvaine Junior Alvarenga Alves and colleagues published a 2023 laboratory study of a South American plant in the bignonia family. The team focused on verbascoside, a compound they found to be the main ingredient in extracts of the plant's leaves. They also built a reliable lab method to measure exactly how much of it an extract contains.

Safety testing in animals suggested the extract was well tolerated at high doses. Both the leaf extracts and the isolated compounds showed activity against the parasites that cause leishmaniasis, a neglected tropical disease. The measurement method gives future researchers a standard way to check the strength of preparations made from this plant.
pmc-10749299:
Chengui Zhuo and nine colleagues published a genetics study in two thousand twenty-three on sexual history and heart disease. Whether earlier first intercourse or more lifetime partners cause cardiovascular disease was unresolved by observation alone. The team used genetic variants as natural experiments, testing both directions.

Genetic evidence linked earlier first intercourse with higher risk of coronary disease, heart attack, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure. The stroke link faded after confounder-linked variants were removed. Lifetime partner number showed no clear causal tie to any of the diseases. Heart disease itself did not genetically predict the sexual factors. The authors suggest the timing finding deserves deeper study, while partner count looks non-causal.
pmc-10751799:
Jan Cz. Dobrowolski and Sławomir Ostrowski published a chemistry paper in 2023 on the HOMA index. HOMA is a number used to judge aromaticity from a molecule's geometry. Benzene, the classic aromatic ring, serves as its reference. The authors ask what the index really measures.

They show the index definition meets the rules of a similarity function. In plain terms, it scores how much a ring resembles benzene. That explains why it works so well for aromaticity. The same idea can compare molecules against other references, even non-aromatic ones. Examples include a saturated ring and a family of fused-ring isomers. For those isomers, the index tracked energy differences and resonance counts closely.
pmc-10751999:
Dan Yang and eight co-authors published a diagnostics study in twenty twenty-three on spotting lymph node spread in colorectal cancer with triple-parameter flow cytometry. Finding cancer in lymph nodes guides treatment, but checking tissue slices is slow and can miss small deposits. The team built a faster test using three cell markers.

First they confirmed the markers appear on colorectal cancer cells but not on normal blood cells, using spiked samples with a near-perfect linear response. Then they tested thirty-six lymph nodes from patients against standard pathology. The flow method caught micro-metastases and isolated tumor clusters that slices alone risked missing. The authors argue it cuts misdiagnosis and speeds staging.
pmc-10755699:
Yiwei Fu and a team of co-authors trace how single copper atoms drive light-based hydrogen making, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. The setup pairs lone copper atoms with titanium dioxide, a strong hydrogen maker whose inner steps were debated. The team ran quantum simulations of the surface at work.

After water lands, the copper atom takes a flat shape that traps hot electrons. It then passes them into a shared orbital with the water. A freed hydrogen atom settles on a nearby oxygen and puts the copper site to sleep. This finding flips an older claim that the atom wakes the site up.
pmc-10809399:
Qian Xu and her team show that a stress-linked protein, when it is kept on all the time in its cut form, blocks the growth of dentin in mice. Their 2024 study looks at teeth in mice bred so that the protein stays on with no need for cell stress.

In the norm, when cells are stressed, an enzyme cuts the note for this protein and turns it into a strong switch form. The bred mice had that form on in the cells that make teeth and in cells that come from them. Scans showed it on in dentin cells and pulp cells. X-ray and fine scans showed change in how the roof and floor of the pulp space took shape. Dentin and cementum growth fell a lot when set next to pups from the same litters with no such change. The drop shows a brake on tooth growth.
pmc-11519699:
Isabelle Meulenbroeks and colleagues published a 2024 study asking aged care residents and community members what allied health services matter to them. Allied health covers support professions such as physiotherapy and similar therapies offered inside residential aged care homes. The researchers wanted consumer priorities to shape future care models.

Sixteen participants joined focus groups where they sorted cards to rank services and say how they would prefer to receive each one. Their rankings and discussion revealed which services people value most and how access should work. Homes designing care packages can use these stated preferences rather than guessing what residents want.
pmc-11540099:
Lizhi Lin, Jialiang Wen, Tiansheng Xu, and Yuhao Si study a protein in thyroid cancer in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Papillary thyroid cancer is rising in incidence, and its drivers are not fully clear. The protein TM4SF4 was much more active in tumors than in normal tissue.

Tests on patient data and a local cohort supported TM4SF4 as a diagnostic marker for this cancer. Related genes pointed to roles in cell junctions and cohesion, and levels tracked with immune activity in tumors. In cell experiments, turning the protein down slowed tumor growth and spread and raised cell death. A drug that activates the AKT pathway reversed those effects. The authors propose the protein as a target and marker.
pmc-11570999:
Lifang Wang and co-authors published a 2024 survey study of nurses who work in intensive care units in China. These nurses care for many patients at the end of life. How a nurse feels about death can shape the quality of that care. The study looked at two inner resources: a sense of meaning in life, and resilience, the ability to bounce back.

A total of 212 nurses from four large hospitals filled in an online survey. Nurses scored highest on calmly accepting death as natural. The team's model fit the data well. Having meaning in life, and even searching for it, both went with stronger resilience. Resilience, in turn, helped shape attitudes toward death. The authors suggest that helping nurses build meaning and resilience could support a healthier outlook on end-of-life care.
pmc-11571099:
Kelley O'Donnell and eight colleagues published a framework paper in two thousand twenty-four on the therapy paired with MDMA in trauma trials. Two large trials tested MDMA-assisted therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder. The drug sessions sat inside a short, intensive course of talk therapy, but the thinking behind that therapy had never been set out in print.

The paper lays out the concepts, theories, and history behind the approach. Its centre is the patient's own inner healing intelligence, with the trusting therapy relationship as the setting that lets it work. The model blends body-based and thought-based trauma care. It avoids labelling the patient's experience as sickness. The authors hope the account clears up common misunderstandings.
pmc-11579799:
Abbi Ward and co-authors test whether web search advertisements can crowdsource a diverse dermatology image dataset, in work published in 2024. Clinical photo collections underrepresent many skin tones and conditions, which weakens research, teaching, and AI tools. The team ran ads against skin-related searches on mobile devices in the United States.

Adults who clicked were invited, after a digital consent process, to contribute photos of their skin conditions plus demographic and symptom details. Contributions went into an open dataset called SCIN, after safety filtering and privacy checks. Dermatologists labelled the conditions, and skin tone was estimated with two standard scales. The study measured how many usable, diverse contributions the ads produced. The authors assess ads as a practical route to broader health datasets.
pmc-11584299:
Thayamkottu and five colleagues model carbon fluxes in an Alaskan rich fen from twenty fourteen to twenty twenty in twenty twenty-four. Boreal peatlands store vast soil carbon because growth outpaces decay. Warming now threatens that balance. The team asked what drives year to year change in carbon dioxide fluxes at the site.

They used an ecosystem model tuned by Bayesian fusion with flux, satellite, and field data. Leaf area rose over the study years in a clear greening trend. The authors attribute that trend to carbon dioxide fertilisation of plant growth. Gross plant production rose by about seventy-five grams of carbon per square metre yearly. Breathing of soil microbes stayed roughly constant. The ecosystem shifted more carbon into foliage than into stems or roots.
pmc-11586399:
Latame Komla Adoli and a large team study why some French patients on dialysis turn down a place on the kidney swap wait list. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, joins counts with talks.

Not all who wash their blood wish for a swap. The count side took all new dialysis patients of swap-fit age from a span of years, from a state list. The talk side heard patients and kidney doctors in three zones. A math model then tied traits and grounds to the choice to refuse. The aim is to learn who says no, and why, so care teams can act with full sight.
pmc-11587699:
Liangyuan Xu, Jing Li, Xiaolin Xu, Tingting Ren, and Jianmin Ma report, published in 2024, a rare growth disorder found in both tear glands of a man of seventy-two. He arrived with swelling of both upper eyelids. Scans showed enlarged lacrimal glands on both sides. Surgeons removed the left mass, and tissue tests named it Castleman's disease of the plasma cell type. The eye socket is an unusual address, and both sides rarer still.

A body-wide check found no disease elsewhere. Steroid treatment followed surgery. A year later the left side had not regrown, and the right eyelid swelling had eased. The authors also sum up earlier published cases. Their advice: when both eye sockets hold masses, keep this disorder on the list. It must be split carefully from look-alikes such as IgG4-related eye disease before treatment is chosen.
pmc-11590299:
Amoozgar and co-authors study why pregnant women are sent for fetal heart scans in Shiraz, in south Iran. A fetal echocardiogram checks the unborn baby's heart for defects. Knowing referral reasons helps clinics see if scans go to the women who need them most.

The team reviewed records from 22,600 pregnant women who had the scan between 2016 and 2021. Data came from a shared electronic record system used by centers tied to Shiraz University of Medical Sciences. The study sorts referral causes at this large center and flags patterns that may guide fairer use.
pmc-11590399:
Shipeng Dai and five co-authors trace how a small RNA molecule drives bowel cancer's spread to the liver, in a study from twenty twenty-four. About half of colorectal cancer patients develop distant spread, mostly to the liver, and treatments for that stage remain limited.

Data mining flagged a microRNA and its target gene as key players. In the spread tumors the RNA ran high and the gene ran low. Lab tests showed the pair boosting cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion through a major survival signaling pathway. In mice, dropping the gene pushed immune macrophages toward a tumor-friendly state and sped liver spread. The authors nominate the axis as a treatment target.
pmc-11593399:
Sarfaraz Niazi, writing alone in two thousand twenty-four, studies how the brain produces the placebo effect. People given inert treatments can show real body and clinical responses driven purely by what they sense and believe.

The analysis traces placebo effects to the rostral anterior cingulate cortex, pontine nucleus, and cerebellum. Niazi links that wiring to how psychedelics, antidepressants, magnetic stimulation, and deep brain stimulation shift brain chemicals. He argues that knowing how placebos work can guide novel treatments, while also complicating the controlled trials watchdogs depend on. A final section asks whether teaching people about belief-driven effects could even soften social and political conflict.
pmc-11598299:
Manera reviews rodlet cells, odd immune cells found in bony fish, as signs of water pollution in twenty twenty-four. The cells have a unique shape and seem to help fish react to stress in their habitat. When fish meet heavy metals, farm chemicals, or tiny plastic bits, these cells change in number and form. The review pulls together what is known so far.

Those steady changes make the cells handy markers for checking river and sea health. The review also traces the history of work on these cells. Little is known yet about the cell signals that drive the changes. The author asks if like cells exist in other backboned animals.
pmc-11598799:
Hyein Jeong and co-authors review clinical studies of bee venom acupuncture for shoulder pain, in work from twenty twenty-four. The cure injects bee venom at acupuncture points. Standard pain drugs can cause dependence and side effects with long use, so other options draw interest.

The team searched eleven databases and found twenty-three clinical studies. Post stroke pain led the causes, with cuff tears and nerve palsy next. Doses per session varied widely across studies. All studies reported gains on pain scores. But proof quality was low, and harms were rarely reported. The authors say the method may serve as an option, yet stronger trials must come first.
pmc-11601899:
Wang and a team including Mootha reported in twenty twenty-four a pill-based way to mimic low oxygen for mitochondrial disease. Mitochondria are the cell parts that make energy, and their failure causes severe illness. Breathing eleven percent oxygen helped mouse models, but that approach is hard to use in daily life.

The regimen pairs two approved drugs. One makes hemoglobin, the blood's oxygen carrier, hold oxygen more tightly. The other blocks a response that would raise hemoglobin and undo the effect. Together they lowered brain oxygen in mice to levels like breathing thin air, and were tolerated for over two months. The team then began testing the pair in a mouse model of Leigh syndrome.
pmc-11602899:
Chang, Yen, Chu, and Kuo present a study from twenty twenty-four on the population genomics of a heat-loving cyanobacterium in Taiwan. The microbe has uses from biofuel to pigment production. Twenty-seven new strains are gathered from nine hot springs. With older strains, thirty-two genomes span eleven springs. Genomes cluster into two clear populations within the species. Distance explains some spread inside groups but not the split itself. The shared gene pool looks closed and nearly fully sampled.

Swept genome regions differ mostly between the two groups. Few swept genes are shared across populations. Photosynthesis, movement, and ion transport genes stand out. The strains and sequences seed future biotechnology work.
pmc-11603299:
Xiuqin Wang and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study of the helicase DDX10 in ribosome building inside mouse embryonic stem cells. Stem cells depend on constant ribosome production to stay viable. Which enzymes control the earliest cuts of ribosomal RNA was incompletely known.

DDX10 sits in the nucleolus and binds the large precursor RNA. Removing it traps a small guide RNA, U3, on the precursor. That blockage stalls maturation of the small subunit's main RNA. The protein also joins droplet-like condensations that speed assembly. A leukaemia fusion version misplaces DDX10 and breaks this control.
pmc-11603799:
Jennie Brentnall and co-authors studied in 2024 how to design a practice week that gets allied health students ready for their first medical placements. Occupational treatment, physiotherapy, and podiatry students in their first year were offered an intensive interprofessional model week, acting out medical cases just before real placements began. A put out method for such design existed, but it rested on theory and expert opinion rather than people' experience.

After the week, the research staff ran focus groups where students discussed what helped, what did not, and what they would change. Those conversations were transcribed and studied for design lessons. The aim was useful guidance grounded in lived experience: how true-to-life cases should be, how professions should mix, and what support novices need. Programs elsewhere can use the findings when building their own placement-preparation models.
pmc-11604299:
Alexander Jans and eleven co-authors run a randomized trial comparing two ways to highlight early cancer growths during colonoscopy in long-standing ulcerative colitis. Their trial came out in 2024. Years of this bowel inflammation raise cancer risk, so surveillance must catch flat, easy-to-miss lesions.

Patients at four European hospitals were assigned to dye spraying or to a digital enhancement built into the scope. Detection of abnormal growths per procedure did not differ significantly between the methods. Per lesion, the digital method caught a higher share and produced fewer false alarms. It also shortened the procedure by about ten minutes. The authors conclude the digital approach can validly replace dye spraying for this surveillance, saving time without losing detection.
pmc-11605099:
Liping Wang and six co-authors mapped how brain structure networks change in people with noise-induced hearing loss, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Long noise exposure harms hearing, and the team asked whether it also reshapes links across the brain. They scanned forty patients and thirty-eight healthy people and built networks from a shape measure of the brain's folded surface.

Patients' networks showed tighter local clumping and longer paths between regions than controls. One region, a frontal area tied to mood and choice, worked less well as a hub. The hub spots shifted to a hearing area and a memory area. Two sub-networks carried odd links, some too strong and some too weak, spread across rest, focus, and movement systems. The work links hearing harm to whole-brain rewiring.
pmc-11607799:
Anna Suarez and Vera Yakupova report a follow up study in 2024 on trauma after childbirth. They ask whether stress symptoms in the first year after birth predict later depression in mothers and behavior problems in children. The study followed four hundred nineteen women in Russia over about two years.

Mothers first completed surveys on birth trauma and depression after birth, then later surveys on mood and child behavior. Higher trauma symptoms predicted higher depression two years later, even after accounting for early depression. Children of mothers with more trauma symptoms showed more behavior problems of all kinds. The authors urge greater awareness of birth trauma among families, health workers, and policy makers.
pmc-11607899:
Binura Taurbekova and four colleagues pooled past studies to test whether two gene variants guard against kidney damage from diabetes. Kidney failure is now the top fate of long-term diabetes worldwide, and genes help set who gets hit. The team searched four databases for work on a variant in the PPARγ gene and variants in the ApoE gene. Eighteen studies fed the first test, twenty the second.

The PPARγ variant cut risk by about a quarter overall. The shield held in both Asian and European groups, and across stages of protein leak in urine, an early sign of kidney harm. The ApoE results add a second thread to the picture. The twenty twenty-four pooled analysis helps explain why some patients keep healthy kidneys for decades while others fail fast on the same sugar levels.
pmc-11608299:
Alimujiang Abudoureyimu and seven co-authors study how high sugar harms heart cells and how the drug carvedilol guards them, in the frame of diabetic heart muscle disease. Gene reads flagged a vast set of changed genes in this state. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Heart cells grown in high sugar lived less, made more reactive oxygen, and fired up a swelling path with raised marker proteins. Blocking that path, its trigger enzyme, or the reactive oxygen eased the harm. Carvedilol raised cell survival and calmed swelling marks. The authors map how the drug acts on reactive oxygen and key proteins in the cells.
pmc-11609299:
Hou, Sun, Cao, Wang, and Jiang show an RNA mark stabilizes a cholesterol enzyme driving ovarian cancer stemness, in a study from twenty twenty-four. High-grade serous ovarian cancer recurs through stem-like, metabolism-shifted cells. The enzyme SQLE is upregulated about fourfold in tumor samples. High levels link to spread and poor prognosis.

SQLE speeds growth, blocks cell death, and boosts stem-like traits. Tumorspheres and animal grafts confirm the stemness effect. An m6A mark on SQLE message, set by WTAP and read by IGF2BP3, stabilizes it. Cholesterol and glutathione metabolism shifts support stemness maintenance. SQLE emerges as marker and drug target candidate.
pmc-11610099:
Hideaki Kuno and seven colleagues measured autonomic nerve damage in patients with non-diabetic kidney disease. Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy is a known warning sign in diabetic kidney disease. Its frequency and features in other kidney diseases were unexplored. The twenty twenty-four cross-sectional study covered 165 patients who had kidney biopsies between twenty twenty and twenty twenty-three. Heart rate variability, from the variation of heartbeat intervals, served as the diagnostic measure.

Diagnosis used age- and sex-adjusted lower limits drawn from healthy people. The median patient age was forty-seven, and about half were men. The team related neuropathy status to biopsy and clinical findings. Extending autonomic assessment beyond diabetes matters because these patients also face high cardiovascular risk. Early detection could change monitoring for a broad group of kidney patients.
pmc-11610299:
Garrett Thrash and co-authors published this review in 2024 on device care for drug-resistant high blood pressure. The state resists three or more drugs and can end in heart failure or torn vessels. When drugs fail, zapping or pacing nerve hubs can help. The team swept a data bank for trials of such nerve-based care and kept thirty-three true trials.

Kidney nerve ablation and neck sensor pacing led, with many trials and hopeful results. Surgical nerve cuts have mostly been dropped for lasting harms. Spine cord pacing is the new path: early results look good, but few trials exist. The authors call for proper trials of spine pacing to set rules for its use. They note the field could not pool results, since trials report gains in unlike ways.
pmc-11611099:
Yoji Tsugawa and colleagues published a 2024 study of an antibody against coronaviruses. The antibody targets a stable part of the spike protein. That region changes little across related viruses. Future animal coronaviruses could jump into humans. Broadly acting drugs would help meet that threat.

The new antibody bound many human and animal coronaviruses. It did not neutralize virus directly in lab tests. Instead, it helped immune cells kill infected cells. In animal models, it slowed disease from COVID infection. Structural work mapped exactly where it attaches. Such antibodies could stockpile protection against unknown outbreaks.
pmc-11611399:
Blessing Kene-Udemezue and four co-authors set blood clot marks next to a key drug in Nigerian children with sickle cell anaemia. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, ran at a Lagos teaching hospital. Hydroxyurea is a strong aid for this disease: it lifts fetal hemoglobin and calms white cells and platelets. Its sway on the clot path in children was not known. Eighty children in a steady state took part over three months.

Half took the drug; half had not. Two marks of clot churn were read in blood. The team set the marks by drug state and age. Readers who treat sickle cell in Africa get child data on a drug whose clot side was a blank.
pmc-11612299:
Yunpeng Zhang and four co-authors sift stress genes for marks of spinal cord harm. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Cell fold-shop stress ties to death calls past such harm, but its paths are dim. Gene lists from two bases were crossed, and sixty-eight split genes came up. Six mark genes were named, all high in harm.

A call chart built on the six guessed harm well. Work reads tied the genes to nerve cells and shield acts. Shield cell mix reads showed guard and NK cells in big roles. A three-way chain web was drawn round the marks.
pmc-11615399:
Molina and co-authors profile lung microbes in sixty-seven COVID-19 patients on breathing machines. Few studies had linked lung microbes to added infections in such patients. Samples came from deep lung wash fluid and airway suction tubes.

Full-length gene sequencing named the bacteria present and their shares. Streptococcus species made up 51 percent of all microbes found. The team checked links with added infections, death, and needing a machine for over seven days. Diversity measures and marker tests compared groups. Results help sort which microbes matter most in severe COVID pneumonia care.
pmc-11616899:
Selma Siagh and co-authors report a man whose new heart valve caught a rare, grim infection two months after surgery, in a case report from two thousand twenty-four. The man, aged seventy, came back with steady high fever and failing health. Deep checks pinned the infection on the germ Serratia marcescens.

Drug care and fresh surgery followed, yet the course stayed poor. The germ is a rare cause of valve infection and kills more often than usual agents. The authors call for more study and clear care guides for such cases. Artificial valve carriers are the group most at stake. Readers get a warning case from a quiet corner of heart infection.
pmc-11618299:
Shanli Nezami, Ahad Ghaemi, and Taher Yousefi tested layered materials in 2024 for pulling radioactive cesium out of nuclear wastewater. Their base material is a MXene, an atomically thin titanium carbide made by etching a precursor in hydrofluoric acid, by two different routes. Structure and surface chemistry were checked with X-ray, microscopy, and spectroscopy methods. In tests at near-neutral pH, the two base materials adsorbed roughly two hundred milligrams of cesium per gram within an hour.

Modifications improved the performance sharply. Treating the MXene with potassium dihydrogen phosphate widened the spacing between layers and added hydroxyl groups, raising uptake well above three hundred milligrams per gram. A chitosan-modified version was also evaluated, as the title indicates. Better cesium sorbents matter because cesium isotopes are among the most mobile and long-lived contaminants in nuclear waste streams.
pmc-11619199:
Celine Monard and colleagues test for a portfolio effect in intensive care handoffs, where later cases get less time as a handoff progresses. Their 2024 study observes morning medical handoffs in two intensive care units.

Research assistants timed each patient case across one hundred sixty-nine handoffs over six months. Nearly twenty-five hundred cases relating to about five hundred patient stays were recorded. Analysis compared case duration before and after the median position, adjusting for patient age, illness severity, organ support, and admission reason. Handoffs strongly shape patient safety, yet their implementation remains unstandardised. The study examines whether ordering effects systematically shorten attention to later patients.
pmc-11625199:
Mohammad Razizadeh wrote on the measles surge in the world and the work to stop it, in a letter published in 2024. The virus was declared wiped out in the United States in 2000, yet a 2024 Chicago shelter case grew to 57 cases, most unvaccinated. A fast mass vaccination drive reached 93 in a hundred there and capped the spread. Similar tales run in Romania and Ethiopia, where war and pandemic gaps fed large counts.

World dose rates sank in the pandemic years to their worst since 2008, with tens of millions of children short a dose. In England no zone meets the herd mark for the joint shot. Doubt, ease of access, and trust drive the gap, he writes. Community-fitted drives, web aids, and steady services are his fixes.
pmc-11629399:
Yimenu Adane and co-authors documented in 2024 what stands between schoolgirls and safe menstrual hygiene in Bahir Dar, a city in northwest Ethiopia. In low-income settings the barriers are known to be pressing, but evidence certain to this city's schools was scarce. The research staff ran a word-based study across three schools, holding focus groups and in-depth interviews with students aged twelve to twenty, girls and boys alike. And with leaders of the school gender clubs.

Four groups of barriers emerged, ranked by how insistently people raised them. Sociocultural factors dominated, stigma, taboos, and teasing around menstruation. Next came inadequate use of the hygiene facilities schools do have, then girls' lack of knowledge before their first period, and finally a general absence of support. The authors turn the findings into lessons for school groups trying to make menstruation manageable rather than a monthly reason to miss class.
pmc-11631199:
A correction notice from 2024 addresses errors in an earlier study of slow wound healing in diabetic rats. Outside reviewers raised concerns that parts of two figures were duplicated, and that the same images appeared in two places. The original authors admitted a figure assembly error, and a second duplication was confirmed as a publisher error.

The authors cooperated with the inquiry and found most of their raw data again. Reanalysis of that data showed the same trends as before, so the study's results and conclusions stand unchanged. Corrected versions of the affected figures are shown in the notice. The notice is a record of the fix, not a new study in its own right.
pmc-11632899:
Junjie Xiao and six co-authors show, in two thousand twenty-four, how one lung cell type can drive the death of another in acute lung injury. Two kinds of macrophage sit in the air sacs during such injury, and both feed swelling and harm. The study asks how the two kinds affect each other.

In mice, the resident sac cells fell in number and died in large numbers during injury. When incoming cells from the blood were kept out, more resident cells lived and lungs fared better. Fluid from the incoming cells killed resident cells in the lab. One signal they released, named in the title, did much of that harm. Blocking that signal cut cell death and eased lung injury.
pmc-11633299:
Zhilang Qiu and co-authors work out how an antimicrobial peptide strips biofilms from a stubborn hospital germ in a 2024 study. The germ, Acinetobacter baumannii, resists the strongest antibiotics in many hospitals, and the World Health Organization lists it as urgently needing new drugs. The team's peptide, Cec4, had already shown it could shrink the germ's mature biofilms, the slimy cities bacteria build for shelter.

Gene activity scans pointed to the genes the peptide switches. One gene, ompH, stood out. The team deleted it with gene editing and restored it with a plasmid to test its role on its own. The work ties the peptide's biofilm clearing to that gene's pathway. Knowing the mechanism is the step that turns a lucky peptide into a drug candidate clinics could one day use.
pmc-11634599:
Raziqah Ramli and colleagues review a decade of emergency presentations of parastomal hernia, the bulge of bowel beside a stoma that can trap and strangle, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Twenty-two admissions reached one large Australian hospital over ten years. The patients were old, median seventy-seven, and medically complex, most with stomas formed for cancer.

Thirteen went to the operating room on arrival; four needed bowel resection, four a new stoma, four a relocated one. One patient died of sepsis afterward. Five hernias recurred on follow-up. Of nine managed without surgery, seven later chose elective reconstruction. The authors stress that emergency repair is common, recurrence is stubborn, and the approach must be individualized, while calling for the guidelines this neglected emergency still lacks.
pmc-11634899:
Irdi Murataj and five co-authors print unclonable tags for fighting fakes in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Counterfeits cost money and can endanger health and security. A physical unclonable function is a pattern that cannot be copied, even by its maker. The team lets block copolymers self-assemble into random nanoscale patterns. Those patterns work like fingerprints and can be stamped on many surfaces.

Computer vision reads the patterns for checks in real settings. The features encode into binary matrices with high uniqueness and entropy. Tests support long-term stable operation. Such tags could guard medicines, parts, and luxury goods. The work joins nanofabrication with authentication practice.
pmc-11638599:
Asma Fatima and five co-authors reported a rare liver tumor case in twenty twenty-four. The patient was a sixty-eight-year-old man with belly discomfort and loss of appetite. Scans showed a large mass growing out of the left lobe of his liver. Tumors of this kind, primary hepatic neuroendocrine tumors, make up only about point three percent of all neuroendocrine tumors.

No source outside the liver was found, so the left lobe was removed. Tissue tests confirmed the diagnosis, with two stains positive even though a standard marker stain was negative. A whole-body scan after surgery found no spread, and the patient recovered smoothly. The authors stress that scans alone cannot name this tumor, since it mimics commoner liver cancers. They back surgery as the best path, with close follow-up for any return.
pmc-11639799:
Wing-Lok Chan and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-four feasibility study of an app-based rehabilitation program for breast cancer survivors on hormonal therapy. Survivors often gain weight, lose fitness, and struggle with daily medication. A phone program could support all three at once.

The THRIVE app paired with a wrist tracker for sixteen weeks at a Hong Kong hospital. Participants logged exercise, medication taking, and self-care. Recruitment, dropout, adherence, and safety formed the main outcomes. Activity, quality of life, stress, and body composition were also tracked. Feasibility evidence sets up a larger trial of digital rehabilitation.
pmc-11642699:
Lorenz Fritsch, Pauline Po Yee Lui, and seven co-authors weigh an added fix in repeat knee ligament surgery. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, looks at a side tendon tightening done with the main repair. The added step aims to steady the knee and cut the chance of a new tear. The team compares patients who had it with those who did not.

Data come from patients treated from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-one. All were followed for at least two years. Scores for pain, function, and activity were tracked, as was knee looseness. Cases with bent leg shape or other ligament harm were left out. The study tests whether the added step truly lowers failure.
pmc-11645899:
Mei Wang and six co-authors hunted the genes of two immune cell types in a child's joint disease, in a study published in 2024. Shifts in those cells track the disease, but cause was unclear. A gene-based cause test tied two cell traits to the illness. Gene readings from seven groups showed the cell mix had shifted in patients. A wide gene screen netted 64 tied genes.

The team then ran more than a hundred blends of twelve machine learning methods to build a test. The best blend sorted patients well across groups. One gene, HRH2, stood out as a key marker in the sort. Laboratory readings backed the markers in patient blood. The authors present the test and the gene as leads for care.
pmc-11646399:
Taohu Zhou and co-authors build a scoring chart that grades the severity of chronic lung disease from CT scans. Their study appeared in 2024. Standard breathing tests grade chronic obstructive pulmonary disease well, but scans show the uneven lung damage in detail. The team gathered 1,099 patients with confirmed disease from two hospitals. Software cut out the whole lung and extracted hundreds of image features.

They built three tools: a clinical model, a scan-feature signature, and a combined chart. The scan tools beat the clinical model alone. Test sets inside and outside the home hospital checked the results. The authors say a scan-based chart can grade severity more finely than breathing tests alone, helping doctors tailor care for a disease that varies widely between patients.
pmc-11646699:
Khurram and Singh present a case report from twenty twenty-four on a rare parasite cyst in a forearm muscle. A sixteen-year-old girl from an endemic region reports two months of forearm pain and swelling. Painkillers fail to help her symptoms. Exam finds a firm, non-tender lump in the forearm. Imaging points to cysticercosis, a larval tapeworm infection. Drugs alone do not shrink the swelling. Surgery removes the cyst from the wrist-bending muscle.

Tissue study confirms the parasite diagnosis. The case is rare in both site and presentation. The authors urge doctors to weigh this infection for soft lumps in endemic areas. Imaging and tissue checks secure the diagnosis. Sanitation and hygiene remain key prevention tools.
pmc-11649499:
Peng Yuan and five co-authors build an AI system to label anatomy in stomach scope images in a 2024 paper. A complete exam of the upper gut is needed to catch lesions, but doctors lack fast tools to confirm every region was viewed. The team trained a convolutional network on a large set of endoscopy images.

More than one hundred sixty thousand images across twenty seven anatomy classes were used. On a held out test set, the system reached accuracy above ninety nine percent, with high sensitivity and specificity. The authors say the tool could help operators check coverage during exams and standardize performance. That support could reduce missed spots in routine screening.
pmc-11650299:
Dóra Edelmann, Arnold Őszi, and Tibor Goda present a new way to study crowd accidents using data stored in multi-way tables called tensors, in a twenty twenty-four paper. Crowd accidents, where the crush of people itself causes deaths, are hard to study after the fact. Records come from mixed sources such as news reports and official reports, and their quality varies. A clear method could help stop repeat events.

Their study covers 186 fatal crowd accidents from nineteen seventy-nine to twenty twenty-three, drawn from public sources. For each event they logged the type, place, date, death count, cause, and setting, plus how much each source could be trusted. They add a score for source trust and find news written two years after an event was the most reliable.
pmc-11652399:
Tongfu Zhang and co-authors compare, in twenty twenty-four, two stent treatments for a torn artery aneurysm in the brain. The tear is in the vertebral artery, which runs up the neck. One treatment uses a flow diverter, a dense mesh tube that redirects blood away from the bulge. Its use here is off-label and its safety was unclear. The other uses a standard stent plus coils. The team reviewed one hundred fifty-two patients treated at one center from twenty eleven to twenty twenty-two.

All procedures succeeded. Forty patients got the flow diverter alone, and the rest got stent plus coils. Full closure rates were near equal in both groups, above ninety percent. Complication and narrowing rates were also similar, with no clear edge either way.
pmc-11653099:
ChangAn Zhu and Chris Joslin speed up in 2024 the transfer of facial performances onto 3D characters. Animators capture a human actor's expressions and retarget them to a digital face. Standard pipelines lose the meaning and strength of expressions, above all on nonhuman characters, and need costly face rigs built by hand.

Their pipeline has two parts: one describes the target face from anatomy, the other reads the source motion in semantic terms. Tests showed the system recreating expressions with matching meaning and intensity. It worked on nonhuman faces without the usual scanning and blendshape modeling. The authors pitch it as a faster route to believable character animation.
pmc-11653799:
Hemming and colleagues lay out a plan in twenty twenty-four to re-analyse many group-randomised trials and see how method choice shifts results. In such trials, whole clinics or villages get a treatment, not single people. Many analysis methods exist, from group summaries to models that account for clustering, and they can give different answers for the same data.

The difference matters most for odds ratios, since each method targets a slightly different quantity. Past comparisons were small and piecemeal. The planned study will gather many trial datasets, rerun them under each method, and report how far estimates move. The authors expect the work to guide analysts on when method choice truly matters.
pmc-11654699:
Ruff and a large team compare microbe life at the surface and deep underground, on land and at sea. Buried habitats rank among Earth's largest homes for microbes. Until now, data were too thin to split sea from land patterns at world scale.

The team analyzed 478 archaeal and 964 bacterial datasets plus 147 metagenomes. Diversity levels were alike in sea and land settings at all scales. Community makeup, though, split sharply between sea and land. Surface and deep communities overlapped, forming a gradient, not a separate deep world. Land diversity fell with depth.
pmc-11655499:
Ping Chen, Dingyi Wang, Zhouwei Zhan, Ling Chen, and Yu Chen test an immune drug for cancer wasting, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Cachexia drains weight and strength in late cancer, and no drug treats it well. Twenty patients got one dose of tocilizumab plus steroids; twenty matched patients got steroids alone.

The drug group eased symptoms far more often, sixty percent against twenty. Blood protein levels, weight, grip strength, and walking speed all improved more with the drug. Infection rates did not rise. The team calls the pairing promising for wasting tied to heavy body-wide swelling.
pmc-11655599:
Paal and five co-authors tracked body-wide inflammation in twenty twenty-four in men receiving radiation for prostate cancer, asking whether treatment feeds the slow inflammatory rise of aging. That rise, called inflammaging, raises the risk of many age-linked diseases.

Three hundred six patients gave blood before treatment, at its end, and three and fifteen months later. During radiation, several markers moved in an aging-like direction: clotting and inflammation measures rose while protective proteins and cholesterol fell. Most values drifted back after treatment ended. A few, though, stayed lower than baseline even at fifteen months. One major inflammation marker never moved at all. The authors read the pattern as radiation stirring lasting inflammatory change. They call for longer studies of how curative radiation shapes the pace of aging itself.
pmc-11655899:
Chenglin Yang, Ziyi Wang, Lingjun Kong, Juan Du, and Jie Yi compared three rapid tests for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a bacterium whose infections surged in China in late twenty twenty-three. All three tests detect the microbe's DNA in nose and throat samples, and all finish in under thirty minutes. The team checked them against reference standards and thirty-five patient samples from a Beijing hospital.

Two Coyote tests detected as few as two hundred copies per milliliter and scored perfectly on the patient samples. The Ustar test needed five hundred copies and caught ninety percent of true cases, though it never cried wolf. All three were exact on samples without the target. The authors say each test gives clinics a sound basis for fast diagnosis.
pmc-11656399:
Agha-Hosseini and co-authors sweep the tie twixt mouth sore ill, OLP, and dry mouth. OLP is a long mouth skin ill that can pair with dry mouth. Proof hints near 45 per cent of red, raw OLP hosts feel dry mouth. The sweep weighs the proof stock on that pair tie. Sense of that tie is key for full care plans in such hosts. Those plans aim to lift host ends in ward care work.

Work past the PRISMA 2020 list framed the sweep set in full. Man work on dry mouth in OLP hosts formed the pick pool. Screen work cut 897 texts to nine works by set rules. Bias was scored with Cochrane tools per work type in the pool. Lot trials took ROB 2; non-lot works took ROBINS-I. Nine works, 1960 to 2023, showed cut spit flow in hosts.
pmc-11657599:
Galic and four co-authors mine weed-killer soil for helpful germs for maize in this twenty twenty-four study. Weed drugs keep fields clean but can stress soil life and plant health. Germs that shrug off the drug and help plants grow could blunt that harm.

Inside, gene scans showed season and crop plan shaped soil germ mix more than the drug did. Rich broth tests still pulled out rare germ types the soil scans had missed. One hundred twenty strains in the haul showed plant-help and pest-fight traits in dish tests. Three team mixes of the best strains were tried on maize in pots. All three sped seed sprout and lifted young shoot mass by a wide share.
pmc-11658999:
Qu and co-authors study patients whose hormone test results land in a gray zone after a saline infusion test. The test checks for excess aldosterone, a cause of high blood pressure. Gray-zone patients show hormone levels between 50 and 100 units after the test. Their traits and organ damage were not well mapped. The team enrolled 611 patients with a high screening ratio at one hospital. Patients were split into three groups by their post-test hormone level.

The gray-zone group was youngest and had the shortest history of hypertension. Kidney damage rates differed across the groups. The team also tied hormone level to heart wall thickness measures. The work helps doctors judge how much concern gray results deserve.
pmc-11666199:
Maryam Nikoonezhad and six co-authors test zinc tablets for rebuilding immunity after stem cell transplant, in a 2024 trial protocol. Transplant patients regrow their T cells slowly, mostly through the thymus, and delay invites infection and relapse. Zinc is known to refresh the aging thymus, and lack of it shrinks the gland.

Forty patients receiving their own stem cells back will be split between zinc and placebo. The zinc group takes three tablets daily for the first thirty days after transplant. Blood tests then track T-cell recovery and thymus output. The protocol paper fixes the design in advance. If zinc speeds immune rebuilding, a cheap supplement could cut the dangerous window after transplant.
pmc-11667599:
Mehwish Khan Mahek and four co-authors review cooling methods for lithium-ion batteries in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Electric and hybrid cars depend on these batteries, which suffer when they run hot. Thermoelectric coolers, solid devices that move heat when powered, are gaining use in battery packs. The review surveys how these coolers are combined with other cooling styles. Four hybrid designs are covered in depth.

The hybrids pair the coolers with air flow, phase change materials, liquid loops, or heat pipes. The authors also study how the shape and layout of heat sink fins change performance. Their survey pulls together core ideas, experiments, and fresh findings. Battery engineers can use it to pick a cooling scheme that fits their pack. The paper supports safer, longer-lived electric vehicle batteries.
pmc-11669799:
Park, Kang, and Kim, with a research team, track in twenty twenty-four how dirty air and green space jointly relate to low mood in older adults in South Korea. Fine dust in the air has long been linked to poor mental health. Whether leafy areas soften that link was not yet clear.

The team followed several thousand people over three survey waves and linked their mood scores to local dust levels and green cover. Dust raised the odds of low mood in all areas, but the rise was far smaller where green cover was high. The pattern held across age, sex, and exercise groups. Green space, they conclude, can blunt part of the harm from dirty air.
pmc-11673099:
Fusong Ju leads a large team presenting a cloud tool for chemistry calculations in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Density functional theory is a core method in chemistry, physics, and materials science. It predicts how atoms and electrons behave, but large jobs can run very slowly.

Their tool, Accelerated DFT, runs the method as a cloud service. It pairs modern cloud systems with algorithms rebuilt for graphics processors. The authors claim about ten times faster runs with no loss of accuracy. They give build details, sample jobs, and speed tests. The pitch is faster results with no change to how scientists already work, plus easy scaling for big jobs.
pmc-11673599:
Richardson and four co-authors reviewed eye problems linked to inflammatory bowel disease in twenty twenty-four. Bowel inflammation can affect the eyes in four to twelve percent of patients, more often in Crohn's disease than ulcerative colitis. The review covers causes, frequency, and treatment side effects.

The most common eye conditions are episcleritis, which flares with bowel activity, and uveitis, which can appear independently and sometimes reveals undiagnosed bowel disease. Surface problems range from common dry eye to a rare corneal ulceration that risks perforation and needs urgent care. Treatments themselves can harm eyes: steroids may cause cataracts and glaucoma, one drug irritates eye tissues, and biologic drugs can occasionally trigger uveitis or serious infections. The authors urge joint care between gut and eye specialists for earlier detection.
pmc-11674299:
A team of co-authors reports a case in two thousand twenty-four of a custom dental device built with computer design tools. Moving lower molars backward is one of the harder jobs in orthodontics, limited by anatomy and mechanics. The usual alternatives include pulling teeth or shaving tooth edges, which a custom device might avoid.

The patient was a girl of fourteen with a bite fault and canines growing in the wrong place. The device was anchored to a small screw set in the jaw shelf, with a rigid arm and a coil that pushed both lower molars back. After eight months of monthly adjustments, the molars had moved as planned.
pmc-11675999:
Garam Byun and colleagues published a 2024 review of how outdoor temperature affects the minds and brains of older adults. Growing research links heat and cold with conditions such as depression and dementia, and people over sixty may be especially vulnerable. The team searched major medical databases for studies on temperature and mental or neurological health in this age group.

Studies using indoor or laboratory exposure were set aside, and each included study was checked for bias using a World Health Organization tool. By gathering scattered evidence in one place, the review helps public health planners judge whether heat warnings and housing policy should treat older adults' brain health as a concern.
pmc-11676699:
Shengli Jing and co-authors compare gene activity in two kinds of brown planthopper, a major rice pest in Asia. Their study appeared in 2024. One kind is beaten by a resistant rice variety; the other has adapted and feeds on it freely. The team read the genes of young insects before and after feeding on the resistant rice. Whole gene clusters shifted between the two kinds.

The shifts covered protein making, fat building, skin structure, and transport. One transport gene stood out in the honeydew the adapted insects produce, hinting it helps them handle the plant's defenses. Longevity and skin genes also moved in telling ways. The authors say the contrast maps how a pest breaks plant resistance, guiding breeders toward defenses that last longer.
pmc-11676799:
Ju Wang and seven co-authors study how a peptide called RHAU grips pairs of G-quadruplexes, folded knots that DNA can form. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Single quadruplexes can link into dimers, the simplest multi-unit form. RHAU was known to recognize such dimers, but its tastes among dimer types were unmapped.

Using size-based chromatography, they timed how long the peptide lingers with six dimer forms. A hybrid tandem dimer offered special binding sites and a weak grip. Bulky ends on one special form blocked the peptide almost entirely. Stacked dimers from separate strands bound tighter than those folded within one strand. The results enrich the picture of quadruplex variety. They also guide anyone designing peptide probes for these DNA structures.
pmc-11676899:
