Andreia Lopes and colleagues published a 2024 study on pulling healthy pigments from seaweed in a cleaner way. Carotenoids are the orange and yellow pigments in many plants and algae. They are prized for food and health uses, but standard extraction uses harsh solvents.

The team's test seaweed is Himanthalia elongata, a brown alga. First they tried classic methods with varied solvents and heat to find a good base method. Then they moved to microwave-assisted extraction, which heats samples fast and uses less solvent. A three-factor design tuned the ratio of solid to solvent, the heat, and the time. The result is a greener recipe for getting these pigments at good yield.
pmc-11681899:
Granovetter and co-authors test vision after one-sided brain surgery in children. Surgery removed part of the occipitotemporal cortex in some patients. The team scanned the spared side in 21 patients and 21 controls. Nine resections sat inside that cortex, and twelve sat outside. Face, object, and word tasks probed visual coding.

Scan patterns for category and item coding matched controls. No group gaps showed in selectivity or adaptation marks. Patients still scored lower on face and object tests. Word reading held at control levels for patients. The authors say one side adapts, but two sides stay needed for full skill.
pmc-11684499:
Ilari Kuitunen and six co-authors test how well ChatGPT-4o judges bias risk in trials, in twenty twenty-four. Reviews of health studies must rate how sound each trial is. That rating takes much time, and human raters often disagree. The team asks whether a large language model can help, building on two small prior tests with mixed results.

One past test used a tool for non-random trials and found low agreement with humans. Another small test used the main trial bias tool and was more hopeful. The authors frame their own test in that gap. Readers get a clear case for why speed and steady ratings both matter in review work.
pmc-11688599:
Anna Hermansen and colleagues ran focus groups with cancer patients in 2024. Sharing health data needs patient consent. Preferences guide that consent in practice. Precision cancer research depends on shared data. Utility models miss how people decide. Gut shortcuts shape real choices heavily.

Several mental shortcuts emerged from discussions. Authority cues built or broke trust. Security needs drove control-seeking behaviour. Transparency wishes appeared alongside control wishes. Familiar examples shaped risk feelings strongly. Emotion also coloured benefit judgements. Together, shortcuts swayed sharing intentions. Consent design should respect these patterns. Trust sits at the heart of consent.
pmc-11690099:
Chi-Tsun Chiu gauges, in a solo 2024 study, how many working years lie ahead for Mexicans at age 50. The country's population ages fast, and pension rules are set to toughen, with early retirement penalized from 2028 onward. Estimates of working life expectancy can tell whether such shifts are feasible. The study draws on a national longitudinal survey of adults aged 50 and older.

At age 50, men face an average life span of 29 more years, of which about 17 are working years. That is close to three fifths of their remaining life. Women live longer, about 32 more years, but work only about eight of them, a quarter of their span. The gap runs hard against women. Chiu urges steps to keep older women in work longer, from training to care support.
pmc-11690299:
Mary Milidonis and three co-authors study phone apps for pain among older adults of two races. Their twenty twenty-four project gave nineteen older adults two of five free pain apps to try. Most were women, and most were White, with about a quarter Black. Each person rated the apps on a standard scale that scores charm, ease of use, looks, and facts. Pain had lasted from three months to twelve years.

Both groups prized clear steps and easy menus. Black users said fear and doubt could deter use, and some prized a personal doctor more. White users cited tangled design and low charm as deterrents. Both groups saw value in some shared features.
pmc-11690499:
Chen Li, Xiaodong Chen, and Lingxiao He study falls and total ability among older adults in Xiamen, China. Their twenty twenty-four paper surveys six hundred twelve people who live at home. Total ability here means the body's built-in reserve across mind, body, and mood. The team asks if a score for that reserve can flag who is at risk of a fall.

Higher scores linked to lower fall risk. A cutoff score split the group well in their test. Adding long-term illness as a factor changed the result only a bit. The authors say the score could help towns target fall prevention to the right people, early and cheaply.
pmc-11691199:
Qingwei Wang, Yu Ma, and Jiayu Chen published a study in 2024 on the refinement of long-term care policies in China, from the 1940s to 2023. China's population has aged rapidly, and its care policies have developed alongside that shift. Gaps persist, however, between what policies intend and what older adults actually need.

The researchers analyzed legislative documents and top-level directives across the period. They found a misalignment: home and community-based services were built up while demand leaned toward institutional care, leaving some resources underused. Regulation was also fragmented across many authorities, which made coordinated governance and implementation difficult. The authors argue that China needs adaptive policy mechanisms that keep pace as the population's age structure changes. They also urge measures that align the care supplied with what people actually want.
pmc-11691599:
Rona Karasik and four co-authors gave a presentation in 2024 on applying antiracist pedagogy to teaching about health disparities in later life. Racial health disparities are well documented across the life course. Merely recognizing them, however, does not prepare future gerontologists, care providers, and policy makers to address their root causes.

The presentation shares newly developed and adapted educational materials, building on the team's earlier work on housing and retirement. At the core is a timeline pairing key historical events with the health policies and programs of their eras. Films and other media accompany the timeline activities. The goal is to lead students toward the roots of the disparities, not only their visible shape. The team also notes the tension of the present moment: strong advocacy for racial equity on one side and laws that restrict such work on the other.
pmc-11692099:
Jieun Yoon and seven co-authors published a study in 2024 on a plantar pressure test as a possible way to detect preclinical Alzheimer's disease. The test measures force through the soles of the feet. It checks how well a person can increase or decrease that pressure. The standard cognitive test for this early stage takes a long time and can be demanding for older patients.

The researchers tested 210 adults aged sixty to eighty-seven with a plantar pressure device and with the standard cognitive score. People whose foot pressure control was worse tended to score worse on the standard test. The group with the poorest foot control also scored far lower than the group with the best control. The associations were weak but statistically clear. The authors suggest that this quick, low-burden foot test could help identify people in the preclinical stage of the disease.
pmc-11692699:
Tina Brinkley and co-authors read lap-by-lap wobble in a six-minute walk test among older adults with extra weight, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Thirty-three adults walked a short course while half-lap times were logged. Curve parts were pulled from the pace lines.

One part, holding over seventy percent of the spread, joined speed with steadiness. High scores there tracked with longer walks, faster starts, and better function scores. A second part tracked pure steadiness and tied to balance and pace drift. Fast starts marked the fitter walkers. The authors ask whether training speed and steadiness can guard independence. Readers get more from a walk test than distance alone.
pmc-11698299:
Edward Harris, Evan Schroder, and Teryn Berks published a 2024 education study on teaching biochemistry in a flipped classroom. Biochemistry is heavy with difficult concepts, and students easily drift during lectures. In a flipped format, students meet the material before class and spend class time working actively.

The authors flipped the first half of an upper-level course, taken mostly by juniors and seniors, and taught the second half as traditional lectures. They compared learning outcomes and student attitudes between the halves. Lower-performing students benefited most from the flipped format. The study offers practical evidence for instructors weighing the effort of flipping against gains for the students who struggle most.
pmc-11706099:
Baku Takahashi and three colleagues report a seventy-year-old whose heart held a giant tumor plus three other diseases, in a case report published in two thousand twenty-four. He arrived with chest discomfort and stomach pain. Echocardiography found a large myxoma filling the right atrium.

The same heart had severe tricuspid valve leakage, a calcified and narrowed aortic valve, and diffuse coronary artery disease. Surgeons removed the tumor, patched the septum with the patient's own pericardium, repaired the tricuspid valve, replaced the aortic valve, and bypassed the coronary lesion in one plan. The authors warn that myxomas can coexist with other cardiac disease. Careful evaluation before urgent tumor surgery prevented missed, lethal companions.
pmc-11712699:
Yi-Ting Wang and a large team of co-authors test a new blood test method, published in 2025, for signs of Alzheimer disease. Blood tests for the disease have grown fast, but each new method must be checked against trusted ones. The method here, called NULISA, was built to spot proteins in blood with very high sensitivity. The team focused on tau protein forms that carry extra phosphate groups.

The study covered three hundred ninety-seven people in a Canadian aging cohort. Each person gave blood for both the new test and older tests, and most also had brain scans. The new test matched the older tests closely, and its tau results tracked the scan results well. For one tau form, the test sorted people with abnormal scans from others with high accuracy. The authors say the method can join the tools used to find and stage the disease.
pmc-11727899:
Jiwon Park and a team of co-authors validate 3D software that checks where spine screws truly sit after surgery. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Metal glare on ordinary CT scans blurs screw edges, and many hospitals lack navigation rigs to guide placement live.

The software rebuilds screws from their known density values. Fifty screws were planted in pig spines with random breaches, and three surgeons judged them by old and new views. The software kept perfect sensitivity while specificity jumped from sixty-three to eighty-three percent. Its positive calls were right ninety-six percent of the time. Nearly four hundred patient screws confirmed the gain, and agreement between readers was excellent. Misread screws mean missed complications, so the sharper view matters.
pmc-11728499: Fine writes in twenty twenty-four an editorial on the fallout of the twenty seventeen world workshop that reclassified gum diseases. The new scheme for periodontal diseases, he argues, opened gaps in knowledge even as it reorganised the field. His piece sets out to expose those gaps and the obstacles the decision created, alongside chances for growth that the shake-up offers. It is a short opinion piece rather than a study.
pmc-11760599:
Julia Wlosik and colleagues characterized an unusual natural killer cell group in two thousand twenty-five. Their setting was acute myeloid leukemia. Natural killer cells can kill leukemia cells directly. Leukemia often weakens them to escape attack. An unconventional subset expands in these patients. Similar expansion occurs in some chronic viral infections.

Advanced cell profiling defined the subset precisely. It carries one surface marker but lacks another. Two master control proteins appear together inside. Lab tests showed the cells can regain the missing marker. Expansion of this subset tracked with worse patient outcomes. That link makes it a treatment target candidate. Restoring killer function could help patients.
pmc-11772299:
Xian Liu and colleagues present a 2024 study of tiny particles built to protect the kidney when blood flow returns after a blockage. That rush of blood, while needed, floods tissue with harmful oxygen by-products. The damage is a top cause of sudden kidney failure and can harden into lasting kidney disease.

The team joined curcumin, a natural compound from turmeric, with the metal ruthenium to form dots smaller than ten nanometers. A coating kept the dots stable in water. In mice with this kidney injury, the dots mopped up the harmful by-products and eased tissue damage. Treated mice showed less swelling, fewer stress markers, and less scarring over time. The dots also slowed the shift toward chronic disease. The work offers a fresh route to guard kidneys at a risky moment.
pmc-11789199:
Heike Fischer and three colleagues review a program that tried to ease the physical strain on home care workers in Norway. Home care staff face heavy lifting and rushed work, with high rates of muscle pain and sick leave. The program, called GoldiCare, spread physical tasks more evenly across the day, aiming for a load that is just right for long-term health. The study asks how well the plan was put into practice.

The team held ten one-to-one talks with managers and five group talks with care workers. Staff broadly liked the idea, yet the reviewers found snags in how strain was measured and in the tool used to plan tasks. Some sites took the plan up only in part. The study shows why a sound idea can still stall on daily work habits.
pmc-11798999:
Rafael Gargurevich, Valeria Campodónico, and Lennia Matos study why fear of COVID-19 led some people to grow and others to suffer stress symptoms. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The pandemic harmed mental health widely, yet many people also reported personal growth.

The team surveyed three hundred ninety-one adults in Peru with standard questionnaires. They focused on three basic needs: feeling free, capable, and connected. When those needs were met, fear linked more weakly to growth loss; growth rose instead. When the needs were frustrated, fear fed growth in a strained way and fed stress directly. The authors say supporting basic needs helps explain who grows after a crisis and who stays stuck in stress.
pmc-11821299:

pmc-11888699:
Swarupa Gnana Sudha Meriam and colleagues check if simple body measures can flag insulin resistance, in this study from South India, published in twenty twenty-four. pmc-12662799:
Choi, Sohn, and Leadbeatter propose a trauma informed care model for dental practitioners, in a commentary from twenty twenty-five. The commentary argues dental teams should assume trauma is common and design care accordingly, rather than waiting for disclosure.
pmc-12663399:
Tina Frodermann and twelve colleagues tracked which bacteria colonize the airways of extremely premature babies. pmc-12669699:
Kawa Kaky and colleagues dope a specialty glass with a rare earth to make it block gamma rays better, in this materials study from twenty twenty-five. pmc-12676799:

pmc-12690399: Yongping Qiu and co-authors describe the nursing care of a very ill patient with severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, a tick-borne viral illness. pmc-12690499:
Takayuki Onishi and colleagues reviewed catheter options for calcified mitral valves in 2025. Heavy calcium complicates mitral valve disease. Surgery is risky for many such patients. pmc-12696099:
Agam Shayit and co-authors published a 2025 chemistry paper reporting the largest exact calculation of its kind for a molecule. pmc-12700899:
David Geary and five colleagues show that how complexly parents talk about numbers predicts preschoolers' later counting knowledge, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. pmc-12702299:
Chih-Chen Tzang and a team of co-authors measure the rebound after patients stop GLP-1 weight and diabetes drugs. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. The medicines work while taken, yet real life is full of interruptions, and the aftermath needed numbers.

pmc-12709699:
Yanfeng Xu, Chong Guo, and Banglin Yang follow Chinese adolescents to trace how stacked family risks feed self injury without suicidal intent, in work from twenty twenty-five. Many single risk factors are known, but how piled up family risk works over time was unclear.

pmc-12714799:

pmc-12715499:

pmc-12716599:

pmc-12722699:
Menwuyelet Melaku and Deribe Hirpo analyze the quantum properties of light formed by superposing two kinds of two-mode cavity beams, one coherent and one subharmonic. pmc-12728999:

pmc-12729199:

pmc-12730799:

pmc-12731899:

pmc-12733299:

pmc-12733399:

pmc-12733899:

pmc-12735899:

pmc-12736199:

pmc-12737299:

pmc-12737599:

pmc-12742199:

pmc-12748799:

pmc-12749899:

pmc-12752499:

pmc-12780199:

pmc-12782599:

pmc-12783099:

pmc-12785299:

pmc-12808999:

pmc-12812399:

pmc-12816299:

pmc-12820299:

pmc-12821999:

pmc-12823599:

pmc-12824299:
Görkem Ata and co-authors run, in twenty twenty-five, a trial of breathing and trunk exercises for children with spinal muscular atrophy. That illness weakens muscles over time, including breathing muscles. Thirty-eight children, with a mean age of about ten, were split into two groups. Both groups did breathing exercises and breathing muscle training for eight weeks. The training used a device set at a share of each child's max breath force. One group added trunk control exercises three times a week.

Both groups gained breathing strength and motor skill. The trunk group gained extra in sitting balance, fine movement control, and upper limb scores. Gains between groups were not clearly distinct in strict tests, the authors note.
pmc-12824399:
Daorina Bao and co-authors test a small wind turbine in real wind, in work from 2025. They set a five kilowatt test machine with blades that can change angle on open land near Hohhot. Sensors logged wind speed, wind path, and strain at the blade base many times each second.

The team compared two spells with like mean wind but unlike gust strength. Stronger gusts raised strain swings a lot and cut the blade life by near a third. Turning the blades to a new angle curbed peak loads and excess power well. The results give builders firm field data for safer small turbines.
pmc-12825199:
Sema Erdem, Kadriye Ağan, and Ipek Midi compare death prediction scores in status epilepticus in a study from two thousand twenty-five. This condition, a prolonged seizure state, is a common emergency with high death rates. Brain wave monitoring helps both diagnosis and prognosis.

The team reviewed two hundred episodes in one hundred eighty-eight patients over four years. They scored each case with two seizure-specific scores and four general severity scores, plus consciousness and comorbidity measures. A general organ failure score performed best, and general scores beat the seizure-specific ones overall. Still, all scores together explained only about half of the deaths. The authors call for better, disease-specific tools.
pmc-12831999:
Jain and co-authors report a woman whose breathing muscle weakness from dermatomyositis was first read as pneumonia. This disease inflames skin and muscle, and lung tissue disease is its best-known lung link. Weak breathing muscles are less often spotted and can mimic lung illness.

The 40-year-old woman first came in short of breath, and scans suggested pneumonia. Three weeks of antibiotics failed as weakness and an itchy rash spread. Later scans pointed to collapsed lung, not infection, and enzyme levels were high. Skin signs, the V sign and Gottron's papules, plus biopsy confirmed the disease. Immune therapy brought clear improvement.
pmc-12836999:
Di Mao and co-authors study whether a hormone that gauges egg reserve links to early miscarriage, in work from two thousand twenty-five. Records covered near nineteen thousand women who conceived through lab-assisted cycles at one Beijing hospital. A gene-based analysis added a check for true cause and effect.

In the lab-assisted group, women with low hormone levels lost pregnancies early more often than women with high levels. The risk fell in steps as levels rose. The gene analysis found no causal link for miscarriage in general. The authors advise calm for natural conception, but care in lab-assisted cycles with low levels.
pmc-12837099:
Shiyin Mu published a solo analysis in two thousand twenty-five on body wear-and-tear in women with infertility. Allostatic load scores the strain that long stress leaves across body systems. Infertility brings heavy stress, yet this marker had barely been studied in affected women.

Using a national United States health survey, the study compared fifty-nine women with infertility against three hundred sixty controls. The infertility group carried larger waists, higher body weight scores, and higher blood pressure. Their protective cholesterol ran lower. Together these gave a clearly higher allostatic load score, which held after survey weighting. The author also hunted for single markers that predict high load in this group.
pmc-12849099:
Yueqing Feng and colleagues compare three milk-derived fortifiers for preterm infants. Their systematic review and network meta-analysis appeared in twenty twenty-five. Fortified breast milk supports growth in babies born early. Bovine, human, and donkey milk fortifiers all exist, with no clear winner.

Ten studies with several hundred infants entered the review. Five studies fed the network comparison across fortifier types. Human milk fortifier linked to fewer cases of a severe gut disease. Bovine fortifier carried higher risk of that disease by comparison. Other illness and death outcomes were also tracked. Neonatal units gain ranked evidence, though the study base remains small.
pmc-12853899:
Shuang Zuo, Guofeng Wei, and Haishan Li build a prediction model for restarting the heart after cardiac arrest in a 2025 study. Survival after out of hospital arrest stays low worldwide, and spotting likely responders early helps teams use resources well. The team reviewed records for about nine hundred arrest patients resuscitated in one Chinese hospital's emergency department.

About twenty percent regained a pulse. More defibrillator shocks predicted success, while larger total adrenaline doses and resuscitation lasting thirty minutes or more predicted failure, with a small positive weight for one blood pressure drug. The model separated outcomes well and calibrated reasonably. The authors offer it as decision support, pending validation elsewhere.
pmc-12860099:
Xinru Li, Jianan Han, Yanan Wang, and Chichen Zhang study older migrants who care for grandchildren in a large Chinese city in two thousand twenty-five. Many older people move to cities to help raise grandkids, yet they can end up cut off from friends and local life. The team asks how grandchild care shapes that sense of isolation.

Survey data from Shenzhen shows that more care went with lower isolation scores. Taking part in local life explained part of that link, about a third of the total. The wish to settle for good also changed how strong the later part of the link was. The work points to local ties as a path to better social health.
pmc-12866199:
Mahram and six colleagues review clinical trials of stem cell therapy after heart attack in twenty twenty-five. The hope is that fresh cells mend dead heart muscle. From over five thousand papers, forty-three trials qualified. Cell type, timing, route, and dose varied widely across them.

Bone marrow and mesenchymal cells drew the most study. Gains were modest but real on pump strength and scar size in the pooled read. Patients with the weakest hearts and younger ages gained most. A three to seven day window after attack looked best. How success gets defined swayed verdicts a lot, they warn.
pmc-12893999:
Helen Leonard and colleagues wrote a policy article in 2026 on Australia. They address how intellectual disability is identified nationally. A new national centre for disability health opened recently. Its aim is high-quality care for all affected Australians. Tracking progress needs a stable count of people affected. That count depends heavily on the definition used. Different data systems define the condition differently. The authors set out a workable shared approach.

Their approach combines several practical markers across systems. Test scores, known conditions, and medical records all count. Education levels and disability scheme codes also count. Each source alone would miss many people. Together they allow fair comparisons across places. Trends over time also become more trustworthy. The article argues this consistency serves policy well. Research quality improves when definitions stay stable.
pmc-12926399:
Katzenelson and eight colleagues compare microbes in the appendix and mouth of children with appendicitis in twenty twenty-six. The microbiome is thought to play a central role in how appendicitis develops. The team studied twenty children under twelve, split into simple and complicated cases. Samples came from saliva and from appendix tissue scrapings.

In complicated cases, three bacterial groups were more abundant in the appendix than in the mouth. No such gap appeared in simple cases. Appendix levels of one group correlated strongly with mouth levels of all studied bacteria. Tooth decay status was alike in the two groups. The authors suggest a link between oral and appendix bacteria across disease phases. Worse disease tracked with larger microbial shifts.
pmc-12947699:
Priulli and co-authors study how money strain and food insecurity relate to a planet-friendly diet in Brazilian children. The study covered 378 children aged eight and nine in Viçosa, Minas Gerais. Diet was recorded with day-long recalls, and a health diet index scored each child. A national scale measured household food insecurity. Surveys captured family income and background traits.

The average diet score was low, at 37.5, showing weak fit with the guide. Children from poorer homes aligned slightly better on parts of the score. Adjusted models tested the links while holding other traits steady. The results complicate the idea that green diets belong to the well-off. Local food habits shape what the index rewards.
pmc-13079999:
Thomas Münzel and colleagues issue a policy statement naming nicotine itself a cardiovascular toxin, in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Twelve evidence-based messages make the case. The novelty is the target: not smoke, not tar, but the nicotine molecule, across cigarettes, e-cigarettes, heated tobacco, and the new synthetic pouches.

The statement covers vascular and metabolic harm, passive exposure, mechanisms, and economic burden, with pointed attention to youth addiction engineered by flavors and marketing. It lands as Europe revises tobacco taxation, setting first minimum duties on e-liquids and pouches. The authors demand the rest of the toolkit too: advertising bans, flavor restrictions, and indoor-use prohibitions applied evenly to every nicotine product. Their aim is to stop a replacement generation of addiction before it calcifies into heart disease statistics.
pmc-13135599:
Four plant breeders, Michaela Jung, Bettina Hänni, Hélène Muranty, and Andrea Patocchi, report in twenty twenty-six on genes that help apple trees fight apple blotch. Blotch is a leaf disease on the rise as growers spray less. Two crosses and a panel of over one hundred twenty kinds of apple were scored in the field across three seasons.

Five spots in the genome shaped resistance, but each one counted for little on its own. Picking single markers will not work well, the team finds. Whole-genome prediction did better, reaching fair accuracy. The authors back that route for breeding. Their work gives apple growers their first genetic tools against the disease.
pmc-13139599:
Yan Zhang and co-authors link pulse pressure to heart disease severity in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Pulse pressure is the gap between the two blood pressure numbers. The team followed patients with stable coronary artery disease whose hearts still pumped at normal strength.

More than seven thousand patients were followed for about three years, during which two hundred eighty-nine major events occurred. Higher pulse pressure tracked with worse artery narrowing and more diseased vessels. After other factors were taken into account, pulse pressure stayed tied to stroke and to combined outcomes. The highest pressure group carried the greatest risk. The authors call pulse pressure a key sign for judging risk.
pmc-13155299:
Lan and four co-authors reported a chemistry method in twenty twenty-six for joining two kinds of building blocks into molecules with a useful shape. The products carry a carbon chain ending in a triple bond next to a handed, or chiral, center, a pattern found in many drugs and probes.

The reaction pairs ring-shaped nitrogen compounds with bromine-tipped chains, using nickel and light-driven chemistry together. Both starting forms of the ring give the same handed product, a trick called convergence, and the join lands at one spot only. The method yields amine products with high handed purity. The team then showed these products can be reshaped into several other useful chiral pieces, including building blocks for proteins. Tests of the mechanism suggest the ring first opens with a halide, then couples in the handed step.
pmc-13155399:
Song and eight co-authors studied why children quit allergy shots for dust mite allergy in Hangzhou, China, in twenty twenty-six. Subcutaneous immunotherapy injects small allergen doses over at least three years to retrain the immune system. Many families stop early, weakening the benefit.

Records from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-three covered six hundred eighty children with allergic asthma, rhinitis, or related disease. About sixty-two percent finished the full course; thirty-eight percent quit early. Doubts about efficacy were the top reason overall, then drug intolerance and family factors. Timing mattered: family issues dominated the first month, intolerance the first six months, and efficacy doubts later. The authors urge better parent education, standard protocols, and quick handling of side effects.
pmc-13156299:
Hassouna, Marzouk, and Fathalla present a low-cost, automated way to find and measure cracks in concrete. Hand checks of cracks depend on skill and site conditions, so results vary and take time. Their method pairs a deep learning model with direct width measurement.

The model builds on YOLO-V11 and was trained on a broad set of crack images. A patching and stitching step measures crack width, and a scaling step turns pixels into real size. Tests used 230 measured crack points from lab samples and real structures. The method kept error low with cheap imaging tools.
pmc-13156599:
Yasar Rashid and co-authors report an uncommon pairing of tumors in a young child in a 2026 case study. Wilms tumor is the most common kidney cancer of childhood. A retroperitoneal teratoma, a growth of mixed tissue behind the belly, is rare on its own. Finding both at once, in different spots, is exceptional, and the second mass raises a hard question: is it spread of the first cancer, or a second primary tumor?

Their patient was three years old, with a Wilms tumor on the right kidney and a mass on the left side. Chemotherapy before surgery shrank the kidney lesion but left the other mass unchanged, a clue they were different diseases. Surgery confirmed a high-risk Wilms tumor on one side and a mature, benign teratoma on the other. The case stresses early recognition and team planning.
pmc-13161799:
Xiao Luo and colleagues trace how a good night's sleep helps the body calm down after stress, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The stress hormone cortisol should fall once a threat passes, and poor recovery is tied to later illness. What the brain does to link sleep with recovery was the open question.

77 adults wore sleep trackers for a night, then faced a stress task in a scanner while giving saliva samples. People who slept more soundly brought cortisol down faster, though their first spike was no smaller. Scans pointed to a circuit between the front brain and the hippocampus, a memory hub. During stress, sound sleepers linked the two areas more strongly. Afterward they unlinked them more, and that unlinking carried the cortisol benefit. Sleep, the team frames it, trains the brain to switch stress circuits on and off in time.
pmc-13173399:
Taechalertpaisarn and co-authors examined this family of ring-shaped peptides in twenty twenty-six. The compounds come from natural products called mortiamides. The team asked how well such rings cross cell membranes without help. They also screened a large library built on the same scaffold for cancer cell killing.

The natural scaffold ranked among the most fat-loving of all its mirror variants. From a library of about sixty-six thousand members, many compounds killed cancer cells at low doses. Closer checks gave a surprise: the compounds barely dissolve and clump into fibers in water. Their killing came from those clumps, not from hitting a specific target. The authors warn that such clumping can fake drug activity in early screens.
pmc-13179399:
Mesude Bicer and co-authors published a 2026 study on using stem cells to fight drug-resistant infections. The cells came from fat tissue in the palate, the roof of the mouth. Such cells release substances that can kill germs. The team tested whether growing the cells inside a soft gel made from cellulose, a plant fiber, would make them stronger.

The cells were set against four germs that often cause trouble in hospitals. Both plain cells and gel-grown cells slowed the germs. The gel-grown cells did far better, cutting two germ types by huge margins within two hours. They also made much more of a natural germ-killing protein. The gel itself blocked the slimy films germs build on surfaces, cutting them by more than half. The authors suggest gel-grown palate cells as a new tool against infections that resist standard drugs.
pmc-13186499:
Rakesh Kodati and colleagues report a lung case of a rare benign growth made of spindle-shaped immune cells stuffed with mycobacteria, alongside a systematic literature review. Their 2026 paper covers a condition usually seen in lymph nodes and skin.

Most reported patients have weakened immunity, particularly from HIV infection or organ transplantation. Lung involvement is less common. Their case arose inside a sequestered piece of lung tissue in a patient with normal immunity, an unusual host for this disease. The review gathers all published cases of the lung form in the English literature. Together the case and review map how this tumour-like infection presents and where it appears.
pmc-13190499:
Heidemarie Abrahamian and colleagues updated Austrian guidance on diabetes and driving in 2026. The paper is a position statement. Public safety is the primary goal. Mobility should not be restricted without risk. Diabetes can affect driving fitness sometimes. Laws leave room for interpretation here.

Specialist medical views clarify grey areas. Traffic relevance guides each topic discussion. New drug classes get specific attention. Some incretin drugs carry no time limits. Older concerns do not apply equally now. Assessors gain a practical reference tool. Patients gain fairer fitness judgements. The update replaces earlier society guidance.
pmc-13192499:
Richard McNeely and co-authors report early results for a new artificial lens implanted in both eyes during cataract surgery. The lens, the Tecnis PureSee, stretches the range of clear focus rather than splitting light. The study enrolls 103 patients and checks them three months after surgery. Tests cover refraction, sharpness at distance, intermediate, and near ranges, plus a reading desk task and questionnaires on vision quality and glare.

Distance and intermediate vision prove excellent, and near vision is good enough for daily function. About 83 percent of eyes land within half a diopter of the target. Patients report few halos or glare effects and rate their vision highly, near 8.7 of 10 by day. Almost all, 98.1 percent, see better than before surgery, and most would recommend it. Spectacle freedom reaches 100 percent for distance and 94 percent for intermediate tasks.
pmc-13193899:
Jianbin Zhang, Sishi Huang, and Hui Shen told of a lung cancer patient switched between targeted drugs after a lung side effect, in a case report from twenty twenty-six. The patient was a sixty-two-year-old woman with early lung cancer carrying a gene fault, treated after surgery with osimertinib, the standard drug for her type. Three months in, scans showed the hazy lung change that marks drug-caused lung disease.

The drug was stopped at once, and her lungs cleared fully within eight weeks, with no steroid treatment. Restarting the same drug risked a return of the lung problem, and chemotherapy promised less. A team decision switched her to a kindred drug, almonertinib. She has stayed free of disease, and free of lung trouble, for thirty-six months. The authors say the switch may be a safe answer to a known treatment bind.
pmc-13195799:
Marie-Agnès Gasqui and colleagues published a retrospective study in 2026 on root canal care. They asked how the quality of a root canal filling and of the crown repair above it relates to health around the tooth root. The work covers teeth that had already been treated.

The team reviewed 257 patients and 798 treated teeth. They graded fillings by length, density, and taper, and graded crown repairs by both exam and X-ray. Infection at the root tip appeared in about half the teeth. Poor fillings linked more strongly to that infection than poor repairs did. A good crown repair alone did not make up for a poor filling.
pmc-13196399:
Christelle Bertsch and colleagues report a proof-of-concept scaffold for cartilage regeneration made from albumin, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Cartilage in the nose, ears, and airways barely regenerates on its own. Current treatments suffer poor integration, donor site harm, or the wrong cartilage type. Most experimental scaffolds use animal collagen, with variability and immune concerns.

Their bilayered scaffold forms by salt-assisted compaction of albumin, with no chemical crosslinkers. One porous layer supports cell infiltration and cartilage-like growth. A smooth layer is meant to later support skin or airway lining regeneration. Human nasal cartilage cells seeded inside stayed alive and proliferated. They produced matrix rich in type two collagen and aggrecan, the marks of real cartilage. The design aims at a translatable, patient-friendly material.
pmc-13198199:
Wange He, Zuyong Chen, Shan Xie, Yuansheng Liu, and Yingge Shu published a 2026 study of trace minerals in tea garden soils in Guizhou, China. The region is known for tea rich in zinc and selenium. Soil minerals pass into tea plants and shape both growth and the quality of the leaf.

The team sampled 36 tea gardens across 12 areas, testing soil layers, rock, and leaves. Selenium levels in surface soil varied widely, and about 69 percent of soils met selenium-rich standards, though only a third met both zinc and selenium standards. Leaf zinc and selenium closely followed soil levels. Rock type and age were the main forces behind soil content. The results can guide where to expand premium zinc-selenium tea.
pmc-13199699:
Xiao Chang and colleagues compared radiation alone versus radiation plus chemotherapy after induction therapy in a 2026 lung cancer study. Unresectable non-small-cell lung cancer cannot be cut out. Strong induction chemoimmunotherapy, drugs plus immune therapy, can shrink it first, but the best local finisher was unclear.

The study covered 153 patients who stayed inoperable after induction. Survival without growth ran alike at one and two years in both groups. Overall survival also matched. Severe blood side effects hit the combined group far more often, about a quarter versus under a tenth. Added immune therapy after local care hinted at gains but not firmly. Radiation alone may spare toxicity here.
pmc-13201299:
Whether cancer drugs built from antibodies need a biomarker test before use is the puzzle taken up in a 2026 review headed by Lei Lei. The comprehensive review examines antibody-drug conjugates, which attach a toxic payload to an antibody that seeks out tumor cells.

Lei and colleagues analyze 40 clinical trials covering 7,879 patients and compare drugs by the chemical linker joining antibody to payload. They report that noncleavable linkers act only in biomarker-positive tumors, while cleavable linkers also kill nearby tumor cells but cause more severe side effects. Their conclusion favors new linkers that release the payload only inside the tumor environment.
pmc-13208999:
Evelyne Benoit and colleagues explain how sea anemone toxin swells nerve fibre nodes. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses frog nerve fibres as the model. The toxin punches cation pores into cell membranes. Treated myelinated nodes roughly double in volume.

Swelling happened only when calcium surrounded the fibres. Removing chloride ions made no difference to the effect. Swapping sodium salts blocked the swelling entirely. A sodium blocker drug did not stop it, ruling out usual channels. Calcium entering through toxin pores seems to start the process. A sodium-calcium exchanger then runs forward and drives swelling. The mechanism clarifies how pore toxins injure nerves.
pmc-13209799:
Jae-Won Lee and co-authors published a 2026 scoping review of botanical extracts as a route to treat asthma, the long-term lung disease in which the airways swell and narrow. The disease is fed by both genetic risk and the environment around the patient. The standard treatment, inhaled corticosteroid sprays, can harm the whole body and fails for some patients whose disease resists it.

Extracts from plant parts, from leaves and roots alike, act on many targets at once, which suits a disease with many causes. The team reviewed work from 2005 to 2025, with a close count of the last ten years. They map which cell signaling pathways the extracts calm, with four named pathways at the core. They also weigh which laboratory models, in dishes and in animals, were used to test the claims, and how sound each model is.
pmc-13210399:
One snake's venom clots blood differently depending on the species bitten, and a 2026 laboratory study authored by Adrielly Viveiros Torres compares that activity across plasmas. The research article tests Bothrops jararaca venom in human, mouse, and rat blood samples, including plasmas missing single clotting factors and blood from engineered mouse strains.

Human and rat plasmas reacted more sensitively to the venom than mouse plasma in the clotting assays. Calcium, phospholipids, red cells, and platelets each amplified the venom's clotting power in the reported experiments. Blocker drugs showed the mechanism itself shifts by species, a warning against assuming rodent results mirror human envenomation.
pmc-13211599:
Writing down everything you eat is hard at any age, and a 2026 validation study led by Yoonjee Sung tests speaking the record instead for older adults. In a randomized crossover trial in South Korea, eighteen adults aged sixty-five and over completed two three-day dietary assessments, one by speech recording and one by paper food diary.

Average daily nutrient intakes from the two methods landed close together, with no large systematic gap at group level in the comparisons. Agreement for individual nutrients ranged widely, from weak to strong correlations depending on which nutrient was examined. Participants also rated the voice tool's usability, and the authors present speech recording as a workable alternative worth refining.
pmc-13214499:
Hannah Morris and a large team review algae as a source of health-linked compounds for use in care and industry. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Sea and micro algae live in harsh zones, which shapes a rich mix of compounds. These span sugars, fats, pigments, and small proteins.

Many show strong anti-oxidant, anti-swelling, and cell-growth effects in the lab, with hints of repair. The team maps uses in four zones: food supplements, skin care, tissue repair, and cancer. Blocks span metal build-up in the algae, mixed extract make-up, and hard rules. Firms in Ireland and Wales name what a workable supply chain needs.
pmc-13215299:
Riccardo Vecchio leads a large team that looks back in 2026 over twelve years of severe pneumococcal disease at a big hospital in north Italy. This germ can invade the blood and lungs. Vaccine makers must know which of its many coat types still cause harm.

The 234 cases sat most in men past sixty-five, most with germs in the blood plus pneumonia. Being obese or having no spleen raised the risk of a bad course. Two coat types led the list. In vaccinated people, other types led instead, a sign that covered types fade and new ones fill the gap. A quarter of germs resisted one drug family. Vaccinated patients left hospital in half the time and cost far less.
pmc-13217599:
Lucas U. Da Ros and co-authors present a 2026 study of how late-life high blood pressure interacts with Alzheimer's pathology in the brain. Midlife hypertension is an established dementia risk, but its effect after sixty-five has looked contradictory across studies, possibly because amyloid status was ignored.

The team followed 637 cognitively healthy people over sixty-five in two independent cohorts, with Alzheimer's status set by spinal fluid or scan biomarkers. Hypertension alone was not the story; combined with amyloid pathology, it predicted faster decline, with memory the domain hit hardest. The pattern replicated across both cohorts after adjusting for age, sex, and genetic risk. The authors cast blood pressure control as a modifiable lever, sharpest in people already carrying amyloid.
pmc-13218099:
Jalpa Devi and co-authors describe the MODIFY-IBD initiative in a 2026 protocol, a consensus project on obesity and heart-metabolic conditions in inflammatory bowel disease. Extra weight, high blood pressure, diabetes, fatty liver, and cardiovascular disease are increasingly common in people with bowel inflammation. These conditions affect disease activity, drug response, surgery, and quality of life, yet guidance for their care rests on scattered findings.

The protocol combines three systematic reviews with a structured expert consensus using the RAND/UCLA appropriateness method. The reviews cover how obesity affects bowel disease outcomes, how large the cardiometabolic burden is, and how such conditions should be managed. An international panel of gut specialists, surgeons, hormone and liver experts, cardiologists, and dietitians will rate statements on a 9-point scale. Agreement is judged with a standard disagreement index. The guidance is meant to direct everyday practice and mark where research is most needed.
pmc-13219899:
Kirsten Seagers and colleagues build a screening system for knee ligament injury risk in athletes in a 2026 study. More than 1.4 million anterior cruciate ligament injuries occur each year, and many are preventable with training, but the assessments that flag risky biomechanics are long and laboratory-bound, so teams skip them. The team wanted the smallest battery that reads the picture.

Twenty-seven female soccer, basketball, and volleyball players performed five activities under three-dimensional motion capture while force plates recorded landings. A selection method hunted for the subset that could reconstruct thirty-five risk factors measured in the rest. Two activities, run cuts and single-leg drop jumps, reconstructed the factors with 88.4 percent accuracy. A composite ACL resilience score built from those two agreed with the five-activity score, with subscores for trunk, hip, knee, and foot. The authors offer the short screen as a route to adoption.
pmc-13221999:
Sayed Mortaza Fayez reviews policy and structural drivers of malnutrition among Afghan women, in a 2026 analysis drawing on literature published after 2021. Women's nutrition has fallen to critical levels, yet most attention goes to child wasting. The review blends gender policy analysis with the geopolitics of aid, a pairing the author says earlier reviews lacked.

Three failures converge: economic collapse and food shortage, Taliban restrictions on women's schooling, work, and healthcare, and suspended development aid that closed hundreds of facilities. Fayez proposes separating nutrition aid from political recognition of the Taliban. Community-based, women-led delivery models feature as a route around access barriers for mothers.
pmc-13222499:
Qingchen Wang and co-authors are the subject of a 2026 retraction note in the Journal of Translational Medicine, withdrawing their article on antiphospholipid antibodies and trophoblast cells. The original study claimed these antibodies block placental cell migration and invasion through a named signaling pathway. After publication, the authors themselves asked for a correction over duplicated images between two figures.

The authors supplied raw data, yet publisher checks then found further overlaps between images said to show different samples and assays. The editor-in-chief states that confidence in the data was lost, so correction gave way to full retraction. Liyan Cui, speaking for all authors, agreed to the withdrawal. The notice preserves the reasons on the public record.
pmc-13222599:
Haytham A Sheerah and co-authors trace a century of Saudi Arabian healthcare, in a 2026 historical and policy analysis running from the 1925 Public Health Directorate to today's Vision 2030 reforms. Milestones include the 1951 founding of the Ministry of Health, national immunization, hospital building, and primary care expansion under successive kings.

Governance stayed centralized, backed by national planning, public financing, and regulation. Recent transformation leans on public-private partnerships, digital records, telemedicine, and early artificial intelligence tools. The system proved resilient through MERS, COVID-19, and the yearly Hajj health demands. Regional gaps, rising chronic disease, and workforce sustainability remain open problems, with lessons for other reforming countries.
pmc-13222999:
Ali and seven co-authors track shelf life of a date sour drink at three heats in this twenty twenty-six study. The drink blends date sour stock with berry juice and honey for taste. Heat in store can wreck its plant goods and taste in weeks.

Inside, jars sat at mild, warm, and hot grades for two months of checks. Plant goods and rust-fight grades fell most at the hot grade. Taste crews ranked the mild-grade jars best by a clear gap. An e-nose rig read scent shifts that tracked the heat grade well. A tree tool sorted store grades with high truth from those reads.
pmc-13223699:
Maria Eduarda Malosá Jorge and co-authors translate and validate a nose surgery quality-of-life form for Brazilian Portuguese, in a 2026 translation study. The 17-item FROI-17 measures how functional rhinoplasty affects concerns about breathing and looks. Brazil had generic tools in Portuguese but nothing built for this surgery, despite high national demand for nose surgery.

The work followed global COSMIN and cross-culture guidelines to preserve meaning across tongues. Soundness checks showed moderate to strong links with two standard scales, a general health survey and a nose outcome scale. A properly adapted tool lets local surgeons measure patient-felt results steadily and compare them with European data collected on the original.
pmc-13223999:
Alicia Valiente-Gómez and colleagues present a 2026 umbrella review linking harmful childhood experiences to physical illness in adult life. Rather than running a new study, the team gathered existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses from three major databases, covering work published up to April 2025. Quality checks and statistical re-analysis graded how strong each link really was.

Across 36 reviews and more than six million participants, any childhood adversity raised the odds of later non-mental disease. Bullying showed the strongest single association, and headache, irritable bowel syndrome, diabetes, and heart and vessel disease each carried highly suggestive links. The grading separates well-supported risks from weaker claims, which helps clinicians and policy makers judge where prevention may matter most.
pmc-13224399:
Benard Odur, Bosco Opio, and Olivia Nabulya investigate a 2026 field study in Apac District, Uganda, on how quickly caregivers seek malaria treatment for children under five. Malaria hits this age group hardest, yet local treatment habits were poorly documented. Interviewers surveyed 240 randomly chosen households, most of them answered by women, and modelled the time until care was sought.

Every caregiver did seek treatment, but timing varied in telling ways. Secondary education sped up the decision to get help. Empty hospital medicine shelves and money shortages caused the clearest delays. The authors recommend steadier drug supply through hospitals and village health teams, plus more teaching for caregivers about acting early.
pmc-13227199:
Janine Myint, Xinfei Miao, and Subhas Gupta mine a 2026 United States injury-surveillance database for all-terrain vehicle injuries to the wrist, hand, and fingers between 2013 and 2022. pmc-13262099:

pmc-13263799:

pmc-13264099:

pmc-13264299:

pmc-13264899:
Catrin Cox, Lucy Neave, and Beverley J Hunt review new approaches to bleeding after childbirth in a 2026 article. Heavy bleeding after delivery is a leading cause of maternal death worldwide. pmc-13264999:

pmc-13265199:

pmc-13265599:

pmc-13265699:
Tera A Scott and colleagues study factors linked to stiffness treatment after knee replacement, in a 2026 database analysis. The authors note season and region effects were modest beside patient factors.
pmc-13267599:

pmc-13267699:

pmc-13267799:

pmc-13268199:

pmc-13268699:

pmc-13269099:

pmc-13269299:

pmc-13269799:

pmc-13269999:

pmc-13273499:

pmc-13273699:

pmc-13273899:

pmc-13274199:

pmc-13274899:

pmc-13275899:

pmc-13276599:

pmc-13276899:

pmc-13277599:

After specialist training abroad she returned to Türkiye and built broad programmes for their care. pmc-13278399:

pmc-13278599:
Barma Naga Raju and colleagues test pharmacist-led care for diabetic foot ulcers in a 2026 randomised study. Foot ulcers are a frequent reason people with diabetes end up in hospital. The trial asked whether structured pharmaceutical care improves quality of life and value for money.

The authors judge the service cost-effective for India.
pmc-13278699:
Nicole F Ruopp and colleagues test a pressure index as a prognostic tool in pulmonary arterial hypertension, in a 2026 registry analysis. The disease raises pressure in lung arteries until the right side of the heart fails. Better risk markers could steer treatment intensity earlier.

Patients in the lowest group walked shorter distances and carried worse functional class ratings. Hospital admission grew steadily more likely as the index fell. Death over three years was also most common in the lowest group, at over a third of patients. The authors support the index as a long-term predictor of events.
pmc-13278799:

Sound-wave lithotripsy cracked the calcium, yet it also split the artery lining and the guidewire slid into the wall layer.

pmc-13278899:

pmc-13279199:

pmc-13279399:

pmc-13279499:

pmc-13280299:

pmc-13280699:

They urge more cost studies in those gaps.
pmc-13281399:
Jane Chungyoon Kim and colleagues weighed spread risk in early stomach cancer in a 2026 study. A scope-based surgery can remove such cancers from inside the stomach. pmc-13281499:

Better labels, they argue, would let software run studies with far less human help.
pmc-13281799:

Path tools charted the cell division cycle as cells moved along. Gene programs for each fate switched on in clear order. The authors say the map gives a base for guiding plant growth. Such control could one day shape crops and blooms.
pmc-13281899:

No findings, data, or conclusions of the original study are changed by the notice.
pmc-13282399:

pmc-13282599:

pmc-13283199:

pmc-13283399:

Lab tests then probed its role in resistant cells.
pmc-13283699:

pmc-13284099:

pmc-13284499:

pmc-13284999:

pmc-13285099:

pmc-13285599:

pmc-13285699:

pmc-13286299:

pmc-13286699:

pmc-13286799:

pmc-13286899:

pmc-13286999:

pmc-13287299:

pmc-13287699:

pmc-13287799:

pmc-13287899:

pmc-13288499:

pmc-13288599:

pmc-13288699:

pmc-13288799:

pmc-13289099:

pmc-13289399:

pmc-13289499:

pmc-13289799:

pmc-13289899:

pmc-13290999:

pmc-13291199:

pmc-13292299:
