Using linked registers for 1.4 million residents of Region Skåne, they measured continuity across all in-person physician visits over 36 months. Regression models weighed personal traits against features of each primary care center.

Low physician turnover was the single strongest tie to higher continuity, joined by older age, chronic illness, smaller centers, and private ownership. Higher education, higher income, and foreign background each tracked with lower total continuity across the system. Center traits mattered more than patient traits overall. The authors note that fragmented care-seeking by people born outside the Nordic countries lowers system-wide continuity without weakening bonds inside one practice.
pmc-13292599:
Fernanda Fortunato and a very large team propose a 2026 operational framework putting European Reference Networks at the center of referrals for babies flagged by genomic newborn screening. Rare diseases affect fewer than 5 people per 10,000, splinter into thousands of entities, and leave families facing diagnostic odysseys. The networks, built since 2017, pool expert centers across borders.

Since 72 percent of rare diseases are genetic and mostly strike children, early genomic screening could shortcut years of searching. The EU-funded Screen4Care project will offer screening to as many as 18,000 infants with a capture panel covering 245 genes tied to treatable conditions, paired with AI-based tools. The framework casts the reference networks as the receiving structure that turns a positive screen into expert care. The authors aim to cut delays and cross-country inequality.
pmc-13292799:
Huixin Liu and co-authors test a two-herb extract in a 2026 study on colibacillosis, a gut disease of chickens caused by harmful Escherichia coli. Drug resistance makes this illness hard to control and costly for poultry farms.

The pair joins Ilex rotunda with Cyperus rotundus, and lab work found 93 active compounds in the extract. Chicks given the extract before infection died less often than untreated sick chicks, with death rates the authors report as 30% to 45% versus 60% in the model group. Treated chicks also showed calmer immune signals, less liver harm, fewer bacteria in blood, and more helpful gut microbes. The herb pair may offer a plant-based guard for flocks.
pmc-13293399: Molly Plovanich and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their study of MICU2, a partner protein that helps control calcium entry into mitochondria. The notice fixes a wrong panel in Figure 2, where one blot image had been duplicated in place of another. The revised figure restores the correct SDHB lysate panel and shows two other panels in their original blot form. Original image data for the figure are now supplied as a supplement. An editorial board member advised that antibody checks support the findings, so the results stand.
pmc-13293599:
Corrin Hepburn and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, telehealth satisfaction between rural and urban liver clinic patients. Video visits can widen reach for rural patients, who face long drives, yet weak technology may spoil the experience.

Of 400 patients surveyed by phone, 164 replied, split between rural and urban homes. Rural patients drove about twice as long to clinic and canceled more often over travel, yet reported far more login and device trouble. Urban patients were more likely to prefer and enjoy video visits than in-person ones. Rural patients favored in-person care instead. Better tech support for rural users is urged.
pmc-13293899:
Raman Sangha and colleagues examine diabetes distress in a 2026 mixed-methods study of teens with type 1 diabetes and their parents. Six adolescents and five parents first completed distress questionnaires, then joined separate focus groups on daily burdens, support already used, and support still wanted. Analysis used interpretive description with collaborative coding.

All six teens scored in the high distress range, while most parents scored low. Five shared themes emerged, including burnout, disruption to daily life, a wish for peer support, and worry about future costs. Parents alone raised concern about handing management duties to their children. The contrast can guide better family support design.
pmc-13294399:
Chang Liu and coauthors build gene tests for pancreatic cancer from blood in a 2026 study. Good early marks are badly missing for this deadly cancer. A chip test on patient plasma found changed genes. Network work on public cohorts crossed those hits with hub gene groups to pick test genes. A risk score came from survival math.

Plasma showed 228 clearly raised gene notes. Five hub genes, including FERMT1 and ITGA3, marked the cancer well. Three of them flagged poor survival on their own. A chart model held value in a public cohort. Lab checks in fresh plasma matched the chip. Blood gene panels could aid early flagging.
pmc-13294999:
Abdinasir Muhidin Abdulle and colleagues report a severe pregnancy emergency in Mogadishu, Somalia, in a 2026 case report. A 17-year-old first-time mother at 35 weeks arrived after seizures, with low oxygen, low blood sugar, and signs of kidney injury. Scans confirmed her baby had already died in the womb.

Care teams stabilised her with seizure prevention, breathing support, and an emergency caesarean delivery of the stillborn baby. Chest imaging showed fluid in the lungs, and intensive care included antibiotics and fluid removal treatment. She came off the ventilator on day five and went home stable on day seven, underlining gaps in emergency obstetric capacity.
pmc-13295299:
Riliang Liu and colleagues set up two embryo-stage models for studying chick gut health, in a 2026 poultry study. What microbes meet a chick before hatching may steer its gut for life, yet hard data are thin. The team injected fertilized eggs with Salmonella Enteritidis, a major foodborne germ, or with a synbiotic blend of two Lactobacillus kin plus inulin, then checked the hatchlings' guts and microbes.

Embryo exposure to salmonella scrambled the gut community, raised likely pathogens, inflamed the intestine, and weakened barrier marks. The blend did the reverse: helpful bacteria settled early, the ileum grew better, lining cells multiplied faster, and barrier marks improved, with hatch rates unhurt. The authors offer both models as starting tools for early-life work, and ask for larger, longer farm trials before field use.
pmc-13295799:
Clare Dinh and Keykavous Parang review drug resistance in children's infections in a 2026 article. Resistance already drives over a million deaths a year worldwide, hitting children under five hardest. Newborns and very ill children face extra risk from immature immunity and scarce drug choices.

Searches covering 2014 to 2026 gathered about 1,840 records, with 69 sources making the final cut. Resistant gut bacteria, hardy staph strains, and carbapenem-proof germs led the harm described in the synthesis. About one in five child bloodstream isolates resisted standard strong antibiotics. Vaccine gains against pneumococcus showed one hopeful route, cutting resistant infections by preventing them.
pmc-13295999:
Alain Bernard and co-authors track, in 2026, how French hospitals' lung cancer surgery results changed over five years. Using a national database of 56,299 operations in 148 hospitals, they model each hospital's risk-adjusted rate of severe complications year by year.

Performance proved sticky, with hospitals tending to stay in their category. Medium-volume hospitals improved most, cutting adjusted complication rates by nearly half. Some small centres worsened sharply, and, surprisingly, a group of busy hospitals also slipped. The authors say routine monitoring of such data can target help where quality is drifting.
pmc-13296699:
Susie Y. Oh and co-authors link perfectionism to the gap between felt and measured sleep in a 2026 study. Some people judge their sleep far worse than wrist sensors record, a mismatch common in insomnia. Sixty adults wore activity trackers and kept sleep diaries for fourteen days while completing questionnaires.

Higher perfectionism went with a larger mismatch, especially the worry about mistakes and doubts about actions. Those perfectionist strands also tied to differences in how long people thought they took to fall asleep. Arousal before bed, particularly racing thoughts, carried much of the connection statistically. Sleep clinicians may do better by asking about perfectionist habits when patients report sleep that tests cannot confirm.
pmc-13296899:
Rahel Looser and colleagues report Swiss experience with checkpoint immunotherapy in organ transplant patients who developed cancer, in a 2026 study. Transplant recipients take immune-suppressing drugs, which raise cancer risk yet also make immune-activating treatment dangerous for the graft. Ten patients with advanced cancers were identified through the national transplant cohort.

Three patients became cancer-free, and two more had disease held stable for months. Four of the ten were alive when the data were analysed. Six patients, however, developed organ rejection during treatment. The authors suggest starting treatment early, note that a few infusions may suffice, and insist each case needs joint discussion with the patient.
pmc-13297499:
Ovidiu-Petru Stan, Marius Misaros, and Liviu-Cristian Miclea design a Parkinson's disease detector whose parts copy brain systems, in a 2026 study. Diagnosis today leans on clinical judgement, which can miss early disease. One model mirrors how the hearing cortex layers sound, for voice recordings; another borrows features from movement circuits, for spiral drawing tests.

A support vector classifier on voice data reached eighty-seven percent test accuracy with no overfitting, beating five rival methods on balance. The sound-mirroring network scored eighty-five percent on spiral drawings. Joining both channels into one system is proposed but not yet built or tested. The authors argue that models grounded in biology make fairer, more objective decision support.
pmc-13297999:
Blood clots complicate a key leukemia drug family, and Jack T Seki with co-authors pooled the evidence on who is at risk in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Asparaginase-based chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia can trigger thrombosis in children and adults alike, at rates that vary widely between reports.

Risk clustered around leukemia subtype, older age, treatment phase, and other clinical features the analysis identified. Newer agents such as cal-asparaginase pegol are spreading as older supplies shrink, making the risk picture more urgent. The authors strongly back preventive steps for patients carrying several risk factors, including heparin-type blood thinners or antithrombin replacement where these can be given safely.
pmc-13298199:
Mikhail Ya. Yadgarov and colleagues build a mortality prediction tool for septic patients with prolonged or chronic critical illness, in a 2026 study using a Russian intensive care dataset. Such patients endure long unit stays, persistent organ problems, and repeated sepsis. Existing sepsis tools were not designed for this group.

Analysis covered 336 patients, split into training and testing sets. Four factors predicted death: age, organ failure score at sepsis onset, type 2 diabetes, and time until sepsis began. The nomogram performed best for short-horizon prediction and weakened at later time points. Prospective testing across several centres is required before clinical use, the authors state.
pmc-13298799:
Victor C Okebalama leads a large author group surveying present and future technology in cancer management, in a 2026 narrative survey. Rising case numbers strain older systems, while digital tools, imaging intelligence, and machine learning reshape diagnosis and treatment planning. Robotics, telemedicine, wearable medical devices, genomics, and nanotechnology all receive coverage.

Nursing uses receive special focus, including symptom tracking and care coordination support. The authors warn that technology assists rather than replaces clinical expertise. Digital literacy gaps among older patients, data protection, and opaque algorithms count among the risks. Rushed adoption without understanding could cause long-term harm, so careful review should accompany rollout.
pmc-13299099:
Age on its own should not bar a fast pill for sore joints, Haruki Matsumoto and his team argue in a 2026 review of proof from Japan. The pills, called JAK blockers, ease rheumatoid joint pain fast. Fears have grown, though, over germ risk, shingles, heart harm, clots, and cancer, in a land where most patients are old.

In Japan's trials and care logs, ill health in the round, steroid use, and off lab marks flagged risk more than years of age. Shingles stood out as the steadiest risk, which backs shots and close early watch. Germ risk was not plainly worse than with shot drugs in old patients. Heart and cancer proof stayed mixed. The team back dose and watch plans fit to each patient.
pmc-13299399:
Elvis Kichana and others assess drinking water quality and health risk in two rural districts of Ghana's Savannah Region, in a 2026 field study. Hundreds of samples came from groundwater sources and household storage containers during early 2025. Testing covered bacteria, nitrate, acidity, chlorine, major ions, and trace metals.

Microbial contamination was widespread in household water, and almost half of groundwater sources exceeded the nitrate guideline, concentrated in one district. No sample held detectable residual chlorine, and many fell outside the acceptable acidity range. Risk modelling flagged nitrate danger especially for infants and children. Source protection, chlorination, monitoring, and household treatment are urged.
pmc-13300099:
Very high blood triglycerides can stem from single genes, gene combinations, or sheer polygenic load. Anastasia V. Blokhina and colleagues examined that mix in 123 patients with triglyceride levels above 5.0 mmol/L, sequencing six known genes and building a risk score from 40 common variants for a 2026 study.

A major genetic driver emerged for 65.0 percent of patients, including rare variants in chylomicronemia genes and an extreme polygenic burden in about a third. Patients fell into five groups, from familial chylomicronemia syndrome to a moderate-risk remainder. The familial group showed the highest triglyceride levels and far greater odds of pancreatitis. Adding APOE testing and risk scores raised diagnostic yield.
pmc-13300599:
Christian X. Lava and a large co-author team compare three implant brands in immediate breast reconstruction in a 2026 multicenter study. The retrospective review covered 631 patients and 1,155 reconstructed breasts treated with acellular dermal matrix support between January 2014 and July 2022, using implants from Allergan, Mentor, or Sientra. The main outcome was return to the operating room for implant removal, with complications tracked in early and later windows.

Beyond sixty days, overall complication rates did not differ significantly between brands. About fourteen percent of breasts eventually had a reoperation, and unplanned removal, seen in about eight percent, was most often driven by infection, capsular contracture, or wounds that failed to heal. Predictors of trouble were patient and surgical factors, including body mass index, diabetes, smoking, chemotherapy, radiation, and incision type. The authors conclude that brand choice can rest on preference and availability.
pmc-13300999:
Heart disease quietly erodes thinking, and Valeria Visco leads a 2026 comprehensive review asking cardiac rehabilitation to take cognition seriously. Roughly one in three cardiology patients shows some cognitive frailty, yet standard rehabilitation programs seldom test for it. The review gathers mechanisms, program components, benefits, and workable strategies for this overlap.

Low cardiac output starves the brain of blood, inflaming tissue and slowing processing speed, the authors explain. Structured exercise counters that path, lifting cerebral flow and fitness-linked gains in attention and mental speed. Adding cognitive screening and training to rehabilitation, they argue, could sharpen recovery and long-term prognosis for a large, often missed group of patients.
pmc-13301899:
Rain scrubs the air over northern Serbia and delivers its catch to the ground, Brankica Kartalović and colleagues measure in a 2026 study of Vojvodina rainwater. Samples gathered through the 2025–2026 heating season at three sites, a petrochemical town, a traffic-heavy town, and an urban background city, were screened for PAHs, phthalates, and BTEX compounds.

The petrochemical site, Kikinda, carried the heaviest load, with total BTEX at 2.818 and phthalates at 0.930 micrograms per liter in the samples. Chemical fingerprints pointed to petroleum sources there, and burning sources at the other sites. Benzene was absent everywhere, while toluene and xylenes ran high. Cancer risk from PAHs stayed acceptable yet non-trivial for children near industry.
pmc-13301999:
E D Merkel and colleagues analyse frailty inside the Budapest CRT Upgrade trial in a 2026 paper on patients whose hearts were weakened by heavy right-sided pacing. Upgrading to a resynchronization device can improve pumping, yet whether it also eases frailty was unknown. Frailty was scored with a standard index counting accumulated health deficits.

The trial randomised 360 patients to an upgraded device or a defibrillator alone. More than ninety percent counted as frail at entry, and three quarters fell in the highest frailty band. Frailty level itself did not significantly predict the combined outcome of death, hospitalisation, or poor heart shrinkage. After twelve months, though, the upgrade group showed a small but real reduction in frailty score compared with controls.
pmc-13302799:
Generative AI entered the world's most-used research data platform carefully, Cathy Shyr and colleagues describe in a 2026 implementation report. The REDCap Consortium shipped three optional features as a minimum viable product in release 15.0: a writing helper, a qualitative data summarizer, and a translator. Security, local choice, and human oversight governed the design, with each institution running its own sandboxed AI tenant.

In the first seven months, eighteen institutions switched the module on and eight sustained use across 1,171 projects. Vanderbilt alone logged 958 projects and over 5,700 AI calls. Uptake hinged on local infrastructure and governance, offering lessons for other data-capture systems.
pmc-13302899:
Costanza Falcidia and co-authors track, in a 2026 single-centre study, how often doctors adjust doses of two JAK inhibitor drugs for severe eczema. Both medicines come in two strengths, inviting escalation when control lags and reduction when side effects bite or skin clears. Real-world habits around those switches were undocumented.

Records covered 212 patients, most taking upadacitinib and the rest abrocitinib. Dose changes were uncommon with abrocitinib but touched about a quarter of upadacitinib patients, split almost evenly between increases and decreases. Escalation typically followed weak control after many months, while reductions followed side effects such as herpes infections and acne, or full clearance. Most adjusted patients reached clear or almost clear skin afterwards.
pmc-13302999:
Yihong Yue and co-authors study, in a 2026 soil study, how long spent mushroom substrate must be returned to rice fields before the soil ecosystem settles. The leftover growing material recycles farm waste and feeds soil, but early effects can be unstable. Fields under rice-mushroom rotation with zero, one, or three years of returns were compared by gene sequencing.

After one year, soil nutrients dipped early in the season and the nitrogen cycle tilted toward higher nitrous oxide risk. After three years, late-season nutrient stores rose and nitrogen-handling genes supported retention instead of loss. Microbe assembly also grew more orderly with time, and interaction networks became more complex. The authors conclude duration decides whether returns destabilise or stabilise the field.
pmc-13303499:
Aaron KH Ho leads a 2026 single-center study of cholesterol control and costs after heart attack in Singapore. Guidelines urge strong lowering of LDL cholesterol after such events, but real-world target rates stay low, especially in Asian groups.

Records for 300 patients admitted to the National University Heart Centre between January and June 2022 were reviewed. After one year, most patients met the local target, fewer than half met a middle target, and under one in five met the strictest target. Strong statin use rose over the year. The gap between guidance and practice carries both health and money costs.
pmc-13303799:
David P. Ruttenberg writes a 2026 commentary on a trial of fecal microbiota transplant for children with autism. The trial used hydrogen nanobubble water and skipped antibiotics and bowel clearing, steps that usually burden young patients.

Scores on a social responsiveness scale fell by about a third over 30 weeks in the original study. The commentary urges caution because the trial had no comparison group. Gains could reflect normal growth over time, extra parent attention, or scores settling after a high starting point, since most children began in the severe range. A controlled confirmatory trial design is outlined.
pmc-13304499:
Olga A. Snytnikova and colleagues map chemical shifts in rat eye lenses as cataracts form in a 2026 study. Fast-aging OXYS rats develop lens clouding early, offering a window on changes that precede visible damage.

Lens chemistry was measured with magnetic resonance methods at two young ages, and clouding was graded by eye exam. Dozens of small compounds were counted. Young affected lenses first piled up amino acids, then weeks later showed steep drops in amino acids, sugar, energy stores, and protective compounds. Clouding grade itself barely shifted the profile, hinting that chemical collapse comes first.
pmc-13304599:
Luis Gil-Gallardo and co-authors compare two shop-bought blood tests for a parasitic worm disease in patients also treated for Chagas disease in a 2026 Spanish clinic study. The worm illness often travels with Chagas among Latin American migrants.

Fifty-five patients took both antibody kits, with infection judged by a combined rule using test results and a blood cell count. About two thirds met the infection rule, and the kits agreed strongly. After worm treatment with ivermectin, both test scores and the cell count dropped clearly by one year. Either kit can screen and track recovery fairly well.
pmc-13304799:
Arunraj Tharamelveliyil Rajendran, Ashwini Prabhu, and colleagues engineer, in a 2026 nanomedicine study, a two-drug particle aimed at resistant glioblastoma. The brain tumor shrugs off its standard drug partly by repairing DNA damage through the PARP enzyme, and the blood–brain barrier blocks reinforcements. Their core–shell particle pairs that standard drug with ellagic acid, a plant compound that inhibits PARP, and steers it with folic acid.

The particles formed evenly, held both drugs stably, and released them in a sustained two-phase pattern. Folic acid coating sharply increased uptake into glioblastoma cells, and the drug pair killed synergistically at much lower doses than either alone. Treated cells showed more DNA damage, more programmed death, less migration, and reduced PARP gene activity. The authors offer the platform as groundwork for translation.
pmc-13305099:
Qi-Long Zheng and co-authors coat aluminum powder to burn more fully in solid rocket fuel in a 2026 study. Aluminum adds energy, but its tough oxide shell makes particles clump and leave unburned residue behind.

A core-shell mix wrapped each particle in an ionic liquid layer holding fluorinated graphene sheets. Heat tests showed the coat triggers a surface reaction that lowers the burning temperature. Fuel using the coated powder left notably less leftover aluminum, and its ash particles shrank to about a third of the plain fuel size. Cleaner burning means more thrust from the same load.
pmc-13305799:
Shu-Jie Zhang examined repair-defect scores and immune cell entry in a common breast cancer type in a 2026 multicentre study. The focus was hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative disease, where outcomes vary widely and the link between DNA repair and immunity was unclear.

A total of 365 patients from three hospitals joined, with immune data for 332 of them. Higher repair-deficiency scores went with slightly fewer tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes in the reported correlation, and high-score patients fared worse in survival analyses. The authors argue the repair score carries prognostic value and may help explain uneven immune activity in this subtype.
pmc-13306499:
Lujia Liu studied a branching brake gene in oilseed rape in a 2026 genetics study. Branch count shapes canopy form, light capture and yield, and the factor BRANCHED1 is known to hold branching back across plants.

Five copies were catalogued in the rape genome, all sharing a conserved core and promoters rich in light and hormone response parts. One copy, BnaA01.BRC1, reacted to shade, sugar and hormone signals in expression checks. Extra copies cut branching while gene knockouts raised branch numbers sharply in reported results, acting indirectly through hormone balance rather than direct partner binding.
pmc-13306699:
Marios Theologou, Nikolaos Syrmos, and Vaitsa Giannouli describe in 2026 a young adult whose brain bleed was misread because a large arachnoid cyst distorted the picture. The man arrived with pain at the back of the head, normal examination, and normal laboratory results. Early scanning suggested an epidural bleed beside a Grade III cyst.

He went home, then returned ten days later when repeat scanning raised fresh concern and brief testing showed mild cognitive problems. Surgery through a burr hole drained what proved to be a chronic subdural collection, not the suspected epidural one. Symptoms cleared fully, cognition normalised, and a scan a month later confirmed the result. The authors warn that cysts can make one bleed type imitate another, and that simple drainage may suffice.
pmc-13306799:
Hailang Huang tailored a detector for small traffic objects in drone views in a 2026 study. Aerial frames hold many tiny, densely packed targets that standard heads built for large objects tend to overlook.

Built on YOLOv8, the YOLO-UTD model swaps the large-object head for a small-object head and adds a shallow-rich feature pyramid for finer detail. A new fusion layer in deep stages blends place detail with meaning through cross-attention. On VisDrone2019 data, scores rose by 3.6% overall and 5.3% for small objects in reported figures, with few added parameters.
pmc-13307799:
Szilamér Ferenczi and co-authors test in 2026 whether a lactic acid microbe can curb aflatoxin output by Aspergillus flavus in corn silage as heat rises. Silage was kept at three heat levels, with and without Limosilactobacillus fermentum. Gene activity and toxin levels were read by lab assays.

Heat, above all the highest level, switched the toxin gene cluster on strongly, master gene included. Adding the microbe cut final toxin level by roughly half to three-fifths at every heat level. Gene readings matched: the master gene and pathway genes were switched down, most sharply one late-pathway gene at the middle heat. A warming world favours this mould, so built-in living brakes matter. The authors propose chosen strains of the microbe as silage seed cultures for high-heat risk.
pmc-13309199:
Maxime J Billick, William K Silverstein, and Isaac I Bogoch lay out in 2026 five key points on Ebola virus disease. A fresh outbreak of Bundibugyo ebolavirus now runs in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Fruit bats are the likely home species, and spread moves through body fluids or soiled goods from sick people or game.

Fever of 38 degrees or more, deep fatigue, muscle pain, and gut upset lead, though under half of patients bleed despite the fever label. The wait from contact to signs runs 2 to 21 days, and a blood gene test confirms the call. Strict gear and rapid expert notice guard staff and contacts. Vaccines and antibodies aid one strain only, so this strain leans on support care.
pmc-13309399:
Manuel Kuelshammer and colleagues analyze registry data from 2026 on newborns with non-immune hydrops fetalis who needed a heart-lung support machine. In this rare condition, fluid builds up in the baby before birth for reasons other than blood group conflict. Many affected newborns need intense breathing and heart support.

Records covering 2000 to 2024 held 171 babies after cases with major heart defects and similar exclusions were removed. Just over half survived until hospital discharge. Babies born heavier, born at 35 weeks or later, and girls survived more often. The type of support circuit made no clear difference. The authors use the data to guide family counseling.
pmc-13309799:
Chong Mao and co-authors study how driver mutations shape immune escape in melanoma in a 2026 analysis. Melanoma tumors differ widely in their immune surroundings, partly by which of three genes, BRAF, NRAS, or NF1, is altered. How mutation type steers inflammation and risk prediction was unclear.

Fifteen inflammation pathways were scored across four patient data sets. A ten-method learning framework built a risk model that reached a five-year accuracy score of 0.95 in the main data set and beat older models in most checks. High-risk tumors showed sparse immune entry and a muted immune tone. Mutation groups differed, with NF1 tumors richest in antigen display signals. A gene called CCNE1 was tested by knockdown in cell lines.
pmc-13309899:
David W. Wang and co-authors study heart strain after liver transplant in patients with high lung artery pressure in a 2026 article. Lung pressure problems raise risk around liver surgery, and newer pressure classes sort patients by where the pressure builds. Whether class predicts early heart trouble was the question.

Twenty years of records at one center covered 2,409 transplant patients, with the pressure group confirmed by heart catheter tests. Patients were sorted into four pressure classes, and heart events within 30 days formed the main outcome, with breathing time, kidney injury, and survival also tracked. The authors compare classes to guide which patients need the closest heart watch after surgery.
pmc-13310699:
Weiyong Si and co-authors wrote a 2026 editorial that opens a set of studies on large language models in robotics. Older robots work well in fixed settings but struggle with safe contact, plain speech, and flexible thought. Language models may help close that gap between what people mean and what machines do.

Five studies in the set cover shop helper robots, two arm remote control, home care guidance, teaching robots, and automated machine learning. One study tested four speech tools and found Whisper most accurate, with language mattering more than speaker sex. Together the pieces map early ways to pair language skill with robot action.
pmc-13310899:
Xiaoya Mao and co-authors review lung organoids for drug finding and safety tests in a 2026 paper. Lung diseases kill many people, yet flat cell dishes and animal tests often fail to predict human results, so drug pipelines lose most candidates. Tiny three dimensional lung models grown from stem cells may close that gap.

Models copy key lung structure and cell mix and serve to study chronic swelling, scarring, viral infection, and lung cancer. Safety uses span fume harm, cosmetic checks, and drug injury, as rules favor non animal tests. Missing blood vessels, weak immune parts, and animal based gels block wider use. Engineered gels and chip systems aim to fix those gaps.
pmc-13310999:
Tekoshar Aram and colleagues report skill based training for a group mental health program in Iraqi Kurdistan in a 2026 paper. Group Problem Management Plus lets non specialist workers aid distressed people and has spread in crisis settings. As refugee care folds into national systems, worker skill must be built and checked in a set way.

Twelve health staff in Duhok who work in Syrian refugee camps took a seven day course, then six months of coaching. Role play and live coaching cut harmful acts and raised facilitation skill on a standard rating frame. Workers also gained confidence and praised problem solving tools. Gains support the training model.
pmc-13311099:
Yijing Xu and co-authors review lysosome driven cell death as a liver cancer target in a 2026 paper. Liver cancer resists many targeted drugs, so a death path that bypasses the usual route draws interest. When lysosome walls leak, cutting enzymes spill and kill the cell from inside.

Natural compounds can trigger that leak through several routes, such as blocking a fat enzyme, freeing iron, shifting acidity, or cutting a growth switch. Such compounds also free trapped drugs from swollen lysosomes, which pairs well with standard targeted drugs. Work joins past proof from major databases to guide resistant cancer care.
pmc-13311199:
Longyu Liu and colleagues find the best spirulina swap level for fishmeal in prawn diets in a 2026 trial. Spirulina algae can replace pricey fishmeal in water farm feeds if growth and health hold. Six diets swapped graded shares of fishmeal for spirulina in river prawn feed over a key egg growth month.

Swaps up to 60 percent kept growth and survival on par with control feed. Higher swaps cut survival and growth sharply. The 60 percent group showed the strongest digestion enzymes and antioxidant shields, and spirulina diets raised egg maturation rates. Muscle amino mix shifted at high swaps. Mid swap earns a clear farm case.
pmc-13311299:
Mohammad Amin Shadman and co-authors present the 2026 survey study from southern Iran on student views of online learning and their links to honest conduct and stress. The work sits in a setting with few resources.

The study drew 256 students at Bushehr University of Medical Sciences between October 2022 and March 2023. Students filled in scales on e-learning views, felt stress, and ethics in online classes. Warmer views of online learning predicted stronger ethical practice, with a modest effect size. No clear link appeared between those views and felt stress. Building good views of online study may support honest habits in virtual classes.
pmc-13311799:
Yizhen Yu and co-authors present their 2026 survey study on confidence, mood, habits, and life quality in Chinese patients with gum disease. Gum disease affects over a billion people and feeds whole-body inflammation.

The survey reached 366 patients. Most brushed at least twice a day, and about half flossed daily. A structural model fit the data well. Low mood tied to lower confidence, while confidence tied to better oral habits in the model. The chain from mood to confidence to habits helps explain why some patients struggle to keep up home care, and where support could break the cycle.
pmc-13311999:
Bing-Yan Zeng and colleagues give a 2026 network meta-analysis on whether newer diabetes drugs change risk of asthma-COPD overlap syndrome. The overlap condition affects a sizable share of chronic airway patients and kills at high rates.

The search swept eight databases and trial registries to April 2026, with a first pass in December 2024. Eligible trials were randomized studies in adults that logged overlap, asthma, or COPD events on diabetes drugs. Classes compared include DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors against standard care or placebo. The pooled set reached 128 trials and 316,832 adults. Dose-split rankings aim to guide drug choice in diabetic patients with airway disease.
pmc-13312099:
Chalita Diandra Natalie and co-authors present a 2026 qualitative study of how Indonesian nursing students perceive and experience end-of-life care during clinical placements. Students often join care for dying patients, yet little was known about what that work feels like from their side.

The team interviewed 10 professional nursing students with end-of-life care experience between February and May 2025 and analyzed the conversations thematically. Four themes emerged, covering students' views of such care, the holistic support they gave patients and families, the challenges and openings the work created, and a growing heart for caring. Students framed good end-of-life care as comfort, dignity, and compassion rather than cure, though weak preparation and emotional strain remained real barriers.
pmc-13312599:
Liuniu Xiao and co-authors compare two forms of hyperventilation syndrome, a pattern of over-breathing that brings on body and mood symptoms. Their study appeared in 2026. One form arises on its own, often from tension. The other follows a chest infection. The team reviewed 167 patients seen between January 2024 and May 2025 and split them by whether a chest infection was present.

Of the group, 91 cases were the primary form and 76 followed infection. Most primary cases began after stress, with 85 percent reporting tension or anxiety first. Patients in the infection group scored higher on a symptom questionnaire. They also showed lower mineral levels, more signs of inflammation, and more repeat episodes within six months. The authors say the two forms look alike but need different care and follow-up.
pmc-13312999:
Yixuan Wang and colleagues run a 2026 randomized trial of stroboscopic training for balance in college badminton players. Flickering eyewear that blinks vision on and off forces the brain to balance with broken visual information, much like the split-second glimpses of real rallies. Yet the method had barely been tested in this sport.

Twenty trained male players were split evenly between stroboscopic and conventional balance work. Both did the same thirty-minute sessions three times a week for six weeks, with the control group wearing identical glasses that never flickered. Afterward, the strobe group improved significantly more on every front: longer eyes-closed single-leg stands, farther reaches on the Y-Balance test, and steadier landings measured by stability indices and pressure traces. The authors recommend weaving stroboscopic drills into badminton training for control and safer landings.
pmc-13313299:
Arpita Mukherjee reviews two linked immune brakes in glioblastoma in their 2026 paper. This brain tumor is known as cold and hard to treat, with worn-out T cells, low oxygen, and strong blocks on immune attack, and it resists standard checkpoint drugs.

One brake is LAG-3, a protein that mutes T cell signals and drains the energy making of those cells. The other is a pair of enzymes, CD39 and CD73, that turn ATP into adenosine, a signal that calms killer cells and feeds suppressive cell types. Gene maps at single-cell level show worn-out LAG-3 cells sitting next to CD73-rich zones, hinting at a loop where each path feeds the other. The review sets out ways to block both paths at once, which may free T cells where single-drug plans have failed.
pmc-13313499:
Shannon Baker, S Mehdi Nouraie, and Richard A Steinman compare residency matches of doctor-scientist trainees in a 2026 study. Staying in a research-rich setting during residency may keep young physician-scientists on a research path, so the team asked where MD-PhD and MD-only students land.

They studied 10,668 students across the 2021 to 2023 match cycles, covering NIH-backed MD-PhD programs, other MD-PhD programs, and MD-only paths. The core measure was the NIH funding level of the department each student matched into. Public match data came from 13 top-funded and 8 mid-funded medical schools, as counted in the report. Top schools housed only the NIH-backed programs, while mid schools had both MD-PhD types. The work shows how school funding and training path shape access to research-heavy residencies.
pmc-13313599:
Zeshuo Zhou and colleagues chart the codon use of a gene called Dnajc15 across birds in their 2026 study. The gene makes MCJ, a protein that reins in the energy chain of mitochondria, and its patterns in birds were largely unknown.

The team studied 27 bird species from 11 orders, using codon bias checks, selection tests with PAML, and gene family study. The gene favored codons ending in A or U, with weak bias overall and a measure the authors give as 51.72 to 61.00 across species, kept mid-sentence here as reported. Selection was mostly purifying, with a rate of 0.33 as stated in the report, meaning harmful changes are weeded out. One test flagged four sites under positive selection near the start and in the J-domain, though a second test did not back that signal.
pmc-13314199:
Hardi Fattah Marif and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, the first molecular detection of Leptospira interrogans in shelter dogs in Iraq's Kurdistan Region. Leptospirosis is a zoonosis, and crowded, unsanitary shelters make dogs reservoirs that can pass the bacteria to staff and adopters through urine. Between May and August 2025 the team collected eighty blood and urine samples from sheltered dogs. They ran PCR against a conserved bacterial gene, sequencing positives to place them among regional strains.

Twenty-three samples, 28.75 percent of those tested, came back positive, split evenly between urine and blood. Young adult males showed the highest infection share among the dog groups at 23.1 percent in the reported breakdown, with females close behind on their own measure. Finding the pathogen in more than a quarter of shelter samples, the authors press for surveillance, shelter biosecurity, and vaccination plans across the region before the reservoir seeds human cases.
pmc-13314599:
Clenise Liliane Schmidt and co-workers link tiredness and work capacity in nurses across two countries in their 2026 study. Fatigue in nursing is a tangled, multi-cause strain that harms both health and care quality, and work capacity shows whether a nurse can keep meeting job demands.

The team surveyed 579 nursing professionals, with 370 from Brazil and 209 from Portugal, as counted in the report. They logged social, job, and health traits and applied two standard tools, a fatigue scale and a work ability index. The cross-country design lets them compare how fatigue tracks with capacity in two health systems that share a language but not a setting. Their results can guide managers who must guard staff health without losing care quality.
pmc-13314799:
Liang Zhang and colleagues mine the genome of a tobacco-root bacterium for new antifungal peptides, in a study published in 2027. The strain, Brevibacillus brevis B011, kills fungi well, but which of its products do the work was not settled.

Genome mining flagged 13 gene clusters for making compounds, among them clusters for edeine, tyrocidine, and gramicidin. Knocking out genes and pitting the bacterium against fungi, read by fine chemical scans, showed edeine as the main antifungal weapon, with tyrocidine second and gramicidin minor. Total edeine yield came to a level of 19.2 mg per liter as stated in the report. The team also built leucine variants of tyrocidines and tryptocidines in dishes, with one variant family split into shares such as 25.6 percent for the first by their measure.
pmc-13315199:
A large team of co-authors wrote a review dated two thousand twenty-six on radiation, cataracts, and how the eye's lens is outlined in treatment planning. The lens is clear tissue that focuses light, and it is highly sensitive to radiation. Cataracts from radiation most often form at the back of the lens.

The team reviewed the anatomy and disease process, including dose thresholds, waiting times, and classification systems for these cataracts. They weighed risk factors such as total dose and how the dose is split. From the evidence they propose standard guidelines for drawing the lens boundary in plans, so dose reports mean the same thing everywhere.
pmc-13315799:
Fahman Saeed and Sultan Aldera present in 2026 an explainable brain-wave system for early sorting of Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Fast, accurate distinction between these dementias is still an unsolved clinical need, and early action depends on early detection.

Their AutoSSM-ICA-EEG pipeline cleans signals with independent component analysis, tunes models with few-shot automated learning, and tracks time patterns with state-space modeling. It classifies dementia type and rates severity at once. Three datasets were used, including open-eyes and resting recordings and an outside Brazilian set, with strict leave-one-person-out checks to test generalization across settings.
pmc-13315899:
Diego Anazco and a large team report a secondary analysis in 2026 of a diet trial for people with obesity who eat in response to emotion. In the main PHENO-Diet trial, care tailored to body phenotype beat a standard lifestyle plan, and this look focuses on the emotional eating subgroup.

Adults were classed by an anxiety score of at least seven, then followed through a twelve-week plan, tailored or standard. Among emotional eaters, 26 on tailored care were compared with 19 on standard care for weight loss, eating behavior, and mood change. Tailoring may matter most where mood drives eating, a common barrier to weight control.
pmc-13315999:
Hee-Soo Kim and colleagues built machine learning models in 2026 to predict long-term death after ischemic stroke, adding the time dimension that older scores often miss. Traditional scores focus on short outcomes and need laborious data gathering, while many newer models only classify and ignore timing.

The building cohort held 3,411 patients from two large hospitals, with 136 deaths, and an outside test cohort held 502 patients from a heart center, with 118 deaths. Several machine and deep learning models were compared with classic risk scores. Feature ranking then sought the smallest set that stays practical for clinic use.
pmc-13316199:
Tajda Laure and colleagues ran a randomized trial in 2026 of ROOM to grow, a phone program for student mental health at Erasmus University Rotterdam. One in four university students faces mental health problems, and the app offers universal plus targeted prevention built around emotion regulation for stress, depression, and anxiety.

Two hundred two students with raised stress were split evenly between instant app access and a three-month waitlist, and 171, or 85 percent, finished the trial. Surveys at set weeks and app logs tracked stress, regulation, symptoms, resilience, and engagement. Headline results showed no clear statistical gain, making uptake patterns central.
pmc-13316599:
Khalid Shahzad and Zainab Asghar report, in 2026, a woman with lupus and Sjögren overlap whose spleen appears to have disappeared without surgery or injury. Loss of the spleen, called autosplenectomy, is best known in sickle cell disease yet seldom reported in autoimmune illness. The 54-year-old had joint pain, fatigue and signs of active inflammation.

Earlier scans had shown a normal spleen, while later computed tomography showed complete absence. Blood tests showed raised anti-double-stranded DNA, low complement and a positive antibody profile. Checks excluded infection, cancer and blood disorders as causes. The authors judge an autoimmune process most likely. Recognising absent spleen function matters because affected patients face severe infection risk and need vaccination and preventive care.
pmc-13316999:
Lucas Cortizo Garcia and co-authors look back, in a 2026 study, at whether custom abduction braces beat rigid plaster casts after hip surgery in children with cerebral palsy. The operation, a thigh bone cut that rotates the hip back into its socket, needs weeks of careful holding while bone heals.

Records covered 14 patients and 26 hips operated in private hospitals between 2021 and 2025. Just 3.8 percent of hips slipped out again and needed reoperation, while 7.6 percent had shallow wound troubles in the reported outcomes. Every chart noted comfort and easy home care for families. The brace matched cast results while easing the daily burden on caregivers, the authors conclude.
pmc-13317599:
Yaping Lyu and co-authors propose, in a 2026 perspective, a new way to use machine learning for tracking how microplastics age in the environment. Current studies lean on small laboratory datasets aged under accelerated conditions and on models for a single setting. Real plastic particles move between water, soil and air while collecting biological coatings.

The authors outline a framework that reconstructs a particle's history from several lines of evidence using Bayesian reasoning. Their TRACE framework links transport, ageing, surface coating formation and ecological toxicity in one model, with physics-aware learning and causal discovery. They also advocate federated learning, where institutions train shared models without exchanging raw data. The goal is better source attribution and risk prediction for plastic pollution policy.
pmc-13318099:
Lorena Torroni and a large Italian team study, in a 2026 population paper, how season and air shape exhaled nitric oxide, a breath marker of airway inflammation used to guide asthma care. Weather can move the marker, so clinics should weigh the season when reading it.

The Verona study covered 412 people with chronic airway diseases and 605 without, aged 20 to 65, examined between 2008 and 2014. Breath levels ran higher in patients during the warm season even after pollen was counted, with a milder rhythm in healthy peers. A ten-unit rise in fine particle pollution over two days nudged levels up by about three percent. Ignoring season and smog, they warn, can distort treatment calls.
pmc-13318799:
Dan Qiao and co-authors give a 2026 case report of lasting severe low platelets during breast cancer treatment. A 50-year-old woman received the antibody-drug conjugate T-DM1 after earlier chemotherapy. After three cycles, her platelet count fell to grade 4 severity and stayed low. That pattern breaks the usual cycle of dip and recovery.

Standard platelet-boosting drugs failed to hold her counts. Checks ruled out spleen problems, platelet destruction, and clonal blood disease. Repeated marrow samples showed faulty platelet-producing cell maturation. Counts fell whenever romiplostim stopped and recovered when it restarted. A threshold-based, on-and-off schedule stabilised her levels long term. Further anti-HER2 therapy was withheld to protect her fragile platelet reserve.
pmc-13318999:
Jee-Hoon Han and Hye Ji Sa offer a 2026 survey study of marine sports intentions in South Korea after Japan's release of treated Fukushima water began. Data came from 250 marine sports participants in September 2023. The study extends the theory of planned behaviour with knowledge and psychological risk. Stats models tested eight hypotheses.

Personal attitude alone did not predict intention to take part. Social norms and perceived control did push intentions upward. Norms also lifted attitudes, and felt knowledge lifted both attitudes and norms. Felt mental risk dragged attitudes and intentions down. The authors say social influence and felt risk shape behaviour when the environment feels unsafe. Officials and organisers should close knowledge gaps and build trust, not just promote the sports.
pmc-13319699:
Alex Nagle and co-authors pilot brain scan feedback for self blame in major low mood illness in a 2026 study. Feelings of guilt and self blame are core parts of this illness and map to a deep brain zone under the front lobe. Training people to shift activity in that zone while they recall hard memories was tested as a new form of help.

Twenty people took part in one session each, split across two training plans that pushed the zone in opposite ways. Mood scores improved across both plans, with no clear gap between them. Control of the target zone varied a lot by person and task. The method proved safe and workable in this small group, but firm effects need larger trials.
pmc-13319999:
Kabelo Leonard Mauco and co-authors ask experts how digital health tools can serve future outbreaks in a 2026 survey study. The COVID years showed that apps and data tools can aid care, tracing, watch systems, and vaccine drives. A field that mines digital traces for health insight has grown from that lesson. Lasting fair use of those tools was the open question.

Experts in outbreaks, public health, and data work from Africa, North America, Oceania, and Europe shared views through a web form built by the team. Most knew the field well and spoke in its favor in the answers gathered. Strengths, weak spots, chances, and threats were grouped from their words to guide joint global planning.
pmc-13320399:
Erika Džajić Uršič presents an interview data set on factory sharing webs in Slovenia in a 2026 data article. In such webs one firm waste becomes another firm food, a core path toward a circular economy where goods loop instead of landing in dumps. Talks with people inside those webs were logged to show how trust and teamwork grow or stall.

All talks ran in Slovene, were turned into note form, scrubbed of names, and rendered into English, giving fifty talks in each tongue. A code book built from the talks sorts themes with clear rules, sample quotes, and edge cases. Files hold both talk sets, two talk guides, and the code book, ready for theme studies, policy contrasts, and training in field coding.
pmc-13320599: Ryan Hass and Sanjiva Lele are named on a 2026 item on shear-free, inhomogeneous turbulence in a stably stratified fluid. The item itself is only a brief image description, with no abstract, methods, or findings supplied alongside it. On its title alone, the work concerns how turbulent mixing behaves when fluid layers differ in density and no shear flow drives the motion, a topic in basic fluid physics. Nothing further about its approach or results can be stated from what the item provides.
pmc-13321299:
Tomoki Nishiyama and co-authors describe a new semiconducting framework material in a 2026 chemistry study. The metal-organic framework mixes copper in two charge states, CuI and CuIII, held by diethyldithiocarbamate ligands and bromide bridges. Single crystal X-ray work confirmed its three dimensional build and its solvent filled pores.

Light tests showed broad absorption out to 2500 nanometres, tied to charge transfer between the two copper states, and magnetic tests confirmed a diamagnetic state. The trapped solvent could be removed gently while pores stayed open, a rare stability for such mixed charge materials. Used as a battery cathode, it gave capacity on par with common LiCoO2 material.
pmc-13321399:
Francesco Petri and a large team examine how success and failure are defined after infected joint replacement in a 2026 meta-epidemiologic study. Prosthetic joint infection affects about 2 percent of joint replacement patients, and varied outcome definitions make studies hard to compare. The team sifted 7585 references down to 461 studies with clear definitions.

Most studies were retrospective, at 90.2 percent, with very few randomised trials. Outcome reporting spread across seven domains, from symptoms and scans to microbiology, death, antibiotics, surgery, and tissue checks, in shifting combinations. Patient reported measures were also gathered. From that map, the authors propose a working core outcome set to steady future research.
pmc-13321799:
Cornelia Lass-Flörl and co-authors set out a framework for reading antifungal drug tests in rare fungi in a 2026 ISHAM review. Many fungi naturally show reduced drug sensitivity, with test values shifted higher across a whole species. Reading the top of that normal range as resistance can mislead care and surveillance, above all where breakpoints are missing.

The framework separates normal sensitivity, intrinsic reduced susceptibility, and true intrinsic resistance from acquired resistance, using species level value ranges and cut-off points. Values inside the normal range should be reported as wild type, even when high. Only clear shifts beyond the range count as non-wild type and possible acquired resistance.
pmc-13322999:
M M Cantagalli and colleagues test robot-assisted surgery for sparing the ovary in children with benign ovarian tumours, in a 2026 comparative study at a specialist centre. They reviewed patients aged 18 or younger treated between January 2023 and December 2025, comparing an earlier group with a robotic group from 2025.

The set held 24 patients, 14 treated before robots and 10 with robot help. Ovarian-sparing surgery succeeded in every robotic case, against most cases in the earlier group, and no robotic case converted to open surgery. Operating time ran longer with the robot. The authors read the results as support for robotic help where saving ovarian function is the priority.
pmc-13323399:
Seong-Min Park and a large consortium present, in 2026, a protein-level regrouping of medulloblastoma, the most common malignant childhood brain tumour. Standard grouping misses much of the disease's variety, and treatments remain blunt and toxic. The team pooled five measurement platforms, including mass-spectrometry protein profiling, for a joined-up molecular portrait.

Seven refined subtypes emerged. One established group split in two and another into three, and two subtypes followed distinct paths of neuronal maturation that pointed to better outcomes. The three poor-outcome subtypes carried unique protein and enzyme-activity signatures suggesting specific drug weak points. Lab tests supported several targeted agents, including blockers of cell-cycle and DNA-repair enzymes and a proteasome inhibitor. The authors propose protein signatures and maturation state as guides for matching children to chosen therapies.
pmc-13323499:
John Onsy Louca leads a large team arguing that perfused donor hearts should serve as a first testing ground for new drugs, in a 2026 perspective. Keeping hearts beating outside the body, a method rooted in Langendorff's nineteenth-century work, now underpins donation programmes after circulatory death.

The proposal uses hearts turned down for transplant, plus hearts removed from transplant recipients, for first-in-human studies with minimal patient risk. Weak drugs could then be dropped long before costly mid and late stage trials, where lack of effect sinks many candidates. Longer perfusion times are the key technical need, and the authors call for joint work among industry, universities and clinicians to spread the model.
pmc-13324499:
Lennart W Sannwald and co-authors measure life quality after surgery for traumatic brachial plexus injury in a 2026 single-center study. These nerve injuries often hit young people and change daily life deeply, yet most past work tracked muscle strength alone.

Records covered 98 patients treated at Ulm University hospital in Günzburg from 2020 through 2023, and 62 returned surveys. Average follow-up was 22.3 months, during which the health utility score rose from 0.41 before surgery to 0.57 at last check. Pain scores fell from 19.7 to 16.5 on the PainDetect scale. Gains in strength lined up with gains in life quality, while sleep showed only a weak trend toward better rest.
pmc-13326999:
Oliver Gould and colleagues describe a 2026 chemistry study on man-made compounds that cut DNA. They joined an acridine unit, which slides between DNA bases, to a click-chemistry scaffold that holds copper ions. The goal was a single molecule that both finds DNA in two ways and breaks it.

Two copper-binding sites from the earlier scaffold were kept, and the third site carried the acridine group, giving a hybrid named DC-PyA. Loaded with copper, the hybrid bound and cut DNA, and its behavior matched a threading style of insertion between bases. Pairing two binding modes in one compound offers a route toward cancer drugs that damage DNA more selectively.
pmc-13327499:
Ganter and four co-authors set out a tighter math fix in twenty twenty-six for scans that split water and fat in the body. Scan fits use a trick that cuts the size of the task by dropping some plain parts. Past tight forms still let water and fat point in flipped ways, which can skew the fit.

Their form bakes the true physical rules in from the start, so flipped fits are barred. A key share, the fat part, gets a closed form tied to two scan traits. On hard data the new form gave more stable reads of all three traits. It keeps the speed of the older forms too.
pmc-13327899:
YongBo Yang and co-authors compare two malnutrition scores before spine surgery in a 2026 prospective cohort study. The Prognostic Nutritional Index, built from blood values, and the GLIM criteria, a wider clinical standard, often disagree. The study followed 1,341 patients at a Chinese center from February 2022 to September 2025.

Low scores were uncommon, at 6.5 percent by the blood index and 6.9 percent by GLIM, yet the two tools flagged almost entirely different patients, with positive agreement of only 5.6 percent between them. Low blood-index scores doubled the adjusted odds of major complications within 30 days, while pragmatic GLIM scoring showed no outcome link. The simple blood index earned the authors' backing for spine surgery screening.
pmc-13328299:
Özge Çolakoğlu and Alaa Altassan use graph mathematics to forecast drug properties in a 2026 study. Molecules can be drawn as graphs of atoms and bonds, and Zagreb indices compress those graphs into numbers. The pair computed several index families for drugs used in bipolar disorder.

From the indices they built quantitative structure-property models for boiling point, vaporization enthalpy, flash point, molar refractivity, and polarizability. Comparing index versions showed which mathematical flavor predicts each property best, all without a single bench experiment. Cheap, fast screening of this kind can rank candidate compounds early, reserving costly lab work for the most promising structures.
pmc-13329899:
Bipin Bhattarai and co-authors report switchable electric order in boron nitride films grown at low heat in a 2026 study. Normal growth needs over 600 degrees, which clashes with patterned silicon devices. The team used atomic layer annealing to grow shapeless films at 350 degrees instead.

Even though the stable crystal form is centred and should show no such order, the new films showed clear switchable polarisation in standard tests. Probe scans agreed with that reading. Chemical checks found mostly boron and nitrogen, with small carbon and oxygen traces that may break local balance. Theory work showed that electric fields can shift atoms enough to create polarisation. The route could bring useful nitride films into device making.
pmc-13330099:
Yi-Ching Chen and four colleagues published an exercise study in two thousand twenty-six on balance training for older adults. Falls are a leading health risk in later life. The team tested whether cuff-restricted blood flow during arm exercise sharpens balance when the mind is busy too.

Twenty-six adults around age sixty-nine did one short arm cycling session, with or without the restriction cuffs. Balance was tested while tapping a light pod and standing on foam. The cuff group swayed less and slower afterward than controls. Brain-to-posture coupling also shifted in one frequency band at the front of the head. The authors say brief restricted arm work may tune balance control.
pmc-13330599:
Aga Natalis, Abdul Jalil, and Sonhaji write a 2026 letter, in Spanish, on contraceptive literacy, women's empowerment, and human rights in Indonesia. The letter responds to a study by Rua and co-authors on women's knowledge of birth control methods in Portugal, where basic knowledge coexisted with gaps on true effectiveness.

Indonesia faces like gaps among teens and remote women despite a national family planning programme, the letter argues. Low literacy leaves choices shaped by husbands, family, and patriarchal norms, with low male involvement. Laws back reproductive autonomy, yet social barriers block it in practice. From a feminist view, literacy empowers women to decide about their own bodies. Schooling and health service access strengthen knowledge, the authors note.
pmc-13331699:
Takeshi Ogura and colleagues share a 2026 technical case report on clearing a blocked bile duct junction in a 68-year-old man with hilar bile duct cancer. Earlier plastic stents had blocked again within a month, so a different approach was needed.

Working through an endoscope, the team placed three fully covered metal stents side by side into the left, rear, and front bile ducts. The stents carry a spiral groove on their outer surface, a design meant to keep side branches open, and scans afterward showed no branch blockage. The patient later died of his cancer after six months, but the stents worked without failure during that time. The authors take that record as support for the grooved design.
pmc-13332799:
Shyamal Sheth and colleagues report a 2026 fulminant mantle cell lymphoma case that first looked like liver cancer. Mantle cell lymphoma is an uncommon, aggressive B-cell lymphoma usually presenting with swollen glands, enlarged spleen, and gut involvement. Liver involvement is rare and usually silent, while liver lesions in practice more often mean metastases from gut, breast, lung, or pancreatic cancers. Here the lymphoma announced itself with tumor lysis syndrome and cholestatic liver injury.

The patient was a 90-year-old man with prior coronary bypass surgery who came with belly pain, nausea, and vomiting. He was first sent home with a presumed chronic lymphocytic leukemia label from blood counts. Days later he returned with worsening jaundice, poor appetite, weakness, and a shuffling gait, plus high white counts and acute kidney injury. The case shows how lymphoma can mimic hepatobiliary malignancy and why rapid deterioration with liver injury deserves urgent lymphoma workup.
pmc-13333099:
Anthony Hong and colleagues report a 2026 case of infant botulism in Costa Rica, the first there supported by local nerve tests. Infant botulism is a life-threatening paralytic condition caused by toxin from Clostridium botulinum. The patient was a four-month-old Costa Rican girl in hospital with poor sucking, feeding difficulty, constipation, low muscle tone, and respiratory failure. History, examination, and nerve tests together strongly suggested infant botulism.

Definitive proof tests can take a long time, so nerve tests may speed diagnosis and prompt earlier treatment. This is only the second reported case in Costa Rica, and the first in which nerve tests were performed locally to support the diagnosis. The case shows clinicians in regions with few reported cases how nerve testing can bridge the wait for proof and justify timely treatment.
pmc-13333299:
Jie Zhao and colleagues test a 2026 PET-guided radiation strategy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with partial metabolic response after R-CHOP. The retrospective analysis included 68 patients with scores four to five after four R-CHOP cycles. Twenty-nine received two more R-CHOP cycles plus risk-adapted residual site radiation: 24 Gray for score four and 40 Gray for score five. Thirty-nine received two to four more R-CHOP cycles without radiation.

The radiation cohort reached far higher end-of-treatment complete response rates, about seventy-two percent versus about thirty-nine percent. Progression-free survival also favored radiation: about eighty-six percent versus about fifty-three percent at two years, and about fifty-seven percent versus about forty-four percent at five years. The study supports PET-guided, dose-adapted radiation for partial responders.
pmc-13333699:
Hannah Burke and co-authors used network analysis in a 2026 study to hunt for gene regulators behind chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Earlier work had flagged eight microRNAs in extracellular vesicles that differ between patients and healthy ex-smokers, and this study looked for their target genes in lung tissue.

Airway epithelial brushings from 24 patients and 20 controls were profiled by RNA sequencing. Computer analysis paired the vesicle microRNAs with genes whose activity moved in the opposite direction, then mapped the pairs into networks. One microRNA, miR-182-5p, stood out as a potential regulator of disease processes. Gene patterns also tracked with CT-based measures of disease probability. The findings nominate candidates for therapies that might one day modify the disease rather than only ease symptoms.
pmc-13333799:
Ana Irina Martin-Lopez and six co-authors study how setting shapes bird malaria germ groups inside two Culex mosquito species in southwest Spain. Most past work looks at the birds, though mosquitoes carry the germs. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Mosquitoes were caught at many sites over two years, and germ strains were read by gene tests. In one species, germ rates rose with greener land, while strain richness fell as land heat rose. In the other, rates and richness rose with low warmth, and diversity fell with land heat. Germ groups split by mosquito species, and place likeness tracked distance in just one species.
pmc-13336399:
Wenbo Ming and co-authors synthesized a fully defined four-part cancer vaccine aimed at the Tn carbohydrate antigen in a 2026 chemistry and immunology study. Tumor sugars like Tn attract vaccine designers but provoke weak immunity and little T cell help, and protein carriers add inconsistency.

Their single molecule packs four functions. Synthetic Tn is the B cell target, vizantin is a built-in Mincle-activating adjuvant, rhamnose recruits natural antibodies for Fc receptor uptake, and mannose guides the construct to dendritic cells through CD206. Precise co-delivery fired all three innate pathways together. In mice the vaccine drove strong IgG class switching, Th1-type cytokines, and meaningful tumor suppression. The design offers a template for next-generation carbohydrate vaccines without carrier proteins.
pmc-13336499:
Yuchuan Zheng and colleagues present 2026 DGIF, a guide for inverse folding in multi-trait protein design. Designing proteins for real-world uses needs many physical and chemical traits met at once. Structure-based de novo protein design has become the main design path and created many proteins.

Trait tuning is often added during sequence making in protein design, that is, inverse folding. Current methods mostly rely on fine-tuning inverse folding models to design sequences with wanted traits. Yet multi-trait tuning through fine-tuning needs data sets tagged with many traits, which remain very scarce. DGIF guides the inverse folding model by adjusting its inner history states through an added discriminator module. The discriminator joins many trait predictors, each trained alone on a single-trait data set.
pmc-13336599:
In 2026, Hao Zhang and colleagues reported a new ceramic electrolyte for safer lithium batteries. The material is a garnet type compound, LLZO, doped with both aluminium and nitrogen in a single heating step. Such solid electrolytes could replace flammable liquids in rechargeable cells, yet their ion flow has stayed too slow for wide use.

The team combined the two dopants to lower the barrier that lithium ions must cross, and measured a high rate of ion flow through the new ceramic. Test cells ran steadily for 600 hours, and a full cell kept 82.6 percent of its charge after 200 cycles. The result points to a practical route toward solid batteries that are safer and longer lasting.
pmc-13336899:
Xiaodong Geng and colleagues explain a warm-up effect in zinc-organic batteries in a 2026 study. Their cathode molecule, DPPT, carries eight nitrogen-based active sites and delivers very long life. Early cycles, though, behave oddly as the molecule transforms from a proton-loaded form into its working form.

Live measurements and calculations showed zinc ions and protons share the storage work, settling into an optimized combined structure. pmc-13342799:
