The twin blends swarm data to test what if paths and guide choices. A simple control layer lets farm and park staff set aims and step in on odd cases, with no need to drive each unit. The road map aims at long, low cost sea watch.
pmc-13369099:
Dost and co-authors map the evidence for a trunk nerve block used in pain control in this 2026 scoping review. The anterior quadratus lumborum block injects anesthetic between two deep back muscles. It promises relief for both surface and internal pain after surgery.

The reviewers searched five databases through February 2026 and kept only randomized trials. From 1,174 records, 119 trials made the final set. Most ran in Asia, at 63 percent, and most enrolled adults. Abdominal and urological operations were studied most. Big questions remain about how the block works and where the drug spreads. The review charts those gaps for future trials.
pmc-13369499:
Liu and six co-authors set a gas-phase coat that lifts sun cell yield to a new high in this twenty twenty-six study. Sun cells of this type lose yield when flaws in the film eat charge pairs. Most flaw fixes use wet coats, which can harm the film and block large-scale builds.

Inside, a dry gas coat grows from a liquid salt layer laid on the film top. Part of the salt reacts with spare lead waste to form a thin link layer. The rest of the salt caps loose lead spots and curbs new flaw growth. Small cells hit a prize yield score and a chart-topping fill score. Big cells kept most of that gain, and aged cells held up well in heat and damp.
pmc-13370299:
Paul Kench and co-workers sum up in 2026 how the coasts of Southeast Asia change, from deep past to now. The zone's coasts face sea rise, storm hits, and fast land sink. Past sea flood took a huge shelf, and a later sea fall built wide low lands in six thousand years.

Now land moves up or down by rock shifts set the true sea rise at each shore, from nil to fast rates that top world means. Shores reply in a patch work: some hold, some grow, some slide. Plans must fit each shore's own path, not a one rate tale.
pmc-13372399:
Marisa van der Graaf and colleagues compare two pulsed field ablation systems for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 registry study. Pulsed field ablation isolates pulmonary veins with electric pulses, yet long-term comparisons between systems were scarce. Patients having a first ablation between early and late 2024 at multiple centres were tracked, with recurrence after a two-month blanking period as the key outcome.

Of 428 patients, 231 received a pentaspline catheter and the rest a circular over-the-wire catheter. Most had vein isolation only, while procedure and left atrium dwell times ran longer with the circular catheter. The registry gives clinicians real-world evidence on whether the two designs differ in lasting rhythm control and repeat ablation need.
pmc-13373299:
Sabine Bischoff and her team set out guide lines for Europe for sleep-drug care in pigs, sheep, goats, and cows used in labs. Their 2026 work-group text fills a gap: safe picks were there for rats and mice but not for these large lab kinds.

Law in Europe calls for steps to use sleep drugs or pain ease, to keep pain at its least. The guide lines draw on norms for care of folk and of beasts in the trade. They aim at sleep-drug care and pain curb that is safe, of use, and good in its acts. Four parts take in calm drugs and ways to hold beasts, base rules for full sleep-drug care, watch work, and pain checks. The text sets norms put forth for labs that work with farm beast kinds.
pmc-13373599:
Conradt and colleagues re-analyze a randomized trial of a parenting intervention to ask whether peer support specialists coach parents as effectively as master's-level clinicians, in 2026 child welfare research. The program, Attachment and Biobehavioral Catchup, trains parents of young children in sensitive responding. The re-analysis covers 79 parent-child dyads: 49 received the program from peer coaches with lived experience, and 30 from clinicians holding master's degrees, with parental sensitivity and intrusiveness as the measured outcomes.

Peer coaches proved non-inferior to clinicians on both outcomes, meaning their results fell within the margin set for being just as good. Parents coached by peers gained sensitivity at rates matching the clinician group, without greater intrusiveness. Conradt argues the finding matters for access. Child welfare systems cannot hire enough clinicians to meet demand, and peer delivery could extend the evidence-based program to far more families without diluting its effect on parenting behavior.
pmc-13375299:
Franciele Saorin and co-authors asked if germs can change hard plastics in a 2026 study. The plastics in view fill food and face-care packs and can last for years in soil and sea. Four germ strains known to gnaw a kin plastic were put to the test.

Each strain sat for 90 days in a thin broth with the plastic blend as the sole food. Growth, life signs, mass loss, and face shifts were checked. Signs of change would be a first for this blend, which most hold to be germ-proof. Even small gnaws could seed new ways to clear waste that now just piles up.
pmc-13376099:
Seolah Lee reports an unusual brain presentation of anti-Ri paraneoplastic encephalitis in a 2026 case report. The syndrome, driven by an immune response to a distant cancer, usually affects the brainstem or cerebellum, not isolated cortex. A 54-year-old woman presented with transient apraxia, confusion, and headache, and MRI showed a tumour-like lesion in the left frontal cortex.

Brain biopsy showed inflammation without malignancy. Blood tests were strongly positive for anti-Ri antibodies, and work-up found breast cancer with axillary lymph node spread. Surgery and chemotherapy plus high-dose steroids and four weekly rituximab doses led to marked lesion resolution. The case expands the known phenotype and warns clinicians not to mistake inflammatory cortex lesions for tumours.
pmc-13376199:
Satoshi Konishi, Fumiya Sano, Yuki Fujimoto, Tomohiro Nakatsuka, and Jin Iguchi give a robot fingertip a sense of smell, in a 2026 paper. Their earlier microfinger already felt force and heat. The new one, twelve millimeters long and half a millimeter thick, bends on air bladders and reports its own motion through a strain sensor. Channels modeled on an elephant's trunk suck samples in at the tip.

Ethanol vapor played the gas target and a colorant the liquid one. The finger sniffed its way across each plume, mapping where the sample ran strongest. Plugged into an outside analyzer, it can identify what it collects. The authors pitch the design for exploring and testing tiny, complex spaces where noses cannot go.
pmc-13376399:
Wang and colleagues present a data-driven method for designing problem-based learning, the teaching style where students learn by solving open problems, in 2026 education research. Instructional designs must balance competing goals on messy educational data. Their framework, Cross-Dataset Robust Multi-Optimization, tunes design settings against three objectives: learning gain, digital literacy, and setup cost and risk. It rewards designs that stay stable when the data vary between institutions and platforms.

The method was tested on three varied datasets, OULAD, EdNet, and KDD Cup 2010, using a shared feature space and design variables for comparison. Scores covered convergence, diversity of solutions, robustness, and stability across the datasets. Under that framework, the method produced higher-quality design trade-offs than the comparison approaches reported. Wang argues robustness-aware tuning is what separates a design that works in one course's data from one a university can trust across programs.
pmc-13377099:
Ho Am Jang and nine co-authors studied a gene called TmKayak in the beetle Tenebrio molitor, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. A signaling path known as JNK helps insects handle stress and infection, but its downstream steps are poorly known in beetles. The gene is a counterpart of a well studied gene in fruit flies.

The team used RNA interference to turn the gene down, then infected larvae with three microbes. Larvae with the gene turned down survived less well than controls. Tests also showed broad drops in the genes for antimicrobial peptides, the small proteins that fight microbes. The effect was strongest against two bacteria and milder against a fungus. The gene thus acts as a key switch in the beetle's defense.
pmc-13377599:
S. Nag and co-authors tried a scan tag for a brain protein in a 2026 study. The protein sits most in deep brain zones and is tied to Parkinson's ill by gene work. It helps set how a key joy and move stuff is let out, and it is off in sick brains.

The tag was built to grip that protein type and skip its two kin. Rat work showed a right map in dish tests but no true grip in live brains. The new work checks grip strength in dish and live tests in apes. A true tag could track the ill's creep and drug acts in the deep brain.
pmc-13378099:
Sharon Lawn and co-authors report how Australians who have lived under community treatment orders describe the experience. These orders compel mental health treatment in the community; their effectiveness is contested and human rights concerns persist, yet Australia uses them at high rates internationally. Their 2026 mixed-methods study surveys consumers recruited across Australia in 2024.

Forty-three people completed the survey, most of them women, and nearly half had been placed on an order more than once. Automated bot responses contaminated further data collection. Answers covered life before, during, and after the orders, attitudes toward them, family involvement, and views of services. Some reported positive care, but many rejected the orders, describing coercion, exclusion from decisions and information, few alternative supports, and a lack of compassion. The authors conclude that reforms emphasising recovery and human rights have not yet improved lived experience, and urge work to close the policy-practice gap.
pmc-13378299:
Soo Yeon Lim and others build a five-target droplet digital PCR test for blood-borne viruses in a 2026 study. The five-target assay detects and exactly counts HIV-1, HIV-2, liver virus C, and hepatitis B plus an internal control in one reaction. Shop-bought blood screening kits multi-target but rely on shared cycle threshold counting, which varies with standard samples and conditions, limiting comparability.

Conventional antigen-antibody tests and single-target quantitative PCR also lack multiplexing or need standard curves. The new assay showed 95 percent detection limits from 2.42 to 6.65 copies per reaction across targets with high specificity. Validation under ISO 20395 showed linearity, sensitivity, and precision with low variation. The test could strengthen blood screening and reference material validation.
pmc-13380199:
Niclas Lutz and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of questionnaires that shoulder and elbow patients complete remotely on digital devices. Such patient-reported measures capture pain and function from the patient's own view. Digital versions let clinics follow large groups without extra visits.

Searching the medical literature to March 2025, the team found thousands of records and, after screening, reviewed 62 papers in full. Eleven studies met all the rules, covering shoulder, elbow, and wider arm problems. The tools fell into five types, and the outcomes into five domains. The review weighs the benefits and practical problems of remote collection for clinics considering it.
pmc-13382199:
Trenton C Agrelius and co-authors report a 2026 study using gene silencing by feeding to study DNA-tagging enzymes in water fleas. The tiny freshwater animals, Daphnia pulex, can reproduce without mating, which makes them a useful system for studying inherited marks that do not change the DNA code. The enzymes studied place those marks.

Two genetic lines of fleas were fed bacteria carrying silencing instructions against three tagging-enzyme genes. Responses differed sharply by line: one line died in large numbers, while in the other the target genes were switched on more strongly, the opposite of the intended effect. The contrast shows that genetic background can dominate such experiments in this model animal.
pmc-13383399:
Quan Zhou's team traced frailty before and after heart disease and stroke in older adults, in a 2026 study across three national cohorts. The team followed 23,307 participants over age 50 from England, the United States, and China, scoring frailty from mobility and daily function. Cardiovascular events were identified from doctor-diagnosed heart disease or stroke.

Frailty was already present before events and worsened afterward, with a sharp short-term jump in mobility scores right after diagnosis in all three cohorts. The pattern suggests frailty screening should start well before events, not only in rehabilitation after them. Prevention and early support could blunt the decline that events accelerate.
pmc-13383499:
Xiaobing Yang's team compared phone-supported versus center-based cardiac rehabilitation in stable coronary heart disease, in a 2026 randomized trial. High-intensity interval training works in rehabilitation, but center programs suffer from access and adherence barriers. The team randomized 98 adults to the same interval protocol delivered either with mobile health support or under center supervision.

The phone-supported group improved more on sleep quality, peak METs, anaerobic threshold, peak oxygen uptake at 20.12 versus 16.70 milliliters per kilogram per minute, and six-minute walk distance. Quality-of-life gains appeared in several domains, though vitality and mental health did not differ. Mobile delivery looks like a strong alternative when center attendance is hard.
pmc-13383899:
Kemler, Sebt, and Banffy set out a changed way to add a brace to a rebuilt knee ligament, in work from twenty twenty-six. The brace, a lateral tenodesis, is a strap on the outer side of the knee. Surgeons add it to an anterior cruciate repair to cut leftover twist and slack. Their way holds it with a knotless anchor of suture alone, plus suture tape. The aim is strength with less harm to soft tissue.

A soft, bendable hold should help the graft knit in at the anchor site. It keeps hard parts from poking up under the skin. The authors say it holds more steady than older ways of fixing the strap. They lay out the steps and why they should work, but give no results from treated knees. Surgeons who want a low add-on for high-risk knees may find it worth a look.
pmc-13383999:
Lavender Micalo and colleagues ask whether GLP-1 drugs link to fewer clots and leg problems in obese patients with vein disease in 2026 work. Adults aged 40 and older with chronic venous insufficiency were drawn from a large United States health network. Patients starting GLP-1 therapy were matched one to one with similar patients who did not start it.

Outcomes tracked over one and three years covered deep vein clots, lung clots, leg ulcers, skin infection, and death. People with earlier clots were excluded so new events could be judged cleanly. The matched design aims to show whether weight-loss drug therapy also protects veins, an open question the authors set out to answer.
pmc-13384899:
Daiyin Liu and a large team trace a circular RNA that drives lymph node spread in bladder cancer in 2026 work. The ring RNA, circFOCAD, runs high in cancers that reached lymph nodes and tracks with poor outlook. Lymph vessel growth depends on activation of the signal VEGF-C, whose controls were unclear.

CircFOCAD boosts two partners that together cut VEGF-C into its active form, one acting as a scaffold. Blocking either partner with antibodies curbed lymph node spread in patient-derived tumor models. The authors nominate circFOCAD as a treatment target for bladder cancer that spreads through lymph channels.
pmc-13386499:
Hayati and colleagues compare Candida albicans yeast isolates from humans and animals in Iran to test whether the same strains cross between species, in 2026 mycology research. Thirty-six isolates from human and animal sources were fingerprinted with RAPD-PCR, a DNA pattern method, using primers, alongside drug susceptibility and virulence profiling. Knowing whether farm and companion animals seed human infections, or the reverse, shapes how clinics and veterinarians coordinate control of this cause of fungal disease.

Genetic patterns separated human and animal isolates into distinct genotype groups. Some relatedness appeared: the highest similarity, 84 percent, linked an isolate from cow feces with one from a human vaginal swab, related but not the same clone. The typing detected no clonal relationship among isolates. Hayati calls the study preliminary, notes the typing method's resolution and reproducibility, and recommends sharper molecular tools before ruling cross-species transmission in or out for Candida epidemiology.
pmc-13391799:
Nada K Gamal and a large team test, in 2026, whether a diabetes drug can protect the brain in a rat model of Parkinson's disease through the gut. Parkinson's involves gradual loss of dopamine neurons and motor symptoms, and gut imbalance is now linked to its development.

Canagliflozin blocks a sugar pump in the kidney. It also calms swelling and cell stress. The team tested if it shields the brain in rats, with the gut as part of its path. The focus was the gut-to-brain relay of swelling signals. Drug readers gain early proof in rats. A drug in wide use for blood sugar might gain a fresh role against this brain disease. Rat work comes first, as it should, before any use in sick people is weighed.
pmc-13392699:
Beilu Duan and a large team tested comic strips warning about elephant skin, sold illegally as a stomach remedy near the Yunnan border with Myanmar, to see which warning cuts demand. Over sixteen hundred residents were split into groups shown legal-risk comics, health-risk comics, or neutral material, then asked what they would do for stomach illness. Beliefs and intentions were modelled together.

Legal warnings cut stated intent to seek elephant skin by about a quarter against the control group, especially when they stressed the product is no cure. Health warnings pushed more people toward hospitals, but among city residents who had never heard of the remedy they unexpectedly raised curiosity to try it. The authors warn that one message can help one audience and backfire with another, so campaigns need tailoring by segment.
pmc-13393699:
G. M. Szafraniec and others map drug-proof germs from lame meat chickens in Poland in a 2026 study. Lameness from bone and joint germs hurts bird health and farm pay. A group of skin germs once thought mild is now blamed more and more, next to the well-known Staphylococcus aureus.

From bone and joint sores in 25 farm flocks, the team typed 93 germ samples across 12 kinds with disk tests, gene tests, strain prints, and full gene reads. Proof against penicillin, doxycycline, and erythromycin was rife, with several proof genes seen often. Vets and farmers now have a map to guide drug choice for lame birds.
pmc-13393899:
Gülay Turgay, Banu Çevik, Sultan Kav, and Ebru Akgün Çıtak interviewed twenty-two palliative care patients and twenty-two caregivers at a foundation hospital in Ankara about spiritual needs at the end of life. Serious illness stirs spiritual struggle in families as well as patients, and the team used open interviews covering challenges, coping, meaning, and shifting beliefs, analysed with a phenomenological method. Kidney failure, liver disease, and lung and ovarian cancers led the patient diagnoses.

Patient accounts organised around disability, transcendence with family support, acceptance, and psychological pain. Caregivers spoke of burden, split into physical, stress, and money strands, alongside missing information, faith in God or a higher power, and even pride in caring. Both groups leaned on God, family, and friends in the hardest stretches. The authors conclude spiritual support is indispensable in palliative care.
pmc-13395399:
Malaak M. Rasheed and Abdulkarim T. Hasan measure, in 2026, forehead shape and sinus size in Syrian adults. X-ray profiles from 216 adults aged 18 to 30 were sorted by jaw pattern into three classes. The team measured sinus height and width plus how far the forehead juts. Men and women were balanced across classes.

Men showed larger values on every measure. Jaw class moved forehead jut but not sinus size, with the class II group jutting least. Bigger sinuses went with stronger forehead jut across the sample. Sex and jaw pattern never crossed in effect. The authors say sex matters most when judging this part of the face.
pmc-13395499:
Spencer Rasmussen and colleagues studied whether dementia present before surgery changes outcomes after hip fracture repair in older adults. Using a large research network, they compared patients aged 65 to 90 who had surgery for two common hip fracture types.

The team drew on records for 68,639 patients, matched on age, sex, and other illnesses. They then tracked deaths, readmissions, and complications such as pneumonia and heart failure. Patients with dementia died at nearly twice the rate of others within 90 days of surgery, for both fracture types. Their readmission and complication rates were also clearly higher at every follow-up point out to five years. The authors argue that care plans and family talks should treat dementia as a major risk factor before hip surgery.
pmc-13396299:
Stefano Mastrangelo and others test watchful waiting for womb-time adrenal lumps in a 2026 one-site look-back study. Womb scans now spot more fetal and newborn adrenal lumps, forcing a choice between swift surgery and watchful waiting.

Nine patients found from 2015 to 2025 were first watched with repeat scans to track lump size. Last calls were four nerve-cell cancers, four kind lumps, and one adrenal cortex cancer. The small set backs picky waiting with close scans, while warning that shares from nine cases need soft reading and more cases to firm them up.
pmc-13396399:
Mohammed and co-authors show, in 2026, that human cystathionine beta-synthase works as a filamentous morpheein, a protein that swaps between assemblies with different activity. The enzyme governs sulfur amino acid metabolism and hydrogen sulfide production. Using cryo-electron microscopy, they mapped three filament types, all stitched through one loop spanning residues 516 to 525 of the protein chain.

Ligand-free dimers formed basal filaments with base activity. Dimers bound to an ornithine analog built a second, stabler filament form. A third form, S-adenosylmethionine-bound dimers, stacked into highly stable, active filaments with boosted activity. The enzyme's lifetime inside cells responded accordingly: adding methionine stretched its half-life by 58 percent to 11.5 hours, while blocking synthesis of its activator cut the half-life by 26 percent to 5.4 hours in their tests. The authors say the filament picture changes how this enzyme is regulated.
pmc-13397599:
Gregory D Whitehill and others name hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae as a new cause of pharyngitis in a 2026 study. This hypervirulent strain rarely causes non-invasive infection, yet throat cultures from eleven pharyngitis cases bore it.

Most cases fell in summer months, patients were spread far apart, and none were diabetic or immune-weak, though near half used inhaled or nasal steroids. The illness mimicked viral or streptococcal sore throat, while genome reads found four strains sharing virulence marks. Clinicians gain a new suspect for stubborn sore throat that keeps coming back despite usual care.
pmc-13398099:
Kristine Salmina and co-authors watch how breast cancer cells patch damage at their chromosome ends after chemotherapy. Their 2026 study treats the MDA-MB-231 cell line with doxorubicin and finds the enzyme that maintains telomeres briefly shuts down before growth restarts. Cells pile up late in division, slip out of mitosis with doubled genomes and lose a key nuclear protein along the way.

In about 11 to 12 percent of cells, telomeres clustered with damage markers inside PML bodies, mimicking a backup lengthening route used by some tumours. By week three the cells shed their extra genome copies and resumed normal cycling and telomere upkeep. Similar bodies appeared in treated melanoma cells, hinting at a shared survival trick.
pmc-13398499:
Chibuzor Onyinye Okonkwo and co-authors review ten years of evidence on how African farming can withstand a shifting climate. Their 2026 survey spans publications from 2015 to 2025 across ten countries, two per region of the continent. Erratic rain, long droughts and heat stress already cut yields and shake food access for millions who farm small plots.

Drawing on three major databases, the synthesis finds climate swings fuelling hunger, displacement and eroded rural livelihoods. Finance shortages head the barrier list, alongside weak policy follow-through and thin local support. The authors weigh adaptive capacity country by country, pressing for stewardship and planning that fit each setting rather than one continental template.
pmc-13398899:
Bisht and Indora write, in 2026, a letter responding to the TOP-ELM trial of tofogliflozin, a sodium-glucose cotransporter inhibitor, in type 2 diabetes. The four-week trial compared the drug with metformin and found similar gains in glycemic measures, alongside a greater reduction in the fatty liver index for tofogliflozin. The letter writers commend the design while probing its negative result: no real group-level improvement in insulin secretory capacity.

They highlight the trial's subgroup analyses, where patients with poorer baseline glucose tolerance, or larger glucose improvements, did show better insulin secretion. That pattern suggests relief of glucotoxicity, the self-harm high glucose inflicts on beta cells, mediates recovery over time. They propose analyzing glucose tolerance as a continuous variable rather than by median splits for a finer picture. They also connect the findings to evidence that early intensive glycemic control can reverse glucose-driven beta-cell damage.
pmc-13399199:
Luiz Sorrenti and colleagues validated a camera-based method for measuring the gap that opens between stitched tendon ends under load, in a 2026 experimental study. Gap size matters because a wide separation after tendon repair weakens healing and raises the chance of adhesions. Their method films a sutured tendon model against backlight from front and side views at once, using a mirror, while software reads the gap from the video.

The test object was a rigid 3D-printed tendon model pulled by a mechanical testing machine, whose own readings served as the reference. The optical method's average error was a few hundredths of a millimeter: bias of minus 0.01 millimeters in the frontal view and 0.04 in the lateral view, as reported in the study. Readings from the two views matched almost perfectly. The authors conclude the cheap video setup is accurate enough to standardize gap measurement in tendon biomechanics experiments.
pmc-13399399:
Burcu İzgi Duman and colleagues tested an erector spinae plane block for pain control after robotic colorectal surgery, in a 2026 prospective observational study. The block is an injection of local anesthetic along the back muscles. The team compared patients who received the block against a control group receiving standard care.

Seventy patients were followed, 36 in the block group and 34 controls, in a non-randomized design. The block group reported lower pain scores both at rest and when breathing deeply or coughing. They used less opioid medication and pressed the patient-controlled analgesia button less often during the first 72 hours, as the results describe. Hospital stay and time to first mobilization did not differ. The authors call the block a safe and effective part of combined pain management, while asking for larger randomized trials to confirm the effect.
pmc-13399799:
Seksan Kukreja and colleagues describe an anchor-free, all-inside meniscal allograft transplant performed entirely by arthroscopy. Their 2026 technical note targets patients with irreparable meniscus damage, including chronic root tears, complex tears, and prior meniscus removal. Donor meniscus transplant can restore load sharing, but anchor-based fixation adds cost and failure risks.

Standard front and side portals prepare the meniscus-capsule junction, and tibial tunnels anchor the front and back roots. The donor graft is implanted from back to front, with hand-tied meniscus-to-meniscus sutures giving secure fixation and controlled tension without anchors. Minor size mismatch can be adjusted during implantation, and ligament or realignment surgery can proceed at the same time. The paper offers a cheaper, less invasive alternative, pending graft survival data.
pmc-13401299:
Seung-Chai Kim and colleagues report a 2026 study of how an NADC34-like strain of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus infects pregnant sows in late gestation. The strain, from lineage 1A, is tied to severe breeding failures in sow herds, yet its behaviour in pregnancy was poorly understood.

The team compared isolate JBNU-22-N01 with a common NADC30-like strain, PJ73, in pregnant sows. The NADC34-like virus peaked earlier in the blood, caused worse illness in the mothers, and restricted fetal growth more, even though overall fetal viral loads were similar. More of its fetuses fell into high viral burden clusters, hinting at stronger crossing of the placenta. Gene and cytokine profiling at the mother-fetus boundary showed weakened barrier and immune genes but raised interferon-alpha, a muted pattern unlike the stronger antiviral response to PJ73.
pmc-13401599:
Stephan Grebien, Julian Gurs, Roman Schnabel, and Mikhail Korobko report a 2026 physics experiment on hyperloss, a newly named failure mode in quantum networks that distribute squeezed and entangled light. Such networks underpin photonic quantum computing, quantum communication, and gravitational-wave detectors, and light loss is their chief enemy.

Designers usually treat spatial-mode mismatch as simple incoherent loss. The team shows that when modes mix coherently with higher-order modes, the apparent loss can exceed the entire starting squeezing. In a minimal two-node network, an 8 percent mode mismatch turned a measurable squeezing level of just under 6 decibels into an effectively thermal, useless state. Crucially, retuning the relative spatial-mode phases recovered the lost correlations, so hyperloss acts as a practical design constraint rather than a fundamental dead end.
pmc-13401699:
Md. Jubayer Hossain and a team of co-authors surveyed community pharmacists in Bangladesh about antibiotic resistance knowledge and training in a 2026 one-time survey study. Pharmacists are front-line medicine sellers in Bangladesh, and resistance is a grave threat that hits lower-income countries hardest.

A tested self-given questionnaire went to 191 pharmacists. It asked about demographics, knowledge and views about antibiotic use and resistance, and dispensing habits. Only about 8 percent showed adequate knowledge of antibiotic resistance, and 38 percent had training in careful antibiotic use. Training was strongly linked to better attitudes and better habits when handing out drugs, though not to overall knowledge scores. The findings expose a workforce handing out antibiotics daily with thin formal training for the problem.
pmc-13401899:
Gengping Zhu, Cesar Rodriguez-Saona, and David W Crowder tested whether habitat suitability models can forecast how abundant a pest will be, in a 2026 study of the blueberry maggot in New Jersey. Pest numbers vary unevenly across landscapes: poor habitat holds almost none, but suitable habitat can hold anything from a few to a swarm.

Six suitability models were built from satellite-derived environmental data and checked against maggot counts from a four-year field survey, 2009 to 2012. The team also modelled how suitability predicts different quantiles of abundance, not just the average. Only two models, BioClim and random forest, caught the positive wedge-shaped pattern between predicted suitability and observed abundance, where the ceiling of pest numbers rises with suitability while the floor stays low. The study shows most models miss that shape entirely.
pmc-13401999:
Michael Ashley, Stephanie Nagy, and David Kosoy report a 39-year-old woman whose stomach twisted around its link to the liver, a form of gastric volvulus they describe as gastrohepatic. She had been born with gut malrotation and came to the emergency room with nausea and vomiting. Her belly was swollen and tense on examination.

A CT scan showed the swollen stomach sitting in the right upper abdomen and the liver on the left, both out of place. At emergency surgery the twist was complete, and both organs looked dusky from poor blood flow. Once surgeons untwisted the stomach by hand, color and flow returned. The authors stress quick surgery when scans show organs out of place with a blocked, swollen stomach, before tissue dies.
pmc-13402099:
Yuya Oishi and co-authors report three women treated for primary urethral carcinoma, a rare cancer of the urine channel with no agreed standard care. The patients were 45, 65, and 71 years old, with three different cell types: adenocarcinoma, clear cell carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma. Two received cisplatin-based chemotherapy before surgery.

All three had robot-assisted removal of the bladder together with the urethra, plus wider cutting that took part of the front vaginal wall or pelvic fascia. One woman had no cancer left in the removed tissue, one had a local return linked to a positive cut edge, and two stayed free of recurrence. Oishi and the team argue that care must be tailored case by case, pairing drugs around surgery with wide removal for locally advanced disease.
pmc-13402299:
Yolanda Benítez and team took a global view of computer predictions linking genes to rare diseases. Their 2026 survey addresses diagnosis: when known gene-disease links fail, exome and genome sequencing yield hundreds to millions of poorly annotated variants needing ranking. Single prediction tools can hide how unevenly genes are represented across databases.

Using a network method, the team explored functional neighborhoods of known disease genes to predict candidates for over 200 rare and Mendelian diseases. A cross-prediction analysis found 192 genes tied to one disease and 251 genes tied to specific disease classes, feeding a gene-disease specificity score. The score aims to help geneticists prioritize variants for validation, while predicted links still require lab and clinical proof.
pmc-13402599:
Liu and co-authors show, in 2026, how doping copper with aluminum steers carbon dioxide electroreduction toward ethylene, a bulk chemical feedstock. Copper alone makes a messy product spread. Using a framework based on six dopants' orbital traits, they predicted p-orbital metals would hybridize favorably with copper centers. pmc-13409699:

pmc-13417599:

pmc-13421799:

pmc-13422699:

pmc-13423999:

pmc-13424699:
Carla Czilczer, Pierre Sachse, and Stephan F Dahm challenge how mental chronometry measures the ability to imagine movements. The standard approach treats imagining in real time as excellence. Many stray factors stretch or shrink imagined durations, though. The team therefore built a new score on Fitts' law, the rule tying movement difficulty to movement time.

With the stylus, larger deviations from real time actually tracked higher self-rated ability, deepening doubt about the old score.
pmc-13424799:
Hideo Fukuhara leads a fifteen-author comparison of laser ablation against standard resection for bladder cancer that has returned without invading muscle, at Kochi Medical School Hospital. The authors call the gentler method feasible and safe.
pmc-13425899:
Sabrina Brito Añez and coauthors present a 2026 protocol for building a human lung tumor on a chip with hot or cold immune surroundings. The Emulate chip system hosts human lung microvascular endothelial cells together with human lung tumor cells to recreate the tumor microenvironment. pmc-13426399:
Francis Lee and colleagues report a young woman with a mitochondrial disease whose stomach outlet narrowed badly, leaving her unable to eat enough. Mitochondrial diseases are inherited faults in the cell parts that make energy, and they can weaken the gut as well as the brain.

When gentler care failed, surgeons cut the tight stomach muscle through small openings, with a camera check inside the stomach. Her stomach then emptied far better, she regained weight, and she no longer needed vein feeding. Restored in strength, she finished her college degree, and Lee urges doctors to weigh surgery in like cases.
pmc-13426499:

Parkinson's-style injury also loosened the barrier and woke the immune cells up. Both injuries raised the same set of inflammatory signals in the chip. pmc-13426899:
Nery and colleagues review in 2026 how genomics of non-model organisms has changed ideas about molecular evolution. For most of the twentieth century, genetics rested on a few lab species such as fruit flies, roundworms, and mice. Those species were chosen for fast breeding and simple genomes, which may make them evolutionary oddballs. Cheap sequencing and better software have now opened the whole tree of life to study.

The wider view has overturned tidy assumptions. Similar adaptations can evolve through several different routes, not one shared path. Speciation turns out to be patchy across the genome, shaped by structural changes and genes borrowed through hybridisation. Genome size, content, and layout vary far more than model species suggested. Using aquatic mammals as their showcase, the authors show how unusual species expose shared and unique solutions to the same challenges. Evolution's rules, they argue, only emerge from life's full diversity.
pmc-13427099:
Akari Abe and Shogo Shirota describe eye findings in Wernicke encephalopathy in a 2026 French-language clinical image article. Their patient drank about ten standard drinks daily, amounting to 108 grams of alcohol, and ate only one small evening meal, with a history of alcohol use disorder, IgA vasculitis, and hypertension. Horizontal gaze was absent while slight vertical movement remained, and vertical gaze-evoked nystagmus appeared on looking up and down, with truncal ataxia also noted. Thiamine deficiency can present through eye signs before classic confusion, making recognition urgent.
pmc-13427499:
Dorothy S. Peng and coauthors report a measles-like drug rash tied to tirzepatide in a 2026 case study with wider prescribing implications. Tirzepatide is the first dual GLP-1 and GIP agonist. Starters reached about 679,000 among roughly 45 million patients.

pmc-13427799:
Thibault Passeri and colleagues describe, in a 2026 technique paper, a skull-base route to tumors sitting deep beside the brainstem. Lesions in the petroclival region, where the temporal bone meets the sloped bone behind the nose, lie close to vital nerves and vessels. Cadaver dissections and surgical drawings support the written steps. Skull-base surgeons gain a detailed refresher on an approach known to be demanding, including extensions for larger lesions.
pmc-13428099:
Keqin Cao and colleagues engineer, in a 2026 study, a living scaffold to repair bone defects too large to heal alone. In rats, the full combination produced the most new bone by scans and tissue checks at eight weeks, with over 70 percent of the defect area filled. Priming cells before implant, rather than dosing the patient, is the strategy on offer.
pmc-13428499:
Nilson Willamy Bastos de Souza Júnior and colleagues map, in a 2026 scoping review, hands-on breathing therapies used for newborns in intensive care. Newborns, especially those born early, have soft airways that collapse easily and trap mucus. Physiotherapists use touch techniques to clear airways and support breathing. The team screened over 1,200 papers and kept twelve clinical studies of babies in their first month of life.

Techniques studied included chest vibration, tapping, drainage positions, speeding the out-breath, lung squeezing with a hand pump, and muscle synergy methods. Studies mostly reported short-term shifts in heart and breathing measures right after treatment. No consistent rise in pain scores appeared. Nearly all evidence came from single treatment sessions, so lasting benefit and safety stay unproven. The authors call for bigger, better-designed trials in a fragile population where habits vary widely.
pmc-13429899:
Yujing Zhang and a large team build, in a 2026 study, a warning model for liver injury caused by a last-line antibiotic. Tigecycline fights multidrug-resistant infections but can damage the liver. Many candidate factors were winnowed to seven that clinics can see easily.

The seven cover treatment length, other liver-stressing drugs, the admission diagnosis, prior liver problems, drinking history, and dialysis. A gradient boosting model, a strong pattern-finding algorithm, performed best and kept high sensitivity when tested at a separate hospital. The team released it as a web calculator that explains its reasoning. Early flags could move a patient to closer monitoring before injury deepens.
pmc-13430199:
Yuezhen Hong and co-authors clarify, in a 2026 concept analysis, what it means for a family caregiver to be activated. Health systems lean ever harder on relatives to manage complex long-term illness at home. The term caregiver activation has been used loosely across cancer, dementia, child, and chronic care. Four attributes define the concept: care capabilities, care autonomy, care resilience, and confidence in providing care. What comes before includes the patient's dependence, teamwork with clinicians, skill gaps, and caregiver burden. Higher activation linked to better service use, caregiver well-being, and care management. Nurses screening families could use the framework to spot who needs teaching or backup before a crisis lands.
pmc-13432899:
Trinh Phan-Canh and colleagues review Candida auris, a yeast that has become a feared cause of outbreaks in hospitals and care homes worldwide. The yeast spreads well on human skin and survives there, passing from person to person by touch.

Many strains resist all three main drug classes used against fungal infections, leaving some cases with no working treatment. Death rates for invasive infections run between 30 and 60 percent even when antifungal drugs are given. The review covers how the yeast colonises skin, which host and germ traits drive its spread, and why stopping it is hard. Phan-Canh stresses early spotting and strict control measures to keep the yeast from taking hold in wards.
pmc-13433499:
Xinyu Wang and colleagues test whether water content rules how lab-made tissue scaffolds stretch and carry charge. These scaffolds, made by stripping cells from animal tissue, draw interest as green biomaterials, yet test results shift with how they were dried and stored.

Sheep aorta tissue from slaughterhouse offcuts was tested in three states: fresh, stripped and freeze-dried, and stripped then re-wet. Pull tests, stretch-and-hold tests in two directions, and simple charge tests charted the gaps. The team shows that wet versus dry handling can fake a material gap, so labs must lock down water content before they claim one scaffold beats another.
pmc-13433999:
Bingxuan Zhang and Xuan Chen optimise a pulse-coupled neural network for image restoration, upgraded with AI to balance detail recovery, structure preservation, and adaptability. The bio-inspired pulse network extracts time-based pulse features from images, while an AI module tunes coupling strengths and firing thresholds on the fly.

An end-to-end system was built and tested on the DIV2K dataset, with diverse degraded images constructed for comparison. Comparative results favoured the optimised model on image quality, including for urban architectural images, where detail and structure matter most. Imaging teams get a restoration model that adapts its own parameters instead of relying on fixed, hand-tuned settings.
pmc-13434699:
Pamela Wong and a large team delete a gene switch in adult mouse immune cells in 2026 to learn what it still does after growth ends. The switch, T-bet, helps build natural killer cells and kin cells that guard tissues. Timed deletion lets the team split growth roles from upkeep roles.

Mature killer cells thinned in spleen and tissues, while bone marrow and lymph node pools held. Liver and gut guard cells also faded without the switch. Deleting a sister switch as well wiped out killer cells fast. In virus tests the sister switch proved vital, while T-bet was not. Tissue by tissue needs differ sharply.
pmc-13434799:
A Alocco and coauthors weave tangled microwave states on demand in 2026. Cluster states let computers work by measuring, a route that may scale better than gate by gate logic. A traveling wave amplifier made from Josephson parts supplies the wide band needed.

Tailored pump tones set which frequency modes link to which. Detectors tuned by frequency confirm the target web of links. Retuning the pumps redraws the web without new hardware. The wide, even band hints at large webs ahead. Superconducting chips gain a flexible source of tangled states for measurement based work.
pmc-13435199:
Vivien Hoof and Julia Schulze-Hentrich reviewed single-cell gene studies in Parkinson disease in 2026, with attention to sex differences. Parkinson disease slowly kills dopamine-producing neurons and involves clumped, misfolded protein. Older bulk sequencing averaged signals across many cells and hid brain cell diversity, while single-cell methods can now separate rare and distinct cell types.

Findings surveyed cover which neurons prove most vulnerable and how support cells, especially microglia and an insulating cell type, contribute to disease in human tissue and in models. Early evidence for different molecular changes in men and women is discussed. The authors urge future single-cell studies to plan for sex from the start.
pmc-13436499:
Simon Röder and coauthors read tree rings to learn why some beech trees bounced back from the 1976 drought in 2026. Wood from a managed stand in central Germany holds both growth and plumbing records. Wide vessels move water fast but risk collapse under drought strain.

Trees with safer, narrower plumbing before the drought recovered best afterward. Fast prior growth did not predict strong recovery. Cautious wood thus beats speedy wood when extreme drought hits. Recent beech die offs across Europe give the old rings fresh weight. Breeding and thinning choices may favor safer plumbing as droughts thicken.
pmc-13437199:
Bhakta and colleagues wrote in 2026 to question a trial that found cheek acupuncture eased sore throat after thoracic surgery with a double-lumen breathing tube. Sore throat is a common, short-lived complaint after such tubes. The letter writers accept the trial's care but raise three points they say cloud its meaning.

First, the trial never measured the air pressure in the tube's cuffs, a known driver of sore throat, so it is unclear whether pressures stayed in the safe range. Second, the cheek point used is not the point best proven against nausea, yet nausea also fell sharply, a result at odds with pooled evidence. Third, after full adjustment the throat benefit lasted only the first half hour. The authors ask whether a needle procedure is justified for so brief a discomfort.
pmc-13437699:
Su Zou and Lisheng Liu studied what protects English-major students in China from anxiety about finding a job. Graduating into a tight market leaves many students tense about whether their skills fit employer needs. Their 2026 survey drew 916 students of English as a foreign language through an online questionnaire. It measured career adaptability, confidence in job hunting, proactive personality, and employment anxiety, then modeled how they connect.

Students with stronger adaptability felt less employment anxiety. Part of that calm ran through confidence: adaptable students trusted their search skills more, and that trust carried about a third of the total effect. A proactive streak sharpened the whole chain, drawing more protection from the same adaptability and confidence. The authors point advisors toward building real adaptability and search confidence rather than offering comfort alone. Career courses, they argue, can train both, and proactive students may gain the quickest return.
pmc-13438199:
Alexandra Anagnostopoulou and a large team asked whether a calm brain rhythm explains how mental reserve protects word skills in sclerosis. People with richer education and mental habits, called cognitive reserve, often keep sharper thinking despite disease. Their 2026 study recorded resting brain waves in sixty-four patients and forty-six healthy volunteers, measured reserve by questionnaire, and tested two kinds of verbal fluency.

Patients showed weaker upper alpha power than controls. That rhythm carried the statistical path from reserve to performance: patients with higher reserve kept alpha activity closer to healthy levels, tracking with better fluency at naming words by meaning. Word naming by letter showed no such chain, and healthy volunteers none either. Disease burden did not formally change the pattern. The authors propose the rhythm as a candidate mechanism of resilience, and a possible target for training or stimulation to keep language quick in this disease.
pmc-13438699:
Huibin Lv and a large team pulled three antibodies from a human antibody library that attack the conserved stem of the flu virus's spike, a spot that barely changes between strains. pmc-13439299:
Hong and Baek wrote an editorial in 2026 asking whether online teaching can raise the quality of cold snare polypectomy, the standard way to remove small bowel polyps during colonoscopy. Small polyps can still hide advanced features, so complete removal matters. The authors argue removal skill is hands-on: margin control, snare position, and a steady close-and-cut motion need guided practice and personal feedback, not lectures alone.
pmc-13439699:

The authors warn that tiny design details in transgenic parts demand hard validation before field use.
pmc-13440099:

pmc-13442799:

pmc-13443099:

pmc-13443399:

Mouse grafts backed the cell tale, so the authors pitch the compound as a targeted lead.
pmc-13443799:

pmc-13443899:

pmc-13445599:

pmc-13445999:

pmc-13446099:

pmc-13446199:

Long disease showed deeper change, with wear markers up across all three types. pmc-13446299:

pmc-13446999:

pmc-13447099:

pmc-13447499:

pmc-13448199:

pmc-13448499:

pmc-13449099:

pmc-13449699:

pmc-13449799:
