pmc-13449999:
Jiao Xue, Xiaodong Wang, and Yi Qiu rank in 2026 twenty strategies for protecting the brain after heart surgery, where delirium and lingering cognitive dysfunction strike many patients. Their Bayesian network meta-analysis wove together 46 randomized trials covering 9,928 patients, spanning anesthetic drugs, add-on medications, and non-drug measures such as cognitive training. Most trials carried low risk of bias, and the network let strategies that never met directly still be compared through shared opponents.

For delirium prevention, intranasal insulin, the herbal compound gastrodin, and cognitive training ranked most effective. For later cognitive dysfunction, gastrodin again led, joined by esketamine and dexmedetomidine. Rankings built on memory test score changes were thinner and treated as exploratory. The authors caution that several top finishers rest on few trials, so the league table is a map for confirmatory research rather than a verdict, and they call for larger head-to-head trials.
pmc-13450399:
Karsten Kaiser and colleagues ran the first randomised trial of dexamethasone in robot-assisted womb removal in 2026, testing whether the steroid eases surgical stress. Dexamethasone suppresses immune responses and may cut infection, adhesions, and slow healing by damping inflammation. The team used C-reactive protein, a blood marker of stress, as the main outcome.

Women scheduled for robotic hysterectomy were assigned at random to a single preoperative dose of 24 milligrams of dexamethasone or placebo. Blood tests, pain scores, nausea and vomiting, and drug use were recorded up to twenty-four hours after surgery. Among 112 women, protein levels were lower in the steroid group at twelve and twenty-four hours, and sickness and vomiting over time also fell. Surgeons gain evidence for a single-dose adjunct to smooth recovery.
pmc-13450499:
Katja Wingenfeld and Eugenia Kulakova review in 2026 what hair tests show about testosterone in borderline personality disorder, a long-term pattern of unstable mood and strained ties with others. Hair holds months of hormone output, so it suits study of a lasting illness. The review pulls together the pair's own past work and studies by other groups.

Across that work, women with the disorder showed hair cortisol in the normal range yet higher hair testosterone than comparison groups. Higher levels tracked with heavier inner symptoms, such as low mood, and with more giving social acts. The authors say the hormone may shape how care is planned, and they call for more work on how it acts in the brain.
pmc-13451299:
Kevin Yang and co-authors run a 2026 pilot trial of gym memberships as a well-being aid for psychiatry trainees. Trainee doctors face high rates of low mood, worry, burnout, and loneliness, yet few tested aids exist. Twenty-eight trainees were split by lot into a group given sixteen weeks of a flexible class-booking pass, or a wait-list group.

Use was high, most passes were spent, and every user backed wider rollout. Worry scores fell by a clear margin in the pass group, while shifts in low mood and loneliness fell just short of firm proof. Burnout did not move. Trainees praised the choice and flex of the pass, plus the social ties it built.
pmc-13451499:
Bernhard Wortmann, Detlef Stolten, and Heidi Heinrichs warn that green hydrogen expansion could collide with the tiny global supply of iridium, in a two thousand twenty-six energy analysis. Proton exchange membrane electrolyzers rely on iridium oxide anodes, and iridium is only a by-product of platinum mining.

Annual production runs near seven and a half tons. Modeling deployment scenarios against catalyst improvements, the authors find net-zero pathways would consume roughly thirty percent of annual production. Shortages could bite as early as two thousand thirty, sooner than previously expected, and demand beyond twenty forty looks significantly underestimated. They urge efficiency innovation, recycling, and resource-aware energy policy.
pmc-13451799:
Jakub Prokop and co-authors rebuild in 2026 the chest of a fossil winged insect to trace how flight gear evolved. The insect, Eubleptus danielsi, comes from the famed Mazon Creek beds in Illinois and lived in the Carboniferous age. Its side chest wall, a part key to wing power, had never been laid bare in such a fossil.

A 3D model of the fossil set its chest traits against a wide range of living insects. The side wall pattern looked less like that of dragonflies or mayflies and more like that of the large modern winged group. The authors suggest the fossil keeps a pattern close to the shared ancestor of all winged insects.
pmc-13451899:
Zhengang Li, Hepeng Zhang, and Daming Dong build in 2026 a device that reads how air particles soak up and scatter light, at two colors at once. Split devices can drift out of step, since the air in each part differs. Their build joins two spheres that catch scattered light and buffer sound, linked by a tube that rings at a set pitch.

Two lasers, blue-green and green, blink at set rates while a chip lock-in reads both channels from one shared air path. Test gases set the scales for each channel. Mist, burn smoke, and outdoor runs checked that the channels stay apart and work in the field. The aim is cleaner climate data on air particles.
pmc-13452099:
Anna-Luisa Kranhold and co-authors study in 2026 how peer bullying ties to mental illness in young therapy patients in Germany. Most past work drew on the general public, not clinic groups with firm labels. The study held 719 outpatients aged six to twenty at one center, with gold-grade checks of their disorders.

Near three in ten patients were caught up in bullying, most as victims, and a third often had painful bullying-linked thoughts that broke in unbidden. Victims leaned toward mood disorders, while those who both gave and got bullying leaned toward acting-out disorders. The authors argue that therapy intake should ask about bullying roles as a matter of course.
pmc-13452299:
Kloosterman and colleagues review in 2026 the role of LR11, also called SorLA, a sorting receptor from the LDL receptor family, in cardiovascular disease. First found in the brain and tied to Alzheimer's disease, the protein also circulates in a shed form, sLR11. Its blood levels rise with vascular injury and with risk factors such as obesity and diabetes.

The review explains how LR11 helps drive vessel wall remodeling, the process that thickens arteries and feeds atherosclerosis. The shed form is not just a bystander marker: it appears to take part in the remodeling itself. The authors discuss how sLR11 could serve as a blood biomarker for vascular damage and risk. They also weigh whether blocking the pathway could become a treatment strategy for heart and vessel disease.
pmc-13453499:
Yuntao Li and ten co-authors build a smart gel that both slicks and treats arthritic joints in rheumatoid arthritis. The disease swells the joint lining, floods it with harmful oxygen species, and grinds down cartilage. Their 2026 gel carries a fat based molecule called 9,10-DiOH, picked out by chemical profiling of joint tissue.

Lab and gene studies show the molecule triggers cuproptosis, a copper driven cell death, in the overgrown joint lining cells. That death quiets two swelling pathways and slows the cells that eat bone. The gel itself releases its load in response to heat, acidity, and oxygen stress, and its fat chains coat the joint surface to cut friction. In mice with arthritis, the gel eased swelling, curbed bone erosion, and kept joint shape.
pmc-13453599:
Opeoluwa Rotimi Dada, Dawit Beza Alemu, and Bolanle Deborah Ikotun publish a dataset and tuning method for a fiber rich concrete used in hard wearing structures. The mix, called SIFCON, pours slurry into a dense bed of fibers; here the fibers are sisal, a plant fiber, and part of the binder is ash from coffee husks. Their 2026 paper reports tests on 10 mixes and 960 data points in all.

Tests covered crushing, bending, and pulling strength plus durability checks, run on a standard testing machine. A response surface method, a math tool for finding sweet spots, then mapped how the two added materials shift each property. The best range came out at 1 to 1.5 percent sisal fiber and 10 to 15 percent coffee husk ash. The authors offer the set as a base for greener concrete design and for prediction models.
pmc-13453999:
Elena Buso and others set dog-watch methods side by side in shelters in 2026, to see how watch choice skews enrichment calls. Shelter dogs live cramped lives with poor welfare, so true counts of conduct matter. Full watch was set next to snap watches at fifteen, thirty, and sixty seconds past enrichment.

Snap watches missed conduct counts next to full watch, with misses growing from fifteen to sixty seconds. With full watch as the gold mark, dog-to-dog play and food-smell treats were tried, and idle lying rose after dog play in the write-up. Dog researchers gain a warning: watch gaps can warp welfare calls.
pmc-13454799: Karolina Krzywiecka and five colleagues published a 2026 correction to their review of fetal bladder rupture in babies with blocked urinary valves. The notice is a correction only, restoring two labels that were dropped from the methods section by mistake. With the labels back, the review's population and comparator lines read as intended, making clear that it rests on case reports without a control group. No findings or conclusions of the review change.
pmc-13454999:
Weigang Luo and six colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether bright spots on brain scans explain the link between poor nutrition and dulled thinking in small vessel disease. Both undernutrition and white matter hyperintensities, the bright spots, predict cognitive trouble in this condition. The team reviewed 383 patients, scoring nutrition with a standard index and thinking with a common test.

Scans were measured automatically, region by region. Patients with impaired thinking ate worse by the index and carried larger bright spot volumes everywhere measured. Higher nutrition scores paired with higher thinking scores, while larger spot volumes paired with lower ones. A mediation check found the spot volume carried about 71 percent of the nutrition effect on thinking. The authors suggest that feeding support might protect cognition partly by slowing this white matter damage.
pmc-13455199:
Manali Patel and others studied prior incarceration and dental spending among older Americans in 2026, using Health and Retirement Study data. Prior research links incarceration history to poorer oral health and lower dental use, but whether out-of-pocket dental spending differs by incarceration history was untested. The team used pooled 2012 and 2014 waves covering 11,438 respondents aged fifty-five and older.

A two-part model first estimated the likelihood of any out-of-pocket dental spending, then estimated spending amounts among those with positive costs, adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, health, and dental factors. About 6.8 percent of the sample reported prior incarceration. The analysis tests whether incarceration history predicts both the chance of spending and the amount spent, informing policies on oral health equity for formerly incarcerated older adults.
pmc-13455399:
Pengfei Li and colleagues find denture use tied to gallstone risk in a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study. Gallstones affect about 6 percent of people worldwide and strain hospitals, yet modifiable risks beyond diet and genes remain sought. The team followed 446,743 adults free of gallstones at baseline for a median of 13.69 years, recording denture use by questionnaire and new gallstone cases from hospital records, with genetic risk scores and mediation checks.

Denture users faced a 29 percent higher gallstone risk after full adjustment. Risk rose to 57 percent higher among users with high genetic risk, though genes and dentures did not multiply each other's effect. Body weight explained 12.96 percent of the link, while diet explained under 1 percent, and a genetic analysis backed a possible causal role. The finding points to oral health checks as one more, unexpected part of gallstone prevention.
pmc-13455499:
Farah Kalagi and six colleagues review, in a 2026 multicenter study, real-world use of GLP-1 drugs in teenagers with obesity in Saudi Arabia. Trial data in this age group remain thin, so the team read medical records from several centers for patients aged 12 to 18 treated between 2021 and 2024. Eighty-one adolescents qualified.

Weight and body mass scores fell modestly during treatment, with median losses between two and seven percent depending on the drug used. No drug beat the others clearly. Side effects were rarely charted and were mostly gut complaints when noted. Specialists wrote most prescriptions. Treatment often stopped early, with a median span of four months, and dose increases were documented in only about a third of cases. Nine percent were referred for weight surgery. The authors call for steadier protocols to get more from these medicines.
pmc-13456399:
Katherine A. Lubina leads a seventeen-author study, from 2026, of forever chemicals in the blood of United States volunteer firefighters. Volunteers form about 65 percent of the fire service, yet their exposure profiles were barely charted. Blood samples from 550 active volunteers across nine states were tested for twelve PFAS compounds between 2020 and 2023.

Levels varied by region, age, and sex. Surprisingly, everyday factors such as demographics and health outweighed fire service duties as predictors of blood levels. Some links differed between men and women under fifty, suggesting distinct routes in and out of the body. The authors read the pattern as a sign that community exposure, through water, food, and consumer goods, rivals the fireground for this workforce. Their findings argue for exposure studies that follow volunteers home, not only to the station.
pmc-13457099:
Mehmet Emin Yelken and six colleagues test, in a 2026 trial, whether adding brain-body coordination drills to ski training changes stress and immune markers in teenage skiers. Twenty under-14 female cross-country skiers were split into two groups of ten. One skied as usual, forty-five minutes three times a week. The other added Life Kinetics exercises, which pair movement with mental tasks, for the same eight weeks.

Saliva was sampled before and after. Cortisol, the classic stress hormone, did not budge in either group. A second enzyme, alpha-amylase, differed between groups overall without a clear time pattern. The clearest signal was immune: a protective antibody in saliva rose in the drill group and fell in controls over the program. The authors judge the added training gentle on stress systems, while urging bigger, longer studies before claiming immune benefit.
pmc-13457499:
Shakeri and colleagues in Iran reviewed in 2026 math models that read PET scans of glioma, a grave brain tumor. After care, scans blur: regrowth and care scars look much the same. The review weighed models that mine scan traits by the score, against plain scan marks. Four banks of past work fed the search.

Trait mining models beat plain marks at both jobs: tell scar from regrowth, and call the path ahead. A blend did best of all, traits plus plain marks in one model. Plain marks alone, like peak tumor to brain ratios, lagged. The authors say such models can shape care per patient. Worth may show in longer life and better days.
pmc-13458299:
Alexander Thomas Brunfeldt and colleagues describe a trainee-run virtual symposium series built inside the American translational science training network. The William Schnaper Visiting Scientist Mini-Symposium lets predoctoral and postdoctoral trainees present research, practice communication, and meet peers across institutions without travel budgets. Their 2026 report covers seven symposia held from 2021 to 2025 under the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences.

Sixty-two trainees presented, drawn from 28 CTSA hubs in 21 states, and about four in five were predoctoral. Talks split across basic science at 34 percent, clinical research at 52 percent, and implementation or public health at 13 percent. Every surveyed presenter called the experience valuable for professional development, roughly half gained useful feedback and new contacts, and 78 percent of attendees rated it a valuable learning experience. The authors offer the format as a cheap, scalable, sustainable model any distributed training program can copy.
pmc-13458499:
Ran Ji and colleagues build a prognostic score for clear cell kidney cancer out of an unlikely cell type: the mast cell. Mast cells cluster in tumors and leak vessel-growing factors, yet their angiogenic signature here was unmapped. Their 2026 study merges single-cell and bulk gene data, trains ten machine learning algorithms, and validates the winners by PCR.

Inside tumors, mast cells ran hot TNF-alpha signaling and conversed with neighbors through pairs such as SPP1-CD44 and CLEC2C-KLRB1, sculpting an immune-suppressed neighborhood. The score separated patients by outlook with satisfactory accuracy. High-risk tumors switched on JAK-STAT3 and other pathways, carried genomic instability, and excluded immunity. Two genes anchored the story: TIMP1, a driver against which herbimycin A docked in screening, and EMCN, a protective counterweight. The authors propose the score and its two poles as prognostic tools and drug targets.
pmc-13459099:
Nancy D. Calzada and colleagues pooled in 2026 what is known about high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy and later asthma in the children born from those pregnancies. The disorders covered include preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, and eclampsia. Searching four databases through December 2024, the team gathered twenty observational studies covering more than three million mother and infant pairs.

Children whose mothers had such a disorder faced a modestly higher asthma risk overall, with pooled odds about 14 percent above comparison groups. Preeclampsia and gestational hypertension each showed a similar rise when examined alone, though results varied widely between studies for gestational hypertension. The link with wheezing fell short of significance. The authors call for closer early monitoring of these children and more work on why the association exists.
pmc-13459199:
Kety Suelyn Ferreira and colleagues trace how birth conditions and social context shape early motor skills in a 2026 study. Motor development in the first five years predicts learning and participation, yet biological and social risks interact in ways single-factor studies miss. The team assessed 626 preterm and full-term children aged 0 to 5 with the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales. It compared gestational age, birth weight, body length, income, schooling and urban versus rural residence.

Most children, 77.8 percent, scored average, while 17.7 percent scored below average. Full-term children outscored preterm children on total motor and grasping measures. Low birth weight children lagged on object manipulation, higher-income children scored better on gross motor and balance, school attenders scored higher overall, and urban children outscored rural children on most subscales. Early screening plus health, education and community support emerges as the equity response.
pmc-13459799:
Cheikh Ibrahima Lo and colleagues announce in 2026 draft genome sequences for 22 Shigella isolates taken from patients with diarrhea in Senegal. Shigella species cause bacillary dysentery and remain a heavy burden in lower-income countries, yet genomic data from West Africa are scarce. The isolates, collected at sentinel surveillance sites during 2020 and 2021, include the sonnei, flexneri, and boydii species.

Genome sizes ran from a little over four million to about five and a half million DNA letters, with similar base composition across isolates. The authors position the collection as a resource for tracking how Shigella lineages spread in the region and which drug resistance traits they carry. Such surveillance can guide treatment choices where resistance is rising.
pmc-13459899:
René Schroedter and colleagues relate knee size to kneecap instability risk factors in growing children in a 2026 MRI study. Chronological age poorly reflects skeletal maturity, so anatomy linked to kneecap dislocation may be better judged against knee size. The retrospective case-control study analysed 630 knee MRIs from skeletally immature patients, half with first-time non-traumatic lateral kneecap dislocation and half matched controls, mean age 14.5 years.

Dislocated knees showed shallower trochlear grooves, greater tilt and lateralisation, and higher patellar height than controls across nearly every measure. Several parameters, including trochlear depth, patellar inclination and the Caton-Deschamps index, shifted significantly with increasing femoral width. Radiologists and surgeons gain a reason to normalise patellofemoral measurements to knee size when judging instability during growth.
pmc-13461799:
Junyang Li and colleagues compare, in a 2026 records review, two keyhole operations for a slipped disc at one level of the lower back. A herniated disc can press on nerves and cause leg and back pain. One method works through two portals. The other passes through a natural side opening. Both remove the disc material pressing on the nerve. The review covered patients treated at one facility in one period.

122 patients were included, 69 with the two-portal method and 53 with the side-route method. Pain scores for leg and back were alike before surgery, the day after, and at follow-up. Daily function scores improved greatly in both groups, and satisfaction sat near 95 percent in each. Scan results matched closely. The two-portal group lost more blood and stayed longer, yet needed far fewer X-ray exposures. The authors rate both as safe and effective.
pmc-13463699:
Berenice M. Román-Calleja, Bryan Adrian Priego-Parra, and Carlos Fernando Martínez-Cabrera introduce a research collection on tailored diets for fatty liver disease tied to metabolic faults. The disease affects nearly a third of adults worldwide, and diet change stays its main treatment. Yet patients respond to the same diet in very different ways.

The editors argue for precision nutrition, which shapes meals around body makeup, blood markers, genes, gut microbes, culture, and daily habits. Papers in the collection cover patient assessment, personal meal plans, and checks of liver and wider health gains. The piece gives clinicians a map for moving from one-size advice to care fitted to each patient.
pmc-13463799:
Robert J Samuel and seven co-authors compare how trials pair radiation with immune therapy for anal cancer. Standard chemoradiation cures most patients, yet about a quarter to a third of those with advanced local disease relapse. New pairings are now in trials, each built in its own way.

Searching three trial databases, the team found twelve trials, with early results from three covering sixty-nine patients. Fourteen immune regimens appeared, given before, during, or after radiation, with wide gaps in patient choice, chemo plans, and study math. No trial used a biomarker to pick patients. The authors urge a shared core of lab tests so future trials can be compared fairly.
pmc-13464299:
Electra Brunialti and colleagues mapped immune signalling in 2026 across the whole mouse body after mRNA vaccination, using reporter mice that glow with inflammation or calm. Vaccine design still leans on trial and error because immune events unfold across many organs at once. The team built a new STAT6 reporter mouse for anti-inflammatory signals and paired it with an existing NF-kB reporter for pro-inflammatory signals.

Two lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines, one with plain RNA and one with modified RNA, drove distinct signal maps over time and space. The liver emerged early as a hub for both signal types after systemic dosing. Early STAT6 activity that faded fast tracked with stronger antibody responses, offering a rapid screen for ranking vaccine designs before long trials.
pmc-13464699:
Soha Abdulrahman Alonaizan and four co-authors grade pre-test handling in a Riyadh biochemistry lab across 2024. Most lab errors happen before the analyzer ever runs, during drawing, labeling, and transport. The team sorted every rejected test into seven quality classes and scored each with Six Sigma tools.

Of more than eight hundred forty-five thousand tests, about one in seventy-eight came back rejected. Broken red cells, called hemolysis, caused three quarters of all rejections on its own. Wrong tube choice added a second slice, and together the two faults drove over four fifths of waste. Root cause work blamed draw technique, needle choice, workload, and long tourniquet time, so training heads the fix list.
pmc-13466299:
Chenyuan Qi and colleagues hunt the main poison inside custard apple seeds, which serve in folk medicine and food despite an unclear safety record, in a 2026 study. Guided by toxicity tests in zebrafish larvae, they separated seed extracts step by step until one compound carried the effect. That compound, squamocin, belongs to the acetogenin family and had not been named an acute seed toxicant before.

Squamocin harmed larvae at extremely low doses, causing death, malformed development, and misshapen face cartilage without much growth stunting. Movement faltered at low doses and coordination failed at slightly higher ones. Chemical and gene readouts showed disturbed amino acid and sugar handling plus stress-gene changes in exposed larvae.
pmc-13466399:
Ristori and colleagues pilot a culture-free blood test for sepsis against the century-old standard. Their 2026 study compares digital PCR performed directly on whole blood with paired blood cultures in 37 samples from 27 patients with suspected bloodstream infection at a hospital. Cultures are slow and miss organisms, especially after antibiotics have started, so a rapid molecular alternative has obvious appeal.

The digital method found a broader range, 34 pathogen species against the culture's 28, with better pickup of fastidious organisms and fungi such as Candida. Against culture as reference it scored 75 percent sensitivity and about 54 percent specificity, a moderate rule-in tool but a weak rule-out one. Many extra positive results looked clinically plausible on chart review, suggesting real infections the culture missed, particularly mixed infections and cases under antibiotic pressure. The authors frame the test as a rapid complement, not a replacement.
pmc-13466499:
Çelebi and co-authors varied the work-to-rest rhythm of mock taekwondo fights in 2026 to see what it costs elite athletes. Twenty male fighters each fought three ways in random order: free-paced combat, bursts with half the rest, and bursts with double the rest. Blood lactate, heart rate, jump height, effort ratings, and muscle soreness were tracked around each bout.

The rhythm mattered for one thing most: lactate, the burn marker of hard anaerobic work. The burst-heavy format produced the highest lactate, free combat came next, and the rest-heavy format the lowest. Jump height dropped after every format, showing leg fatigue regardless of rhythm. Heart rate, effort ratings, and soreness did not differ between formats. The authors conclude rest spacing tunes metabolic stress specifically. General combat fatigue seems set by the sport's stop-start nature itself, at least in highly trained fighters.
pmc-13467499:
Laura Herkner and colleagues test in 2026 how well automated planning software chooses pedicle screw sizes for spine surgery, compared with what surgeons actually implant. The software proposes screw paths and sizes, but matching a plan on average is not the same as agreeing case by case. The study drew on 103 consecutive patients who had thoracic or lumbar spine fixation at one center between January 2021 and January 2024, giving 351 paired screw records.

Screw diameter from the software correlated moderately with the implanted diameter, with a correlation value of 0.635 across the records. Screw length showed a similar moderate link. The authors also checked whether the type of spinal disease or uneven left-right planning changed the agreement, and they tracked available safety outcomes. The findings help surgical teams judge where automated starting plans can be trusted and where surgeon judgment still rules.
pmc-13467699:
Erol Imren and co-authors use machine learning in 2026 to tune a biodegradable plastic strengthened with lignin nanoparticles. The base plastic, polylactic acid, was melt-mixed with lignin pulled from black pine using a deep eutectic solvent, plus a coupling agent, then molded into test pieces. Strength was measured in pulling and bending tests, and fracture surfaces were examined under a scanning electron microscope.

Plain polylactic acid was strongest in tension, at 61 megapascals. Small lignin additions slightly lowered tensile results but raised bending strength to about 58 megapascals, and microscope images showed the particles spread evenly without cracks. Two learning models, Random Forest and XGBoost, were trained to predict strength from the recipe, so future mixes can be optimized on a computer before anyone melts plastic. The approach blends green materials with data-driven design.
pmc-13468199:
Yiyao Gong and co-authors test in 2026 whether ginsenoside Rg1, an active compound from ginseng, can protect the brain against lead harm. Chronic lead exposure damages the hippocampus and thinking, partly through ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. The team used lead-exposed mice and a lead-exposed brain cell line, checking behavior, tissue damage, inflammation, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis markers together.

Rg1 improved cognitive performance and reduced hippocampal neuron loss, inflammatory activation, and oxidative injury. Iron accumulation and mitochondrial damage linked to ferroptosis also eased. The compound restored two protective proteins, SLC7A11 and GPX4, and strengthened the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway; blocking Nrf2 with an inhibitor weakened the protection, tying the benefit to that pathway. The work puts forward a ginseng compound as a possible defense against an environmental toxin that still harms many communities.
pmc-13468599:
Yafei Li and co-authors screen in 2026 sixty local melon varieties from Xinjiang for drought tolerance at the germination stage, the moment a dryland crop either starts or fails. Seeds were germinated in polyethylene glycol solutions of four strengths, a standard stand-in for dry soil. The team measured germination, rootlet growth, osmotic adjustment substances, and antioxidant enzyme activity.

Drought simulation suppressed germination overall, and every germination index trended downward as the solution strengthened, though moderate stress oddly stimulated rootlet growth in some varieties. The spread of responses at each strength let the authors rank the sixty accessions and build toward a prediction model for rapid screening. Xinjiang melon farming is throttled by water scarcity, so identifying seed lots that sprout under drought is the cheapest drought adaptation there is: it costs a seed test, not an irrigation scheme.
pmc-13468799:
Jiawei Fu, Guanhua Xu, Jiajia Chen and Zhiming Cui published this 2026 study predicting who suffers a new vertebral fracture after cement procedures for osteoporotic spinal fractures. Vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty inject bone cement to stabilise a crushed vertebra, but some patients fracture again. Reviewing 107 patients treated between May 2023 and May 2024, the team compared those who refractured with those who did not, across bone density, blood markers of bone turnover and surgical details. They built a prediction nomogram.

Six factors predicted a second fracture: older age, more vertebrae treated, cement leaking, higher levels of the bone-formation marker PINP, lower vitamin D, and lower bone mineral density. The nomogram built from these six discriminated almost perfectly in validation, with an area under the curve of 0.975, and predicted risk matched actual risk well. The authors recommend using the score to flag high-risk patients for closer monitoring and preventive treatment after their procedure.
pmc-13468899:
Povilas Kavaliauskas and colleagues report a laboratory and animal study, published in 2026. It tests a natural mineral used in animal feed. The question is whether it blunts gut inflammation from bacterial endotoxin. The mineral is clinoptilolite zeolite. It soaks up substances strongly. The team asked whether it lowers the activity of lipopolysaccharide. This toxin triggers immune responses.

In immune and gut cell models, the mineral helped. It reduced inflammatory signalling. Nitric oxide output fell. Selected inflammatory messengers fell too. Pre-mixing it with the toxin lowered the toxin's effect. This suggests simple binding. Rats fed the mineral for weeks showed no damage. Doses went up to a set level. Blood and organs stayed normal. This supports its safety as a feed material.
pmc-13469899:
Reham Bassem Ibraheem and colleagues compare in 2026 heart health and blood fats between garment workers in Egypt who face loud factory noise and those who do not. Noise on the job is common, yet its link to heart and vessel disease has stayed unsettled. The study enrolled two equal groups of about two hundred workers each at a denim plant in Ismailia. The groups were split by at least three years of exposure above or below a standard noise threshold.

Noise was measured with room meters and personal devices, and workers gave interviews, exams, heart tracings, and blood tests. The exposed group showed higher pulse pressure and systolic blood pressure, plus higher cholesterol and triglyceride readings. Abnormal lipid profiles were more common among them, affecting about six in ten workers. Heart tracing problems also appeared more often in the exposed group.
pmc-13470199:
Shi Chen and co-authors uncover in 2026 a chemical tagging route by which radiation teaches tumors to resist further radiation. Radiotherapy reshapes sugar metabolism in cancer cells, and the resulting lactate buildup is tied to treatment resistance. The team traced the chain to an enzyme called GCN5, which adds a crotonyl tag to a metabolic protein named ACAT1 at one specific site.

The tag boosts ACAT1 activity, which in turn marks and switches off a key enzyme for burning pyruvate. Sugar breakdown then stalls into lactate production. A mutant version of ACAT1 that cannot receive the tag made cells more sensitive to radiation and cut lactate output sharply. The authors propose blocking that single tagging site as a way to restore tumor sensitivity during radiotherapy.
pmc-13470499:
Egbase and a large team showed in 2026 that blocking an enzyme called NAMPT shields insulin-making beta cells from autoimmune attack. The enzyme raises levels of NAD, a core metabolic molecule, and the team suspected excess NAD fuels islet inflammation killing beta cells. They tested a blocker on mouse and human islets bathed in inflammatory signals, and a mouse diabetes model received it for 16 days.

Protection was broad: in isolated islets, the blocker preserved insulin release and prevented cell death under cytokine attack. Gene profiling showed it silenced inflammatory and cell-recruitment programs, and in diabetic mice treatment improved blood sugar control and beta-cell survival. Immune invaders inside islets thinned out, and killer T cells lost their ability to migrate into islets in dish tests. The authors float NAMPT blocking as a therapy candidate, and caution that NAD-boosting supplements deserve scrutiny in people at risk of this disease.
pmc-13470699:
Abd Rahman and co-authors strengthen a plant-fibre absorbent so it survives getting wet. Their 2026 paper works with kapok, a hollow natural fibre, formed into handsheet absorbents for wet environments. Paper-like materials usually collapse when soaked. pmc-13508799:

pmc-13513199:

pmc-13520899:

pmc-13531199:

pmc-13534199:

pmc-13534399:
Jagdish Prasad Meena and colleagues set out in 2026 a trial plan testing bevacizumab added to standard first-phase chemotherapy for children with high-risk neuroblastoma. pmc-13534499:

pmc-13534699:

pmc-13535899:

pmc-13536799:

pmc-13538499:

pmc-13538999:

pmc-13540699:

pmc-13540899:

pmc-13541599:

pmc-13541899:

pmc-13542099:
Kamla Imtiaz and colleagues model heat flow in a 2026 study. The fluid is a Bingham fluid. Such a fluid stays put until pushed past a threshold force. It then flows past a heated wedge. Nanoparticles are stirred into the flow. The field is applied mathematics, with industry in mind.

They also reacted most sharply to setting changes. Higher yield stress raised surface drag.
pmc-13542699:
Hamna Danyal Barry and colleagues present a blocked eye vein in a young woman that pointed beyond the eye, in this case report from twenty twenty-six. pmc-13543499:

pmc-13544699:

pmc-13545199:

pmc-13545799:

pmc-13545999:
Hongying Cai and six co-authors profiled fat tissue chemistry in mice made obese by a rich diet, in a study from twenty twenty-six. pmc-13546599:

pmc-13546799:

pmc-13547199:

pmc-13547899:

pmc-13548599:

The work points past treatment alone toward lasting activity habits.
pmc-13548999:

pmc-13549299:

pmc-13549599:

pmc-13549699:

pmc-13550399:

pmc-13550499:

pmc-13550599:

pmc-13551299:

pmc-13551699:

pmc-13551799:

pmc-13552299:

pmc-13554899:

pmc-13555999:

pmc-13558599:

pmc-13560299:

pmc-13561299:

pmc-13562499:

pmc-13562699:

pmc-13563899:

pmc-13568199:

pmc-13568699: Bassem Hassan reflects on a fruit fly study showing that what each fly learns reshapes how alike its behavior is to others, in a short piece from two thousand twenty-six. pmc-13569799:
