No serious side effects were blamed on the drug, and the one death in the program was judged unrelated. Virus DNA fell over time but could still be detected past day twenty-eight in some patients. With no comparison group, the authors cannot tell drug effect from the illness fading on its own.
pmc-13616399:
Hyeonjin Park and colleagues cook ultrabright carbon dots, tiny glowing particles, without any solvent, and reach near-perfect light efficiency for use in light-emitting diodes. Making these dots in liquid usually tangles the recipe, since the solvent interacts with the starting material and leaves a messy, uneven product. Their solvent-free route starts from a single compound that melts and shields its own growing cores from oxygen at first.

As the melt thins, oxygen reaches the surface and caps it in a controlled way, sealing defects that would waste light. Energy absorbed in the core then funnels to the bright surface. Careful heat studies and modelling traced this two-stage birth. A simple, dry recipe for dots this bright could cut cost and waste in display and lighting manufacture.
pmc-13616499:
Sangho Hyun and colleagues analyse in 2026 early readmissions after left atrial appendage closure. This catheter procedure seals a stroke-prone heart pouch. They compare patients sent home the same day with those kept overnight. Their records come from a national United States readmissions database covering 2016 to 2020, limited to stays of zero or one night. In all, 39,705 procedures qualified, with 1,621 same-day discharges against 38,084 overnight stays.

Same-day discharge grew from 1.6 percent of cases in 2016 to 7.7 percent in 2020. Seven-day readmission was slightly lower after same-day discharge, at 2.0 percent against 2.4 percent, and the models adjusted for patient, hospital, and income factors. Going home early, at least for the patients hospitals chose, did not bring people back through the door sooner, easing a key fear about the practice.
pmc-13619199:
Lloyd P Provost wrote an essay on why measurement sits at the heart of healthcare quality improvement. He opens with a study in the same journal issue that compared ways of detecting blood clots acquired in a children's hospital. His point is that improvement work cannot show whether care got better unless the numbers behind it are accurate and steady over time.

Provost draws on Shewhart and Deming, two founders of quality science, who both warned that unstable measurement makes every later conclusion shaky. Hospital data pulled automatically from records or billing codes can miss real cases or flag false ones. Readers get a practical reminder to check the measuring process itself, not just the results it reports, before trusting claims that a change in care worked.
pmc-13620199:
Ewerton Lourenço Barbosa Favacho and six colleagues report testicular tumors in a twenty-year-old male capuchin monkey kept under human care in Brazil. Leydig cell tumors are uncommon in nonhuman primates, and tumors on both sides are scarcer still. Ultrasound first spotted a nodule in the right testicle, which had been enlarged since the year before.

The monkey died the following year from neurological problems and went to necropsy at a university pathology lab. Both testicles held masses, the right one larger and orange on cut surface with fluid-filled spaces, and microscopy confirmed Leydig cell tumors on both sides. No major lesions appeared in other organs. Tissue features described include varied cell shapes in a solid pattern with rich pink cytoplasm. The authors present the case as documentation of a rare finding in this species, adding to the short list of such reports.
pmc-13620399:
Dhaniel Anderson Olimpio Barbosa and twelve colleagues measured the faces of Brazilian children born with congenital Zika syndrome, the set of birth defects tied to Zika virus infection in pregnancy. Their cross-sectional study compared twelve children with virus-caused microcephaly, a smaller-than-usual head, against fifteen typically developing children, all aged four to five. Eight marked points let the team compare the upper, middle, and lower thirds of each face.

Only one difference cleared statistical testing: children in the syndrome group had a measurably larger upper lip than controls. Ratios involving the upper lip also ran higher, and lower-face measures trended larger, yet those gaps could easily reflect chance in such small groups. The authors present the upper lip finding as the solid result of the study. Small, careful measurements like these help clinicians describe the syndrome's physical pattern for follow-up care.
pmc-13621199:
Toshiaki Toshima led a long author list and study group examining whether a simple nutrition index can forecast surgery outcomes for colorectal cancer patients in their nineties. The index combines blood albumin with body weight relative to ideal weight. Records covered 225 patients operated on at fifteen institutions between 2011 and 2022, split into high and low index groups at two different cutoffs.

Complication rates did not separate the groups. With the standard cutoff, better-nourished patients left the hospital sooner on adjusted analysis, but survival matched. With a lower, data-derived cutoff, the better-nourished group also lived longer, a link that held up after adjustment for other factors. The authors say the index offers a cheap way to flag fragile patients before surgery and target nutrition support, while the lower cutoff needs outside validation before use.
pmc-13621999:
Jaspreet Kaur and colleagues map how fluid moves through the spinal cord in mice, and what happens to that flow after injury. The glymphatic system is a cleansing flow that uses fluid channels around blood vessels to wash waste out of nervous tissue. It is well studied in the brain but poorly understood in the spine.

The team injected tracer dyes into spinal fluid and tracked them with scans and tissue imaging. Narrow spots in the space around the cord sped the tracers up, and the injection site changed which cord regions lit up. Larger tracer molecules stayed trapped in the membranes, while smaller ones spread through the tissue and cleared within a day. After a small injury, tracers moved faster yet cleared far worse, lingering up to seven days. Mice lacking a key water channel protein fared worst, with bigger lesions and weaker recovery.
pmc-13622599:
Priyadarshni Patel leads a team asking whether cheek swab DNA can reveal how much illness burden a very preterm baby carried in intensive care. Babies born before thirty weeks often face several serious problems at once. The researchers used methylation marks, small chemical tags on DNA, to build scores that estimate levels of proteins in the blood.

Cheek samples came from 537 infants in the NOVI cohort at discharge from intensive care, and 111 protein scores were tested against having two or more major morbidities. Eighteen scores showed links at a loose threshold, and one, tied to a growth-related protein called MIA, survived stricter correction. A side check in paired blood and cheek samples found that many scores matched well across tissues. The linked scores pointed to immune, inflammation, metabolic, and growth pathways. The team suggests such swab scores could one day flag babies needing closer follow-up.
pmc-13623099:
Carmen Arteaga-Jordá leads the authors of a protocol, a published plan, for a scoping review on how strategic communication shapes nurses' professional identity during cultural change in health organisations. A nurse's professional identity means how nurses see and carry out their role, and it affects satisfaction, teamwork, and staying in the job. Whether planned communication strengthens that identity has rarely been mapped.

Following Joanna Briggs Institute methods, the planned review will search seven databases plus grey sources for work published from 2000 to 2025 in any language. Only studies linking communication, identity, and cultural change together will qualify, not studies of each topic alone. Two reviewers will screen and extract data, guided by three published frameworks covering communication parts, identity models, and change dimensions. The end product will be an evidence map with guidance for nurse leaders, teachers, and policymakers.
pmc-13623199:
Aléxia Bezerra de Mendonça Belarmino and co-authors review endoscopic treatments for stubborn benign narrowings of the oesophagus, the tube carrying food to the stomach. These strictures are harmless in origin but keep closing after stretching, and they arise either at surgical joins or elsewhere. The review sorts results by that split to see which origin fares worse.

Eighteen studies published between 2005 and 2025 met the rules, covering hundreds of patients treated by stretching, steroid or drug injections, cutting, stents, or self-dilation. Procedures usually succeeded on the day, with technical success above eighty percent overall. Lasting success was lower, near fifty-eight percent. Strictures at surgical joins did worse over time and caused more complications than other strictures, which the authors blame on complex scar rebuilding after surgery. They also found four rival definitions of stubbornness in use, and they call for one shared standard.
pmc-13624299:
Wenna Xu and colleagues review how neutrophils, the first-responder white blood cells, turn heart attack treatment into fresh injury. Restoring blood flow saves heart muscle, yet the returning flow summons neutrophils whose attack overshoots, killing cells that survived the blockage. Mapping that chain reaction points to places where medicine might interrupt it.

The review follows neutrophils from recruitment into the reopened tissue through their three main weapons. These are a burst of corrosive oxygen chemicals, packets of digestive enzymes, and web-like traps of DNA thrown out to snare microbes. Each weapon damages heart cells and stirs more inflammation, feeding a loop that enlarges the final scar. Counter-strategies surveyed include blocking cell movement, melting the DNA traps, calming internal signals, protecting the cells' energy factories, reshaping immune behaviour, and delivering drugs in targeted carriers. The authors frame neutrophil control as a promising complement to reopening the artery.
pmc-13624499:
SeungHye Han and colleagues summarize a 2026 workshop report from the U.S. National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute on lung stem and progenitor cells and the early roots of chronic lung disease. Lung function peaks in young adulthood and then declines, yet that trajectory may be open to change if repair cells can be protected or boosted. The virtual workshop, held in November 2024, brought together lung researchers, stem-cell biologists, and technology developers to map what is known and what is missing.

The report reviews how lung progenitor populations maintain and repair tissue. It also asks where their regulation remains unclear, and which questions matter most for early diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and pulmonary fibrosis. It flags gaps in how these cells respond to injury, aging, and exposures like smoke and pollution.
pmc-13625199:
Daniel O'Sullivan, Aref Pariz, Daniel Trotter, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It builds a computer model of myelin, the coating on nerve fibers, and asks how changes in that coating reshape the way single nerve cells behave.

Myelin does more than speed signals up; it also tunes their timing. The model shows that when signal speed along a fiber is off, the pattern of inputs a cell receives changes too. That shift alters how excitable the cell is and how it adjusts its connections based on timing. Both too little and too much speed caused unhealthy patterns in the model. The authors offer signal speed as a key link between myelin changes and brain computation.
pmc-13626899:
Zhixue Ye and five co-authors draft a feeding protocol for severe brain injury care. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, uses expert consensus rounds. Patients with grave head wounds burn energy fast, break down tissue, and often cannot tolerate feeds. No joined-up feeding guide exists for this group.

The team first gathered and graded evidence from the literature. Seventeen studies passed their quality checks. A draft guide took shape with five top areas and dozens of detailed items. Fifteen experts then rated each item for use and weight in two rounds. Agreement scores show where the panel truly converged. The final protocol aims to steady feeding care across hospitals.
pmc-13630499:
Simone Foti Randazzese and eleven colleagues review the widening off-label use of dupilumab in children, published in 2026. The antibody blocks the shared receptor for two messengers that drive type-2 inflammation, and it already holds approvals spanning eczema, asthma, swollen nasal tissue, and an inflamed oesophagus, some reaching into infancy.

Beyond those licences, case reports and small series describe benefits across inflammatory skin diseases, immune defects with severe allergy, transplant-related immune chaos, selected lung conditions, and food allergy. Reported gains in severity and quality of life come with a reassuring safety picture, yet nearly all evidence is uncontrolled. The authors call for prospective trials to define who benefits, at what dose, and with what long-term safety.
pmc-13630799:
Irina Danilova and five colleagues tracked how the protein p53 pulses inside breast cancer cells after radiation. They pushed the measures down to very low doses. The protein halts the cell cycle and can order damaged cells to die. It normally rises and falls in waves with its partner MDM2. Earlier models predicted those waves should vanish at low exposure.

The team used protein blots and gene activity measures across doses. At high doses they found the famous wave pattern. At the lowest dose a single brief peak still appeared. It arrived later and smaller. Target genes followed the pattern. The authors say low-dose responses are delayed, not absent. That correction carries weight for radiation risk models.
pmc-13634299:
Sahar Ashari and four colleagues built an active packaging pad to keep fresh-cut pomegranate seeds fresher for longer. The seeds, called arils, spoil fast once separated from the fruit, losing water, nutrients, and brightness. The team spun a mat of fine fibers from two food-friendly polymers. Into the fibers they loaded carbon dots, tiny glowing carbon particles, plus a plant essential oil in both free and nanoencapsulated forms for slow release.

Four versions of the pad were tested on arils over twenty days in cold storage. The nano-enabled pads cut weight loss, membrane leakage, and microbe growth compared with plain pads. Treated arils kept their acidity, sugars, vitamin C, and protective plant compounds far better. Enzyme patterns inside the fruit showed calmer oxidation and slower aging. The authors present the combined system as a practical route to longer shelf life for ready-to-eat fruit.
pmc-13634599:
Boris Nikolic wrote this ethics essay questioning medicine's oldest motto: first, do no harm. The Latin maxim still stands as a symbol of medical restraint. Yet modern treatment routinely accepts injury on purpose, the author notes. Surgery cuts tissue, chemotherapy poisons the whole body, and burning or blocking tissue is exactly how some procedures cure. Nikolic asks how such deliberate injury fits the old rule, working through classic ethical frameworks, not data.

His answer is that practice no longer runs on literal non-harm. Doctors actually practice comparative harm management, choosing among foreseeable harms under uncertainty. A growing class of treatments harms as its very mechanism, which older frameworks address only sideways. On his account, the motto survives as caution and restraint, not a description of daily work. Physicians are better seen as stewards of proportionate therapeutic injury, weighing benefit against the damage a cure requires.
pmc-13635599:
Bridget Laging and three colleagues synthesized interview studies on how people view hospitals as places where nursing home residents die. Policy pushes to keep dying residents out of hospitals, yet transfers remain common. The team searched four databases for qualitative studies published between 2012 and early 2024. Using a method that translates findings across studies into fresh interpretations, they built two overarching themes from residents', families', and clinicians' accounts.

One theme covered symptom control: hospitals felt impersonal but offered strong tools against pain and distress. The other covered acceptance: a hospital death felt legitimate because medicine's authority confirmed that everything possible had been tried. The authors call this a paradox worth facing honestly. They advise strengthening symptom care inside nursing homes, planning ahead with residents and families, and talking more openly about dying. Such steps could cut avoidable transfers while honoring what families actually seek at the end.
pmc-13639599:
Huimin Chen and two colleagues offer a 2026 commentary on how the source of dietary protein may shape colitis, prompted by patient demand for food guidance in bowel disease. Protein advice usually ignores the wider meal pattern that comes with each source.

The authors review mouse experiments comparing beef protein with pea protein in gut inflammation models. Beef-fed mice fared worse, and the gap depended largely on gut microbes. Beef feeding also shifted bile acids, and one bile acid worsened colitis when given directly. The piece links diet, microbes, and bile chemistry as a joint influence on intestinal inflammation.
pmc-13641699:
Ujwal R Bagal and twenty-one colleagues present a genome study of two Sporothrix fungi behind sporotrichosis, a skin infection now epidemic in South America and often passed from cats to people. One species, Sporothrix brasiliensis, drives the outbreak.

Sequencing ninety-five isolates, the team found far less genetic variety inside the outbreak species than in its relative, whose family tree split deeply between continents. Copy number changes clustered near chromosome ends, and a scan for resistance to the drug itraconazole flagged eighty-one positions spread across many genes. The pattern suggests drug tolerance rests on many small genetic contributions.
pmc-13644599:
Kelsie Marks and co-authors report a 2026 monkey study of bispecific antibodies that hitchhike across mucosal barriers into protected tissues. Ordinary antibodies barely reach the lungs, gut lining, or other protected spaces. A receptor that ferries antibodies across tissue layers offers a smuggling route.

Receptor expression in cynomolgus monkeys closely matched humans, backing the animal model. Built bispecific antibodies vanished quickly from blood while piling up many-fold in lung wash fluid, far above normal antibodies. Gut mucosa showed the same build-up. Barrier-crossing antibody delivery, long a drug-science wish, gains primate proof of concept.
pmc-13644699:
Christian Tischer and seventeen colleagues present a 2026 report on an open training resource for bioimage analysis, the craft of extracting numbers from microscopy pictures. Microscopes now produce data too large and complex for manual handling, and expertise is scarce.

The resource is modular: each unit teaches one compact topic with hands-on activities on real biological images, runnable in tools such as ImageJ or Python. Trainers use it to build courses, and the community can add or improve modules through a public repository. Over the past three years many trainers have run courses with it, refining the material continuously.
pmc-13645799:
Sarah Bastkowski led a 2026 genome-scale study mapping which genes shape Escherichia coli susceptibility to antibiotics, using a gene-disruption method called TraDIS-Xpress. Treatment failure often reflects bacteria that drugs fail to kill, yet the gene set behind it in Gram-negative bacteria was incomplete. The team disrupted genes across the E. coli K-12 genome and tested survival against thirteen antibiotics spanning major classes at multiple concentrations.

Beyond resistance genes, the core genome proved central. Disrupting energy, growth, and amino acid pathways improved survival, suggesting that slowing energy use shields cells during drug exposure. By contrast, pathways for DNA copying, cell wall and outer membrane building, transfer RNA charging, and vitamin and terpenoid making aided survival when intact. Defined mutants confirmed that breaking energy and breathing pathways protected against drug classes. Drug makers get a framework for reversing drug tolerance by targeting cell workings, not just resistance genes.
pmc-13648299:
How poverty-linked worry may drain working memory is theorised by Hunter in a single-author review. Socioeconomic status tracks with many barriers to success, including cognitive gaps. Most explanations focus on external influences during development rather than mental processes operating in the present. Hunter proposes the Bucket Model of Socioeconomic Working Memory Disparities, arguing that worry and social comparison passively occupy working memory and pull attention away from the task at hand.

Working memory is the mental workspace that holds and manipulates information briefly. It matters for learning and problem solving, and the model claims a portion of socioeconomic gaps in that workspace reflects this ongoing drain. Hunter first reviews evidence linking socioeconomic status to cognition and to working memory in particular, then maps pathways by which worry and comparison divert resources. The review offers the model as a complement to developmental accounts.
pmc-13649399:
Qiaoli Hua and four colleagues reviewed how children with solid tumours fared on drug plans built around anlotinib at one Chinese hospital. The drug blocks blood vessel growth in tumours. Records covered 45 patients treated from 2020 to 2025, all under 18 years old at diagnosis.

Four children had tumours shrink, and 14 more held stable, so about two in five gained some control of their disease. Children with tumour types other than sarcoma did much better than those with sarcoma. Side effects were near universal, and most children had at least one severe event, most often in the blood. The authors present this as real-world safety and outcome data for a group with few options.
pmc-13649699:
Xingru Chen and six colleagues sorted intensive care nurses in Shandong Province, China, into types based on mindful self-care, then asked how those types relate to grief felt at work. Care unit nurses face death often and carry heavy loads. The survey covered 355 nurses at nine hospitals.

Two types emerged: a low self-care group of about one third, and a high self-care group of about two thirds. Good health and strong self-kindness made the high group more likely. Nurses in the high group felt clearly less grief from their work. The authors say these links give a base for programmes that build mindful self-care in care units.
pmc-13649999:
Xuanming Hu and one colleague ask whether the time of day when people exercise changes how well they sleep and how they feel. Advice on morning versus evening workouts conflicts across earlier studies, so the pair pooled trial results for both single sessions and regular exercise habits.

Thirteen studies supplied 81 effect sizes drawn from searches of eight English and Chinese databases. Exercise beat no exercise for sleep in the standard model, although a stricter statistical check made that result uncertain, and head-to-head timing comparisons showed no steady winner among morning, afternoon, or evening. Mood results followed a similar pattern, with one afternoon-versus-evening signal resting on only two studies. The authors conclude that exercising at all likely matters more than the hour chosen, and they stop short of firm timing advice.
pmc-13650299:
Jingjing Sun and six colleagues map the literature on how nurses and technology work together in home rehabilitation for older adults covered by long-term care insurance. Home rehab faces too few care workers and growing needs, while digital health tools and social robots promise relief only if staff and machines genuinely collaborate.

Following formal scoping methods, the team searched six databases for studies of nurse-technology teamwork in this setting and found 15 studies from 10 countries. Their three-stage lens sorts the work into tools replacing tasks, tools raising staff capacity, and a still-unexplored stage where technology blends into the whole care environment. Monitoring of body signals and risk warnings carried the strongest evidence, while supervision of exercise quality lagged. The authors also catalog barriers built into institutions, aiming to guide policy as much as practice.
pmc-13651099:
Anqi Ju and ten colleagues develop a rapid on-site test for avian colibacillosis, a poultry disease caused by E. coli strains that produces heavy losses through blood poisoning and organ inflammation. Farm-side diagnosis normally needs culture work or laboratory PCR machines, both too slow or too costly for routine screening where birds are raised.

Their method copies DNA at one steady temperature and reports the answer by color: positive tubes turn yellow-green while negatives stay orange, readable by eye within forty-five minutes. Samples came from eleven poultry farms in Jilin Province, and hundreds of isolates informed the design of four primer sets. The finished assay detected far smaller amounts of target than conventional PCR, showed no cross-reaction with other bacteria, and matched PCR verdicts on clinical samples completely. The authors offer it as a field screening tool needing no thermal cycler or gel equipment.
pmc-13652099:
Alexander Muacevic and seven colleagues review surgical options for repairing abdominal wall defects in patients who live with a stoma. An opening for an ostomy weakens the belly wall by design, and hernias beside the stoma are common, especially after earlier surgery or mesh infection. The review compares repairs that use mesh alone against repairs that add a flap of the patient's own tissue for coverage.

Mesh repairs lower the chance of the hernia coming back, yet they struggle in infected fields, in repeat hernias, and where large areas of soft tissue are missing. Flap techniques answer those gaps by bringing in healthy tissue, at the cost of a bigger operation. By weighing recurrence, complications, and patient selection across the published studies, the review helps surgeons match the repair method to the difficulty of the defect.
pmc-13676799:
Tereza Stastny and colleagues asked whether mechanical power, a combined measure of the energy a ventilator delivers to the lungs, predicts survival in dogs on breathing machines. The measure bundles rate, volume, and pressures into one number and is studied in human intensive care. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team reviewed cases from three teaching hospitals and one referral center over six years. All dogs had primary lung tissue disease. Power was computed for each of the first three days of ventilation with a simplified formula, and survivors were compared with nonsurvivors.

Dogs that survived had clearly lower mechanical power on every one of the first three days. Even a small rise in power tracked with worse survival odds in the analysis reported. The authors also compared the combined measure against single ventilator settings and oxygen measures to judge which forecast best.
pmc-2707599:
Moher, Liberati, Tetzlaff, and co-authors publish the PRISMA Statement itself, listing the reporting items that systematic reviews and meta-analyses should follow. Reviews that gather all studies on a health question carry great weight in medicine. Poor reporting, though, can hide bias and weak methods from readers.

The statement gives authors a checklist and flow diagram to follow when reporting a review. It covers how studies were found, chosen, and combined. PRISMA became the standard reporting frame for evidence synthesis, helping readers, editors, and guideline panels judge reviews quickly and fairly.  Editors could point authors to one short document instead of long debates.
pmc-4469799:
Bowden, Davey Smith, and Burgess wrote in 2015 on Mendelian randomization with invalid instruments. Such analyses were growing fast as genome-wide studies multiplied and teams wanted sharper causal estimates. A problem arises when some gene variants used as instruments affect the outcome through other paths.

The authors present effect estimation and bias detection built on Egger regression. The method can flag when instrument assumptions fail and adjust the estimate. That matters because a biased causal claim can point policy and drug work in the wrong direction. Their approach gave the field a routine check for a flaw that had often gone unnoticed.
pmc-4991899:
Sender, Fuchs, and Milo revised a famous count in 2016: how many cells, human and bacterial, a body holds. Reported values in the literature differed by orders of magnitude and were seldom backed by measurements or calculations. The often-quoted claim that bacteria outnumber human cells ten to one rested on shaky ground.

The authors integrated the most up-to-date information on both cell counts. Their careful estimates put the numbers of human and bacterial cells in the same ballpark. Most bacteria live in the colon, so counts swing with gut contents. The paper gave a firm base for a factoid repeated in countless textbooks and talks.
pmc-6223899:
Amira Sirelkhatim, Shahrom Mahmud, Azman Seeni, and coauthors reviewed zinc oxide nanoparticles in 2015. These tiny particles can kill bacteria, which has drawn wide interest for coatings and dressings. Their size is close to that of the microbes they target.

The review gathers evidence on how the particles damage bacterial cells. Reactive oxygen forms and zinc release both play a part. The same powers can harm human cells, so dose and contact matter. The authors press for care in judging safety claims. The paper remains a cited entry point on both promise and risk.
pmc-7619199:
Niharika Sharma and colleagues investigate the methane paradox in two Austrian lakes. Their study from twenty twenty-six samples lakes Mondsee and Attersee across seasons. Surface waters hold more methane than air contact alone explains. Algae were suspected of making that extra methane.

Both lakes stayed methane-saturated through the year. Summer peaks sat in the middle water layer of each lake. In one lake, methane tracked algae abundance closely. The other lake showed no such link at all. Isotope labelling showed algae made almost no methane directly. Algae likely feed other microbes that produce it instead. Lake carbon budgets need that indirect pathway counted.
pmc-8026399:
Benjamin Buchfink, Klaus Reuter, and Hajk-Georg Drost presented in 2021 a greatly improved version of DIAMOND, a tool for aligning protein sequences very quickly. Biology is entering an age when the genomes of all known species may be sequenced, and comparing a new sequence against millions of known ones is a daily need. Older alignment tools are accurate but slow at that scale.

The improved DIAMOND keeps high sensitivity, catching distant matches that faster tools miss, while running at a pace suited to tree of life scale data. The authors benchmark it against alternatives on large collections. For comparative genomics, a tool that is both fast and sensitive decides which questions are even practical to ask.
pmc-8238499:
Yuhan Hao and a large team of collaborators presented in 2021 a method for analyzing single-cell data that measures several kinds of information at once. New instruments can record, for the same cell, its gene activity plus other molecular features. Making sense of such combined data requires methods that can define a cell's state from all the measurements together.

Their approach, called weighted-nearest neighbor analysis, learns how much weight each kind of data deserves for each cell. It then builds a single map of cell states that uses every measurement. The authors show the method clarifying cell types that any one data type alone would blur, a step toward richer single-cell atlases.
pmc-8991999:
Scott Marek and colleagues showed in 2022 that studies linking brain scans to behavior need far larger samples than the field had been using. Brain imaging transformed understanding of the human brain by mapping abilities to structures and activity patterns. Mental health research hoped to find scan based markers of illness the same way, but its findings often failed to repeat.

The authors demonstrate that brain wide associations with behavior and mental health are real but small, so studies with a few dozen or hundred people produce unstable, exaggerated results. Thousands of participants are needed for findings that replicate. The paper reset expectations across neuroimaging and pushed the field toward shared, large scale datasets.
poems-1799:
Robert Southey published a volume simply called Poems in 1799, when he was still a young writer making his name. The book mixes long narrative verse with ballads and eclogues, and its contents show Southey trying many forms at once. An epigraph from Spenser sets the modest tone: please the better reader, displease the worse, ask no more.

The longest piece is the Vision of the Maid of Orléans, in three books, on Joan of Arc. Ballads follow, including the sailor who had served in the slave trade, the surgeon's warning, and Jaspar, while the English eclogues turn to cottages, funerals, and grandmothers' tales. Poems such as the Complaints of the Poor show the social anger of the young Southey. The volume captures a future poet laureate in his radical, experimenting years.
royce-world-individual-vol-1-1899:
Josiah Royce published The World and the Individual, Volume 1, in 1899. The book prints the first series of his Gifford Lectures. Royce, an American idealist, asks what it means for ideas to be true. An idea, he argues, seeks its object and is fulfilled only in a larger whole of experience.

Royce describes the Absolute as a community of interpretation linking all minds. Four historical views of being are tested and found partial. The lectures state American idealism as a full system. Royce writes with warmth and literary skill. The volume rewards readers who like grand questions handled with care.
russell-atonement-vol5-1899:
At the center of Russell's system stands The At-One-Ment Between God and Man, the fifth Studies volume of 1899. Charles Taze Russell explains the ransom: Christ's death buying back Adam's fallen race. The hyphenated title itself makes his point, that God and man are made at one again.

Doctrine fills these pages in careful, lawyerly steps, from man's fall to his restoration. Where other volumes treat prophecy and church order, this one carries the theology that holds the series together. Bible Students treated it as the heart of Russell's teaching, the volume to master first.
schiller-death-of-wallenstein-1799:
The Death of Wallenstein closes Schiller's trilogy on the great general of the Thirty Years' War. Samuel Taylor Coleridge translated the play into English in 1800, the year after its German debut. Wallenstein, accused of treason by the emperor he serves, hesitates too long between loyalty and revolt.

Stars, omens, and spies crowd around the general as his camp melts away. His friend Max Piccolomini dies for a hopeless cause, and hired killers close in at Eger. Coleridge's version is a landmark of English Romantic translation in its own right. Schiller's climax stands at the summit of German classical drama. The trilogy is completed by The Piccolomini and Wallenstein's Camp.
schiller-piccolomini-1799:
The Piccolomini forms the middle part of Schiller's Wallenstein trilogy, in Coleridge's English of 1800. General Wallenstein's army gathers at Pilsen while Vienna plots his removal. His trusted aide Octavio Piccolomini spies on him for the emperor, even as Octavio's son Max serves him with love.

Max falls for Wallenstein's daughter Thekla, binding the two houses in hope and danger. Banquets and councils in this part build the pressure that the final play releases. Coleridge translated both this play and The Death of Wallenstein with a poet's ear. Readers need this middle panel to feel the full weight of the fall. Schiller balances war, love, and fate across the three plays.
sea-monster-relation-1699:
A True and Perfect Relation of the Taking of a Sea-Monster is an English broadside of 1699. A quarter century after the famous sheet of 1674, another monster rose from the deep in print. Late Stuart readers still bought marine marvels with undimmed hunger, and printers still supplied them.

The sheet reports the capture of the creature as sober news. Its woodcut and plain claims belong to the street literature of the age. Such broadsides mixed report, rumor, and salesmanship in one penny package. Read together with the 1674 sheet, it shows a durable market. England's appetite for wonders from the sea outlasted kings and fashions.
sextus-empiricus-greek-scepticism-patric:
Mary Mills Patrick published Sextus Empiricus and Greek Scepticism in 1899. Patrick, a philosopher and college president, studied the ancient Greek skeptics. Her book contains the first English translation of Book 1 of Sextus Empiricus's Outlines of Pyrrhonism, the chief source for that school.

Patrick explained how Pyrrhonists suspended judgment on every claim, setting argument against argument until the mind rested. Sextus's outlines list the modes, the standard moves by which skeptics unsettled dogma. His work survived while other skeptic writings were lost. Patrick's study gave English readers a full door into ancient scepticism. That philosophy later shaped Hume and modern thought on the limits of knowledge.
sibylline-oracles-terry-1899:
Milton Spenser Terry translated the complete Sibylline Oracles into English in 1899. The Oracles are prophetic poems composed by Jewish and Christian writers over centuries. Their authors spoke in the voice of pagan prophetesses, the Sibyls.

Doom, moral warning, and messianic hope mix across the collection's books. The poems foretell the rise and fall of kingdoms in hexameter verse. Church Fathers quoted the Oracles as proof of Christian claims. That ancient endorsement kept the texts copied and read for centuries. Terry's translation gave English readers the whole strange collection at once. Prophecy with many authors speaks here in one urgent tone throughout.
spencer-gillen-the-native-tribes-of-cent:
Baldwin Spencer and Francis James Gillen wrote the founding classic of Australian anthropology in The Native Tribes of Central Australia, published in 1899. Spencer, a biologist, and Gillen, a telegraph officer at Alice Springs, worked from the Horn expedition and years of residence. Arunta totemism, the Alcheringa dream times, initiation, and magic fill their record.

Their account shaped how the whole world thought about early religion for a generation. Durkheim and Freud both built on its pages, whatever later fieldwork revised. The book remains the great early source on Arrernte life, written close to the people it describes.
spr-proceedings-vol14-1898-1899:
Parts thirty four and thirty five make volume fourteen, dated 1898 and 1899. As the century ends, the SPR Proceedings keep their mix of trial, case, and dispute. Thought transference work takes new statistical forms under careful hands. The census of hallucinations still frames how apparition cases get weighed.

Trance sittings, including the long Piper record, fill many pages with transcripts. Thompson and other mediums of the period appear in the case files. Skeptical members publish their counter readings in the same binding. Volume fourteen closes the society's Victorian era in fitting style. Its evidence fed the next century's arguments. The record stays open for readers to judge.
still-philosophy-of-osteopathy-1899:
Andrew Taylor Still, a Kansas doctor, set out the ideas behind osteopathy in his Philosophy of Osteopathy in 1899. Still had lost faith in the drugs of his day and built a new way of healing with his hands. He saw the body as a machine whose parts must sit and move rightly.

When structure goes wrong, Still taught, function suffers, and a lesion, a spot of strain or blockage, lies behind much disease. Free the body's own flows, he held, and nature does the healing. As the founding text of osteopathy, the book still anchors how the field tells its own story.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i: Only the title page of Volume 10 is present for this record, so no issue or article appears here. Published by J. Limbird at 148 Strand, the title page promises original essays, historical narratives, biographical memoirs, and sketches of society. It also lists topographical descriptions, novels and tales, anecdotes, poetry original and selected, and the spirit of the public journals. Discoveries in the arts and sciences and useful domestic hints round out the catalogue. An engraving of the Lord High Admiral heads the page.

The Mirror's No. 366, dated Saturday, April 18, 1829, illustrates Harrow School under a line from Thomson. Harrow-on-the-Hill had consideration before its school: the Archbishops of Canterbury occasionally resided there after the Conquest and won its people a weekly market. The Free Grammar School now ranks among England's eight great schools. It began small, like most foundations of its kind.

In Elizabeth's fourteenth year John Lyon, a wealthy yeoman of Preston, obtained letters patent to found the school. For years he contributed only thirty marks annually. In 1590 he declared his full intentions and drew up regulations. He would build meet rooms for the master and usher and a large school house with a chimney, plus a cellar for wood and coals. The master's salary was fixed at twenty-six pounds, thirteen shillings, and fourpence, with fuel money besides. Readers meet a great school inside one yeoman's careful arithmetic.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, March 26, 1831, No. 482, illustrates Bray Church, home of the turning Vicar of Bray. Who has not heard of the vicar and his turning, turning again, the article asks. The editors turn his church in turn to their pages' illustration, disclaiming any sinister motive. If the shot hits the black of such variableness, the galled jade may wince.

Bray village stands about a mile from Maidenhead. Camden supposes the Bibroci, who submitted to Caesar, occupied the spot, so submissiveness seems the very air of the place in all times. Queen Philippa held rents from Bray and neighbouring Cookham. The manor now belongs to the royal domain under Windsor Castle's liberties, exempt from tolls in adjacent market towns. Its church is a spacious structure of mixed materials and almost every architectural style. Readers get a proverb of political trimming anchored to one Thames-side parish.

No. 469 of The Mirror, dated Saturday, January 1, 1831, begins the year with verse rather than news. The opening lines link Petrarch with Arquà in Italy, and Ariosto and Tasso with Ferrara. Lord Byron's pilgrimage through Italy supplies the quoted stanzas.

Byron's poem lingers at Arquà, where Petrarch, the lover of Laura, lies buried in a tomb raised on pillars. The verses praise the poet for lifting his language and his country, and they describe the plain mansion and grave shown to passing strangers. A soft, quiet mountain village, shaded by a green hill, closes the picture. Readers meet Italian literary geography through poetry before any plain description begins.
tob-0099:
George Lincoln Burr, a historian of Cornell, surveyed the literature of witchcraft itself: the books through which Europe learned to hunt witches and, eventually, to stop. Demon-hunters' handbooks, skeptics' rebuttals, and trial narratives pass in review. Burr writes for readers who want the whole craze mapped through its printed remains.

From the Malleus Maleficarum's authority to the doubts of Scot and others, the walk covers roughly three hundred years of fear and law. Burr's scholarship helped found the modern academic study of witch trials. For anyone entering the subject, his guide remains a key orientation to Europe's witch craze and its paperwork.
tob-10099:
Thomas Commerford Martin, an electrical engineer, edited a volume gathering Nikola Tesla's talks and articles. Tesla was then explaining the alternating-current system that would come to power the modern world. Martin's collection let readers hear the inventor in his own vivid words rather than through newspaper summaries.

Inside are Tesla's induction motor, his work on high-frequency currents, and early tests with wireless transmission. Lectures and papers show both finished inventions and research still in progress. For anyone curious how a new electrical age argued for itself, Martin's volume preserves Tesla presenting his ideas, experiments, and hopes at the moment they were new.
tob-10499:
Flavius Josephus lived through the Jewish revolt against Rome and then wrote its definitive history, The Wars of the Jews. He had served as a commander in Galilee before being captured and later attached to the Roman side. His account runs through the siege of Jerusalem and the Temple's burning in 70 AD.

The narrative ends with episodes like the last stand at Masada, where defenders chose death over surrender. Josephus writes eyewitness narrative with a general's eye for siege warfare, logistics, and morale. Flawed and self-interested as he may be, his history is the essential source for one of antiquity's great catastrophes, read ever since.
tob-10799:
The second volume of H. P. Blavatsky's Isis Unveiled came out in 1877 and takes up the faiths of the world. She argues that all faiths spring from one old stock of secret wisdom. The churches, she charges, have buried that stock under dogma and priestcraft. The book is huge in scope, fierce in tone, and stuffed with odd lore.

She ranges over the early church, the Gnostics, and the faiths of the East, with quotes piled high. Set beside the first volume, on science, it launched the movement known as Theosophy. Read it as a gauntlet thrown down, not as calm scholarship, and note how much later occult thought starts here.
tob-10899:
Edward J. Ruppelt headed the United States Air Force's Project Blue Book investigation, and his 1956 Report on Unidentified Flying Objects gives an insider's account. Ruppelt coined the term UFO itself, preferring it to flying saucer. His book reviews the best cases, the investigations, and what the files actually showed.

Radar sightings, pilot reports, and famous incidents are weighed without hysteria for hoaxes, balloons, or honest mistakes. Ruppelt stays balanced and unsensational, while admitting some cases resisted explanation on the evidence then available. The result is often called the soberest book on the subject, written by the officer who had run the official inquiry.
tob-4099:
G. R. S. Mead's 1906 English Corpus Hermeticum presents the Greek dialogues of Hermes Trismegistus to modern readers. Mead, a theosophist and careful scholar, translated works like the Poimandres, where Mind reveals God and man to Hermes. His English is lucid where the Greek is dense and strange.

Renaissance magi had treated these dialogues as their bible, older than Moses and full of secret power. Mead brought that whole inheritance into the occult revival of his own day. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Mead's version nonetheless fixed the Hermetica in the modern imagination.
tob-4199:
Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, built the Spiritual Exercises out of his own conversion and years of guiding others in prayer. Elder Mullan's translation follows the saint's text closely. The Exercises form a four-week retreat, led by a director, with each week shaped around a stage of the soul's turning.

Retreatants picture Gospel scenes, examine conscience, and learn the discernment of spirits: how to tell consolations and desolations apart and choose well between them. Jesuits and lay seekers have made the retreat for nearly five hundred years. Few manuals of prayer have formed so many lives, or lasted with so little change.
tob-4299:
Mead's Pistis Sophia appears again in this further record of his 1896 translation. The Coptic Gnostic gospel stages the risen Savior teaching his disciples the mysteries of the soul's ascent. Pistis Sophia, a fallen wisdom-power, repents through the rulers' realms in psalms of grief and hope.

Jesus expounds her songs as maps of the spirit's fall and return. The cosmology is elaborate: treasuries of light, archons, and aeons in ranked array. Verified from the 1919 edition, the entry keeps Mead's famous version in circulation. For many modern readers, this strange gospel was Gnosticism's first open door.
tractatus-septem-de-lapide-philosophico-: Seven treatises on the philosopher's stone, drawn from a very old codex, are named on a garbled Latin title page after repeated ProQuest reproduction slips. The Latin title says the tracts were cleaned of errors and brought into print. The philosopher's stone was alchemy's goal, a substance said to transform metals and extend life. Lettering beyond the title is broken and unreadable in what is present. The damaged title page is what is present here, so the seven treatises themselves do not appear.
tristan-iseult-gottfried-weston-vol1-189:
Gottfried von Strassburg wrote the deepest medieval version of Tristan and Iseult in German verse around 1210. Jessie Weston translated it into English, and this first volume came out in 1899. Gottfried never finished his poem, but what he left stands near the top of medieval literature.

The tale opens with Rivalin, Tristan's father, and his courtship in Cornwall. Then comes the voyage to Ireland and the fateful drink the lovers share by mistake. Gottfried looks inward, studying love as both joy and wound. Weston's first volume carries the story from its roots toward the potion that changes everything.
tristan-iseult-gottfried-weston-vol2-189:
Jessie Weston's second volume of Gottfried von Strassburg's Tristan and Iseult appeared in 1899. It continues the German master's unfinished poem from the point where suspicion closes around the lovers. The translation lets English readers follow the tale to the place where Gottfried's own life cut it short.

Tristan and Iseult pass through tests, exile, and uneasy returns to court. Gottfried probes their hearts with a care few medieval poets match. Then the poem stops, mid-story, and no ending from his hand exists. Later writers finished it in their own ways, but readers still prize Gottfried's part above theirs. The great love story was never completed.
un-ga-res-54-99:
Three years into Guatemala's peace, the General Assembly passed Resolution 54/99 in December 1999 to keep the UN watch in place. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 1999 by a vote of 1998. The Assembly had the mission's ninth report on human rights before it. It also had the report of the Commission for Historical Clarification, the truth body that had named the crimes of the civil war.

The mission's role in the peace is stressed, and the need for all sides to back it is pressed. Both sides had voiced their wish for the mission to stay in the land. The Secretary-General's counsel on its work is weighed: how to shape it to meet the needs of the peace through the end of the year 2000.
un-ga-res-999:
Two days after its first Suez cease-fire call went unheeded, the UN General Assembly returned to the crisis with Resolution 999, adopted on 4 November 1956. The text notes with regret that not all sides had agreed to obey Resolution 997. That call had put an instant cease-fire first, with a halt to all movement of troops and arms into the area, and a pull-back behind the truce lines.

The Assembly states the 2 November call again, in full force. The Secretary-General is given power to arrange the cease-fire with the sides at once. He must report back on how the call is being kept, within twelve hours of the vote if he can.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
In resolution 54/99, adopted on 8 December 1999, the General Assembly again renews the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala, the ceasefire-to-peace operation known as MINUGUA. The text works from the mission's latest verification reports and from the findings of the country's Commission for Historical Clarification on the civil war.

The mandate runs through 2000. Guatemala's government and former insurgents are urged to finish carrying out the peace accords and the truth commission's recommendations. The Assembly frames full implementation as a condition for lasting peace and democracy. The resolution also asks for better international help in investigating the killing of a bishop. The case had tested public faith in the settlement. Each yearly renewal kept the peace process under sustained international scrutiny.

Resolution 999 (ES-I) of 4 November 1956 records the Assembly's frustration that its Suez cease-fire demand had not been obeyed. It reaffirms that demand and again calls on the parties to comply at once. The Secretary-General is authorized to arrange implementation of the cease-fire and the halt to force and arms movements. He must report within twelve hours. With the Truce Supervision Organization's help, he is to obtain the withdrawal of all forces behind the armistice lines. The Assembly decided to meet again as soon as his report arrived.
un-sc-res-1199:
When the Council met on 23 September 1998, it adopted Resolution 1199 on Kosovo. Serb security forces and the Yugoslav army had used heavy force against Kosovo Albanians. More than 230,000 people had fled their homes. Tens of thousands lacked shelter as winter neared.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands an instant halt to the fighting. Belgrade must pull back the units used against civilians and let foreign monitors move freely. Refugees must be able to return home with aid groups at their side. Kosovo Albanian leaders are told to reject violence and seek their goals by peaceful means alone.
un-sc-res-1299: The record catalogued as Resolution 1299, dated 2000, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1399:
Fighting flared in the Congo's Moliro pocket in March 2002. Rebel troops of RCD-Goma seized the town on Lake Tanganyika. On 19 March 2002 the Security Council condemned the attack. It called the capture a major breach of the Lusaka ceasefire. That ceasefire had held since January 2001. Peace talks between Congolese parties were under way. No side, the Council stressed, could grab land while a peace process ran.

RCD-Goma had to pull out of Moliro at once and without conditions. All parties had to return to the defensive lines set by the Harare plans. RCD-Goma also had to leave Pweto, which it held against the same plans. The demands defended the ceasefire's basic bargain.
un-sc-res-1499:
The plunder of the Congo's natural resources kept a panel of experts at work under a Security Council decision of 13 August 2003. A transitional government had just been formed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The panel's chairman had briefed the Council on 24 July that the looting continued, above all in the east. The panel had also opened dialogue with the people, firms, and states named in its reports.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to extend the Expert Panel's mandate. It repeated its demand that all states concerned act at once to end the illegal exploitation of Congo's wealth. The panel would pass governments the information required under resolution 1457 and keep updating its findings. It could remove from its lists the names of parties that settled their cases. The text ties the resource trade to the illicit flow of small arms that fed the war.
un-sc-res-1599:
Timor-Leste's support mission gave way to a smaller office on 28 April 2005. The Council praised the peace and stability the Timorese had built and UNMISET's work in its consolidation phase. The prime minister had written in January about the road ahead. The Secretary-General judged that a United Nations presence should stay past 20 May 2005, at a reduced level. Justice, policing, and public administration still needed help.

The Council established the United Nations Office in Timor-Leste, UNOTIL, as a one-year follow-on political mission. It would stay until 20 May 2006. Its mandate centered on building state institutions, training the national police, and backing democratic governance and human rights. Advisers would pass on skills and knowledge to Timorese staff as they worked. A special representative would lead the office. Donors and agencies were urged to keep their support flowing as the country took over its own affairs.
un-sc-res-1699:
Police work meets diplomacy in Resolution 1699, adopted in September 2006. It strengthened cooperation between the United Nations and Interpol, the global police network. The Council wanted Interpol's tools, including its databases on stolen documents, used more fully against listed terrorists.

Inside, sanctions committees are urged to share information with Interpol and to make use of its special notices for listed people. The text is short and practical rather than dramatic. It matters because modern sanctions only work when border officers can identify a name, and this resolution wired the UN's lists into police channels.
un-sc-res-1799:
Congo sanctions were given a short renewal by the Security Council on 15 February 2008. Illegal weapons kept flowing within and into the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Armed groups and militias still held ground in North and South Kivu and in Ituri. The Council said it would review the measures of resolution 1771 (2007) and adjust them as security, army integration, police reform, and disarmament allowed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the arms measures of resolution 1493 (2003), as widened by resolution 1596 (2005), to 31 March 2008. The transport controls of resolution 1596 ran for the same six weeks. So did the money and travel measures aimed at embargo breakers and armed group backers. The Group of Experts' mandate was extended over the same period. The brief rollover kept every tool in place while the Council prepared a fuller reset of the regime.
un-sc-res-1899:
UNDOF's renewal in December 2009 carried a new standard clause. On 16 December 2009 the Security Council extended the Golan force until 30 June 2010. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission in November. Alongside the usual terms, the Council welcomed the force's work on conduct. UNDOF was applying the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse. Its personnel had to meet the United Nations code of conduct in full.

The parties again had to carry out resolution 338 at once. The Secretary-General owed a report at the term's end. The conduct clause now appeared in most mission renewals. It marked a shift in how the Council wrote mandates after abuse scandals elsewhere.
un-sc-res-199:
Congo's crisis was handed to African diplomacy on 30 December 1964. The Council deplored the recent events in the country and noted the worsening state of affairs. It held that the answer lay in national reconciliation and restored public order. The Organization of African Unity had passed its own Congo resolution on 10 September 1964.

The Council asked all states to keep out of the Congo's domestic affairs. It appealed for a cease-fire on the terms of the African body's September resolution. Mercenaries were to be withdrawn from the Congo as a matter of urgency. The Organization of African Unity was encouraged to press its efforts to bring the government and the factions to reconciliation. All states were asked to help it reach that goal. The African body had to keep the Council fully informed, and the Secretary-General would follow the Congo and report when the time was right.
un-sc-res-399: Western Samoa asked to join the United Nations in 1976. On 1 December 1976 the Security Council examined its application. It recommended to the General Assembly that Western Samoa be admitted to membership. The vote was unanimous, and the text is one sentence. The Pacific island state had been independent since 1962. It took its seat as the world body kept growing.
un-sc-res-799:
Israel sent hundreds of Palestinians to Lebanon in December 1992. The move came on 17 December, from land held since 1967, including Jerusalem. On 18 December 1992 the Council condemned the act in strong terms. It said the act broke the Fourth Geneva Convention. That treaty guards people under foreign rule in war. The Council said it covers all the land Israel held.

Israel had to bring all those sent away back home at once, and keep them safe. The Council voiced firm protest against any such act. It also backed Lebanon's freedom and its borders. Those expelled spent months in a camp in south Lebanon. Their case drew world focus to the rules on forced removal.
un-sc-res-99:
Judge Sergei Alexandrovich Golunsky resigned from the International Court of Justice in 1953 because of ill health, and Resolution 99 deals with the empty seat he left behind. The Security Council adopted the text on 12 August 1953, with no member objecting.

The resolution notes that the vacancy must be filled under the terms of the Court's Statute. Under Article 14 of that Statute, the Council fixes the date of the election. It decided the vote would take place during the eighth session of the General Assembly. The record is brief, but it shows how the Council handles one of its steady duties: keeping the world court at full strength.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Fighting in Kosovo brings a Chapter VII response in Resolution 1199, adopted on 23 September 1998. Serbian security forces and the Yugoslav Army had used excessive, indiscriminate force, killing civilians and driving over 230,000 people from their homes. Refugees were flowing into Albania and elsewhere, and tens of thousands inside Kosovo lacked shelter. A humanitarian catastrophe loomed.

The Council demands an immediate ceasefire and an end to hostilities by all parties. It orders the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to halt security-force action against civilians, pull out units used for repression, and allow continuous international monitoring. It also orders that refugees return safely with aid access. It calls for urgent talks with the Kosovo Albanian leadership on a political settlement with greater autonomy. It backs the new Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission and demands full cooperation with the Yugoslavia tribunal's prosecutor. If the measures are not taken, further action will be considered.

Security Council resolution 1299, adopted on 19 May 2000, rapidly reinforces UNAMSIL in Sierra Leone as security on the ground deteriorates. The Council expands the mission's military component to a maximum of 13,000 personnel. That includes the 260 military observers already deployed. It thanks states that sped up troop deployments or offered support. Acting under Chapter VII, it exempts arms supplied for the sole use of states cooperating with UNAMSIL and the Sierra Leone government from the restrictions of resolution 1171 (1998).

A lakeside town's fall broke Congo's truce in March 2002. Rebel troops of RCD-Goma seized Moliro by force. The Lusaka truce had held since January 2001. Peace talks among Congolese were in full flow. Resolution 1399 passed with no dissent on 19 March 2002.

The grab was damned as a grave breach. RCD-Goma had to quit Moliro at once, with no terms set. It had to quit Pweto too. All sides had to fall back to the lines the Harare plan set. Kisangani had to be cleared of arms. Rwanda was told to use its clout on the rebels. No side could grab land while talks ran. UN troops in both towns won the Council's thanks and a plea for safe work.

Resolution 1499, adopted unanimously on 13 August 2003, extends an investigation into the looting of Congo's wealth. An expert panel had documented how natural resources, especially in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, were being plundered during the conflict, feeding the trade in small arms. A transitional government had just been installed in Kinshasa.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to extend the panel's mandate until 31 October 2003 so it could finish its remaining work. The panel was also updating its findings and resolving cases with named individuals, companies, and states through dialogue. The resolution kept international attention on the link between resource theft and Congo's war.

Resolution 1599, adopted unanimously on 28 April 2005, creates a small political office to succeed Timor-Leste's big peacekeeping mission. UNMISET was ending on 20 May, but the Secretary-General judged that a reduced UN presence was still needed; Timor-Leste's prime minister had asked for continued support back in January. Young state institutions remained fragile, above all in justice and administration.

The Council created a small UN office for Timor-Leste, known as UNOTIL, for one year. Instead of troops, it would field civilian advisers to help build state institutions, train police, and support democratic governance and human rights. The mission shrank from thousands of peacekeepers to a few dozen specialists, marking Timor-Leste's graduation from UN administration.

Cooperation between the United Nations and Interpol on sanctions is deepened on 8 August 2006. Interpol already helped the Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions committee, notably through special notices that alert police worldwide to listed people. Scope for the same help across the other sanctions committees was now seen.

The Secretary-General is asked to take the steps needed to increase that cooperation. All sanctions committees are invited to consider closer work with Interpol, each drawing its own conclusions. Sanctions, the Council stresses, are applied through national law, often criminal law, so stronger police cooperation would help states enforce asset freezes, travel bans, and arms embargoes against listed people and groups.

Resolution 1799, adopted on 15 February 2008, is a short bridge for the sanctions regime on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The Council condemned the continuing illicit flow of weapons into and within Congo. Armed groups and militias in North and South Kivu and in Ituri kept the east insecure, and the Council said it would keep watching how the embargo and related measures worked.

Acting under Chapter VII, it extended the arms measures first imposed in 2003, as amended since, until 31 March 2008. The six-week span was deliberate: members intended to review the whole regime and adjust it to progress in army integration, police reform, and disarming Congolese and foreign armed groups.

The last Golan renewal of the 2000s came in the year's final days. The chief's report of 18 November 2009 had found the zone calm. UNDOF's term was close to its end. Resolution 1899 passed on 16 December 2009.

The force won six months more, to 30 June 2010. The Council rang its old bell once more: act on the 1973 text at once. A long clause on staff conduct stands out in this text. The force must hold the UN's zero-tolerance line on sexual abuse. Troop states must probe and punish such acts by their own men. A report was due at the term's end. Few files show peace work's twin face so plainly: a still line abroad, and strict rules for the watchers.

Congo's chaos at the end of 1964 is addressed in Resolution 199, adopted unanimously on 30 December. The Council noted with concern that Congo's crisis was deepening and deplored the recent violence there. It backed an African-led path out: the Organization of African Unity had resolved in September to pursue reconciliation, including removing the mercenaries fighting in the country.

All states were asked to keep out of Congo's domestic affairs. The Council appealed for a ceasefire on the African organization's terms and said the mercenaries should be withdrawn as a matter of urgency. The OAU was encouraged to keep working for a peaceful settlement and to inform the Council.

Resolution 299, adopted unanimously on 30 September 1971, concerns the application of Oman for United Nations membership. The Security Council reviewed the Gulf sultanate's request and found it ready to forward. Oman, at the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, had stayed outside the UN long after many neighbors joined.

The Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Oman, and that one sentence is the entire decision. Under the Charter, no state joins without this recommendation first. The resolution is a small formal step, yet it marks the point where Oman moved from the margins of the organization into full membership, with a vote in the General Assembly.

The first trust land to win freedom waited fourteen years for its UN seat. On 1 December 1976, the Council adopted Resolution 399 without dissent. Western Samoa had reached self-rule in 1962. The Polynesian state chose to firm up its house first. Close ties with New Zealand marked those years. A seat in New York was not its first concern.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Western Samoa. The Assembly acted two weeks later. The country later shortened its name to Samoa, in 1997. It grew into an early Pacific voice in the Assembly. Seas, islands, and climate topped its list of causes from the start.

On 18 December 1992 the UN Security Council voted unanimously to condemn Israel for deporting hundreds of Palestinian civilians across the border into Lebanon one day earlier. The Council said the expulsions broke the Fourth Geneva Convention, the wartime treaty that protects civilians living under occupation.

Beyond condemning the move, the members demanded that Israel bring every deported person back to the occupied territories safely and at once. They also reaffirmed Lebanon's independence and asked the Secretary-General to consider sending an envoy to press the Israeli government and report back. The vote kept the expulsions at the top of the Council's agenda.

A judge of the International Court of Justice resigned because of ill health in 1953. Judge Sergei Alexandrovich Golunsky, named in the text, had submitted his resignation. His seat stood vacant for the rest of his term. Resolution 99 was adopted on 12 August 1953.

Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the Security Council fixes the date of the election for such a vacancy. The Council decided that the election would take place during the eighth session of the General Assembly. No single date was set in the text. The decision is a short, routine step in the Court's life. It kept the bench of the World Court on the way back to full strength.
un-un-res-special-report-of-the-secretar:
Crisis forced this special report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, document S/1999/20, at the turn of 1999. Rebel forces were closing on Freetown, the capital, in a drive that would soon flood the city with violence. The small observer mission had to pull back for its own safety.

The report explains the emergency, the evacuation of observers, and what the attack meant for the peace effort. It asks the Council to weigh the mission's future in harsh new conditions. The document is the record of a mission overtaken by the war it watched.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The third report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/3899, reviews the force through 1957 and 1958. UNEF had cleared its first hurdles and now held set positions between Egypt and Israel. The report comes from the force's second year, when its methods were still being tested.

It describes observation posts, patrol habits, and the handling of minor border incidents. It also addresses supply lines and the force's money troubles. For readers tracing how peacekeeping grew up, this early report shows the experiment in its raw, formative stage.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6599:
Section 6599 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the use of outside aid by the Sergeant at Arms of the Senate. It sits in Chapter 65, on Senate officers, in a part on the make-up of that office. For each year of funds, from the year that ends on 30 September 1982, a grant is given. The Sergeant at Arms may spend a sum from his account in the contingent fund of the Senate. The sum may not top $300,000 in a year.

The first use named for that sum is the hire of outside experts. The hire may be of single men and women, or of firms of such experts. The hire is on a short-term base in each case. The grant of the Committee on Rules and Administration must be had first.
veblen-theory-leisure-class-1899:
Thorstein Veblen published The Theory of the Leisure Class in 1899. Veblen, a Norwegian-American economist at the University of Chicago, studied the rich as an anthropologist studies a tribe. His dry, ironic book founded institutional economics and gave the language a lasting phrase.

That phrase is conspicuous consumption: spending not for need but to display rank. Veblen traced the leisure class from barbarian chiefs to modern wealth, arguing that honor, not usefulness, drives much spending. Dress, sports, manners, and even learning served as proof of standing in his account. Later scholars disputed his history, but his lens on status spending remains one of the sharpest tools in social thought.
waddell-among-the-himalayas-1899:
Laurence Waddell marched the Himalayas as a soldier and scholar in the 1890s and heard strange tales at altitude. Among the Himalayas, printed in 1899, is his travel book of the high ranges. Waddell served with the British Indian Army and dug in Tibet's lore as he went.

In its pages he sets down legends of hairy wild men who haunt the snows. His notice is among the first in the West to print yeti folk tales. The book mixes march, map, and myth in a soldier's clear prose. It planted the seed of the yeti in Western minds.
ward-naturalism-agnosticism-vol1-1899:
James Ward delivered the Gifford Lectures that became Naturalism and Agnosticism in 1899. Ward taught at Cambridge and held a pluralist view of the world. Volume one opens his case against naturalism, the view that nature alone explains all things. The lectures address scholars and general readers alike.

Ward tests the claims of science when science steps beyond its own field. He asks whether mind, will, and value can shrink to matter in motion. His answer defends a world of many real agents, not one blind machine. The volume sets up the argument volume two completes. It shows British idealism in debate form.
ward-naturalism-agnosticism-vol2-1899:
Volume two of James Ward's Naturalism and Agnosticism completes the Gifford Lectures published in 1899. Ward, the Cambridge pluralist, spends the first volume testing naturalism's claims. Here he carries the same argument to its second half. Agnosticism, the claim that deep truths lie beyond knowledge, also faces his questions.

Ward presses on the limits that both views set for mind and faith. He defends room for spirit, purpose, and a theistic reading of the world. The lectures keep a measured tone even when the stakes run high. Read after volume one, the book gives his full case. It captures a key British debate of the 1890s.
wells-tales-of-space-and-time-1899:
H. G. Wells set his short tales in a book in 1899. Tales of Space and Time holds five of his best short works. The tales range from the end of the world to a shop in London. Wells was then at the height of his first fame.

The Star tells of a rogue world that near hits Earth and remakes its skies. The Crystal Egg gives a shy shop man a live view of Mars. The Man Who Could Work Miracles closes the set with a clerk whose wishes all come true. The tales show Wells's range in brief, bright form.
white-yajurveda-griffith-1899:
Ralph T. H. Griffith translated the texts of the White Yajurveda into English in 1899. The White Yajurveda, or Vajasaneyi Samhita, is one of Hinduism's four Vedas. Its forty chapters hold the sacrificial formulas of Vedic ritual.

Priests chanted these verses while offering at fire altars in ancient India. Mantras accompany the building of altars, royal rites, and daily sacrifices. The collection also preserves hymns and prayers of great antiquity. Priests composed parts of the text more than three thousand years ago. Griffith's translation made the full Samhita readable in English. Austere and rhythmic, the formulas remain foundational to Hindu tradition today.
wilde-importance-of-being-earnest-1899:
Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest first saw print in 1899, four years after its triumph. The subtitle calls it a trivial comedy for serious people, and many agree it is perfect. Its first run in London made Wilde the toast of the town in 1895.

Jack Worthing invents a wicked brother, Ernest, to escape to town and woo Gwendolen. His friend Algernon invents an invalid, Bunbury, for the same sport in the country air. False names, a handbag at Victoria Station, and Lady Bracknell's cross-examining tangle the lovers' plans. A lost manuscript and a christening plot sort the pairs out in the end. Wilde's lines sparkle so brightly that the play feels brand new each staging.
yeats-wind-among-reeds-1899:
W. B. Yeats published The Wind Among the Reeds in 1899, a book of poems rooted in Irish myth and legend. Yeats was an Irish poet helping to lead a revival of Irish culture. Lovers, heroes, and fairies from old tales move through these lyrics. Names like Aengus and the Sidhe recur in dreamlike settings.

The poems are musical, wistful, and full of longing for a lost beloved. Yeats wrote notes explaining the legends behind many pieces. The book marks the height of his early Celtic Twilight style. Later his verse grew harder and more public. These poems still charm readers with their mist and music. They show a young poet finding his voice.
